1975-12-13-la-vanguardia-john-st-field-c.kurz: Short review in a round-up column of new records (page 57; alongside People's Choice, Orleans and Miguel Ángel, among others).
inhalt: Short review in a round-up column of new records (page 57; alongside People's Choice, Orleans and Miguel Ángel, among others). John St. Field's "Control" is described as an album of singer-songwriter songs ("canciones de autor") that are carefully arranged, and praised as a record of rare charm. The tone is clearly positive. At the end comes the reference Movieplay S-32.738, exactly the catalogue number of the original Spanish pressing. A sentence about folk roots convincingly reshaped into a rock aesthetic appears on the same page; whether it still belongs to this review cannot be decided with certainty from the snippets.
zitate_kontext: The core of the short review (OCR lightly cleaned).

1975-12-13-pueblo-que-un-cantautor-ingle.titel: [Music column of "…Que" glosses, including John St. Field]
1975-12-13-pueblo-que-un-cantautor-ingle.kurz: *Pueblo*'s music page in the run-up to Christmas 1975. It consists of a series of short glosses, each beginning with "…Que".
inhalt: *Pueblo*'s music page in the run-up to Christmas 1975. It consists of a series of short glosses, each beginning with "…Que". One of them marvels that an "English cantautor" called John St. Field, who had found no musical response in his own country, had found open doors at a Spanish record company, while many (Spanish) artists waited in vain. The tone is mocking rather than a judgement of the music. The neighbouring glosses concern Fernando Arbex/Micky and the band Camel, not yet released in Spain.

inhalt: Small finds without substance of their own on the Spanish presence of "Control" and John St. Field. The BNE pages after 1940 are locked for copyright reasons (only search snippets can be read). The Prensa Histórica pages are free (CC BY 4.0). The three reviews and the gloss from December 1975/January 1976 are listed individually (see notes).

**1975 – named among rock visitors.** *¡Hola!* (Barcelona), 2 August 1975, p. 58: a page of new records. A note lists rock artists whom someone had "brought to Spain in a short time": Stomu Yamashta, **John St. Field**, Nektar, Focus, Status Quo, Leo Sayer, Rory Gallagher, Electric Light Orchestra, Kursaal Flyers. Who is meant (record company or promoter), and whether "brought" refers to concerts or releases, cannot be told from the snippets. 1976-01-09-marca-john-st-field-control.kurz: In 1975/76 the sports paper *Marca* ran a rock and records column that rated albums with points.
inhalt: In 1975/76 the sports paper *Marca* ran a rock and records column that rated albums with points. On page 29, alongside items on Deep Purple/Tommy Bolin and a cancelled Madrid concert, there is a review of "JOHN ST. FIELD: «CONTROL» (Movieplay)". The critic begins by saying he had been told about the record and now wants to find out what there is to it. A sentence fragment praises St. Field's brilliant technique. The rating and the overall tone cannot be determined with certainty from the snippets: judging by the word order, the "7 puntos" just before the title probably belongs to the previous review.

1976-01-28-ya-folk-rock-escoces-john-st-.titel: Folk-rock escocés [John St. Field at La Boîte, Madrid]
1976-01-28-ya-folk-rock-escoces-john-st-.kurz: Concert review in the Madrid daily *Ya* under the headline "Folk-rock escocés" (Scottish folk rock).
inhalt: Concert review in the Madrid daily *Ya* under the headline "Folk-rock escocés" (Scottish folk rock). It has been reconstructed only from snippets of the BNE full-text search, so the wording is incomplete.

The critic reports that John St. Field came to Madrid without any publicity, almost unnoticed. He calls him an excellent Scottish folk rocker whose album had recently come out on the Spanish market. St. Field played at **La Boîte** to a small but knowledgeable audience. He performed without a backing band, with only a steel-string guitar and his voice. Few dare to do that, and St. Field manages it "more than well". His line runs, if distantly, parallel to Cat Stevens, but St. Field's music and delivery are much harder: he is a man of cutting expression, very inventive and technically accomplished as well. Successful performances of "Dog Star" and "Dune Voices", both songs from "Control", are singled out. The article says explicitly that St. Field was in Spain to present this record and that he played songs from "Control". A passage on his background mentions some thirty concerts and the recording of the "great album" "Control"; the context of that figure (where and when) is not preserved in the snippets.
Tone: very positive.
zitate_kontext: On the purpose of the visit.

1978-06-zigzag-doll-by-doll-acne-club-ay.titel: [Short review of Doll by Doll, Acne Club, Aylesbury] ("URGENT!! The proverbial hold-the-presses review!")
1978-06-zigzag-doll-by-doll-acne-club-ay.kurz: A hurried stop-press review in ZigZag no. 84 (June 1978), in which Kris Needs reports on Doll by Doll at Aylesbury's Acne Club and says they blew his head clean off.
inhalt: Kris Needs's "hold-the-presses" review appeared in ZigZag no. 84 in June 1978. He says there was no room or time for a full article, but that he could not wait to tell readers about the band: he had not been so bowled over by a new group since the 1976-77 heyday. A proper feature was promised for the next issue, and he joked that by then every other glory-grabbing rock writer would have planted a Union Jack in the band's backside.

The night itself: on a Wednesday in Aylesbury Steve Hillage was playing the Friars club to about a thousand people, while Needs went to the backroom of a small, dark pub that doubles as a disco and on Wednesdays becomes the Acne Club, a showcase for breadline bands. About 40 or 50 diehards saw Doll by Doll, then based in London, "wring a magnificent but tortured set" from a situation that would have daunted many bands. There was no stage. The crowd went mad and called them back; the band returned shaking their heads in depression, and Leven, whom Needs calls "the big, Glaswegian singer-guitarist" (he was from Kirkcaldy in Fife), told the room they did not deserve them and had been rubbish that night. Needs's verdict: if that was a bad set, Doll by Doll had blown his head clean off, and everyone else's.

Describing the music, he first tries Stranglers, Television, rock 'n' roll and inventive West Coast rock, then gives up. Their strength is originality: riffs you have not heard, passages where Leven sings alone (which takes some nerve in a pub), weird, angular guitar solos shot through with melody and texture, a dynamite unison vocal touch, and a spring-tight, claustrophobic, on-the-edge menace. The heaviness is constant, yet they can play a melodic slow number as though holding feathers rather than guitars.

Needs caught the titles "Guts" and "Butcher Boy". He started chatting with Leven afterwards but his lift home was waiting, so they arranged to meet at a gig the following week. He wants to know what is behind the band, notably why they hand all their gig money to an American charity for nervous-breakdown victims while living in a London squat. They once described their music as "a nature ramble through Hell", and he has learned that they have sent a whole bunch of cheque-waving record companies packing. The tone is breathless throughout.
zitate_kontext: Kris Needs on the Acne Club gig
How the band described its own music, according to Needs

1978-07-zigzag-doll-by-doll.kurz: Kris Needs's interview with Doll by Doll in ZigZag, July 1978 (about 3,900 words, before the band's record deal), is accessible only as metadata and a teaser quoting lyrics of the early song “The Perfect Bride”.
inhalt: Kris Needs's early interview with Doll by Doll appeared in the magazine ZigZag in July 1978 and runs to 3,864 words according to Rock's Backpages. It was made before the band's record deal with Automatic. The freely visible teaser is an excerpt from the early song “The Perfect Bride”; the content in detail is behind the paywall. Needs was the band's most important advocate in the music press. The interview is not identical with the short review in ZigZag no. 84 (June 1978, of a gig at the Acne Club, Aylesbury); it is probably issue no. 85, though the issue number is not documented.

1978-09-16-melody-maker-entropy-is-just-.kurz: A long Melody Maker interview by Ian Birch with Doll by Doll from September 1978, one of the first major press pieces about the band; the full text sits behind the Rock’s Backpages paywall.
inhalt: The interview “Doll By Doll: Entropy Is Just Another Word For Nothing Left To Lose” by Ian Birch appeared in *Melody Maker* of 16 September 1978. According to Rock’s Backpages it runs to 3,353 words; it is one of the first major press pieces about the band. The teaser quotes lines from “Teenage Lightning”. The full text is behind the archive’s paywall and was not consulted.

1978-10-21-music-week-automatic-signs-do.titel: [News items: first signing for Nick Mobbs' Automatic Record Company / “Automatic signings”]
1978-10-21-music-week-automatic-signs-do.kurz: Music Week reports in October 1978 that Nick Mobbs's new label Automatic has signed the London band Doll by Doll as its first act, with debut recording starting that same month.
inhalt: The trade paper Music Week carries two items on Doll by Doll in its issue of 21 October 1978. The news column says the first signing to Nick Mobbs's Automatic Record Company has now been announced: a long-term worldwide deal with the London-based band Doll by Doll. Recording of a debut LP starts that month, for release early the following year. Mobbs, who had been some time in seeking his first signing, said he had been waiting for “artists who are going to change the world”. Doll by Doll are currently playing club and concert dates around Britain. Automatic product will have its own logo in the UK through WEA, but is on the Warner Brothers label for the rest of the world.

In the “Tipsheet” section under “Automatic signings” Mobbs looks for more acts for the label: having just signed Doll by Doll, whom he describes as “the first British act in the last year who are capable of changing the world”, he wants acts other acts will get compared to – the kind you can't quite compare to any other. His image requirement is “contemporary rock and roll”, deliberately broad. Because of the American connection with Warner Bros. Mobbs will commute back and forth; his three-year plan calls for signing about six acts. The label's contact address is 5 Avery Row, London W1.
zitate_kontext: Nick Mobbs on Doll by Doll in the “Tipsheet” section.
Mobbs on what he had waited for in his search for a first signing.

1978-10-28-record-mirror-doll-by-doll-ro.kurz: Alex Skorecki reviews Doll by Doll at the London Roundhouse in Record Mirror of 28 October 1978: booked between two reggae bands before a modest crowd, they were the most interesting band of the evening, with Leven sounding “like a stronger version of Elvis Costello”.
inhalt: Skorecki writes about the Sunday night at the Roundhouse: though not top of the bill, Doll by Doll were “far and away the most interesting band of the evening”, inappropriately sandwiched between two merely pleasant reggae bands. Their “evocative / provocative” music seemed a bit wasted on a lukewarm, modest-sized audience.

The band had been formed ten months earlier and had been gigging fairly consistently around London for the last three or four. Their reputation for severity is misleading, he says; it is just their serious manner. The music itself is as accessible as the best heavy rock has always been. Their songs contain elements of the “more creative aspects of earlier heavy metal”, an appellation that has since become derogatory as that music decays into tired clichés: “Doll by Doll are the real HM of today, true progressive music of the late seventies.”

Among their assets is Jackie Leven’s voice, which can be “mature and vibrant” as on “Lose Myself”, or soulful as on “Janice”. In vocal partnership with lead guitarist Jo Shaw he sounds rather like a stronger version of Elvis Costello. There are fruitful moments of partnership in the guitar work too. Skorecki singles out “Butcher Boy”, which features all their strong points: excellent double vocals, multitudinous guitar phrases in the intro and Dave McIntosh’s “untheatrical but solid” drumming. Recorded product from this band, he says, will be something to look forward to. (According to the gig listings the show was on 22 October 1978.)
zitate_kontext: Skorecki on the band’s place in rock

1978-11-18-record-mirror-chris-westwood-.titel: [Band profile with interview: “Chris Westwood dresses Doll By Doll up”]
1978-11-18-record-mirror-chris-westwood-.kurz: One-page Record Mirror profile in which Chris Westwood – later the band's most important champion at Record Mirror – introduces Doll by Doll ahead of the release of their debut.
inhalt: One-page Record Mirror profile in which Chris Westwood – later the band's most important champion at Record Mirror – introduces Doll by Doll ahead of the release of their debut. He begins with the lower-case spelling after E. E. Cummings that Leven adopted, and places the band on an axis running from Cochran and Holly through the Velvet Underground into something of the future. Automatic Records, Nick Mobbs' new project, signed Doll by Doll as its first band; as the piece is written, Leven (guitar, vocals), David McIntosh (drums), Robin Spreafico (bass) and Jo Shaw (guitar) are working on the album. The interview took place in the band's squat in Maida Vale near Warwick Avenue tube station, though only with Shaw and McIntosh. Shaw explains the connection with the Philadelphia Association (shared houses for people in psychological crisis, inspired by R. D. Laing's ideas): the band played benefit concerts and donated part of the Automatic advance, but the connection has been exaggerated in other articles – as has the influence of Artaud, who mainly inspired Leven. McIntosh says that about two and a half years earlier he played with Leven in Dorset in another band that never performed; after it ended he went abroad, and then Shaw, Leven, Spreafico and he found each other – about a year ago. Since then almost a hundred concerts, support slots for John Otway and Ultravox, and next the Devo tour with two nights at the Hammersmith Odeon. Both talk about the risk on stage (“like a tightrope”). Leven's earlier album, available only in Spain, is also mentioned. Tone: enthusiastic, presenting the band as a genuine, uncompromising alternative to commercialised punk.

1979-02-24-nme-how-to-change-the-world-i.kurz: Nick Kent’s *NME* interview with Doll By Doll, “How To Change The World In Ten Easy Stages”, shortly before the release of *Remember* (about 2,800 words), introduced by a long Artaud quotation about “the void”.
inhalt: On 24 February 1979 the *NME* published an interview by Nick Kent with Doll By Doll under the title “How To Change The World In Ten Easy Stages”, shortly before the release of their debut album *Remember*. According to the archive Rock’s Backpages the text runs to about 2,800 words. It is headed by a longer quotation from Antonin Artaud about “the void”, which mirrors the band’s self-styling after Artaud. The full text is only available behind a paywall.

A recollection by the music manager Mick Houghton (2011) suggests that Kent vanished into the band’s squat for a weekend after an interview appointment and that the article was therefore postponed; whether this is the text that finally appeared is not certain.

1979-02-24-record-mirror-doll-by-doll-th.titel: [Single review] Doll By Doll: 'The Palace Of Love' (Automatic Records)
1979-02-24-record-mirror-doll-by-doll-th.kurz: Record Mirror reviews Doll by Doll’s debut single ‘The Palace of Love’ in its singles column: less threatening than expected, reminiscent of The Who, a “formidable” accessible song – ignore the review, buy the single.
inhalt: In the singles column ‘A Single Day in a Life: Music to Wake Up To’ in the issue of 24 February 1979, alongside short reviews of Van Morrison, Joe Jackson and The Cure, there is one of Doll by Doll’s ‘The Palace of Love’ (Automatic Records). The reviewer, whose name is not identifiable, writes that the record is “not as threatening as I’d been led to believe”.

Instead the song reminds him of The Who: “a formidable, highly accessible universal song”, melodic, fresh and emotional and “no way near as clichéd as my review”. The recommendation at the end is blunt: “Ignore this and buy the single.” The ending is ironic: the reviewer applies the charge of cliché to his own review.
The short review is one of the earliest press records of Doll by Doll, shortly after the release of their debut single on the Automatic label.

1979-02-28-bbc-radio-1-john-peel-show-pa.kurz: A fan documentation of John Peel's shows lists Doll by Doll's single “The Palace Of Love” in the BBC Radio 1 programme of 28 February 1979.
inhalt: The fan documentation of John Peel's shows, reconstructed from tapes, lists the Doll by Doll single “The Palace Of Love” (Automatic K17330) for 28 February 1979, played between Alan Libert's Parabola and the Glaxo Babies. The same excerpt appears on the fan tape “PM142”. No Peel session by Doll by Doll is listed.
The entry shows that Peel played the band at least occasionally, which counters a common claim that he positively hated them.

1979-03-24-melody-maker-remember.kurz: Ian Birch reviews the debut album *Remember* in Melody Maker; his opening sentence suggests a balanced verdict after the initial hype.
inhalt: Ian Birch, who had interviewed the band at length half a year earlier, reviews Doll By Doll's debut album *Remember* (Automatic Record Co.) in Melody Maker (24 March 1979). His opening sentence speaks of the “rock and roll romance” first running hot, then cold, before settling into a realistic relationship – suggesting a measured verdict after the initial hype. Full text and rating are not freely accessible.

1979-03-24-sounds-remember-dull-by-doll.kurz: Dave McCullough pans the debut *Remember* in Sounds under the headline “Dull by Doll”, a pun on the band's name; the Rock's Backpages archive lists it with two stars.
inhalt: Dave McCullough's Sounds review of Doll By Doll's debut *Remember* (Automatic K56618) carries the headline “Dull by Doll”, a pun with “dull” standing in for “Doll”. The Rock's Backpages archive lists the review with two stars. The headline is apparently the earliest documented source of the nickname, which the press officer Mick Houghton later describes as current (“Dull By Dull”). The full text of the review is available to subscribers only.

inhalt: Trade-oriented short review of the debut (producers: Bill Price and the band): a disappointing album that stands out precisely for its lack of originality – nothing that hasn't been done before. Tone: negative. In the same issue WEA advertises “Remember”.

1979-03-31-record-mirror-doll-by-doll-sp.titel: [Tour news: Doll by Doll after the release of “Remember” – “Spring Offensive” tour]
1979-03-31-record-mirror-doll-by-doll-sp.kurz: Record Mirror reports on 31 March 1979 that Doll by Doll, after the release of their debut album *Remember*, are starting an extensive club tour of England, with dates from Wolverhampton to Middlesbrough.
inhalt: In its news-in-brief column Record Mirror writes under the heading “Doll by Doll” that the band, who released their first album *Remember* “last week”, begin an extensive tour this month. The item lists the dates: Wolverhampton Lafayette (30 March), Manchester Factory (31 March), Jacksdale Grey Topper (1 April), Leeds Fan Club (5), Burton on Trent 76 Club (6), Nottingham Sandpiper (7), Norwich Boogie House (8), York Pop Club (9), London Marquee (10), Liverpool Eric’s (12), Retford Porterhouse (13), Birmingham Barbarellas (14), Newbridge Club (15), London Marquee again (18), Chesterfield Fusion (19), Lincoln AJ’s (20) and Middlesbrough Rock Garden (21 April).

The item says nothing about the music; it documents the release period and tour plan: the debut was thus out around 23 March 1979, and the tour went mainly through small clubs in the north and the Midlands. The same issue also lists the Wolverhampton show in its gig guide.

1979-03-zigzag-night-of-the-psychotic-wo.kurz: Major Doll by Doll piece by Kris Needs shortly before the release of the debut album *Remember* (23 March 1979), nine months after the first interview in ZigZag No. 85. Needs raves about the album, which was recorded live, apart from a few overdubs, at Wessex Studios with Bill Price, describes “Sleeping Par…
inhalt: Major Doll by Doll piece by Kris Needs shortly before the release of the debut album *Remember* (23 March 1979), nine months after the first interview in ZigZag No. 85. Needs raves about the album, which was recorded live, apart from a few overdubs, at Wessex Studios with Bill Price, describes “Sleeping Partner”, “Chances”, “Janice”, “More Than Human” and “Palace of Love” (as a shortened single, because “Teenage Lightning” could no longer be pulled off after three attempts). He recounts the path since summer 1978: ZigZag as a port of call for record companies, the contract with Nick Mobbs' Automatic (WEA distribution), being thrown off the Devo tour after two concerts (“not Devo enough”), the band still living in a squatted house in Maida Vale (“Hard Ventures HQ”). Leven is annoyed about an advance review in *Sounds*. In conversation, over whisky, Leven (and Jo Shaw) explain that the band are “amateur”, its members “all fucked up”, standing outside political camps and rock clichés. Then the interview turns dark: Leven speaks of a “death trip” of the band, predicts his own end “within the next three LPs”, compares himself to Sid Vicious (whom he knew from Maida Vale) and tells of a suicide attempt before Christmas 1978. The next day in the pub he is relaxed again; at night Needs listens to Leven's “Spanish only” solo album (*Control*). Outlook: tours, a second album in the autumn, new songs such as “Hell Game” and “An Honest Woman”. Tone: fanlike, moved.
zitate_kontext: Leven on the band on stage.

1979-04-06-wb-wax-lou-seal-doll-by-doll-.titel: [Column “Ancestral Swags Haunt Literate Lower Case R&R” – section on Doll by Doll]
1979-04-06-wb-wax-lou-seal-doll-by-doll-.kurz: A chatty column in the Warner Bros. house magazine: “Lou Seal” writes that his notes on Doll by Doll vanished from his luggage; the band are the first signing to Warner’s Automatic label, and “Palace Of Love” is literate, risk-taking, high-velocity stuff.
inhalt: The column “Ancestral Swags Haunt Literate Lower Case R&R” by “Lou Seal” appeared on 6 April 1979 in *WB Wax*, the house magazine of Warner Bros. Records. The columnist writes from Los Angeles, where he fled from the London weather in mid-February. There he has “trouble deep”: the important notes he took about a group called Doll by Doll somehow went missing from his ravaged luggage. He jokingly attributes this to the group’s “Special Powers”, as they keep their profile, if not low, then deliberately shrouded in mystery.

Doll by Doll are the first signing to a new label called Automatic, distributed by WB and masterminded by Nick Mobbs, whose avowed intent was to sign only a band which could change the world. That is shooting pretty high, so he asked an “impartial expert” to assess their chances. The man just said it was a terrific and exceptional band of the sort bound to engender impassioned remarks like Mobbs’s. The sheaf of press cuttings with “delirium and rapture” as their common denominator made him put on the single himself: “Palace Of Love”, written by “jackie leven”, who expresses himself exclusively in lower case. It is literate, risk-taking, high-velocity stuff – very modern, but with swags of ancestral voices linking it to rock & roll’s noble dawn.

The piece documents the label hype around the band in the company’s US promotion; of the music itself there is only this description of the single. On the same page follow items on the Searchers (Sire) and a Todd Rundgren benefit concert.
zitate_kontext: On Nick Mobbs’s ambition for the Automatic label
Lou Seal on the single “Palace Of Love”

1979-04-21-sounds-doo-laing-doo-laing-do.kurz: Sounds profile and interview by Hugh Fielder (21 April 1979) on Doll by Doll: the standfirst urges readers to forget the label “R. D. Laing / music for psychotics” and give the band a chance.
inhalt: The profile with interview by Hugh Fielder (about 1,700 words) appeared in the British music paper Sounds on 21 April 1979 and is archived today on Rock's Backpages; the full text is available to subscribers only. The standfirst urges readers to forget the label “R. D. Laing / music for psychotics” and give the band a chance. Fielder is thus writing against the image of Doll by Doll that was current at the time and arose from the benefit concerts for Laing's Philadelphia Association. Nothing is known of the rest of the conversation.

1979-05-05-record-mirror-chris-westwood-.titel: [Tour report with interview: “communication that only some have heard”]
1979-05-05-record-mirror-chris-westwood-.kurz: Chris Westwood's second major Record Mirror story, written on the spring 1979 tour after the release of “Remember”.
inhalt: Chris Westwood's second major Record Mirror story, written on the spring 1979 tour after the release of “Remember”. The starting point is the recent pannings in the rock press, to which the band, by their own account, reacted almost with relief: Dave McIntosh says they had expected a kicking sooner or later, and that the criticism had welded the band back together. Westwood attacks a critic who, after earlier praise, has now torn into Leven's songs, singing and guitar playing – two of the passages praised as Jo Shaw solos were in fact played by Leven; Leven mockingly calls the journalist “a human with a pencil”. There follow ironic mini-biographies of the members (Spreafico as a “Dutch peasant” who keeps silent about the past; Leven with “three divorces, five months in jail”; Shaw with a boarding-school past in Fort Augustus), a concert scene at the York Pop Club, where the punk audience reacts with unease to the open emotionality, and long Leven passages: on the “death trip” from the ZigZag interview, the lack of understanding of death in the modern world, the “war” over whether people will ever feel one another, and the announcement that the band will change radically – the new songs “Forbidden Lands” and “The Hell Games” already lead away. Westwood confesses that the band have fundamentally changed his attitude to rock. Tone: avowedly partisan.
zitate_kontext: Leven against the charge of morbidity.

1979-06-09-record-mirror-in-cold-storage.kurz: Under the heading “In Cold Storage”, Record Mirror reports on 9 June 1979 that Doll by Doll's planned European tour is in danger of collapsing over bassist Robin Spreafico's tangled papers; the same issue announces a benefit concert by the band.
inhalt: The story begins with a ringing phone: at the other end is Bruce, Doll by Doll's manager, telling of the problems facing the planned European tour, which ultimately look like knocking it out for the time being. At the centre is bass player Robin Spreafico's “involved and twisted” state of citizenship. He was born in Italy, moved to Holland, then Britain, then to the south of France for some two years of work, and then came back specially to join Doll by Doll; drummer Dave McIntosh had travelled to France to invite him. Somewhere along the line he had been “bafflingly” banned from Germany, a ban that now appears to have been lifted. On top of that, his foreigner's and EEC ID cards had expired, and because he had lived in Britain only for a limited period he remains an Italian citizen who needs the necessary papers.

He was literally en route to the airport when word came through that if he touched Italian ground he would be accosted by the police, there being a warrant out for his arrest as a deserter. The reason for this “astounding state of affairs” is that when he was 22, two years earlier, he failed to send in a form detailing his absence and the reason for it, his work abroad; he never realised the form should be sent. A small organisation looking after health and social security problems of Italian migrants in Britain has stepped in, but by no means is the air clear yet. Spreafico cannot enter Italy until the warrant is smashed and therefore cannot sort out the passport and ID situation: “A real dead end.”

The issue also carries, on page 4, the news that Doll by Doll play a benefit concert at the Factory in Chippenham Mews, London, on Saturday 9 June 1979, with all proceeds going to the Caribbean Labour Solidarity Organisation. The report is unsigned, and the OCR text of the scan is patchy in places.
zitate_kontext: Record Mirror on the state of the European tour

1979-07-28-record-mirror-dolls-to-split-.kurz: Record Mirror reports in July 1979 that bassist Robin Spreafico is leaving Doll by Doll amicably; Nick Whiffen makes his debut on 4 August at the Nashville, followed by a break from British dates until November.
inhalt: The short news item “Dolls to split” in Record Mirror (28 July 1979, p. 4) reports that Robin Spreafico, bass player with Doll By Doll (spelt “Speafico” in the text), is leaving the band. The split is a friendly one; a group spokesman is quoted as saying that for Robin the fun went out of it, so it went out of it for all of them. Spreafico is auditioning musicians for his own band, and the band “look forward to seeing him in action soon”.

His replacement, Nick Whiffen, plays his debut with the group on 4 August at the Nashville in London; apart from an appearance at the Reading Festival it will be their last British date before November. The band plan to work on their second album, with the working title “One Cold Vibe Don’t Stop Dis, Ya Boogie”, until late autumn. A European tour is fixed for October, and the band return to Britain for a tour the following month. The item names Whiffen, not Tony Waite, as the successor.
zitate_kontext: A Doll by Doll spokesman on the bassist’s departure
Record Mirror on the replacement and the dates

1979-07-zigzag-zigzag-10th-birthday-part.titel: [Report from the ZigZag birthday party at the Venue, London – excerpts on Doll by Doll]
1979-07-zigzag-zigzag-10th-birthday-part.kurz: Kris Needs reports in ZigZag no. 95 (July 1979) on the magazine’s tenth-anniversary party at the Venue in London: Doll by Doll play a deliberately uncompromising set, grow angry at a drinking, chattering crowd and end in noise as Joe Shaw smashes a guitar.
inhalt: This is an extract from Kris Needs’s report on the party for ZigZag’s tenth birthday, held at the Venue in London in June 1979. Needs was part of the magazine’s own team and writes accordingly as a partisan: for him Doll by Doll are the band of the night.

The group had put together a special set made up largely of numbers they had not played since their pub-gig days. The first half was slow, unfamiliar and uncompromising, opening with “Stripshow”. The band were visibly annoyed that much of the audience simply carried on drinking and talking through it. The volume rose accordingly, until by “Honest Woman” they were playing, in Needs’s words, at a frightening level of noise and anger. “Palace of Love” was the closing onslaught, ending in a wall of feedback in which guitarist Joe Shaw (spelt “Jo Shaw” in the piece) snapped in frustration and demolished a rare, trusty guitar worth about £500.

Needs insists this was no cheap stunt for the press and takes a swipe at Sounds, which he says skimped on coverage of the party. After Doll by Doll many guests left, partly because the DJ followed with going-home music and partly because, as Needs puts it, a body can only take so much.

The printed thank-you list says the party would never have happened without the Doll by Doll crew. Colin, road manager from the “Dolls House”, is singled out for helping organise the event for weeks and for working about 24 hours non-stop on the night. Guests are said to have included Siouxsie, all of The Clash and John Lydon; the bill included Levi and the Rockats, John Otway and Doll by Doll.
zitate_kontext: Kris Needs on the start of Doll by Doll’s set
Needs on how the set escalated
Needs on the end of the performance
The ZigZag team’s thanks to the band and their crew

1979-09-01-record-mirror-reading-festiva.kurz: Westwood in Record Mirror on Friday at Reading Festival 1979: Doll by Doll were the “fall guys”, hated by the crowd and leaving without a trace of sympathy; Motörhead and The Cure the real winners.
inhalt: The festival report “Reading Matter?” in Record Mirror of 1 September 1979 describes Friday as a day “shot through with innate complacency”, awash with fags, booze, drugs and denim, which was above all Motörhead's day and made “the total and utter pointlessness of the outdoor festival” obvious. The writer (signed WESTWOOD) praises Motörhead, dismisses The Police as a comfortable “business unit” and calls Wilko Johnson simply R&B.

On Doll by Doll he writes only a few lines: they were “the fall-guys, hated to such an alarming extent by almost everyone, it gave the crowd an early opportunity to sort themselves out and get all the crap out of their systems”. Leven later pointed out that each of the bands was there to fulfil some kind of function within the ludicrous spectacle Reading represented. It was “just sad” to see Doll by Doll dumped into this totally unsuitable environment and emerging without the slightest sympathy. The most overtly impressive and immediate band, he says, were The Cure. Of the festival as a whole he thinks little: a place where a band's greatness is determined by its ability to play as loud and as garishly as possible.
zitate_kontext: Westwood on Doll by Doll at Reading.

1979-11-17-record-mirror-doll-by-doll-mu.kurz: In *Record Mirror*, Chris Westwood hails Doll By Doll at London’s Music Machine as “the most real band” he has ever seen: they do what they have to rather than what they want, and need only time, which the rock business does not give.
inhalt: Chris Westwood reviews a Doll By Doll concert at London’s Music Machine in *Record Mirror* (17 November 1979). The difference between Doll By Doll and other “expressionists”, he writes, is that the others do what they want, while Doll By Doll do what they have to. Rock and roll should not dictate lifestyle but motivate individuals to acknowledge their roles, to adjust to them, to break from the distorted values of rock “culture” and one’s own self-doubts, to come to terms with what you are fighting for; Doll By Doll, unlike others, have understood that.

They play songs of urgent power and simple beauty, songs of substance and involvement: communication, information to be used as the individual inquires. They are of the dark hours, moody but not hopeless; their music is of fear, violence and romance, as in “Butcher Boy”, “The Human Face” and “Palace Of Love”, and accumulates whole new areas of meaning as it surfaces in differing live situations. The Music Machine appearance was notably happy, relaxed and devoid of frustrated tensions or shocks, an ironic reflection of the band’s and the audience’s calm state of mind.

Westwood calls them the most real band he has ever seen, at a time when the industry sluggishly sidesteps realism for the sake of hard-sell cartoon pantomime pop stars and blank, ineffectual escapism. Their main problem is the extent of their task: they are a growing, gradual thing, still presenting themselves to audiences of would-be fun-grabbers. Something like Doll By Doll needs time to take effect, and deserves it, but in rock and roll time is patient for no one. They are certainly getting more accessible, more perplexing and more deceiving. His closing line: they are still waiting for you, patiently – your move.
zitate_kontext: Chris Westwood, opening of the review

1979-11-17-record-mirror-gypsy-blood-gyp.kurz: Contemporary review of the second album by Chris Westwood, which at the same time defends the debut: “Remember” was slated by form-obsessed critics although it was a very powerful record of disturbing honesty.
inhalt: Contemporary review of the second album by Chris Westwood, which at the same time defends the debut: “Remember” was slated by form-obsessed critics although it was a very powerful record of disturbing honesty. “Gypsy Blood” seems almost relaxed on the surface but is subtle and deceptively accessible; Westwood singles out Jo Shaw's “Endgame”, which is about Shaw's experiences of the heroin scene. Rating: high (stars not legible in the scan), tone enthusiastic. In the same issue (p. 31) Westwood's live review from the Music Machine.

1979-11-22-bbc-radio-1-john-peel-show-te.kurz: A fan tape of the John Peel show of 22 November 1979 includes Doll by Doll's “Teenage Lightning” among reggae and punk tracks.
inhalt: The Peel wiki documents the fan tape “PM209”, a recording of BBC Radio 1 programmes from 20 to 26 November 1979. The tape was recorded by Peter Mitchell and later digitised; the time marks denote edits. The date of the broadcast is taken from the dates attached to the tracklisting.

Side A lists, under 22 November 1979, Doll by Doll's “Teenage Lightning”, after the Comsat Angels session (“Total War Girl”) and a track by Errol Dunkley and Roddy Moody, and before Twinkeys. Side B carries more material from the same day, including the Dickies and Essential Logic. The wiki has no separate page for that broadcast date, and the entry says nothing further about Leven's band.
zitate_kontext: Entry in the tracklisting of tape PM209

1979-12-08-record-mirror-doll-by-doll-ni.kurz: Record Mirror reports Doll By Doll's split from Hawkwind's anniversary tour after the Hammersmith show: an allegedly amicable parting after a confrontation with Hawkwind's road crew, accompanied by a sarcastic band statement.
inhalt: Under the headline “Doll By Doll nixed”, Record Mirror reports on 8 December 1979 that Doll By Doll have split from Hawkwind's tenth-anniversary tour following their Sunday appearance at London's Hammersmith Odeon – literally a year to the day since they were due to support Devo at the same venue (a tour from which they were also removed).

The allegedly “amicable” split was, say Doll By Doll and Hawkwind management, the result of a confrontation between certain band members and some of the Hawkwind road crew. Hawkwind manager Doug Smith says that in the end the two sides just could not get on together; the conflict had built up gradually and came to a head on Sunday night.

The band replies with a sarcastic statement: the vibe was right, but eventually certain members of the band and some of the Hawkwind road crew couldn't tell the difference between a strobe and the white lines on the road – with the addendum “Simon King rules OK” (King being Hawkwind's drummer). Doll By Doll still play two more dates in their own right before Christmas, at London's Nashville on 17 December and the Marquee on 21 December, and a January UK tour of their own is being planned. A photo of Jackie Leven accompanies the item.
zitate_kontext: Doll By Doll's statement on the split (OCR corrected).
Hawkwind manager Doug Smith on the conflict.

1979-12-15-record-mirror-forbidden-words.kurz: Chris Westwood rides with Doll by Doll in a van from Glasgow to Newcastle and lets Leven talk at length about *Remember* and *Gypsy Blood*, birth and death, media control and his half-Romany heritage.
inhalt: Chris Westwood wrote this piece for Record Mirror of 15 December 1979 during a van journey through the Borders from Glasgow to Newcastle; the band had recently left the Hawkwind tour and announces dates at the Nashville (17 December), the Venue with U2 in support (18th) and the Marquee (21st). Westwood loves Doll By Doll not as a “rock band” but as a community, an emotional force, “four people fighting”. Against the accusations (morbid, pretentious, joyless, pessimistic) he sets “facts”: the band is gradual, challenging, euphoric, optimistic, “emotionally anarchistic”. *Gypsy Blood* begins a second phase. The Leeds-born bassist Tony Waite is new; the line-up is now Leven, Jo Shaw, Dave McIntosh and Waite.

Westwood talks to Leven in a flat in the “haunted valley” community near Warwick Avenue (Bristol Gardens, Formosa Street), with vodka, a mutual friend named Claire and four hours of talk. Leven calls *Remember* a “black classic”, “an album of death”, and earlier “a huge vomit”, while *Gypsy Blood* is “an album of life”. For him the act of love is the “definitive act of violence”, and the supposed separation of the two is the root of many of society's problems. The band, he says, paid a price out of all proportion to its crime for its “massively violent honesty”. He speaks of losing his son after a woman left him holding the baby: it taught him not to fear death, since having a child is the absolute sense of creation, and he recovered his innocence. The title *Gypsy Blood* refers to his half-Romany heritage: Gypsies believe in souls and that nobody owns anything.

The longest stretch is about media and power. Leven says the ruling class, the “dead people”, decide through language and the media how everyone else sees life; the media are a “system of mirrors” in which people cannot see themselves, and the rulers “are breaking their own mirrors”. Doll By Doll are destroying the domineering concept of success, which is why people think they will not succeed. Westwood compares Leven with Jim Morrison, Lenny Bruce and Antonin Artaud: Morrison was called a sexual politician, they are called “emotional anarchists”. He ends alone at night with Lou Reed's *Berlin*; Leven is, according to the text, 29, and the warm flow of his Fife accent almost belies the remarkable power of his words. The piece is idealistic and demanding, less report than credo; Westwood closes: “Doll By Doll matter a lot to me.” A gossip item in the same issue says Mick Jones bought a Doll By Doll album at Smiths.

Leven on *Remember* and his view of the world
Leven on success and the media

1979-12-22-record-mirror-jahresbestenlis.kurz: At the end of 1979, *Record Mirror* published its staff writers' personal lists of the year on page 15.
inhalt: At the end of 1979, *Record Mirror* published its staff writers' personal lists of the year on page 15. Doll by Doll are conspicuously well represented: Chris Westwood puts the debut *Remember* at number 1 and *Gypsy Blood* at number 2, and also names the York Pop Club show among his best concerts of the year. Robin Smith lists *Gypsy Blood* at number 3 and names Doll by Doll as his hope for the eighties; Graham Stevens puts the album at number 4, Simon Ludgate at 8 and Daniela Soave at 9. On the same page John Shearlaw wishes Doll by Doll world domination in the eighties.

So five writers on one of the major British music papers put *Gypsy Blood* in their personal top tens of the year. That is weighty evidence against the version, often told later and held by Leven himself, that Doll by Doll were rejected by the British music press across the board. What it proves, however, is only that the band had several committed advocates within this one paper, not an overall verdict of British criticism.

1979-12-29-record-mirror-doll-by-doll-u2.kurz: Record Mirror, probably by Chris Westwood: an enthusiastic report on the evening at London's Venue when U2 supported Doll By Doll; Doll By Doll's music is “strong and lasting”, their set “a steady, good-humoured confirmation”.
inhalt: The review opens with an attack on the London club The Venue: its layers of stodgy tables and dodgy in-business types out to compare wallets and tour jackets, Space Invaders, ugly bar prices, pointless jukeboxes, predictable “I-say-what-ho” applause, dopey table service regulations and pseudo-exotic furnishings. “This is the first time we've done cabaret,” announces U2 singer Bono, and the audience greets it with self-conscious hums of approving tee-hees. A band at The Venue is like a band on “New Faces” or at a Working Men's Club variety night, performing for a studio audience that laughs and claps in all the right places.

U2, the reviewer says, are aware and promiscuous, warm enough to draw people in yet stubborn enough to deflate a cosy situation and stick their flag in the painful parts. They have conquered the art of dynamics and hustled it into a remarkably fresh and frisky new rockpop. In Bono they have a uniquely expressive front-figure, an irrepressible schemer who can create interest with a flick of the hand. Polite applause flickers at the close of their set.

“Doll By Doll are harder to explain”: they make him feel alert, challenged, confronted, self-sufficient, aware, romantic (even). Watching them in this grand slab of night-club grandeur is a terrible irony, the poor attempting to guide the misguided rich, and he interleaves lines about the rich losing what the poor have won. Their music is “strong and lasting”, “poetic, aesthetic, magnetic”, sweet and sour, beautiful ugliness: four people playing twelve songs and inspiring “so many abstract thoughts and feelings”. He names “The Fountain Is Red” (“gorgeous, spiralling”), “An Honest Woman” (“elongated, dark, brilliant, euphoric”), “Hell Games” and “Palace Of Love”, and notes that their Venue set was still heavily restrained. He leaves immediately, to remember Doll By Doll and not the Venue: their relaxed hour was a steady, good-humoured confirmation. The photograph shows Jackie Leven and Tony Waite.

The reviewer on Doll By Doll

1980-01-26-music-week-doll-by-doll-virgi.titel: [Photo item: Doll by Doll sign publishing deal with Virgin Music; single “Gipsy Blood”]
1980-01-26-music-week-doll-by-doll-virgi.kurz: A picture story in Music Week: Doll By Doll sign a long-term worldwide publishing deal with Virgin Music; the single “Gipsy Blood” is out on 8 February 1980.
inhalt: The item in the trade paper Music Week of 26 January 1980 accompanies a photograph of the band “saluting in respectful awe”. Doll By Doll have signed a worldwide publishing deal with Virgin Music on a long-term basis. The new single, “Gipsy Blood”, from their second album of the same name, will be released by Automatic on 8 February, backed with “Lose Myself” from the first album, *Remember*.

The photograph shows, from left, band manager Bruce Williamson, the Dolls Tony Waite, Dave McIntosh, Jackie Leven and Jo Shaw, and Virgin Music managing director Rob Gold. The item sits on the publishing and songwriter news page, which is otherwise filled with reports on threats to the music publishing business (piracy, home taping) and deals by other firms.
zitate_kontext: Opening of the Music Week picture story

1980-02-02-record-mirror-doll-dates.kurz: Record Mirror announces a short headlining tour for Doll by Doll in February 1980; their album Gypsy Blood counted among the magazine's albums of 1979, and the dates partly replace cancelled slots supporting Hawkwind.
inhalt: The item "Doll Dates" in Record Mirror (2 February 1980) reports that Doll by Doll, "whose second album 'Gypsy Blood' was voted one of Record Mirror's Albums of 1979 by the staff", begin a short headlining tour in February. The new dates make up in part for the cancelled appearances after the band were "dropped" as support to Hawkwind late the previous year.

Confirmed dates: Colchester Institute (1 February), Bedford College (2), Gwent Newbridge Institute (3), London Marquee (5), Loughborough University (6), Leeds Fan Club (7), Middlesbrough Rock Garden (8), Hull University (9), Dublin Trinity College (22) and Cork University (23). More dates were still to be added, and "Gypsy Blood", the title track of the album, would be released as a single on 8 February. The item is short but documents the magazine's regard for the album and the timing of the single and the Irish dates.

1980-02-09-record-mirror-doll-by-doll-gy.kurz: A short Record Mirror review (9 February 1980) calls “Gypsy Blood” difficult but ultimately rewarding material. The reviewer took weeks to warm to the album and demands more attention for Doll by Doll.
inhalt: The review appears in Record Mirror’s singles column. The single “Gypsy Blood” (Automatic) is taken from the album of the same name and is “an example of the difficult, but ultimately rewarding stuff of which Doll by Doll are capable”. The reviewer says he spent weeks listening to the album without liking it particularly, but that it “clicked eventually”.

The band deserve far more attention than they are receiving, and he hopes some DJ picks up the single and thrashes it, “because that’s the only way”. Of Jackie Leven, “vocalist and penman”, he notes a “thick theatrical voice” that would be sensational in another setting; the sentence is cut off in the scan. The reviewer is not named.
zitate_kontext: Reviewer on the album and the band

1980-02-23-sounds-doll-by-doll-marquee-l.kurz: A Sounds live review by Hugh Fielder of a Doll By Doll concert at London's Marquee, headlined “Shattered Dolls”; the text itself could not be seen.
inhalt: On 23 February 1980 the music paper Sounds printed, under the headline “Shattered Dolls”, a live review of a Doll By Doll concert at London's Marquee. The author is Hugh Fielder and the piece runs to 456 words. Its content and verdict could not be seen, so nothing can be said about the tone of the review.

1980-05-10-sounds-doll-by-doll-without-l.titel: [News item: Doll by Doll without a record company – Automatic does not take up option]
1980-05-10-sounds-doll-by-doll-without-l.kurz: In May 1980 *Sounds* reports that Doll By Doll are without a record company because Automatic Records did not take up its option; label boss Nick Mobbs says the band had not sold any records. Tour dates and a US visit in June follow.
inhalt: *Sounds* reports on 10 May 1980 that Doll By Doll are now without a record label. Automatic Records, the company founded and run by former EMI A&R man Nick Mobbs, has failed to take up its option on the band’s third album. Mobbs is quoted as saying “quite simply, they haven’t sold any records”: there was lots of interest internationally but no sales, “and I mean no sales”. Whatever his personal belief in the band, taking up the option would have been too expensive. He is sure they are not as depressed at being dropped as he is at dropping them.

Following a recent European tour, the band start a short tour of England before visiting the States in early June. The British dates begin at the Moonlight, London, on 19 May and move on to the Taboo Club in Scarborough, the Bungalow in Paisley, the Apollo Lounge in Glenrothes, the Nite Club in Edinburgh, the College of Technology in Glasgow, the Rock Garden in Middlesbrough, Belsay Castle in Northumberland, the Greyhound in London and the Troubadour in Port Talbot on 29 May. Glenrothes is in Leven’s home region of Fife.

In the same issue Hugh Fielder, in a Genesis tour report, says that the night before he left for Scotland he checked out Doll By Doll playing an unannounced gig at the Hope And Anchor. Their being without a record deal, he writes, is a criminal state of affairs and a damning indictment of British record companies. He got a very different but equally exhilarating buzz from them and from Genesis: both perform to the limit of their ability and provide intense stimulation.
zitate_kontext: Nick Mobbs, head of Automatic Records
Hugh Fielder in a Genesis tour report in the same issue

1980-05-zigzag-doll-by-doll.kurz: Kris Needs’s ZigZag interview with Doll by Doll (May 1980, about 3,000 words) appeared in the month the record company did not take up its option on a third album; its teaser is Leven’s defiant “we’re just not going away”.
inhalt: Kris Needs’s interview with Doll By Doll appeared in May 1980 in the music magazine ZigZag and runs to about 3,000 words. It came out in exactly the month in which Automatic did not take up its option on a third album (Sounds, 10 May 1980). The teaser is a defiant quotation from Leven: the band are “just not going away”.
The full text is behind a paywall; the freely visible part gives only this teaser.
zitate_kontext: Leven in the teaser of the ZigZag interview, May 1980

1980-06-28-record-mirror-doll-by-doll-ne.titel: [Tour news: Doll by Doll negotiating a new record deal]
1980-06-28-record-mirror-doll-by-doll-ne.kurz: Record Mirror reports on 28 June 1980 that Doll by Doll are negotiating a new record deal, play a single London date in July (the Half Moon, Herne Hill) and head off on a lengthy US tour in August.
inhalt: The short item appears in Record Mirror’s tour-dates column of 28 June 1980, among announcements for other bands. It says Doll by Doll are “currently negotiating a new record deal”. Before a “lengthy Stateside tour” in August the band play one London date the following month, at the Half Moon in Herne Hill on 5 July.

The item documents an interim phase between the two Automatic albums and the later move to Magnet (signing in September 1980, according to another source). Whether the announced US tour took place cannot be told from the notice.

1980-08-09-record-mirror-doll-by-doll-to.kurz: Graham Stevens praises a Doll by Doll show at the Torrington in Record Mirror as an emotionally charged event on a full-moon night: honest, shaky, yet superior to ‘musical robotics’.
inhalt: Graham Stevens opens his short live review in the Record Mirror of 9 August 1980 by remarking that when a band with the emotive abilities of Doll by Doll appears on the night of a full moon, one can be assured of an “atmospherically loaded event”. So it was at the Torrington in north London.

The band opened with ‘Hey Sweetheart’, “a soulful giant of a song”, building wave upon wave of emotion until the pressure is almost intolerable before calming down and leaving you drained and moved. Musically the band succeed through the honesty and sheer feeling they put into their playing. They “blunder onward”, flashes of brilliance interspersed with broken strings or suspect timing, but always come out ahead of the “plastic song and precision technique of musical robotics”. The set rarely faltered.

The new material showed all the power and commitment of the first two albums, *Remember* and *Gypsy Blood*, represented on this occasion by ‘Binary Fiction’, ‘Lose Myself’ and ‘Stripshow’: powerful, menacing passages complementing Jackie Leven’s “almost manic” style of guitar playing, from which he produces almost frantic runs of deft notes. The closing line reads: “Doll by Doll are essential listening, are emotions essential?” – a phrase that is both verdict and question.
zitate_kontext: Stevens on the opening song ‘Hey Sweetheart’

1980-09-13-melody-maker-doll-by-doll-the.kurz: In *Melody Maker*, Ian Pye calls Doll By Doll “so enigmatic it hurts” and praises an evening in Richmond despite a weak PA: Jo Shaw’s hypnotic guitar, Leven’s voice and an encore ending in retching feedback; time for their breakthrough.
inhalt: In the “Caught in the Act” column of *Melody Maker* (13 September 1980) Ian Pye reviews a Doll By Doll gig at The Castle in Richmond, west London. The band are “so enigmatic it hurts”: they continue to confound and disturb, veering from twisted layers of screaming noise, almost painful in magnitude, to exquisite moments of dazzling innovation which threaten to fulfil the astonishing promise shown when they first came under the media’s eye. The early gigs were received with the enthusiasm of the converted, supported by a mystique that slowly evolved around their lyrics, redolent with literary references and dark psychological confessions; Jackie Leven emerged as a forceful, charismatic figure.

The first album, *Remember*, was typically confusing, with passages that only hinted at the band’s live presence; some commercial credibility was regained after the second, *Gypsy Blood*, which contained some excellent songs but again paled in comparison to their frequently stunning live performances.

At Richmond a dodgy PA and an initially fuzzy mix only marginally marred a performance of consuming passion. On “Teenage Lightning” and “Strip Show” they explored territories few will have heard before; Leven’s voice soars over the top like a prehistoric bird. Jo Shaw has evolved into a guitarist of hypnotic intensity and breathtaking range, picking out penetrating lines behind Leven’s vast banks of rippling electronic sound, over the insistent rhythm of drummer Dave McIntosh and bass player Tony Waite. Only Leven’s fear of sounding familiar prevented them from fully relaxing into the veins of white soul that run through their music. Everything is delivered with a glowering menace, occasionally punctuated by the band’s exclusive, whispered conversations; slow, curling intros establish the mood before a creeping menace comes from behind to grip like a vice. Pye quotes lines from “Teenage Lightning” and “Hell Games”.

Now that bands like Joy Division and Echo And The Bunnymen have opened the way for new music of risks and adventures, Doll By Doll should, if there is any justice, have their day. Encoring with “Palace Of Love” (printed “Place Of Love”), they left amidst a tangle of retching feedback; Leven stood transfixed, glaring into the distance one last time before he led the band quickly away.
zitate_kontext: Ian Pye, opening of the review

1980-10-13-record-business-doll-by-doll-.titel: [Photo item: Doll by Doll sign long-term worldwide deal with Magnet Records]
1980-10-13-record-business-doll-by-doll-.kurz: A photo item in Record Business records that Doll by Doll, after leaving Automatic, have signed a long-term worldwide deal with Magnet Records and will shortly go into the studio.
inhalt: The photo item in Record Business of 13 October 1980 reports that Doll by Doll, who left the Automatic label earlier that year, have signed a long-term worldwide deal with Magnet Records. The band will shortly go into the studio to begin work on new material.
The picture shows, left to right: Dave McIntosh, Jo Shaw, manager Bruce Williamson, Magnet managing director Michael Levy, Jackie Leven and Tony Waite.
zitate_kontext: Text of the photo item (OCR corrected).

1981-05-23-record-mirror-make-good-doll-.kurz: In Record Mirror Mark Cooper awards four pluses to Doll by Doll’s self-titled third album: a shimmering, more compact work in which Leven remains “a truly strong voice”.
inhalt: Mark Cooper reviews, under the heading “Make Good”, Doll by Doll’s third, self-titled album (Magnet MAGL 5039). He opens by saying the band’s romanticism is of the kind in which only the roughest men indulge. *Remember* came out two years ago on a different label, and now “finally” comes the third album, a shimmering, designed work that has not lost the band’s rough edge. The trademarks – choruses, lyricism and repressed anger – are all here, “present and correct”.

Jackie Leven remains a truly strong voice, combining raw blues with something of the pastoral mystic. Once again these trademarks are allowed to exercise over a wide variety of musical styles and echoes, but in a more compact manner than before. As usual Doll By Doll sing of deep matters in a poetry with roots in a brutal, mythic folk past, content for the most part to remain obscure. Cooper points to the sudden contrasts between the tender ballad “Main Travelled Roads” and the disco pulse of “Caritas”; handclaps recall sixties dance music throughout, here turned to heavier, darker purposes. Despite the exuberance the music never quite overcomes its brooding, sorrowful quality. He also counts among the high points the humble “Soon New Life”, a celebration of birth, and the folk tenderness of “Main Travelled Roads”.

His verdict: the record has an electric vision and a unity of purpose, with a pop cleanliness that Doll By Doll have never previously achieved. “Perhaps now the pirates will stand aside for the sorrowing warriors. As Jackie Leven has it, ‘Eternal is the warrior who finds beauty in his wounds.’” The review carries four plus signs (the picture caption reads “The sands of time run out for Doll by Doll”). The full headline reads "Eternal Warriors Make Good".
zitate_kontext: Mark Cooper on Doll by Doll.

1981-06-08-record-business-doll-by-doll-.titel: [Album review] Doll By Doll: Doll By Doll (Magnet MAGL5039)
1981-06-08-record-business-doll-by-doll-.kurz: Record Business calls Doll by Doll's third album on Magnet a turn-round: now fashionably psychedelic in the manner of Teardrop Explodes, yet with the muscle in Leven's and Shaw's voices, which could raise the band's profile.
inhalt: In the “Best of the rest” column of its album page of 8 June 1981, Record Business reviews *Doll By Doll* (Magnet MAGL5039; producers Tom Newman and Jackie Leven). The unsigned review speaks of “quite a turn-round” for the band, newly ensconced at Magnet and still searching for that elusive media acceptance. They now sound fashionably psychedelic, with ethereal guitar harmonics and one-paced drumming in the style of Teardrop Explodes.

They cannot hide the inherent muscle in the vocals of Jackie Leven and “Joe” (that is, Jo) Shaw, however, who can make even the most melancholy material sound urgent and dramatic. That Doll By Doll were among the first into this genre could enhance their profile this time around. The tone is benevolent overall. The airplay guide in the same issue also lists “Main Travelled Roads” by Doll By Doll.
zitate_kontext: Record Business on Leven's and Shaw's singing

1981-06-13-music-week-doll-by-doll-album.titel: [Album and single review] Doll By Doll: Doll By Doll (Magnet MAGL 5039) / Main Travelled Roads (MAG 188)
1981-06-13-music-week-doll-by-doll-album.kurz: In June 1981 Music Week reviews Doll by Doll's first Magnet album, Doll by Doll (rock with hazily romantic lyrics that you love or hate), and the single "Main Travelled Roads" (fine live band, dramatic ballad, but no hook that sticks).
inhalt: The trade paper Music Week printed two short dealer-oriented reviews on 13 June 1981. Of the album *Doll by Doll* (Magnet MAG L5039), produced by Tom Newman and Jackie Leven, it says: the group's third LP but their first for Magnet. Their brand of rock with "hazily romantic lyrics" seems to provoke "a varied and sometimes violent reaction - you love it or hate it". Some songs sound "strangely dated" at first but grow on you after a few plays. The band has a fair following, so with UK and European dates planned plus a single release the LP "could skirl charts" (sic).

Of the single "Main Travelled Roads" (Magnet MAG 188, distributed by EMI), in the singles column: "Fine live band, dramatic ballad, pleasing effect but no staying line." The same issue's radio-airplay listing prints the catalogue number as "MAG 88", a misprint. The gossip column mentions a party at The Venue for the signing of Doll by Doll to Magnet. The review shows that the album appeared in May/June 1981.
zitate_kontext: Music Week on the album Doll by Doll
Music Week on the single "Main Travelled Roads"

1981-06-15-record-business-doll-by-doll-.kurz: John Hayward on Doll By Doll at London's Venue: the band, now tagged “psychedelic”, played new material from the Magnet album; the full house preferred the tougher numbers to the single “Main Travelled Roads”.
inhalt: In Record Business, John Hayward reviews a Doll By Doll show on Monday at The Venue in London. He finds it strange that a band that has stuck to its own version of rock 'n' roll for so long is now saddled with a “psychedelic” tag, more usually associated these days with a certain type of band from the north-west of England. Still, he can see how it might have happened: the band unveiled a batch of new material from the new Magnet album that drifts around leader Jackie Leven's folkie roots while the husky singer delivers his heady lyrics and then tends to explode into powerful guitar figures from Jo Shaw, who specialises in the sort of brain-frying feedback effects that get a reaction from any crowd.

The band made a big feature of the long single “Main Travelled Roads”, but the full hall seemed keener on tougher numbers like “I Never Saw The Movie” and “The Street I Love”. Doll By Doll have a strong following, and Hayward would like to see it translated into the sort of album success for which the band has striven uncompromisingly for some years.
zitate_kontext: John Hayward on the Venue show

1981-06-20-record-mirror-crystal-balls-u.kurz: Robin Smith is disappointed by Doll by Doll's London Venue gig in June 1981: he expected an earthquake and got only a few tremors; Leven seemed petulant, and the old manic style was largely gone.
inhalt: The concert review (Record Mirror, 20 June 1981, page 18) opens with an image of disappointment: Smith feels like a kid who has been promised a pound of wine gums. After so long underground, Doll by Doll should have come up fighting and determined at their big gig at the Venue, at last to start hitting mass appeal. “I expected an earthquake, but all I got were a few tremors.”

Leven appeared to him to be in a petulant mood, anxious to play the bashful musician and sensitive artist. Largely gone was the old manic style that could have you gripping the edge of your seat with your eyeballs bulging. A sentence about old numbers such as “Palace of Love” is not reliably legible in the scan; the band played all the songs competently, but “Main Travelled Roads” was savagely cut short. The verdict: “Adequate but not inspired”; Leven and his lads should really pull their fingers out, because 1981 and the new deal are going to be make or break time for the band.

1981-06-zigzag-doll-by-doll-part-1.kurz: Kris Needs's two-part 1981 ZigZag interview accompanies Doll by Doll's third, self-titled album on Magnet; part two names "The Perfect Romance" as a collaboration between Leven and Claire Verve.
inhalt: Kris Needs published a two-part interview in ZigZag on Doll by Doll's third, self-titled album for Magnet (part one in June 1981, about 2,200 words; part two in July 1981, about 1,600 words). Part one opens with lines from Leven's song "A Bright Green Field".

Part two apparently goes through the album track by track, beginning with side two. "The Perfect Romance" is the hardest piece, in the band's old style, dates from their early days and is a collaboration between Leven and Claire Verve, who, like manager Bruce (Williamson), stayed loyal to the band throughout. Claire Verve later worked for the PR agent Judy Totton. This co-writer is not named in discographies. The full texts are accessible only through paid archives; only the teasers are known.

1981-08-22-music-week-doll-by-doll-carit.titel: [News item and band profile: new single “Caritas” / Rock on the Tyne]
1981-08-22-music-week-doll-by-doll-carit.kurz: Music Week reports on 22 August 1981 Doll by Doll’s new Magnet single “Caritas” (28 August) and prints a short band profile in a Rock on the Tyne supplement, plus a Magnet advert featuring Jackie Leven.
inhalt: In its “News in brief” column Music Week states that Doll by Doll release a new single on the Magnet label on 28 August 1981. Entitled “Caritas”, it will be available in picture sleeve in both 7" (MAG 195) and 12" (12MAG 195).

A supplement for the Rock on the Tyne festival (Gateshead) carries a short profile: in September 1980 the band signed to Magnet Records following much gigging at home and abroad and a “significantly prolific writing period”. Their first album for the label, *Doll by Doll* (MAGL5039), was released earlier in the year “to much praise from the critics”, and a new single was scheduled for the end of August. Earlier albums are listed as *Remember* (Automatic K56618), *Gypsy Blood* (K56755) and *Doll by Doll*. A full-page Magnet advert shows Jackie Leven of Doll by Doll and promotes the 12" with a bonus track, “from the album Doll by Doll”, also available on cassette (ZCMAG 5039).

1981-09-12-record-mirror-doll-by-doll-ni.kurz: Bob Flynn hails Doll by Doll at Edinburgh’s Nite Club as “mystic guerillas”: dark, deep, hallucinatory songs between romance and rough reality, whose time, he says, will yet come.
inhalt: Bob Flynn’s short live review in the “Gigs” section of Record Mirror (12 September 1981, p. 18) describes Doll by Doll as “mystic guerillas of music, forever turning in the breeze of their imagination, conceding to no style or movement”. Uncompromising but not consistent enough to move beyond cult barriers, they annoy critics by jumping out of every box they are put in. Front man Jackie Leven looks as if he has just undergone “a 48-hour interrogation with the Iranian police” – “probably usual”; he looks a dark and troubled man.

“Teenage Lighting” (as printed) and “The Street I Love” are, Flynn says, the first stirrings of their talent and of this set. Hung on dreams, the songs plunge into the mind, with lyrics “a foot or so too deep for these days” but buried in the harsh guitar and drive of the numbers; the band tread hallucinatory terrain with confidence. The emphasis is on the joining of two extremes – hard and soft, natural and supernatural – into a strong and disturbing mixture of romance and rough reality, “a potent hemlock that few can stomach”. The songs are knocked out with the speed and immediacy of your latest nightmare. Doll by Doll are the essence of the new psychedelic strivings of younger groups, forming “something finer” from the raw materials of the imagination.

The chameleon sound changes back and forth, with a side-step into the new single “Caritas”, “all swirling guitars and voices, aching with feeling”. The closing warning: “All the wrong dudes are making it while they are slagged off for thinking too much. Softly, softly, the time will come for the dreams of the Doll. The timing is wrong, this is not the summer for D by Ds ‘Main Travelled Roads’, it is the summer of mixed-up urban streets.” The text gives no concert date; it probably falls in festival time, late August or early September 1981.
zitate_kontext: Bob Flynn on Leven’s stage appearance
Flynn on the music of Doll by Doll

1981-10-03-record-mirror-tour-by-doll-li.kurz: Record Mirror item of 3 October 1981: ahead of a major UK tour Doll by Doll change their line-up; Leven and Jo Shaw stay, Andy Anderson (drums) and John Read (bass) replace the rhythm section.
inhalt: The short news item “Tour by Doll” in Record Mirror of 3 October 1981 reports that Doll by Doll, “shortly to embark on a major British tour”, have changed their line-up. Founder members Jackie Leven and Jo Shaw remain, while the rhythm section of Dave McIntosh and Tony Waite is replaced by Andy Anderson on drums and John Read on bass.

According to the OCR text the decision came after the band's recent sold-out London dates and the release of “Caritas”, which many consider their best single to date; it coincides with a shift in the group's musical emphasis. Both newcomers have distinguished musical backgrounds: the bassist has just completed a series of dates with a well-known artist (not clearly legible in the scan) and is an in-demand session musician. The scan is very noisy, so the spelling “John Read” is uncertain (elsewhere given as John Reid).

1981-10-19-zdf-disco-doll-by-doll-main-t.kurz: According to the episode list of the ZDF show “Disco” (episode 125, 19 October 1981), Doll by Doll appeared with “Main Travelled Roads”; a three-minute clip of the performance has been on YouTube since 2014.
inhalt: The episode list of the ZDF music show “Disco” (Wikipedia) records Doll by Doll with “Main Travelled Roads” for episode 125 of 19 October 1981. The same programme featured, according to the list, Matchbox (“Love’s Made a Fool of You”), Tony Holiday (“Rio”), Kirsty MacColl (“There’s a Guy Works Down the Chip Shop Swears He’s Elvis”), Roland Kaiser (“Dich zu lieben”), Soft Cell (“Tainted Love”), Aneka (“Japanese Boy”), Lonzo (“Della und der Dealer”), Leif Garrett (“Uptown Girl”) and The Teens (“New York”); the dancers named are Ramona Wulf, Janina Richter, Elke Kast and Olivia Pascal.

A three-minute recording titled “Doll By Doll – Main Travelled Roads 1981” has been on YouTube since 4 February 2014 (channel “fritz51332”, length 3:03); its description contains only the song text. The link between the clip and the “Disco” episode follows the episode list. As usual on the show, it was probably a playback performance. Leven later said the band appeared on television shows in “strange places like Munich” alongside Sting and Kirsty MacColl, which fits this episode.
1981-10-19-zdf-disco-doll-by-doll-main-t.titel: Disco (episode 125, 19 October 1981): Doll by Doll – Main Travelled Roads

1981-rowohlt-rock-session-5.autor: Editor/author of the contribution not identified
1981-rowohlt-rock-session-5.kurz: In the German rock yearbook *Rock Session 5* (Rowohlt, 1981) Doll by Doll and *Gypsy Blood* are named among the musicians expected to shape rock in the 1980s.
inhalt: The yearbook *Rock Session 5* (Rowohlt, Reinbek 1981) mentions Jackie Leven with Doll by Doll and the album *Gypsy Blood* (WEA 56 755) among the musicians who, in the contribution's view, would shape rock music in the 1980s. The author of the contribution cannot be seen in the available excerpt. It is an early German-language sign that Leven and his band were noticed in Germany as early as the start of the eighties.

1982-05-15-nme-doll-by-doll-off.kurz: In May 1982 the NME reports that Doll by Doll have cancelled their largely sold-out UK tour after “traumatic rows” with Magnet Records, with Jackie Leven severing all ties with the label.
inhalt: The item on page 41 of the NME of 15 May 1982 is short but consequential: Doll by Doll have called off their current UK tour, which was largely sold out. The paper puts it down to what it calls “traumatic rows” with their record label, Magnet Records.

Jackie Leven, the band’s leader, says he felt compelled to sever all relations with the company. The band, he says, had delivered two albums’ worth of original material on time, but Magnet did not fulfil its agreed part of a financial agreement. According to the group, the relationship collapsed through broken promises, and the tour had to be halted because the agreed money was not forthcoming.

The item is an early record of the break between Doll by Doll and their label, which followed the album *Grand Passion* (1982) and heralded the end of the band. It gives the band’s side only; no response from Magnet is quoted. The online transcript used here carries a stray ZigZag header (July 1979) by mistake; the text itself is from the NME.
zitate_kontext: Opening sentence of the NME item
The band’s reason for halting the tour

1982-08-28-sounds-under-whose-thumb-doll.kurz: Sounds reports that Doll by Doll have patched up their dispute with Magnet: the single “Under My Thumb” is out this week, *Grand Passion* follows in September; the band now consists of Leven, Helen Turner and Tom Norton.
inhalt: The item “Under whose thumb?” in Sounds of 28 August 1982 reports that Doll by Doll have repaired the traumatic rift with their record company Magnet which for a while threatened the band's career earlier in the summer. “A new understanding and unity of purpose” has now been established, according to the band's leader and sole-remaining founder member Jackie Leven (pictured with Helen Turner).

The first fruit of this new understanding is a single released that week, a version of the Rolling Stones' “Under My Thumb”. The album *Grand Passion* will emerge towards the end of September, and the band – currently consisting of Jackie Leven, Helen Turner and Tom Norton – are now working on more material. There is no news of any live gigs at present.
zitate_kontext: Leven's formula for the new relationship with Magnet, according to Sounds.

1982-10-02-record-mirror-grand-passion-r.titel: [Brief news item: new album “Grand Passion” on 24 September]
1982-10-02-record-mirror-grand-passion-r.kurz: A short item in Record Mirror: Doll by Doll release their new album *Grand Passion* on 24 September, with twelve Jackie Leven compositions and a cover of the Jagger/Richards number “Under My Thumb”.
inhalt: The item in Record Mirror of 2 October 1982 states that Doll by Doll release a new album, *Grand Passion*, on 24 September. It features twelve Jackie Leven compositions and Doll by Doll’s cover of the old Jagger/Richards number “Under My Thumb”. The note appears in the magazine a week after the date it names.

1982-12-02-34th-street-doll-by-doll-gran.titel: [Album review] Doll By Doll – Grand Passion (Magnet, UK)
1982-12-02-34th-street-doll-by-doll-gran.kurz: Daniel Silverman praises *Grand Passion* in the student supplement 34th Street as “some of the finest AOR to come along in years” and ranks it sixth in his 1982 albums list.
inhalt: Daniel Silverman reviews *Grand Passion* in the Thursday supplement of the Daily Pennsylvanian in Philadelphia. He starts with a sigh: for four years the virtually unknown Doll By Doll have been releasing “near-classic albums to an utterly indifferent public”, and unless Magnet Records has a major promotion scheme up its sleeve, this will unfortunately continue with the fourth album.

Jackie Leven, he says, has the rare combination of writing instantly classic melodies and having a voice capable of doing them justice. ‘Cool Skies’ and ‘Lonely Kind of Show’ have the relaxed, plaintive feel of today’s best FM pop (Steely Dan, Roxy Music), yet Leven gives his blend of percussion, sparse synthesizer and guitar a timelessness not heard since prime Dylan or, “dare I say, The Beatles”. Not all is easy listening: ‘Natural’ is powerful and uplifting, with impassioned vocals and “an absolute killer chorus”; on ‘City of Light’, Leven and second vocalist Helen Turner create nightmarish images of a war-torn society with wailing guitar, a hauntingly repetitive vocal and a rigid military beat.

The one weakness is Leven’s “unrelenting and humorless pursuit of some ‘grand passion’” – excluding a most credible cover of ‘Under My Thumb’ – which eventually grows tiresome. The lyrics, such as the title track’s lines about singers opening up and strong men finding their tenderness, border on the melodramatic, but that is a minor flaw. The verdict: *Grand Passion* contains some of the finest AOR to come along in years. A week later Silverman places the album sixth in his list of the best albums of 1982, between R.E.M.’s *Chronic Town* and Peter Gabriel.
zitate_kontext: Silverman at the start of the review

1983-01-17-record-business-doll-by-doll-.kurz: John Hayward describes Doll by Doll's last London gig at the Marquee in Record Business: Leven is determined to end the Doll by Doll side of his life and retreat to the Outer Hebrides.
inhalt: In Record Business of 17 January 1983, John Hayward reviews "Doll By Doll - London: Marquee", the band's last metropolitan gig, on a Friday night at the Marquee. Many of the stalwarts who watched the outfit make its impression on the London clubs "back in the optimistic days of Automatic Records" were there. The "emotion-charged" Leven is determined to finish with the Doll by Doll side of his life and is about to take himself off to the Outer Hebrides to write new songs and emerge in a new persona, probably on a new record label. He hammered that point home with a rocking-style "Skye Boat Song".

As a farewell concert, Leven did not milk the old favourites, preferring to keep progressing right to the end, and even dumped most of the recent Magnet repertoire in favour of a selection of new heartfelt rockers.
