A blast of "Cool Skies" and a rocking "Dancing Shoes" were good representatives of the *Grand Passion* album, finding co-vocalist and keyboard player Helen Turner in good voice. Leven himself took lead guitar honours with confidence. There was, however, no show-stopping version of "Lonely Kind of Show", which might have been expected.

Hayward ends wistfully: what a shame that the "combative, mature and wholly original" Doll by Doll could never gain the national acceptance it deserved. Perhaps Leven's next project will be the one to spark the public's imagination. The report does not give the exact date, and Jo Shaw is not mentioned.

1983-03-19-nme-bred-by-leven.kurz: NME item “Bred by Leven”: Jackie Leven, who disbanded Doll by Doll a few months ago, has formed a new group under his own name, signed to Charisma Records; first London dates at Fulham Greyhound, Woolwich and the Embassy Club.
inhalt: The item in the “Forthcoming Visitors” column of the New Musical Express of 19 March 1983 reads: Jackie Leven, who disbanded Doll By Doll a few months ago, has now formed a new outfit which will operate under his own name. It comprises Chris Clarke (drums), Mark Fletcher (bass), Garry Jackson (keyboards) and Carol Pearrett (vocals). Leven has been busy writing new material, and the band have signed a long-term deal with Charisma Records, with an initial release expected shortly.

The dates: “this Saturday (19)” the band play London’s Fulham Greyhound, in one of the venue’s benefit shows in aid of muscular dystrophy; further London dates are the Woolwich Tramshed on 24 March and the Bond Street Embassy Club on 1 April. “More gigs are being added.” An advertisement in the same issue lists Jackie Leven with Ukraine for Sunday 20 March at £2 – the date differs from the news item.

1983-09-10-nme-jackie-leven-debut-solo-s.titel: [Brief news item: debut single “Love Is Shining Down On Me” on Virgin/Charisma]
1983-09-10-nme-jackie-leven-debut-solo-s.kurz: In a brief item on 10 September 1983 the *NME* reports that Jackie Leven, former leader of Doll By Doll, released his debut solo single, “Love Is Shining Down On Me”, through Virgin/Charisma on 9 September.
inhalt: In a column of record news, the *New Musical Express* of 10 September 1983 notes briefly that Jackie Leven, “former leader of Doll by Doll”, releases his debut solo single through Virgin/Charisma on 9 September. It is titled “Love Is Shining Down On Me”, backed by “Mindless Sweethearts Underground”, and is out as both a seven-inch and a 12-inch. The item says nothing more.

1983-facts-on-file-hounsome-rock-record.titel: Rock Record / New Rock Record / Rock Record 6 (entries for John St Field and Doll By Doll)
1983-facts-on-file-hounsome-rock-record.kurz: The Rock Record directories list “John St Field (Jackie Leven)” with *Control* and Doll By Doll with Leven as vocalist and guitarist and *Remember* (1979), cross-referenced to other musicians.
inhalt: Terry Hounsome's musician directories (*Rock Record*, *New Rock Record*, *Rock Record 6*) with album and line-up details contain an entry “JOHN ST FIELD (JACKIE LEVEN)” with *Control* and one for Doll By Doll, listing Leven on vocals and guitar and *Remember* (1979, Automatic K 56618), cross-referenced to other musicians. Rock Record 6 (1995) also links Leven with David McIntosh and other studio musicians.
It is an early link between the pseudonym John St Field and Leven in a printed reference work; which edition first carried the entry is not established.

1983-music-week-radio-airplay-love-is-sh.titel: [Collected file: radio airplay of the solo singles "Love Is Shining Down On Me" (1983) and "Uptown" (1984) in Music Week]
1983-music-week-radio-airplay-love-is-sh.kurz: Music Week's weekly airplay pages ("Based on plays Friday–Thursday") list Leven's first solo single "Love Is Shining Down On Me" (Virgin/Charisma JACK 1) in four consecutive issues: 10, 17 and 24 September and 1 October 1983, with playlist entries and "hitpicks" at numerous stations.

1983-scribner-robbins-trouser-press-guid.kurz: The book editions of the Trouser Press guides (1983, 1985, 1991) describe Doll by Doll with Leven as the increasingly sole driving force; Gypsy Blood is "the group's finest", the third album suffers from "creeping relaxation".
inhalt: The Doll by Doll entry in the book editions of the Trouser Press guides (The Trouser Press Guide to New Wave Records, Scribner 1983; The New Trouser Press Record Guide, 1985; The Trouser Press Record Guide, Collier Books 1991) is the source of the entry still maintained online today. In 1983 it calls Leven the singer, guitarist and songwriter who had become increasingly solely responsible. *Gypsy Blood* is "the group's finest". The third album suffers from delay and "creeping relaxation", while *Grand Passion* is the result of a complete upheaval.

The text is expanded in the 1985 and 1991 editions. In 1991 a sentence about the last concert "in late 84" and a cross-reference "Concrete Bulletproof Invisible - See Doll by Doll" (p. 145) are added. The claim of a last concert in late 1984, still repeated today, comes from the 1991 edition and conflicts with other sources that place the band's end earlier.
zitate_kontext: Trouser Press on the third album

1983-unwin-jakubowski-wit-and-wisdom-of-.kurz: Maxim Jakubowski’s quotation collection *The Wit and Wisdom of Rock and Roll* prints a remark by “Jackie Leven – Doll by Doll”: he always lives as if he were in a film.
inhalt: The collection was published by Unwin Paperbacks in London, probably around 1983/84. Among the voices from the rock world is a sentence by “Jackie Leven – Doll by Doll”: he always lives as if he were in a film. The continuation of the quotation is not visible in the available excerpt.
The remark probably comes from an interview around 1979/80, when Doll by Doll were getting attention from the music press on Automatic and Magnet; its origin is not given.

1984-04-21-music-week-studio-chipping-no.titel: [Studio column “Buzzes”: new Charisma signing Jackie Leven in Chipping Norton]
1984-04-21-music-week-studio-chipping-no.kurz: A studio item in Music Week of 21 April 1984 names “new Charisma signing Jackie Leven” among the artists working on albums at Chipping Norton Studios in 1984.
inhalt: In the studio column of the trade paper Music Week (issue of 21 April 1984) a short paragraph covers Chipping Norton Studios (“Chippie”). Artists who have been there this year working on LPs include Level 42’s Mark King, working with engineer Jeremy Green on his solo album for Polydor; Shakatak with producer Nigel White; Jim McDiamond of PhD with producer Pip Williams on his solo project; and “new Charisma signing Jackie Leven with Barry Hammond engineering”.

That single mention is all there is: no album title, no producer, no details about the music. But the item shows that by spring 1984 Leven was already signed to Charisma and working on an album at the Oxfordshire studio. The column also mentions, among other things, a Chris Rea single (co-produced by Dave Richards) and The Kane Gang.
zitate_kontext: Music Week on Leven at Chipping Norton Studios.

1984-08-04-music-week-jackie-leven-uptow.kurz: Music Week calls "Uptown", the second solo single from the ex-Doll by Doll singer, a big, stirring sound that should get plenty of airplay thanks to Geoff Emerick's production.
inhalt: In the singles section of Music Week (4 August 1984) an unnamed reviewer covers Jackie Leven's "Uptown" (Charisma/Virgin JACK 2, 12-inch JACK 212, distributed by EMI). He hears "a big stirring sound" for the second solo single from "this ex-Doll By Doll singer/songwriter", featuring emotive vocals and acoustic guitar that builds into a brash chorus with full backing vocals and uplifting horns.

Thanks to "its big production by Geoff Emerick" (the engineer and producer best known for his work with the Beatles), the single "should receive plenty of exposure". On page 12 of the same issue "Jackie Leven - Uptown - Charisma/Virgin" also appears in the list of records that continue to "bubble under" the main airplay grid, having appeared in the column before. The review is a trade recommendation without any critical reservation.

1985-pierian-whos-new-wave-in-music.kurz: Data-sheet entry no. 207 on Doll By Doll in *Who's New Wave in Music* (1985): formed 1977, style “offbeat folk rock”, line-up Leven and Joe Shaw, album list with some mix-ups.
inhalt: The reference book *Who's New Wave in Music: An Illustrated Encyclopedia, 1976–1982*, published by Pierian Press (Ann Arbor), lists Doll By Doll as entry 207. It is a brief data sheet: country United Kingdom, “Formed 1977”, style “Offbeat folk rock” – the only group in that category in the book's style index –, line-up with Jackie Leven (vocals, guitar, songs) and Joe Shaw, and an album list. The book dates *Gypsy Blood* to 1980 and calls the debut “Doll By Doll” instead of *Remember*; both are obvious mix-ups.

1986-harmonie-park-music-index-1978-1980.titel: The Music Index – Annual Cumulation 1978 and Vol. 31–32 (1979–80): entries “Doll by Doll, The” and “Leven, Jackie”
1986-harmonie-park-music-index-1978-1980.kurz: The US music-periodicals index lists contemporary press articles on Leven and Doll by Doll, including a Melody Maker interview, “The eyes of Jackie Leven”, of 13 September 1980.
inhalt: *The Music Index* (Harmonie Park Press, Detroit/Warren) lists contemporary press articles. Under “LEVEN, JACKIE” there is an interview, “The eyes of Jackie Leven”, by S. Taylor (Steve Taylor) in *Melody Maker* of 13 September 1980 (vol. 55, no. 22), with biography and portraits. Under “DOLL BY DOLL, THE” are, among others, *Melody Maker* of 31 March 1979 (vol. 54, pp. 15 f.) and a review of *Gypsy Blood* in *Melody Maker* of November 1979.

The 1978 volume (published 1989) also lists a Doll by Doll article titled “Entropy is just another word for nothing …”, with the periodical illegible in the snippet; so there was press coverage as early as 1978. *Melody Maker* of 31 March 1979 is also the source of the phrase “a mystery shrouded combo by the name of Doll by Doll” in Kenneth Hudson’s *Dictionary of the Teenage Revolution* (1983).

1989-banyan-frame-harp-beat-rock-gazette.kurz: In Pete Frame's rock gazetteer, the entry for Glenrothes in Fife says the new town was the birthplace of Jackie Leven, leader of the late-70s challengers Doll By Doll, and an inspiration for the Skids.
inhalt: Under the entry GLENROTHES (Fife), the rock gazetteer names the new town as the birthplace of Jackie Leven, “leader of late 70s challengers Doll By Doll”, and as an inspiration for the Skids. The 1989 edition includes a photo of Leven. The same statement appears in the revised edition of 1999 (*Rockin' Around Britain*).
It is the earliest printed source found for Glenrothes as his birthplace. Most other sources give Kirkcaldy; Leven grew up in Glenrothes.

1990-10-10-nursing-standard-core-trust-d.titel: [News item: CORE Trust Day Centre for drug addicts opens in London]
1990-10-10-nursing-standard-core-trust-d.kurz: A short item in Nursing Standard (10 October 1990) reports the opening of a CORE Trust day centre in London that combines acupuncture, herbal remedies and meditation with conventional detoxification.
inhalt: This short news item in the British nursing journal Nursing Standard (vol. 5, no. 3, p. 11) reports that a new rehabilitation facility for drug addicts with holistic treatment had opened in London. The programme of the CORE Trust Day Centre combines acupuncture, herbal remedies and meditation with conventional detoxification methods.

The item is one of the few contemporary sources on the work of the trust founded by Jackie Leven and Carol Wolf. Leven is not named in the part that is freely visible; whether he or Carol Wolf is quoted remains open. The day centre opened in autumn 1990.

1990-12-the-company-the-core-trust-fish.kurz: The former Marillion singer Fish writes in the first person about his friendship with Leven and about the CORE Trust.
inhalt: The former Marillion singer Fish writes in the first person about his friendship with Leven and about the CORE Trust. He says he met Leven in the bar of the Marquee in Wardour Street, in the middle of his own “Incommunicado” phase; in the conversations of the following years the subject kept returning to Leven's idea of a clinic that would treat not only the body but the soul of those suffering from addiction. Fish contrasts this with the government's anti-heroin advertising campaign, which he criticises as superficial, and says he donated at Leven's request. Through Judy Totten, a CORE PR consultant, he met the New Zealand acupuncturist Murray Douglas in 1987; a large part of the text is a testimony to acupuncture, hypnotherapy, Bach flower remedies and medicinal herbs. On Leven: a Scot “through to the core”, formerly the frontman of an underrated band, who came to CORE after his own drug problems; he is no longer involved in the clinic, and the last Fish heard was that Leven was in Australia preparing a career as a poet and singer. CORE is now run by Carol Wolf, who founded the Trust with Leven; the centre in Lisson Cottages (Lisson Grove) has been renovated and was reopened by Princess Diana on 19 September, and the WHO is interested in the model. The text ends with an appeal for donations.

1991-08-31-nme-great-lost-albums-doll-by.kurz: Stuart Maconie presents Doll by Doll’s self-titled third album (1981) in NME’s “Great Lost Albums” column as an uninfluential but passionately loved discovery, praising Leven’s guitar playing and voice.
inhalt: Stuart Maconie includes Doll by Doll’s third, self-titled album (Magnet, 1981) in his NME series “Great Lost Albums”. He opens with a deliberate understatement: the record had no influence on pop and hardly anyone has heard it, yet he loves it to bits. He knew nothing of the band when it appeared; to him they are a shifting outfit built around the Scot Jackie Leven, a passionate, intense character who seemed more interested in R. D. Laing and drug rehabilitation than in the words of “Chairman Lydon”. He heard the album by accident and was knocked sideways.

On paper this is music to avoid – heartfelt guitar rock with Celtic mysticism, style-hopping and chest-beating bravura – yet it works thanks to Leven’s “smouldering genius”. It is his show, built on liquid, heart-breaking guitar playing and an extraordinary voice, by turns a swaggering Yankee bullhorn, a falsetto sob and the suavest of growls; you feel he means every word. He singles out “Up” (an anthem to elation), “Bright Green Field” (a luminous, almost medieval allegory), “Main Travelled Roads” (a Scottish lament) and “Caritas” (a tormented howl of disco rock).
Maconie ends by asking where the band are now: they made one more, inferior album and fizzled out. Anyone with information or a good copy is asked to get in touch.
zitate_kontext: Stuart Maconie opens his appreciation of the 1981 album.
Maconie on Leven’s guitar playing and voice.
Maconie on the state of his own copy.

1993-mcfarland-edwards-rock-n-roll-1970-.kurz: The American discography reference for chart artists lists Doll by Doll under ‘Synth-Rock – British’, with line-up and albums 1979–1982.
inhalt: The reference work by Edwards, *Rock ’n’ Roll, 1970 through 1979* (McFarland, 1993) catalogues discographies of all performers who hit the charts. Doll by Doll have an entry of their own, filed under the style heading ‘Synth-Rock – British’, which does not describe the band’s music. It lists the line-up – Jackie Leven (vocals, guitars), Jo Shaw (vocals, keyboards and more) and David McIntosh – and the albums of 1979 to 1982, including a title ‘DXD’ (1981) which appears nowhere else and is probably an error or a compilation.

The book’s name index lists Leven, McIntosh and Shaw with a reference to the band. The entry is an example of how the band was perceived in American reference works: as a British new-wave group with a small discography.

1994-04-09-fremtiden-songs-from-the-argy.kurz: An enthusiastic short review of the mini-album *Songs from the Argyll Cycle*: after twelve years' silence the reviewer never thought a comeback possible and hears the Doll by Doll magic fully intact.
inhalt: The Drammen newspaper Fremtiden hails the mini-album *Songs from the Argyll Cycle* (distributed in Norway by Amigo) under the headline “An incredible comeback!” Twelve years after his last album, the reviewer had never believed this would be possible. He recounts that Leven lived a hard life with alcohol and heroin that brought him close to an overdose, followed by a brutal assault on London's streets in which he was nearly strangled. The attempted strangling, he says, damaged Leven's vocal cords in the mid-1980s.

Leven, “an incredible singer and songwriter with gypsy blood in his veins” (the text's words), led the hottest band on London's club circuit in 1978–79; Doll By Doll made “three fantastic albums” (in fact four), and it is a strong feeling to hear that the magic is still completely intact. The five very varied songs tell “more than a book about feelings and hope”. The mini-album is also a thank-you to his Scottish roots; a full album follows in the summer, and the reviewer awaits the sequel with great excitement.
zitate_kontext: The reviewer on Doll by Doll and the comeback.
On the five songs of the mini-album.

1994-08-10-arbeiderbladet-mektig-og-jord.kurz: Arbeiderbladet praises Leven's debut *The Mystery of Love …* as bigger than most of what is on the market: cinemascopic sound of mandolins and fiddles beside synthesisers and, above all, a voice between crooner, folk and soul singer, “mighty and likeably down-to-earth”.
inhalt: The short review in the Oslo daily (10 August 1994) sits in a column of new releases under the headline “Mektig og jordnært”, “Mighty and down-to-earth”. It opens with a tribute: over the past decade Leven has spent less time on his career than on helping fellow musicians dry out – honour to him for that – even though *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* is bigger than most other things on the market. The reference is to his work with the CORE Trust.

The music has a “cinemascopic” breadth of sound, created by mandolins and fiddles as well as synthesisers and electric guitars. Most of all, though, Leven's voice towers: the former Doll by Doll chief is crooner, folk singer and soul singer at once, “pathos-filled mighty and likeably down-to-earth”. He does “I Say a Little Prayer” with Scott Walker-like elegance and fills the rest of the record with self-written, well-written, lyrical, slow songs. The reviewer signs as “Haakon Lars” (the OCR is not fully legible).
The same text appeared slightly expanded under the headline “Leve Leven!” in Haugesunds Avis on the same day, adding that it was the most poetic pop music of 1994.
zitate_kontext: On the rest of the album

1994-08-20-fremtiden-sigoyner-i-blodet.titel: [Profile/review:] Sigøyner i blodet – JACKIE LEVEN «The mystery of love is greater than the mystery of death»
1994-08-20-fremtiden-sigoyner-i-blodet.kurz: Johnny Andreassen welcomes Leven's comeback *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* as one of the year's best albums and retells his story from London's streets to his return to Scotland.
inhalt: The Drammen music journalist Johnny Andreassen reviews Leven's solo debut (Amigo) in the local paper Fremtiden under the headline “Sigøyner i blodet”, “gypsy blood”. Like a cat, the former leader of the “legendary” Doll By Doll undoubtedly has more than one life: overdoses and attacks in London's streets, with attempted strangulation, should long ago have sent him to his grave, yet he has clawed his way back to life unnoticed after returning to the Scotland of his childhood, where he has blossomed with a pearl of an album. In the late seventies he was the hottest thing on the London club scene, with a charisma that hardly lags behind a Jim Morrison, and has one of the most beautiful and charismatic voices in the world.

A section under the subhead “Avvenning” (withdrawal) says that in 1985 Leven founded the drug-rehabilitation institution CORE, which, thanks to new treatment methods, has very good results to show and, according to the article, is supported by the Prince of Wales, Genesis, Eric Clapton and Mike Scott of the Waterboys. It helps people out of a squeeze that almost killed Leven himself some years earlier.

On the music: Leven has gypsy blood in his veins, and that restlessness has shaped his music all along; strong feelings swirl around his lyrics and melodies. His friend, the American poet Robert Bly, reads poems on the album, and towards the end Leven's melody takes over and strengthens the mood to rarely effective ends. Mike Scott and the jazz saxophonist Ed Jones contribute. The music reflects Scottish folk and a distinctive troubadour pop sound; Leven's voice alone is worth the price, especially in “Call mother a lonely field” (presumably “Cold Mother of Lonely Fields”). The album is better than a good film, and Andreassen is sure that it will be one of the three or four records he will hold closest to his chest at the end of 1994.

1994-cooking-vinyl-man-of-mysteries-and-.kurz: Cooking Vinyl's 1994 press biography for the comeback album: Leven as former Doll by Doll frontman, the attack, heroin and recovery in Oban, then his three ventures (CORE Trust, men's work with Robert Bly, his own whisky) and his own note on the album title.
inhalt: The text introduces Jackie Leven as a great singer, a writer of beautiful, telling songs and a fine guitarist, best known in Britain as the former “wild frontman” of the critically acclaimed rock band Doll by Doll. That phase of a promising career, it says, ended “in savage circumstances”: in an unprovoked attack in a North London street he nearly died of strangulation and was silenced for years. The biography quotes Paul Du Noyer calling his voice “one of the best male voices of the time”. (Its claim that Doll by Doll made “five stunning albums in as many years in the early eighties” is not accurate; the band ran from 1977 to 1982/83.)

Unable to sing and deeply traumatised, Leven turned to heroin, “the classic drug of despair”, and, adding insult to injury, his girlfriend ran off with the Dalai Lama's bodyguard. The wise decision was a return to Scotland, to Oban and the West Coast, to recover, reflect and make new and lasting friendships with “the canny natives”. With his humour restored, he then threw himself into several significant and controversial ventures.

First comes the CORE Trust College, which on this account he founded in 1985: “a cost effective community health model for the future”, then the UK's only fully holistic service for healing addictions, also used by casualties of the music business. CORE, it claims, shook up the established “Addiction Industry” with its radical holistic programmes, college-style classes and success rate. Its champions are listed as the Princess of Wales (who has headed four events for CORE, with more promised), Genesis, Westminster City Council, John Paul Getty Jr, Eric Clapton and, singled out, Mike Scott of the Waterboys.

Second is his friendship with Robert Bly, author of the American bestseller *Iron John* and recognised originator of the mytho-poetic men's movement. For five years, the text says, the two have stayed with each other in Britain and the USA; together with Richard Olivier, son of Laurence, this has produced ten Bly-led men's retreats of up to a hundred men each, with more promised for the autumn. The “men's work”, with its visible themes of warriorship, grief and shame, has polarised feminist thinkers in Britain and America and made Leven a spokesman, appearing with Gloria Hunniford, on *Kilroy*, at the Tate Gallery (with Sara Kent), at the Royal College of Art and on BBC Scotland television.
Third is his own malt whisky, Leven's Lament, “the lonely spirit of the glens”, due in the shops that autumn as an “unusual and strong” uisge beatha, the water of life.

The biography ends with a note by Leven on the album title, *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*. Cooking Vinyl, “people of genuine charm and a certain recklessness”, found his two other title ideas too long. “Mystery”, he explains, is meant in an earlier pagan sense, not the Christian one; the line is used at men's retreats to stun the intellect, after which one can slip images into the men's hearts. The first rejected title was an off-the-cuff remark by Robert Bly at a retreat in Dorset, when told a thunderstorm might cut short an outdoor activity: there are thunderstorms longing to come into the world through the minds of women. The second came from a television scene with Prue Leith (Leven is not sure it was she): she told an Oban fishmonger that she had eaten a fish elsewhere in Scotland that had been swimming five minutes earlier and asked whether he could beat that for freshness. The fishmonger replied that you get a sweeter taste when rigor mortis sets in, and Leith took an involuntary step back in horror.
zitate_kontext: Leven on the title of The Mystery of Love …
The Oban fishmonger's reply, as told in Leven's note
Robert Bly at a men's retreat in Dorset, as quoted by Leven
Paul Du Noyer on Leven's voice, quoted in the biography

1994-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.titel: [Collected finds Nasjonalbiblioteket 1994: brief news items, announcements, listings]
1994-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.kurz: In 1994 Leven appears in the Norwegian press as a solo artist: the distributor Amigo releases *Songs from the Argyll Cycle* and *The Mystery of Love…*; there are reviews, new-release lists, syndicated short notices and year-end lists.
inhalt: 1994 is the year Leven appears in Norway as a solo artist: the distributor Amigo (later Bonnier Amigo) releases *Songs from the Argyll Cycle* in the spring and *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* in August. The National Library's full-text search records around 45 issues from 1994 mentioning “Jackie Leven”.

Besides the reviews (Fremtiden 9 April, Arbeiderbladet/Haugesunds Avis 10 August, Fremtiden 20 August) there are mainly new-release lists (Arbeiderbladet and Nordlys in March, Arbeiderbladet and Tønsbergs Blad in August), a short notice printed identically in at least eight local papers in August (“JACKIE LEVEN er kult-figur i Skottland …”), a note in Hamar Arbeiderblad of 8 July (the mini-album was actually intended for Scotland only, Amigo secured a few copies), a club programme in Tromsø in which a DJ plays tracks from Leven's first solo CD, and year-end lists in December: Arbeiderbladet places *The Mystery of Love* at no. 49 in its top 50, and Fremtiden's list hails the return of the Doll by Doll leader after years of silence as “fairy-tale beautiful” Celtic music. No concerts in Norway are documented for 1994. The magazine *Beat*, then the leading Norwegian rock magazine, mentions Leven in five issues in 1994, and *Puls* in one; these are readable only with Norwegian access, as are possible longer pieces in Klassekampen (14 April), Adresseavisen (21 December) and Bergens Tidende (27 December).
zitate_kontext: Start of the short notice printed in several local papers in August 1994.
Fremtiden's year-end list on the comeback.

1995-01-04-nordlands-framtid-kraftig-og-.kurz: Kjell Nordeng praises Leven's solo debut in Nordlands Framtid as powerful in sound and thoughtful in lyrics, one of 1994's records that should not go unnoticed.
inhalt: In early January 1995, Kjell Nordeng reviews *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* (Cooking Vinyl) in Nordlands Framtid (Bodø). At the start of the eighties Leven led the critically praised but commercially unsuccessful British soul-rock band Doll By Doll. On this, “as far as I know”, his first solo CD, he had help from, among others, the Waterboy Mike Scott, and that collaboration is a small pointer to where the music lies.

The soundscape is spacious and powerful, the lyrics thoughtful. There are elements of pop, rock and folk in fine union, and Leven's vocal carries the melodies excellently amid acoustic and electric instruments. The songs have atmosphere, weight, nerve and melody, making this one of the records of 1994 that should not go unnoticed.

1995-02-02-fremtiden-jackie-leven-er-til.kurz: By its own account the first and only Norwegian newspaper interview with Leven after his comeback (Fremtiden 03.05.1995).
inhalt: By its own account the first and only Norwegian newspaper interview with Leven after his comeback (Fremtiden 03.05.1995). Andreassen had put *The Mystery of Love* in third place on his 1994 year-end list. Leven tells the story of the attack like this: at two in the morning he left the studio and wanted to walk home, was attacked and almost strangled, for two or three years he could neither speak nor sing, and he endured a severe depression only with constant heroin; years of training in the “Alexander Technique” repaired his voice. He describes the centre he founded, The Core Trust, which treats all kinds of addiction with acupuncture, among other things.

On his helpers: Mike Scott later rescued the Core project with badly needed money, and a joint album is under discussion; Robert Bly he has admired since he was 16 and regards as the greatest performer of his time. Leven left Scotland as a teenager to escape gangs and fights; on his return he found a changed country with a better relationship between women and men, and Scottish men now had to free themselves from English dominance. He sees close ties between Norway and Scotland (Shetland, the north-east), hopes for a tour or an Oslo concert in early March with his keyboard friend “James Halliway”, and announces the next album, *The Year I Left My Heart*, for April – he has asked Van Morrison to take part.
zitate_kontext: Leven on the evening of the attack.

1995-03-10-the-big-untidy-jackie-leven-i.kurz: Long fanzine interview, conducted backstage at the Pfefferberg in Berlin on 10.03.1995, shortly before Leven introduced Andy White; on tour with keyboard player James Hallawell for the EP with “I Say A Little Prayer”.
inhalt: Long fanzine interview, conducted backstage at the Pfefferberg in Berlin on 10.03.1995, shortly before Leven introduced Andy White; on tour with keyboard player James Hallawell for the EP with “I Say A Little Prayer”. The introduction sums up Doll by Doll, the attack, heroin and the return to Oban and the west coast, praises *The Mystery Of Love…* and *Songs From The Argyll Cycle*, reports on the Cooking Vinyl package tour with Tom Robinson and Andy White at the Knaack in Berlin (October 1994) and mentions CORE (acronym spelt out), the men's movement around Robert Bly and the whisky “Leven's Lament”.

In conversation Leven says: Doll by Doll (founded ’76/’77) fell between two stools – too heavy for punk's opponents, not punk for punks; he regards punk as a middle-class phenomenon. The band broke up because nobody bought the records. He describes the attack here without embellishment: drunk, walking from the studio near the Caledonian Road to Maida Vale, “just got mugged”. Afterwards about two years without a voice, steroids (“electric fur”), isolation, heroin, which he describes as a journey of initiation. He developed the CORE Trust out of his own withdrawal programme, with his girlfriend Carol, who was in the last Doll by Doll line-up, on the advice of her homeopathic doctor. He came to Cooking Vinyl through his lawyer, who recommended Martin Goldschmidt. He says he was the first schoolboy in Scotland to be caught for drugs and discovered Bly in the school library; he explains the Dylan co-authorship of “As We Sailed Into Skibbereen” with a shared train journey from Berlin to St Petersburg. Finally, explanations of “Call Mother A Lonely Field” (ploughed winter fields) and “The Garden” (Machado's image of the soul as a garden, his own years in London pubs).
zitate_kontext: Leven on Doll by Doll between punk and rock.

1995-04-24-bergensavisen-leven-pa-garage.kurz: Bergensavisen announces Leven's concert at Garage in Bergen on 27 April 1995 with a pun on his name and sketches his turbulent biography, from rehab and heroin to Doll by Doll and the acclaimed comeback album.
inhalt: In a short preview, Bergensavisen announces Jackie Leven's concert at Garage on Thursday 27 April 1995, with a pun on his name: “it could get really lively” (Norwegian “leven” means commotion). The Scottish artist has led, to put it mildly, a turbulent life and carries his experiences into his lyrics. Among the more serious ones are a stay in a rehab clinic in Scotland and a period as a “heroin slave” in the 1980s. He had barely got back on his feet when his girlfriend ran off with the Dalai Lama's bodyguard.

Many will remember the group Leven led from 1979 to 1982, Doll By Doll, whose four LPs have long since become collectors' items. Last year came the “knock-out” solo album *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*, which Bergensavisen reviewed with a five and which several papers named album of the year. The conclusion: Leven is a truly distinctive artist, and a concert with him is unforgettable.
zitate_kontext: Closing sentence of the concert preview.

1995-04-26-arbeiderbladet-mystisk-leven.kurz: Interview on the day of his concert at the Rockefeller, Oslo, as part of a “magical week” on the theme of healing.
inhalt: Interview on the day of his concert at the Rockefeller, Oslo, as part of a “magical week” on the theme of healing. The standfirst: the cult hero has quit drugs and turned to whisky production instead. On the album title, which Robert Bly tossed out on an occasion he hardly remembers, Leven says he has no clear idea what it means – what is mystic is the mystery itself. Sandnes recalls Doll by Doll and the silence after the attack, broken only by Mike Scott's cryptic thanks on *This Is the Sea* (Leven had let him “take the bus”).

Leven tells it soberly: after the attack he lost his voice, sat at home for a few years and took heroin; the silence led him back to a place he knew. His lyrics are about universal loneliness and the need to accept being alone; he likes to write about sadness, but “in a loving way”, and humour is the basis of life. He rejects being compared with Nick Drake, Syd Barrett or Kevin Ayers: he is neither dead nor a junkie nor mad, although he works with many mad people. He describes himself as a rough, tough, poetic guy. He started the whisky as a joke and then discovered the kinship of “spirit” and “sprit”.

1995-04-29-bergensavisen-bra-med-leven.kurz: Julie Forchhammer praises Leven's solo concert at the Garage in Bergen: holding the room with just an acoustic guitar, a strong voice despite the aftermath of an attack, and rough stories between songs that had everyone laughing.
inhalt: Julie Forchhammer reviews Leven's show at the Garage on Thursday 27 April 1995 for Bergensavisen. The Scot is one of the few who can sit alone on a stage with just an acoustic guitar, she writes; one mostly wants to tie him down so he can go on and on. Despite a break of almost twelve years he keeps a high standard in both melodies and delivery.

She finds the voice remarkable: it is hard to believe that in the mid-eighties he was beaten down so brutally (and almost strangled) that he could neither speak nor sing for several years. His guitar playing shows how well he commands the instrument, and the sound engineer added plenty of echo, so that the sound was full despite the slender set-up. Leven is often compared with Van Morrison, and as the first encore he played a splendid version of Morrison's “Slim Slow Slider”.

The reviewer arrived somewhat late, but judging by the audience's engagement she assumes the troubadour held the level from beginning to end. He kept the mood going with chat between songs, and despite tough stories from his wild years there was plenty of laughter, from Leven himself and from the very attentive audience. The photo caption adds that there was no kilt, but at least the socks were in place.

1995-05-03-fremtiden-jackie-leven-rockef.titel: [Concert report with interview: Jackie Leven at the Rockefeller, Oslo]
1995-05-03-fremtiden-jackie-leven-rockef.kurz: Report on the solo concert in the “magical week” at the Rockefeller, Oslo – according to Andreassen Leven's first visit to Norway in over ten years.
inhalt: Report on the solo concert in the “magical week” at the Rockefeller, Oslo – according to Andreassen Leven's first visit to Norway in over ten years. Only Fremtiden and the rock magazine *Beat* were on the guest list; a small, enthusiastic audience would not let Leven leave the stage. Alone with a guitar, he had the audience holding their breath with pleasure; pieces from *The Mystery of Love* (including “Call Mother a Lonely Field”) and from the forthcoming album *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West*, due out in August, were played.

In conversation after the show Leven says he feels at home in Norway, although his last stay, in a band “with Glen Matlock, among others”, was not a happy time. As chairman of a London centre for people addicted to everything from sex to money, he believes in healing and acupuncture – for himself it is probably too late. On the new album: he asked Van Morrison to read a poem by the Belfast poet Louis MacNeice, Andy White takes part; the album is assembled like a film from speeches, poems, noises and songs, the range greater than before. The title means that in the West there are forbidden things one does not talk about – the West is slowly dying.

1995-05-11-eye-weekly-the-wild-boy-at-re.kurz: Feature in the Toronto free culture paper on the North American release of *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death* (True North/MCA), based on a telephone interview with Leven in London.
inhalt: Feature in the Toronto free culture paper on the North American release of *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death* (True North/MCA), based on a telephone interview with Leven in London. Anderson frames the piece with his own scepticism towards Robert Bly's *Iron John* and introduces Leven as the British spokesman of the “Mytho-Poetic Men's Movement”. He calls Doll by Doll an unjustly overlooked band, best on *Remember* and *Gypsy Blood*. Leven tells the Oban story: after the attack, heroin and a break-up, a night drive through a snowstorm to the west coast, in a bar the invitation from a half-Scottish, half-Polish giant to an arm-wrestle, from which a lifelong friendship grew – for him a turning point in his life. The “Argyll Cycle” (15 songs on an album and two EPs in 1994) documents the dying of his younger, wild self; you have to be defeated and betrayed to know who you are (“ignominy” as “no name”). Leven distances himself sharply from commercial men's courses (the warrior is an archetype we live in) and defends Bly against the charge of misogyny. On the cover of “I Say A Little Prayer” he develops the idea of the “black woman in you” for whom Bacharach/David wrote. Tone: very positive, compares the album with *Fisherman's Blues*.
zitate_kontext: Leven on his youth and Doll by Doll.

1995-09-28-moss-dagblad-forbidden-songs-.titel: [Record review: Jackie Leven – Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West]
1995-09-28-moss-dagblad-forbidden-songs-.kurz: A short review in Moss Dagblad: the former Doll by Doll singer follows last year's “pearl” with *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West*, a cross between Bryan Ferry and Van Morrison who again sets poems to music.
inhalt: The music section of Moss Dagblad carries a short, favourable review of Jackie Leven's *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West*. The former Doll By Doll singer is back with a follow-up to last year's pearl, *The Mystery of Love…*. For the uninitiated, Leven is best described as a kind of cross between Bryan Ferry and Van Morrison, and on the new album he proves once more what a capable singer he is. Most of the material he wrote himself. As last time, he has again set poems by authors such as James Wright and Emily Dickinson to music.

1995-09-29-arbeiderbladet-liv-og-leven.kurz: In Arbeiderbladet Haakon Larsen praises *Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West* as warm-hearted, soothing and almost spiritual, and as a fine successor to *The Mystery Of Love*; Leven only goes slack when he flirts with country, jazz and old rock.
inhalt: This short record review in the Oslo paper Arbeiderbladet (29 September 1995) presents *Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West* (Cooking Vinyl/Amigo) as an album about big boys who cry, mothers who took their own lives, and blessed, beautiful moments. The title, it says, must not be taken literally: Leven wrote the songs himself, and they are about personal growth and the need to redeem the unredeemed within oneself.

The basic tone is “in no way depressing” but kind-hearted, soothing and nearly spiritual. Even Sylvester Stallone in *Judge Dredd* could be moved by “Men In Prison”, in which Leven, on top of sixty sacred male choir voices, sings of the sea, the darkness and loneliness with a crooner’s pathos and a soul singer’s heartfelt power. Three of the sixteen tracks are recitations of poems the Scot has borrowed from Emily Dickinson, James Wright and Louis MacNeice.

Musically Leven draws his raw material from Celtic folk tunes, spaghetti westerns, rock and much else. Perhaps he goes too slack when he flirts with country, jazz and old rock, but all in all the album is a fine successor to *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death*. The piece is signed Haakon Larsen; the rating symbol is illegible.
zitate_kontext: Haakon Larsen on the album’s basic tone

1995-10-22-bergensavisen-lite-leven.kurz: Tore Bø calls *Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West* a gloriously melancholy record free of pop clichés, one critics will love and few will buy; Leven “steals with style”.
inhalt: Under the tongue-in-cheek headline “Lite Leven” (roughly “not much Leven” or “little noise”), Tore Bø reviews Jackie Leven's album *Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West* (BMG) in Bergensavisen. Leven has again made a record doomed to become a critics' favourite; it is unlikely to sell in large numbers, since TV advertising is reserved for bigger names.

Even so, it is a “deilig melankolsk plate”, a delightfully melancholy record, full of catchy melodies and arrangements so refreshingly free of pop's clichés that one can only bow in the dust. Bø concedes that Leven is a master at borrowing from other capable folk: “he steals with style”. In his music and lyrics you can hear touches of Morricone, Chris Isaak, Big Country and Morrissey. But only this Scot, he says, could come up with lines like those he quotes as a sample: “We sat in a bar / She went for a piss / I confessed the emptiness / In every kiss”. The rating cannot be read in the newspaper scan.
zitate_kontext: Tore Bø on *Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West*

1995-10-24-fredriksstad-blad-ujevn-leven.kurz: Terje Carlsen finds *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West* atmospheric but “ujevn” (uneven) in *Fredriksstad Blad*: plenty of good music, but some songs remain mere parentheses.
inhalt: Under the pun “Ujevn Leven” (“Uneven Leven”), Terje Carlsen reviews Leven’s new album *Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West* (Amigo) in a round-up column. It is a collection of “atmospheric, slightly pompous songs”. Ireland is the starting point for this “third-part concept album”. Leven has a soft, warm voice and there is a lot of good music here. A number of the songs, however, amount to nothing but parentheses, and overall the album is rather uneven.
zitate_kontext: Terje Carlsen on *Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West*

1995-11-03-rolling-stone-de-auf-den-spur.medium: Rolling Stone (German edition), online archive rollingstone.de
1995-11-03-rolling-stone-de-auf-den-spur.kurz: Early German-language interview profile from the time of “Forbidden Songs of the Dying West” (1995), written by Doebeling, long-standing Leven champion at the German Rolling Stone, after a visit to Argyll at Loch Feochan.
inhalt: Early German-language interview profile from the time of “Forbidden Songs of the Dying West” (1995), written by Doebeling, long-standing Leven champion at the German Rolling Stone, after a visit to Argyll at Loch Feochan. The text begins with cultural criticism of the nineties music business, which Leven shares “meaningfully”, and describes him physically (short trousers, white knee socks, sturdy footwear; at 45 “gnarled like an old oak”). Leven explains why he moved to the west coast: the people there are straightforward and have Irish blood, whereas the Scandinavian-Protestant east coast of his origins suits him less (self-statement). He presents himself and keyboard player James Hallawell as Celts (Fife and the “Kingdom of Cornwall” respectively). Doebeling recounts the personal catastrophes up to addiction, the independent heroin withdrawal and the founding of the CORE Trust, as well as Leven's role in Robert Bly's men's movement; Leven tells of wilderness weekends with a hundred men, poetry, drumming and stories. Doebeling ironically declines an invitation to take part. At the end he praises Doll by Doll as a band “between all stools” and the new double album as a near-perfect realisation of Leven's vision, much more fully worked out than its predecessor. The whisky “Leven's Lament” is also mentioned. Tone: ironic and detached towards the men's esotericism, full of admiration for the music.

1995-guinness-larkin-whos-who-of-indie-a.kurz: The reference book describes Doll By Doll as a vehicle for Jackie Leven, formed in 1977; the self-titled album on Magnet is said to have produced a minor hit with “Carita” (meaning “Caritas”). An album list for 1979–1982 follows.
inhalt: The entry “Doll By Doll” in the *Guinness Who’s Who of Indie and New Wave Music* (edited by Colin Larkin, 1995) is worded identically to the article in the *Guinness Encyclopedia of Popular Music*. It describes the group as a vehicle for Jackie Leven, formed in 1977. The self-titled album on Magnet is said to have produced a minor hit with “Carita” (the single is actually “Caritas”, 1981). A list of the albums from 1979 to 1982 follows.

Elsewhere the book also lists the bass player Marc Duncan (born 9 May 1960) “of Doll By Doll”, who later moved to another band. This claim also appears in other reference works by the same editor but cannot be reconciled with other sources on the band’s line-up.

1995-hachette-guide-du-routard-ecosse.titel: Le Guide du routard: Écosse (editions 1996–1997 and 1999)
1995-hachette-guide-du-routard-ecosse.kurz: The French travel guide Guide du routard: Écosse gives Leven a box: the life of this man from the ‘kingdom of Fife’ is a novel; he founded Doll by Doll and the Core Trust, supported by Eric Clapton, Genesis and Princess Diana.
inhalt: The Scotland volume of the travel guide series *Le Guide du routard* (Hachette, Paris; editions 1996–1997 and 1999) includes a box on Jackie Leven. The life of this man from the ‘royaume de Fife’ is a novel: with Doll by Doll he founded one of the best Scottish rock bands, whose promising career broke off after four albums. To help addicts he founded the Core Trust, supported by Eric Clapton, Genesis and Princess Diana.
That a travel guide of the mid-1990s should portray a musician in this way is unusual; Leven’s life story was evidently thought worth telling as part of Scotland.
