1995-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.titel: [Collected finds Nasjonalbiblioteket 1995: brief news items, announcements, listings]
1995-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.kurz: In 1995, Norwegian newspapers cover Leven's first solo concerts in the country (Oslo, 26 April; Bergen, 27 April) and, in autumn, the album *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West*. Around 70 issues mention his name.
inhalt: 1995 brings Leven's first Norwegian solo concerts: at Rockefeller in Oslo on 26 April, part of a “magical week” on the theme of healing, and at Garage in Bergen on 27 April. According to Fremtiden it was his first visit to Norway in over ten years. In autumn comes the album *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West* (Cooking Vinyl/Amigo, given as BMG in Bergensavisen), with numerous reviews. A concert in Oslo announced in February for early March (with James Hallawell) is not documented.

Individual pieces include an interview in Fremtiden (2 February), a preview in Bergensavisen (24 April), an interview in Arbeiderbladet (26 April), Bergensavisen's concert review (29 April), a concert report with interview in Fremtiden (3 May) and album reviews in Moss Dagblad (28 September), Arbeiderbladet (29 September), Haugesunds Avis (4 October) and Bergensavisen (22 October). In all, around 70 issues mention “Jackie Leven”, many of them in major papers such as Dagbladet, VG, Aftenposten, Bergens Tidende and Klassekampen; the magazine *Beat* mentions him in seven issues, issue 5/6 with eight mentions, presumably in a larger article or interview.

Among the shorter mentions: in Firda (8 April) a local musician, Geirmund Henjum, names Leven as his favourite artist. In Nordlands framtid (1 August) Leven serves as a point of comparison in another artist's review. Arbeiderbladet (20 November), reviewing a Mike Scott concert, speaks of “sjelefrenden Jackie Leven” (soul friend), and Fremtiden (7 December), reviewing Mike Scott's *Bring 'em All In*, mentions a conversation with Leven in a Scottish bar. Nordlandsposten points on 13 December to a cover CD with the magazine *Beat* featuring a Leven track. Romerikes Blad lists *Forbidden Songs* in a year-end round-up on 12 December as “mindre kjent, men veldig bra” (less known, but very good).
zitate_kontext: Arbeiderbladet, 20 November 1995, in a review of a Mike Scott concert
Romerikes Blad, 12 December 1995, on *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West* in a year-end round-up

1995-papermac-olivier-shadow-of-the-ston.kurz: The director Richard Olivier mentions Leven in his book on his path into the men's movement as a good friend who gave him a poetry reading and accompanied him to an event on male initiation.
inhalt: The theatre director Richard Olivier, son of Laurence Olivier, describes in *Shadow of the Stone Heart: A Search for Manhood* (Papermac, 1995; US edition *Melting the Stone*, 1996) his path into the men's movement around the poet Robert Bly.

Leven appears as a good friend who gave him a recording of a poetry reading, and as a companion: the following Saturday Olivier drove with Leven to Victoria for an event on male initiation. The book shows Leven's role in the British men's movement of the early 1990s from a contemporary outside view; which reading it was (presumably one by Bly) is not clear from the passage. Leven himself refers to the book in his columns.

1996-02-14-jaerbladet-forbidden-songs-of.kurz: Jærbladet praises *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West* as one of last year's strongest records and *The Mystery of Love …* as even more majestic, and passes on Dylan claims from Leven's own self-presentation.
inhalt: The short review (column “Musikk”, signed “Ved Helge Barane”, Jærbladet, 14 February 1996, in Nynorsk) sits between reviews of Jah Wobble, Joan Osborne, Runrig and Nick Cave's *Murder Ballads*. The reviewer says he is writing about the album “for the second time” because no record shop in Bryne has yet had it, or Leven's previous album, on its shelves: “a great shame”. It is one of the “absolutely, decidedly strongest” records of the previous year, in any genre. The 1994 record *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*, on the same label, is more majestic and stronger still; that almost nobody in the Jæren district knows these two “masterpieces” is a “great mystery” to him.

He then relays claims that largely rest on Leven's self-presentation: Leven is “one of Bob Dylan's biggest favourites”, the two have composed songs together, and Dylan was a guest throughout the whole studio session. This echoes a legend spread by Leven's circle at the time and is not substantiated. Leven was also the singer of the fabled Doll by Doll, whose “fine records from the eighties” are hopefully due on CD before summer 1996. The sentence on what Leven's two solo records ought to sell breaks off at the column break.
zitate_kontext: The reviewer on Forbidden Songs of the Dying West

1996-03-09-bergensavisen-leven-laerer-la.kurz: Bergensavisen announces three three-day seminars at the 1996 Ole Blues festival, including Jackie Leven's songwriting course, whose participants are to appear on a single as "The Celtic Orchestra of Bergen".
inhalt: On 9 March 1996 Bergensavisen reports, under the headline "Leven lærer låter" ("Leven teaches songs"), that Bergen's Ole Blues festival will offer three three-day seminars: Sonny Landreth (slide guitar), Jackie Leven (songwriting) and Michael Hill's Blues Mob (blues on various instruments). Landreth and Leven each have room for 15 participants, while Hill's Blues Mob is split into four groups with many more places. The seminars are run with the Norwegian Music Council.

Festival director Gisle Johnsen says it has always irritated the organisers that artists visiting Bergen leave as soon as their concerts are over; now they finally have the chance to keep them longer. Expectations are high, he says, "perhaps especially of Jackie Leven". Leven has persuaded his record company to back a single on which his seminar participants take part under the name "The Celtic Orchestra of Bergen", so local songwriters can follow the whole process from a song's birth to the finished recording. Frank Nes says the seminars were decisive in getting Landreth and Hill's Blues Mob to come.

A photo caption says Leven will make a record with those taking part in his songwriting seminar, and the festival's artist list is printed alongside, including The Chieftains (opening), Fairport Convention, Andy White, Martin Stephenson, Pinetop Perkins, Hubert Sumlin and the Fabulous Thunderbirds (closing six days later). The article does not say whether the single actually appeared.
zitate_kontext: Festival director Gisle Johnsen on Leven's seminar

1996-04-26-the-independent-man-trouble.kurz: Early profile from the first Cooking Vinyl decade. Paul Du Noyer visits Leven at the CORE Trust near the Marylebone Road, where a portrait of the Princess of Wales hangs in reception, and introduces the former “psyche-punk” singer as co-founder of the addiction charity and British spokesman of Robert Bly's Men's Movement.
inhalt: Early profile from the first Cooking Vinyl decade. Paul Du Noyer visits Leven at the CORE Trust near the Marylebone Road, where a portrait of the Princess of Wales hangs in reception, and introduces the former “psyche-punk” singer as co-founder of the addiction charity and British spokesman of Robert Bly's Men's Movement. Leven wears knickerbockers and is a hard-drinking Scot. The attack of 1983, the end of Doll by Doll and the story of the girlfriend who ran off with the Dalai Lama's bodyguard and left Leven Bly cassettes are recounted. Leven defends the Men's Movement as common sense without a guru, speaks of “endarkenment” as the counterpart to enlightenment, promotes his whisky “Leven's Lament” (reportedly sold at Selfridges and Harrods) and bars as places of reflection. On the CORE Trust: no compulsory abstinence as in twelve-step programmes; ten staff, 30 therapists, supporters such as John Paul Getty Jr., Genesis, the Pet Shop Boys and Eric Clapton; Mike Scott donated a library. Musically current: The Argyll Cycle Volume One, with an album “Fairy Tales for Hard Men” planned.
zitate_kontext: Leven on spirituality in the therapy scene.

1996-04-27-tromso-en-skotsk-personlighet.kurz: Helge Matland previews Leven’s concert at Tromsø’s Blå Rock Café and retells the legend of Doll by Doll, the attack and withdrawal, in the manner of press-release folklore; the same issue reviews *The Argyll Cycle – Volume One* as “smelling a little of whisky”.
inhalt: The preview “En skotsk personlighet” (“A Scottish personality”) in Tromsø (27 April 1996) announces Leven as a man “with the big personality, musically and humanly” who plays at Blå Rock Café the following evening (28 April). Some will have seen him the day before on NRK’s “Helg i solnedgang”. The Irishman Andy White opens; then Leven plays alone with his guitar.

Matland retells the familiar legend: Leven fronted Doll By Doll, who released four records between 1979 and 1982, were declared geniuses by the critics but largely overlooked by record buyers in a time when the new wave drew attention away from those who stayed rooted in rock’n’roll. The band split in 1982 and Leven started recording his first solo project. Walking home from the studio after an argument, he was attacked and nearly killed in one of London’s seedier districts, saved at the last moment by musicians who had followed him; the stranglehold cost him speech and song. Two years in hospital, heroin and alcohol, and a collapse in his love life followed. Then he got back on his feet with his own withdrawal model based on tapering down – which, according to the text, earned him Britain’s highest civil honour and is continued in a facility he runs. These details belong to the press stories of the time and are unverified.

Leven also runs his own whisky distillery with the brand “Leven’s Lament”, which the author Salman Rushdie is said to have certified with the words: “Try it, you’ll get sadder – but wiser.” On the Wednesday of that week his third solo album, *The Argyll Cycle – Volume One*, came out, after *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death* (1994) and *Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West* (1995). Together these records give the picture of a distinctive musician with beauty, poetry, atmosphere and thoughtfulness; Celtic melancholy cannot be avoided but is never allowed to steer the music alone.

On page 31 of the same issue Matland reviews *The Argyll Cycle* as “Lukter litt whisky” with a dice rating of four. The album contains four new songs and a handful of earlier B-sides and offers a small glimpse behind the curtains of the period after the murder attempt and the mute phase, up to 1990. It is a small step back from his two previous solo records but still beautiful, poetic and atmospheric, not without Celtic melancholy. Leven has long had good reviews but trouble breaking through with buyers; perhaps the time has finally come. But try *Forbidden Songs* and *The Mystery of Love* first, he advises.
zitate_kontext: Matland in the record review of *The Argyll Cycle – Volume One*

1996-05-02-haugesunds-avis-terapeutisk-j.kurz: Conversation held in Oslo by the NTB/Arbeiderbladet critic Haakon Larsen on the occasion of *The Argyll Cycle Vol.
inhalt: Conversation held in Oslo by the NTB/Arbeiderbladet critic Haakon Larsen on the occasion of *The Argyll Cycle Vol. 1*. Larsen opens by telling the familiar story – the stranglehold 13 years ago, heroin addiction, the woman who disappeared with the Dalai Lama's bodyguard, the return to Scotland. According to the article, the album's twelve songs all date from the second half of the 1980s; four of them were already on the two previous albums. The rest would have remained unreleased without pressure from fans who wanted to hear more from his convalescence; a second and final part is expected for the end of 1997.

Leven himself says that songwriting served him as therapy at the time; he sees himself more as a soul singer, “soulful” fits better than “spiritual” because his music is mostly sad – there is strength in sharing the experience of melancholy. Larsen describes him as calm and composed, praises his melodies and the “most graceful crooner voice this side of Scott Walker”, and thinks buyers of Van Morrison or Mark Knopfler might like him. The first album from 1971 and Doll by Doll as a “new wave” band from 1979 are mentioned.

The CORE Trust is described as a London foundation that works with acupuncture, poetry, music and rhythmics and is (according to the article) financed by Eric Clapton, Pete Townshend and other rock greats. At the time of the article Leven was in Bergen to lead a songwriting course for local musicians and to appear at the Ole Blues festival as the finale of a shorter Norwegian tour with the Irish troubadour Andy White.

1996-05-03-arbeiderbladet-mer-snadder.kurz: Erik Valebrokk's short review in Arbeiderbladet of *The Argyll Cycle Volume One*: twelve brilliant songs by a craftsman, wistful melodies, a songwriter who deserves his breakthrough.
inhalt: In the column “Mer snadder” (“More goodies”) of the Oslo paper Arbeiderbladet on 3 May 1996, Erik Valebrokk reviews Jackie Leven's *The Argyll Cycle Volume One* (Cooking Vinyl/Amigo). The project will comprise two records; all songs were written in Scotland, where Leven lived from 1985 to 1990 “while trying to recover from his time as a heavy heroin user”. Some of the twelve tracks had been released before.

Valebrokk calls them uniformly “brilliant songs, written by a professional”. The base throughout is an acoustic guitar, seasoned with band players, saxophone, violin, mandolin, pedal steel and keyboards; the melodies are good and wistful and suit the lyrical content. His conclusion: “yet another beautiful record from a songwriter who still deserves his breakthrough” – and he asks his readers, “Are you listening?” The review sits between pieces on Bob Mould and Ocean Colour Scene on the music page; clearly positive, but brief.

1996-05-04-bergensavisen-leven-pa-verfte.titel: [Conversation with Jackie Leven at Verftet, Bergen]
1996-05-04-bergensavisen-leven-pa-verfte.kurz: Bergensavisen meets Leven at the 1996 Ole Blues festival in Bergen: he recalls a school trip 33 years earlier, announces a seminar on the soul and laments Scotland’s battered folk soul. A concert review alongside praises his poetic songs.
inhalt: The paper introduces Leven as a Scot perhaps best known as songwriter, singer and front man of the cult band Doll by Doll, who made a comeback two years ago after 13 years in musical hibernation. The acclaimed *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* (printed as “Stranger than”) brought him back, and its successor *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West* was lauded at least as much by music experts.

The reporter meets Leven for an informal chat at the Verftet cultural centre, a place he swore 33 years ago he would never go near again. On a school trip by ship from Edinburgh the vessel had been met on its approach to Bergen by an unbearable stench coming from the factory at Verftet. Since then, the piece says, culture has displaced the sardines and the place smells of fresh coffee. A photo caption mentions a herring stench thirty years ago, so the paper itself wavers on figure and fish.

Leven has come for the Ole Blues festival, where he is giving a concert and leading a seminar. It is called “Thought of the Heart: Concern of the Soul” and is meant to show how to express feelings as well as possible in words and melodies, to speak from the heart and to grasp the meaning of the soul. In the West, Leven says according to the report, we have lost the ability to understand this, which has damaged our experience of life. The Scottish folk soul and self-esteem are also badly damaged, he says, by the behaviour of English soldiers down the ages: they robbed men of their pride and women of their self-respect, and it has been passed down through generations.

With “Leven’s Lament”, according to the article his own whisky, he wants to get across the message that the Scots must find their way back to the splendid people they once were – “and it certainly doesn’t hurt that it is also ‘damn good’”. Leven wants to make timeless music, to wake people’s sleeping souls and let them discover forgotten parts of themselves, men above all, whom he finds rather backward in some situations. “I’m gonna get those bastards!” he says, full of fight, thanks the reporter politely and strolls off to his seminar.

On the same page the same author reviews the concert at Garage, where the Irishman Andy White had warmed up the crowd (with an Abba cover and an Eurovision satire). With his eminent guitar playing and warm voice Leven hit the audience “right in the stomach”; his songs are poetry for the ear and the soul, about the West’s disrespectful treatment of life and men’s fear of their feminine side, and funny stories between the songs kept spirits high.
zitate_kontext: Leven on his mission to reach men
From the same author’s concert review on the same page

1996-05-09-fremtiden-jackie-leven-kom-ti.kurz: Double page by the Fremtiden music journalist Johnny Andreassen, who had already conducted the interview with Leven in 1995.
inhalt: Double page by the Fremtiden music journalist Johnny Andreassen, who had already conducted the interview with Leven in 1995. Leven is back in Norway; last time only Fremtiden readers got to know him better, this time he visited all the big cities and appeared on the NRK1 Friday programme from Tromsø. Andreassen repeats Leven's earlier statement that he learned to speak and sing again with the Alexander Technique and that his voice is now better and stronger than ever.

Under the subheading “En kveld i magiens tegn” he describes the concert at the venue Rebekka West, Oslo: a good-humoured Leven alone with a guitar, a stomp board on which he beats time with his foot, and his voice; plus hours full of funny stories and songs of the last two or three years. One of them, told by Leven on stage: in a London restaurant he saw the football manager Terry Venables at the other end of the room; a note he wrote and an Indian waiter who did not understand English led to an angry Venables – a punchline story that Leven evidently used as a stage number.

The profile section sums up Doll by Doll (late 1970s on London club stages, white soul, Celtic and rock elements, in 1978 the hottest thing on the scene), the attack in 1982 after a studio session (three years without a voice, depression, heroin) and The Core Trust; the latter treats addictions of all kinds (alcohol, drugs, sex, money) with acupuncture and healing, and even the Queen has visited the centre. Leven released three albums in one year and announces more; his bond with Norway has grown stronger (subheading “Bånd til Norge”).

1996-05-11-harstad-tidende-en-juvel.kurz: A hymn of praise by John Storhaug in Harstad Tidende for *The Argyll Cycle*: an “unparalleled masterpiece”, nothing but pearls, a dark, clear voice and arrangements that never turn pompous.
inhalt: Under the headline “En juvel” (“A jewel”), John Storhaug reviews Jackie Leven's *The Argyll Cycle* (Cooking Vinyl/Amigo) in Harstad Tidende on 11 May 1996. Some records captivate the listener from the first second and hold them fascinated, he writes – and this is one: “a masterpiece without equal”, with “kun perler” – only pearls. Leven's musical career started in the late seventies with Doll by Doll, who never got the attention they deserved; after the “brilliant” album *Grand Passion* in 1982 he vanished from the music scene (the text then garbles the next years: drug problems and 1984), and in 1994 he released the “brilliant” *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*. *The Argyll Cycle* surpasses “most of everything”.

Leven delivers great music: the voice is dark and bell-clear and looms in the sound without ever sounding strained; the music is dressed in lavish arrangements that never become pompous or pathetic; the melodies “grow straight into the sky”. His Scottish roots lurk in the background, give the music a unique stamp, but never dominate. It is “classic good pop”, firmly anchored in acoustic instrumentation, a record you get dependent on. The biographical details in the OCR text are partly garbled.
zitate_kontext: Storhaug's overall verdict on the record.
Storhaug on the character of the music.

1996-06-14-moss-avis-the-argyll-cycle-vo.kurz: Morten Brunslid recommends *The Argyll Cycle, Volum 1* in *Moss Avis* as music “for building up the mind and peace in the soul”, written in Argyll while Leven fought his way back to life.
inhalt: In a round-up column of album reviews by Morten Brunslid there is also a brief appreciation of *The Argyll Cycle, Volum 1* (Cooking Vinyl/Amigo). Jackie Leven delivers music for building up the mind and peace in the soul. The record was written in Argyll in Scotland between 1985 and 1990, while Leven was fighting his way back to life – for which the author says thanks. The music has graceful movements and soft curves. He announces that “Volume 2” is ready and just around the corner.
zitate_kontext: From the short review in *Moss Avis*

1996-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.titel: [Collected finds Nasjonalbiblioteket 1996: brief news items, announcements, listings]

1996-natt-og-dag-the-argyll-cycle.kurz: In the Oslo city magazine *Natt&Dag*, Anita Håland recalls Doll By Doll’s small but enthusiastic Norwegian following and finds Leven back after whisky and heroin: his romantic voice and the melancholic, slightly bombastic songs of *The Argyll Cycle* are made for Norwegians.
inhalt: Anita Håland reviews *The Argyll Cycle* (Cooking Vinyl/Amigo) in the new-releases section of the Oslo magazine *Natt&Dag*. As frontman of Doll By Doll, Leven had a small but enthusiastic following in Norway in the mid-Eighties; *Grand Passion* was the high point then. After many years of far too much whisky and heroin, he is back, with the “great passion” still on the agenda.

Not many illusions remain, but with his distinctive, romantic voice, melancholic songs and a not insignificant amount of bombastic mood, Leven is a man “we Norwegians” like. At times it borders on pompous trickery, but Leven’s sentimental Scottish songs, all written in “the town of Argyll” (properly, the region of Argyll) between 1985 and 1990, after he had rid himself of his heroin addiction, still touch something in the sentimental Northerner. In a “Best akkurat nå” list in the same issue the album gets the short verdict “Svulstig, vakkert og melankolsk” – bombastic, beautiful and melancholic.
zitate_kontext: Short verdict in the “Best akkurat nå” list

1996-schirmer-heylin-bob-dylan-a-life-in.kurz: Clinton Heylin's Dylan chronicle already carries, in 1996, Leven's anecdote of meeting Bob Dylan in a Berlin bar, reported on Leven's word as “ex-singer of British punk band Doll By Doll”.
inhalt: Clinton Heylin's day-by-day chronicle *Bob Dylan: A Life in Stolen Moments – Day by Day 1941–1995* (Schirmer Books, 1996) takes up Leven's story of an encounter with Dylan. Under an entry headed “September to Early October” it says that, according to Leven, “ex-singer of British punk band Doll By Doll”, he met Dylan in a Berlin bar. The anecdote had thus entered Dylan literature by 1996; Heylin reports it as Leven's own statement. The year of the entry is not visible in the extract.
zitate_kontext: Heylin's description of Leven in the Dylan chronicle

1997-03-26-haugesunds-avis-myknings-midd.kurz: A mildly critical review of *Fairytales for Hard Men*: four albums in three years are plenty even for Leven, but his programme of softening men and women and setting great poetry to music remains warm and appealing.
inhalt: Haugesunds Avis reviews Jackie Leven's *Fairytales for Hard Men* (MD/Cooking Vinyl) under the headline “Myknings middel” (roughly “softener”). Four albums in barely three years are, the reviewer says, on the generous side, even for Leven. He was deeply touched by the 1994 comeback *The Mystery of Love…* but has increasingly experienced the records as repetitions.

Leven's programme is to soften men and women, to peel away pride, fear and false ideals and cultivate tenderness, empathy, poetry and joie de vivre instead; “Boy Trapped In A Man” and “Fear of Women” are among the titles. His respect for great poetry has this time led him to set W. B. Yeats, James Wright and – with an exclamation mark – the Norwegian poet Rolf Jacobsen to music. Musically it is the same sonorous, warm mix of heartfelt vocals, acoustic guitar, engaging keyboards and instruments one mostly associates with Celtic folk. Leven's old group Doll By Doll play on three of the tracks.
zitate_kontext: On the poems set to music.

1997-03-record-collector-jackie-leven-in.medium: Record Collector (interview for the magazine; transcript on Leven's website)
1997-03-record-collector-jackie-leven-in.kurz: Long conversation over Guinness on the eve of Leven's debut at the Royal Festival Hall as support for Bruce Cockburn (March 1997), shortly before *Fairytales For Hardmen*.
inhalt: Long conversation over Guinness on the eve of Leven's debut at the Royal Festival Hall as support for Bruce Cockburn (March 1997), shortly before *Fairytales For Hardmen*. Leven says the pseudonym (Sir) John St. Field came about when he was stopped by the police in the street and spontaneously assumed another identity; as St. Field he opened in the early 70s for ELO, Man, Quintessence, East of Eden and Colosseum II. *Control* was recorded in 1971/72 at Mayfair Studios and released only in Spain. He mentions a duo “Saint Judas” with Colin Soutar and a BBC session from Newcastle in 1969, as well as Walkman recordings from Greece (material for later Haunted Valley CDs). On Doll by Doll: the concert with U2 at the Venue in 1979 (he says he delivered a drunken monologue to U2), no live recordings, the recording of *Grand Passion* and of the unreleased *A Last Flick Of The Golden Wrench* in parallel in both Utopia studios with Tom Newman, the rights situation of the Automatic albums at Warner and a planned box set at Cooking Vinyl. He corrects the story of the attack himself: not his throat cut, but almost strangled, and not two years but “a year and a bit” without a voice; at the time he was living behind a fish-and-chip shop in Lisson Grove. Further: the genesis of *Fairytales* from two B-sides (“Poortoun”, “Sir Patrick Spens”), a planned live album at the 12 Bar Club, *Argyll Cycle Vol. 2* (with the Hilliard Ensemble?), the Argyll songs as the conclusion of a separation after which his ex-partner gave him Bly cassettes, the path to Cooking Vinyl (Sony interest, the lawyer's advice) and traditionals (Dick Gaughan, “Jim o Windygates”).
zitate_kontext: Leven on the time without a voice.

1997-04-02-glamdalen-leven-rolf-jacobsen.titel: [Jackie Leven and Rolf Jacobsen's «Solsikke» – Fairy Tales for Hard Men]
1997-04-02-glamdalen-leven-rolf-jacobsen.kurz: Thor Martinsen introduces Leven and *Fairy Tales For Hard Men* to Glåmdalen readers: the album ends with Rolf Jacobsen's poem “Solsikke”, via Robert Bly, with news of an imminent Norwegian tour.
inhalt: Under the headline “Store stemmer gjør verden mindre” (“Big voices make the world smaller”), Thor Martinsen combines an album introduction with local pride in Glåmdalen, the Kongsvinger newspaper. Rolf Jacobsen came from Flisa and was this paper's editor during the war; he changed its name to Glåmdalen and drew the logo, and is said to be the indirect origin of its regular music columns. He is regarded as perhaps Norway's greatest post-war poet and one of the few with an international name.

This week a new CD appears from Jackie Leven, a Scottish singer and songwriter “with clear political awareness and a good literary orientation”, blessed with one of the most expressive voices on the airwaves, although, the paper says, it was nearly silenced for ever by an attempted strangling a few years ago. Jacobsen's poem “Solsikke” closes Leven's *Fairy Tales For Hard Men*, so it is the words of the fellow countryman that ring in your ears once the powerful séance is over. The link is Robert Bly, the American poet of Norwegian descent (his name comes from Bleie in Hardanger), who translated Norwegian poets, first Olav H. Hauge and then Jacobsen. “Sunflower” is a fairly literal rendering of the original, recited with a discreet rhythmic accompaniment. Martinsen is always sceptical about how poems are treated in music, but ranks this among the best results.

Alongside Jacobsen the CD includes James Wright and William Butler Yeats. Wright's “Saint Judas” has become a song, which Leven carries off with great honour. The big victory, though, is how Leven's own songs blend so appealingly with the contributions of the bigger names; he declaims them against the violent person in all of us. “What ambition, what courage, and what an expressive voice!”

Leven arrives in Norway in the next few days for a long solo tour, starting at Dixie in Oslo the next day and continuing to eight other places until 12 April. According to Jan Saghaug, who made Leven's home pages on the Internet, there is also some hope that Leven will return in the autumn with his old group Doll By Doll. Saghaug, originally from Slåstad in Sør-Odal, adds that Leven has a special relationship with Norway and regards it as his second homeland.
zitate_kontext: Thor Martinsen on *Fairy Tales For Hard Men*

1997-04-03-arbeiderbladet-leven-i-levend.kurz: Major interview on the day the tour starts in Oslo. Leven says Robert Bly stays with him when he comes to Britain; then they sit up for a week exchanging poems and life experience, and every time Bly has his “Norwegian night” – that is how he came to appreciate Rolf Jacobsen.
inhalt: Major interview on the day the tour starts in Oslo. Leven says Robert Bly stays with him when he comes to Britain; then they sit up for a week exchanging poems and life experience, and every time Bly has his “Norwegian night” – that is how he came to appreciate Rolf Jacobsen. “Sunflower” is a hard poem by any standard of manhood: we take things too personally, while an energy streams through the universe beside which one's own happiness is a trifle.

Asked about the closeness of his lyrics to depression and madness, Leven says he seeks the “freezing moment” that a good poem gives; on this record the images are clearer to him than ever before. Some, such as “Sad Polish Song”, are so strong that he cannot sing them on stage without being completely knocked over; Yeats and Jacobsen overcame themselves – that is his aim too.

Leven now wants to write more, including an autobiography, once his parents can no longer read it. To that end he stepped down as head of the centre for drug addicts: after eleven years with two full-time jobs, withdrawing is a relief, the staff are carrying on the ideas and concept, and *The Big Issue* wants to set up a similar facility in Glasgow. Announced are: a CD reissue of the Doll by Doll catalogue with a reunion tour, due to begin in August in Oslo and Bergen, a live record and a “sister album” to *Fairy Tales* entitled “Injured Women” – poems by women about women wounded in the soul, by his own account “hopefully my most miserable record”.

Steinkjer acknowledges the loyal Norwegian following since Doll by Doll and mentions the whisky Leven's Lament. On the album's second Norwegian reference, the thanks to the bar of the Grand Hotel in Tromsø, Leven says that on his last visit he spent a lot of time there working through a difficult question of life; the bar is a peaceful reminder of a world he is afraid of. He openly admits that he sometimes wishes he were not alive.

1997-04-04-arbeiderbladet-ikke-lett-a-va.kurz: A positive review of *Fairy Tales For Hard Men* in Arbeiderbladet: Leven has plenty to say after the lost years of addiction and wrestles with the male role in his songs; the Celtic grounding and poetic sense are praised.
inhalt: The short review, headed “Ikke lett å være mann” (“Not easy being a man”), appeared on 4 April 1997 in the Oslo paper Arbeiderbladet. With *Fairy Tales For Hard Men* the Scot shows “once again” that he has a great deal to say after all the lost years that drugs took. Titles such as “Boy Trapped In A Man”, “Extremely Violent Man”, “Fear Of Women” and “Sexual Danger”, the reviewer notes, make clear that he has not exactly found himself and is much preoccupied with working out the male role.

Musically the album is, as usual, strongly Celtic, with the expressive melodies the theme calls for. Some songs are reinforced by quotations from pop history; “Yesterday” and “Unchained Melody” are woven in without seeming out of place in Leven’s own universe. Three of the songs were recorded with his old group Doll by Doll and do not stand out noticeably. Throughout the record lies a self-assured, folksy playing that makes Leven’s big thoughts all the more moving.

The reviewer praises most the poetic sense: besides his own emotional lyrics, in which nature and people merge, Leven set William Butler Yeats’s “Mad As The Mist And Snow” to music, and at the very end he declaims “Sunflower” – Rolf Jacobsen’s “Solsikke” in Robert Bly’s English translation. That is a worthy end to an album which underlines that the heaviest thoughts can be very uplifting in difficult times.
zitate_kontext: Closing verdict, on the final track “Solsikke”

1997-04-04-nordlys-fairy-tales-for-hard-.kurz: Stig Nilssen gives *Fairy Tales for Hard Men* 5 out of 6 in Nordlys: a “knowing man” tells, in small novellas, of things men rarely discuss, without finger-wagging or sentimentality; demanding, with “Old West African Song” as the high point.
inhalt: The review in the Tromsø daily (4 April 1997, rating 5) also announces the concert at Blå Rock Café the following Sunday. Nilssen begins by saying that the singer-songwriter Jackie Leven has “been through a lot, a very great deal”, but unlike most of us the Scot seems to have learned from his mistakes. On *Fairy Tales for Hard Men* it is a “knowing man” who delivers his thoughts. Song titles such as “Boy Trapped in a Man”, “Extremely Violent Man” and “Fear of Women” give a good idea of what is on Leven's mind: he offers “small novellas, or fairy tales if you like” that touch on subjects few men dare to talk about, still less write about and then release on record. He does it with the greatest matter-of-factness and without raising a finger or becoming mawkishly sentimental, although the record sounds rather melancholy. As an example the reviewer quotes lines from “Boy Trapped in a Man” about the sunlight outside, pretending nothing is wrong, and heading for the bar.

The album is not, however, “fully consumed” after one spin in the CD player. It is demanding, not just because the content is so intense but because the man is a Scot and a couple of songs have English strongly marked by it, and because some tracks carry (crushing) sound samples that fall into place only gradually. Not all the lyrics come from his own head. The high point “at the time of writing” (it has varied from play to play) is “Old West African Song”, a text of unknown origin set to music by Leven, who has managed “in an exquisite way” to combine African rhythms with Scottish tones. There is also a poem by the Norwegian poet Rolf Jacobsen, clad only in percussion – “naked and beautiful”. The conclusion: the man will stand with guitar and voice at Blå Rock in Tromsø on Sunday evening. “The record promises a great night.”
zitate_kontext: Closing sentence, looking ahead to the Blå Rock concert

1997-04-08-nordlys-ikke-bare-for-harde-m.kurz: Ulf Sverresvold describes Leven’s late-night show at Tromsø’s Blå Rock Café as “fairytales for hard men”: guitar, stamping foot, self-irony and stories about whisky, pizza and sex; Leven spoke with the audience, not just to it.
inhalt: The concert review “Ikke bare for harde menn” (“Not just for hard men”) in Nordlys (8 April 1997) covers the late-night concert at Blå Rock Café in Tromsø on 6 April 1997, between eleven and two, billed as *Fairytales for Hard Men*. Fairytales for hard men do not really rhyme, the critic says – yet that is exactly what Leven delivered. The café, with guitars of famous musicians under the roof beams, many odd corners and nooks and pictures of big stars everywhere, was intimate: a man with a guitar sits on a stool in the corner by the jukebox and tells fairytales for grown-ups while the guitar plays and his foot stamps the beat. The sound system worked so well that you did not even need to see him.

The audience got the points even though he speaks English with a Scottish accent. Leven told jokes to steady guitar accompaniment and played interludes that revealed he can do flamenco too. He could be delicate and lyrical, then “pure dynamite”; the floor served as percussion while his fingers conjured guitar music. He told what hard men do not do – talk to their children – and sang of what life offers and of experiences that can harden people: longing, hopelessness, drink or drugs. With self-irony he told, for instance, of the girlfriend who left him for the Dalai Lama’s bodyguard.

As the night went on, the stories became, as befits a late show, “more of the kind that suits adults under the duvet”: he spoke of the likeness between whisky, pizza and sex – good, and also when it is bad. He captivated and “enchanted” the audience of about a hundred with fairytales and stories, mostly reflections on his own experience. Like few others, the critic writes, Leven could speak with the audience, not just to it: about longings and pains that have been themes of song and popular music for hundreds of years, but Leven did it “so directly, so vividly, so damn convincingly”.
zitate_kontext: Ulf Sverresvold on the opening of the concert

1997-04-09-bergensavisen-eventyr-for-har.kurz: Espen Børhaug praises *Fairy Tales for Hard Men* in Bergensavisen as a poetic, beautiful record with Celtic roots about ‘hard men’, but warns of Leven’s high output.
inhalt: The review in Bergensavisen of 9 April 1997 starts from the cover: Peter Howson’s painting ‘The Bodybuilder’ shows a muscleman whose muscles speak of a hard man. He wants respect from men and love from one special woman; she never comes, because the woman in him is gone, and men meet him with disgust rather than respect. That, Børhaug writes, is the starting point of Jackie Leven’s latest release. Leven is preoccupied with hard men – “just boys trapped in men’s lives, pretending to be men”, as he explains.

As before he is inspired by the poet and philosopher Robert Bly, who in 1990 published his manifesto on masculinity, *Iron John*. The songs carry titles such as ‘Boy Trapped in a Man’, ‘Extremely Violent Man’ and ‘Sexual Danger’; yet, the reviewer says, this is “first and foremost a poetic, beautiful record”. The music has deep Celtic roots, the melodies are strong, and ‘Poortoun’ is downright stunning. On some tracks his old band Doll by Doll play with him; other songs lie beyond rock’s fortified guitar-bass-drums constellation.

The reviewer’s caution: Leven maintains a “surprisingly high productivity”, and the danger of repeating himself is certainly present. Still, anyone could do with a new – “or should we say ancient” – perspective on the man, a decade after Norway’s own government commission on the male role collapsed without leaving visible traces. A picture caption notes that, according to the reviewer, the melodies of the new record are at times stunningly beautiful.
zitate_kontext: Leven on the ‘hard men’ of his songs (quoted in English in the article)

1997-04-09-nordlandsposten-leven-for-bod.titel: [Interview before the Bodø concert: «Dere kan vente en veldig loud Scotsman»]
1997-04-09-nordlandsposten-leven-for-bod.kurz: Preliminary interview ahead of the first Bodø concert (Den Siste Glæde, Sunday 13.04.1997) on the music page, alongside a short review of *Fairytales for Hard Men* (“folksanger i stor-format”: raw, hard and yet warm and humorous; you need strong nerves to take the whole album in one go).
inhalt: Preliminary interview ahead of the first Bodø concert (Den Siste Glæde, Sunday 13.04.1997) on the music page, alongside a short review of *Fairytales for Hard Men* (“folksanger i stor-format”: raw, hard and yet warm and humorous; you need strong nerves to take the whole album in one go).

Leven announces that the audience can expect a very “loud” Scotsman with a loud guitar and sad rock songs, plus funny stories. The biggest problem when playing solo, he says, is the audience's beer consumption; but his guitar makes enough noise, and he even plays drum solos on it. Doll by Doll played on three tracks of the new album; in the autumn they intended to reissue the old albums and do a small Norwegian tour. Norway, he says, is the country he values most after Scotland. He has already been to Tromsø and thanks the bar in the Grand Hotel on the sleeve; during a stopover in Bodø the previous year he had decided to ask his Norwegian tour manager for a gig there.

He has only good things to say about Mike Scott, with whom he worked on his first solo album. He got to know Rolf Jacobsen through Robert Bly, who translated “Solsikke” for him; with Bly he occasionally holds poetry evenings at which a lot of Jacobsen is read. He hears for the first time of Henning Gravrok from Bodø, who has made a whole album of Jacobsen texts, and would like to meet him. At the end he asks about Bodø; asked about salmon, he says wild salmon is good anywhere, but he rejects farmed salmon – and reacts drastically when he hears that Ian Anderson (Jethro Tull) runs a salmon farm.

1997-04-11-lofotposten-hvit-soul.kurz: Lofotposten previews Leven's concert at Præstengbrygga in Kabelvåg: the writer recalls seeing Doll by Doll in a dreary venue in east London in 1977, and a friend who saw the tour in Tromsø praises the show.
inhalt: Under the headline "Hvit soul" ("White soul"), Lofotposten (11 April 1997) announces Jackie Leven's concert on Saturday at Præstengbrygga in Kabelvåg. He is "a musician's musician, Scotland's finest supplier of white soul, a bandless edition of Van Morrison". The writer (the byline is legible only as "Refs") says he had the pleasure of seeing Leven with Doll by Doll in a dreary venue far out in east London in the summer of 1977, an experience that still stays with him.

Then the outline: after four "genius" records with Doll by Doll between 1979 and 1982, Leven was working on a solo record when he was nearly killed by a street gang in 1983. He lost his voice and entered a period of depression and drug abuse, though also one in which he wrote a lot of poetry. In 1985, the article says, he opened a drug-rehabilitation centre, and later, ironically, he appeared as producer of his own whisky, "Levens Lament". After 13 years of musical hibernation he returned as an artist in 1994 and has several critically acclaimed albums behind him. The latest CD is about to enter the Norwegian charts, and he is on a solo tour of Norway.

Tor-Harald Bergsrud, a music enthusiast from Kabelvåg now living in Tromsø, heard Leven the previous weekend and is full of praise: Leven, whom he has seen before, was in top form and delivered a really good concert for a full house at the "Blå Rock Café". Between the songs he tells crazy stories, and a brilliant guitarist and an artist with great charisma is coming to Kabelvåg.

1997-04-12-bergensavisen-historiefortell.kurz: Espen Børhaug praises Leven’s Garage concert in Bergen: poetic ballads, coarse stories, a guitarist who “howls at the moon”, and a conspicuously quiet audience.
inhalt: Bergens Avisen reports on Leven’s solo concert on Thursday evening (10 April 1997) at the well-attended Garage. The “sympathetic Scot” was in pearly good humour: he sits not on the chair but on a monitor beside it, his fingers fly across the strings and the audience gapes. Børhaug recalls the Doll by Doll era (he wrongly places it in the eighties; the band was mainly active around 1979–83) and the heroin addiction that followed and nearly killed him. Heroin, Leven says today, is “like an old love”: you think about it now and then, but you cannot go back. Since the 1994 solo debut *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*, three more CDs have appeared, the freshest being *Fairytales for Hard Men*, though Leven devoted himself just as much to the earlier releases in concert.

The songs are minor-key and poetic, standing in sharp contrast to the coarse, unpolished, at times hysterically funny stories between them, but there are red threads: boys who grow up into hard men, beautiful mood pictures from the Scottish Highlands, love without optimal conditions for growth. “Love is all it takes to start a relationship,” Leven says, quoting his good friend Robert Bly, “but only the warrior manages to stay in it.”

Børhaug admires the guitar technique: Leven caresses the strings, hammers and slaps the body, stamps the beat, whistles, hums and “howls at the moon”. He plays “Stranger On The Square” and gets lost in “Young Male Suicide Blessed By Invisible Woman”; he often forgets the words, he says, “but don’t mind, I don’t get embarrassed”. One has to like Leven, and contact with the audience is immediate. The audience is “much quieter” than last time, he remarks – almost embarrassingly reserved at the feet of the “master”. In late summer he plans to return with Doll by Doll and promises to hurry up the sister album to *Fairytales for Hard Men*, to be called “Injured Women: The Jackie Leven Report”.
zitate_kontext: Leven on his former heroin addiction.
Leven on stage, quoting Robert Bly.
Espen Børhaug on Leven’s guitar playing.

1997-04-14-lofotposten-hvit-manns-soul.kurz: Ole-P. Refsahl celebrates Leven’s concert at Kabelvåg in Lofotposten, before about 120 guests: a story about building fences in the rain, self-mocking anecdotes, deadly serious songs – “white soul” that goes straight to the spine.
inhalt: Refsahl writes about the concert at Præstengbrygga in Kabelvåg on Saturday evening (12 April 1997). We have seen many singers with guitars, he says; Leven belongs to the few who deliver a concert that bites into the “heart bark”. The Scot came on stage around 11 pm, tuned his guitar and told a story about what it was like to be young, homesick and forced to build fences in the rain on a farm in northern England. Then he sang “Farm Boy”, about exactly that, “and the evening was Leven’s”.

Of about 120 present, Refsahl guesses only some 20 had any idea of the Scot beforehand; the rest took a chance on meeting the unknown and got songs of a quality rarely heard in licensed venues. Leven has a deep, powerful voice that interprets raw rock songs and intense ballads with the same commitment. As a Doll by Doll musician he had, by his own tales, lived the life of a “bastard”; the strongly self-ironic and partly bizarre stories between songs showed that he had been through some hard rounds with himself. If the stories were insane, the songs were marked by deep seriousness: strong love stories combined with commitment to those who have not lived in the sun, songs about women’s fates and coexistence like “Peace Comes Dropping Slow”. The self-irony peeled away as soon as the first chords rang out on the “troll-tuned” guitar, which also served as a rhythm instrument together with his shoe soles: “simple and straightforward, just how Leven wants it”.

“I’m not depressing you?” he asked some way into the show, and got a clear no. Refsahl’s punchline: if the white man can sing soul, Leven is among the foremost; if the white man cannot, he is still a bloody great artist. After two hours without a break the audience could hardly bear to let him go; Leven found many similarities with his native Scotland and said: “and I hope I’ll soon be back”.
zitate_kontext: Refsahl on the switch from anecdote to song

1997-04-14-troms-folkeblad-ekte-vare-fra.kurz: Ronny Trælvik describes in Troms Folkeblad Leven's two-hour solo show at Sumaloftet in Finnsnes as a format that looked “stillborn” on paper but worked through honesty and humility; before just over a hundred listeners Leven proved “a pleasant acquaintance”.
inhalt: The concert review (“Ekte vare fra skotske Leven”, “The real thing from Scottish Leven”) opens with the coarse joke with which Leven began the Friday evening (11 April 1997) at Sumaloftet in Finnsnes: had they heard about the Scotsman who appeared in a porn film and ran the film backwards so he could see the whore give him his money back? He then delivered a two-hour performance, just him and the six-string. The critic calls the starting point a “rather stillborn” idea: it was bound to be monotonous, boring, tame.

But that is not how it went. Those willing to listen got a good example that evening of how an “honest and humble attitude” can lift an artist. Leven has experienced most things and more; he sings unvarnished about everyday events “in all their charm and brutality” and tells “juicy stories”, but never in a way that abandons the believable picture on which his music is founded. Trælvik adds a criticism: the construction and melodic lines of the songs are, to put it mildly, simple, and despite “exquisite subtleties” on the guitar Leven could do little to vary the sound. As an “inexhaustible source” of everything a musician should carry with him, he ought to have given even more of himself and spiced up the menu a notch. It picked up towards the end, and he was never close to falling through.

With telling use of his voice and a “genuine” Scottish attitude he held a good hundred followers – at least those who wanted to listen – “in the palm of his hand”. The critic would have given a lot to hear an accordion, fiddle, flute or harmonica in the arrangements, yet Jackie Leven was “undoubtedly a pleasant acquaintance”. The photo caption carries the same line.

1997-04-15-nordlands-framtid-en-poetisk-.kurz: Jo Petter Furuhovde celebrates Leven's first concert in Bodø: stories about beer, whisky and sex, but above all music. The critics' favourite became the audience's favourite too.
inhalt: Under the headline “En poetisk grisegutt” (“A poetic piggy-lad”), Jo Petter Furuhovde reports in Nordlands Framtid on Jackie Leven's first concert in Bodø, at Den Siste Glæde on Sunday 13 April 1997, before about 150 people and lasting just under two hours. When Leven plays or tells stories the audience sits still and listens; he is an authority whether singing or telling stories. He introduces him as a critics' favourite for years, a Scot who sings in dark, bleak, poetic moods with his head full of stories, and who even makes his own whisky (“Leven's Lament”). Two weeks earlier his fourth solo album, *Fairytales for Hard Men*, had come out.

Anyone at the “Glæden” who did not know Leven beforehand surely does now: his arrival was like saying thank you for last time to an old pal, and his leaving nearly two hours later like saying farewell to a close friend. He began with “Farm Boy” from the debut *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* and followed it with the prison story “Shadow in My Eye” from the same record, and with that had set the standard.

Between songs he took his time to tell stories, often about beer, whisky and sex. That sounds crude, and some may have thought Leven was, but he tells them so casually and decadently that he avoids seeming a simple old pig; it is simply overwhelmingly funny. One of his remarks, “far from the strongest”, was delivered with an ambiguous glint: sex is like pizza, even when it's bad it's good. But the stories were only part of the concert; the music mattered most. With the guitar serving as both guitar and drum, his left foot as a manual rhythm box and his voice like a soulful highland horn, he filled the room with Scottish Highland soul. So on Sunday Leven became not just the critics' favourite but the audience's too.
zitate_kontext: Leven on stage in Bodø (as reported by Furuhovde)

1997-04-15-nordlandsposten-leven-pa-glae.kurz: Torgeir Eikeland praises Leven’s solo concert at Bodø’s Den Siste Glæde: atmospheric, witty and self-mocking, with many songs from *Fairytales for Hardmen* and coarse stage patter.
inhalt: Torgeir Eikeland reports in Nordlandsposten of 15 April 1997 on the Sunday-evening concert of 13 April at Den Siste Glæde in Bodø, before a good 150 people. The Scottish troubadour told wild stories and sang sad and beautiful songs and ought to have felt at home in Bodø, the paper says, having grown up in the Kingdom of Fife, “Scotland’s most windswept landscape”. Alone with his acoustic guitar he gave a thoughtful, atmospheric concert. Some lyrics deal with life’s harder questions, such as what happens when the one you love does not love you back.

The punchlines came from the man himself: “Then you tend to think: maybe it helps if I spray that Calvin Klein stuff under my arms,” said Leven, who “only occasionally shut up” between songs. The audience laughed a lot at the subtlety and self-irony. Most songs came from the new album *Fairytales for Hardmen*; not all lyrics were equally deep, for example the one he wrote in honour of his better half’s behind. Musically he moves within the Dylan tradition of singer-songwriters but has made his own form: sitar-like unpredictabilities on the guitar, drum solos on the guitar body, a voice stretched into the “primitively guttural” without hurting the ears. He also whistles a theme that sounds like something from Sergio Leone’s Clint Eastwood westerns – a pity, the reviewer says, that he used it in at least three songs.

Midway came “one of the loveliest ballads the Glæden has heard”; otherwise the Scot was a little long-winded and uninspired in between, but not enough to spoil a good concert. The jokes between songs contributed as much as the music to a successful evening. Leven threatened to go back to the hotel to watch the porn channel if he was ruining the evening, threatened to open ‘Jackie Leven’s Scottish Bastard Pub’ in Bodø, and told how he once emptied a hotel minibar in Hamburg and filled the whisky bottles with piss to avoid paying. At the end he threatened to return next year to give them more Leven: “Gladly.”
zitate_kontext: Leven on stage, on unrequited love

1997-05-03-firda-eventyr-fra-jackie-leve.kurz: Firda is lukewarm but kindly about *Fairytales for Hardmen*: consistently pretty, melodic folk-rock sounds to stories about hard role models, but nothing that stands out from the average; guitar and voice carry you “quite okay” through the 16 tracks.
inhalt: The record review in Nynorsk (initials “AH”, Firda, 3 May 1997) sits in a column of new releases that also takes in a Norwegian hard-rock debut. The reviewer begins with a reflection: in pre-Christian times fairy tales had a larger place in people's lives; how you reacted to and felt about the events in them could often be a sign of difficulties and dilemmas that met you later. On *Fairytales for Hardmen* Leven delivers some of those stories, about how men and women in historical times lived up to expectations of how tough they should be. Both sexes had the hard-boiled as role models; that is Jackie's frame, and he links it with “pretty and melancholy folk-rock tones”.

The verdict is cool but friendly: consistently beautiful and melodic “but nothing that stands out from the ordinary”. Jackie Leven's guitar and voice carry you through all 16 songs in fairy-tale land, “in a quite okay way”. No mark is given. The paper had announced the concert in Førde (Studentkroa/Kulturkafeen) on 8 April 1997.

1997-06-q-bawdy-jackie-leven-shocks-scan.kurz: Report on Leven's solo concert at the basement club Garage in Bergen on 10.04.1997, combined with quotations from conversation.
inhalt: Report on Leven's solo concert at the basement club Garage in Bergen on 10.04.1997, combined with quotations from conversation. Aizlewood describes the coarse stage stories with which Leven introduces songs such as “In The Greenwood”, and notes a changed Leven: slimmer, better dressed, country life in Hampshire with Deborah Greenwood, reduced commitments at the CORE Trust. Leven calls his career “spectacularly unsuccessful” and openly admits two legends to be a “scam”: the whisky “Leven's Lament” was only a small bottling of a respected whisky, and Bob Dylan's co-authorship of “As We Sailed Into Skibbereen” after a shared train journey was invented. Bergen, where Leven allegedly played his first professional gigs in 1966, had taken *Fairytales For Hardmen* to number 40 in the Norwegian charts. Two hours solo, no encores, with requests from the audience; “Marble City Bar” is about a suicide attempt in Ireland, “Desolation Blues” is dedicated to the late Q writer John Bauldie. Leven announces a return with the reunited Doll by Doll in the same year and the album *Injured Women: The Leven Report*, and talks about lost self-esteem since his heroin addiction. Tone: amused and admiring.

1997-08-28-bergensavisen-lager-plate-i-b.kurz: Bergensavisen reports on 28 August 1997 that Doll by Doll would record their concert at Garage the following evening, their first together in almost 15 years, for a live CD; all four albums and a so-far unreleased fifth were to appear on CD.
inhalt: The item (“Lager plate i Bergen”, “Making a record in Bergen”) announces that the English band Doll by Doll will record their concert at Garage the next evening (29 August 1997) for release as a live CD. It describes Doll by Doll as an innovative band in the years 1979–82 which broke up in the early Eighties after four strong LPs. Since then the group's status has reached “legendary heights”, largely because their records have been all but impossible to find.

Now it is reported that all four albums are to appear on CD, plus the fifth record the group made but never released. The live CD would thus be number six. The producer of the recordings is “Pytten” (the Bergen producer Gunnar Andersen, named in the article only by that name). Doll by Doll consist of Jackie Leven, Joe Shaw, David McIntosh (“Mclntern” in the paper) and Kevin Foster; the Garage show is their first together in almost fifteen years. The item is signed Bård Ose and accompanied by a photograph of the band. Whether the recording was later released is not stated.
zitate_kontext: Bård Ose on the reunion concert

1997-08-31-bergensavisen-dukker-i-fint-d.kurz: Lars Olve Hesjedal sees Doll by Doll at Bergen’s club Garage in their first concert in 15 years: intimate, at times reverent, at times driving. The band is in hardly any history book, he writes, but more than good enough for its fans.
inhalt: This concert review in Bergensavisen (31 August 1997) reports on the British band’s reunion gig in the basement club Garage. It was the group’s first concert in fifteen years; Leven joked, “We are four living dolls.” Barely a step to the left or right was needed before the cheering hit the ceiling, and he hardly had to take more than a few sips from his plastic beer cup. That, the critic says, is part of the charm of playing to devoted fans: you can allow yourself a few gestures.

Yet nobody could complain about quality or intimacy. In the quiet songs the group at times created an almost reverent atmosphere, and when it was time to swing, it swung. Leven and guitarist “Joe” Shaw (presumably Jo Shaw) entered some fruitful guitar dialogues, Kevin Foster delivered both steady and more brilliant bass lines, and drummer David McIntosh (“Mdntern” in the paper) had plenty of juice in sticks and bass-drum pedal.

By way of context the critic notes that Doll by Doll are absent from most books on rock history and never became big commercially in the early 1980s. Among their own, however, they are “more than good enough”, which is perhaps why the experience of punch and drive felt especially strong at Garage. The piece is signed Lars Olve Hesjedal and describes the concert of Friday 29 August 1997.
zitate_kontext: Opening of the review: Leven jokes on stage

1997-10-25-drammens-tidende-fram-fra-ska.kurz: A short reissue note on Leven’s *Control*: a “funny curiosity” for fans from his youth, with the anecdote of his first trip abroad, to Bergen.
inhalt: The record page of Drammens Tidende reviews the CD *Control* in a few sentences under the heading “Fram fra skapet” (“out of the closet”). It is a “funny curiosity” for the many who have since become hooked on Jackie Leven’s and Doll By Doll’s wonderful world of Celtic soul and British rock. The album was recorded “back in 1966” by a young Scot on the run from the law. In the booklet Leven writes that he was completely hooked on LSD at the time, and the record was released only briefly in Spain in 1973.

You can hear it is the same voice with the same soulful build-up of melody. It is no great experience like Leven’s later albums, but absolutely fun to hear for fans. The text adds that in 1969 Leven jumped aboard a ship to Bergen – his first trip abroad – and that his relationship with Norway today is “very special”. The 1966 dating is the article’s own.
zitate_kontext: Opening of the short review of *Control*.
Closing sentence on Leven’s first trip abroad.

1997-12-wavelength-jackie-leven-ulrich-b.kurz: Interview by the German Van Morrison fan Ulrich Begemeier for the British Van Morrison newsletter, conducted on 22.09.1997 at the Sinkkasten in Frankfurt am Main (Morrison once played there as “Storyville” with the Monarchs).
inhalt: Interview by the German Van Morrison fan Ulrich Begemeier for the British Van Morrison newsletter, conducted on 22.09.1997 at the Sinkkasten in Frankfurt am Main (Morrison once played there as “Storyville” with the Monarchs). Leven talks about the reissue of *Control* (LSD imagery), the pseudonym John St. Field (trouble with the police in a northern English town), years in Madrid, Berlin, South America and Dorset, Doll by Doll falling between two stools (like The Yachts, The Original Mirrors, The Only Ones), unreleased Virgin recordings, the attack, heroin and the CORE Trust, which he said he had handed over to his friend Jason Wright but remains a “father-figure”. He reports on the Doll by Doll concert in Brussels with Jo Shaw and David McIntosh (Shaw is currently building a studio for George Martin), on a song not used for the film *Sid & Nancy*, and on having received the German critics' annual prize in Bonn the day before (after a journey from Bautzen via Hannover, Hamburg and Düsseldorf), where he sang “The Bonnie Earl O' Moray” unaccompanied. A large part concerns Van Morrison: “Slim Slow Slider” on *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow*, “Hungry For Your Love”, Hillman's term “pathos”, *Veedon Fleece* as favourite album, being neighbours in Notting Hill, the 1995 Q Awards. Plans: Doll by Doll CDs, Charisma/Virgin material, *Argyll Cycle Vol. II*, *Injured Women*, an album setting Russian poetry to music (Mandelstam, Akhmatova). At the end he explains the Artaud photo on the covers.
zitate_kontext: Leven on Van Morrison's song imagery.

1997-clearspot-jackie-leven-tower-arts-c.kurz: Mike Plumbley hails Leven as a Celtic bard and raconteur at a solo gig in Winchester: percussive guitar playing, a Clapton anecdote, requests read off a CD booklet, and no encore ritual.
inhalt: Mike Plumbley describes a solo concert by Jackie Leven in the small, packed Tower Theatre of the Tower Arts Centre in Winchester, around the time of *Fairy Tales for Hardmen* (1997). Leven asks the audience what time it is – according to his contract he finishes at ten and can go – yet plays on past half past ten. Plumbley calls him a master raconteur, a latter-day Celtic bard who brings philosophy to the bar room, and a songman whose tradition of spoken word and song stretches back to Homer. The atmosphere, he says, is that of friends gathered in a cosy snug.

He places the four solo albums then out: *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* takes up where Van Morrison left off, followed by *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West*, *The Argyll Cycle Part 1* and now *Fairy Tales for Hardmen* – enough philosophy to fill a thesis, enough song to sink a boat. On stage Leven's voice has the grip of a boat hook; as a one-man band he beats time with heel and toe, whistles like a Uillean pipe and uses every inch of the guitar, hitting the soundboard and strings and hammering melodies like a cross between a Mississippi bluesman and a flamenco guitarist. Leven explains that his guitar is a Gallagher once owned by Doc Watson.

The set begins with “Farm Boy” and ends with “Gylen Gylen”, written on the Isle of Kerrera, where Macbeth is said to be buried. In between come thundering anthems such as “Call Mother A Lonely Field” and “Marble City Bar” and sparse, gentle numbers like “Working Alone” and “Men In Prison”. Plumbley's favourite story involves Eric Clapton, who turned up in the studio as Leven was about to record “Call Mother A Lonely Field”, listened, and afterwards only wanted to know what Leven thought of his coat. Plumbley considers the song one of the finest he has heard about the Irish spirit – by a Scotsman.

Leven refuses the encore ritual, stays where he is and takes requests after the “official show”. “As We Sailed Into Skibbereen” is too difficult; he cannot remember “Snow in Central Park”, so a fan in the front row hands up the sleeve of *The Mystery of Love…* and Leven reads the words from it. For “Main Travelled Roads” a listener again offers the lyrics: the front row is lined with Doll by Doll fans holding album covers. After two rusty readings “Gylen Gylen” closes the night; Leven picks up his half-eaten prawn mayonnaise sandwich, courtesy of the venue, and walks out. The report ends with the full 19-song set list and a rundown of his Cooking Vinyl releases, including a four-track CD with a version of “Say A Little Prayer”.

Leven recounting Eric Clapton's reaction after listening to “Call Mother A Lonely Field”.
Closing lines of “Gylen Gylen”, as quoted by Plumbley.

1997-cooking-vinyl-the-fairytale-so-far.kurz: Cooking Vinyl’s 1997 press biography for *Fairytales For Hardmen* traces Leven’s path from Fife through Doll by Doll, the London street attack and his heroin years to the founding of the CORE Trust and a fresh start with Cooking Vinyl.
inhalt: This is an unsigned label biography from the year of *Fairytales For Hardmen*, and it reads as a self-contained heroic narrative. It opens in Fife, where Jackie Leven was born in 1950 and spent his childhood and teens among dying coalfields and fading woollen mills; his song imagery, it says, is still shaped by this early witnessing of a culture in crisis. His mother loved jazz and black American blues such as Lightnin’ Hopkins, and to that were added Protestant hymn-singing at school and the “dark salty common songs of Fife”, which the biography names as the melodic root of his songwriting.

The 1960s layer on further influences: a lasting love of Russian and American poetry, and the pull of West Coast and acid rock. Both, the text says, surface in the acid-hazed album *Control*, made under the pseudonym John St. Field and dated here “1971 (?)” – the question mark is the text’s own. Through the early and mid-1970s he played music mainly to observe life in different parts of the world, including half-year stays in Madrid under Franco and in a still-divided Berlin.

In 1976 Leven moves into an ancient farmhouse in deepest Dorset with guitarist Jo Shaw and percussionist David McIntosh, and Doll by Doll is born, “the truly great rock band” in the biography’s words. Between 1978 and 1982 they make five albums – *Remember*, *Gypsy Blood*, *Doll By Doll*, *Grand Passion* and *A Last Flick Of The Golden Wrench*, the last never released. The first two appeared on Automatic Records, the next three on Magnet. The band disbanded in 1982, tired of the struggle of making consistently beautiful music that seemed fatally out of sync with the taste of the times.

The darkest chapter follows. In 1983 Leven resumes recording as a solo artist and releases two singles on Charisma/Virgin, “Love Is Shining Down On Me” and “Uptown”. The same year, according to this account, he is almost strangled to death in an unprovoked street attack in north London. Unable to speak or sing for a considerable time and in exceptional psychological and physical pain, he finds solace in heroin, which the text calls “the classic drug of despair”.

Recovery leads to the founding of the CORE Trust in 1985, a holistic approach to addiction treatment based on Leven’s own experience, using acupuncture, reflexology and counselling. CORE, the biography says, has since treated thousands of people and has had active and financial support from Diana, Princess of Wales, Mike Scott, Genesis, Eric Clapton, Westminster City Council and John Paul Getty Jr., among others; it works from premises in Marylebone. Leven remained chairman of the trustees but scaled down his duties and in 1994 returned to his solo career with Cooking Vinyl: *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death* (1994), *Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West* (1995) and *The Argyll Cycle Vol. 1* (1996).

The text closes with the current album, *Fairytales For Hardmen*, which the Norwegian paper Bergens Tidende is quoted as calling “naked, sad, beautiful – masterpiece”. A sister album, *Injured Women – The Leven Report*, is announced; it never appeared under that title. A final note calls Leven a senior spokesman on the UK men’s movement, a role that came to him through his friendship and artistic collaboration with the American poet Robert Bly. The dates given (break-up in 1982, attack in 1983) differ from later label texts.

The label on the end of Doll by Doll
The label on the period after the attack

1997-expose-john-st-field-control.kurz: Mike Ohman reviews the CD reissue of John St. Field’s *Control* for the progressive-rock magazine Exposé: pleasant electric British folk, but of little interest to prog readers beyond two tracks.
inhalt: Mike Ohman reviews the Cooking Vinyl CD of *Control* (COOK CD 131) for Exposé, a magazine covering music “from the fringes”. He takes it to be a 1975 release put out only in Spain on the Movieplay label, and doubts it is of general interest to the magazine’s readers. The review does not say that St. Field is Jackie Leven.

The basic sound is electrified British-style folk – “not about to give Fairport Convention a run for their money, but nice” – with touches of blues, light rock and, on one track, space-rock; flute, sax, Farfisa and Moog supplement the guitars. Vocally St. Field oddly resembles Joe Jackson. Ohman finds only the ten-minute “The Problem” (most like Jethro Tull) and the short “Dune Voices”, a sound collage of filtered white noise and backwards voices, really interesting – probably the best track. Without the eminent label, he thinks, the album would have received little notice.

Ohman on John St. Field’s voice.
Ohman on the second track he singles out.

1997-musikexpress-night-lilies.kurz: Musikexpress celebrates Leven's comeback as “one of the unexpected triumphs of the decade”: on his fourth solo album, *Night Lilies*, he takes a bigger step towards pop.
inhalt: The short album review in Musikexpress (signed “tw”) opens with a grand gesture: Jackie Leven's comeback is one of the unexpected triumphs of the decade. After the break-up of the new wave band Doll By Doll in 1983, its former leader seemed entangled only in a “thicket of depression and drug addiction”. Only an intensive engagement with Scottish mythology, poetry and folk gave him new strength and optimism.

The album *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death* was audibly influenced by these cultural studies and, thanks to warm compositions and a recitative delivery, got Leven talked about again. Now the healing process seems complete and the way open for new ideas. On his fourth solo album Leven takes a bigger step towards pop music: he adapts fifties rock 'n' roll, has female backing voices breathe doo-wop vocals, quotes country and blues, and always lays a cleanly formulated melody over the top. The performer's sensitivity and maturity prevent an abrupt break of style and strengthen Leven's “already considerable position as an expressive, independent songwriter at the edge of the mainstream”.
