1997-sanctuary-hinton-celtic-crossroads.kurz: In Brian Hinton’s *Celtic Crossroads: The Art of Van Morrison* the author compares a Morrison anecdote with a story Leven “recently” told on stage about seeing Van Morrison, and calls him “another great Celtic soul singer”.
inhalt: In his book on Van Morrison (Sanctuary Publishing, London 1997, reissued 2000), Brian Hinton compares an anecdote from Morrison’s life with a story that Jackie Leven “recently” told on stage about how he once saw Van Morrison. Leven is described as “another great Celtic soul singer”, alongside Morrison.

Hinton mentions Leven in other books too, for example *South by South West* (2003), *Let Them All Talk* (on Elvis Costello, 1999), *Joni Mitchell: Both Sides Now* (1996) and the *Bob Dylan Complete Discography* (2006), where Leven says of Dylan’s “Visions of Johanna” and the “Proust” poem that it gave him a feeling of healing.
zitate_kontext: Hinton on Leven, in comparison with Van Morrison

1998-03-06-nordlys-live-med-leven.kurz: Half-page portrait ahead of Leven's tour of northern Norway in March 1998, largely assembled from British interviews (Q, Mojo) and memories of the Tromsø concert in 1997.
inhalt: Half-page portrait ahead of Leven's tour of northern Norway in March 1998, largely assembled from British interviews (Q, Mojo) and memories of the Tromsø concert in 1997. Emberland begins with the image of the man with his own whisky, his own detox clinic, men's work and “more and coarser bawdy jokes than an entire Rorbua clientele”, and recapitulates the legend: start as John St. Field, “punk band” Doll by Doll, a choking attack in a side street in north London, heroin, the girlfriend who vanished with the Dalai Lama's bodyguard, then the “CORE Thrust college” with (alleged) support from Princess Diana.

On the whisky Leven's Lament he quotes Leven's stage joke from 1997 (the crate of samples disappeared at Fornebu airport) and – from Q – the admission that the whisky was bottled by his favourite brand and merely relabelled; after all, you can also have “Sting cognac and Tina Turner chardonnay”. Leven is a great fibber, but an even greater storyteller. Further: Leven as a kind of English branch of Robert Bly's men's movement; his own statements on *Fairy Tales* (fairy tales as stories for everyone, men who are mostly still boys, the “impoverished woman” in men) and a coarse stage anecdote from Tromsø 1997 about his partner Deborah. From Mojo: he loves telling fragmented stories on stage and seeing when people are really moved; from Q: heroin cost him a lot of self-confidence and he needs reassurance that he has not messed it up.

Outlook: Doll by Doll are slowly reuniting; in a month Leven goes into the studio for “Injured Women – The Leven Report”, due in the autumn, together with a Doll by Doll box of six albums including the unreleased “Last Flick of the Golden Wrench” and a regular best-of. Tour dates in the box: Huset, Hammerfest (Wednesday), Blå Rock Café, Tromsø (Thursday), Præstengbrygga, Kabelvåg (Saturday).

1998-03-12-nordlys-fin-by-a-vaere-ensom-.kurz: Nordlys talks to Leven on the day of his Tromsø concert: Tromsø is a fine city to be lonely in; he doesn't want to be called a poet; “Burning the Box of Beautiful Things” was partly written in the Grand bar.
inhalt: The piece “Fin by å være ensom i” (“A fine city to be lonely in”), credited to Lisbeth Skøelv (photo: Yngve Olsen Sæbbe), ran in Nordlys (Tromsø) on 12 March 1998, the day of the concert at Blå Rock. “I think Tromsø is a fine city to be lonely in,” says the “melancholic Scottish artist”; you shouldn't be afraid of being alone now and then. Loneliness is one of the many things he sings about. It is his third visit to the city in two years.

He is a singer, guitarist and songwriter – but don't call him a poet, even if his lyrics resemble beautiful poetry more than anything else: “A poet is not something you just decide to become. It is something others perceive you as.” It frightens him when young people wake up one day and think they are poets; that has to be earned. You can be good at writing without being a poet, and he compares this crudely to being good at masturbating without being a good lover. The paper adds that Leven is otherwise better known for the addiction clinic that Princess Diana supported and for his girlfriend running off with the Dalai Lama's bodyguard.

In Tromsø, though, he is known for his music: he never appears on the charts but has a loyal audience that buys the records and comes to the concerts. Ideas come from tiny things – “the way an old lady turns on the street can be enough to give me new ideas for writing”. He has a very close relationship with the Grand bar in Tromsø, which he also mentioned on his previous CD cover; “Burning the Box of Beautiful Things” was partly written there: “I saw the barmaid's reaction to a situation, and the third verse came.” He draws much on his own tough experiences at an earlier stage of life. “I write all the time. And I write well, though I don't want to boast. Even when I was at the bottom.” That evening he planned to play a few new songs for the first time in Tromsø.
zitate_kontext: Leven on why he doesn't call himself a poet.

1998-03-16-lofotposten-leven-for-dove-or.kurz: Ole-P. Refsahl describes in Lofotposten a concert in Kabelvåg ruined by a chattering audience: Leven grew irritated, the stories dried up, and the reviewer felt cheated of the evening.
inhalt: Under the headline ‘Leven for deaf ears’, Ole-P. Refsahl takes the audience of a concert in Kabelvåg to task in Lofotposten of 16 March 1998. The Scot Jackie Leven came to Kabelvåg to sing, “a large majority of the audience came to talk”. That quickly makes for bad chemistry. Leven first tried to shout down the talkers, grew irritated and asked the chatterers to shut up.

The audience took offence and answered with a chorus of shushing that was, if possible, even more irritating to listen to than the talking had been. The artist did his job with voice and acoustic guitar, but the evening was strongly marked by duty: joy and glow vanished, and the good stories that had spiced the previous – “excellent” – concert in Kabelvåg were missing entirely. The talking was taken care of by the people in the hall.

For the reviewer the concert was “totally ruined”. He can only hope that the “very capable Scottish artist” does not drop Kabelvåg the next time he is in Norway: the chatterers have inflicted a great loss on them. The piece is less a criticism of Leven than of the listeners, and it confirms how much his concerts then depended on his storytelling.
zitate_kontext: Refsahl at the start of the review

1998-04-25-yahoo-groups-leven-mailinglis.kurz: Group page of the fan mailing list “leven”, founded 25 April 1998: its description, 252 members by February 2003 and a monthly message count that works out at roughly three to ten posts a day.
inhalt: The group page for the mailing list “leven” at Yahoo! Groups (earlier eGroups) describes it as a place to discuss the “life, work and times” of the Scottish folk and rock singer Jackie Leven, his artistic influences and his past work as John St. Field and with the band Doll by Doll. It also supplies news of live performances and record production, with a “limited exchange of mp3's” in the Files section, and points to the fan site jackieleven.com. It is listed under “Rock and Pop”, the language is English, and the group details give a founding date of 25 April 1998 – so the list predates the Yahoo era, and moved to Yahoo only in 2001.

The page as captured on 27 February 2003 shows 252 members and restricted membership; the message archive was only ever open to members, so only the description and the figures are public. The figures are informative: the fan site always gave the list's traffic as “3–10 messages per day”, and the monthly statistics bear that out. The archive starts in September 2000 with 147 messages (October 347, November 201, December 214). In 2001 the monthly totals ran between 103 and 290, about 2,000 in all; in 2002 they varied between 50 and 230 (about 1,700), and in January and February 2003 they were 284 and 311.

The membership can be traced through the captured pages too: 171 at the end of 2000, 169 in February 2001, 177 in April 2001, 216 in mid-2002, 252 in February 2003 and 285 in autumn 2004. It was a small but steadily growing community that exchanged views and live recordings for years and followed the releases of an artist who barely featured in the mainstream press. After Yahoo Groups closed, a later forum post says, many former members gathered in a Facebook group.
zitate_kontext: The group's own description of the mailing list.
Second part of the group description.

1998-07-rip-it-up-jackie-leven-robert-du.kurz: Preview of Leven’s first Australian tour in July 1998: in a phone interview he talks about his popularity in Europe, the Celtic Soul Men, a planned Doll by Doll box set and a possible album of Tim Hardin songs.
inhalt: In the Adelaide free weekly *Rip It Up*, Robert Dunstan introduces Jackie Leven as an artist barely known in Australia who is now arriving for a first solo tour. If it goes well, he might return the following year with his band for the Womadelaide festival. Leven says he is “not even that well known in the UK” but has been pretty big in Scandinavia and Germany over the past two years. Dunstan also mentions Leven’s reputation for riding his horse across the English countryside, stopping at pubs to sample whisky and cider, and quotes Q magazine – credited here to Stuart Maconie – calling him a songwriter of rare gifts and one of the greatest voices these islands have produced.

The author reproduces at length the liner notes of the Cooking Vinyl sampler *Cooking Rhythms*. According to them, Leven’s voice graced the Doll by Doll albums of the late 1970s and early 1980s; after the band’s demise and a spiral of personal disasters he founded the Core Trust, described as Britain’s only holistic service for the healing of addictions, supposedly championed by Princess Diana, Eric Clapton and Mike Scott. Leven is called a seminal figure of the Men’s Movement around Robert Bly and the creator of Leven’s Lament, his own malt whisky, about which Salman Rushdie (“Salmon” in the text) is said to have remarked that you would be sadder but wiser for trying it. This is label copy rather than independent verification.

On his lower profile at home, Leven says it concerns him a little but not enough to cause stress; he left Britain young, lived in Berlin, Madrid and South America and lost touch, so he is “kind of an outside figure now”. When Dunstan remarks that acoustic music is popular again, Leven answers that music runs in cycles rather than along the “straight arrow of time”. Dunstan admits he does not know Doll by Doll; a friend once compared them to the Violent Femmes, which Leven finds a new one. The band recorded four albums and keep a cult following although the records have long been out of print; Cooking Vinyl plans a box set under the working title “Swimming In A Lonely Pool”. Leven is also contemplating an album of Tim Hardin songs. Neither project materialised.

He will bring copies of the limited live album *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow*, with its songs and “highly amusing stories”, plus EPs that are hard to find in Australia. He plans plenty from the Cooking Vinyl albums, material from the just-finished *Night Lilies*, brand new songs, “some very ancient Scottish songs” and, as he puts it, a few stories. The last show of the tour is at the Governor Hindmarsh in Adelaide on Thursday 30 July; his latest album, *Fairy Tales For Hard Men*, is out through Festival on Cooking Vinyl.

Leven on why he is better known in Europe than in Britain
Leven on trends and cycles in music
Leven on what his Australian shows will include

1998-09-07-bergensavisen-whiskyen-pa-hyl.kurz: Interview on the release of *Night Lilies* (mistakenly “Night Lines” in the standfirst), which Leven describes as emotional songs in a rocky wrapping.
inhalt: Interview on the release of *Night Lilies* (mistakenly “Night Lines” in the standfirst), which Leven describes as emotional songs in a rocky wrapping. He wanted to trace how a particular smell, sound or movement triggers intense memories of very specific episodes. The album is less melancholy than *Fairy Tales*: the colours still dark, but clearer; the aim is a sad record that at the same time lifts you up. Nothing does him as much good as walking the streets and watching people – in the past he did not do that.

Guitarist Joe Shaw from the Doll by Doll days plays on the album. Leven: Joe has always been a good friend, but the band years were traumatic in many respects; nobody liked them, they themselves were convinced of their class and sometimes took a perverse pleasure in flattening the audience with an overwhelmingly heavy live show until the hostility became palpable. Today he can laugh about it and is proud of the records. Releasing the climax of a song is like wrestling with an angel.

On the whisky Leven's Lament he says that, ironically, he no longer likes whisky: after a bout of nausea he has to turn away at the mere smell – bad advertising, as the “workers” pointed out to him. Halleraker recalls that at earlier Bergen gigs Leven talked more than he played; Leven: friends call him a lying bastard, but he likes inventing little stories that put the big things in perspective. Announcement: Garage, 30 October 1998, “one of his hardest rock concerts in a long time”.

1998-09-08-dagsavisen-mye-liv-i-leven.kurz: Leven has become a kind of “Norgesvenn”; he is releasing his fourth album in four years and is coming in October with a full band for the first time.
inhalt: Leven has become a kind of “Norgesvenn”; he is releasing his fourth album in four years and is coming in October with a full band for the first time. The songs “just poured out of him”; four albums, singles, EPs and a lot of touring have made him known above all in Germany and Norway. Nilsen summarises Doll by Doll (critically acclaimed “post-punk” band, silence after *Grand Passion* in 1982), the legend of the girlfriend, the choking attack and heroin, and the comeback in 1994. Leven laughs: apart from his “accidents”, it was wonderful to do nothing for years; all he ever had to do was live and observe – but when the songs came, he had to write them down, record them and play them.

*Night Lilies* is about memories and the tricks memory plays. On Robert Bly and the “Men's Movement”, Leven says Bly has sensible things to say about men and women. The hardest thing he has experienced was the break-up with his girlfriend two years ago because he had fallen in love with another woman; today he lives on the Scottish west coast with his new partner and her children. He wants to process this chapter on “Injured Women: The Leven Report”, which is meant to show that he does not write only about masculinity. Planned: a 6-CD box with Doll by Doll's complete work including the unreleased fifth album, and next year a new, differently sounding, possibly more electronic album with new people.

Tour dates in the text: Stavanger (20.10.), Kabelvåg (21.), Bodø (22.), Trondheim (23.), Førde (24.), Oslo (29.), Bergen (30.10.1998). Leven: apart from the reunion concerts with Doll by Doll in Bergen the previous year, he has never brought a band to Norway.

1998-09-08-tonsbergs-blad-levende-minner.kurz: NTB Pluss interview conducted in Oslo on *Night Lilies*. The key words of the album are memory and remembrance: how with age one forgets and falsifies memories, until a smell, a taste or a sound suddenly brings them back.
inhalt: NTB Pluss interview conducted in Oslo on *Night Lilies*. The key words of the album are memory and remembrance: how with age one forgets and falsifies memories, until a smell, a taste or a sound suddenly brings them back. That is exactly what happened to him in the summer of 1997 on a small Greek island: the scent of a flower took him straight back to childhood and youth in Scotland and awakened forgotten memories, some of which ended up on the album; all eleven songs have a real basis, even if not all of them describe his own experiences.

On Doll by Doll Leven says the band deserved a better fate but had only itself to blame for never breaking through: so aggressive and unfriendly that it made many enemies; he himself was violent at the time and thought that was right because his friends were the same. He led a life on the edge, and ironically it was precisely the severe assault that saved him: for two years he could not speak, for six years he could not sing, but he had time to withdraw to Scotland and take stock of his life – he emerged from convalescence a better person. A great deal of energy afterwards went into the centre for homeless drug addicts that he founded. He has enjoyed telling stories since childhood and gives them a fitting mood; *Night Lilies* is considerably warmer than *Fairy Tales*. The ending (destroyed by OCR) mentions Rolf Jacobsen, plans to set more poems by his “good friend” and other poets to music on the next record, and the October tour.
zitate_kontext: Leven on the Doll by Doll years.

1998-09-11-jaerbladet-leven-ikke-leven-i.kurz: Interview from the youth pages of Jærbladet just before *Night Lilies*: Leven talks about his Oslo gig for 40 people, buried memories, working “militarily” in the studio, his hatred of the word “lifestyle” and the story behind “Irland For Loosers”.
inhalt: Sølve Friestad conducts a very relaxed interview for Jærbladet (Bryne) on 11 September 1998, shortly before the release of *Night Lilies* (Monday 14 September). He introduces Leven as not the best-known artist in Norway and not music for the very youngest. The album has a reputation for being his best; Leven is on the same label as the Oyster Band, comes from Scotland and is called “Celt/soul” by Q magazine. He lives in the small town of Titchfield between Southampton and Portsmouth.

Of his release concert in Oslo, a small club with room for only forty, Leven says it was hard work to play for so few; afterwards people came up and told him the songs had made them cry. Good, he told them: then they had understood something about the lyrics. The lyrics come from his own experiences, not always good ones. *Night Lilies* is, in brief, about memories we bury and leave lying for a long time, until they grow angry. Some are bad memories: “Bad memories remain bad until you learn something from them.” His favourite song on the album is “Burning the Box of Beautiful Things”.

On his way of working: he writes and produces everything himself, which can be lonely but gives him a lot. He is self-taught, tunes and plays the guitar his own way and in fact cannot play “normally”. In the studio he is “a fairly military person” but open to suggestions. He thinks in images and then has to find words for them; there is no humour in the lyrics, only “jokes”. The story of “Irland For Loosers”: he thought he was in love with Helen Turner, now playing with Paul Weller; they went to a cottage in Ireland, found out after a month that they were not in love, and spent the rest of the summer together anyway, happily but sadly, knowing they would part. In the studio an Irishman objected to the title (“It better not”).

Asked about a commercial breakthrough, he quotes a pub saying (“All things come to he who waits – as long as he who waits waits a bloody long time”) and says he has no control over his career but controls his work. A big house with a swimming pool would not be bad. He has been an artist since 1967. He hates “lifestyle” as a term used when you stop living. He names Chet Baker as a vocal model (not to copy, but to match in vocal use), listens to Carmen McRae and Will Oldham, likes the Scottish band Wolfstone, enjoys walking by the sea and the first hour after the pub opens with a newspaper and a drink. Words such as “snack” and “nick nack” make him angry. He prefers *Rob Roy* to *Braveheart*; his favourite film is Wim Wenders’s *The American Friend*. A short album review is appended: disappointing at first, then growing considerably, atmospheric and pleasant to listen to.

Leven on his work in the studio

1998-09-12-drammens-tidende-det-store-hj.kurz: Music page by Johnny Andreassen (formerly Fremtiden) with an interview on the sofa at the Hotel Savoy and a short review.
inhalt: Music page by Johnny Andreassen (formerly Fremtiden) with an interview on the sofa at the Hotel Savoy and a short review. Andreassen describes Leven as an artist who puts more soul and heart into it than anyone else he has met; Leven is slowly becoming prominent in Norway after frequent acoustic tours, and a Norwegian (Jan Saghaug) made his official website. At the last meeting the talk was of fairy tales for men and the ability to cry; at that time Leven announced an album about injustice towards women (“Injured Woman”). Now he says that, unfortunately, he has since hurt his partner again; something of what he wanted to say about women's fates is also in *Night Lilies*.

According to Leven, the album title goes back to large night lilies that grew in his youth along a disused railway line in a forbidden area and opened only late in the evening; at 16–17 he mostly brawled and drank. He forgot the flowers until he found them again late one evening on a remote Greek island – the scent hit him like a shock. He speaks of “memory chances” and warns that being open can destroy you (example Bill Clinton). On the whisky: Leven's Lament is still being produced but is hardly available, Harrods is said to be a safe source; in his youth one could choose between the paper mill, the coal mine and the whisky bottling plant, workers received eight bottles a week, and his home town had Europe's highest unemployment and the most suicides for three years. He no longer drinks whisky himself.

Announcement of the big Norwegian tour in October with Steafan Hannigan (Irish flutes, percussion) and Michael Cosgrave (keyboard, trumpet). The review calls *Night Lilies* a pearl with some of his most beautiful melodies and more experimental rock moods, “Celtic soul” with “perhaps the most beautiful male voice of our time”. A box quotes Leven's love of Gothic horror storytellers.
zitate_kontext: Leven (from the earlier conversation, as a headline quotation).

1998-09-16-dagsavisen-liv-og-leven.kurz: Geir Rakvaag praises *Night Lilies* in Dagsavisen as nearly as strong as its predecessor: deeply personal stories, familiar yet distinctive melodies, Celtic earthiness – and Leven remains one of the world’s most underrated rock singers.
inhalt: The review opens with an observation: smell is probably the only phenomenon that can conjure up a feeling of time and place even more strongly than music. Leven has let himself be inspired by the scent of night lilies, which he says shaped his life and helped make him the man he is today – “not the worst influence he has been exposed to”, Rakvaag writes.

The previous album (wrongly called “Ballad Of The Hard Men” in the text; *Fairy Tales for Hard Men* is meant) was one of last year’s highlights, and the new record is hardly worse. Leven tells unusually strong stories in painfully personal songs about the difficult relationship between women and men, supported by melodies so good they seem familiar yet are entirely his own. An earthy Celtic mood hangs over the songs, and the playing by Leven and his friends is exquisitely tasteful throughout. At times he almost comes across as “the Roy Orbison of our time”.

The critic places Leven in Norway: in recent years the “cult hero” has become big in small circles – that his previous album reached no. 40 on a Norwegian sales list caused a stir in the British rock press – yet he must still be one of the world’s most underrated rock singers. There is little chance that *Night Lilies* will change this, “and that is perhaps best. Sometimes great secrets are good to have.” A photo caption announces that Leven plays Oslo again on 29 October.
zitate_kontext: Geir Rakvaag on Leven on *Night Lilies*.
Rakvaag at the start of his review.
Closing lines of the review, on Leven’s obscurity.

1998-09-18-glamdalen-liljedugg.kurz: Tommy Rønningen praises Night Lillies in Glåmdalen as "pure" Celtic soul from the same well as Van Morrison's: eleven carefully chiselled songs full of wisdom, faith and hope.
inhalt: In Glåmdalen (Kongsvinger) on 18 September 1998, Tommy Rønningen reviews Jackie Leven's album *Night Lillies* (Cooking Vinyl) under the headline "Liljedugg" ("Lily dew"). Leven is a Scot, ex-vocalist of the semi-legendary Doll by Doll, ex-junkie, singer-songwriter and solo artist. He has fought his way back after "the biggest portion of bad luck in history", and his previous album, *Fairytales for Hard Men*, brought him well-deserved success.

*Night Lillies* is more conventional than its predecessor but is still about so-called "Caledonian soul": Celtic soul with strong folk elements, from the same source as Van Morrison once drew on. The album is "pure as silver and fresh as dripping morning dew". It contains eleven brand-new, carefully chiselled songs whose latent explosive power wipes out all bad vibrations in the surroundings, eleven tales full of wisdom, faith and hopes. Verdict: it is for those who have lost their faith, those who want to believe in something, or those who simply want to hear beautiful music. The rating scale is illegible in the scan.
zitate_kontext: Rønningen's overall verdict on Night Lillies

1998-09-25-bergensavisen-night-lilies.kurz: Frank Johnsen in Bergensavisen on *Night Lilies*: a gloriously melancholy record with a Dylan feel and stories that cut through the skin – music for late autumn evenings with Leven's own whisky in the glass.
inhalt: The record page of Bergensavisen on 25 September 1998 carries Frank Johnsen's short review of *Night Lilies* (Cooking Vinyl). He calls Leven “the Scottish friend of Bergen” and describes how the title track opens with the lines “Come gather round assholes and chop me a line, I'll tell you a tale of a good friend of mine”, and with its “Dylanesque feeling” starts off a “gloriously melancholy” record, in the same vein as Leven's earlier solo outbursts.

With his paws firmly planted in British folk music, Leven tells stories “that cut through the skin”. The airy atmosphere surrounding the songs gives the music a cool, dreamlike feel, and he never provokes with “loutish ball-kicking”. This is music for late autumn evenings, “preferably with Leven's own whisky in the glasses”, when you are trying to find out what went wrong – “Jackie Leven knows the answer.” According to a later issue the paper gave the album a 5 on its dice scale; the rating itself is not legible on this page.
zitate_kontext: Johnsen at the end of his review.

1998-09-30-romerikes-blad-skotsk-livseli.kurz: A positive review of *Night Lilies*: Leven has only got better since the end of Doll by Doll; the album is mature, warm music and a tribute to the small important things, with “Burning the Box of Beautiful Things” and “Alvis Green” as highlights.
inhalt: Romerikes Blad (Lillestrøm) reviews Jackie Leven's *Night Lilies* (Cooking Vinyl) under the title “Skotsk livseliksir” (“Scottish elixir of life”). Leven has received much praise for his records and for his concerts. The Scot has only got better and better since he dissolved Doll By Doll, who “unfortunately never got the attention they deserved”. With his fourteenth album, the reviewer writes, Leven offers “noble goods”: music from a mature man, for comfort and joy as autumn takes over our part of the world.

He sings with a confidence built up over years and has a band who know exactly what is needed. Leven's words and melodies are the kind that grow stronger each time you hear them. It is hard to judge whether this is the best he has done, but *Night Lilies* is in any case among the cream. Lyrically it is a sort of tribute to the small, important things that shape us and which we do not know how to appreciate enough; musically it is warm, melodic and memorable. The critic singles out “Burning The Box Of Beautiful Things” and “Alvis Green” as songs you do not soon forget.

1998-10-02-helgelands-blad-night-lilies.kurz: Helgelands Blad gives *Night Lilies* a mixed review: melodic, poetic folk rock with airy arrangements and lyrics about betrayal and love, though Leven can seem overly pompous. Still worth a try for friends of dramatic, romantic rock.
inhalt: The review (author not identifiable in the print) introduces Leven as making no exactly “noisy” music: it is rock, but in a melodic, folk-inspired form that should not frighten delicate ears. In the early 1980s Leven was front man of the cult favourites Doll by Doll. Personal problems and drug abuse swept him away for some years before, “three years ago”, he debuted as a solo artist with the “grand” *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West* (so the paper; this is only partly right, since Leven had released solo records earlier and *Forbidden Songs* was not his first work since the comeback). Two more albums followed before *Night Lilies*.

Leven is again out on “dramatic wanderings” along dark paths in the Scottish Highlands, drawing from them inspiration for melodic, poetic rock ’n’ roll with clear touches of folk. The arrangements are airy and the music rich in detail. Lyrically it is still about betrayal and lost or won love, this time with the underlying theme of how memories from the past can catch up with us.

The weakness: Leven can seem overly pompous, with no limit to how much pain love inflicts on us. Add a tendency to pitch the voice a little too velvet-soft, and the feelings can simply take over. But anyone who likes melodic rock with dramatic depth and a romantic touch should definitely check out this kind of Leven. It is an album on which Leven wanders on.

1998-10-16-harstad-tidende-ujevnt-fra-ja.kurz: A slightly disappointed review of *Night Lilies* in Harstad Tidende: glossy production and good material but signs of stagnation – the feeling of having heard most of it before. “Empty In Soho Square” is the highlight; still worth buying.
inhalt: John Storhaug reviews *Night Lilies* (Cooking Vinyl/MNW, 1998) in Harstad Tidende on 16 October 1998 under the heading “Ujevnt fra Jackie Leven” (“Uneven from Jackie Leven”). Leven has become “a man to reckon with”, he writes; from his Doll by Doll days to his solo career he has kept the quality at a comfortably high level. On this year’s album, however, there are “unfortunately small things pointing to stagnation”.

The production is glossy and the song material good, but something grates: where Leven used to renew himself in small details, this time he treads too much on familiar ground. The feeling of having heard most of it before is “irritatingly present all the time”. The mood and the landscapes are the same, “at least as beautiful as before”. Naturally there are highlights: the ballad “Empty In Soho Square” is of a very high standard, with Leven singing “at his most magical” and holding the interest throughout the song. Living up to the quality the man delivered in the nineties with each release is hard; the record disappoints a little but is worth buying anyway.

1998-10-23-lofotposten-en-perfekt-kveld.kurz: Anki Gerhardsen describes Leven’s solo concert in Kabelvåg as a “perfect evening”: two hours of gallows humour, a rough voice and guitar, with the audience in his hands from the first anecdote.
inhalt: The review in Lofotposten was written twelve hours after the concert, and the music, songs and stories were, the author says, still in her ear. Leven came up the stairs to the first floor of Præstengbrygga in Kabelvåg shortly before 11 pm on Wednesday evening; it was half dark and quiet, and the audience of about 80 chatted over a beer and lit candles. “Good evening,” said Leven, and struck the first chords. After the first song and a first anecdote from his “manifold life” she thought: yes, here we stay for the rest of the evening.

From that moment he had the audience completely in his “roomy embrace” for two full hours. Leven is an authority on stage; with a combination of gallows humour, wounded depth, a raw, strong voice, outstanding guitar playing and a lot of lived life he delivered a performance to remember. Alone with a well-worn acoustic guitar he led the audience through a selection of his songs, interspersed with insanely funny stories. She describes him affectionately and mockingly: somewhat stout, in worn tracksuit bottoms, scuffed patent-leather shoes, a hole-ridden denim shirt and white ski socks round his ankles – and yet livelier than any one-man band she had heard for a long, long time.

Leven’s storytelling talent also marks his songs with their uniquely well-composed lyrics. Without lapsing into tough sentimentality he sang his way through the back streets of grief, lost lovers, the lonely muscle mass of the bodybuilder and straight into rakish Celtic folk tunes. The great musical range characterised the concert; the reviewer takes her hat off to the people at Præstengbrygga for repeatedly bringing in artists of this quality.
zitate_kontext: Anki Gerhardsen on the concert in Kabelvåg.

1998-10-24-nordlands-framtid-takk-for-si.kurz: Nordlands Framtid reports on the Bodø concert at Glæden through the eyes of Leven's biggest local fan, whose own life story suddenly meets the new song "Single Father".
inhalt: Under the headline "Takk for sist Thor Arne!" ("Thanks for last time, Thor Arne!"), Freddy Toresen describes on 24 October 1998 the reunion of the Scot Jackie Leven with his biggest fan in Bodø, a 36-year-old. He is in love with the music of the then 48-year-old cult figure and had just attended his third Leven concert, at Glæden on Thursday. He came to Leven through a free CD on the music magazine *Beat*: "The song hit me right in the heart, and I've been hooked ever since." The voice, the songs, the whole atmosphere give him goose bumps.

An anecdote: on Leven's previous visit to Bodø, the fan joined his fan club by paying the subscription to Leven in person after the concert; neither the promised CD nor the members' magazines ever arrived. When he emailed to ask, the club's manager Mick Nolan replied that you must not give money to Leven, because it disappears at once "into the drug sewer". When Leven met the fan on Thursday he had been warned by Nolan: "Ah, it's you, the CD is coming, make sure of that", he reassured him. "That's just how he is," says der Fan, "and I have no problem accepting it."

Under the heading "Hardt liv" ("Hard life") the article says Leven has lived a very hard life since his first records with Doll by Doll: for a long time in a narcotics hell, with enormous alcohol problems as well. The fan says the way he got back to life commands respect; he was found drunk and wrecked in a London gutter until someone got him back on his feet, and his descriptions of life's dark side are enormously strong.

The concert: Leven sat alone on a stool with the guitar placed in front of his somewhat growing belly, conjuring up his strong melodies bare and alone, interrupted only by his usual humorous stories from travels around the world. The roughly 90 listeners for once kept quiet and followed what he had to say, a pleasing novelty in the concert city of Bodø. Halfway through, Leven called the fan up on stage, whispered something in his ear and introduced him to the audience as "my male north-Norwegian sweetheart". Then he announced a new song he had written on a plane a few days earlier: "I'll probably make a fool of myself now, but why not, you are my friends", and played "Single Father", about suddenly losing your beloved and becoming a lone father.

Ten years earlier the fan had lost his wife in an air crash and become a single father; he told Leven so after the concert, and Leven was astonished. The writer expects the story to turn up in Leven's concerts in future. Next time Leven comes to Bodø the two plan to go fishing at Saltstraumen.
zitate_kontext: The fan on how he found Leven

1998-10-24-nordlandsposten-stakkars-jack.kurz: Jo Petter Furuhovde is furious in Nordlandsposten that about ten noisy young men turned Leven’s concert in Bodø into background music – Leven himself, he says, delivered professionally anyway.
inhalt: The concert review is less an appreciation than a scolding of the audience. Furuhovde writes that he would not wish on anyone the audience Jackie Leven met on Thursday at Den Siste Glæde in Bodø – “poor man”. It is “downright sad” when so fine an artist is reduced to providing background music at his own concert. About ten people ruined the evening for those who had paid to hear Leven, and not “idiots” who evidently find what they are saying so important that everyone else in the room must hear it too.

Furuhovde is almost surprised that “dear Leven” put up with being drowned out as he was. Last autumn Ole Paus told the audience at Samfunnet to go to hell because they were noisy; had Leven done the same, he would have understood. But since it is not the artist’s task to make an audience shut up, the staff could have been a bit more grown-up and asked the loudmouths to take their loud words elsewhere. Even if you paid only 60 kroner (a very friendly price), you want to hear what you came for: the artist on stage.

Despite the noise Leven at times managed to get across his songs, which have strength and nerve, as do his singing and guitar playing. Out with his new CD *Night Lilies*, he “did his job professionally”, which makes it all the sadder that ten bawling young men were allowed to spoil it. The concert box gives an audience of about 60.
zitate_kontext: Jo Petter Furuhovde at the start of his review.
Furuhovde on Leven’s performance despite the disturbance.

1998-10-26-bergensavisen-spirituell-berg.kurz: Conversation after Leven's course on “guitar-based songwriting” for local musicians at Hagstrøm (Ole Blues with Norsk Musikkråd).
inhalt: Conversation after Leven's course on “guitar-based songwriting” for local musicians at Hagstrøm (Ole Blues with Norsk Musikkråd). Leven says he made his professional debut in Bergen in 1967, together with an American gospel singer, and fell in love with the city at once; its “spiritual aura” is like coming home and reminds him of a small town on the Scottish west coast where he lived for a long time. Tours are normally just work for him – except in Bergen, where he always takes a day off. On Friday he comes to Garage with the “virtuoso The Celtic Soulmen”, the only place where he wants to play in Bergen. The concert in Førde the day before was “a bit wild”, most of the guests drunk.

What became of the planned live album of the Doll by Doll concert at Garage in 1997, Leven does not know – he forgot about it, and it does not mean much to him, so many people record his concerts. He prefers to tour alone: in bands one person always gets depressed and infects the others until nobody is talking to anybody any more.

From the seminar: images are the most important thing, which is why he always carries a notebook; you should write with your heart and not analyse. He deliberately allows himself only one cliché per song, warns against “biblical” images such as deserts and suggests drastically more interesting alternatives; American country singers use so many clichés that it becomes surreal and therefore exciting (k. d. lang). Caption: Leven plays a 58-year-old guitar that once belonged to Doc Watson.

1998-10-30-bergensavisen-leven-om-inspir.titel: [Jackie Leven, in town for his concert, on his sources of inspiration]
1998-10-30-bergensavisen-leven-om-inspir.kurz: A short box on the day of his concert: Leven names Van Morrison, Lou Reed and Neil Young as inspirations, Chet Baker as his favourite vocalist and Ani DiFranco as the author of one of the century’s best songs.
inhalt: On the day of his Bergen concert Bergensavisen (30 October 1998) ran a short box by Frank Johnsen in which Leven describes his influences. Van Morrison, Lou Reed and Neil Young are important sources of inspiration. “Madame George” from *Astral Weeks* has an incredibly pictorial lyric; sadly Morrison has become less interesting over the years, while Lou Reed’s great period ran from *Transformer* to *Berlin*, in Leven’s view.

Surprisingly, Leven names the jazz trumpeter Chet Baker as his favourite vocalist: “He made these silly jazz songs, with a strange, creeping atmosphere. A great vocalist.” He prefers individual albums and songs to an artist’s whole output, for example the latest Grant Lee Buffalo album or compilations of Soweto artists with “incredible power in the songs”, and even likes some Ace of Base hits. His “label friend” Ani DiFranco – both were on Cooking Vinyl – has written one of the century’s best songs, “Untitled Face”.

Finally Leven says he toured folk clubs with Elvis Costello “before he became Elvis”; an album like *Imperial Bedroom* has a lot of beauty in it, and the artist Rocky Burnette is a personal favourite. “I like many kinds of music,” he says. The Costello tour is Leven’s own claim and not otherwise documented.

Leven’s claim, as reported by the journalist

1998-11-01-bergensavisen-kveld-med-jacki.kurz: Frank Johnsen praises a concert at the “Garage” club in *Bergensavisen* with the Celtic Soulmen: tragicomic stories, percussive guitar and a bagpipe moment when “the world stood still”; the set drew mainly on *Night Lilies*.
inhalt: Under the headline “Lyrisk kjeller!” (“Lyrical cellar!”) Frank Johnsen reviews a Leven concert at the Garage club in Bergen. An evening with the “hefty Scot” at one of his favourite clubs was bound to be wonderful, and Leven did not disappoint this time either, firing off tragicomic stories from his stool to the audience’s wild delight. With him were The Celtic Soulmen, Michael Cosgrave on keyboards and Steafan Hannigan on percussion and Uilleann pipes, who gave Leven the airy sound that characterises the records. Hannigan’s “synchronised swimming” between bodhrán, djembe and pipes was nothing short of impressive.

Cosgrave and Hannigan are also prominent on Leven’s latest album, *Night Lilies*, so much of the programme came from that “fabulous” record, which the critic does not hold against him; best-of concerts, he says, can wait for the compilation. Leven tells stories, whether about golf on the moon, Van Morrison’s stage paranoia or a car sale with a fatal outcome, and beneath this “purgatory” there is always a humorous bottom; few artists deliver the message as clearly as the Scottish veteran. But it is also about music: Leven is a creative guitarist, and his percussive play on the guitar body while he works the strings is a joy to watch.

The great artistic moment came when Hannigan played a personal ode to his father on the pipes, over a beautiful synth carpet, and the piece gradually melted into “Burning The Box Of Beautiful Things”: “the world stood still for a moment”. The start of the article is partly cut off in the newspaper scan.
zitate_kontext: Johnsen on the high point of the evening

1998-11-09-taz-soundcheck-taraf-de-haido.kurz: On 9 November 1998 the taz recommends Leven in its “Soundcheck” column for the Logo in Hamburg: hard years, a comeback in 1994, ever since “songs of captivating fragility”, most recently *Night Lilies*.
inhalt: In the taz's “Soundcheck” concert column of 9 November 1998, Leven is the second tip of the evening alongside the Romanian Roma orchestra Taraf de Haidouks, playing at the Curio-Haus. For Leven (9 pm, Logo, Hamburg) the short piece, signed “cbu”, compresses his story into a few sentences: the man has had “hard years”; after a “brawl” in the mid-Eighties, meaning the 1983 attack, he lost his voice “and with it his inner voice”. He sought oblivion in heroin and nearly died.

In 1994 the singer of the “post-punk band Doll By Doll” reported back, and ever since “the colossus” has written songs “of captivating fragility”. *Night Lilies* is already the fourth album since the new start. The text is an announcement and does not confirm the concert afterwards.
zitate_kontext: The short text on Leven, opening
The taz on Leven's new start

1998-11-soundi-night-lilies.kurz: Jussi Niemi gives *Night Lilies* the maximum five stars in the Finnish magazine Soundi: a mature, timeless, soulful album with Leven’s singing as its high point.
inhalt: The review in issue 11/1998 of the Finnish music magazine Soundi carries a rating of 5 out of 5 stars. Jussi Niemi recalls that Jackie Leven’s “fatefully melodic” Doll By Doll stayed with him from the late seventies as one of the most individual rock bands of the era. He has come across Leven’s solo records – 14 in all – only now; *Night Lilies* makes him regret their long separation.

The Scot Leven has dug deep into his Celtic roots: besides inspired melodies they are reflected in tin whistle, fiddle and mandolin. Yet Leven filters the Celtic through blues, rock, jazz and country, like Van Morrison or Mary Coughlan, especially in his acoustic guitar playing. The sound of the album is spacious, dark and stripped down; the acoustic base impression is underlined with minimalist, almost avant-garde synthesizer touches.

The best of it, though, is Leven’s singing: “What a voice and presence!” Effortless and yet intense, it breathes a hard-lived life, mirroring tenderly the autobiographical lyrics in which light and shadow constantly measure themselves against each other. The imagery has dizzying poetic depth; as an example Niemi quotes from ‘Live or Die’ the lines about a man who has injured women so many times and is now on his knees. The “stunning” title track opens the album as its most traditional piece, but there is no filler afterwards. The conclusion: a mature, timeless, rarely soulful and utterly self-expressive work “with the flavour of a future classic”.
zitate_kontext: Lines from ‘Live or Die’ quoted by Niemi

1998-12-22-lofotposten-ikke-helt-det-sam.kurz: In Lofotposten Anki Gerhardsen finds *Night Lilies* decent but less compelling than the solo performer she saw live in Kabelvåg: with a band and a tidier concept the mood is different, and she prefers Leven alone with stories, song and guitar.
inhalt: The review (“Ikke helt det samme”, “Not quite the same”) starts with the writer's caveat: she has no deep knowledge of Jackie Leven's musical history, but has heard a couple of his records and seen him live at Præstengbrygga in Kabelvåg. There she was “thoroughly charmed”, by the man himself, by his “incredible gift for storytelling” and, most of all, by the crooked, soulful essence of the whole concert: Leven “raw and alone” with his songs, his captivating voice and the acoustic guitar – a “tired” guitar, according to the standfirst.

*Night Lilies* is something else. Here Leven has a handful of other musicians with him, now and then an extra voice and a tidier set-up than she remembers from his previous record, which she calls “The peace comes dropping slow” (probably *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow*). The “Leven-esque” expression is certainly present on the new album, but the atmosphere is different: Scottish blue tradition, “pub pop” and absolute quality. Leven delivers skilled craftsmanship with able musicians, and the CD is good to listen to on dark December evenings. The bottom line: “Decent, but not quite the same” – she prefers Leven alone, with his stories, his singing and his acoustic guitar. The photo caption says the same in a nutshell: “Pub pop: Leven delivers skilled craftsmanship with able musicians.”
zitate_kontext: Anki Gerhardsen at the end of the review
Gerhardsen on the atmosphere of Night Lilies

1998-cooking-vinyl-jackie-leven-biograph.kurz: Cooking Vinyl's press biography for *Night Lilies*: Leven as a “Celtic Soul” singer, Doll by Doll, the street attack, heroin, self-cure, the CORE Trust, the friendship with Robert Bly – plus press quotes on the 1994–97 albums.
inhalt: The biography that Cooking Vinyl issued with *Night Lilies* (1998) opens with a superlative: with this album, “one of the very best of 14 albums” he had made since 1971, Jackie Leven was “in danger of becoming a national living treasure”. He is described as a formidable singer, guitarist, songwriter and storyteller whose work, like that of many greats, falls into a category of its own. It had been called “Celtic Soul” with some justification, and Leven stands in an ancestral line with Van Morrison, Lightnin' Hopkins and the unnamed work-song singers of every corner of the earth.

Doll by Doll, the text says, made a serious impact in the late 1970s as a classic two-guitars, bass and drums outfit that beguiled audiences when they were not scaring the pants off them with a rare on-stage intensity. The band made five “superb” albums of warped melodic rock (one unreleased) but were “perhaps fatally” out of step with the punk and new wave preoccupations of the day. The serious illness the biography refers to is an attack: “in the early 1980's”, it says, Leven was nearly murdered by strangulation in an unprovoked assault in a London street while walking home from recording. He could neither speak nor sing for over a year and, in considerable pain, turned to heroin as pain management. After a year of addiction he decided he “wanted his life back” and freed himself with a method of his own making that combined acupuncture, psychic healing and reflexology.

The method worked so well that it was formalised: Leven co-founded the CORE Trust, a registered addictions charity in central London that still offers the same treatment. The biography claims its success rate is among the highest in Europe, and says Diana, Princess of Wales championed the Trust in her lifetime, was guest of honour at fundraisers and officially opened the premises. In the early 1990s Leven became close friends with the American poet Robert Bly, described as the foreshadower of the so-called men's movement. With Richard Olivier and the psychologist James Hillman they brought large groups of men together in the UK and the USA to consider manhood for up to a week at a time in remote locations; Leven has since become a spokesman on such issues.

His return to record-making is marked by *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*, with poetry readings by Bly and Mike Scott, followed by *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West*, *The Argyll Cycle* and *Fairytales for Hardmen*; *Night Lilies* continues the series. The page closes with a “What they said” collection from *The Independent*, *Q*, *Vox*, *Independent on Sunday*, *Detroit News*, *Time Out* and *BUZZ*, without authors or dates. According to these quotes, *The Mystery of Love…* was one of *Q*'s top 20 albums of 1994, and the *Detroit News* called *Forbidden Songs…* “nothing less than astonishing – a true masterpiece in a marketplace of replicas”. It is a label text, so promotion first, but a revealing one: it shows how Leven's story was meant to be told publicly in 1998.
zitate_kontext: Opening sentence of the Cooking Vinyl press biography.
Press quote attributed to The Independent.

1998-cooking-vinyl-jackie-leven-intervie.kurz: A short Cooking Vinyl Q&A on *Night Lilies*: Leven talks about the title, the Böcklin-inspired cover, the Disastrodrome festival with David Thomas and his audience in Germany and Scandinavia, plus some joke answers.
inhalt: The interview was conducted by Cooking Vinyl around the release of *Night Lilies* (1998) and runs as a string of short questions and answers. On the title, Leven says the smell of night lilies takes his life “round in a full circle” from now to when he was seventeen and back. A sound, a gesture or a smell can cause a “draught of remembrance”, and we should not overlook unusual moments in our lives.

On the album’s reception, he recalls that each new Beatles album sounded different, strange and confusing to him as a young man, and that many fans feel the same about his own work at times. *Night Lilies*, however, is getting a more immediate, enthusiastic response, although some people think the first line stupid and disgraceful. He says he is always totally involved with cover art; this one is Ferdinand Keller’s “Tomb of Böcklin”, a homage to Arnold Böcklin’s “Isle of the Dead”, and he loves its mystery, intrigue and “divine sense of dread”.

Disastrodrome, the four-day festival of voice and vision at London’s South Bank Centre directed by David Thomas of Pere Ubu, changed his understanding of what is creatively possible. Thomas was stunning as director, performer and human being, and Leven would like to work with him again; he laments how suddenly it ended and hopes it will be released on record. The two plan an EP led by a duet of “You’ve Lost That Lovin’ Feeling”, about which he jokes over the line about closing one’s eyes during a kiss.

He explains his popularity in Scandinavia and Germany by saying audiences there appreciate the unfolding depths of his images – like Van Morrison’s “going down the old mine with a transistor radio”, which none of us has done, yet the image is immediate and sustained; it grows. He sees his songs as a community he works for as honestly as he can. Music in the UK is more about lifestyle, in Germany and Scandinavia about life, death and beauty – which is why they love jazz.

Asked about major labels in the Doll by Doll days, he says they are the kind of people who take you out for a £200 lunch to explain why they cannot lend you £200, with one genuinely supportive person for every two-faced one who damages the partnership; he praises the care he and Cooking Vinyl have invested in each other. The closing answers are jokes: without music he would train as a barman in Ireland, and in a card game in high-security prison with Rev Hammer and Martin Goldschmidt he lost the forfeit of not wearing long trousers.
zitate_kontext: Leven on his audiences in Germany and Scandinavia.

1998-muze-macmillan-larkin-encyclopedia-.titel: The Encyclopedia of Popular Music (entries “Doll By Doll” and “Leven, Jackie”)
1998-muze-macmillan-larkin-encyclopedia-.kurz: Colin Larkin’s encyclopedia of popular music carries entries on Doll by Doll, described as essentially a vehicle for Leven, and on Jackie Leven with his solo career from the 1990s.
inhalt: The *Encyclopedia of Popular Music* (Guinness Publishing 1995, Muze/Macmillan 1998, Muze/Oxford University Press 2006), the standard reference on popular music, carries two entries across several editions. ‘Doll By Doll’ describes the band as essentially a vehicle for Jackie Leven, formed in 1977; the third album, on Magnet, was ‘accomplished’ and the group had a minor hit (meaning ‘Caritas’). There are also star ratings for albums, in the 1998 edition four stars for *Gypsy Blood* and three for *Doll By Doll*.

The entry ‘Leven, Jackie’ (born in Fife) begins with Doll by Doll splitting up in 1983 and then describes his solo career of the 1990s. The fourth edition (2006) additionally mentions Leven in the entry on David Thomas, with whom he collaborated as ‘UbuDoll’.

1998-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.titel: [Collected finds from Nasjonalbiblioteket 1998: news items, announcements, lists]

1998-natt-og-dag-night-lilies.kurz: A pointed mini-review in Natt & Dag that describes the artist rather than the album: Scottish, fat, melancholic, “full of the devil”, funny and very gifted – missing him on the Norwegian tour would be foolish.
inhalt: The Oslo magazine Natt & Dag (issue 10/1998) devotes a short review to *Night Lilies* (MNW) that almost entirely characterises the artist. He is Scottish, fat, a “reformed junkie, punk and alky – no, not alky, at least not reformed”, very, very melancholic, “full of the devil”, funny and very, very gifted. He bears the mark of the beast, “Norgesvenn” (friend of Norway), on his forehead and can be seen around the country in the autumn in connection with the record.

It would be stupid not to see and hear him if you have the chance. He will probably come alone, so it will be “one on one”. The reviewer (initials “JEF”) ends by borrowing what he calls the apparently brilliant device of the author Dag Solstad: “Yes, that will be stupid of you.” The text passes no judgement on the music itself.

1998-ted-smart-heatley-encyclopedia-of-a.kurz: The entry for *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* in the *Encyclopedia of Albums* (1998) gives a data header and line-up and describes the album as a rebirth of a singer whose earlier band Doll by Doll were “perennial underachievers”.
inhalt: The entry in the reference book, published in London in 1998 by Ted Smart, opens with a data header: artist, label Cooking Vinyl, producer, line-up (including James Hallawell and Glen Nightingale) and a track list running to “I Say a Little Prayer for You” and “Bars of Dundee”. The release date is given as “June 1995”; the album in fact appeared in 1994.

The text calls the album confirmation of the rebirth of the singer and guitarist, whose former band Doll by Doll had been “perennial underachievers”, that is, perpetually falling short of their ability. It then turns to the mugging, which plays a central part in Leven’s life story.
zitate_kontext: The reference book on Doll by Doll

1999-03-16-rockol-la-musica-in-televisio.kurz: Rockol's TV music listing for Tuesday 16 March 1999 gives “Roxy Bar” on TMC2 at 8.30 pm with Jackie Leven, Puertorico, Carmen Consoli and Negrita.
inhalt: The item is a television programme note from the Italian music site Rockol, titled “La musica in televisione martedì 16 marzo”. For 8.30 pm it announces the programme “Roxy Bar” on the channel TMC2, in which, besides Jackie Leven, the acts Puertorico, Carmen Consoli and Negrita appear or are guests.

The entry thus names an Italian television date for Leven. It is a pure announcement: which songs or conversation Leven contributed, and whether he really appeared, cannot be gathered from it, and no recording of the programme is known.

1999-05-27-radio-bremen-konzert-club-mom.titel: [Radio Bremen: concert recording of Jackie Leven, Club Moments Bremen, 27.05.1999]
1999-05-27-radio-bremen-konzert-club-mom.kurz: Radio Bremen recorded Leven's solo show at Club Moments in Bremen on 27 May 1999; in 2024 MiG released it as half of the four-CD box *Live Or Die – Live In Bremen 1999 & 2004*, with many stories between the songs.
inhalt: The page of the Hanover label MiG Music for the box *Live Or Die – Live In Bremen 1999 & 2004* (four CDs, released 26 April 2024, total running time 202:49) describes two recordings made by the broadcaster Radio Bremen “in the usual excellent sound quality”. Jackie played the 1999 concert at the Bremen music club “Moments” solo; in 2004, in Radio Bremen's broadcasting hall, he was accompanied on keyboards by his long-time friend and “web companion” Michael Cosgrave. The label's introductory text traces Leven's path: born in 1950 in Kirkcaldy (as the “son of an Irishman and a Roma”, the label's claim), starting in the late Sixties under the name John St. Field, under which *Control* was recorded in 1973, founding Doll by Doll in London in 1978, then, after the band disbanded in 1983, a solo career that took off only eleven years later with *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*. Leven died in 2011, aged 61, after a long, serious illness.

For the 1999 concert (CDs 1 and 2, 27 May) the track list gives: Intro, “Stranger on the Square”, “Call Mother a Lonely Field”, “Looking for Love”, “The Crazy Song”, “Jim O'Windygates”, “I Saw My Love Walk into Clouds” and, on CD 2, “Marble City Bar”, “Universal Blue – Poortoun”, “Single Father”, “Men in Prison” and “Gylen-Gylen”. Between the songs the spoken passages are separate tracks: “Jackie Talking About Football (Soccer)”, about the Irish singer Andy White, about city life, about his son Simon and about St. Kitts & Nevis, some almost seven minutes long and so longer than many songs. The 2004 concert (CDs 3 and 4, 29 March) includes “Single Father”, “My Philosophy”, “Fly”, “Alvis Green” (with a spoken lead-in track), a spoken track titled “Glen Matlock is drinking…”, “Empty in Soho Square”, “Classic Northern Diversions”, “Little Brown Box”, “Poortoun”, “Exit Wound”, “Call Mother a Lonely Field”, “Tied-Up House” and “Live or Die”. Whether and when Radio Bremen broadcast the 1999 recording the page does not say.
zitate_kontext: The label MiG Music on the two recordings
MiG Music on the Radio Bremen recordings

1999-08-bbc-radio-scotland-celtic-connec.kurz: Doug Anderson preserves on his fan site a BBC Radio Scotland session he happened to record in August 1999: five live tracks and a long conversation in which Leven talks about bursts of writing, a customs anecdote from Perth and his role models.
inhalt: Doug Anderson, who runs the fan site Rock Review, reproduces a session he happened to record in late August 1999 from the programme “Celtic Connections” on BBC Radio Scotland – his first contact with Leven’s music. The presenter, whose name he does not remember, played five live tracks: “Stranger on the Square”, “I Saw My Love Walk into Clouds”, “Call Mother a Lonely Field”, “The Crazy Song” and “Single Father”. In between came a longer conversation, which Anderson retells at length and partly transcribes.

Leven says he is still hung over from the gig “the other day” in Edinburgh and explains his high rate of releases – 14 albums by then – with a burst of creativity brought on by two months each year on a Greek island; he wants to record everything before “something terrible” happens to him. Songwriting, he says, has become easier with age. He writes on behalf of other people, not just about himself. At length he retells, in what he calls a “cleaned-up” version, the anecdote of the Australian customs officer in Perth who made him explain the meaning of a line from *Man Bleeds in Glasgow* and then had tickets for his concert.

Leven also says he has become a kind of representative of Scotland in the WOMAD world (Australia, New Zealand, Bali, South Africa). In Britain he plays solo because audiences want the stories; in Germany he plays with a band. Cooking Vinyl lets him make one solo live album a year; *The Wanderer* is in progress. He names Chet Baker (as a singer), Nat King Cole and Ani DiFranco (“Untouchable Face”) as role models, plus an interest in old, traditional music and the guitarist Martin Brown, with whom he had played in Aberdeen the year before. An addendum from 2001 dates the Edinburgh concert mentioned, using the Fringe programme, to Saturday 22 August 1999.
zitate_kontext: Leven at the start of the conversation, according to Anderson’s transcript

1999-3pbs-fm-brain-massage-jackie-leven.medium: 3PBS FM Melbourne, programme “Brain Massage” (recording on YouTube, channel Owlsley Burroughs)
1999-3pbs-fm-brain-massage-jackie-leven.kurz: A good 21 minutes of studio conversation with two live pieces, broadcast in Steve G. Mileham's programme “Brain Massage” on 3PBS FM Melbourne; the presenter uploaded the recording in 2022 under his stage name Owlsley Burroughs.
inhalt: A good 21 minutes of studio conversation with two live pieces, broadcast in Steve G. Mileham's programme “Brain Massage” on 3PBS FM Melbourne; the presenter uploaded the recording in 2022 under his stage name Owlsley Burroughs. Leven is on his second Australian trip, shortly after the first: by his own account he has come straight from a television programme with Bert Newton and goes back there afterwards, was at WOMADelaide and the Port Fairy Folk Festival, plays in Melbourne at the Continental and the Dan O'Connell, and travels on to WOMAD offshoots in Johannesburg and Auckland. He raves about Dan Penn and Spooner Oldham, says “Night Lilies” was made with “ruthless military precision”, explains the album title by the scent of night lilies on a Greek island that reminded him of a railway embankment in Scotland, and interprets the album as an arc spanning some 30 years of memory. He plays “Sick Harbour Lament” (the record company wanted to shorten the title) and, at the end, a second piece, tells the story of how “Elvis Green” came about (an American woman with a green vintage car, an interest in buying it on David Gilmour's part, her death the same night), describes the tension between dark lyrics and light music using Chet Baker as an example, and names John Cale/Terry Riley's “Church of Anthrax” as a model for “Carnival Dark”. Tone: relaxed promotional conversation rich in anecdotes; all stories are self-reports.

1999-balafon-bacon-london-live.kurz: Tony Bacon's book on London live clubs lists five Doll by Doll appearances at an unnamed club, starting on 6 October 1977, and shows the band in monthly calendars next to Squeeze, the Skids and Wilko Johnson.
inhalt: *London Live: From the Yardbirds to Pink Floyd to the Sex Pistols* (Balafon Books, 1999) tells the story of London's live clubs and contains lists of appearances. In one chapter, the club not being evident from the search snippet (the Marquee is presumed), a chart lists Doll by Doll with five appearances: on 6 October 1977, 2 December 1977, 7 February 1979 and 10 April 1979, plus one further date.

The book's monthly calendars show the band among groups such as Squeeze, Five Hand Reel, the Skids, Wreckless Eric and Wilko Johnson. The details matter because they document dated London club gigs by the band from October 1977 on, and so contribute to the question of when Doll by Doll actually began playing. The club's name and the complete list appear only in the book.

1999-collectors-guide-fitch-pink-floyd-e.kurz: Vernon Fitch's *Pink Floyd Encyclopedia* (1999) and Glenn Povey's *Echoes* (2010) list Leven and *Grand Passion* because of David Gilmour's guest spot: a personal entry, a band entry and full credits.
inhalt: Because David Gilmour guested in 1982 on *Grand Passion*, Doll by Doll's last album, Vernon Fitch's *The Pink Floyd Encyclopedia* (Collector's Guide Publishing, Burlington, Ontario, 1999) gives Jackie Leven an entry of his own (“Scottish musician. Guitar. Vocals. Former …”). There is also an entry “Doll By Doll – A British band” and song entries with full credits: produced by Tom Newman and Leven, with Tom Norden, Rod Bedall, Graham Broad and Tori Josias among the players. Glenn Povey lists the album (UK: MAGL 5047) in his Gilmour session discography in *Echoes: The Complete History of Pink Floyd* (Chicago Review Press, 2010).
The two books are mainly useful as a source for the line-up and production details of *Grand Passion*.

1999-cooking-vinyl-jackie-leven-kuenstle.kurz: Cooking Vinyl's 1999 artist page: Leven's life from Fife through *Control*, Doll by Doll, the attack, heroin and the CORE Trust to Robert Bly, plus a discography with press quotes, his notes on *Control*, an interview and a fan-club box.
inhalt: The label's biography begins with Leven's origins: born in 1950 in the Kingdom of Fife, he grew up among dying coal fields and fading woollen mills, and his song imagery is still shaped by that early witnessing of a culture in crisis. His mother loved jazz and the black American blues of Lightnin' Hopkins; add Protestant hymn-singing at school and “the dank salty common songs of Fife”, and these are named as the melodic root of his songwriting. In the Sixties, a love of Russian and American poetry and the pull of West Coast and acid rock layered over that, all of it, the page says, surfacing on the “acid-hazed” album *Control* of 1971, made under the pseudonym John St. Field. Through the early and mid-Seventies he played mainly to observe life in different parts of the world, including half-year stretches in Madrid under Franco and in a still divided Berlin.

“Celtic Soul” is the label's description of his work, placing him in an ancestral line with Van Morrison, Lightnin' Hopkins and the unnamed singers of work-songs from every corner of the earth. His first serious impact on the UK scene came in the late Seventies with Doll by Doll, a hard-hitting classic outfit of two guitars, bass and drums that beguiled audiences when it wasn't “scaring the pants off them”. The five albums are listed as *Remember*, *Gypsy Blood*, *Doll By Doll*, *Grand Passion* and *A Last Flick of the Golden Wrench*; the group disbanded in 1982, tired of struggling against the punk and new wave preoccupations of the time.

In 1983 Leven began recording as a solo artist but was, in the same year, nearly murdered; of the attack he remembers only “a powerful arm coming around my neck”. His larynx was almost destroyed, he was silenced for years and turned to heroin, and his girlfriend ran off with the Dalai Lama's bodyguard. After a year of addiction he decided he “wanted his life back” and freed himself with a method of his own using acupuncture, psychic healing and reflexology. Out of this came the CORE Trust, a registered addictions charity in central London; the page wrongly dates its founding to 1995 (elsewhere 1985). Diana, Princess of Wales, it says, was guest of honour at fundraising events and officially opened the premises, and CORE's success rate is among the highest in Europe.

Later came the friendship with Robert Bly, author of *Iron John*, and Leven's role as spokesman for “men's work”, with appearances for Gloria Hunniford, on *Kilroy*, at the Tate Gallery, the Royal College of Art and BBC Scotland television. “No wonder”, the paragraph concludes, that he has earned a reputation as the thinking man's rock star. Since signing to Cooking Vinyl he has released five albums (*The Mystery of Love …*, *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West*, *The Argyll Cycle Volume 1*, *Fairy Tales for Hard Men* and *Night Lilies*). The biography also names the Jahrespreis der Deutschen Schallplattenkritik, “the most prestigious and serious critical German award”, and predicts that he will “go down in history as a genius of his time”. A MOJO line serves as motto at the top.

The discography sub-page gives each album's details, track listing and press extracts, among them Q (calling *The Mystery of Love …* one of the top ten albums of 1994 and “Call Mother a Lonely Field” the most awesome song of the year), MOJO and the Rheinische Post. For *Control*, reissued in 1997, the page lets Leven speak: his favourite track is “Soft Lowland Tongue”, written when he was married to a wealthy young woman and living in her parents' castle in the Scottish Lowlands, riding out alone to remote country bars. The cover is an illustration of Balzac's story *The Devil's Heir* by R. A. Brandt, and on interpretation he says nothing is more culturally important than not solving mysteries. A fan-club box promotes The Haunted Valley (£14 or £20, four newsletters, one free CD a year, the first of rare 1960s material by the duo St Judas); the only web link is Jan Saghaug's fan site.

1999-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.titel: [Collected finds from Nasjonalbiblioteket 1999: news items, announcements, lists]
1999-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.kurz: In 1999 Norwegian newspapers mention Jackie Leven only in passing: listening tips, a look back at blues courses and a Bodø fan’s top ten, but no concert and no new album.
inhalt: After the strong Norwegian years of 1995 to 1998, 1999 shows a clear decline in Norwegian press coverage: the National Library’s full-text search finds only 14 issues naming Jackie Leven. A Norwegian concert by Leven that year cannot be established from this, nor a new album.

The freely readable hits are mentions. In February several papers (Fremover, Nordlands Framtid) carry an NTB sports piece noting that the ski racer Lasse Paulsen listens to Jackie Leven, among others, to relax. On 17 March Bergensavisen looks back at the sold-out Ole Blues seminars of autumn 1998 with Leven and Nils Lofgren, whose waiting lists were long. In July Lofotposten mentions Cooking Vinyl as the label of XTC and Leven in connection with the Andy White reissues. In October Nordlandsposten profiles a reader in Bodø, whose top ten includes *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West*; in November Jærbladet cites Leven as a listening recommendation from a singer.

Further mentions in Bergens Tidende, Stavanger Aftenblad, Strilen and Hallingdølen are accessible only via the National Library and, judging by their extent (one to three mentions each), do not suggest longer articles. The sum: Leven stayed present in the background, but not at the centre.

1999-rough-guides-rough-guide-to-rock.kurz: Justin Lewis's signed entry in *Rock: The Rough Guide* outlines Doll by Doll (London, 1977–83) and Leven's path from John St Field solo performer to prolific solo artist in the 1990s – an often underrated talent.
inhalt: The “Doll By Doll” entry in *Rock: The Rough Guide* (1st edn 1996, 2nd edn 1999, 3rd edn 2003) was written by Justin Lewis; Leven is indexed on p. 257 (1st edn) and p. 291 (2nd edn). The heading reads “Formed London, 1977; disbanded 1983”.

Leven first appeared on the club circuit as a solo singer and guitarist under the name John St Field; “Strip Show” is said to date from that time. In 1977 he founded the guitar band with Jo Shaw, Robin Spreafico and David McIntosh; Tony Waite replaced Spreafico. The third album feels lighter, with the folky ballad “Main Travelled Roads”; *Grand Passion* followed, and another album was recorded but never released. In the 1980s Leven played with former members and Glen Matlock; in 1994 a mini-CD available only in Scotland appeared, after which he was relatively prolific through the 1990s. Lewis calls him an often underrated talent.
zitate_kontext: Heading of the Doll By Doll entry.

2000-01-26-bergensavisen-plate-jackie-le.kurz: Tore Bø calls *Defending Ancient Springs* melancholic and resigned: the opening cover cannot match the Righteous Brothers, but “Single Father” is probably the loveliest song Leven has written; he also flags the 1 March concert.
inhalt: Tore Bø reviews *Defending Ancient Springs* (Cooking Vinyl/MNW) in Bergensavisen in a short, benevolent record review. A predominantly melancholic, resigned mood hangs over Leven's latest record. The tone is set by the opening cover of “You've Lost That Loving Feeling”, which sounds good but cannot bear comparison with the Righteous Brothers' classic version.

By contrast Leven's own “Single Father” is probably the loveliest song he has ever written: full of grey weather, fog and lost love, it tells of lost industrial jobs and a type of person who has simply disappeared. “I Saw My Love Walk Into Clouds” is Scottish soul at its most effective. The review ends with a pointer that you can see the man live on 1 March at Stundik'en in Bergen – “Be there”, as they say in Nynorsk.
zitate_kontext: Tore Bø on the album's overall mood.

2000-01-29-drammens-tidende-skotsk-magi.kurz: An enthusiastic short review of *Defending Ancient Springs* in Drammens Tidende: nobody sings like Leven, this is the “friend of Norway’s” 18th album, with David Thomas of Pere Ubu on a duet – “Recommended!”
inhalt: This short review in Drammens Tidende (29 January 2000) opens by saying there is no one who sings like the Scot Jackie Leven. He is a folksy troubadour, a “pop carpenter” and former rocker with Doll By Doll in the late 1970s. After many years away from music he returned with *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death*, one of the ten best albums of the 1990s. Over the following years he has been very productive, and now the “friend of Norway”, who will soon tour there, is back with *Defending Ancient Springs* – album number 18, the paper says.

Singled out are David Thomas of the cult band Pere Ubu, who sings with Leven on the classic “You’ve Lost That Lovin’ Feelin’” (“incidentally a lovely version”), and the ballad “Single Father”. On a couple of tracks Leven tries new paths that are “a little more *Paris, Texas*”, more Ry Cooder and Tom Waits. Musicians from the circles of James, The Christians and Lighthouse Family take part. The critic is once again “completely lost” in this special singer’s world of poverty, fate, love and the belief that it will all work out in the end.

Leven, he concludes, is an artist you develop a personal relationship with; anyone who has not yet heard his fine voice should do so now. Verdict: “Recommended!” (MNW). The author cannot be identified.

2000-01-cooking-vinyl-defending-ancient-.kurz: Cooking Vinyl's announcement of Leven's 18th album *Defending Ancient Springs*: a life sketch from Fife via *Control* and Doll by Doll to the Cooking Vinyl albums, five audio samples and a London launch gig on 1 February 2000.
inhalt: The page announces Jackie Leven's “18th full-length album” *Defending Ancient Springs*. Leven is “in the true sense of the word, a remarkable man”, a songwriter “virtually without peer”, a natural raconteur, an unusual and brilliant guitarist and above all a singer of the rarest beauty. The music writer and biographer Brian Hinton (author of books on Joni Mitchell, Elvis Costello and Van Morrison) is quoted as saying that Leven's subjects are “love, violence, drink, poverty”. The man's own experience of these conditions, the text says, gives him the edge when he turns to his central theme, “the spirit at bay”.

Leven spent his childhood and teens in the dying coalfields of Fife in the fifties and sixties, where he had to reconcile his emerging musicality and enduring love of American and Russian poetry with the need to be “hard”, because the community regarded him as somehow an outsider. The resulting blend of tenderness, honesty and menace still informs his writing. At eighteen he left Scotland and became “a wonderer with a guitar”, living in Berlin, Madrid, the west of Ireland and Dorset. Throughout these years he distilled the themes of his songs, making the “acid-tinged” album *Control* as John St. Field in London in the early 1970s and moving on without regard to its release; it eventually came out in Spain only.

Next came five critically acclaimed albums (one unreleased) with the “hugely underrated” rock band Doll by Doll, who called it a day “through sheer exhaustion” in 1982. After the “serious illness” to which the page refers without describing it, his return to record-making came on Cooking Vinyl with *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* (with poetry readings by Robert Bly and ex-Waterboy Mike Scott), then *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West*, *The Argyll Cycle*, *Fairytales for Hardmen* and *Night Lilies* in 1998. It closes by saying that Leven “has no vision as such, but sees the extraordinary dreams of ordinary people”, of whom he is one; the coming year will see him tour the world to sing them again “with black humour and unlikely tales”.

On the practical side, five tracks (*You've Lost That Lovin' Feeling*, *Single Father*, *Your Winter Days*, *The Keys to the Forest*, *Paris Blues*) were offered as RealAudio samples, and the launch gig was on Tuesday 1 February 2000 at the Spitz, Commercial Street, London.
