The label on the end of Doll by Doll.

2000-01-wandering-dog-defending-ancient-.titel: [Review of Defending Ancient Springs, start-of-year column]
2000-01-wandering-dog-defending-ancient-.medium: wandering.dog (private music site at Virgin Net)
2000-01-wandering-dog-defending-ancient-.kurz: Reviewed in an early-2000 end-of-year column on a private music site: *Defending Ancient Springs* takes several plays to open up because its varied sounds can smother the strong lyrics, but the title track, the Tsvetaeva setting and “Your Winter Days” make it worth the effort.
inhalt: The anonymous review opens a column written at the start of 2000: the beginning of the year is quiet because new releases are slow to arrive, so it is a good moment to look back at the best CDs of 1999. First comes Jackie Leven, whose album *Defending Ancient Springs* (Cooking Vinyl, made with David Thomas) only just qualifies as a 2000 release. The writer recalls that Leven played at the end of the Wessex Poetry Festival in 1997 and toured as support for Bruce Cockburn around that time, noting “some similarities” between the two. Originally from Fife, Leven is no newcomer, but after years of being strangely ignored his latest album is receiving favourable attention.

The sepia-coloured sleevenotes, the reviewer says, trace the title to an idea of the poet Kathleen Raine and include quotations from John Burnside, Antonio Machado and Juan Ramón Jiménez (in Robert Bly's translation), Rumi and Mandelstam. It is odd for a singer-songwriter to open with a cover version, here the Righteous Brothers' “You've Lost That Loving Feeling”, but it has a “strange edginess” that sets a bleak tone for the rest.

The album took several plays to get into, partly because the lyrically very strong songs are hindered by the varied mix of sounds around Leven's soulful vocals: a full band on most tracks, occasional brass, orchestra, backing vocals, clanking industrial effects and spoken word. It is worth persevering. The title track and the setting of a poem by Marina Tsvetayeva, “Hand Is Pale With Holy Kisses”, are particularly haunting, and the spare acoustic “Your Winter Days” is, for the reviewer, the best track of all. The verdict: plenty of loss and pain on this fine album, even menace in the closing “Morbid Sky”, and a soulful lyricism that shines through.
zitate_kontext: The anonymous reviewer on getting into the album

2000-02-01-dagsavisen-liv-og-leven.kurz: Geir Rakvaag finds *Defending Ancient Springs* very fine but not different enough from its two near-superb predecessors – the price of being so thoroughly one's own thing; the closing “Morbid Sky” with David Thomas is its peak.
inhalt: Geir Rakvaag reviews *Defending Ancient Springs* (Cooking Vinyl/MNW) in Dagsavisen. Leven is “true to himself”, with a series of emotionally charged songs about men and women and the great loneliness that follows. He opens with Phil Spector's “You've Lost That Loving Feeling” to underline where he stands and continues with painful but highly poetic observations on life's commonest afflictions.

David Thomas of Pere Ubu joins on accordion, with a band of former members of James, The Christians and Lighthouse Family, yet it is once again Leven's own life that stands at the centre in his characteristic folk rock. The only exception is the closing “Morbid Sky”, actually taken from a performance by David Thomas's Pale Orchestra with Leven in the ranks, and perhaps the album's strongest moment.

Rakvaag's verdict: the new songs are very fine but not different enough from the two nearly formidable preceding records – perhaps the price to pay for being so utterly something of one's own. Leven plays Oslo on 28 February and then tours the country.

2000-02-03-the-daily-telegraph-the-lost-.kurz: Large portrait on the release of *Defending Ancient Springs*, Leven's sixth solo album for Cooking Vinyl, which McCormick considers perhaps his best.
inhalt: Large portrait on the release of *Defending Ancient Springs*, Leven's sixth solo album for Cooking Vinyl, which McCormick considers perhaps his best. Leitmotif: talent and fame have little to do with each other – Leven is the “great lost British rock star”. McCormick portrays Doll by Doll as the industry's hottest hope at one time, undone by a ruinous contract with Automatic; around 1982 Leven was solo and signed to Chrysalis. Leven tells of the attack in north London (choking, kicking, rescue by his producer in a Range Rover), the broken ribs, the injured larynx, almost 18 months without a voice, steroids with weight gain and the feeling of being “covered in electric fur”, then a year of heroin. Self-healing with acupuncture and “psychic healing” led in 1985 to the founding of the CORE Trust, whose centre Princess Diana opened. The girlfriend who had accompanied him through everything ran off with the Dalai Lama's bodyguard (Leven's punchline: she had met him as an acupuncturist). Leven reflects at length on the loss of his falsetto, which made him a terser, more considered writer, and on his position “more like a poet than a pop musician”, who has to make a brilliant record every 18 months. The connection to Robert Bly and the men's movement is mentioned. Tone: admiring, with blunt remarks about Leven's appearance (double chin, belly).
zitate_kontext: Leven on the consequences of the attack.

2000-02-07-wiseacre-defending-ancient-sp.kurz: A short review: apart from the lame opening cover of “You've Lost That Loving Feeling”, *Defending Ancient Springs* is a strong album, with Leven in fine voice and in form as a songwriter.
inhalt: The review in the webzine wiseacre opens with a joke about the acronymed buttons on a CD player that nobody ever works out: start learning them, it says, because anyone who slots in *Defending Ancient Springs* is in for a nasty shock unless they can skip track one. The culprit is the “insipid” version of “You've Lost That Loving Feeling” that opens the album.

After that comes relief: the rest of Leven's “zillionth” album, a collaboration with Pere Ubu's David Thomas, is considerably better. Leven is on terrific form both vocally (he has rarely sounded better) and as a songwriter. “The Working Man's Love Song” and the “gorgeous” “Single Father” are near-perfect, with “Your Winter Days” not far behind. That makes the decision to open with a lame cover all the more mystifying, but for anyone who can work the auto-skip on their hi-fi the album is well worth time and money.

2000-02-08-nordlands-framtid-gode-sanger.kurz: Kjell Nordeng praises Leven’s *Defending Ancient Springs* in Nordlands Framtid as an album between American rock and British folk – lonely, yearning, earthy and acoustic – and notes that Leven is “topical in Bodø”.
inhalt: Nordeng opens with a play on words: “Talk about timing” – Leven is topical in Bodø just as he releases these excellent new songs on CD. Like Mike Scott and Van Morrison, Leven stands in the cross-pressure between American rock elements and the folk music of the British Isles, “perhaps a little Springsteen” in a couple of the ballads. But he does not remind one of any of his more famous musical brothers.

The lyrics often have an undertone of loneliness and longing, which is reflected in the melancholy melodies. The arrangements are earthy, full and acoustic-based, with occasional more experimental moods. Leven’s expressive voice conveys this superbly. The material ranges from wistful ballads such as “Single Father” and “Paris Blues” to the tougher beats of “Morbid Sky”. In the classic “You’ve Lost That Loving Feeling”, with guest David Thomas of Pere Ubu, one hears that Leven is enough of an artist to give valuable personal interpretations. The paper prints the title as *Defending the Ancient Springs*.

2000-02-09-hamar-dagblad-poetisk-musikk.kurz: Geir Hovensjø recommends Leven’s 18th album *Defending Ancient Springs* as a simple, growing record between folk, country and blues; a box recounts the attack and recovery story.
inhalt: Geir Hovensjø’s review in Hamar Dagblad presents *Defending Ancient Springs* (Cooking Vinyl). The Scot is not that widely known, he says, but is in fact out with his 18th album. Leven is a musical wanderer who has lived in many places around Europe; the “poetry lover” always has something on his heart. He writes about life’s essential sides, love and misery, in a dark, simple and striking way.

The music is also quite simple, on the borderland between folk, country, blues and similar earthy things, the songs naturally and plainly built. He opens with Phil Spector’s old “You’ve Lost That Loving Feeling”, the rest being his own. When the set-up is so simple, mood and nerve must do the work, and Leven captures “all willing listeners”. The arrangements are very deliberate and underline text and melody without disturbing them. “This is a record that grows.”

An accompanying box, “Nesten drept, fant kur” (“Almost killed, found a cure”), summarises Leven’s story: in the early eighties he was almost strangled to death in an unprovoked attack on a London street while walking home from the studio; for a year he could neither speak nor sing and eased the pain with heroin. After that year he devised his own cure of acupuncture, physical healing and “reflexology”, so successful that he turned it into a system and founded The Core Trust. Princess Diana was among the supporters (the paper’s claim). Leven is also active in the men’s movement.

2000-02-18-glamdalen-en-fyr-uten-om-det-.kurz: Full-page portrait on the release of *Defending Ancient Springs*, according to a note at the end based on a text by Kjell Haglund in the magazine *Pop* (no. 24/1997).
inhalt: Full-page portrait on the release of *Defending Ancient Springs*, according to a note at the end based on a text by Kjell Haglund in the magazine *Pop* (no. 24/1997). The biography is told in Leven's version: born some 50 years ago among the dying coalfields of Fife, on the road at 18 as a hippie (Dorset, Madrid, Berlin, western Ireland), living for two months in an abandoned lighthouse on dog biscuits and water; in this period the “acid-soaked” album *Control* as John St. Field. Doll by Doll is compared with Television (long, complex songs, Verlaine-like poetry); after ever quieter records the band split up in 1983 out of exhaustion.

The attack is described like this: Leven was walking home at night with a freshly signed solo contract in his pocket when someone choked him from behind until he lay unconscious in the gutter; prescribed painkillers led to pill addiction, then heroin addiction. A withdrawal took him to little Argyll, where he recovered after a year of addiction and began writing again in 1985, while building up the CORE Trust. After a failed relationship he moved to London; meeting Robert Bly and his men's movement (*Iron John*, in Norwegian “Mannen”) shaped his career – five albums in four years – and spun on the Celtic thread of “Main Travelled Roads”. Musically he sounds like a sharpened Van Morrison at his best. Conclusion: Leven's life is the message that one can stumble and get up again.

2000-02-18-jaerbladet-jackie-leven-defen.titel: [Jackie Leven: Defending Ancient Springs – review with profile boxes]
2000-02-18-jaerbladet-jackie-leven-defen.kurz: Sølve Friestad in Jærbladet: a review of *Defending Ancient Springs* praising the woven folk but faulting the opening cover and “Keys to the Forest”, plus biography boxes and an announcement of the Café Sting gig in Stavanger.
inhalt: The music page of Jærbladet (Bryne) of 18 February 2000 combines Sølve Friestad's record review with biographical boxes on Leven. The review: “the Leven mood can be heard once again” when Leven gets going with his atmospheric, accomplished melodies; one could almost call him a “poetic artist”. On his 18th album he weaves folk music masterfully together with poetic lyrics, the sound is mostly calm but there are some livelier arrangements. Friestad sees two mistakes: “Keys to the Forest” is too sorrowful and dead, with an irritating chorus, and the re-recording of “You've Lost That Loving Feeling” is “just ugly” and, worse, put first on the album. “Otherwise everything is totally maximal”; folk fans should check it out. Tips: “Paris Blues”, “The Working Man's Lovesong” and “Defending Ancient Springs”.

The boxes tell Leven's story briefly: he left Scotland at 18, lived by playing the guitar and stayed in Berlin, Madrid and Dorset; during these “drifter years” he wrote the songs of the album *Control* (early seventies) as John St. Field, “released only in Spain?”. In the late seventies and early eighties he made five records with Doll by Doll, “one was never released”. In the early eighties Leven was “nearly murdered” after an unprovoked attack on the way home from a London studio, could neither speak nor sing for over a year, took heroin for the pain and after a year freed himself with a method of his own, combining acupuncture, psychic healing and reflexology. This led to the CORE Trust, which Lady Diana visited and opened. In the early nineties he befriended the poet Robert Bly, who together with Mike Scott (Waterboys) read poems on *The Mystery of Love…*.

A photo caption headed “Melankoli” says his one-man show is “warmly recommended”: he comes from Scotland but is not stingy with either good songs or “crooked stories” when he plays. The photo is from last year's concert at Café Sting in Stavanger. On Sunday 5 March “the Scot” comes to Café Sting again.
zitate_kontext: Friestad on “You've Lost That Loving Feeling”.

2000-02-28-gaesteliste-bodenstaendigkeit.kurz: First of five Gaesteliste interviews by Ullrich Maurer with Leven, on the release of “Defending Ancient Springs” (2000).
inhalt: First of five Gaesteliste interviews by Ullrich Maurer with Leven, on the release of “Defending Ancient Springs” (2000). Maurer introduces Leven as an “oddball” who found a home at Cooking Vinyl after Doll by Doll. Leven says he has rediscovered the magic of songwriting from his beginnings; as Doll by Doll's singer he was a boy, today he is a man. He explains the album title with the (pseudoscientific) idea that water has a memory: every person is born with a kind of inherited memory, which one defends in old age by reflecting on one's roots. He goes on to explain individual pieces: “Your Winter Days” is based on a folk song from Oban, “Hand Is Pale With Holy Kisses” on a poem by Marina Tsvetaeva, “You've Lost That Loving Feeling” is a dark, paranoid, underrated song; plus short poems from the Spanish. He relates that an American friend told him during his Berlin period that for the British it is never about travelling, but about homesickness and return. David Thomas (Pere Ubu), whom he got to know through “Mirror Man”, Maurer calls a kindred spirit; “Morbid Sky” from the project is on the album. “Paris Blues” goes back to a scene in a Paris café with Thomas (self-report). Tone: benevolent, slightly ironic towards Leven's philosophy.

2000-03-01-bergensavisen-berost-leven.kurz: Preview of the concert the same evening at Den Stundesløse (“Stundik'en”) with an interview. Leven (49) says he is lucky: nobody steers him, he is with a small company that lets him get on with it – quite unlike Van Morrison or Bob Dylan, who always have someone above them.
inhalt: Preview of the concert the same evening at Den Stundesløse (“Stundik'en”) with an interview. Leven (49) says he is lucky: nobody steers him, he is with a small company that lets him get on with it – quite unlike Van Morrison or Bob Dylan, who always have someone above them. The reviews of *Defending Ancient Springs* are overwhelming; Rolf Sejersted, who brought him back to Norway, sees him on the verge of the big breakthrough, and a big American label has offered him a contract – “then freedom is probably over”.

Asked whether “The Working Man's Lovesong” might be about the closure of the shipyard in Laksevåg, Leven answers that he believes everything goes in circles. His songs are more joy at having experienced something good than blues; he shares an African view of death as a reunion with the ancestors. Inspiration: poets, philosophers, Chet Baker, R. L. Burnside, Johnny Dowd and “David Munyan”, who inspired him to write “Single Father”. One should not analyse his music to death, but see the images. Turning 50 feels good, he never liked being young.

2000-03-02-nordlys-leven-med-leven.kurz: Telephone interview on the day of the concert in Tromsø (Blå Rock Café). Leven, with a cold, promises old songs (“easier to play”) alongside new ones.
inhalt: Telephone interview on the day of the concert in Tromsø (Blå Rock Café). Leven, with a cold, promises old songs (“easier to play”) alongside new ones. On the theme of *Defending Ancient Springs* he says that the “straight arrow of time” of the modern world troubles him; he likes the idea that time runs in a circle. The album is about the water you have in your body at birth and which is gradually replaced; all your life you long for it, and at death you should have the same water back. Where the idea came from he no longer remembers; he is interested in a holistic view of body and health.

On the tour: the Oslo concert went well, 260 spectators, he played “bloody well” but was nervous – it was his first concert since a gig in Pittsburgh in December; after a flu infection he even had to go to hospital. The day before had been the second tour concert, in Bergen. With its snow, Tromsø reminds him of the Scotland of his childhood, he would like to come in summer one day; he values Egon (Holstad) of the Blå Rock and the Grand Hotel, where he always stays, especially its bar.

2000-03-02-rogalands-avis-stilsikker-fra.kurz: Two pieces by Svein Reidar Myklebust in Rogalands Avis: a review of *Defending Ancient Springs* (a “stylish performer of his own set-to-music short stories”) and a preview of the Stavanger concert with a long life sketch.
inhalt: On 2 March 2000 Rogalands Avis (Stavanger) prints two texts by Svein Reidar Myklebust side by side. The review calls Leven “a crooked observer of life with a rare gift as a songwriter” who enchants with his songs, sung in a melodic baritone to his own unique guitar playing. All his albums have plenty of beautiful songs, but it is sometimes hard to tell them apart. *Defending Ancient Springs* is “somewhat rawer than usual” – thanks to David Thomas of Pere Ubu, who sings on a couple of tracks, especially on the last one, “Morbid Sky” with David Thomas and the Pale Orchestra, where Leven is the vocalist. He dares to start the album with Thomas in their own unique take on “You've Lost That Loving Feeling”, so that you forget the Righteous Brothers and hear the words. The title track and “Single Father” are built so that they can be heard many times. With six solo albums for Cooking Vinyl, the former Doll by Doll singer has established himself as “a stylish performer of his own set-to-music short stories”.

The preview “Jackie Leven til Stavanger igjen” announces Leven “from the Kingdom of Fife” at Sting Nere next Sunday, for the fourth time, to present his 18th album. It was recorded at the Bryn Derwen studio in western Snowdonia in Wales, in the shadow of the world's largest slate quarry, with views of palm trees, forest, mountains and lakes. Myklebust quotes the music writer Brian Hinton that Leven's subjects are “love, violence, drink and poverty”, and retells the familiar story: childhood and youth in the dying coalfields of Fife, Doll by Doll and their debut *Remember*, four more albums (the last unreleased), the band stopping in 1982 from exhaustion. Then the attack on the way home from a London studio, a year without speech or song; for the pain the doctor first gave him anabolic steroids, which made things worse, then heroin, the “classic drug of desperation”, the self-cure with acupuncture, physical healing and reflexology, and the founding of the CORE Trust. Finally Robert Bly, Richard Olivier, James Hillman and the men's groups. The closing line: Leven is a singer you must be in the right mood to appreciate, but when you are he always gives the audience “full reward”.
zitate_kontext: Myklebust at the end of his review.
Myklebust at the end of the preview.

2000-03-02-tromso-jackie-leven-vender-ti.kurz: Helge Matland in the daily Tromsø: a preview of Leven's fifth visit – probably the only international artist to thank Tromsø bars on record sleeves – with promoter Egon Holstad on critical acclaim and disappointing sales.
inhalt: The preview “Jackie Leven vender tilbake” (“Jackie Leven returns”) appeared in the paper Tromsø on 2 March 2000. Helge Matland asks which international artists give thanks to Tromsø bars on their record sleeves – “hardly anyone other than the Scot Jackie Leven”. First the Blå Rock Café was honoured on one of his many records, listed among the bars that had meant something to the Scottish musician; on the next release it was the Grand bar. And this evening, his fifth visit to the town “he has fallen in love with”, he plays, as always, the intimate stage at the Blå Rock Café.

Promoter Egon Holstad (Blå Rock Café and the record shop Feedback) says: “I always think it's great to have Jackie Leven back,” and welcomes the media attention; he “could hardly believe” what he saw when Leven appeared on the NRK news Dagsrevyen on Monday. Critics have always been enthusiastic, but he has largely been let down by record buyers; mostly only the specially interested have bought the records, hence no big media coverage – “unless that is now about to change”.

About the man: Leven fronted Doll by Doll, who released four records from 1979 to 1982, were declared geniuses by critics but largely overlooked by buyers at a time when the new wave grabbed the attention. The band broke up in 1982 and Leven began his first solo project, but his solo career took off only in the nineties; since 1994 albums have come out roughly annually. They show “a peculiar musician with beauty, poetry, atmosphere and reflection”; Celtic melancholy cannot be avoided, but it never gets to steer the music alone. Holstad describes Leven as a live act: some still live under the delusion that Jackie is “a travelling troubadour with a guitar, warbling his sad songs”; those who know what he stands for live agree that this capacity and brilliant songwriter, “not to mention entertainer”, is among the most captivating and magical things one can experience live. Leven himself thinks the Tromsø concerts are something special, mainly because of an enthusiastic and disciplined audience.
zitate_kontext: Egon Holstad on a common misconception about Leven.
Egon Holstad on critics and record buyers.

2000-03-03-bergensavisen-gudbenadet-kar.kurz: Frank Johnsen credits Leven at Den Stundesløse in Bergen with a stage authority beyond most song-writers: a God-given voice, acoustic guitar, stamping foot and a loose tongue, plus autobiographical stories full of humour.
inhalt: Frank Johnsen reviews Leven's concert at Den Stundesløse for Bergensavisen. Leven has a stage authority that surpasses most singer-songwriters, he writes: with a God-given voice, an acoustic guitar, a steady-beating foot and a foul mouth he drew the audience into his own tragicomic universe.

What sets him apart from many artists of similar standing are the mostly autobiographical stories between the songs. He has a great deal to convey, and humour always lies like a steady carpet beneath the bittersweet episodes from a long life. Leven has also discovered a central point of the Norwegian folk soul: Norwegians always phone when you are sitting on the toilet. He can be at home enjoying the throne, the phone suddenly rings, and he thinks at once that it is surely Frank Nes (of Ole Blues); the room fell about laughing.

In the end, though, it is the music that counts, and Leven disappointed nobody, whether one is a fan of the latest record, *Defending Ancient Springs*, or wants a deep dive into his rich song archive. The classics came like pearls on a string. A microphone placed at foot level picked up his stamping beat, which together with a fantastic guitar technique in which the whole body of the instrument is used to evoke moods meant that a band was hardly missed.

2000-03-03-rolling-stone-de-defending-an.kurz: Jörg Feyer sees *Defending Ancient Springs* as the meeting of two awkward spirits: Leven and David Thomas's pared-down “You've Lost That Loving Feeling” exposes its paranoia, while the overloaded title song persuades less than the concentrated pieces; appreciative with reservations.
inhalt: The review in the German Rolling Stone (3 March 2000) begins: “Two people have found each other.” Jackie Leven and David Thomas would not be themselves if they did not immediately want to set a beacon for their joint cause. So the pop monument “You've Lost That Loving Feeling” is not ground to crumbs by force, but the drop from Spector's sound mania to this reduced, moderately modern interpretation is there, and behind the romantic shell lets one feel the paranoia Leven always suspected in the song.

If *Night Lilies* was merely “the fragrant wake-up call for all sorts of amorous entanglements”, Leven's reminiscence of youth on Scotland's east coast is spread decidedly wider this time, musically too: in the ambitious title song he aims at “the big picture” with “monstrous sound bites and mighty riffs”, but he is better and more compelling when he does not force everything into one picture and concentrates on striking details. Feyer cites the quiet suffering of a “Single Father” who can only shrug laconically and bitterly at the end (“Now half the world is working, half is watching T.V. Some take smack and fall right back, it's all the same to me”), the gentle promise of the “Working Man's Love Song” (“We will have music, everywhere we go”) and a dying love in winter.

It is winter here at all times anyway: “The snow was like a razor, cut his mind away”, David Thomas whines in “Paris Blues”; there is much “cruelly still, impenetrable snow” also in “Hand Is Pale With Holy Kisses”, the setting of a poem by Marina Tsvetayeva, whose picture is on the cover. In the “fairy-tale-cruel folk étude” “The Keys to the Forest” the unhappy man even lands in the latrine, where “kiss” rhymes with “piss” – “that is on the very edge”. And then, under “Morbid Sky”, it becomes utterly unbounded again: “In my head morning never comes”, Leven rants, the Pale Orchestra swells cacophonously and menacingly, against which even their “You've Lost That Loving Feeling” does not sound paranoid in the least. Leven and Thomas had found each other, the review notes, at the “Mirror Man” project at London's Queen Elizabeth Hall. No mark is given.

Feyer on the end of the album

2000-03-03-tonsbergs-blad-poeten-leven.kurz: Portrait distributed via the NTB Pluss agency at the start of the tour. The “friend of Norway” sees himself above all as a poet.
inhalt: Portrait distributed via the NTB Pluss agency at the start of the tour. The “friend of Norway” sees himself above all as a poet. It recounts the near-death after a mugging in the early 80s (almost strangled, without a voice for over a year), then heroin – and his girlfriend running off with the Dalai Lama's bodyguard. His 18th album has now been released; the European tour began “this week” at John Dee in Oslo and continues to Bergen, Tromsø, Trondheim and Stavanger.

Leven says he does not know exactly why he starts in Norway; he likes the country at this time of year, especially Tromsø; he has never played in Norway or Sweden in good weather. He likes the Norwegian audience, even if it is sometimes rather drunk, especially in Bodø and Kabelvåg. He takes it as a compliment that he is called the great lost British rock star: in every generation some get lost, he lost commercially, but he is more a poet than a rock star and only ever wanted to play in a rock band. His boyhood wish to travel the world with a guitar has come true; he got lost and was found. He lives in a happy relationship with a jazz singer; “Single Father” is about his adult son.

2000-03-04-nordlys-grisete-sentimental.kurz: A concert review from Tromsø: Leven alternates between “howlingly funny” and “tear-drippingly sentimental”, in sharp contrast to the poetry of his songs. Open-D tuning and virtuoso fingerpicking recall an acoustic Rory Gallagher.
inhalt: Torkil Emberland reviews Leven’s concert at the Blå Rock Café on Thursday 2 March in Nordlys (4 March 2000). The headline “Grisete sentimental” (“grubbily sentimental”) sums up the evening’s two faces. When Leven invites you to a concert, the chat goes something like this: he was apparently on national television but had no time to watch it – too busy watching porn films in his hotel room. If you switch channels very fast you can watch two films at once without paying, but then it is “almost impossible” to find relief at the same time. Emberland finds this in “sharp contrast to the exquisite poetry” of the songs: “howlingly funny” and “tear-drippingly sentimental” by turns.

The old Doll by Doll rocker has travelled alone with a guitar for years, a rattly old guitar that is “more a body part than an instrument”. He underlines the sadness of the songs with open D tuning and virtuoso fingerwork with elements of both Delta blues and Highland folk tunes, “like an acoustic Rory Gallagher”. The Blå Rock, with its tight corners and small stage, suits this format “like a glove”; the audience was disciplined, so quiet you could hear a pin drop. There is not room for many, but everyone should buy his latest album, *Defending Ancient Springs*.
zitate_kontext: Leven’s patter, as reported by Emberland

2000-03-04-tromso-en-opplagt-jackie-leve.kurz: A positive review of the solo concert at Tromsø’s Blå Rock Café: a “brilliantly in-form” Leven with sensitive songs and subtly witty stories; a folksy aura, Celtic melancholy, a solid guitarist.
inhalt: Helge Matland reviews Thursday night’s concert at the Blå Rock Café (2 March) in the newspaper “Tromsø” (4 March 2000). A “brilliantly in-form” Jackie Leven, with sensitive renderings of new and older songs linked by funny, subtly witty stories, created a dense, good atmosphere. When Leven enters the stage it has to be an intimate concert in a hushed mood: words matter, both in the songs’ beautiful lyrics and in the stories shaped by good storytelling and Leven’s own humour, and one simply has to listen intently. That gives a particular calm while the music plays and a warm, humming mood between the songs. Only one man, drunk and more interested in hearing his own voice than Leven’s, disturbed the evening – without being able to spoil it.

The reviewer has been enthusiastic about Leven’s records since his solo breakthrough with *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death* (1994) and *Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West* the year after; annual releases have followed. Although Leven first visited Tromsø as early as 1996, he had never managed to catch a gig – and hearing him on stage was “another dimension”. “Jackie Leven has charisma.” He is unpretentious in delivery, and his easy-going way with the audience makes him seem a very folksy artist, “a man on our level”. The songs feel like results of his lived life, with beauty, poetry, atmosphere and reflection. Celtic melancholy is unavoidable but never allowed to steer the music alone; the big rock’n’roll factor is not there, and nothing in the situation invites it. Besides being a good singer with a sensitive voice, Leven is a solid guitarist, which matters especially when he performs entirely solo.
zitate_kontext: Helge Matland on Leven’s stage presence

2000-03-16-haugesunds-avis-lavmaelt-og-m.kurz: Tor Tessem praises Leven's album *Defending Ancient Springs* in Haugesunds Avis as quiet, melodic songs between American rock and Scottish heritage, with gems such as “Paris Blues”, “Keys To The Forest” and “Morbid Sky”.
inhalt: Tor Tessem reviews *Defending Ancient Springs* (Cooking Vinyl/MNW) in Haugesunds Avis. Leven has by now become what one might call “a friend of Norway”, meant in a positive sense, with a fabulous voice and a fantastic joy in storytelling that he conveys at the crossroads of Celtic music, rock and folk. On the current album he carries on doing what he does best: quiet, melodic songs that lean on the one hand towards American rock like John Hiatt and on the other keep faith with his Scottish roots. As a finishing touch he fills the songs with sound textures usually heard in more experimental music.

The reviewer concedes that the album has its less happy moments: Leven's attempt at “You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin'” and the simple, slightly sentimental “Single Father” do not quite suit him. But that matters little when there are also gems such as “Paris Blues”, “Keys To The Forest” and “Morbid Sky”.

2000-03-25-westfaelische-rundschau-die-g.kurz: Bernd Berke celebrates Leven’s concert at the Zeche in Bochum: a voice “from a chest the size of Pavarotti’s”, deeply moving songs and “Celtic soul” that, as an insider tip, is staggeringly underrated.
inhalt: For the Westfälische Rundschau Bernd Berke describes a “nicely smoky club atmosphere” in Bochum’s Zeche, full of the initiated: someone calls out “Single Father” and everyone knows what that means – the sad song about the single father, a subject not everyone sings about. Leven’s full-toned voice, saturated with folk, blues and partly bitter life experience (two failed marriages, overcome heroin addiction), comes from a chest “of Pavarotti’s dimensions”; if necessary, it would probably carry across the sea.

In these “ice-hot” songs the hard, razor-sharp menacing sides of life are preserved as much as floating poetic states of soul on the edge of trance; Leven’s guitar speaks all these languages too and becomes a living being that knows about melancholy and hope. Most songs come from the recent albums *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West* and *Defending Ancient Springs*. The music is of today and often about the everyday, yet has archaic roots and a leaning towards mysteries; at times one imagines hearing from the Scottish Highlands the call of a knight or wizard conjuring the spirits of life. The man cannot really be classified; the label “Celtic soul” fits a little.

They are mostly the old stories of loss and despair, yet they sound freshly told: the cutting cold of abandonment pours like a primal scream out of “Paris Blues”, and one rarely hears so compelling a version of a pop classic as “You’ve Lost That Loving Feeling”, which in Leven’s version goes far deeper to the heart than in the rather shallow original. Leven’s companion Deborah Greenwood (vocals) and Michael Cosgrave (keyboards) are intimately part of it. Berke’s conclusion: it is basically incredible that such haunting music is still regarded as an insider tip.

2000-04-05-bergensavisen-i-arkiv-forbidd.kurz: In the “I arkiv” column Tore Bø recommends *Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West* as a forgotten gem; after his first Leven concert in Bergen he considers *Defending Ancient Springs* the album of the year.
inhalt: In Bergensavisen's archive column “I arkiv”, Tore Bø recommends Jackie Leven's *Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West* (Cooking Vinyl). The occasion is Leven's recent concert in Bergen, the first Bø had seen. The Scot has, he says, already delivered the album of the year: *Defending Ancient Springs* is a brilliant album, full of heartfelt, melancholy and infinitely beautiful songs. On stage sat a “half-old fatty in Harry clothes”, alone with his guitar, giving a concert that went straight to the soul.

Now Bø is hunting for forgotten gems, and *Forbidden Songs* is the record some consider Leven's best. Leven places himself somewhere between Van Morrison and John Martyn but has an unmistakably personal style. Bø singles out a series of first-class songs, among them “Young Male Suicide”, “Some Ancient Misty Morning” and “The Wanderer”, and says your own life seems to pass in review when you play Leven. He also recommends *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death* (1994) and *Night Lilies* (1998).
zitate_kontext: Tore Bø on the concert in Bergen

2000-08-05-sydney-morning-herald-celtic-.kurz: Bruce Elder praises *Defending Ancient Springs* in the *Sydney Morning Herald* as a clear success: a modern, unvarnished Celticism between sweetness and abrasiveness, with David Thomas and an eccentric version of “You’ve Lost That Loving Feeling”.
inhalt: Bruce Elder reviews the Australian release of *Defending Ancient Springs* (Cooking Vinyl) under the headline “Celtic post punk”, summing it up as “Scottish new wave folk meets Cleveland post punk”. Leven, once lead singer of the Scottish post-punk group Doll By Doll, has matured into a hugely talented and highly original singer-songwriter. He has eschewed his violent, drug- and booze-influenced punk roots and embraced folk, delicate Celtic melodies, the men’s movement, serious poetry and worthy causes. Elder’s labelling of Doll By Doll as a punk band is a simplification.

On his unusual route out of punk he has picked up David Thomas, one-time lead singer of the Cleveland avant-garde group Pere Ubu, and headed into territory previously inhabited by Van Morrison, Mike Scott, W. B. Yeats and Seamus Heaney. It is a particularly modern Celtic spin on the way the world works: not a Brigadoon world of kilts, bagpipes, glens and gloamings, but a world of pain, too much booze, difficult family relationships, unemployment, poverty and rundown industry.

The result is a strange musical and lyrical collision in which the natural Celtic impulse towards sweetness and gentle melody battles with a need to be abrasive and discordant. Leven thus has no embarrassment about reading poetry against washes of synthesiser before launching into songs about lost love. Elder singles out the mix with Thomas’s strange vocals (the shared vocals on “Paris Blues”), the intense confessional lyrics about being a single parent, wanting to escape pain and loneliness, and the blend of abrasiveness and sweet melody on the title track and the strangely discordant “Morbid Sky”.

Leven has always had a hit-and-miss quality, but this is clearly a hit. The album is worth buying just for the brilliant eccentricity of its version of “You’ve Lost That Loving Feeling”, and it is the best collection of songs he has released since *Fairytales for Hard Men* of 1997.

Elder on the tension in the music

2000-09-21-head-heritage-doll-by-doll-gy.kurz: Dave Furgess on Julian Cope's Head Heritage (Unsung) celebrates Doll by Doll's *Gypsy Blood* as one of his all-time favourites: Leven as Scott Walker crossed with Tim Buckley, “Highland Rain” the peak.
inhalt: In September 2000 Dave Furgess writes in Head Heritage's “Unsung” column about Doll by Doll's *Gypsy Blood* (1979, Automatic). He recalls that the group were “very big news” in the UK music papers in 1979, with some writers suggesting they would change the face of pop. In a “very strange” Melody Maker interview Leven confessed the whole group's heavy LSD use and even admitted that he heard voices and could communicate with the dead. So Furgess bought the debut *Remember* and was impressed: a couple of bum tracks but mostly “immense promise”, which only the second album would reveal fully.

*Gypsy Blood* is “a magnificent album” and one of his all-time favourites. For the sound he suggests traces of Traffic, John Cale, Moby Grape, Family and Love. Leven is “a spectacular singer with a mind shattering control and range. Try to imagine Scott Walker crossed with Tim Buckley”, and the band provide a fluid and colourful backing. Furgess goes through the record track by track: the two short openers “Teenage Lightning” (issued as a single) and “Gypsy Blood” remind him of Moby Grape's Peter Lewis in Leven's voice; “Strip Show” is a reflective ballad, “The Human Face” even better, recalling George Harrison's *All Things Must Pass* and looking ahead to The Teardrop Explodes' *Wilder*; “Hey Sweetheart” recalls Scott Walker's *Scott 4*. Side two: the muscular psychedelic funk pounder “Binary Friction”, then “Hell Games” with the line “I lived for awhile in the shadow of Castle Frankenstein” – “this should have been a number ONE single” – and “Forbidden Worlds”, another missed hit.

The record closes with three “knockouts”: “Highland Rain”, his favourite Doll by Doll song of all (“a mindfucker supreme”), “Endgame”, a ghostly solo acoustic number that is a “dead ringer” for the Teardrop Explodes B-side “Use Me”, and the barely-a-minute “When a Man Dies”, a dark solo piece that ends the album on a twisted, disturbing note. He has been trying to turn people on to this record for over twenty years. Doll by Doll made some great records after *Gypsy Blood* before Leven was sidelined by a crippling heroin habit; the good news is that he has recovered and is touring England. “If you're living in England please support the great man, he's too good to lose!!!!”
zitate_kontext: Furgess on the album's high point.

2000-09-26-the-independent-jackie-leven-.kurz: Gavin Martin reviews an evening with Leven, Andy White and Michael Weston King at London’s Purcell Room for *The Independent*: Leven outshines both, is coarsely funny and deeply moving on stage, and deserves recognition as a “living treasure”.
inhalt: Gavin Martin describes a song evening at the Purcell Room of London’s South Bank Centre, where Jackie Leven, Andy White and Michael Weston King sit side by side and take the lead in strict rotation. Their strengths and weaknesses soon show: King is an unfortunate combination of borderline pomposity and whingeing piety, while the callow-voiced White is airy, skittish, inoffensive and sometimes pleasant enough. Neither can compare to Leven, whose formidable bulk matches a huge talent, moulded by a life and career teeming with hard experience and inspiring regeneration.

Martin sums up the biography in one paragraph: an itinerant guitarist and singer who left the abandoned coalfields of his native East Fife in the wake of Sixties acid rock, played in Franco’s Spain and a Berlin divided by the wall in the Seventies, and as frontman of Doll By Doll presented a blend of transcendent hard rock and Celtic blues invocations in the post-punk era. Nearly strangled in a street attack, he could not use his voice for a long time, sank into heroin addiction and devised his own cure by setting up the Princess Diana-supported Core Trust. Since 1994 he has released records that few can match for tender beauty and consistency; the current *Defending Ancient Springs* may well be his best, built on his recovered voice, a “wondrous, wounded bellow” with elisions and melisma straight from black American gospel.

In the flesh he is something else again, “like a trawlerman at rest”: baggy denim work shirt and, for those at eye level, a disconcertingly tight pair of shorts, drinking a cocktail of gin, vodka and ginger wine that he has topped up with lager from a front-row punter. His conversation is deprecating, offhand and often off-colour, obsessed with bodily functions, Izal toilet rolls and scurrilous reminiscences involving Patsy Kensit, Salman Rushdie and the country legend Will Oldham. At first the chat seems a mask for the deeply spiritual blues he mines in “Chevin” (inspired by a lover’s tryst on a Yorkshire hillside) and “Single Father” (a meditation on loss and loneliness); but through his often wordless, slurred, drunken improvisations and his rancorous, percussive guitar he is immersed in messy, visceral emotion.

He ends with “Madame George”, and Martin says he reclaims its jazzy spaces, dark rhythmic nectar and deathly intimations – an approach Van Morrison long since forsook, whose later writing Martin dismisses as “new-age nonsense”. The verdict: a cult artist with a cognoscenti following he may be, but on this showing Leven deserves to be recognised as a living treasure.
zitate_kontext: Gavin Martin on Leven’s solo albums since 1994

2000-09-29-bergensavisen-kulttreff-pa-ga.kurz: Bergensavisen announces the duo UbuDoll, Jackie Leven and David Thomas of Pere Ubu, for 23 November 2000 at the Garage club in Bergen.
inhalt: Under the headline "Kulttreff på Garage med Leven og Thomas" ("Cult meeting at Garage with Leven and Thomas"), Bergensavisen reports on 29 September 2000 that "Bergen friend" Jackie Leven and the American cult artist David Thomas are joining forces as a duo and will play Garage in Bergen on 23 November. They call themselves UbuDoll, a name alluding to their band affiliations. Thomas is singer and leader of Pere Ubu, the art punks from Cleveland who have "ruled" the US underground since 1975, while Leven had a career in the British post-punk band Doll by Doll "in the 80s" (the author, Frank Johnsen, dates the band too late; it began in the late 1970s) before breaking out to "rule" pubs and clubs with his acoustic guitar, beautiful songs and biting lyrics.

The promise is a unique performance, a happening with vocals, guitars and accordion. In the press release Leven himself threatens that it might be a one-off: "Even though we like each other, we are both loners." Thomas and Leven met in England four years earlier and clicked at once. They first collaborated on Thomas's pioneering theatre project *Mirror Man*, which premiered in London the previous autumn (with the record released at the same time), and Thomas then took part in Leven's critically acclaimed album *Defending Ancient Springs*, which Leven promoted with a beautiful concert at Den Stundesløse in Bergen in the spring. Together, two men with over 50 years of rock experience between them and 35 records, large and small, so the author reckons they will have something to say.
zitate_kontext: Leven in the press release on working with David Thomas

2000-11-22-bergensavisen-leven-pa-garage.kurz: Preview of the UbuDoll concert on 23.11.2000 at Garage, according to the paper their third concert together.
inhalt: Preview of the UbuDoll concert on 23.11.2000 at Garage, according to the paper their third concert together. Leven promises to “break all the rules”. On David Thomas: one of the great American artists of the present, with a mysticism that many great musicians lack; both have a short fuse. He says he met him when he found out that Thomas lived on the English west coast – he phoned him because they were on the same label, they drank a lot of cognac and walked Thomas's dogs on the beach.

Leven says that on the night of the concert he should actually have been in Scotland at the “Spirit of Scotland” awards, where he is nominated as an ambassador of Scottish art; he doubts he will win and chooses Bergen – typical of him to be Scottish abroad and never popular at home. Scottish television made the documentary “East Coast Boy, West Coast Man” about him, filmed all over Scotland, plus a concert in Glasgow; since then he has no longer been “Jackie who?”. He recorded *Defending Ancient Springs* in Wales with an almost blind sound engineer with phenomenal hearing; the record sold well in Europe. Right after New Year he is going back into the studio with the same musicians and David Thomas. A second piece carries a short interview with Thomas (47), who thinks he remembers having been in Norway once before in the 80s.

2000-11-24-dagsavisen-kulthelt-for-sin-h.kurz: Geir Rakvaag previews the joint Oslo concert of David Thomas and Jackie Leven as UbuDoll in Dagsavisen. Mostly Thomas speaks, about cult status, their collaboration and why a record is unlikely.
inhalt: Geir Rakvaag's preview is headlined “Kulthelt for sin hatt”. On the evening of 24 November 2000, David Thomas and Jackie Leven play Oslo (according to the listings, at John Dee) as UbuDoll. Twenty years ago, Pere Ubu and Doll By Doll were cult bands on either side of the Atlantic; the groups have kept reappearing at irregular intervals, but the frontmen have mostly worked separately. Now there are two exclusive concerts in Norway. As evidence of their cult status the piece notes that, according to the international music press, Leven scraped into Norway's top 40 best-selling albums for one week.

Almost only Thomas is quoted. A cult hero is not something one tries to become, he says; it is probably the same as not being very popular, but popular enough, and too stupid to give up. He does not remember exactly how the collaboration began; they had been on the same label for a while, and at some point he asked Leven to join his show *Mirror Man*, and Leven returned the favour by having Thomas guest on his latest album *Defending Ancient Springs*. They share the same poetic passion and an understanding of geographical visions, he from urban Cleveland, Leven from rural Scotland, with similarities complemented by contrasts. Both come from dark, cold places, which is probably why they go to Norway.

The concerts consist mainly of each taking part in the other's songs; there is no new joint material and no songs from their old bands. They will probably keep appearing together “until we end up in a terrible fight”, but whether records will come is doubtful, since much of what they do is talking and telling stories on stage, which is hard to capture on record, and both are very busy. Thomas plans a new Pere Ubu album, one with the Pale Boys, and further work on *Mirror Man*. A companion piece (“Kulere som kult”) calls it the cult heroes' weekend in Oslo, with concerts by Leven, Thomas and The Bevis Frond.
zitate_kontext: David Thomas on cult status (as rendered by the paper)
Thomas on what he shares with Leven

2000-11-25-bergensavisen-trivelig-pa-gar.kurz: Frank Johnsen in Bergensavisen praises the half-full UbuDoll concert (Jackie Leven and David Thomas) at Garage as a quiet, bittersweet and funny cuddle hour for grown-ups, and welcomes the unusually early start.
inhalt: Frank Johnsen reviews the concert by Jackie Leven and David Thomas at Garage in Bergen on Thursday evening (23 November 2000; the house was half full). The “brand-new duo UbuDoll”, he writes, delivered a “quiet, bittersweet, funny and beautiful cuddle hour”. Because the club had been granted an exception from the city’s “curious licensing rules”, the show started at 9.30 pm, and Johnsen enjoyed a concert without noise, drunks or workmen racing for the last bus; he hopes this will become a trend.

The audience was reverent and grown-up. The two portly men sat on stools, Leven with acoustic guitar, a threadbare shirt and tracksuit bottoms tucked into his socks, Thomas in a butcher’s apron with accordion, and they delivered “beautiful poetry performed with soul and humour”. They opened with Thomas’s “Morbid Sky” from Leven’s *Defending Ancient Springs*, and that song and another collaboration from the same record, “Paris Blues”, were played in long versions with much improvisation. Between the songs they chatted: autobiographical stories from Leven’s adventurous life alongside Thomas’s tragicomic poetry, “in the same landscape as Tom Waits or Robbie Robertson”. The humour was loose, the audience laughed, even though most of the material was unknown to most of the room.

No encore ritual: the pair did not bother leaving the stage, as merely getting up from the stool would have been an exercise in itself, so they went straight into “Call Mother a Lonely Field” and Van Morrison’s “Cyprus Avenue”, “beautiful and melancholy”. Then everyone could walk happily into the night, knowing that, had the “puritans in the city council” had their way, the concert would have started half an hour after it ended.
zitate_kontext: Frank Johnsen, opening of the review

2000-11-28-puls-ubudoll-nerve-humor-og-e.kurz: Frank Stener-Andersen hails Leven’s joint show with David Thomas as ‘Ubudoll’ at Oslo’s John Dee as an overwhelming evening of nerve, humour and simplicity.
inhalt: The music paper Puls reports on 28 November 2000 on a concert “last Friday” at the John Dee in Oslo: a blend of British storytelling tradition and early American punk, accompanied by guitar and accordion, as David Thomas and Jackie Leven took the stage as ‘Ubudoll’. The collaboration arose from many years of mutual admiration, and the audience clearly appreciated it over nearly two hours. Apart from applause it was so quiet “you would think light beer was coming out of the taps at the bar”; most present knew better than the reviewer what they were in for, and had the sense to listen to two men with much to say.

The writer introduces both artists: Leven founded the London band Doll by Doll “a little over 20 years ago” and, after four albums virtually declared works of genius, carried on alone; he had played the John Dee in February and given a concert that was very well reviewed. Thomas founded Pere Ubu with Peter Laughner in the mid-seventies, a band counted among early American punk and inspired by, among others, the Velvet Underground. The two had already worked together on Thomas’s stage production ‘Mirrorman’ and on Leven’s latest record, *Defending Ancient Springs*.

The programme ranged from pure poetry, supported by monotone, sombre tones, in which Thomas exposed himself with such intensity that one hardly dared cough, to Leven’s lighter, melodic songs. There was also “masses of humour”, for example when the two ironised each other and the world between songs. The common denominators of the evening were “nerve, humour and simplicity”. The reviewer, who came with high expectations, says he was surprised, “not to say overwhelmed”; it is odd, he writes, that the two are not better known. He means to buy records and urges anyone who likes “simple and genuine music with soul and nerve” not to miss them next time they visit Oslo. He repeatedly spells the name ‘Levin’.
zitate_kontext: On the pair’s lack of fame

2000-11-28-rockol-jackie-leven-non-verra.kurz: In November 2000 Rockol reports the cancellation of Leven’s two Italian concerts in Turin (28 November) and Rome (29 November) because of an illness he caught during his previous stay in Norway.
inhalt: This short item from the Italian music site Rockol of 28 November 2000 is headed “Jackie Leven non verrà in Italia” (“Jackie Leven will not come to Italy”) and reports that the Scot’s two planned concerts are off: at the Zoobar in Turin on 28 November and at Big Mama in Rome on 29 November. The reason given is an illness Leven fell ill with during his preceding stay in Norway. The item is contemporary evidence that these two dates did not take place and must not be counted as concerts played.

2000-miller-freeman-thompson-alternative.titel: Alternative Rock (Third Ear: The Essential Listening Companion) – entries “Doll by Doll” and “Jackie Leven”
2000-miller-freeman-thompson-alternative.kurz: Dave Thompson's Alternative Rock (2000) gives Jackie Leven and Doll by Doll entries of their own: Control under the name John St. Field, Doll by Doll's "menacing, angry post-rock sound", and appearances at Reading and Pinkpop.
inhalt: Dave Thompson's reference work *Alternative Rock* (Miller Freeman Books, San Francisco, 2000, in the "Third Ear: The Essential Listening Companion" series) has a separate Leven entry on page 460 ("Jackie Leven, born 6/18/50, Kirkcaldy, Scotland") and an entry on Doll by Doll. According to the text excerpts available, *Control* was recorded at Mayfair Studios in London under the name John St. Field and released in Spain and Latin America.

Doll by Doll are described as having a "menacing, angry post-rock sound"; they made their first national tour as a support act, in parallel with the album *Remember*, followed by appearances at the Reading Festival and the Dutch Pinkpop festival, then a move to Magnet. Tony Waite left, and Leven carried the band on alone. The discography lists, among other things, "Control (MCA - Spain) 1971"; label and year contradict other accounts (Movieplay, 1973 or 1975). Leven also appears in the book's acknowledgements list.
zitate_kontext: Thompson on Doll by Doll's sound

2000-serpents-tail-lane-from-blue-to-bla.kurz: Joel Lane mentions, in the afterword to his music novel From Blue to Black (2000), experiences from a tour with "the blues singer Jackie Leven", including some comically bleak stories.
inhalt: The Birmingham writer Joel Lane tells the story of a band in his music novel *From Blue to Black* (Serpent's Tail, London, 2000). In the afterword or acknowledgements he mentions experiences from a tour with "the blues singer Jackie Leven", including some comically bleak stories. The surviving excerpt does not make clear whether Lane himself toured with Leven or used other people's stories.

2000-virgin-larkin-virgin-encyclopedia-o.medium: Virgin Books in association with Muze UK, London
2000-virgin-larkin-virgin-encyclopedia-o.kurz: Entry on Leven in the *Virgin Encyclopedia of Nineties Music* (2000, pp. 230–31): Doll by Doll fell apart in 1983 without much commercial success, *Control* appeared only in Spain as John St. Field, *Night Lilies* is “desperately bleak”.
inhalt: The *Virgin Encyclopedia of Nineties Music* (Virgin Books with Muze UK, London 2000), edited by Colin Larkin, gives Jackie Leven an entry of his own on pages 230–31. From the visible parts: Leven, born in Fife in 1950, saw Doll by Doll fall apart in 1983 without major commercial success. His album *Control* appeared only in Spain, under the pseudonym John St. Field. The EP *Songs from the Argyll Cycle* marks the new beginning, and *Night Lilies* reunited him with Joe Shaw and is “desperately bleak”.
It is a brief reference entry, available only in excerpts; it shows that Leven was included in a general British music encyclopedia of the nineties.

2001-01-01-globalguest-inoffizielles-gae.medium: globalguest.com/gb/TOUT – guestbook of the fan site jackieleven.com
2001-01-01-globalguest-inoffizielles-gae.kurz: The fan site's “Unofficial Jackie Leven guestbook” began on 01.01.2001 with a test entry by the webmaster (“PT”, Italy) and collected almost 100 entries by the end of 2001.
inhalt: The fan site's “Unofficial Jackie Leven guestbook” began on 01.01.2001 with a test entry by the webmaster (“PT”, Italy) and collected almost 100 entries by the end of 2001. At first fans praise the new site, which they say they found through the eGroup mailing list; organiser Mick Nolan is thanked, and the webmaster is addressed as “Paul”. He replies himself, for instance on the quality of the RealAudio samples (deliberately low, to encourage purchase) and with a forwarded message from Deborah Greenwood (24.08.2001) explaining the delays with the Haunted Valley CD *Munich Blues* and the bootleg *Deep in the Heart of Nowhere* (live at The Greys) by new British CD licensing procedures.

The entries trace the concert year: a tour with Andy White and Michael Weston King in Belgium and the Netherlands (AB Brussels, Assen, Eindhoven, Haarlem/Solingen relocation), Fareham, Winchester (Tower Arts Centre, 06.04.), Kirkcaldy (Path Tavern, 14.06.) and Dundee (15.06.), the Mirror Man concerts, a free concert on Southsea Common (29.07.), the 12 Bar Club with three new songs, Southampton, Leicester (The Musician), Jim's Cafe in Colne, two evenings at the Edinburgh Fringe, Stockholm and the German tour in October with Ron Sexsmith (Bremen, Bielefeld, Krefeld, Münster, Frankfurt, Hannover), with memories of the stage stories about Heineken, the “Schweinehund” and Sting's alleged helicopter crash. Fans from Australia recall performances in the Barossa Valley and at WOMAD, and a New Zealand visit in November is announced. A former DJ and stage manager at London's Dingwalls (1979–83) calls Doll by Doll a crowd favourite; fans ask about the announced Doll by Doll reissues and a best-of. The musician Chris Connelly writes from Chicago that Leven's songs saved him; Ecki Stieg links to a German interview on grenzwellen.com, and Liam Carson announces his interviews for the Irish Examiner and Irish News on the Ireland tour. On 09.12. a fan reports on the Christmas concert in Milford with the “Girls” (The Stornoway Girls).

2001-02-19-jackieleven-com-new-release-g.autor: Webmaster jackieleven.com (with a quotation from the Cooking Vinyl newsletter)
2001-02-19-jackieleven-com-new-release-g.kurz: Announcement of the four-CD box *Great Songs From Eternal Bars* (Cooking Vinyl, 19 February 2001, 1,000 copies), which first made the live album *The Wanderer* commercially available; with Leven’s comments on the recordings, on *Control* and on his next album.
inhalt: On 19 February 2001 the webmaster of jackieleven.com announced the release of a four-CD box set from Cooking Vinyl, *Great Songs From Eternal Bars* (COOKCD212). It contains *Control* (the album Leven made as John St. Field), *Fairytales For Hardmen*, *Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West* and the live album *The Wanderer*, previously issued by the fan club Haunted Valley. Only 1,000 sets were pressed, the first fifty signed by Leven; the price was £15 (£11.50 for Cooking Vinyl members) plus postage. Orders could be placed by telephone or fax; the label’s online ordering did not yet work at the time of writing.

The main part is a long quotation from the label’s newsletter. Leven had previously sold *The Wanderer* only at gigs; for the box it gains tracks that had only been on vinyl, among them “So My Soul Can Sing”, an adaptation of a poem by the late black American prison poet Etheridge Knight, and “Donna Karan”, which Leven says is about “lonely Knightsbridge women”. The recordings come from concerts in Australia, Poland, Norway and the UK; named are “Poortoun”, “Stranger On The Square”, “Heartsick Land” and a medley of “Newfoundland Blues”, “Some Ancient Misty Morning” and “Working Alone”, together with the storytelling that is part of his live shows, including a tale from Aberdeen. Leven explains that he had been collecting recordings of interesting concerts from Sydney to Poznań and chose tracks and stories that define different phases of his live act. Sydney stuck in his mind because he was so tired he almost fell asleep on his guitar, yet it was an important media gig; the audience was raucous but also reserved, and found his language a little colourful.

The three studio albums are described briefly. *Fairytales For Hardmen*, his fourth solo album for Cooking Vinyl, keeps the passion of his earlier work but is more contemplative, with the familiar Celtic mellowness in the arrangements, “steeped in mists, poetry and alcohol”; the sleeve notes list 17 pubs in which he found “moments of solace and reflection”. Highlights named are “Boy Trapped In A Man”, “Poortoun” and “Fear Of Women” with its version of “Unchained Melody”. *Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West* (1995) was recorded in Cornwall and contains the famed “Argyll Cycle”, with “Some Ancient Misty Morning”, “The Wanderer” and “Young Male Suicide Blessed By Invisible Woman” singled out.

On *Control* the text says the album dates from long before Doll By Doll. Leven himself linked it to an intense period of taking LSD in many places and circumstances; by the late Seventies he had decided on a life with career structures and all but forgot the record, until it felt right in the Nineties to release it. “Raerona” sings of a dream location, a strange sprawling village he kept visiting in his sleep; “I’m Always A Prinlaws Boy” is about a very poor working-class area of Leslie where he lived as a child. The newsletter dates the album to 1971; the webmaster corrects this in brackets to 1973.

Asked about the future, Leven says he is going back to Snowdonia in Wales to record and may call the new album *The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ*, although everybody tells him it is a terrible title, which only encourages him. Other song titles include “Friendship Between Men and Women” and “Hidden World Of She”: more songs about the stress of living and loving and the long, lonely, secret lives we learn to endure.

2001-04-10-hot-press-lorraine-sammelreze.kurz: In *Hot Press*, Duan Stokes covers two singles in one review: Jimmy MacCarthy’s “Lorraine” and Leven’s “The Right To Remain Silent”, where Leven superbly blends modern and ancient sounds on intelligent, fluent songs.
inhalt: Duan Stokes covers two singles in one short review in Ireland’s *Hot Press*: Jimmy MacCarthy’s “Lorraine” (Sony Music) and Jackie Leven’s “The Right To Remain Silent” (Cooking Vinyl). He speaks of two master songwriters displaying their respective talents. MacCarthy builds a vivid image of Lorraine and yearns for her company; the song is well constructed but suffers from having been done before: ballads bemoaning the absence of a fair maiden are three a penny, and this fails to deviate significantly from the standard.
Leven, meanwhile, manages to rise above the usual fare by superbly blending modern and ancient sounds on songs that are intelligent and fluent. The review says no more about Leven’s contribution.

2001-06-28-the-independent-always-look-o.kurz: Interview in a London pub (“Railway Tavern”) a few days before the release of *Creatures of Light and Darkness* (3 July 2001), which Martin counts as the 21st album of a 30-year career.
inhalt: Interview in a London pub (“Railway Tavern”) a few days before the release of *Creatures of Light and Darkness* (3 July 2001), which Martin counts as the 21st album of a 30-year career. Leven says that as a schoolboy in Glenrothes he won the Scottish Round Table essay competition (topic: the career he wanted – he wanted to travel the world with a guitar), shortly before becoming the first pupil in the country to be expelled from school for drug possession. There follow the LSD years, Madrid under Franco, divided Berlin, Doll by Doll as a “defeat” he still carries, the 1983 mugging with the loss of his falsetto, heroin together with his then girlfriend and, from that, the CORE Trust (funded by Shirley Porter's Westminster Council, supported by Princess Diana). Leven says Diana asked him to sing after a charity lunch – his way back into music; later he also sang for the aged Laurence Olivier. He explains “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” (a mining community with 14 churches and one pub, allegedly the highest male suicide rate in Europe, voices of laid-off shipyard workers), his studio method of withholding the other tracks from musicians, his own whisky “Leven's Lament” and a Bly men's gathering in the Highlands on the subject of grief. Overall tone: respectful, with a sense for Leven's contradictions.

2001-07-03-dagsavisen-en-naturbegavelse.kurz: Geir Rakvaag praises *Creatures Of Light And Darkness*: Leven's poetry of wild nature needs time, the music leans towards soul this time, and the high point is a setting of a Robert Frost poem.
inhalt: In Dagsavisen (Oslo), under the headline “En naturbegavelse” (“A natural talent”), Geir Rakvaag reviews Jackie Leven's album *Creatures Of Light And Darkness* (Cooking Vinyl/VME). For a long time Leven released an album every year, almost as though it were a matter of urgency for him after he was cured of his drug abuse. This time he has let three years pass, Rakvaag says (not quite right, as the previous album, *Defending Ancient Springs*, appeared in 2000), and he has a great deal on his mind.

Leven takes both words and music seriously, so it takes a while to digest his poetry, which is “full of big images of wild nature and even wilder emotions”. The music is rooted as usual in Celtic song tradition, but this time it moves some way towards soul on several songs, for instance “The Sexual Loneliness Of Jesus Christ”, which was apparently meant to be the title track of the whole album but perhaps became too strong in the end. As a friend of Norway, Leven does not deny himself this time either: “Rainy Day Bergen Women” is lyrically almost an update of the Bergen favourite “Jenter fra Bergen er nåkke for seg”, set at the fish market, with David Thomas dropping by with big words.

The boldest project is a setting of Robert Frost's poem “Stopping By Woods On A Snowy Evening” (here called “Stopped By Woods…”), one of the great treasures of American literature, to which Leven has set a truly beautiful melody and which becomes the album's high point. The closing line: “Han er fortsatt noe helt for seg selv” – he is still something entirely his own.
zitate_kontext: Rakvaag, closing line of the review

2001-07-03-rolling-stone-de-creatures-of.kurz: A positive review in the German edition of Rolling Stone: Leven, a “hunted Iron John and king of the restless”, delivers a quiet, coherent album with more distanced lyrics, including about his late father; it opens up fully only with the booklet.
inhalt: The anonymous editorial review begins: “The eagle flies again.” Jackie Leven, a “hunted Iron John and king of the restless”, has once more put some order into the hut. In the “small Scottish village of Agryll” (sic) he once wrote the “liberating” *Argyll Cycle*; the last spark of life ignited, the world was back in joint. Yet Leven is still more hunted than hunter – as the live albums, issued in tiny editions and often more reading than concert, “speak volumes”.

His soul, battered by heavy drug abuse and personal blows of fate, seems to have found some relief; the lyrical motifs are more distanced than usual this time. “My Spanish Dad” and “Rainy Day Bergen Women” come from Leven’s memories of his late father, and for “Exit Wounds” he even poached in the books of the ancestors – with a quotation from the mouth of Queen Elizabeth I: “If you could look inside my heart, you’d see a body without a soul.”

It is about the seriousness of a broken life, the ceaseless interplay of hopeful trust and wailing despondency. Leven has kept his hand for thought-through, mature songwriting. The consistently quiet pieces, hardly any under five minutes, “live, hiss, chirp and fight” and are, despite the renewed involvement of the “art poser” David Thomas, produced very coherently: no unnecessary pomp, carefully placed accents – “a gruelling battle, only this time without war”. The record opens up fully only to those who study the lyrics and liner notes printed in the booklet attentively. The review ends on the punchline: “Reading broadens the mind.”

2001-07-05-the-independent-creatures-of-.kurz: In The Independent, Andy Gill calls *Creatures of Light & Darkness* another fine offering after *Defending Ancient Springs*, singling out “My Spanish Dad” and “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ”.
inhalt: Reviewing the album in The Independent on 5 July 2001, Andy Gill calls it “another fine offering” that builds on the (artistic) success of the previous year's *Defending Ancient Springs* and uses much the same group of musicians: David Thomas (the “Ubu-man”, of Pere Ubu), the former James trumpeter Andy Diagram and the former Christian Henry Priestman.

Leven's recurrent interests of poetry, people and a heightened sense of place dominate, Gill says, particularly where they touch on gender differences and relations between parents and children. “Hidden World Of She” and “Billy Ate My Pocket”, in which the narrator's adulterous leanings are spookily laid bare by a horse's bite, wield the mythopoeic power of traditional folk forms. “My Spanish Dad” simply and movingly celebrates small but significant moments shared with Leven's late father.

Gill hears in the arrangements the familiar, folksy Caledonian Soul that Leven has made his own. On “Rainy Day Bergen Women”, Michael Cosgrave's accordion and David Thomas's melodeon add warmth and mystery; Thomas's coughing fit and glimpses of the eponymous women combine into a gestalt apprehension of the death of Leven's father. The most striking song, though, is “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ”, another paternal rumination in which the saviour laments a solitude that persists despite his apparently limitless powers. The verdict is clearly positive.

2001-07-06-the-guardian-creatures-of-lig.kurz: Adam Sweeting gives *Creatures of Light and Darkness* four stars: Leven marshals bleak, difficult songs into a whole with icy composure, while tumultuous emotions rage beneath. The verdict: “frequently awesome, and frequently terrifying”.
inhalt: Adam Sweeting’s short review in The Guardian (6 July 2001, four stars) sits in a round-up with contributions from John Aizlewood, Alexis Petridis, Maddy Costa, Michael Odell and Betty Clarke. Leven “marshals bleak and difficult songs into a coherent whole with icy composure”. It is his seventh album for Cooking Vinyl, so his complete control of the studio comes as no surprise. But behind the skilfully crafted surfaces, “tumultuous emotions battle for supremacy”.

Brisk folk-rock and soulful balladry, with artful assistance from trumpeter Andy Diagram and “off-centre genius” David Thomas, harbour “stunning reworkings of Biblical myth and Oedipal trauma”. And you have to doff your cap to anybody who can write a song called “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ”. The verdict is summed up as “frequently awesome, and frequently terrifying”.
zitate_kontext: Adam Sweeting on the contrast within the songs

2001-07-11-tromso-jackie-leven-pa-tomgan.kurz: Helge Matland has loved Leven’s records since 1994 but finds *Creatures of Light & Darkness* over-arranged and over-instrumented: it lacks dynamics and engagement, and the lyrics grip less too.
inhalt: Helge Matland writes under the title “Jackie Leven på tomgang” (“Jackie Leven idling”) about *Creatures of Light & Darkness* (Cooking Vinyl/Voices of Wonder). Personally, he says, he has been thrilled by everything Leven has released since his solo breakthrough with *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* in 1994 and the follow-up *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West* a year later; since then the productive Scot has put out records annually. Leven has presence, is unpretentious in the way he performs his songs, and his easy-going way of communicating with the audience makes him seem a very down-to-earth artist, a man on our level. The songs seem like results of his lived life, with beauty, poetry, mood and reflection, but also room for a portion of sly humour. Celtic melancholy is unavoidable but is never allowed to steer the music alone; blues, soul and pop seem nearer influences than rock’n’roll. Leven is also a good singer with a sensitive voice and a solid guitarist.

On the new album, however, he disappoints a little: the music is more arranged than before, and what the critic perceives as excessive instrumentation hinders the dynamics, drive and engagement usually found in Leven’s music. So he does not engage him as he used to. It does not help that Leven flirts with Norwegians by singing about the “fantastic” “Rainy Day Bergen Women”, or sees reality and history through different eyes as usual, as in “The Sexual Loneliness Of Jesus Christ”. When the musical side does not quite stretch, the words do not catch either, as they could have done.
