2001-07-13-tonsbergs-blad-norgesvennen-j.kurz: Erik Munsterhjelm hails *Creatures of Light and Darkness* in Tønsbergs Blad: Leven survived a hard life and over ten years earned the status of a ‘friend of Norway’.
inhalt: The short review in Tønsbergs Blad of 13 July 2001 is of *Creatures of Light and Darkness*. Erik Munsterhjelm begins with the life: Jackie Leven is “a man who has lived life”. As leader of the “legendary punk group” Doll By Doll the menu was “not exactly carrot juice”, and when, after a “raw and very brutal assault”, he began using heroin as a painkiller, things looked very dark for him for a while – as musician and as human being. But he got back on his feet, “fortunately for all of us who appreciate British rock” rooted in traditional folk elements with a good, funny or moving, at any rate always well-written lyric on top.

The conclusion concerns Leven’s role in Norway: over the past decade he has built up the status of a ‘Norgesvenn’ – “with a positive sign, for heaven’s sake” – and it is well deserved, for Leven is an artist “with personality, integrity and credibility”. The text gives no rating or track-by-track critique; it is more a portrait in miniature.
The paper misprints the label as ‘Cocking Vinyl’ and the band as ‘Doll By Holl’; ‘punk group’ is the paper’s simplified classification.
zitate_kontext: Munsterhjelm on Leven’s role in Norway

2001-07-18-hamar-dagblad-det-fins-ingen-.kurz: Hamar Dagblad calls Leven, in a short review of *Creatures of Light and Darkness*, an original artist with something on his mind, whose complex, dark soundscape demands concentration and at times clouds the lyrics.
inhalt: Geir Hovensjø's short review (headline “Det fins ingen maken”, “There is nothing like him”) introduces Leven as the Scottish frontman of Doll by Doll (1977–1983) who then went solo. He suffered unprovoked violence and had drug problems but came back stronger than ever. He is an “original and distinctive artist with something on his mind”, as this album, *Creatures of Light and Darkness* (Cooking Vinyl), also clearly proves.

His lyrics have lyrical ambitions, and he also uses other people's poetry as words (Robert Frost). The music is mostly marked by dark tones. Leven demands the listener's concentration, because a lot happens in the complicated, detailed soundscape, “perhaps so much that the lyrics get somewhat muddled and clouded”. No mark is given. The band years are the paper's own dates. The same text ran in Østlendingen on the same day.

2001-07-19-gaesteliste-das-leben-ist-ein.kurz: Interview on “Creatures of Light and Darkness” (2001). To begin with: Leven has his own whisky brand, “Leven's Lament”; he says a company called MacDuff produces it, and the label shows a Scottish and an English soldier from the last war as an image of a changing Scotland.
inhalt: Interview on “Creatures of Light and Darkness” (2001). To begin with: Leven has his own whisky brand, “Leven's Lament”; he says a company called MacDuff produces it, and the label shows a Scottish and an English soldier from the last war as an image of a changing Scotland. Maurer mentions that Leven worked in the Haig distillery in his youth. Leven describes himself as a “counterpart to the clown”: happy in private, committed to dark undertones in his work. The album's central theme is the relationship with his recently deceased father, from “My Spanish Dad” to “Bergen Girls” (with David Thomas); his father was unmusical but in old age found a way into music and into Leven's work through his enthusiasm for Spain (he learned Spanish) (his own account). Leven interprets “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” as a question of where Jesus had to take his human feelings, linked with Scottish shipyard workers. On the writing process: some songs arrive finished, others he works on for months; he only recognises an album's guiding motif afterwards, and his greatest worry is losing the ability to write. Outlook: an autumn tour, possibly with the trumpeter David Diagram.
zitate_kontext: Leven on his relationship to the clown figure.

2001-07-25-harstad-tidende-stemningsfull.kurz: John Henry Storhaug praises *Creatures of Light and Darkness* in *Harstad Tidende* as a solid album with echoes of Van Morrison, big words and dramatic sound effects: music that demands listening and is “to live with”.
inhalt: Under the headline “Stemningsfullt” (“Atmospheric”), John Henry Storhaug welcomes Jackie Leven’s return with *Creatures of Light and Darkness* (Cooking Vinyl, 2001): the boss of the old legendary Doll By Doll is once more behind a solid product. In phrasing and approach he reminds one strongly of Van Morrison, but is even fonder of dramatic effects: slamming doors, trickling rain, cheers and the like. Lyrically he loves big words and big visions.

“The Sexual Loneliness Of Jesus Christ” is hardly an average pop title; “Rainy Day, Bergen Women” is more familiar to Norwegians. Leven’s strength, as before, is the mood and atmosphere he conveys and the closeness to the music in which he places the listener. The music demands that you listen, and cannot be filed away as background. It is music to live with, it more than holds up, and it is a record you will return to long after the autumn darkness has set in.
zitate_kontext: John Henry Storhaug on *Creatures of Light and Darkness*

2001-07-26-the-guardian-i-am-an-abject-f.kurz: Conversation over a pint at Marylebone station. Aizlewood begins with Leven's annual ritual: every spring he travels with a sleeping bag, a few books and little money to a randomly chosen country station and sets off walking to walk off his aggression.
inhalt: Conversation over a pint at Marylebone station. Aizlewood begins with Leven's annual ritual: every spring he travels with a sleeping bag, a few books and little money to a randomly chosen country station and sets off walking to walk off his aggression. Stages of the biography follow, some told this way only here: son of a carpet fitter from Fife, work in a rocket factory, married at 16, driven out of the neighbourhood by a gang at 17, farm work from Cornwall to Glasgow, in Franco's Madrid in the early 70s, where *Control* was allegedly the only thing easily obtainable. Doll by Doll (“Dull By Dull” to their detractors), the 1983 attack in Market Street in Islington with a cut across the throat, loss of his falsetto, heroin, withdrawal, the CORE Trust (discreetly supported by Princess Diana); his partner and CORE co-founder ran off with the Dalai Lama's bodyguard. Leven has since withdrawn from running the trust and lives in Hampshire with Debbie, who is teaching him “80/20” organisation. *Creatures of Light & Darkness* processes the death of his father the previous year. Leven half-amusedly calls himself “an abject failure”, rejects a crossover in the manner of David Gray, describes the rigours of long German tours and his reserve of unrecorded songs. Overall tone: sympathetic, with regret at the little recognition he has received.

2001-07-jam-creatures-of-light-and-darkn.kurz: Ezio Guaitamacchi gives *Creatures of Light & Darkness* a mark of 8 in the Italian magazine JAM: ten masterful songs of personal memory on a simple, elegant sound backdrop, with “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” as the best.
inhalt: The review (mark: 8) opens with a portrait: Leven is an eccentric personality, inspired songwriter and refined musician who escapes the clichés the music business demands today, and for that reason is popular with those seeking emotion, meaning and solid artistic content. Born in 1950 in the Scottish county of Fife, he heard Lightnin' Hopkins and other masters of Afro-American music at home thanks to his mother; blues, jazz, marching anthems from school and the popular traditional songs of his homeland all left deep marks on his writing. When *Defending Ancient Springs* appeared a little over a year earlier, the whole musical world welcomed the return of this heavyweight folksinger, whom some remembered as John St. Field, who recorded *Control* (now reissued by Cooking Vinyl as an “acid” album), or as a member of Doll by Doll, or as author of a handful of Charisma singles in 1983. After the attack on a London street and a separation from his girlfriend, he fell into depression and heroin in the Eighties; towards the end of the decade came the hoped-for exit from the tunnel, and he found himself and started to write again.

Now a “serene fifty-year-old”, he builds with David Thomas (ex-Pere Ubu, already at his side on the previous record) on the excellent result of *Defending Ancient Springs*. The disc is full of fascination, beautiful melodic songs, poetic and captivating accounts, and electro-acoustic arrangements that improve with every listen. The ten tunes open with the autobiographical “My Spanish Dad”, a classic folk-rock number with plenty of violin and accordion in the vein of Steve Earle's best, in which Leven traces a vivid memory of his father. Next comes “Exit Wound”, the only rather weak piece (melodically), which leaves no mark, but it matters little, for straight after comes the best song of the album: “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” rests not only on a beautiful text but on a hypnotic melody and an effective harmonic base, as good as anything he has written. With a simple arrangement in which violin and mandolin add lovely colours, the song flows magnificently, lyrically too. S4, Leven's Italian record company, has cleverly translated it into Italian, as they did for Ani DiFranco, and the review prints the opening lines.

From there the disc moves between ballads of nostalgic melancholy, like the “gorgeous” “Washing by Hand”, fears of unknown worlds (“Hidden Word of She”), and almost theatrical pieces such as “Rainy Day Bergen Woman”, where, between pounding rain and a hacking cough, a solitary harmonica lays down an evocative intro over a long diatribe by a man; there is also a swinging song for the great forests, “Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening”, whose words are a poem by Robert Frost. Among more or less Dylanesque pieces (“Friendship Between Men and Women”, “Wrapped Up in Blue”), Leven crowns the work with the “winning” “Billy Ate My Pocket”, a fascinating sonic story with a surprise ending. The verdict behind the mark of 8: Leven confirms his moment of great inspiration, and with David Thomas's help gives ten masterful songs of personal memories and old emotions against a simple but most elegant sound backdrop. (The text survives on the fan site only as the webmaster's English translation.)

2001-08-11-drammens-tidende-jackie-leven.kurz: Conversation before the 2001 Norway tour (last updated online in 2010). Leven says his youth was marked by trouble in a rough environment, which is why he left Scotland; Bergen was the first city outside Britain in which he lived, and a photo from his young Bergen days hangs at his mother's.
inhalt: Conversation before the 2001 Norway tour (last updated online in 2010). Leven says his youth was marked by trouble in a rough environment, which is why he left Scotland; Bergen was the first city outside Britain in which he lived, and a photo from his young Bergen days hangs at his mother's. “Rainy Day Bergen Women” came about after a night of heavy drinking, on the morning walk to the fish market. On his whisky “Leven's Lament” he says that after a serious whisky illness in Paris he no longer drinks it – a dangerous drink.

Andreassen describes the music as “white Scottish soul”; *The Mystery of Love* brought him Norwegian fans and tours as far as Australia. Leven would like to record Tim Hardin songs but shies away from the time it would take from his own pieces. He talks about working with David Thomas (Pere Ubu) on the new album and the duo Ubudoll, who last played in Oslo; he considers another Ubudoll album unlikely. He is now becoming a little well known even in Scotland.

2001-08-21-glamdalen-opphengt-i-det-bla.kurz: Tommy Rønningen gives *Creatures of Light and Darkness* a mixed verdict in Glåmdalen: brilliant lyrics, but sometimes too few strong melodies. Some tracks belong on any best-of, yet it trails *Forbidden Songs* and *Fairy Tales for Hard Men*.
inhalt: Rønningen starts with Leven’s productivity since his comeback: ten years of dammed-up writing had to come out, and a string of albums, singles and EPs followed. On record Leven comes across as a blend of Van Morrison and a Celtic Henry Rollins. On *Creatures of Light and Darkness* he has his old Doll by Doll comrade Jo Shaw (printed “Joe Shaw”) on guitar, and David Thomas of Pere Ubu, always present in Leven’s world.

Heard from outside, the album sounds not much different from its predecessors, still “Caledonian soul”, but there are signs that the musical engine has begun to slip “just a little”. The lyrics are brilliant as usual, yet Leven sometimes seems too absorbed in his big thoughts and their romantic sheen and forgets to write melodies strong enough to carry them. He keeps seeking new musical roads to get his basically classic folk-rock songs into our hearts, and does not always succeed. An example is “Rainy Day Bergen Women”, which should never have left the drawing board.

At the same time Rønningen names songs that would make any best-of on any day: “My Spanish Dad”, “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” and “Wrapped Up in Blue”, as well as “Friendship Between Men & Women”, where Leven jazzes himself up to a level only “Van the Man” had reached before him. Leven’s most devoted followers will surely love everything on the album, he suspects, and he himself probably will in time, since there are obviously depths still to discover. For the moment, though, the record ends up in the shadow of the monuments *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West* and *Fairy Tales for Hard Men*.
zitate_kontext: Rønningen on the album in relation to its predecessors

2001-09-04-dagbladet-na-blir-det-leven.kurz: Short interview piece at the start of the Norway tour in September 2001. The hook is not the new album but Leven's own whisky: Grønneberg presents him as probably the first artist in the world with his own whisky label.
inhalt: Short interview piece at the start of the Norway tour in September 2001. The hook is not the new album but Leven's own whisky: Grønneberg presents him as probably the first artist in the world with his own whisky label. Leven says that in winter 2001 a fan approached him in a pub, revealed himself as the director of the Islay Mist distillery and asked him to “compose” a whisky of his own. Leven stresses that he does not care what is in the bottle; what matters to him is the label: it shows the motif “The Order of Release” (a woman freeing a Scot captured after Culloden). Leven interprets the picture as a depiction of female strength that humiliated Scottish men and contributed to violence against women; Scotland is far ahead in Europe for domestic violence, and the label is meant to make people think – a typical Leven interpretation, hard to verify.

On the album *Creatures of Light and Darkness* (summer 2001, according to the article his 21st studio album, praised by critics) Leven says it is exactly the record he always wanted to make; he compares his role with a fixed line-up of musicians to that of a football manager. He likes Norway because of the weather, which reminds him of Scotland, especially the rain in Bergen – hence the song title “Rainy Day Bergen Women”. The article lists the tour dates.

2001-09-05-bergensavisen-hyller-jenter-f.kurz: Preview of the concert on 06.09.2001 at Den Stundesløse, where Leven's own whisky can also be bought at the bar.
inhalt: Preview of the concert on 06.09.2001 at Den Stundesløse, where Leven's own whisky can also be bought at the bar. Leven says he loves picturesque Bergen and its women; “Rainy Day Bergen Women” was hard to write, he wanted it to take off at the end, and the lyrical song gradually became a humorous one. Being compared with Van Morrison flatters him, even if Morrison no longer achieves anything at the level of *Astral Weeks* and *Moondance*, but has one of the best voices.

Personal matters, as his own account: he is better than ever, he has come to terms with the death of his father, with whom he reconciled towards the end of his life; he lives with a woman who teaches him to live in the now, and her son. In the 80s he was addicted to heroin and completely on the floor. Writing is often therapy for him; his songs are more descriptive than sentimental. He sees his soul as influenced by black masters such as Lightnin' Hopkins, Blind Lemon Jefferson and R. L. Burnside – the latter making his best records at over 70. For the concert the venue is launching “Leven's Lament”; the album received the top rating of 6 in BA.

2001-09-06-lofotposten-rolig-leven-traff.kurz: Bjørnar Larsen sees Leven at Præstengbrygga in Kabelvåg: a quiet, spellbinding evening of ballads, idiosyncratic guitar playing and stories before 110 people, with a late blues waking the room from dreamland.
inhalt: This concert review in Lofotposten (6 September 2001) describes the performance of Tuesday evening, 4 September, at Præstengbrygga in Kabelvåg, before an audience of 110. A “receptive audience” was captivated by quiet songs, glittering guitar playing and fine singing. Little suggested that the Scot and “friend of Norway” has a past as a punk musician in Doll By Doll (the paper’s words) as he conjured up one quiet song after another.

In a T-shirt, shorts, white tennis socks and “pub-to-pub shoes” he looked uncannily like AC/DC singer Brian Johnson, but musically he was the opposite. Leven is known for his versatile style, from pop through soul and rhythm and blues to Celtic tradition; on this evening the ballads were the focus. It was not just the voice that held the audience: his unusual guitar style, with steady slaps on the guitar body and stamping on the floor, left people sitting as if paralysed. The humorous interludes, in which Leven told stories of things he had experienced and dreams, were well received.

Some in the audience had probably expected a faster concert, and the reviewer felt that some were waiting for him to shift gear. Near the end he launched into a blues that woke the gathering from dreamland; the audience, used to more punch in the music at this venue, clapped along in time through the whole song. The only criticism the author offers is for people at the back who could not keep quiet and so spoiled some of the atmosphere. The piece is signed Bjørnar Larsen.
zitate_kontext: Larsen on the effect of Leven’s playing

2001-09-08-bergensavisen-altfor-mye-leve.kurz: Tore Bø finds Leven’s solo show at Bergen’s Den Stundesløse “far too much Leven”: the singer told overlong stories and tried stand-up comedy, so that the songs were squeezed out.
inhalt: Tore Bø of Bergensavisen writes about the concert at Den Stundesløse (‘Stundiken’) on the night to 7 September 2001. The headline is a pun: there was “far too much life/Leven”, and Jackie Leven was mostly to blame. For some reason he insisted on telling “loooong stories” from his more than fifty years of life. No wonder many dropped out and started entertaining themselves; only those closest to the stage and the biggest fans kept their ears pricked for the two hours.

The reviewer missed the artist and poet Leven when he tried his hand at stand-up comedy – about as successful, he says, as when Jonas Fjeld played Thomas Giertsen at the Nattjazz festival in spring. “It’s a shame that so great a singer can’t stick to what he does best”: he is a brilliant songwriter and a sovereign singer. The lyrical texts about love, nostalgia and his late father became contrasts in an evening where Leven wanted to chat with the audience.

Leven came alone with his guitar and, though he is a capable musician, there were few high points. They came with the “lovely” ‘Rainy Day Bergen Women’, ‘Single Father’ and ‘The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ’. A picture caption mocks that Leven insists on performing in shorts – given his build, “not exactly smart”.
zitate_kontext: Bø on how the evening went

2001-09-10-rogalands-avis-leven-uten-dod.kurz: An enthusiastic review of the tour finale at the Stavanger club Sting Nere: two hours, 16 songs, not a minute of dead time; Leven “looked like a tramp but entertained like a king”. Only about 50 people attended.
inhalt: Einar Owe Einarsen reviews Saturday night’s concert at Sting Nere in Stavanger in Rogalands Avis (10 September 2001). Leven played two straight hours without a minute of dead time. “The Scot looked like a tramp but entertained like a king.” The reviewer had only received Leven’s new album *Creatures of Light and Darkness* that week and had played it a double-digit number of times. He had no prior relationship with Leven and asks: why do some end up as superstars while others, just as big, remain a secret for the few? Leven has released around 20 records and fronted Doll By Doll, “but that means little to anyone but the initiated”.

Leven walked on in shorts, a ragged shirt and with a patched-up guitar and took possession of the Sting with outstanding guitar playing, lyrics without easy rhymes and clichés, a vocal delivery of great commitment and a good portion of self-irony. He gets away with swearing, sex talk with the most private details and corny jokes thanks to his disarming style. The two-hour show of 16 songs was spiced with anecdotes from Norway and Scotland, a few digs at Mette-Marit and some baiting of Americans. Even when some of the verbal sequences ran to several minutes, it never became boring.

Leven is also an outstanding songwriter who romps through folk rock, soul and blues and can sing “like the smoothest crooner” when necessary. The music lies not only in the melodies but just as much in the “lush and spirited” language. That he played only four songs from his latest album, and neither of the reviewer’s two favourites from it, was a good sign: not a single song was indifferent. Leven promised to return to Stavanger next year – “Then I will come too.” But there should be more than the roughly 50 who came that night.

2001-09-12-sarpsborg-arbeiderblad-en-man.kurz: Erling Brøndmo: *Creatures Of Light And Darkness* is atmospheric, tradition-inspired music that demands listening and then gives a lot back, though not as strong as *Fairy Tales For Hard Men*.
inhalt: Sarpsborg Arbeiderblad heads this short review “En mann å stole på” (“A man to rely on”). Erling Brøndmo writes that Jackie Leven sends out one record after another and always has the critics on his side, including after *Creatures Of Light And Darkness*. The reason, he says, is that Leven is a bearer of tradition. This is tradition-inspired fare from the former member of Doll By Doll, mood-creating music, not the kind that goes straight into your head but the kind that demands you listen and get into it; if you do, you get a lot back.

Leven is also a good storyteller who wants something with his music and words. Everything is written with heart and solid presence, and delivered simply and feelingly. Melodically he has been even stronger, but this CD also grows and keeps getting stronger, “though hardly as strong as Fairy Tales For Hard Men”. The record is on Cooking Vinyl.
zitate_kontext: Erling Brøndmo on *Creatures Of Light And Darkness*
Brøndmo on the album's melodic strength

2001-09-18-grenzwellen-creatures-of-ligh.kurz: A rave review of *Creatures Of Light And Darkness*: Ecki ranks Leven above Nick Cave and calls him “one of the last great storytellers of our time”. The centrepiece is “Rainy Day Bergen Women”, about the death of Leven’s father.
inhalt: In the online magazine of the radio programme “Grenzwellen”, “Ecki” (Ecki Stieg) wrote a lengthy review on 18 September 2001. He opens with Leven’s life: in the seventies singer and head of the “criminally underrated” Doll by Doll, then heroin dependency, then the “unexpected rebirth” with the solo debut *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death* and seven further albums, “all without exception moving”. (He dates the rebirth to the eighties; the debut actually came out in 1994.)

Leven, he argues, has perfected the art of songwriting – not by using familiar templates but by observing things, condensing them, linking them to his own history and drawing new conclusions. Asked for peers, one keeps arriving at Nick Cave, whose career also has its highs and lows; but unlike Cave’s “affectedly pathetic” lachrymosity, Leven manages without whininess, literary navel-gazing or “concern”. He is at once a well-read literary man, an incurable romantic, a humorous person and sometimes a cynic. Ecki recalls that in 1994 Leven wrote in his autograph book that it never rains in Scotland, which is why the songs are so happy. In Leven’s sound-world Scottish folklore, blues and jazz fuse into a unity that quickly makes one forget genre labels.

The new album, he writes, does not quite reach the “dark intimacy” of *Fairytales For Hardmen* (1997) and *Night Lilies* (given as 1999; actually 1998), but is more convincing than the “somewhat frayed” *Defending Ancient Springs*, made the year before with David Thomas. It offers ten songs, compressed despite their length, ranging from quiet contemplations (“Stopped By Woods On A Snowy Evening”) through amusing and blasphemous thought-games (“The Sexual Loneliness Of Jesus Christ”) to hymn-like pieces (“Washing By Hand”). The “hard-to-digest centrepiece” is the almost ten-minute, tormented, bluesy lament “Rainy Day Bergen Women”, again recorded with David Thomas of Pere Ubu, in which Leven works through his father’s death – one of the extremely intimate and at the same time heavily veiled moments of an otherwise warm and transparent album.
Beneath the text are a photo of Leven by Uli Kniep, a link to an interview and the tour dates: 30 October Schlachthof, Hamburg, and 31 October Räucherei, Kiel.
zitate_kontext: Ecki on Leven as a storyteller
Leven’s inscription in the reviewer’s autograph book, 1994

2001-10-05-uncut-jackie-leven-borders-ox.titel: [Concert review] Jackie Leven at Borders Bookshop, Oxford Street, London
2001-10-05-uncut-jackie-leven-borders-ox.kurz: Gavin Martin reports on a solo in-store show at a London bookshop: Leven is irreverent and coarse between songs, crystalline in his fingerpicking, and for Martin the most naturalistic and profound blues artist in these islands.
inhalt: Gavin Martin reviews, for Uncut, a solo in-store performance by Jackie Leven at Borders bookshop on London's Oxford Street on 5 October 2001. The “big denim-clad man” looks at home among the shelves in front of a generation-spanning audience, Martin writes: in three decades on the troubadour trail Leven has drawn deep inspiration from the written word, from German literature to detective fiction. His well-documented hard times, addiction and past commercial failure, Martin adds, have strengthened his resolve and fed his creativity, and the “stupendous” new album *Creatures of Light and Darkness* is further proof of his standing as the most naturalistic and profound blues artist operating in these islands.

The in-person solo Leven is a different proposition from the warm arrangements on his records, Martin says. His attitude is irreverent, casual and offhand, and contrasts with the wounded but loving solemnity at the heart of his songs. Leven opens by saying he almost forgot to come to London, having just got back from northern Russia. Then he asserts his authority and his link to British folk blues with a cascade of crystalline finger-picking and long sustained notes that fill the room during “Universal Blue”.

False modesty is not in Leven's remit. He has to grab a copy of his latest CD from the shelf to refresh his memory, and is immediately gratified by what he finds. The evidence follows: “Exit Wound”, with an extraordinary vocal that veers between fractured staccato and agonised rumble; the Robert Frost-inspired “Stopped By Woods”, pitched between warm invitation and dark forewarning; and best of all the semi-comic “Billy Ate My Pocket”, about a horse that becomes a detective – not in the police force, which Leven calls silly, but a private detective specialising in adultery.

Between songs Leven's talk ranges from literary reminiscence through outrageous claims about the origin of an esteemed organ to a gruesome excursion into bowel matters aboard a ferry crossing the Barents Sea. No Leven performance is complete without such a stomach-churning tale, Martin notes, but he is no fool: he knows the ugly story only highlights the beauty of the music. The verdict is warmly positive throughout.

Leven on the horse in “Billy Ate My Pocket”.
Gavin Martin on the solo Leven.
Gavin Martin's verdict on Leven and the new album.

2001-10-triste-the-triste-interview-jack.kurz: Longest interview in the website archive, conducted before a concert at Jim's Cafe in Colne (Lancashire) on the tour for *Creatures of Light and Darkness*.
inhalt: Longest interview in the website archive, conducted before a concert at Jim's Cafe in Colne (Lancashire) on the tour for *Creatures of Light and Darkness*. Leven describes the Bryn Derwen studio near Bethesda on the edge of Snowdonia (sound engineer David Wrench), which feels to him like the Scottish west coast, and his way of working: intensive pre-production with demos sent several times to the musicians, so that studio time runs “like a military operation”; he always gives a safe brief but hopes for better ideas from the musicians. He calls sound collages “landscaping” and cites the producer John Sinclair (Doll by Doll days). He tells how the shipyard workers' voices in “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” came about (a tip from Michael Cosgrave over a beer in Bethesda), of “Billy Ate My Pocket” (a horse eats a note from his pocket) and of the Blackwood song after an encounter on a bridge in Regensburg. Album titles are “stalking horses”; *Defending Ancient Springs* was meant to be provocatively called “The Total Poetry of Industrial Language”. He distinguishes male “concept” from female “imagination”, sneers at Kevin Rowland, speaks openly about the death of his father (in “My Spanish Dad” and “Rainy Day Bergen Women”), praises Michael Weston King (whose next album he wants to produce at Bryn Derwen in January 2002), explains invented bars in his booklet thank-you lists (Royston Vasey) and admits to having deliberately smuggled the “Small Faeces” joke into the Cooking Vinyl newsletter. To close: merchandising is vital in Germany (up to £1000 per night), and he changed agents three times in three years in order to play away from the usual club circuit.
zitate_kontext: Leven on sound collages on his albums.

2001-11-21-irish-examiner-jackie-leven-f.kurz: Preview of Leven's Ireland tour in autumn 2001, written by Liam Carson (then at Lilliput Press, later founder of the Irish Language Literature Festival IMRAM) for the *Irish Examiner* and the *Irish News*.
inhalt: Preview of Leven's Ireland tour in autumn 2001, written by Liam Carson (then at Lilliput Press, later founder of the Irish Language Literature Festival IMRAM) for the *Irish Examiner* and the *Irish News*. The text opens with Leven's quotation from a Yeats poem about the feeling of being blessed and able to bless, and makes blessing, friendship, community and poetic tradition its leitmotif. Leven talks about Fife's coal mines, wool and paper mills in the 50s and 60s and about women washing at stone communal troughs in the snow. He describes Doll by Doll as the opposite of punk's “cartoon violence”; formerly a vision drove him, today he is interested in the dream world. He criticises a culture that wants to analyse everything – images should work on their own. He explains at length how “Call Mother A Lonely Field” came about (a winter morning on a frozen field by the Thames at Maidenhead, a sudden longing for his mother). *Defending Ancient Springs* refers to Kathleen Raine's study, *Creatures of Light and Darkness* contains “My Spanish Dad” about his late father and a setting of Robert Frost. With Bly he sees “unexpressed grief” as the root of collective evils. To close: Leven as a bard with rogue's tales, who has spent a lot of time in Cork and Kerry. Overall tone: hymnic.
zitate_kontext: Leven on the change since Doll by Doll.

2001-12-03-mescalina-creatures-of-light-.kurz: Christian Verzeletti praises *Creatures of Light and Darkness* for its ancestral emotion and modern production: ten matured ballads somewhere between Van Morrison and a more rural Costello.
inhalt: On Mescalina, Christian Verzeletti introduces Jackie Leven as an “omone scozzese”, a big Scotsman, with a troubled past: first in the rock band Doll by Doll, then getting off heroin after a near-fatal attack on the streets of London. None of it undermined his deep humanity; he set up a detox centre, The Core Trust, and relaunched his solo career, for instance with the “excellent” *Defending Ancient Springs*. The new *Creatures of Light and Darkness* is the result of a true, genuine passion that Leven has learned to refine over time, in the company of his friend David Thomas, formerly of Pere Ubu.

Ten ballads, “each aged by years of listening and silence”, each with a different aroma that recalls something already heard but, once consumed, reveals its uniqueness. The sound is ancestral in the emotions it provokes but very modern in production: choirs, mandolins, winds, violins, bells, a pinch of electronics and noise on an intimist rock structure. The younger Van Morrison and a more rural, less pedantic Costello are shadows that lengthen over it, but Leven's creatures are guided by a light of their own.

The lyrics centre on the elements of nature (river, snow, rain, sea above all) and on life as their sacred projection. Singled out are “Hidden World Of She”, which wraps the silent flow of female sensuality in a Gregorian chant, “Rainy Day Bergen Women”, a deeply nocturnal blues lament in which harmonica and coughs create echoes, and “Stopped By Woods On A Snowy Evening”, a snow-covered mantle from which Leven's voice rises uncontaminated. The notes in the margin of the lyrics add to the charm: Robert Frost's poetry finds the same space as provincial life. “The Sexual Loneliness Of Jesus Christ” stands out for images that alternate sexual and religious attraction; first a mandolin and then an electric guitar mark the anxious need for answers that runs through the whole album. It closes with the delicate “Wrapped Up In Blue”, a farewell song that proceeds as slowly as the best slow soul and, the reviewer says, may warm your soul in the cold winter to come.
zitate_kontext: Christian Verzeletti on the album's sound

2001-12-17-pennyblackmusic-great-songs-f.kurz: Malcolm Carter recommends the four-CD box Great Songs from Eternal Bars as the best and cheapest introduction to Leven's "Celtic soul", praising The Wanderer, the sleeve notes and "Working Alone / A Blessing".
inhalt: Malcolm Carter reviews the four-CD box set from Cooking Vinyl for Pennyblackmusic (17 December 2001). Leven, "former frontman of the early eighties rock band Doll By Doll", has developed into one of our greatest songwriters and storytellers, and there are few artists who keep getting better with each album, which is exactly what he does. His "unique brand of Celtic soul" mixes folk, rock and poetry and blends sweet melodies with biting but passionate lyrics. The box contains *Fairy Tales for Hard Men*, *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West*, *Control* (recorded in 1971 but released later) and the live album *The Wanderer*. Carter dates *Fairy Tales* to "1977" (it was 1997) and says *Control* was not released until 1997.

*The Wanderer*, previously sold only at gigs, is available commercially for the first time, with three bonus tracks from different periods and shows, including ones in Australia, Norway, Poland and Wales. Live albums are generally of interest only to those who were at the concert, Carter says, but here Leven conveys his stage presence through the speakers so the listener feels part of the show, and the humour of his between-song tales lightens the dark mood. *Control* is interesting because his voice had not yet developed the deep, warm sound of his later records; according to Leven it was made after an intense period of taking LSD, which he feels shows, though what shows more is a maturing talent.

Carter praises the sleeve notes ("compelling reading"; if Leven wants a break from music, success as an author is guaranteed) and notes that his songs are often described as steeped in mists, poetry and alcohol. "Working Alone / A Blessing", from *Forbidden Songs*, starts as a typical Leven song about a man alone in a field and ends with Leven reciting James Wright's poem "A Blessing" over his own music; in other hands it could have been mawkish, but it works as if Wright had written it for that purpose. Surprises also come in the acoustic "Fear of Women" on *Fairy Tales*: halfway through, Avril Jamieson's angelic voice sings "Unchained Melody" while what sounds like crashing plates adds a disturbing touch, before Leven returns singing about walking through Glasgow in freezing gloom and intones "Be suspicious". Verdict: there is no better or cheaper introduction, but beware: you will end up buying the rest of his records.

2001-cooking-vinyl-jackie-leven-biografi.kurz: The 2001 label biography traces Leven from Glenrothes through his wandering years and Doll by Doll to the assault, heroin, acupuncture and the founding of the CORE Trust.
inhalt: To mark *Creatures of Light and Darkness* (2001), Cooking Vinyl presents Jackie Leven as the man from the Kingdom of Fife who was, until relatively recently, perceived as little more than another wayward son from the wilder shores of rock – the unnerving front man of the “genuinely enigmatic” band Doll By Doll. Time and a consistently superb series of albums for the label, it says, have revealed an artist of endurance and candour with a hard poetic eye for the vicissitudes of life.

He spent his childhood and teens in the Fife glen villages and the new town of Glenrothes, built mainly to serve the Rothes Colliery, which flooded shortly after the Queen opened it and was never used. Unemployment was high and school-leavers were expected to sign up with one of the two main employers, the Fettykill Papermill or the Haig whisky factory, known locally as ‘the Kill’ and ‘the Bond’. Leven gave both a miss and became an itinerant musician in his late teens, sleeping rough through harsh winters. The pattern, the text says, still prevails: to the consternation of friends and record company he tends to disappear every early spring to road-walk and sleep rough. He lived in Carlisle, Newcastle, Poole, Berlin, Madrid and Tralee; at the time of writing he is in “darkest Hampshire” beside his horse, an enormous English cob called Eric.

In 1975, we are told, he half-settled in southern Dorset, where he met the drummer David MacIntosh and the guitarist Joe Shaw and formed Doll By Doll, “one of the most ferocious live rock acts” of the late seventies and eighties, whose intensity was at odds with what Leven called the ‘cartoon violence’ of punk. Their five albums (one unreleased) were surprisingly melodic. After the band dissolved he began a solo album for Tony Stratton-Smith’s Charisma label, but the project ended when he was attacked in a north London street while walking home from recording, nearly strangled, and left unable to sing or speak for the best part of two years. In pain, he turned to heroin and was addicted for a while.

Wanting his life back, he rejected existing treatments and, with a sympathetic doctor, devised a holistic programme of addiction release whose mainstay was traditional Chinese acupuncture. Its success led in 1985 to his co-founding the CORE Trust in Marylebone, London, which still offers a holistic approach to addiction; Princess Diana formally opened the centre and contributed to its fundraising without being asked. Throughout, Leven kept writing; after much hesitation he recorded a demo that became the core of *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*, with contributions from Robert Bly and Mike Scott. The biography dates the album to 1995; it was released in 1994.
The page also offered a RealAudio sample, ‘My Spanish Dad’.

On the attack in north London

2001-milo-nolan-i-swear-i-was-there.kurz: In Nolan’s book on the Sex Pistols gig in Manchester in 1976, one eyewitness is said to have later worked with Leven, the former singer of the “Scottish New Wave/folk nutcases” Doll by Doll.
inhalt: In *I Swear I Was There* (Milo Books, 2001), Dave Nolan’s book on the Sex Pistols gig in Manchester in 1976 and its aftermath, one of the eyewitnesses is said to have later worked with Jackie Leven, the former singer of the “Scottish New Wave/folk nutcases” Doll by Doll, and to have toured with his band The Philistines. Which eyewitness is meant is not clear from the available excerpt.

2001-orion-rankin-resurrection-men.kurz: Jackie Leven appears for the first time in Ian Rankin’s Rebus novel *Resurrection Men* (2001): a character swaps Led Zeppelin for a Leven CD in the car, exactly the album Rebus would have chosen. The friendship between the two grew from it.
inhalt: *Resurrection Men* (Orion, London, 2001) is the Rebus novel in which Jackie Leven features for the first time. A character changes the CD in his car, taking out Led Zeppelin and putting in a record by Leven; it is “just the album” that Rebus himself would have chosen.

According to Rankin and Leven themselves, the musician discovered the mention by chance and got in touch with the author. That was the beginning of their friendship and of the later collaboration that produced stage shows and the double CD *Jackie Leven Said* (2005). The encyclopedia *British Crime Writing* (Greenwood) names this very book as the starting point. The passage is also found in the novel’s translations (French *Une dernière chance pour Rebus*, 2008; Dutch *Lazarus*, 2007).
A divergent claim that the first mention occurs only in a novel after *Shining Brother, Shining Sister* (2003) does not fit this book’s year of publication.

2002-01-wondrous-stories-experiencing-ja.medium: Wondrous Stories (magazine of the Classic Rock Society), no. 120; web version on rockreviews.co.uk
2002-01-wondrous-stories-experiencing-ja.kurz: Doug Anderson, an English fan, accompanied Leven through Germany for two weeks in October 2001 as merchandiser – he got the job through a call in an email group.
inhalt: Doug Anderson, an English fan, accompanied Leven through Germany for two weeks in October 2001 as merchandiser – he got the job through a call in an email group. His report for the Classic Rock Society's magazine (January 2002, “slightly altered” as a web version) first describes the daily routine of the tour: short drives anticlockwise around the country, late soundchecks, often poorly prepared equipment, up to seven hours of work per evening. At the merchandise stand the Haunted Valley CD *Deep in the Heart of Nowhere* sold best, because the audience mostly already owned the new studio album.

The second part describes the concert: Leven and Michael Cosgrave opened with “Call Mother a Lonely Field”, after which the programme varied according to mood; fixtures were “Billy Ate My Pocket”, “Jim O'Windygates” (introduced with memories of Leven's work in the Haig whisky factory) and a train story of up to ten minutes. There were no encores (“Jackie doesn't believe in them”). Shows lasted almost two hours. Anderson compares Leven to a mixture of Billy Connolly and a bass-baritone Bob Dylan. Also included are a complete setlist and the December 2001 dates. Enthusiastic fan tone.

2002-08-23-rolling-stone-forum-jackie-le.kurz: Oldest Leven thread in the forum of the German Rolling Stone, 29 posts from August 2002 to March 2024 (two pages).
inhalt: Oldest Leven thread in the forum of the German Rolling Stone, 29 posts from August 2002 to March 2024 (two pages). It begins with fans compiling their own best-ofs and assessments of the production; people discuss whether Leven would be better off staying unknown. In 2003 people are waiting for the tour with Midnight Choir and Richard Thompson presented by the magazine and for the promised Doll by Doll reissue. One user remembers a poorly attended Doll by Doll reunion concert in the mid-nineties at which Alan Bangs was said to be in the audience. The user “hasenschnitte” announces in February 2003 a new German Yahoo group on Leven and posts the March 2003 dates (Tuttlingen, Tübingen, Frankfurt, Essen, Bremen, Kiel, Singwitz, Hannover, Bielefeld). In August 2003 a concert recording on Radio Eins is discussed, in September 2005 a studio guest appearance on Radio Eins about “Elegy for Johnny Cash”, and a user recalls Leven's appearance at the Nuremberg Bardentreffen in 2001. After his death “stefane” announces the NDR Info obituary “Elegie für den Celtic Soulman” by Uli Kniep (14.01.2012) with the announcement text; “thomas-zimmer” posts his own concert review of the appearance at the Jubez in Karlsruhe in 2008 (Olivier story, “Museum of Childhood”, Roberto Duran song). Last post: a pointer to the Radio Bremen Zwei programme of 01.04.2024 with the recording from the Sendesaal Bremen of 29.03.2004.

2002-ashgate-reising-every-sound-there-i.kurz: In the essay collection *Every Sound There Is* on the Beatles’ *Revolver*, a chapter on “She Said She Said” quotes Jackie Leven of Doll by Doll: he loves the confusion the song creates.
inhalt: The scholarly collection (Ashgate, Aldershot, 2002), edited by Russell Reising, deals with *Revolver* and its significance for rock and roll. In a chapter on “She Said She Said”, drawing on a survey of musicians, probably from Mojo, Leven “(Doll By Doll)” is also quoted. He loves the confusion the song creates.
The original source of the remark is not given in the visible excerpt; the wording is not preserved here.

2002-entertainment-law-gregg-freedom-of-.kurz: A legal article on the blasphemy warranty in music contracts mentions Leven in passing: in 1994 the MP for Selby instigated blasphemy proceedings over “So My Soul Can Sing”, without success.
inhalt: Lindsay D. Gregg, a London solicitor, examines in the journal *Entertainment Law* (2002) the customary warranty in recording and publishing contracts that submitted material is not obscene, defamatory or blasphemous. He traces the history of English blasphemy law in the light of freedom of expression (Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights) and concludes that the major record companies have by now dropped the blasphemy warranty from their standard contracts, but that the offence remains on the books and its abolition is overdue.

In the section “Blasphemy and Music” Gregg lists cases in which music was attacked as allegedly blasphemous: Crass (1978), Christian Death, Depeche Mode, Creaming Jesus, James, Cradle of Filth. Leven appears in this series with a single sentence: in 1994 the MP for Selby instigated blasphemy proceedings in respect of the song “So My Soul Can Sing”. The footnote cites the *Yorkshire Evening Press* of 29 March 1994, quoted via Martin Cloonan’s book *Banned!* (1996), and states that the track was from the Cooking Vinyl album *Songs from the Argyll Circle* (sic) and that the attempt was unsuccessful.

The MP is not named. “So My Soul Can Sing” in fact appears on *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* (1994), not on the Argyll Cycle releases, so Gregg’s footnote evidently gives the album inaccurately.

2002-globalguest-inoffizielles-gaestebuc.medium: globalguest.com/gb/TOUT – guestbook of the fan site jackieleven.com
2002-globalguest-inoffizielles-gaestebuc.kurz: Around 60 entries. Fans thank him for the Christmas concert in Milford (December 2001, with praise for organiser Mick Nolan and the “Girls”) and for the live albums *Greetings From Milford* (“finally Main Travelled Roads on CD”) and *Barefoot Days*; people ask about Doll by Doll reissues a…
inhalt: Around 60 entries. Fans thank him for the Christmas concert in Milford (December 2001, with praise for organiser Mick Nolan and the “Girls”) and for the live albums *Greetings From Milford* (“finally Main Travelled Roads on CD”) and *Barefoot Days*; people ask about Doll by Doll reissues on CD and about Doll by Doll concerts hinted at in the Haunted Valley newsletter. The writer Liam Carson is looking for a copy of the Concrete Bulletproof Invisible record and in August asks for news. Concert reports come from Otley, Leeds, Watford, Vienna (Aera, 16.05.), Hebden Bridge, Ruthin (North Wales; some women in the audience took offence at coarse stories), Tregaron and Leicester (The Musician); a promoter from Portsmouth (City Bar) reports a poorly attended but great evening. A Norwegian mentions concerts with David Thomas in Oslo, a Japanese writes that he sent Doll by Doll poems by airmail over twenty years ago, which were printed in a magazine. The fans' complaints about a Haunted Valley membership that never got a reply begin here. In December a German fan announces a new German Yahoo group.

2002-mercat-strong-great-scots-musicogra.kurz: Martin C. Strong’s Scottish music lexicon gives Leven his own entry: beginnings as John St. Field, founding Doll by Doll, the solo years, links to Robert Bly and Richard Jobson, and a complete discography to 2001.
inhalt: In *The Great Scots Musicography* (Mercat Press, Edinburgh, 2002) Jackie Leven has his own entry in Section 8 (“Rock, Pop & Indie”), to which the folk section cross-refers; it continues on a following page. The text expands the Doll by Doll entry from Strong’s *Great Indie Discography* into a Leven biography: beginnings as John St. Field with appearances including with Man, the move to London and the founding of Doll by Doll, the Magnet albums, the solo years, a link to Robert Bly and to “fellow ex-punk Fifer” Richard Jobson.

The entry includes a complete discography to 2001, among others *Control* (COOKCD 131, “rec. 1973–5”, LP “iss. 1975” in Spain), the box set COOKCD 212 and *Creatures of Light & Darkness* with David Thomas (COOKCD 213, August 2001). The dating of *Control* (recorded 1973–75, LP 1975) differs from other accounts (1971/1973).

2002-modernista-feber.kurz: The Swedish collection *Feber* includes a review by Lennart Persson dated 14 August 2001 that leads from Van Morrison to Leven, a Scot who needs and deserves attention.
inhalt: The collection of Swedish record reviews (Modernista, Stockholm, 2002) contains a piece by Lennart Persson, dated 14 August 2001, on Jackie Leven's album *Creatures of Light and Darkness* (mis-set in its heading as “Greetings of Light & Darkness”). Persson starts with Van Morrison and moves on to Leven: a Scot who needs and deserves attention and whose life fits the romance and drama of his music.

He tells of the attack by a street gang, which he dates to the mid-Eighties; afterwards Leven could not even listen to music. Persson sees the time with Doll by Doll as the real start of his career and recommends *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* as the entry point. The extract does not give the review's original place of publication, presumably a newspaper.

2002-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.titel: [Collected finds Nasjonalbiblioteket 2002: news items, announcements, lists]
2002-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.kurz: Four finds from Norwegian newspapers in 2002: Leven’s lyrics in translation (“Tre tekster”, Friheten), a Kabelvåg venue naming him as a memorable guest, and two record reviews using him as a yardstick.
inhalt: In 2002 the Norwegian press carried no new concert and no new studio album, but four mentions. The most striking: on 15 March 2002 the Oslo paper Friheten printed, under “Jackie Leven: Tre tekster”, three song lyrics in Norwegian translation, among them “Billy spiste lomma mi” (a song Leven introduces by saying it is about a horse that, under unusual circumstances, becomes a private detective, “based on a true story”), the setting of a Robert Frost poem (“Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening”) and “Tullet inn i sorg”. The paper notes that the texts were translated from the lyric booklet of the album *Creatures of Light and Darkness*, released in summer 2001.

On 29 January 2002 Nordlys, in a report on the Nordland Art and Film School in Kabelvåg (Lofoten), names the pub Præstengbrygga as the students’ meeting place: Jackie Leven, Unni Wilhelmsen, Vidar Busk and Misvær Ska forening have “all held some memorable concerts” there. Two further mentions are comparisons in record reviews: on 1 March 2002 Jærbladet reviews an album by David (Knopfler), saying it has the same musical expression as Leven, who however has “that little extra” David lacks. On 31 December 2002 Bergensavisen judges of Michael J. Sheehy’s *No Longer My Concern* that he has more in common with Jackie Leven lyrically than with Tom Waits.
