Jærbladet (1 March 2002) in a record review
Tore Bø in Bergensavisen (31 December 2002) on Michael J. Sheehy

2002-pearson-railway-holiday-in-scotland.kurz: In Pearson’s railway travel book Leven appears several times: as the singer of Fife’s places, who sings of bars, time and place, and as a song that ends with the sound of a steam train.
inhalt: *Railway Holiday in Scotland* (J. M. Pearson & Son) is a railway travel book with several references to Leven. Passing through Fife, the author links the area’s paper-making history with Leven, who sang of these places. He admires in him – besides the number of bars he seems to know – the sense of time and place. Elsewhere the journey through the Lammermuir Hills reminds him of a Leven song that ends with the sound of a steam train.

2002-viking-heylin-can-you-feel-the-sile.kurz: Clinton Heylin dedicates his Van Morrison biography *Can You Feel the Silence?* to Jackie Leven, “who continues to steal the highlights” – evidence of the friendship between the rock historian and Leven.
inhalt: Heylin's biography *Can You Feel the Silence? Van Morrison: A New Biography* (Viking, London 2002; Chicago Review Press 2003) carries a dedication to Jackie Leven that begins by calling him the one who continues to steal the highlights (from Van Morrison). The dedication documents the friendship between the rock historian and Leven; Heylin was also among the contributors to Leven's fan club. Whether Leven appears in the main text of the book cannot be told from the search extracts.
zitate_kontext: Start of the dedication in Heylin's Van Morrison biography

2003-01-20-bergensavisen-cd-jackie-leven.kurz: Tore Bø praises *Shining Brother Shining Sister* in Bergens Avisen as the work of a poetic storyteller with one of the best soul voices in the business, who deserves an audience on Leonard Cohen’s scale.
inhalt: The short review in Bergens Avisen opens with a superlative: there is nobody, “absolutely nobody”, who can sing so poetically about trains leaving grimy industrial towns in lashing rain, or about the romance one can experience in the back streets of cities like Stockholm, Bergen (“Levin”, as the paper spells it, must have good memories of it) and Amsterdam. Great lyricism, too, is the story of the old woman who sits thinking of the man who used to love her so warmly in winter.

The critic praises Leven’s voice as one of the best soul voices in the business; he singles out the “utterly lovely” “My Philosophy”, where he says one hears Leven together with Ron Sexsmith (the attribution is the review’s). Leven is “Scotland’s best-kept secret” and would deserve an audience the size of Leonard Cohen’s. As a future classic he names “A Little Voice In Space”, quoting a love line from it, and for “Heroin Dealer Blues”, about a drug dealer’s dreams, he notes a story with real background behind it.

Bø closes by pointing to Leven’s lived life: he has fallen flat more than once, and so it is good to be able to report that he is now doing well and is “more together than ever”. His advice: “Lytt og lær!” – listen and learn.
zitate_kontext: Tore Bø on Leven’s songwriting on *Shining Brother Shining Sister*.
Bø on Leven as “Scotland’s best-kept secret”.

2003-02-03-rockol-jackie-leven-nelle-can.kurz: The Milan interview accompanies “Shining Brother Shining Sister”. Leven explains why he includes poems and reciting guests in his recordings.
inhalt: The Milan interview accompanies “Shining Brother Shining Sister”. Leven explains why he includes poems and reciting guests in his recordings. In doing so he distinguishes his song lyrics from actual poetry: in his estimation, poetry is found only in places in his songs. He combines his enthusiasm for literary language with a criticism of the rock of the time.

Leven names Fontella Bass and Feodor Chaliapin as early inspirations. He explains “Heroin Dealer Blues” as an attempt to approach Randy Newman's art. He traces the sound backdrop of “Classic Northern Diversions” to train journeys; he also links “Irresistible Romance” with observations made on the road. These are the songwriter's statements about his work, not independently verified records of how the songs came about.

Further topics are his interest in the music that taxi drivers listen to and the pub as a public place of encounter. He explicitly explains the Neruda reference of the album title against the background of the looming Iraq war and the humanity of the people living there. At the end the editors list five planned Italian concerts in March 2003. No author is named in the visible version.

2003-02-03-the-guardian-jackie-leven-kor.kurz: Dave Simpson’s enthusiastic live review from a pub in Otley: Leven, “big and beautifully damaged”, is a true modern troubadour; a third of the evening is dark songs, the rest funny and abysmal stories.
inhalt: Dave Simpson reviews Leven’s gig at Korks in Otley in the Guardian (3 February 2003). He first summarises Leven’s life story as Leven tells it: he led the feted band Doll By Doll, who, he says, never achieved success because they were more interested in chasing “a terrible beauty” than writing platinum albums. In 1983 he was slashed across the throat as he walked down a street in London; he couldn’t speak for months and his unmistakable falsetto was lost. Shattered, he spent years losing his pain in heroin before founding a charity for addicts. Then his long-term girlfriend and charity co-founder ran off with the Dalai Lama’s bodyguard.

These remarkable experiences, Simpson writes, have inspired scores of great, warped songs, and hearing Leven perform them – the voice now recovered to a coruscating, metamorphosing tremor – is an unforgettable experience. The man could fill venues with his presence: 52, big and beautifully damaged, with his socks rolled up over his trousers, looking like a great, confused creature who just wandered in off the moor. He is a true modern troubadour, and this is just another stop in his career journey from pub to pub, fiasco to adventure.

Dark, twisted songs such as “Heroin Dealer Blues” from his new album, *Shining Sister Shining Brother*, form about a third of the show. The rest of the time Leven introduces them with often entirely unrelated stories that are “compulsive and hilarious”: how he alienated the entire city of Munich, the time his partner mistook dog food for his excrement, and a budgerigar with a coarse name. Alternating between triple vodka-and-lime and lager without any dip in sharpness, he roams the surreal netherworld of pubs and alcoholism and is fascinated by people who have “the despair of poverty bleeding into their life”. He romanticises Glasgow’s Shat Inn, but a bleak horror haunts songs like “Three O’Clock Men” and “Dustelegia”, about a hapless dreamer and small-time dealer who was shot dead. Leven is “like a cocktail of Van Morrison, Nick Drake and Irvine Welch” (Welsh is meant); the humour and the horror increase exponentially until you literally don’t know whether to laugh or cry, “and many end up doing both”.
zitate_kontext: Dave Simpson on Leven’s stage presence
Simpson on the effect of the show

2003-02-06-gaesteliste-der-tod-der-traeu.kurz: Long interview on “Shining Brother Shining Sister” (2003). Leven explains the choice of guests who recite poems: David Thomas reads Rilke, Ron Sexsmith a poem by E. E. Cummings at the end of “My Philosophy”; you have to be careful about who you give which text to.
inhalt: Long interview on “Shining Brother Shining Sister” (2003). Leven explains the choice of guests who recite poems: David Thomas reads Rilke, Ron Sexsmith a poem by E. E. Cummings at the end of “My Philosophy”; you have to be careful about who you give which text to. Former Doll by Doll colleagues also appear on the album. He speaks at length about “Savannah Waltz”, which is based on a series of powerful, “cinematic” dreams of an old, dignified woman waiting for a male angel; the dream world is, for the West, a lost world (his own account). Of the dealer Dusty in “Heroin Dealer Blues” he says he does not choose the characters, they find him; society passes responsibility down the line. Good creativity has a healing quality (example Chet Baker), but nobody buys CDs for that. “My Philosophy” is about the time when his life was falling apart: he holed up with newspapers in the Marylebone underground station until two friendly policemen asked if everything was all right; he replied that he was working on his philosophy – the sign to carry on (his own account). Also: praise of clichés and Euro-pop (“the music in the lifts”), production of Michael Weston King's album, announcement of the tour with Richard Thompson and Midnight Choir, accompanied by “Michael Cosgrove” [sic].
zitate_kontext: Leven on the dream behind “Savannah Waltz”.

2003-02-11-dagsavisen-gamle-helter.kurz: Geir Rakvaag reviews the new Cooking Vinyl albums by Richard Thompson and Jackie Leven together in Dagsavisen: both are more than good enough, he says, but are beginning to repeat themselves.
inhalt: In the double review "Gamle helter" ("Old heroes") in Dagsavisen on 11 February 2003, Geir Rakvaag takes Richard Thompson's *The Old Kit Bag* and Jackie Leven's *Shining Brother Shining Sister* (both Cooking Vinyl) together. Both have made so many brilliant albums that "even more in the same direction as before" becomes slightly too much, even if each new record is more than good enough on its own. Made by young debutants, he says, they would quickly have been small sensations.

Of Leven he writes that he carries on with a tried and tested formula: his sensitive voice in ambitious poetry about life's big questions, to arrangements that are often "very large-scale" for a man who likes to tour alone with a guitar. He also keeps wooing his international audience, and lines like "I love Hamburg / Oslo too / Greetings from Bergen / Mmmm Milano" do not live up to his otherwise high lyrical level. Otherwise the album is "entirely exemplary in execution", but Leven makes an album almost every year and, like Thompson, has begun to repeat himself. Conciliatory ending: good things cannot be said too often, and if you have listened a lot to these two before, you almost have to hear them once more.

Thompson, the review says, sounds almost too contented and has written songs that burned themselves into the memory far more deeply; after Linda Thompson's underrated *Fashionably Late* he is less impressive than hoped. On the same page Leven's album also appears in a list of new releases.

2003-02-12-sarpsborg-arbeiderblad-en-bed.kurz: Erling Brøndmo recommends Shining Brother Shining Sister in Sarpsborg Arbeiderblad: Leven sounds lighter, easier and more varied than before, and it is high time to discover him.
inhalt: Under the headline "En bedre Jackie Leven" ("A better Jackie Leven"), Erling Brøndmo writes in Sarpsborg Arbeiderblad on 12 February 2003 about Leven's *Shining Brother Shining Sister* (printed as "Shining Brothers Shining Sisters"; Cooking Vinyl). Some musicians are left to get on with their thing without the big commercial spotlight falling on them, however solid and good they are, and Leven is one of them.

He works in a musical landscape that should please all fans of Van Morrison: the starting point is firmly rooted in traditional music, and while Morrison draws on the Irish and Celtic, Leven takes from Scottish folk traditions. On this album he is lighter and easier in mind and varies his expression more than on earlier records. That is positive, since he had a tendency to become a bit too closed and almost one-track. Leven, who may well be called a critics' favourite, still has the same starting point, but the backdrops vary from synthetic via rock (only to be expected from the old Doll by Doll man) to jazz, which strengthens the overall impression. His closing advice: if you have not opened your ears to Jackie Leven before, it is high time to do so.

2003-02-15-hamar-dagblad-noe-a-tenke-pa.kurz: Geir Hovensjø reviews *Shining Brother, Shining Sister* warmly: Leven has something to say and puts the modern world in perspective, but tends to over-arrange here and there; the sleeve with lines of poetry deserves close study.
inhalt: This short record review, “Noe å tenke på” (“Something to think about”), in Hamar Dagblad (15 February 2003) calls Leven a Scottish poet, musician and songwriter who has given us a series of good albums in recent years and evidently has more in store. He has “something on his mind”, puts our debatable modern world in perspective and chooses music that supports the words.

As usual he offers several highlights, but also some songs that are not especially interesting musically. Perhaps there is a tendency to over-arrange here and there; he is just as good when he under-arranges and keeps it simple and bare. The sleeve is “worth a close study”: it carries verses by several well-known poets, for instance words by the American Robert Bly on paradise (men and women spend only a moment in Paradise; the lovers watch Charlie Chaplin eat his shoe and a moment later find themselves barefooted in the grave). The critic’s comment is a terse “Akk ja…” (“Ah, well…”). The review is signed Geir Hovensjø.

2003-02-19-stavanger-aftenblad-poesi-for.kurz: Geir Flatøe reviews *Shining Brother, Shining Sister* with goodwill: poem recitations and guests make it a rock-meets-poetry album for melancholy evenings, even if many songs run too long.
inhalt: Geir Flatøe opens in Stavanger Aftenblad by observing that rock and poetry are closely related and that Leven ties the bonds tighter by including poem recitations on his latest album. David Thomas of Pere Ubu is allowed to take on Rainer Maria Rilke’s “Faces”, Ron Sexsmith contributes a few lines to “My Philosophy”, and Leven’s friend, the ageing American poet Robert Bly, appears in the opener “Classic Northern Diversions” with a line from a French medieval prayer (“Lord help me, because my boat is so small and your sea is so immense”), which Flatøe says Norwegian Sunday-school children should know well.

Leven is seldom among those who rein themselves in: the songs usually spread out wide, and at times Flatøe wishes he would stop in time and tighten up a few minutes here and there. He is not one to keep to the three-minute rule; “a bit more Scottish miserliness could do wonders”. At the same time the singer-songwriter character is strong, and the songs often deal with what he experiences on his many travels – for example “Another Man In The Old Arcade”, inspired by a man in Cardiff who drinks in the same bar every day since his wife left him, or “Irresistible Romance”, in which Leven mentions Oslo and Bergen but forgets Stavanger.

Finally the critic places him: Leven, born in Fife in 1950, released several records with Doll By Doll before trying on his own in 1983 (his solo career in fact began later). The big breakthrough never came, but he has delivered a series of fine albums that are “a blessing in melancholy evening hours”.
zitate_kontext: Geir Flatøe on the length of many of the songs.

2003-02-23-gaesteliste-koeln-gloria-mit-.kurz: Ullrich Maurer reports on a three-act evening in Cologne with Midnight Choir, Richard Thompson and Leven; Leven and Michael Cosgrave stretch the songs beyond ten minutes, and Leven’s stories are what make the songs make sense.
inhalt: This Gaesteliste.de report, headed “Depression ist Scheiße” (“Depression is shit”), covers a short package tour date at Cologne’s Gloria on 23 February 2003 with Midnight Choir, Richard Thompson and Jackie Leven. As Leven explained later, the running order was swapped by mutual agreement from night to night; here the Norwegian band Midnight Choir opened, Thompson played solo, and Leven closed. Maurer describes a comparatively mature audience for “solid, story-driven songwriting without any hipness factor”.

Leven, he writes, brought keyboard player Michael Cosgrave, a good idea because the rich but transparent keyboard carpets already carry the atmosphere on Leven’s records. Besides the familiar stories – for example about his youth in a whisky distillery (“Haigh” in the review) – there were new ones for the songs of the then current album *Shining Brother Shining Sister*. Again the contrast showed between Leven the introverted, melancholy songwriter and Leven the life-affirming, at times hilarious performer. He uses it deliberately, Maurer says, because only so can the sometimes complex, rather metaphorical contents of his songs be even half appreciated.

“Classic Northern Divisions” (spelled “Diversions” in the review) and “My Philosophy” made sense only with Leven’s absurd background stories. “My Philosophy”, Maurer explains, is about two London policemen who saved him from the worst depression of his life; “Classic Northern Divisions” is a kind of metaphysical travelogue. Between the lines there was a lesson too: sadness is good because positive things can grow from it, depression is useless because it inhibits action.

Musically, Leven used the possibilities of the duo to break the songs into epic, freely built sections and explore them at length. That was not to everyone’s taste – no piece ran under ten minutes – but for fans it was a fine chance to see the mostly solo performer interacting with another musician. All in all, the verdict runs, the three-act bill worked better than expected, as the different approaches complemented each other in mood “in an almost magical way”.
zitate_kontext: Maurer on Leven’s two sides on stage
Maurer on the message in Leven’s stage patter
Maurer on the extended duo versions

2003-02-26-tromso-jackie-leven-leverer-i.kurz: Kjetil Vik hails *Shining Brother Shining Sister*: Leven has never made a bad album and is on top form, with one of the best soul voices around and guests including Ron Sexsmith, David Thomas and Robert Bly; concert at Blå Rock on 2 March.
inhalt: Kjetil Vik reviews *Shining Brother Shining Sister* (Cooking Vinyl) in the Tromsø newspaper. The Scot from a remote spot in the Kingdom of Fife on Scotland's east coast has “yet to release a bad album”, and with his eighteenth record on Cooking Vinyl (the paper's count) he is back in splendid form, perhaps better than for a long time. Leven belongs to the artists who captivate with personal lyrics and strong melodies, and it is not for nothing that he has been called “Scotland's answer to Van Morrison”. Words and melodies possess a rare power and energy, delivered by one of the best soul voices in the business. He sings with such intensity that you have to believe him, whether he is singing about drug dealing, immortal love or romantic back streets in Stockholm or Bergen.

The album also features the Canadian Ron Sexsmith (like Leven “an all too well preserved musical secret”), the American David Thomas and the poet Robert Bly – an “incredibly strong all-star cast”. It was recorded in Wales but rehearsed and prepared in California, so the result is in many ways both sunny (California) and rain-heavy (Wales), “as life is too”. Conclusion: a well-rounded album firmly planted in the singer-songwriter tradition. Leven plays Blå Rock on Sunday 2 March.

2003-02-28-tromso-jackie-leven-pa-blaroc.kurz: Helge Matland previews Leven's concert at Blå Rock Café in Tromsø: the promoter Egon Holstad describes him live as intimate and gripping, with just a guitar and a miked-up floorboard, plus wild stories.
inhalt: In the paper Tromsø, Helge Matland previews Leven's concert on Sunday 2 March 2003 at Blå Rock Café. He opens with a curiosity: probably no other international artist thanks bars in Tromsø on his record sleeves. First Blå Rock Café was named on one of Leven's many records, and on the next release it was Grandbaren. Now the Scot is back in the city he has fallen in love with, and as always he plays the intimate stage at Blå Rock Café.

The promoter Egon Holstad (Blå Rock Café and Platebaren Feedback) describes the difference between records and stage: Leven's albums are something in their own right, but quite different from the man live. The records are in part pompous and loaded with arrangements and guest artists, whereas on stage he is one of the most intensely gripping and intimate things you can see: just himself, a guitar and a miked-up floorboard. Leven is a one-off as guitarist and singer, and between his beautiful, solemn songs he tells some of the wildest and most twisted stories you have heard, provoking both laughter and thought; all one can do is bow in the dust and feel privileged to be part of it. Holstad deserves much credit for Tromsø repeatedly getting to experience this songwriter, singer and guitarist.
The photo caption shows Leven at Blå Rock Café on 2 March 2000; on 2 March 2003 the Scot is back.
zitate_kontext: Egon Holstad on the difference between records and live shows

2003-02-cooking-vinyl-pressemitteilung-s.titel: [Press release] Jackie Leven – Shining Brother Shining Sister (COOKCD250)
2003-02-cooking-vinyl-pressemitteilung-s.kurz: The tongue-in-cheek label text for *Shining Brother Shining Sister* (2003) runs Leven’s life in parallel with that of Chancellor Gordon Brown, while telling the story of Doll by Doll, the attack, the heroin years and the founding of the CORE Trust.
inhalt: This press release for the album of 10 February 2003 is a piece of deliberately wry label prose. It sets two men from the Kingdom of Fife side by side: Gordon Brown, then Chancellor of the Exchequer, who has provided economic stability, and Jackie Leven, who has provided “an immense series of beautiful records” about inner poverty, the spirit at bay, and the greatness that can spring from such duress. The parallels are mostly punchlines: Brown’s father was a minister, Leven’s a carpet fitter. In the source the sentence breaks off mid-word; the fault lies with the label’s own text.

On Leven himself the text says: in the 1960s he joined the angry hardman tribes of Fife’s dying coalfields, doing meaningless jobs in bleak factories until his musical gifts revealed him as an outsider. Facing growing hostility from his peers, he had to leave Fife and then Scotland. For years he was rootless, often in real hardship, living in Carlisle, Newcastle, Poole, Exeter, London, Berlin and Madrid; the hunger to understand the mysteries of the world was stronger than the desire for comfort. What he learned became songs at once starkly beautiful and forbidding, which found expression in the five albums with his “infamous” rock band Doll By Doll (all now on Warner, one never released).

Then come the anecdotes. The Dolls once played the Reading Festival before Motörhead, having fortified themselves with LSD; Paul Du Noyer, then at the NME, wrote that “perversely the sun chose to shine as their set began”. The band wrong-footed audiences and the music establishment alike, the text claims, by playing charity concerts for the Philadelphia Association of the controversial Scottish psychiatrist R. D. Laing, and by hand-delivering an expensively produced calendar with graphic scenes of oral sex to the fifty most prominent people in the music business, bearing the strapline “You’re welcome to stay, but you won’t hear many jokes.”

On the band’s end, the text says the records were timelessly stunning but the image kept darkening, and the Dolls called it a day in 1983. While touring Ireland they toyed with the idea of vanishing entirely, but feared the world might say “thank god for that”. A year later, while recording a solo album for Charisma/Virgin, Leven was nearly strangled in an unprovoked attack as he walked home from the studio late at night in north London. For nearly two years he could neither sing nor speak, and retreated into heroin, “the classic drug of despair”. Watching children listen to a jazz band by the canal in Little Venice decided him to take his life back; he freed himself from addiction through traditional Chinese acupuncture and psychic healing.

From the method of his release came the CORE Trust, “an holistic approach to addiction” in central London, founded with the help of sympathetic complementary practitioners. Leven is now its patron; in its early days it was championed by the late Princess of Wales, and it enjoys support from the music business, notably from Leven’s friend Mike Scott. Leven returned to records on Cooking Vinyl with *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death*, featuring spoken contributions from Robert Bly and Mike Scott. “Eight great studio albums later” comes *Shining Brother Shining Sister*. The release closes by anticipating greater things from “these two outstanding Fifers”. Its dates differ from other sources.
zitate_kontext: The label on Leven’s youth in Fife
The label on the end of Doll by Doll
The label on the aftermath of the attack

2003-03-01-bergensavisen-leven-gar-i-fen.kurz: Preview of two Bergen appearances: on 07.03.2003 at the small venue Madam Felle and on 08.03. (International Women's Day) at Bergen Landsfengsel.
inhalt: Preview of two Bergen appearances: on 07.03.2003 at the small venue Madam Felle and on 08.03. (International Women's Day) at Bergen Landsfengsel. Leven says he was addicted to heroin and knows what it means to be an outlaw; he is looking forward to the prison concert. The prison's leisure activities manager, Frode Trefall, calls it a big thing to have a “world name” as a guest and expects lively interest from the prisoners.

Bergen has a special place in his heart, he says; the atmosphere reminds him of Scotland, and he mentions Bergen in at least one song on every new album. On the guests on *Shining Brother Shining Sister* (David Thomas, Ron Sexsmith, Robert Bly): none of them is ordinary, all are difficult, and that is exactly what makes them exciting; Sexsmith was at first afraid of him because of his past. He says he himself worked in a London women's prison, looking after women whose children were growing up without fathers and needed male values. He understands people who prefer alcohol or drugs to television (he himself is at times addicted to television), but has no time for state intervention – one has to want to stop oneself. Today he drinks alcohol in moderation and has his own whisky, Leven's Lament. The album had received 5 out of 6 in BA.

2003-03-01-nordlys-kiltkledd-helt-tilbak.kurz: Mariell Tverrå Løkås announces Leven’s fifth Tromsø concert at Blå Rock Café in *Nordlys*: his friend Egon Holstad calls him “the toughest Scottish export since malt whisky”, one of the world’s best guitarists and a charismatic storyteller.
inhalt: The feature “Kiltkledd helt tilbake i byen” (“Back in town in a kilt”) announces Leven’s concert on the following Sunday (2 March 2003) at Blå Rock Café in Tromsø, his fifth in the city. It opens by calling him “the toughest Scottish export since malt whisky”. His friend Egon Holstad says: “He’s a totally incredible guy with a unique ability to make people fond of him.” Leven arrives a day early to wander around in the snow in a kilt, which he nearly always wears.

Holstad recalls the first Tromsø gig at Easter 1995 with Andy White and praises Leven as one of the world’s best guitarists, “insanely authoritarian on stage”. He is also known for his stories: you get the feeling of becoming smarter each time you talk to him; what he says provokes as much thought as laughter, while he is very self-revealing and self-ironic. Leven has just toured Germany with Richard Thompson and Midnight Choir and will also play Kabelvåg, Bergen and Oslo during his stay in Norway. A photo caption in the paper calls him a “unik skotte”, and the “Tromsø Guide” listings of the same day “a one-off both as guitarist and vocalist”, compared with Mike Scott, Elvis Costello and Van Morrison.
zitate_kontext: Characterisation at the start of the article

2003-03-06-lofotposten-ettertenksom-leve.kurz: Kurt E. Holm in Lofotposten on Leven's concert on 4 March 2003 in Kabelvåg: a hushed, attentive audience, a quiet yet powerful soul-blues-rock version; the story of the heroin dealer's dream “both moving and funny”.
inhalt: The review “Ettertenksom Leven” (“Thoughtful Leven”) in Lofotposten (Svolvær) of 6 March 2003 reports on the Tuesday-evening concert at Præstengbrygga in Kabelvåg before 50 people. There was “not much noise”; the audience was attentive and you could “almost hear the famous pin drop”. Leven had just released the album *Shining Brother Shining Sister*, which had won glowing reviews worldwide. Those who came to experience the drive of the album, however, got a completely different version of this “well-preserved Scottish secret”: “quiet but at times powerful soul/blues/rock of absolutely the best brand”.

The man has lived a life that shapes the lyrics; most of it is self-experienced. The story about the heroin dealer's dream is “both moving and funny”, and humour and irony marked many of the spoken passages. One attendee, Svein Roger Jensen, who had only just discovered Leven, says: “This is exactly as good as I had hoped.” He had heard about Leven by chance in the capital and, with his newly bought CD, found out that the Scot would play in the Lofoten. Those who preferred to spend the Tuesday evening with the judge “Amy” or the catchphrases of “Friends”, the text consoles, will surely get another chance. A fact box sums up his life: born 1950 in the Kingdom of Fife, more than thirty years in the business, frontman of Doll by Doll (four acclaimed albums 1978–1982), nearly killed by blind violence in 1983.

2003-03-07-tonsbergs-blad-cd-jackie-leve.kurz: Øyvind Sætre reviews *Shining Brother Shining Sister* in Tønsbergs Blad very positively: after years of drug problems Leven is more together than ever and his “pop noir” works almost perfectly.
inhalt: Øyvind Sætre’s review in Tønsbergs Blad (“Vestfold puls” section) opens with Leven’s life story: after years of drug problems, Leven seems to be managing to stay on “the narrow path”. Judging by *Shining Brother, Shining Sister* he is more together than ever. His slightly alternative “pop noir” works almost perfectly this time.

Leven reminds Sætre a little of Lou Reed, but offers more intensity and magic. The record is gripping in a “subtle” way – partly of course because of the good song material, but also because of a particularly creative production in which surprises are constantly lurking. The lyrics range from sensitive love (happily without many clichés) to black everyday realism and bizarre humour. Sætre’s closing words: Leven is an artist it is hard to be indifferent to, at least after the “surplus phenomenon” of this record – “lots of good Leven at once”.

2003-03-09-bergensavisen-leven-bak-muren.kurz: Bergensavisen reports on Leven's hour-long concert for inmates of Bergen prison on 8 March 2003: he told stories from his heroin years, prisoners recognised themselves in them, and the paper says he himself served several sentences in British prisons in the Sixties.
inhalt: The headline “Leven bak murene igjen” plays on his name: “Leven behind the walls again”, and “lage leven” also means “to make a racket”. Kaspar Synnevåg's report opens by saying that the blues artist Jackie Leven sat in prison several times in the Sixties; the day before he was back behind the walls to make a racket for an hour. It was “high under the roof” in the sports hall of Bergen prison where he played for the inmates, but not so high that about ten officers did not conscientiously keep a firm eye on the audience.

Leven, whom the article calls “Scotland's answer to Van Morrison” and a frequent visitor to Norway, had played at Madam Felle the night before and used Women's Day to entertain the inmates. “I could have been sitting in a bar, as I normally do”, the Scot smiles to the paper. Between songs he told stories from his time as a heroin addict, in which, the report notes, many inmates recognised themselves. A prisoner in the sixth year of his sentence, who plays guitar in his own cell, calls him “a wonderful person” and gives his message as: it is possible to get away from drugs, prison and all the crap.

The writer portrays Leven as clearly on the side of the outsiders. As a young man he served several sentences in British prisons and struggled with drugs for years; now he has his life in order but still represents the outsiders. Nobody would have reacted had the blues veteran swapped places with someone in the hall: “He was a ragged soul in a worn denim shirt and never made a secret of it.” If anyone stood out, it was the guards with their uniforms and ID cards. When Leven picked up the tempo halfway through, rock feet began to tap there too. The prison claim comes from the paper; Leven himself is not quoted on it.

An inmate on Leven's message (name withheld here)

2003-03-uncut-shining-brother-shining-si.kurz: Uncut calls *Shining Brother, Shining Sister* (2003) earnest and open-hearted, with poems read by Sexsmith, Bly and Thomas. Where it fails to click it sounds like Chris Rea; the love songs move “to the marrow”.
inhalt: The short, unsigned review in Uncut (1 March 2003) introduces Leven as a “wilfully weathered” Scottish cult hero whose first album since 2001’s *Creatures of Light and Darkness* this is. He wears his art on his sleeve: the new work incorporates poems by Rilke, e. e. cummings and Edith Sitwell, read by Ron Sexsmith, Robert Bly and David “Pere Ubu” Thomas. Despite Leven’s wry sleevenotes, it is nothing if not earnest.

When it doesn’t click, it’s a bit Chris Rea/Dire Straits; but when he allows himself to croon songs of honest personal heartbreak, like the lovely “Another Man in the Old Arcade”, the light and shade come in and his lilting voice moves you to the marrow. The page shows a rating of 3 (scale not stated).

2003-05-08-pennyblackmusic-shining-broth.kurz: Reviewer Carter of Pennyblackmusic calls *Shining Brother, Shining Sister* Leven’s strongest album since *Night Lilies* and possibly his best: poems, guests and long, gripping songs. His verdict: “Leven’s best album to date? I’d say so.”
inhalt: The reviewer (Carter) calls *Shining Brother, Shining Sister*, Leven’s eighth solo album for Cooking Vinyl, his strongest since 1998’s *Night Lilies*. *Defending Ancient Springs* (2000) and *Creatures of Light and Darkness* (2001) each had classic Leven songs scattered through them but could not top the eleven excellent tracks of *Night Lilies*. Here, all twelve tracks carry Leven’s soulful, unique vocals married to beautiful melodies, making it a contender for his best album yet.

Part of this is down to new elements. Lifting portions of other songs is nothing new for Leven, Carter notes, recalling Avril Jamieson’s lines from “Unchained Melody” on “Fear of Women” from *Fairytales for Hardmen*. On the eight-minute opener “Classic Northern Diversions” Leven intones the title of Big Joe Williams’s “Baby Please Don’t Go”, and at the end the American poet Robert Bly recites part of a medieval French prayer. The song itself is pure Leven, with strong vocals, insightful lyrics (“it took me fifty long years just to work out, that because I was angry didn’t mean I was right”) and a melody that, uneasy at times, is always coloured with beauty. Film composer Geoffrey Burgon plays the trumpet elegy that precedes “Savannah Waltz”, and Carter enjoys Leven’s sleeve-note stories behind the songs.

It is hard to name a single best track. “My Philosophy” at times seems to be it: Deborah Greenwood’s background vocals (Carter asks whether he is the only one longing for a solo album from her), Leven’s dark-brown voice and, at the end, Ron Sexsmith reciting a poem by e. e. cummings. Next comes “Another Man in the Old Arcade”, to him one of the best songs Leven has ever recorded. The long songs hold the attention, such as the nearly ten-minute “A Little Voice in Space”, which closes with Leven reciting a poem by Osip Mandelstam. “Heroin Dealer Blues” is affecting, a warning without preaching, as a weary Leven sings of the dealer who “died as he lived, and he lived in vein”. David Thomas of Pere Ubu performs a text by Rainer Maria Rilke, a short horror story, “a stroke of genius”. The album closes with “Tied-Up House” (voice and acoustic guitar) and two poems set to music, Edith Sitwell’s “Bells of Grey Crystal” and Ciaran Carson’s “1798”.
Carter’s closing verdict: “Leven’s best album to date? I’d say so” – although he had thought Leven reached his peak with *Night Lilies*.
zitate_kontext: Line from “Classic Northern Diversions”, quoted by the reviewer

2003-05-uncut-jackie-leven-the-borderlin.kurz: Uncut calls Leven's Borderline gig one of the oddest in a long time: he drowns his sad songs in bawdy anecdotes. “You come expecting Johnny Cash; you leave having witnessed Johnny Vegas.”
inhalt: The live review in Uncut (online 1 May 2003) opens with the verdict “one of the oddest gigs I've seen in a long time”. The weathered Leven sings mournful songs of loss and regret in a rich, soulful voice, and is a “big poetry man”, quoting Pablo Neruda on his new album *Shining Brother Shining Sister*. Yet more often than being a melancholic, working-class minstrel, he is a man of the people in an entirely different manner: for at least half his time onstage he tells bawdy shaggy dog stories. If he were not sitting on a stool, he would be a great stand-up.

Most of his tales are filthy; one explores the similarity between cheap dog food and human faeces at interminable length. He is a natural, and his fiftysomething followers are in fits of laughter, but it means any mood evoked by the songs is chucked out with the bathwater. “You come expecting Johnny Cash; you leave having witnessed Johnny Vegas.” You would say he is in the wrong line of work, except that he is a lifer, an authentic folk-hero, once in post-punk enigmas Doll By Doll but touring for decades as a broody balladeer; he has survived a troubled personal life of addictions and crashes and clearly relishes the role of wiser, wizened, antipretty spokesman for fans who mostly share his Scottish/Irish connections and his age group.

Flanked by two colleagues, ironically named his “Sex Trio”, Leven lilts through his sorrowful songs; one thinks of L. S. Lowry, noble stooping northerners and all that. “Another Man In The Old Arcade” and “Classic Northern Diversions” are splendid examples of the new material. But mostly one is thinking of Johnny Vegas's jowls: the scatological anecdotes stretch on for ever. He is either shooting himself in the foot or, after a life fully lived, displaying “cavalier career apathy”. We learn that on a train Leven engaged in a surreal conversation with a drunk, that in Cardiff he stared at an enormous human mess on the pavement, and that his girlfriend, through “comic misunderstandings”, thinks he has trouble with his bowels. He is supporting Richard Thompson in Europe, then touring the UK; the reviewer hopes his inner Roy Orbison turns up, not his inner Roy Chubby Brown.
zitate_kontext: The Uncut reviewer on Leven's stage anecdotes

2003-06-10-firda-frodige-jackie.kurz: Firda celebrates Leven’s solo show at the Antonius Festival in Førde: a raggedly dressed Scot who, alone with guitar and floorboard, gave a concert “of the rare kind” to a tiny audience. The festival itself made a loss.
inhalt: The report “Frodige Jackie” (“Luxuriant Jackie”) in Firda (10 June 2003, in Nynorsk) covers Leven’s performance on Whit Sunday, 8 June, in the Storehagen room of the Sunnfjord Hotel at the Antonius Festival in Førde. Thanks are due to the doormen, it says, for letting Leven in: the “Scottish mountain of a long-haired, middle-aged man” turned up in a worn denim jacket barely holding together around his ample torso, shorts a size too small, wool-coloured knee socks and shoes resembling folk-costume shoes with silver buckles – “in sovereign contempt of etiquette”. But once “Jackie from the Kingdom of Fife” grabbed his Morgan guitar and sat down alone on the stage, any sneers had to be wiped away.

What followed, in the critic’s words, was “a concert experience of the rare kind”. Many regard Leven as at least as great a songwriter and singer as Van Morrison, and the parallels are there. With a simple acoustic guitar and a microphone-amplified floorboard he served songs from a long career. He attacked the guitar physically, hammering, drumming and rubbing; one tormented string held the bass line while plump fingers played over the others. His voice covered the whole register, from delicate moods to raw power. That only one musician stood on stage was at times hard to grasp, because Leven made a lot of noise – “sweaty, powerful” noise.

The songs mostly came from *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death*, *Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West* and *Shining Brother, Shining Sister*. Between them Leven chatted with the audience, serving lush, forceful Scottish humour with anecdotes from his childhood and artist’s life. Afterwards the small crowd did not bother him: “Quality is better than quantity. And the audience today was of the former category.” Then he disappeared, still in his unorthodox outfit, into the Sunnfjord hall to catch Bertine Zetlitz’s concert. A side article reports that the festival organisers sold about 600 tickets for eight events – only half last year’s figure – and expect a deficit.

2003-11-05-kanaliena-gr-jackie-leven-int.medium: Kanaliena.gr / programme “Rockzone” (recording on YouTube, channel Dimitris Antonopoulos)
2003-11-05-kanaliena-gr-jackie-leven-int.kurz: A good five-minute edit of a conversation which, according to the on-screen caption, the Greek presenter Dimitris Antonopoulos conducted on 5 November 2003 for Kanaliena.gr or his programme “Rockzone”; the questions have been cut out, leaving only Leven's answers.
inhalt: A good five-minute edit of a conversation which, according to the on-screen caption, the Greek presenter Dimitris Antonopoulos conducted on 5 November 2003 for Kanaliena.gr or his programme “Rockzone”; the questions have been cut out, leaving only Leven's answers. The caption lists as topics Peter Hammill, Van Morrison, “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” and concerts. Leven says that anyone who wants to become a singer takes on responsibility: one's own voice speaks for others, for love, hatred and anger – Hammill understands this particularly well. He admires Van Morrison for his early work but finds the last ten years monotonous; he himself wants to carry on the tradition that Van embodied at his peak, and thinks that Michael Cosgrave does the same. He wrote “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” on the Greek island of Astypalaia, alone on a hot day, thinking of a Jesus with human fears. He will stop when there are no good songs left in him; the tour through Germany, Spain, Britain and now Greece is tiring but lovely. Advice to young musicians: do not look to fame, but be artistically satisfied with yourself. Overall tone: a short, reflective promotional conversation during the trip to Greece with Cosgrave and Michael Weston King.

2003-bbnc-oors-pop-encyclopedie-2004.kurz: The Dutch standard reference work from the magazine Oor gives Leven his own entry in the 2004 edition; only a discography line with *Defending Ancient Springs* is visible.
inhalt: Oor's Pop-encyclopedie, the Dutch standard reference work from the music magazine Oor, gives Jackie Leven an entry of his own in its 2004 edition. Only the discography line with “(97) Defending Ancient Springs (Cooking Vinyl …)” is known. The number before the title is unclear: the album appeared in 2000, so it may be an error or a rating figure.

2003-canongate-strong-great-indie-discog.titel: The Great Indie Discography (2nd ed.; 1st ed. 1999 as The Great Alternative & Indie Discography) – entry “Doll By Doll” with Jackie Leven
2003-canongate-strong-great-indie-discog.kurz: In Martin C. Strong’s *The Great Indie Discography* the entry “Doll By Doll” tells of Leven’s beginnings as John St. Field, the band in punk’s wake, its albums and his solo career, followed by a discography with catalogue numbers and star ratings.
inhalt: The entry “Doll By Doll” in Martin C. Strong’s *The Great Indie Discography* (Canongate, 2nd edition 2003; first edition 1999 as *The Great Alternative & Indie Discography*) begins “Formed: London, England … 1977 by Fife-born Jackie Leven”. It tells of Leven’s beginnings as a singer under the name John St. Field, with gigs including some with the band Man, the band “in punk’s wake” on Warner, the Magnet albums of 1981/82, the formation C.B.I. with Glen Matlock and the subsequent solo career. In the 1999 edition a cross-reference elsewhere reads “Jackie LEVEN (see under ⇒ DOLL BY DOLL)”.

A full discography with catalogue numbers follows, for instance Charisma JACK 1 (August 1983) and COOKCD 131 for *Control* (September 1997), the latter with the note “rec. 1973–5” and the remark that the LP was issued in 1975 on a Spanish label, as well as the 2001 box. The star ratings: *Remember* 6, *Gypsy Blood* 7, *Doll By Doll* 5, *Grand Passion* 4 and *Control* 5. The entry is the main source for the biography section of the English Wikipedia article.

2003-globalguest-inoffizielles-gaestebuc.medium: globalguest.com/gb/TOUT – guestbook of the fan site jackieleven.com
2003-globalguest-inoffizielles-gaestebuc.kurz: With well over 90 entries, 2003 is the strongest year of this guestbook. It accompanies *Shining Brother Shining Sister* (February 2003), which fans from Cornwall, France (a record dealer who wants to sell 200 copies), Kiel, Asker and Hamm (Radio Runde Hamm: “CD of the month”) celebrate; the radio DJ…
inhalt: With well over 90 entries, 2003 is the strongest year of this guestbook. It accompanies *Shining Brother Shining Sister* (February 2003), which fans from Cornwall, France (a record dealer who wants to sell 200 copies), Kiel, Asker and Hamm (Radio Runde Hamm: “CD of the month”) celebrate; the radio DJ Ecki Stieg writes that the album almost saved his life. The February/March tour with Richard Thompson and Midnight Choir can be followed place by place: Haarlem (19.02., with Michael Cosgrave), Hamburg St. Pauli-Theater (20.02.), Berlin (21.02.), Vienna (25.02.), Oslo John Dee (06.03.), then a German tour whose dates a fan posts (Tuttlingen, Tübingen, Frankfurt, Essen, Bremen, Kiel, Singwitz, Hannover, Bielefeld), with an argument over whether Kiel took place at the Halle 400 or the Räucherei. A host in Tübingen recalls conversations about Rilke and Blake. Further traces: Bein Inn (Fife, January), Penzance, Flowerpot Derby, Førde (Norway, June), Edinburgh Fringe (August), New Roscoe Leeds, Midlands Arts Centre as support for Cara Dillon (July), a US thank-you for Leven's contribution to the Frankie Miller tribute.

Many entries revolve around Doll by Doll: one fan saw them in 1979/80 “blowing Devo off the stage”, a musician from Leeds played support in the Clifton Villas era and saw Jo Shaw smash his Stratocaster, a pedal steel player lived with Vincent Crane in Warwick Avenue in the 1970s, and people keep asking about CD editions of the Doll by Doll albums, until someone mentions CD-R bootlegs. Fans praise the monthly columns and wish for them as a book. At the end of the year a buyer complains that his cheque has been cashed but the CD has not arrived – a foretaste of the problems of 2008.

2003-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.titel: [Collected finds Nasjonalbiblioteket 2003: news items, announcements, lists]

2003-netrhythms-shining-brother-shining-.kurz: Mike Davies hears Leven's 15th solo album as poetic, Celtic-tinged soul-pop about loss, rich in poem settings and crowned by the trumpet instrumental “Dust Elegy”.
inhalt: Mike Davies of NetRhythms describes the album as Leven's 15th solo record, following 2001's *Creatures of Light and Darkness*, by which point he is “firmly ensconced in the ranks of cult”. Lending his “rich peat whisky voice”, Leven delivers a collection of poetic, Celtic-infused soulful pop veined with rockabilly, jazz and even hip hop, “all aged in the oak of reflective melancholy”.

Even the apparently buoyant “Irresistible Romance”, with its skirl of pipes and a drum fade-out, inspired by Peter Ackroyd's London, is full of ragged street kids and people trapped in relentlessly imprisoning jobs. The songs are concerned with loss, through death, ended relationships or the passing of industries, or, as in “Another Man In The Old Arcade”, with the halting resolution not to let things slip away. The despairing realisation of wasted life and misguided anger in “Classic Northern Diversions” and the dreams blown away in “Heroin Dealer” (a bitter fable about a man Leven once knew) are counterpointed by rays of optimism: the hope of healing in “A Little Voice In Space” and the centuries-spanning love of “1798”.

Davies particularly stresses Leven's commitment to poetry: “1798” sets a poem by Ciaran Carson, and there are lines by Edith Sitwell, Rilke (the short horror story “Faces”, spoken by David Thomas), e. e. cummings (read by Ron Sexsmith), Robert Bly (who contributes his own spoken words) and Osip Mandelstam. This restates a commitment to a form whose power the world and the industry largely overlook. He is not sure that any single song matches “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” or “Exit Wounds” (properly “Exit Wound”) from the previous album, but finds the cumulative effect haunting, and the evocative trumpet instrumental “Dust Elegy” “something quite special”.
zitate_kontext: Mike Davies on the voice and style of the album

2003-orion-rankin-a-question-of-blood.kurz: In Ian Rankin's Rebus novel A Question of Blood (2003), Rebus lies in the bath while Leven plays on the stereo, singing about the romance of hard men.
inhalt: In *A Question of Blood* (Orion, London, 2003), a novel about the Edinburgh Inspector John Rebus, Jackie Leven appears in a brief scene: Rebus lies in a lukewarm bath, has ordered a curry, and on the stereo is Leven, singing "about the romance of hard men", an allusion to Leven's album *Fairytales for Hard Men*.

The passage is among the most frequently quoted mentions of Leven in Rankin's work, which has repeatedly taken up Leven's music and lines since the two became friends. The novel also appeared in translation, for example as *Een kwestie van bloed* (Dutch), *Una cuestión de sangre* (Spanish, 2010) and *Die Kinder des Todes* (German, Goldmann 2006), each containing the scene.

2003-sanctuary-hinton-south-by-south-wes.kurz: In his history of alternative country, *South by South West*, Brian Hinton briefly discusses *Shining Brother, Shining Sister*: a lament for “Dusty”, a young heroin addict, and a duet with David Thomas.
inhalt: Brian Hinton discusses Leven in the context of British relatives of Americana. Of *Shining Brother, Shining Sister* he remarks that Leven writes on it a lament for “Dusty”, a little heroin addict. He also mentions the duet with David Thomas on a bleak “Surf’s Up”, the Beach Boys song.

2004-01-05-kindamuzik-for-peace-comes-dr.kurz: An enthusiastic review of the regular reissue of the live album *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow* (London, Twelve Bar Club), originally released in 1996 for fan-club members only: a beautiful setlist, covers and three spoken pieces as special attractions.
inhalt: Maurice Dielemans reviews the reissue of *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow* on Cooking Vinyl/Bertus on KindaMuzik (5 January 2004) under the heading “Voor laat in de avond” (“For late in the evening”). In their “wild enthusiasm” the editors had almost shouted it into their 2004 album lists, but it is merely the simple reissue of a “somewhat obscure but superior” live record. In 1996 it appeared only in a very small edition for fan-club members; it would have been a crying shame not to share this beautiful, intimate concert recording of the Scottish ex-punk, ex-heroin addict and ex-frontman of the “English punk group” Doll by Doll (the reviewer’s description) with the rest of the world.

The setlist is “wonderful”: many songs from the masterpieces with philosophical titles such as *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*, *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West* and *Fairy Tales for Hard Men*, plus interesting covers, including as closer Van Morrison’s “Slim Slow Slider” and The Velvet Underground’s “Pale Blue Eyes” (given several times as “Pale Blues Eyes” in the booklet). The intimate atmosphere of Leven’s solo show at London’s Twelve Bar Club is captured in a unique way. With three short spoken pieces – “Acid Roast Beef”, “Whisky Story” and “Jackie Losing It” – the Scottish bard ties together the heartbreaking songs and the “wanly beautiful” guitar playing in unsurpassed fashion.

Anyone who listens late in the evening imagines himself unnoticed among the attentive audience of the Twelve Bar Club “or, if need be, the Hague Schouwburg”, since shortly before Leven had been seen live in The Hague at the Crossing Border festival. Finally the author quotes the last words of Doll by Doll’s “Main Travelled Roads”: “Eternal is the warrior who finds beauty in his wounds”, which Leven, who saw life’s dark side several times, is said to have borrowed from the Japanese writer Yukio Mishima (1925–1970) – the reviewer’s attribution, unchecked.

2004-01-24-rolling-stone-forum-jackie-le.kurz: A short forum thread from January 2004 lists the dates of the spring tour (24 March Bonn to 3 April Vienna) and collects concert memories, from disappointed to entertained, including a Doll by Doll show in Hamburg for a handful of paying people.
inhalt: On 24 January 2004 an anonymous user opens a thread in the German Rolling Stone’s concert forum with the dates of Jackie Leven’s spring tour: 24 March Bonn (Harmonie), 25 March Hamburg (Knust), 26 March Kiel (Räucherei), 27 March Northeim (Kunst & Kultur), 28 March Hannover (Blues Garage), 30 March Frankfurt (Sinkkasten), 31 March Munich (Muffatcafé), 1 April Berlin (Quasimodo), 2 April Dresden (Starclub) and 3 April Vienna (Chelsea).

Six further posts follow within hours and again in February. The verdicts are mixed. One has seen Leven live once and found it one of the most disappointing concerts he has ever seen, “even if it was a U&D” (free open-air show). Another saw him twice and found it very entertaining, even though it was indoors and paid. A third had seen him supporting Richard Thompson, was surprised, found him very entertaining and likeable and a great artist, and notes the tour down. Another user pencils in the Berlin date.

An anonymous post recalls a Doll by Doll reunion concert in the 1990s at the Fabrik in Hamburg in front of about 15 paying people; he remembers little of it and it left no lasting impression. On 20 February a user points to a gig by Michael Weston King & The Decent Men featuring Jackie Leven on 29 May at the Knaack in Berlin: anyone who wants can hear him twice.

User brightwhitebird on Leven opening for Richard Thompson

2004-01-26-gaesteliste-for-peace-comes-d.kurz: On Gaesteliste.de Ullrich Maurer recommends the reissue of the live album *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow* as a “calling card of the performer Leven”: relaxed versions, a few covers and above all the funny stories between songs.
inhalt: Ullrich Maurer opens his review of 26 January 2004 with a thesis: anyone who knows Leven only from his records knows “really only the box” in which his soul – his songs and his nature – is packed. Anyone who wants the Jackie Leven “of flesh, blood, whiskey and sweat” must see him live. On stage he plays much looser and more relaxed than a studio CD allows, and one notices that the man himself is “not nearly as brooding, serious and dark” as his music suggests.

The album, a recording of one of his intimate pub gigs that Maurer dates to 1993 (“10 years old”), conveys a good idea of what to expect from a Jackie evening: an unpredictable, eclectic mix of his own songs in “impressively lively” versions that sometimes depart considerably from the preserved originals and are played with technical brilliance, plus a few covers – some blues tracks, Lou Reed, Van Morrison. (Other sources say it was recorded in 1997 at London's 12 Bar Club.) Above all, there are “the small, hair-raising and stunningly funny stories and dialogues” he conducts with the audience, from his “standard whiskey stories” to passages where he loses the thread in his typical way (“Jackie's Losin It”) and babbles preposterous nonsense.

Incidentally, the recordings show how little has changed and how true to himself Leven has stayed over the years. For fans who could not buy the disc at a concert, the reissue on Cooking Vinyl/Indigo is the chance to pick up this “gem”; for everyone else it is “a kind of calling card of the performer Leven”.
zitate_kontext: Maurer on the album's main appeal.

2004-01-27-celtic-connections-pressemitt.titel: [Press release] Ian Rankin and Jackie Leven present 'Jackie Leven Said'
2004-01-27-celtic-connections-pressemitt.kurz: Announcement of the premiere of *Jackie Leven Said* on 27 January 2004 in Glasgow: Ian Rankin recites a specially written short story in instalments, and Jackie Leven answers each with songs.
inhalt: This press release announces the premiere of *Jackie Leven Said* on 27 January 2004 in the Strathclyde Suite of Glasgow's Royal Concert Hall, as part of the Celtic Connections festival. It presents the project as the work of “two brilliant minds from the Kingdom of Fife”: the crime novelist Ian Rankin, best known for his novels about the “haunted” Detective Inspector John Rebus, and the singer Jackie Leven, with three decades of critically acclaimed albums behind him.

Rankin has written a short story that he recites in short bursts, punctuated by songs from Leven that reflect what has gone before. The theme is the mystery of how, at its lowest ebb, life can suddenly become beautiful, though that beauty may take many forms. Rankin names the soul, the passions, the past, Celtic ties, Scottishness and masculinity as the story's concerns. Leven talks about “the spirit at bay” and about hard men desperately clutching at a silver sliver that cannot be held; without it, he says, we become merely cunning survival machines. He promises jokes as well.

The release bills the evening as a powerful show of “forensic drama” by two men who admire each other's work so much that they have become friends and artistic collaborators. Both are accompanied by the “Breton” multi-instrumentalist Michael Cosgrave. It closes with a pointer to the festival website.
zitate_kontext: Ian Rankin on the short story written for the evening
Jackie Leven on Rankin and the shared theme

2004-01-30-bbc-folk-awards-2004-folk-clu.titel: Jackie Leven 2004 Live or Die [recording; presentation of “Folk Club of the Year” for the BBC Folk Awards]
2004-01-30-bbc-folk-awards-2004-folk-clu.kurz: A fan recording on YouTube shows Leven performing “Live or Die” at a club gig in January 2004, where at the BBC's request he presented the pub with the “Folk Club of the Year” award; it aired next evening on BBC Four.
inhalt: The video “Jackie Leven 2004 Live or Die” by the user “dhatboy” is a shaky handheld clip (“Shaking due to beer I think”), the sound of which the uploader nonetheless calls not too bad for a camera clip. According to the description, Leven was playing that night at a folk-club pub, and the BBC asked if he would present the “Folk Club of the Year” award to the pub during the night's show. It was aired on television on BBC Four the next night (31 January 2004). The uploader recalls wondering at the time what the two girls with a high-tech camera were filming for, and by chance watching the folk awards the following night. The video's tags include “Rockingham Arms” and “Rotherham”, pointing to the venue; the text does not name the club.

The uploader also writes personally: he misses “the big man” and chatting with him at gigs, which began at the Otley Folk Festival in 1998; a friend, Richard McFarlane, had told him he would like him. He then caught him for many years in Yorkshire and sometimes further afield, a New Year's (or Christmas) show in Belper being “a great night”. He has not got over Leven's passing and posts one of a few clips from the night that he managed to save on an old hard drive. The video's content itself was not viewed; the BBC broadcast was not found.
zitate_kontext: The uploader in the video description

2004-02-17-drammens-tidende-herlig-uform.kurz: Johnny Andreassen in Drammens Tidende on the reissue of *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow*: a gloriously informal solo recording with guitar and foot rhythm, monologues, and in his view one of today's greatest artists.
inhalt: On the music page of Drammens Tidende on 17 February 2004, Johnny Andreassen reviews the Cooking Vinyl edition of *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow* under the headline “Herlig uformelt” (“Gloriously informal”). It is a concert recording of Leven as a soloist with his acoustic guitar and rhythms stamped with his foot on the guitar case lid. The album was originally released in 1996, he writes, but never officially – probably sold only through Leven's own fan club.

It contains many of Leven's best songs since his comeback in the early nineties, among them the soul-stirring “Call Mother a Lonely Field”, and some of his “restless monologues”, in which you experience what a storyteller the former Doll by Doll frontman is. One is about Arctic sex after a tour of Norway that took Leven to Tromsø. Very few artists can fill a live album with only themselves and an acoustic guitar; Leven does it “with the greatest ease and all his Scottish pride and vocal splendour”. He recently toured Germany with Norway's own Midnight Choir, and the reviewer recommends him “warmly” as “one of the very greatest artists we have today, in my opinion”.

2004-03-02-mescalina-shining-brother-shi.kurz: Christian Verzeletti considers *Shining Brother Shining Sister* not Leven’s masterpiece but an open, many-voiced album about humanity – “a necessary record”.
inhalt: The review appears on mescalina.it about a year after release; Christian Verzeletti finds it nevertheless “a duty”, because Leven’s records deserve and provoke “a step back, a pause for reflection”. *Shining Brother Shining Sister* is not a masterpiece and not the Scottish songwriter’s best album, but an example of how music can open itself and open others.

The names printed on the cover – Robert Bly, Rainer Maria Rilke, Ron Sexsmith, E. E. Cummings, David Thomas, Edith Sitwell – already suggest a multi-voiced work; the twelve songs form a mosaic whose every tile is a small hymn to humanity. Leven has worked like a modern craftsman to build an “auteur pop” that transcends genres and absorbs them to catch their single, common soul: songs with a living core, able to sound ancestral and look ahead. Compared with *Creatures of Light and Darkness* it is a more open record, with more voices and more light; even the poetic quotations (Neruda, Rilke, Mandelstam, Sitwell, Cummings and Ciaran Carson) are part of one flowing current.

In detail Verzeletti names the opener “Classic Northern Diversions” (train whistle, siren, Moog and synth touches, a fragment of a medieval prayer and an insert of “Baby Please Don’t Go”), “Irresistible Romance” and “My Philosophy”, whose spirit surpasses that of any of today’s pop greats, the trumpet in “Dust Elegy” leading into “Savannah Waltz”, African roots in “A Little Voice in Space”, the shadows in “Heroin Dealer Blues” and the loving “1798”. Not every song reaches such peaks, perhaps “something too much” was added, but the album opens and closes like a sacred circle and offers a view of life that is never generic or rhetorical. His conclusion: it introduces a fraternal relationship with music and with the world.
zitate_kontext: Christian Verzeletti on *Shining Brother Shining Sister*.

2004-03-15-rolling-stone-forum-jackie-le.kurz: In the Rolling Stone forum’s rating thread, users award stars to Leven albums between 2004 and 2020: *The Mystery of Love* and *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West* are called masterpieces, and condolences follow in 2011.
inhalt: The thread in the forum’s “sober rating” section, “Sterne an”, runs to 83 posts over six pages and begins in March 2004 with one user’s ratings of five albums. Over sixteen years members add their stars for Leven’s albums and argue over them. The consensus: *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* (mostly 4 to 5 stars) and *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West* (often 4.5 to 5) are the peaks; one user says the first two records are “among the best of the entire 90s”, another puts them in his personal top-100 and top-500 lists. *Fairy Tales for Hard Men* generally sits a notch lower (2.5 to 4.5), *Night Lilies* and *The Argyll Cycle* at 3 to 4.5. Later albums such as *Defending Ancient Springs*, *Creatures of Light and Darkness* and *Shining Brother, Shining Sister* are rated highly and defended by individual users, with special praise for David Thomas (Pere Ubu) as collaborator. There is also criticism: one user finds *Forbidden Songs* too “inhomogeneous” musically, another finds *Mystery* in retrospect “tame and limp – and too much spoken word”.

One fan’s long list shows how widely Leven’s work was heard: he rates the John St. Field album *Control*, the Haunted Valley releases, the Sir Vincent Lone albums and all four Doll by Doll albums. Asked what the Haunted Valley releases are, another explains that it is Leven’s small label, mostly issuing concert recordings or alternative versions that were usually only on sale at gigs; nine have since come out officially on Cooking Vinyl. Several posters ask for Doll by Doll reissues, later for vinyl reissues. One user says he narrowly missed a Leven concert in 1995 while on holiday in Oban, then Leven’s home town; another saw him often between 1997 and 2007 and in 2010 helped bring him to his own home town.

On 15 November 2011 the condolences begin: “Jackie died today. It makes me sad,” writes one user, planning to relisten to a good deal in his honour the next day; another had meant to attend the Münster concert, which no longer took place. A third wishes the singer “always one (better two) full bottles of whisky in the hotel bar”. Asked whether he really drank that much, the poster replies by pointing to a Deutschlandfunk programme, “Ein großer Unbekannter”, on 19 November. The thread is thus a record of German reception: a small, loyal audience who consider him underrated.
zitate_kontext: Forum user on *Mystery of Love* and *Forbidden Songs*
User explains the Haunted Valley label
A critical voice on *The Mystery of Love* (2019)

2004-03-16-ostlendingen-live-helt-alene.kurz: Østlendingen reviews Leven's live album For Peace Comes Dropping Slow: hardly something the world asked for, but Leven is in top form at London's 12 Bar, especially solo with a guitar.
inhalt: Under the headline "Live helt alene" ("Live all alone"), Østlendingen (Elverum, 16 March 2004) carries a short review of Jackie Leven's live album *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow* (Cooking Vinyl). The reviewer says the world has hardly been crying out for a 75-minute, 16-track live album from the Scot, but here he is in top form ("i kjempeslag") at the music pub 12 Bar in London.

Four of the tracks are humorous chat, one of which starts from Tromsø; the rest is "almost songwriting" (visesang), and Leven's distinctive voice comes out especially well when only his own guitar accompanies it. Then the objection: it is a little hard to keep one's concentration when the set-up is so "thin", and his good lyrics are not printed in the sleeve booklet. The closing line, "But you're allowed to eat small portions!", advises taking the record in small helpings. The author is probably Geir Hovensjø (the byline in the scan is unclear).

2004-03-26-wdr-rockpalast-crossroads-jac.kurz: The WDR Rockpalast page gives line-up and setlist of Leven’s set at the Crossroads festival in Bonn’s Harmonie on 26 March 2004: Leven, Kevin Foster and Michael Cosgrave play eight pieces from “A Little Voice in Space” to “Exit Wound”.
inhalt: WDR presents Leven in its Rockpalast series under “Crossroads March 2004”. The festival, the page says, is “our very own festival” and a “Rockpalast matter of the heart”: twice a year, in spring and autumn, the broadcaster invites people to the Harmonie in Bonn for four evenings of music. At the March 2004 festival Aynsley Lister, Five Horse Johnson, The Ian Parker Band, Imperial Crowns, Ivan Neville, Vanilla Fudge and Willard Grant Conspiracy also appeared. Leven played on the last evening, 26 March.

The line-up: Jackie Leven (vocals, guitar), Kevin Foster (bass), Michael Cosgrave (keyboards, backing vocals). The setlist: 1. “A Little Voice in Space”, 2. “Classic Northern Diversions”, 3. “Live or Die”, 4. “Poortoun”, 5. “My Philosophy”, 6. “Call Mother a Lonely Field”, 7. “Empty in Soho Square”, 8. “Exit Wound”.

On the material: the Rockpalast channel released a 44-minute version in 2018 with four songs and three short interview segments; MIG Music put the whole concert of about 75 minutes online in 2024, with storytelling passages such as “Jackie Talks About Kiel And His Mother” and “… Norwegian Prisoners”. The material was issued as the DVD *Live at Rockpalast* (2011) and as the CD+DVD *Live at Rockpalast 2004* (2024).
2004-03-26-wdr-rockpalast-crossroads-jac.titel: Jackie Leven live | Rockpalast | 2004 [Crossroads Festival, March 2004, Harmonie Bonn]

2004-03-29-radio-bremen-konzert-sendesaa.titel: [Radio Bremen: concert recording Jackie Leven & Michael Cosgrave, Sendesaal Bremen, 29.03.2004]
2004-03-29-radio-bremen-konzert-sendesaa.kurz: The label MiG’s page for the 4-CD box *Live Or Die – Live In Bremen 1999 & 2004* (2024) documents the duo concert with Michael Cosgrave in Radio Bremen’s Sendesaal on 29 March 2004, with track list and a biographical sketch.
inhalt: The release page of the label MiG Music (box dated 26 April 2024) presents *Live Or Die – Live In Bremen 1999 & 2004*: four CDs with two Radio Bremen recordings, running to just over 202 minutes. CDs 1 and 2 hold the solo concert at the Bremen club Moments on 27 May 1999; CDs 3 and 4 hold the concert in Radio Bremen’s Sendesaal on 29 March 2004, at which Leven was accompanied on keyboards by his “long-time friend and web companion” Michael Cosgrave.

The 2004 programme includes “Single Father”, “My Philosophy”, “Fly”, “Alvis Green”, “Empty In Soho Square”, “A Little Voice In Space”, “Classic Northern Diversions”, “Little Brown Box”, “Poortoun”, “Exit Wound”, “Call Mother A Lonely Field”, “Tied-Up House” and “Live Or Die”. Between them sit the stage announcements (“ad lib”) as separate tracks, including stories about “Butterfly”, about Alvis Green, about “Glen Matlock is drinking…” and about “certain German places”.

The accompanying text summarises Leven’s career, partly with details that differ from other sources: born in 1950 in Kirkcaldy, son of an Irishman and a Roma woman; he began in the late 1960s as John St. Field (*Control*, 1973) and founded Doll by Doll in London in 1978, whose emotional, psychedelic-tinged new wave went down very well live but did not meet commercial expectations. After the break-up in 1983 he focused on his solo career, which took off only eleven years later with *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*. Three albums as Sir Vincent Lone are described as songs too unusual for his folk-musician image. Leven died in 2011, aged 61, after a long, serious illness.

The label text on the line-up of the two concerts

2004-04-24-music-week-green-man-festival.titel: [Festival preview 2004: Green Man Festival with Jackie Leven]
2004-04-24-music-week-green-man-festival.kurz: In a festival preview of 24 April 2004 Music Week lists Jackie Leven among the confirmed acts for the second Green Man Festival at Baskerville Hall, Powys, billed as the home of the “new folk movement”.
inhalt: The unsigned item on page 8 of the issue of 24 April 2004 runs under the headline “Smaller festivals line up impressive range of acts”. It reports that alongside the big festivals a handful of smaller, independent events are taking shape, among them Summer Sundae in Leicester (headlined by Super Furry Animals on 13–15 August, with Amy Winehouse, Dogs Die in Hot Cars, Easyworld and Paul Burch), the Big Chill at Eastnor Castle, Guilfest in Surrey (with UB40, Simple Minds, Blondie and Katie Melua) and the independent Green Man.

Green Man, it says, is put together by the folk duo Jo and Danny at Baskerville Hall in Powys and, only in its second year, has already been extended to two stages and more than forty acts. So far Four Tet, James Yorkston and the Athletes, Jackie Leven, Aidan Smith, Adem and the Fence Collective have been confirmed, “marking it out as the event which accommodates the new folk movement”. The printed date is “July 21 to 22”, “the same weekend as the V Festivals”; that cannot be reconciled with the V Festivals (August) and is probably a misprint. Leven appears here in the company of the young Scottish folk scene around Yorkston and the Fence Collective.
zitate_kontext: Music Week on the 2004 Green Man Festival

2004-04-the-word-ian-rankin-and-jackie-l.kurz: Report and conversation on the evening “Twa Twisted Fifers” at the Celtic Connections festival in Glasgow (January 2004), at which Ian Rankin read his new short story “Jackie Leven Said” and Leven sang songs at suitable points, accompanied by Michael Cosgrave on keyboards.
inhalt: Report and conversation on the evening “Twa Twisted Fifers” at the Celtic Connections festival in Glasgow (January 2004), at which Ian Rankin read his new short story “Jackie Leven Said” and Leven sang songs at suitable points, accompanied by Michael Cosgrave on keyboards. Du Noyer describes the story (two brothers from Fife, one of whom becomes a pop producer in London) and sketches Leven's life story: John St Field (Leven: trouble with the law), Doll by Doll, the attack and addiction, the solo albums. Leven mentions 130 concerts a year (previously 200). Rankin explains that Rebus would like Leven's music because they are stories about disappointed hard men; Leven announces “The Haunting Of John Rebus”. The two talk about emotional reticence in Fife, about pubs as an outlet, about a “Celtic” view of the world (Leven: reality lies in the in-between, for instance between tree and bark) and about the differences between Glasgow and Edinburgh. Rankin thinks Leven's life would make a great book. Songs sung include “Man Bleeds In Glasgow” and “Gylen Gylen”.

2004-05-28-gaesteliste-orange-blossom-sp.kurz: Ullrich Maurer’s festival report: at Orange Blossom Special 8, Leven played quiet ballads and stories with Michael Cosgrave on the Saturday and later as lead guitarist in Michael Weston King’s new band. The tone is very positive.
inhalt: Ullrich Maurer reports for Gaesteliste.de from the Glitterhouse festival Orange Blossom Special in Beverungen (28–30 May 2004). Jackie Leven appears twice in this first part. On Saturday 29 May he and his keyboard player Michael Cosgrave walk on “very leisurely”. Anyone who knows Leven knows he is “not a man of loud tones”, and so he plays a mixture of “wonderfully atmospheric, slightly elegiac ballads”, underpinned by his “inimitable stories taken from life”. To reproduce these here would be, Maurer says, as pointless as it is impossible and embarrassing. Leven plays songs from across his career, including older material such as “Single Father”, for which one of his stories fits “excellently”; Cosgrave adds carpets of atmosphere, pearling keyboard glissandi and springy bass lines. A fan remarks afterwards that it is astonishing such an enormous man can produce such gentle sounds. Legend has it that the whisky level backstage dropped rapidly afterwards – a minor inconvenience, the author says, that organisers must accept.

Later the same day Leven is on stage as guitarist in Michael Weston King’s new band, The Decent Men (named after the title of King’s last CD), with Cosgrave also playing trumpet – a surprise, since he had always been hesitant about it. On pieces like the “majestic” “Decent Man” a nearly solemn mood arises, and Leven in particular on lead guitar, which at times looks like a mere accessory against his massive body, adds mighty drive. King’s set is “definitely the first highlight of the festival”, the best anyone has seen him; peaks include a jazzy version of Neil Young’s “Love In Mind” and, fittingly for King’s friendship with Townes Van Zandt, “Waiting Around To Die”.

The rest of the report concerns other acts (Markus Rill, Mountaineer, Neal Casal as surprise guest, the Creekdippers, Hugo Race, Savoy Grand) and the festival setting, including criticism of video projections and trouble with a neighbour who wanted quiet.
