A festival-goer, as reported by Maurer
Maurer on Leven’s guitar playing with Michael Weston King’s Decent Men

2004-11-15-gaesteliste-the-meeting-of-re.kurz: In his review of the DVD *The Meeting Of Remarkable Men*, Ullrich Maurer warns that it is not a proper Leven concert but a festival recording shared with David Thomas, Ian Rankin and Ciaran Carson: charming, but more for specialists.
inhalt: Ullrich Maurer reviews the DVD *The Meeting Of Remarkable Men* (Cooking Vinyl/Indigo) for Gaesteliste.de and opens with a warning: it is not a proper Jackie Leven DVD at all. It is a recording of a peculiar evening at the Crossing Border Festival in The Hague the previous year. Besides Leven and his musical partner Michael Cosgrave, the bill features David Thomas, Leven’s occasional partner in crime, the Scottish bestselling crime novelist Ian Rankin and the Irish poet Ciaran Carson.

In loose sequence the programme offers several Leven songs, an excerpt from David Thomas’s “Mirrorman”, a reading by Rankin and a performance by Carson, who plays flute, sings a cappella and recites poems. The DVD is rounded off with four interviews the participants gave around the event. Maurer finds it not without charm, especially if you like Leven’s habit of illustrating his sets with adventurous anecdotes in which everyone present gets their share of the teasing.

Still, he would rather have had a complete Leven concert, perhaps even with a band. As it is, the disc is more for specialists and close friends of the master, not least because of the ultimately amateurish quality of the recording. A final aside: Leven wears one of his dreaded baggy shirts with a big hole on the left shoulder, and after ten minutes you find yourself staring at it like a rabbit.

2004-11-23-kindamuzik-jackie-leven-blijf.kurz: Backstage conversation at the Crossing Border festival in The Hague, held on a Friday afternoon (from the context, 12.11.2004, Leven's second Crossing Border appearance), published on 23.11.2004. Dielemans describes a subdued mood: Leven drinks canned beer, stares at the just-released …
inhalt: Backstage conversation at the Crossing Border festival in The Hague, held on a Friday afternoon (from the context, 12.11.2004, Leven's second Crossing Border appearance), published on 23.11.2004. Dielemans describes a subdued mood: Leven drinks canned beer, stares at the just-released DVD “The Meeting Of Remarkable Men” and lost his mother a few days earlier. The author summarises the biography (Control 1971, Doll by Doll from 1976, attack in a London alley, heroin addiction, comeback in 1994 with the albums up to “Creatures of Light and Darkness”).

Leven says that for “Control” he took a lot of LSD, like everyone at the time; because of trouble with the police the record came out under another name and only in Spain, and he forgot about it for a long time. He describes the 2003 Crossing Border evening at the Koninklijke Schouwburg with Ian Rankin, Ciaran Carson and David Thomas in detail: an invitation from the organiser Louise Behre, no rehearsal, Rankin and Thomas had been on a bender the night before, he himself was very nervous; a scene captured on the DVD in which Thomas urges him to hurry and then apologises. As follow-up projects he mentions an appearance with Rankin and James Yorkston at Celtic Connections, an evening in Fife with an English author, a new album to be recorded in Beirut with a large “gypsy orchestra” and released in summer 2005, and the double CD “Jackie Leven Said” for January. In closing: in the Netherlands he hardly sells any records, but he feels at home in The Hague (narrow streets, dark pubs, rain like in Glasgow) and wants to keep trying. Overall tone: a warm, slightly melancholy portrait.
zitate_kontext: Leven on his attitude to touring.
on the unprepared Crossing Border show in 2003.

2004-cooking-vinyl-for-peace-comes-dropp.autor: Cooking Vinyl (unsigned; with a quotation from Leven)
2004-cooking-vinyl-for-peace-comes-dropp.kurz: In 2004 Cooking Vinyl announces the re-release of the live album *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow*, said to be recorded at London’s 12 Bar Club in 1993 and limited to 2,000 copies. Leven says it gave him back his stage confidence.
inhalt: On its artist page, Cooking Vinyl presented the 2004 reissue of the live album *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow* (catalogue number COOKCD282). It is headed by a line from W. B. Yeats that gives the album its title ("and I shall find some peace there, for peace comes dropping slow").

According to the text, after *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* and *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West*, both on Cooking Vinyl, Leven listened to the clamour from die-hard and new fans for a live album that accurately reflected his stage work at the time and released a recording of a live show in a highly limited edition. It was recorded at London’s 12 Bar Club in 1993, sold out quickly and has since become a “must have” for Leven fans. It is now re-released, “owing to popular demand”, again limited to 2,000 copies worldwide. The label describes it as an accurate reflection of his shows of the time: a raft of great songs, warm and affectionate banter with an engaged audience, and some classically dubious stories of rare humour.

Leven himself is quoted at some length. He says he never thought he would get on a stage again, but good old-fashioned A&R skills at Cooking Vinyl, and their genuine belief that treading the boards once more would do him a power of good, gave him his self-belief as a performer back. The record, he says, is the sound of him enjoying the first fruits of re-acquainting himself with the smell of the crowd. He particularly likes the affectionate shambles of the audience teaching him Lou Reed’s “Pale Blue Eyes”, everyone muddling along on what they could collectively remember.

The text closes by calling it a small record with a huge heart, from a small club, first released as an “official bootleg” and now available again for lovers of the immense landscapes often displayed on his studio releases. The page also offered audio streams of “Sacred Bond” and “Uist Tramping Song”.
zitate_kontext: Leven on the effect of Cooking Vinyl’s faith in him
Leven on his favourite moment on the album

2004-globalguest-inoffizielles-gaestebuc.titel: [Unofficial Jackie Leven guestbook (jackieleven.com / home.xnet.it/tout), 2004 to January 2005]
2004-globalguest-inoffizielles-gaestebuc.medium: globalguest.com/gb/TOUT – guestbook of the fan site jackieleven.com
2004-globalguest-inoffizielles-gaestebuc.kurz: Around 50 entries up to early 2005. One fan was at the evening with Ian Rankin in January 2004 and once saw Doll by Doll as the support act for John Otway and Hawkwind.
inhalt: Around 50 entries up to early 2005. One fan was at the evening with Ian Rankin in January 2004 and once saw Doll by Doll as the support act for John Otway and Hawkwind. The AllMusic critic Thom Jurek asks in January for review copies, as Leven's records are hardly available in the USA. In March 2004, in response to an appeal from Leven, around ten fans apply to be merchandise sellers for the German tour. Concert greetings come from Brighton (The Greys, with David Thomas), Botley, Kiel (together with Tony Joe White, 24.03.), Munich, Cologne, Berlin, Frankfurt, Dresden, Essen (with Michael Weston King), Moers (festival with David Thomas), Leicester (with Dan Britton) and Glastonbury (with Michael Weston King's band). On 04.04.2004 Robin Spreafico, a former Doll by Doll member, gets in touch from Indonesia and asks how he can reach Leven. One fan points out the reissue of *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow*, another complains that the news page has not been updated for a year. There are birthday wishes on 18.06. (a “midsummer party” is mentioned). The last recorded entry (13.01.2005) asks about the dates of the tour with The Earlies and a concert at the Morden Tower, Newcastle.

2004-mcfarland-mitchell-great-composers-.kurz: A reference book on composers on screen lists a ‘Jackie Leven’ in a film’s cast list; whether this is the musician is unclear.
inhalt: The book *The Great Composers Portrayed on Film, 1913 through 2002* (McFarland, 2004) lists films about composers. In an entry for a film with music by Richard Strauss – probably Ken Russell’s BBC film ‘Dance of the Seven Veils’ of 1970 – the cast list names a ‘Jackie Leven’ alongside Murray Melvin, Sally Bryant and Ken Russell.

That would be a possible sign of a minor appearance by the later musician in a Ken Russell film around 1970. It may equally be a coincidence of names; the film title is not visible in the available excerpt, so the attribution is inferred.

2004-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.titel: [Collected finds, Nasjonalbiblioteket 2004: short news items, announcements, listings]
2004-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.kurz: A round-up of 2004 mentions in Norwegian newspapers and magazines: besides the review of *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow*, mostly asides, including a vinyl reissue of *Control* as John St. Field and Leven's European tour with Midnight Choir.
inhalt: For 2004 the search of the National Library of Norway's holdings shows thirteen issues mentioning Jackie Leven, eight of them freely readable. Treated individually are the reviews of the Cooking Vinyl reissue of the live album *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow* (Drammens Tidende 17 February; Østlendingen 16 March; Hamar Dagblad 20 March). No concerts in Norway are documented for 2004 in the freely readable finds.

The other hits are mostly asides. The reissue column of the magazine “Musikkavisen Backstage” (2004, no. 2) reports under vinyl: “John St. Field, or rather Jackie Leven, is now releasing his ‘Control’ album on vinyl” – i.e. a vinyl edition of *Control*; the item sits among reissues of Love, Caravan, Vanilla Fudge, the Undertones and others. Another issue of the same magazine (no. 1) calls Leven an “ex-junkie” in an article on drugs in rock and cites the song “Dealer”. The Tromsø paper reported on 23 September 2004 on a solo concert at Blå Rock by the Midnight Choir singer Paal Flaata; promoter Egon Holstad says there: “Midnight Choir toured Europe with Richard Thompson and Jackie Leven, which says something about how big they were. Still the Norwegian media didn't care.” Elsewhere, Firdaposten (8 May) has a reader saying he listens to “a bit of Jackie Leven”, and a record-shop advertisement in the paper Tromsø (23 April) lists Leven's name.

Several further mentions (Dagbladet 3 January, Adresseavisen 10 January and 2 June, Aftenposten 16 March, Bergens Tidende 3 April) can only be read through the National Library with Norwegian access; the Adresseavisen text of 2 June with three mentions is probably a longer article.
zitate_kontext: Egon Holstad in the paper Tromsø, 23 September 2004.

2004-orion-rankin-fleshmarket-close.kurz: In Ian Rankin's Rebus novel *Fleshmarket Close*, Siobhan Clarke drums on the steering wheel and hums along to a Jackie Leven CD that Rebus gave her for her birthday.
inhalt: In Rankin's novel (Orion, 2004; US title *Fleshmarket Alley*), Inspector Siobhan Clarke drums on the steering wheel and hums along to Leven; the CD is a birthday present from John Rebus. Elsewhere she has bought Leven, Lou Reed and John Mayall but not yet listened to them. Craig Cabell refers to this passage in his monograph on Rankin.
The novel appeared in German as *So soll er sterben* (Goldmann, 2007) and in French in 2010.

2005-01-31-paul-hegeman-the-meeting-of-r.kurz: A concert-film entry: *Jackie Leven Live: the Meeting of Remarkable Men*, directed by Paul Hegeman, 122 minutes, shot in The Hague, with Ian Rankin and Ciaran Carson, released on 31 January 2005.
inhalt: The database entry lists *Jackie Leven Live: the Meeting of Remarkable Men* as a video from 2004 with a running time of 2 hours 2 minutes. It was directed by Paul Hegeman, with Jackie Leven, Ian Rankin and Ciaran Carson credited, each as himself. It was filmed in The Hague (Zuid-Holland); the country of origin is the United Kingdom, the language English, the category “Music”. Production companies are Cooking Vinyl and Paul Hegeman Productions, with a UK release date of 31 January 2005.

The page carries no plot summary; the description is limited to the names. According to Leven's own column, the concert was recorded at the Crossing Border Festival in The Hague in November 2003, where Leven, in largely improvised fashion, met the Pere Ubu singer David Thomas, Rankin and the poet Ciaran Carson, accompanied by Michael Cosgrave. In the entry's short description Carson's name is misspelt “Charsom”.

2005-02-19-whisperin-and-hollerin-twiste.kurz: Sam Saunders catches The Earlies and Hem on the Twisted Folk Tour in Leeds; Leven, well known locally, wins him over with his richening voice, a guitar train impression and old folk-club storytelling: “The world needs the likes of Jackie Leven.”
inhalt: Sam Saunders reviews the Twisted Folk Tour evening at Leeds City Varieties for Whisperin & Hollerin, featuring The Earlies, Hem and Jackie Leven. He finds the mix not entirely comfortable, noting people sitting out one set or another in the bar, but “safe programming never baked any muffins”. Most of the review goes to The Earlies (eleven musicians, big multi-part singing, at their best in “Devil's Country”, with a Tim Buckley song winning him over) and to the more controlled, warmly tender Hem, centred on singer Sally Ellyson.

Of Leven he writes that he is “well known in these parts” and had his song about Leeds “ready and oiled”. Strictly speaking it is a song about leaving Leeds on the train, “but that's a nice way to go”; Leven's fine voice and guitar playing did it proud, ending with a convincing train impression tapped and scraped out on the guitar. His set always balances gritty Glaswegian anecdotes with sorrowful songs, and the voice gets richer and more decorated as time goes by: “It really is quite an instrument.”

His presentation is much more like the old folk-club raconteur and singer, though he still claims to be the “bitter and twisted, rather than just twisted, end of folk”. Saunders found some truth in that this evening: the mournfully wry tale of his mother's recent death maybe told the audience more than Leven wanted them to know. He closes the Leven section with the line that the world needs the likes of him.

Saunders on Leven's voice and stage manner

2005-04-26-drammens-tidende-jackie-leven.kurz: Preview with a telephone interview (“vel hjemme i England”) ahead of Leven's appearance closing the 2005 Working Class Hero festival in Drammen on Sunday, 1 May – according to the paper his first concert there in two years.
inhalt: Preview with a telephone interview (“vel hjemme i England”) ahead of Leven's appearance closing the 2005 Working Class Hero festival in Drammen on Sunday, 1 May – according to the paper his first concert there in two years. Andreassen introduces Leven as the former frontman of Doll by Doll, whose voice Q had counted among the greatest British voices; the solo albums since 1994 are first-rate without having made him widely known. Åge Aleksandersen is named as a prominent fan.

Leven says (self-report) that he has just come back from Beirut, where he recorded new songs with Lebanese and Greek musicians – it still sounds like a Western Jackie Leven record, but it is the most exciting thing he has done. He does not measure success in sales: he knows many successful musicians, but none of them gets to travel to Tromsø. At length he repeats the Diana anecdote: after the attack (in the paper “1982”, “mugged and stabbed”) he worked for years with addicts and met Princess Diana in the course of it; her “Why don't you sing something” was perhaps the most important moment of his life, and he did not dare to sing again for over ten years.

On the festival's name, Leven says he is himself a “working class man”; in England a festival would not call itself that, because under Tony Blair people want to forget their industrial roots. Andreassen closes by noting that Leven's concerts are never boring – he has seen “quite a few”.
zitate_kontext: Leven on more successful fellow musicians.

2005-04-30-dagsavisen-leven-i-litteratur.kurz: Major interview on the double album *Jackie Leven Said* with Ian Rankin, shortly before Leven's next visit to Norway.
inhalt: Major interview on the double album *Jackie Leven Said* with Ian Rankin, shortly before Leven's next visit to Norway. Rakvaag stresses that the collaboration began, in a way, in Norway: according to the booklet, Leven discovered on a flight from Bergen to Tromsø that he appears in Rankin's novel *Resurrection Man* (in the paper “Ressurection Man”, Norw. “Botsgang”) as Inspector John Rebus's favourite singer. Leven confirms this (self-report): he was reading it over a few drinks before a difficult landing. Norway is for him the “extreme version of Scotland”; he has played here since 1966, then as guitarist of the blues singer Doris Henderson – his first trip abroad as a professional musician.

Rankin and Leven then exchanged emails and worked out a joint stage show for festivals in Glasgow and Edinburgh in 2004. Rankin's story is about a musician who travels from London to Fife for his mother's funeral. Leven describes the shared theme: men whose lives are becoming blurred and whose inner lives are a mystery to them. He sings old songs that inspired Rankin, and three new ones, including “The Haunting of John Rebus”; the rest of the double album is a retrospective chosen jointly. The title alludes to Van Morrison's “Jackie Wilson Said”; a character quotes “My Spanish Dad”.

On drinking, Leven says he has not been addicted to heroin for 20 years and does not want to go on appearing as an ex-junkie for ever; he believes in good company when drinking, but also spends a lot of time at home sober. He loves the melancholy of travelling alone; as a young man he won a national writing competition with a travel story. Outlook: solo at the Working Class Hero festival in Drammen on 1 May, a week later with David Thomas (Pere Ubu) as UbuDoll at Bergenfest. Fact boxes on Leven (including: the Doll by Doll albums soon to appear on CD for the first time, next album recorded in Beirut with Greek and Lebanese musicians) and on Rankin.

2005-05-02-gaesteliste-jackie-leven-said.kurz: Ullrich Maurer reviews the double CD *Jackie Leven Said*, with Ian Rankin's short story and Leven's songs: entertaining, but, for all his affection, one for hardened fans only.
inhalt: Ullrich Maurer places *Jackie Leven Said* (Cooking Vinyl/Indigo) in Leven's turn to literature as a live medium. After the DVD *Remarkable Men* it is already the second document on which Leven sets off against humanity together with his “Fife neighbour”, the bestselling author Ian Rankin (Maurer calls him a neighbour because both come from Fife).

The twist: Rankin reads a short story he wrote about Leven – “Jackie Leven Said” – while Leven, with his musical partner Michael Cosgrave, illustrates it, including with new songs about characters from Rankin's books. The performance is framed by the inimitable, hair-raising chatter that makes up a good part of every Leven show. The rest of the double CD consists of a few songs from Leven's songbook which he and Rankin chose together, among them Burt Bacharach's “Say A Little Prayer”.

Maurer's verdict: for all his love, this work too is only for hardened fans, though it will probably not be the end of the story. The songwriter James Yorkston recently told him that he also comes from Fife and that Leven had already phoned him.

2005-05-04-bergensavisen-bombedrama-beir.kurz: BA meets the “Bergensvenn” Leven at the start of a six-day stay in Bergen. Leven says (self-report) that a few months ago he was sitting in a street café in Beirut when, two blocks away, the car bomb exploded that killed the former prime minister Rafik al-Hariri; he w…
inhalt: BA meets the “Bergensvenn” Leven at the start of a six-day stay in Bergen. Leven says (self-report) that a few months ago he was sitting in a street café in Beirut when, two blocks away, the car bomb exploded that killed the former prime minister Rafik al-Hariri; he had been there to record his forthcoming record with local and Greek musicians. He was terrified for his life and refuses to go back for cover photos.

The reason for the long stay is Bergenfest: on Friday he plays with David Thomas (Pere Ubu). Bergen is his “spiritual centre”, the festival head Frank Nes invited him for six days; he wants to relax and write. On *Jackie Leven Said* he repeats the flight anecdote (Bergen–Tromsø, Rankin's novel, Rebus as a fan); Rankin's publisher first turned the project down and then postponed its marketing by eight months. A tour is open: his mother died last year, after his father's death he buried himself in work, and now he wants to be at home with his wife and write songs.

On Doll by Doll: Warner did not care about the four albums, and now someone has finally woken up – partly thanks to the Rankin record. He rules out a live reunion, but says they have talked about a new joint studio album. Ending with “Rainy Day Bergen Woman” and a wish for rain.

2005-05-31-bergensavisen-jackie-leven-sa.kurz: Tore Bø recommends the live double album *Jackie Leven Said*: Ian Rankin tells Scottish stories, Leven adds three new songs, and CD 2 offers classics that stand up to a second listen.
inhalt: This short review in Bergensavisen (31 May 2005) introduces the live album from Edinburgh: Ian Rankin, it says, is Scotland’s leading crime writer, best known for his novels about the policeman John Rebus, while Jackie Leven is an “outstanding singer and songwriter” who has visited Bergen many times.

The background to the record, it explains, was a flight between Bergen and Tromsø on which Leven passed the time reading a Rankin novel. There he read that he himself is one of the hero’s favourites. He contacted Rankin, and a joint concert project came about: Rankin with the story “Jackie Leven Said”, Leven with songs that slip naturally into the text. On the first disc Rankin tells Scottish stories and Leven serves three new songs; CD 2 gives some of the classics and Leven’s own favourites from old albums, which “can stand a second hearing”. The review is signed Tore Bø; the rating is illegible.
zitate_kontext: Bø on the content of the double album

2005-05-goodreads-jackie-leven-said-orio.kurz: Goodreads’ publisher blurb for *Jackie Leven Said*: CD 1 holds Ian Rankin’s story from their joint show at the 2004 Edinburgh Festival, Leven’s songs and a “wildly funny” discussion of what it means to come from Fife.
inhalt: Goodreads lists *Jackie Leven Said* by Ian Rankin and Jackie Leven as an audio CD (first published 5 May 2005); the page shows 4.20 stars from 15 ratings. The catalogue text describes the first CD: it contains the story “Jackie Leven Said”, written and read by Rankin, from the pair’s live show at the 2004 Edinburgh Festival. Rankin tells it in short chapters illustrated by musical interludes and complete songs performed by Leven and keyboard player Michael Cosgrave.

The story evokes the suffering and healing of a Scottish family coming together for a funeral in Fife on the east coast. Although a work of fiction, it resonates strongly with the life experiences of Rankin and Leven, who both come from that part of the world, and it “sparkles with humour”. At the end of the storytelling, Rankin and Leven have a “wildly funny knockabout discussion” of what it means to come from Fife, with Leven departing from the subject in his uniquely crazy way. The songs blend the lives of both men and also touch on the inner life of Rankin’s fictional hero, Detective Inspector John Rebus, “the haunted genius”, himself a Fifer. The page also carries a short biography of Rankin (born in Fife in 1960, first Rebus novel in 1987, translated into 22 languages, OBE).

Publisher’s text on the conversation between Rankin and Leven

2005-06-22-sarpsborg-arbeiderblad-et-sja.kurz: Erling Brøndmo retells the origin of the double CD *Jackie Leven Said* in Sarpsborg Arbeiderblad and calls it “a charming mess”: Rankin’s story not at its best, Leven’s songs mostly familiar, but winning through humour and Scottish dialect.
inhalt: The review, in the “spoken word/folk” column, begins with the “fascinating story” of the record: the old Doll by Doll singer Jackie Leven sits on a flight from Tromsø to Bergen reading a book by Ian Rankin and discovers that the hero John Rebus is a fan of his. A double CD came of it, “and not just any record”. When Leven got in touch they agreed that Rankin should write a short story; the title became “Jackie Leven Said”.

Brøndmo’s verdict on the story: “not Rankin at his very best, but not bad either”. It is read on the CD live from Edinburgh, with a few musical interjections from Leven and Michael Cosgrave. On the second disc Leven “struggles on”; three new songs are included, the rest the fans know already. And the fans, says Brøndmo, are the ones who will buy it, those already hooked on Leven’s warm voice and cosy music.

His conclusion: it all appears a bit messy, “but it is a charming mess”, charming because of the “cosy humour lurking” and the Scottish dialect. (The paper prints Rankin as “Rankings”, and the direction of the flight differs from other accounts.)

2005-07-03-rolling-stone-de-short-cuts-j.kurz: In his “Short Cuts” column in *Rolling Stone* (German edition), Wolfgang Doebeling describes *Jackie Leven Said* as a delightful rendezvous of two Scottish art oddballs, Ian Rankin and Leven, and gives it a rating of 3.0.
inhalt: In his round-up column “Short Cuts” for the German edition of *Rolling Stone*, Wolfgang Doebeling gives *Jackie Leven Said* (Cooking Vinyl) a short paragraph headed “Jackie Leven & Ian Rankin”. The album, he says, is the document of a “most enjoyable rendezvous” of two Scottish “art oddballs”: the bestselling author Ian Rankin, speciality crime fiction, and the “not overly popular but immensely productive” songsmith Leven, speciality “iron manhood”.

He describes a performance in Edinburgh: Rankin reads his short story “Jackie Leven Said” about the life conflicts of a record producer, Leven and the keyboardist Michael Cosgrave provide musical interludes, there is an “absurd discussion” about their shared homeland, the Kingdom of Fife, and Leven plays new songs, with Doebeling calling him the “mystic”. To the question “Funny?” he answers “You bet.” The rating is 3.0.

2005-08-01-jackieleven-com-elegy-for-joh.kurz: Press text for the album *Elegy For Johnny Cash* (12 September 2005), said to have been recorded in Beirut with Lebanese and Greek musicians, followed by Leven's own notes on several songs.
inhalt: The information page on Leven's website announces his studio album *Elegy For Johnny Cash* (Cooking Vinyl, COOKCD331) for 12 September 2005. It was recorded, the text says, in Beirut and mixed in Bethesda, Wales, with musicians and singers from Lebanon, Greece, the USA, Northern Ireland, Ireland, England, Wales and Scotland. It describes a “different kind of studio album” with touches of Americana and hip-hop, and insists that despite the Lebanese and Greek guests it is not a “world” album: the musicians mostly play in western styles, though nobody in the West could play the viola solos of the Greek musician Mixalis Kataxanis.

The title track grew out of Leven's admiration for Johnny Cash's late recordings with Rick Rubin. Leven says he had admired Cash the artist but only really engaged with him through those records; he sings his song as if he were Cash, imagining his last performance as he passes from this world to the next. It is followed by “The Law Of Tide”, in which Robert Fisher of Willard Grant Conspiracy also takes on Cash's persona. Leven recalls singing Fisher a snatch of it at a soundcheck “in the style of Johnny Cash”, after which Fisher agreed to sing the whole song, “a scary performance”. Other highlights include the hip-hop track “All The Rage” with Leven's old friend, the Ulsterman Martin Okasili. Leven and his engineer David Wrench produced the record, and the cover is a painting by the Münster-based artist Mirjam Rückert.

As to why Beirut, the text gives this account: after the funeral of his mother, long-standing family friends asked Leven to sing at a gathering of Roma singers south-east of the city, a concert exclusively for Roma. Being Romany himself, he was honoured and went there in December. Wrench then suggested recording with the musicians he would be meeting, and Leven, who had already decided to work with two Greek friends, took it from there.

Most space goes to Leven's own song notes. For “Museum Of Childhood” he tells of the two boxing matches between Sugar Ray Leonard and Roberto Duran: in the second, Duran stopped fighting mid-round, walked to his corner and smiled quietly at Leonard, and Leven says he will never forget the commentator saying Duran “looks like a man who just wants to go home”. Recording the title song, he says, Kataxanis first refused to play, because the genre was so far from his experience and he did not know who Cash was; only the video of “Hurt” changed his mind, and he nodded and went back into the studio. “All The Rage” is about the fading men of the heavy industrial age, whom he and Ian Rankin had met in a Kirkcaldy bar earlier that year. “Vibration White Finger” is an industrial injury that “kills your hands”, and “King Of The Barley” portrays the lone Scotsman drinking whisky in English city bars. The page ends with the full line-up by country, including Michael Cosgrave, Deborah Greenwood, Michael Weston King and Alan Cook on pedal steel.
zitate_kontext: Leven on “Museum Of Childhood” and the Leonard–Duran fight

2005-08-08-rolling-stone-forum-jackie-le.kurz: A forum thread of tour announcements for Jackie Leven in Germany, Austria and Switzerland: autumn 2005 with the Small World Orchestra, April 2006, and April/May 2007 with Michael Cosgrave.
inhalt: The Rolling Stone forum thread consists of nine posts and exists solely to swap tour dates. It opens in August 2005 with an anonymous announcement of the tour by “Jackie Leven’s Small World Orchestra (UK)” for the new album *Elegy for Johnny Cash* (Cooking Vinyl/Indigo), running 16 to 30 November 2005: Münster (Gleis 22), Dortmund (FZW), Frankfurt (Sinkkasten, to be confirmed), Thun (Café Mokka), Vienna (Chelsea, tbc), Ingolstadt (Neue Welt), Stuttgart (Laboratorium, tbc), Erfurt (Museumskeller), Berlin (Quasimodo), Singwitz (Kesselhauslager), Halle (Theater), Hanover (Bluesgarage), Hamburg (Knust) and Kiel (Räucherei).

In September 2005 a user adds changes according to Cooking Vinyl: three dates at the Galerie Augenweide in Münster (27–29 October) and one on 16 November at the Steinenhaus/Irish Pub in Solingen, the rest unchanged. Another user notes Hamburg. In March 2006 two lists of the spring tour (31 March to 8 April) follow: Kufstein (Kulturfabrik), Göppingen (Odeon), Dresden (Dreikönigskirche), Vienna (Chelsea), Augsburg, Nuremberg (Ruhestörung), Magdeburg (Feuerwache), Einbeck (Beim Esel) and Wredenhagen (Scheune). The Augsburg venue appears once as “Striese” and once as “Kilobuch”. One user calls Leven the “guitar highlander”; another regrets he is not playing nearby, since he was in Dortmund only recently.

In April 2007 a tour “together with Michael Cosgrave” is posted and later extended: 19 April Bremen (Kioto), then Kiel, Verden/Aller, Berlin, Hamburg, Bonn, Oberhausen, Hanover, Dresden, Offenburg, Erfurt, Halle and, on 4 May, Stuttgart – the first list also had Zurich on 5 May. One user plans to be at the Stuttgart show and calls the Laboratorium “exactly the right intimate setting for a Jackie concert”. The dates are announcements, not proof that the concerts took place.

2005-08-30-drammens-tidende-kloverod-sma.titel: [Eivind Kløverød plays with Jackie Leven] (subheading “KLØVERØD MED LEVEN”; main headline not reliably legible in the OCR)
2005-08-30-drammens-tidende-kloverod-sma.autor: anonymous (not reliably attributable in the OCR)
2005-08-30-drammens-tidende-kloverod-sma.kurz: Profile of the percussionist Eivind Kløverød ahead of Leven’s concert opening the Union Scene in Drammen: Kløverød had joined Leven’s solo show spontaneously on 1 May and now tours with his new band through Norway, Germany and Switzerland.
inhalt: Under the heading “Vestfossens uslepne diamant” (“Vestfossen’s uncut diamond”), Johnny Andreassen profiles the drummer Eivind Kløverød in Drammens Tidende (30 August 2005). The occasion: on Saturday 24 September the new Union Scene in Drammen is officially opened with a concert by the Scot Jackie Leven. According to the paper, Leven has put together a band “for the first time since he led the legendary Doll By Doll in the early eighties”, with Kløverød on percussion. That claim is the newspaper’s own.

Andreassen calls the background a “tall tale”: at the Working Class Hero festival on 1 May, which the critic Øyvind Gundersen had rated a six, Leven played solo. Kløverød, who had played as support with the Bent Bredesen Trio, walked on “completely impulsively” with his kit. The roughly 150 present still talk about the magic between the two. Kløverød says he had listened to Leven – “This is good. I could have played here” – and asked the sound man to set up his drums; “after a couple of beers” he was probably a bit cocky, and it was “cheeky”, since you never know what reaction you will trigger. Bredesen was horrified and shouted “no, no”.

For the collaboration he is building a “very special instrument”. After the Drammen concert he is to tour Germany and Switzerland with Leven and the new group, Leven’s “Small World Orchestra”. Kløverød, drummer in Jonas Fjeld’s band and lately in the Jensengruppen, is called a “find” and perhaps Norway’s most exciting drummer by Dagbladet. Of playing together he says, “We talk to each other without talking”; he dislikes the word jam because it is far more constructive and structured. He never went to music school – “The school I attended is called Jonny Aasgaard”.
zitate_kontext: Eivind Kløverød on joining Leven’s concert spontaneously
Johnny Andreassen on Leven’s new band

2005-09-03-rolling-stone-de-elegy-for-jo.kurz: Germany’s Rolling Stone praises *Elegy For Johnny Cash*: Leven’s tonne-heavy songs need no Rick Rubin; two pieces are directly for Cash, and “King Of Barley”, on the lonely drinkers at the bar, shows who can sing them so well.
inhalt: The unsigned review by the German Rolling Stone editorial staff (3 September 2005) opens with a quip: no, Rick Rubin did not produce this record – he is busy doing his best to reincarnate Neil Diamond artistically – but he probably could not have added much to Leven’s songs, “always equipped with a tonne-heavy mood”. Leven did not choose the title without reason: he is a Cash admirer and believes he has got to the bottom of the singer otherwise too, even if, like so many, he found his way to Cash for good only through the *American Recordings*.

The supposedly last paths, the reviewer says, Leven has famously walked more than once: a beaten track of misery and ruin, heroin and whisky, self-abandonment and withdrawal cures, things that tattoo themselves on your heart and whose aftereffects he has sung about for years. *Elegy* too mostly treats the side-worlds, but two songs are dedicated directly to Cash: the “fantastic” title track, which Leven imagines as Cash’s last singing performance and which is lightened by pedal steel and the virtuoso violin of Mixalis Kataxams, and “The Law Of Tide”, sung “no less grandly” by “dark rumbler” Robert Fisher (Willard Grant Conspiracy; spelt “Fischer” in the text).

Otherwise Leven digs, as usual, in the territory far from breakfast families and ordered circumstances. “Blue Soul Dark Road” is a Leven standard, “No Honour In This Love” and “Vibration White Finger” are wonderful. And then he describes the lonely man from the pub: “King Of Barley” is what English and Scottish bars call the stranded and broken-off who talk to nobody and stand drinking at the bar for hours. Everyone knows such types, and we may sometimes be them ourselves, “but who could sing them as beautifully as Jackie Leven”. The verdict is clearly positive; the page gives no star rating.
zitate_kontext: Opening of the Rolling Stone review

2005-09-06-dagsavisen-i-johnny-cashs-fot.kurz: Mode Steinkjer reviews *Elegy for Johnny Cash* in Dagsavisen as a record full of love for Cash and for Americana: recorded in Beirut, with a Memphis feel and Scottish lyrics, a must for fans of both artists.
inhalt: Mode Steinkjer opens in Dagsavisen: if you miss Johnny Cash or are a fan of Jackie Leven, Leven’s *Elegy for Johnny Cash* is “a necessity in everyday life”. The singer-songwriter with a Doll by Doll background has made a record that exudes love for Cash and for the genre springing from country rock and Southern Americana, and he pairs it, in his own way, with “honest and harsh Scottish lyricism”.

The album was recorded in Beirut, but the feeling is Memphis. Not every song is as obvious a Cash tribute as the “fine title track”, written in gratitude to Cash’s producer Rick Rubin, but all are inspired by the same atmosphere, whether about Sugar Ray Leonard or a lonely barstool experience, whether the country is the US or Leven’s own Scotland. As a poet Leven is more advanced than Cash, though the atmosphere is the same, and he shows a “new, warm and perhaps even more melancholy side”. Steinkjer quotes the line “I got a blue soul and a dark road” and notes that on that road Leven touches on many kinds of fates, which have in common that they can laugh at themselves.

Equally important is how the record was made, a kind of geographical round trip that echoes instrumentally, from Lebanon, Greece, the USA, Northern Ireland and Wales to England, with the Scottish in the lyrics. It is neither a covers album nor a “world” album, but Leven’s way of showing that his songs are universal and humanist and that he owes his mentors a great debt, for the words as well as the musical inspiration. The review appeared in Dagsavisen on 6 September 2005; the paper’s rating, according to a later notice, was five out of six.
zitate_kontext: Steinkjer on Leven as a poet

2005-09-09-the-independent-album-jackie-.kurz: Andy Gill writes in The Independent (9 September 2005) that *Elegy for Johnny Cash*, recorded in Beirut, remains Leven’s customary soulful Caledonian folk-rock. He praises the portraits of hard men; the love songs convince him less.
inhalt: Andy Gill places the album in time: it arrives only five months after the *Jackie Leven Said* collaboration with Ian Rankin and was recorded late the previous year in Beirut, where Leven, “a Romany himself” according to Gill, had been invited to a gathering of Romany singers. Stylistically it is barely altered from his customary soulful Caledonian folk-rock, apart from the occasional flurry of Arabic percussion or Greek rembetika viola.

The lyrical concerns are likewise unchanged: the iron in the souls of hard men struggling to retain their dignity in an age that has no use for them. Gill cites the “broken men of the Mersey and the Tyne” stricken with industrial injuries in “Vibration White Finger”, the bitter, hard-drinking misanthrope in “King of the Barley” and the husband kicked out by his wife in “Blue Soul, Dark Road”. The calloused nobility is embodied by a few figures: the boxer Roberto Durán, turning his back on Sugar Ray Leonard mid-fight in “Museum of Childhood”, and Johnny Cash, a gnarled monument of pained solitude borne with stoic grace, whom Leven imagines singing the title track.
The love songs are less effective, with the romances always doomed. Women, Gill adds, play in Leven’s work much the same kind of support roles as in Scorsese’s films.
