Gill on Cash as a figure on the album

2005-09-13-drammens-tidende-gjennombrudd.kurz: Johnny Andreassen hails *Elegy for Johnny Cash* in *Drammens Tidende* as a possible breakthrough in Norway and “one of the year’s biggest albums” (“En perle!”); also a preview of the concert at Union Scene.
inhalt: Under the headline “Gjennombruddet” (“The breakthrough”), Johnny Andreassen announces Leven’s appearance at Drammen’s Union Scene with his Small World Orchestra, with Eivind Kløverød on percussion, and, judging by the new album, promises an under-the-skin experience of a rare kind. *Elegy for Johnny Cash* should be the Scottish veteran’s definitive breakthrough in Norway. The closeness of his blend of Scottish white soul, Celtic singer-songwriter folk tradition and pop songs that feel like a long-missed relative surprisingly coming home is unique.

He stresses that Leven conjures up Johnny Cash’s soul as he has never heard anyone but the Man in Black himself do, particularly on the dark, dramatic “The Law of Tide”, which according to the critic is sung by Robert Fisher of Willard Grant Conspiracy: “Magisk!” The album, he says, is made for establishing Leven as a friend of Norway, as Leonard Cohen and Van Morrison have become, and without compromise: he has simply collected some of the finest songs he has written, such as the opener “Blue Soul Dark Road”, and let voice and guitar do the rest. The closing flourish: if God likes music, he is sure God has already burned himself a copy.
He concedes weaknesses: a programmed drum sound and a couple of somewhat anonymous songs that could have been better. Even so it is, for him, one of the year’s biggest albums: “En perle!”
zitate_kontext: Johnny Andreassen on *Elegy for Johnny Cash*

2005-09-15-halden-arbeiderblad-leven-pa-.kurz: A preview in Halden Arbeiderblad for the concert at the pub Siste Reis on 25 September 2005: Leven’s life story, the promoter Tom Skjeklesæther and the comparison with Van Morrison and Mike Scott.
inhalt: On 15 September 2005 Halden Arbeiderblad announces that the pub Siste Reis in Halden will receive “fine visitors” on Sunday 25 September: Jackie Leven (55), “a well-known Scottish singer-songwriter” and cult artist with a past with Doll by Doll among others. Tom Skjeklesæther of Halden, who ran the rock club Ratz in Oslo in the early 1980s, came into contact with Leven then: “Doll by Doll was the first band we had at Ratz.”

The article retraces Leven’s life as Norwegian media told it at the time: born into a Romani family, father Irish, mother from northern England, raised in Scotland. A tough childhood ended with him ‘fleeing’ the country and living in London, Berlin and Madrid, in underground scenes and playing the music played there. While working on his first solo record he was the victim of a random assault in London, was nearly strangled and was without a voice for a year; a heavy time in which he sought comfort in narcotics. He got back on his feet and since 1985 has been involved in CORE, an organisation that helps people dependent on narcotics and other intoxicants; Princess Diana was an important supporter for years, and Eric Clapton is also involved.

Leven also gradually returned to music, has released fifteen solo albums, still works for CORE and is an artist who arouses attention and enthusiasm, preferably in small clubs. Skjeklesæther: “Jackie Leven likes best small, intimate venues where closeness to the audience is great.” What can the audience expect? “A fine evening. Leven has a fantastic voice and is in a musical landscape somewhere between Van Morrison and Mike Scott of the Waterboys.” The paper once spells the name ‘Jacke Leven’; the biographical details are the newspaper’s own.
zitate_kontext: Skjeklesæther on the Oslo club Ratz

2005-09-19-mescalina-jackie-leven-said.kurz: Christian Verzeletti finds the double CD *Jackie Leven Said* with Ian Rankin a record of noble intentions but for fans only, better as a DVD. He likes best the three new songs from Rebus’s viewpoint, above all “Linseed Oil”.
inhalt: Verzeletti begins with Leven’s path: already on *Shining Brother, Shining Sister* he had engaged with other voices, including literary ones. In his career one can see a human and artistic journey that has made his pop ever more conscious and refined; the song has become a container at times too narrow and constricting, so it is logical that it spills into projects and collaborations beyond pure music.

*Jackie Leven Said* is a record “for four hands” with the writer Ian Rankin. The first CD and part of the second contain the recording of the evening the two gave at the Queen’s Hall in Edinburgh in August 2004, a concert-reading in which Leven’s songs alternate with Rankin’s reading; there are also three new songs and a handful of older ones. The title, Verzeletti says, comes from a Van Morrison song (evidently “Jackie Wilson Said”). It all began when Leven found his name in a text by Rankin and, also curious because Rankin, like him, was from Fife, contacted him. Verzeletti calls Fife a little village in Scotland, an error, since it is a county. Rankin wrote a story about a family gathering at Fife for a funeral; it became the basis for a date on which the two read, played and talked, a show full of humour and reflection, of folk and witty words.

But transferred to CD, the evening loses much of its effectiveness, especially for those not fully fluent in English; the songs also drag on too long, passing seven and eight minutes, although Leven brings all his usual depth as an author. If one can enter the show entirely, one can recognise the pride and dignity both artists bring to their work from real experience, but it is an arduous task, even when they break into a lively conversation about what it means to live in Fife.

More accessible are the three new songs in which Leven adopts John Rebus’s view. “Linseed Oil” stands out, about the oil that makes the whole town of Kirkcaldy stink, a perfect example of combining bitterness and hope, tragedy and humour, with the arrangements themselves poking ironic fun at life. The already released pieces he finds negligible. His conclusion: an album with noble intentions, but intended only for fans, which would have deserved to be published exclusively on DVD.
zitate_kontext: Verzeletti on the CD version of the evening

2005-09-20-drammens-tidende-liten-verden.titel: [Jackie Leven and the Small World Orchestra open the Union Scene] (caption “LITEN VERDEN
2005-09-20-drammens-tidende-liten-verden.kurz: Preview of the opening of Union Scene in Drammen: Leven tells how the idea for the Small World Orchestra was born in Drammen and talks about *Elegy for Johnny Cash*, which helped him come to terms with his father's death.
inhalt: Drammens Tidende announces Jackie Leven's appearance at the opening of the new cultural centre Union Scene on Saturday (24 September 2005). Dagbladet dubbed him “Scotland's answer to Van Morrison” a couple of years ago. With percussionist Eivind Kløverød from Vestfossen, a Greek violinist and an English keyboardist and trumpeter, Leven says he is more excited than he has been since touring with Doll by Doll in the late 1970s. It is a fantastic feeling to inaugurate a cultural centre like Union Scene; he last played there at the Working Class Hero festival.

The idea for the Small World Orchestra, Leven says, was born in Drammen. On his earlier visit he was playing a song about a train journey from Drammen to Bergen, his first in Norway, when Kløverød “cheekily and boldly” walked on stage, sat down beside him and began to play. “First I thought: ‘Who the f… is this bastard?!’ Then Eivind started to play. He was so good that I fell head over heels in love.” None of the orchestra has played together before and there is only one morning to rehearse, but with such musicians he is not in the least afraid; it is only the band's second concert, in Drammen, where the idea was conceived.

The article points to the new album *Elegy for Johnny Cash*, which strengthens Leven's position in Germany – he tours there in November with Kløverød and the orchestra – and might bring the final breakthrough in Norway. Leven says he did not foresee the Cash feeling; it arrived after he was enchanted by Cash's video for “Hurt”. He had not liked Cash much before, but in his last recordings found a feeling that helped him come to terms with his own father's death. He then began collecting pictures as if from Cash's life, which became the song “Elegy for Johnny Cash”. As background the article says Leven led a distinctive, charismatic rock band until the mid-1980s, when he was attacked without provocation in London and believed he would never sing again; ten years later Princess Diana removed his doubts by demanding that he sing for her – and in Drammen he now appears with his first band in twenty years.
zitate_kontext: Leven on the moment Eivind Kløverød walked on stage unannounced.
Leven on how *Elegy for Johnny Cash* came about.

2005-09-21-nordlys-jackie-vokser.kurz: A positive short review of *Elegy for Johnny Cash*, flagging Leven's visit to Tromsø: a record full of good stories whose songs grow on repeated listening; the reviewer's favourite is “King of the Barley”.
inhalt: Nordlys (Tromsø) reviews *Elegy for Johnny Cash* (Cooking Vinyl) in a round-up column under the headline “Jackie grows”. The Scot, who visits Tromsø the following week, is a formidable singer-songwriter, and the album shows no loss of form: it is stuffed with good stories and songs that grow strongly after several listens. It is the kind of album on which you constantly find new favourites. The reviewer himself currently needs large daily doses of “King of the Barley”, a sauntering song that explodes into a chorus “sent from heaven with a jetpack”.

Leven has no ambition to revolutionise the singer-songwriter genre – and that is unnecessary as long as quality is so high all round. The review praises fine details from musicians from the British Isles, Greece and Lebanon (!) and stories from a universe outside the usual “woe, loneliness” (the surviving text excerpt ends here).
zitate_kontext: The reviewer on his favourite, “King of the Barley”.

2005-09-26-drammens-tidende-naervaer-av-.kurz: Øyvind R. Gundersen criticises the band sound at the opening-weekend concert of Union Scene in Drammen, but hails Leven as a poet, storyteller and master guitarist with a huge voice.
inhalt: Øyvind R. Gundersen reviews Leven's concert on Saturday 24 September 2005 at 10 pm at Union Scene in Drammen, before about 250 people. Leven's concert at the Working Class Hero festival in the spring had been “two hours of pleasure” with an undeservedly little-known star from Scotland; this time he had upgraded from just himself to a four-piece band, and expectations were sky-high.

The critic first gets some irritations out of the way: the band's sound disappointed. Synthetic synth sounds and a thudding bass have nothing to do with Leven's music. The best-sounding member was the Drammen percussionist Eivind Kløverud, whose percussion and quirks were the perfect accompaniment to Leven's rhythmic guitar playing; he singles out a percussion duel between the two. Leven himself comes off well: a big man with a big voice and enormous presence, whose friendly and at times quite coarse chat between songs created the communication such a low-key concert needs. His stylistic range runs from heavy blues-tinged numbers through playful jazz pieces and more exotic touches to classic singer-songwriter art; none of it is pure or perfect, but Leven makes something of his own from it, driven by the voice.

Further back in the room the audience's chatter took over. Leven must be experienced with intense presence, a listening audience and preferably sparse instrumentation; since the Saturday evening lacked some of that, it was a pity, because with the right setting he makes a tremendous impression. The dice rating cannot be read in the scan.

2005-09-27-avisa-nordland-elegy-for-john.titel: [Review: Jackie Leven – Elegy for Johnny Cash]
2005-09-27-avisa-nordland-elegy-for-john.kurz: Short review in *Avisa Nordland* (27 September 2005): *Elegy for Johnny Cash* captures the mood of Cash’s last albums with unusually strong songs; also a concert tip for Kabelvåg.
inhalt: On a page of record reviews, *Avisa Nordland* urges anyone living nearby who likes great songwriting to catch Leven when he plays with a band at the Præstengbrygga in Kabelvåg the following Thursday. The man who fronted the cult band Doll By Doll in the Eighties, it says, keeps releasing better and better records on his own.

On *Elegy for Johnny Cash* he tries to recreate the mood of Cash’s last records. It is that mood and expression he chiefly pays tribute to, and he delivers a set of strong songs with an unusual and arresting nerve. Leven is close and alive, and lyrics, melodies and the fine production take hold the way great artists do. He is a well-kept secret with a loyal core of followers, who will get their fill in Kabelvåg on Thursday. Placing Doll By Doll in the Eighties is a simplification (the band began in 1977–78).
zitate_kontext: From the review of *Elegy for Johnny Cash*

2005-09-27-rogalands-avis-enigmatisk.kurz: In *Rogalands Avis*, Helge O. Svela calls Leven “enigmatic” and praises *Elegy for Johnny Cash*: even odd production choices cannot spoil Leven’s classic songwriting; a big record that needs some getting used to.
inhalt: Helge O. Svela writes under the headline “Enigmatisk” about *Elegy for Johnny Cash* (Cooking Vinyl/Bonnier Amigo). The “enigmatic Scottish artist” comes to Checkpoint in Stavanger in just under a month, and it is a concert he intends to catch. The album demonstrates that even odd production choices cannot ruin Leven’s classic songwriting and lyrics.

It is a tribute to the late Johnny Cash; on the title track and on “The Law Of Tide” Leven stays close to the country king’s vocal expression. Although several songs can be classed as Americana, there is more to the album: the reviewer gives Lebanon as the recording location and hears echoes of folk music from both the Middle East and the British Isles. His verdict: “a big record that requires a little getting used to”.
zitate_kontext: Helge O. Svela on the album

2005-09-28-bladet-tromso-leven-pa-bla-ro.kurz: A preview of Leven's concert at Blå Rock in Tromsø that same evening: he presents *Elegy For Johnny Cash*, is touring northern Europe, and, according to “well-informed sources”, will not go on stage until after the Liverpool–Chelsea match.
inhalt: Under “Leven på Blå Rock”, Bladet Tromsø (by Kjetil Vik) announces the Scottish troubadour's concert that same evening at Blå Rock, where he is a regular guest. Leven returns to Tromsø “with new songs in his guitar case”. He recently released *Elegy For Johnny Cash*, an album with musicians from Lebanon, Greece, the USA and Britain, recorded in Beirut and, the paper says, well reviewed on the whole.

He also has a solid back catalogue: for the last ten years he has released solo records steadily, with songs “beyond most hit lists, in a positive sense”. An evening with Leven on stage is a great experience and seldom boring: he gives a lot of himself, spices the music with funny stories and anecdotes from his many tours, and is also “a devil on guitar”, with strings and wood taking a beating when he hammers away. The concert is part of an extensive northern European tour taking in Norway, Sweden, Germany, England and Switzerland. The paper adds a punchline: Leven is a big football fan and, according to well-informed sources close to the artist, will probably not go on stage at Blå Rock until the Liverpool–Chelsea match has finished on TV. The same issue's events listing names a local Tromsø band as the support act.

2005-09-28-nordlys-skotsk-tromso-patriot.kurz: On the day of his concert at Blå Rock in Tromsø, Leven tells Nordlys that he wrote some of his best songs in the city's hotel rooms, senses an “end-of-the-world feeling” there, and explains his turn to Johnny Cash through the “Hurt” video.
inhalt: Christine Kristoffersen Hansen profiles Leven in Nordlys on the day of his concert at Blå Rock (Wednesday 28 September 2005; according to the concert listing with Elias Jung as support) as a “Scottish Tromsø patriot”. Tromsø has a kind of “end-of-the-world-feeling”, Leven says, but he does not mean it negatively, quite the opposite: a truly special place whose magic he finds hard to explain.

His Tromsø patriotism arose during four earlier visits. He says he has actually written “some of my very best songs” in hotel rooms in the city; something about the atmosphere inspires him. He is currently on a big Norwegian tour that has taken him to Oslo and Trondheim, among other places, and jokes that he hardly needs to say that this is the concert he is looking forward to most.

Of his latest album, *Elegy for Johnny Cash*, Leven says it is a very special record for him. He initially did not care much for Johnny Cash until he saw the “Hurt” video and was “really moved”; he then went back through Cash's work and came to appreciate especially his last album. He promises tastes of the album and songs from earlier years, plus “a lot of humour” and “quite a few funny stories”. He feels very good at the moment and is sure it will be a very good concert.
zitate_kontext: Leven on Tromsø (as rendered in the paper)
Leven on what led to *Elegy for Johnny Cash*

2005-09-musikexpress-elegy-for-johnny-ca.kurz: Peter Felkel places Leven beside Van Morrison and Rory Gallagher as a Scottish-Irish “soul brother in spirit”; *Elegy for Johnny Cash* is no flat Cash tribute but Leven's most unusual, though not his best, album.
inhalt: Peter Felkel opens his Musikexpress review with Van Morrison's claim that the blues really came from Scotland and Ireland, the former Caledonia, and took a roundabout route to the cotton fields of the American South. Endless arguments speak against this, Felkel says, but three support it: Van Morrison, Rory Gallagher and Jackie Leven. The last, a melancholic poet from Fife, battered by life yet unbowed, has nothing formally to do with the twelve-bar scheme but can certainly count as a “soul brother in spirit” – someone who does not bother with the superficialities of pop and titled his first solo work in 1994 *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death*.

*Elegy for Johnny Cash* is again a mix of folk, Celtic soul, soft rock, ethnic touches that thankfully never drift into dungaree-clad multicultural bliss, and pop with plenty of pathos, sometimes decidedly too much – but definitely not a flat tribute to the “Man in Black”. There are no country tunes, but fine melodies, irritating rap interludes and, in “Blue Soul Dark Road”, a capital killer song that will delight even Dire Straits fans. The record was made in Beirut of all places. The verdict: Leven's most unusual album, but not his best. Release date: 12 September.

2005-09-plattentests-de-elegy-for-johnny.kurz: In "Schwarzer Anzug" on Plattentests.de, Oliver Ding describes Leven's Cash album as a walk through the last stations of the Man in Black with vagabonds and the forgotten, recorded in Beirut; the polish occasionally grates. Rating: 6/10.
inhalt: Oliver Ding reviews *Elegy for Johnny Cash* (Cooking Vinyl/Indigo, released 12 September 2005) under the headline "Schwarzer Anzug" ("Black suit"). Leven, he says, has one of those voices in which you can hear life: the scars, the pain his larynx had to endure when he was almost strangled in a street attack in the mid-eighties and lost not just his voice for a time. But self-destruction turned into respect, despair into hope, and Leven into "one of Scotland's most profound musicians".

The famous albums on American Recordings made Leven a Cash fan. For this record he walks, with his own views, the last stations of the great Man in Black. The morbid title track links a pleasant shiver with strings resigned to fate ("I'm a real gone man"), short, concise, laconic. Elsewhere, too, a kindred spirit accompanies him: exactly two years after Cash's death the Scot revives one of Cash's main narrative threads, lonely vagabonds and resigned figures, outcasts and the forgotten, people who, like him, have the blues and find their lament in the minor key.

Despite all the wistfulness, no heavy burdens weigh on the album, because together one is strong. It was recorded in Beirut during a Roma festival with friends such as the Lebanese percussionist Reza Almieri, the Greek viola player Mixialis Kataxanis and Robert Fisher (Willard Grant Conspiracy), with softly lamenting guitars, whispering drum loops and nasal brass, "without fear of bitter truths, without desire for depression". Only occasionally does the gentle polish grate like a thorn in the ear; the result is "music with one laughing and one crying eye". Listed highlights are "Blue Soul Dark Road", "Elegy for Johnny Cash" and "The Law of the Tide". Rating: 6/10 (readers' average 7/10).

2005-10-01-lofotposten-bla-leven.kurz: A disappointed concert review from Kabelvåg: everything as usual – vodka, beer, guitar, dry quips, flawless singing – yet after barely an hour many left the hall. Perhaps Leven lacked energy after his northern Norway tour.
inhalt: Anki Gerhardsen reviews Leven’s concert at Præstengbrygga in Kabelvåg on Thursday 29 September in Lofotposten (1 October 2005). The headline “Blå Leven” plays on “blue” (sad, but also tipsy). Leven can serve “a whole evening” of guitar, singing and anecdotes, she writes, “we know that from before” – and asks what failed this time at Præstengbrygga.

Everything looked as it has every time the troubadour from Scotland enters the stage in Kabelvåg: a vodka glass and a half-litre of beer on the floor, the guitar resting against his ample belly, his fringe falling over the bridge of his nose, and laid-back quips that made the audience chuckle or roar – at least at first. There was nothing to criticise in the singing: Leven has a fullness in the throat that puts him in the same class as Cornelis Vreeswijk, and with no stage show beyond the lifting of a beer glass he usually keeps people spellbound for a whole evening. The support act, Hot Club de Norvège, had warmed up the audience with first-class string swing, and a packed Brygge was ready for Leven’s oblique look at Norwegians, Britons and existence. Even a long sequence of sound adjustments did not stop people sitting quietly with their ears on stalks.

But after about an hour it was somehow “enough”. A good part of the audience went home or gathered in the smokers’ corner outside. Gerhardsen suggests two reasons: either the jazz fans left once Hot Club de Norvège had finished, or Leven lacked energy after touring northern Norway for a while, “where it has rained for a long time”. He sang “Universal Blue” among others, “yet another of Leven’s yearning songs”; perhaps he was “on the bluest side” on Thursday. The caption sums it up: Leven is a distinctive storyteller in text and tone, but he has had more punch on stage than he had on Thursday.

2005-10-08-firdaposten-elegy-for-johnny-.titel: [Review: Jackie Leven – Elegy for Johnny Cash]
2005-10-08-firdaposten-elegy-for-johnny-.kurz: A longer review in Nynorsk in Firdaposten of *Elegy for Johnny Cash*: recorded in Beirut, no lament for Cash but a tribute to Rick Rubin's sound; “Celtic soul”, more accessible than usual, closer to Doll by Doll than in years.
inhalt: The review in Firdaposten (Florø) of 8 October 2005, written in Nynorsk, begins with a career outline: Leven has made music almost continuously since the early seventies, as or with John St. Field, Doll by Doll, Concrete Bulletproof Invisible, Sir Vincent Lone and under his own name, yet has never had the big breakthrough. In the early eighties the record company tried to make him a pop star, but after a studio session for the planned album he was one late night subjected to blind violence and nearly strangled. His ability to speak and sing vanished, he lost the record deal and followed several years of physical and mental problems from drug and alcohol abuse, until he made a “formidable comeback” in 1994 with the EP “Songs from the Argyll Circle” (as printed) – when Leven was seen for the first time as he has stood ever since.

The biggest surprise of this release is the recording location: of all places Beirut, Lebanon. Those who expected an album coloured by its surroundings will be disappointed, and anyone who assumes from the title that it sounds like Johnny Cash is wrong too. It is “not a lament for Cash” but rather a tribute to the producer Rick Rubin and the sound and mood he achieved on Cash's last records. Musically it is, “as usual”, what Leven calls Celtic soul; he has also been called a Scottish Van Morrison.

Again he has written a handful of songs that will last, but this time he has put it all in a more accessible mode – so that he may now “perhaps get the breakthrough he so absolutely deserves”. And he has probably not been so close to the sound of Doll by Doll since they split. Highlights are “Blue Soul Dark Road” and “King of the Barley”. The review sits under the sub-heading “Skotsk avdeling” (“Scottish department”); author and rating cannot be made out on the page.
zitate_kontext: The reviewer on the character of the album.
The reviewer on the album's sound.

2005-10-16-bergensavisen-bergensblod.titel: […] bergensblod (headline only partly legible in the OCR)
2005-10-16-bergensavisen-bergensblod.kurz: This week Leven was “official Scottish ambassador” in Bergen: on Wednesday (12.10.2005) he appeared as musical guest of the British Week at Galleri Nygaten, for the 60th anniversary of the Norway–Shetland ferry link; in the second set the audience was very drunk, he…
inhalt: This week Leven was “official Scottish ambassador” in Bergen: on Wednesday (12.10.2005) he appeared as musical guest of the British Week at Galleri Nygaten, for the 60th anniversary of the Norway–Shetland ferry link; in the second set the audience was very drunk, and he had to sing the more cheerful songs. On Friday (21.10.) he plays solo at Kamelon, his second Bergen concert of the year. Leven says (self-report) that he never liked Johnny Cash – Cash stood for him for Scottish “rednecks” – until a few years ago he saw the video for “Hurt” in a hotel room in Svolvær; the Rubin albums are fabulous. The title song became the “locomotive” during the recordings in Lebanon as the most positive piece; the release date of 12 September, the second anniversary of Cash's death, is a coincidence. Plans: a Bergen concert with Ian Rankin the following year, a house swap for a week with Frank Nes (Leven and his wife Deborah in Bergen), perhaps a record in Bergen. *Elegy* got a 5 on the dice scale in BA.

2005-10-17-stavanger-aftenblad-leven-lov.kurz: Preview with an interview on Leven's concert at Stavanger's Checkpoint Charlie (the Thursday after publication, so probably 20.10.2005).
inhalt: Preview with an interview on Leven's concert at Stavanger's Checkpoint Charlie (the Thursday after publication, so probably 20.10.2005). The 55-year-old has been very active for ten or eleven years after a long break. Stavanger reminds him of small Scottish towns, and he plans to use the day off after the concert to explore.

At the centre is *Elegy for Johnny Cash* (2005). Leven says the album came about in Beirut: at a music event he met old friends again and got to know Lebanese musicians; rather than bringing them to Scotland, he travelled to Lebanon with the producer. The title came only during the recording. He did not like Cash as a young man; he discovered him only about two years earlier, when he heard “Hurt” on the radio in a hotel in Kabelvåg and fell in love. At the concert he intends to play old, new and unreleased pieces; he thinks his music appeals to all age groups, likes to talk to the audience after concerts and treats pushy fans politely but firmly. The article closes with an overview of the concert week in Stavanger (Zoom finale, Brian McFadden, Dungen and others).

2005-11-11-nrk-no-nordaforr-med-jackie-l.autor: anonymous (NRK; journey and photos: Arne Berg, NRK P2)
2005-11-11-nrk-no-nordaforr-med-jackie-l.kurz: NRK presents “Ukas P2-artist” Jackie Leven: Arne Berg accompanied him to concerts in Tromsø and Kabelvåg and travelled with him on the Hurtigruten, through a landscape that reminds Leven of Scotland and of his childhood.
inhalt: On 11 November 2005, under the title “Nordaførr med Jackie Leven” (“Northwards with Jackie Leven”), the Norwegian broadcaster presents the P2 channel’s artist of the week. The programme runs Monday 14 to Friday 18 November, 9.30 to 10.00 each morning. The strapline: Jackie Leven lived so close to the edge of the abyss that he had to stare down into it to see the reflection of light.

After four records as frontman of Doll By Doll, things went downhill for Leven; with heroin as an aid he tried to medicate his own anxiety. In the end he had to have it out with himself, and succeeded. On the other side of that reckoning waited a very strong run of records, both self-examining and honest yet with a skewed, humorous view of the world and of himself. Throughout he asks the basic question: what does it mean to be human? And not least, what does it mean to be a man?

NRK P2’s Arne Berg has followed Leven’s music for decades, and when he got the chance to accompany him to concerts in Tromsø and Kabelvåg he seized it without hesitation. The journey between the places was made on the Hurtigruten coastal steamer, through a landscape that reminds Leven of his own Scotland and brings back memories of a childhood outside good society. A photograph shows Berg with Leven on board.

2005-11-16-gaesteliste-der-furchtlose-so.kurz: Interview on “Elegy for Johnny Cash” (2005). Leven says that both his parents died the previous year, his father after a long illness at about the time of Cash's death; only through his father's death did he come to Cash's music, and the title song “wrote itself” (self-report).
inhalt: Interview on “Elegy for Johnny Cash” (2005). Leven says that both his parents died the previous year, his father after a long illness at about the time of Cash's death; only through his father's death did he come to Cash's music, and the title song “wrote itself” (self-report). He avoided country for a long time because in his youth in Scotland mainly insufferable “rednecks” listened to it; Michael Weston King showed him the way in. The songs are more about other people, for instance “King of the Barley” (the brooding Scottish pub-goer) and “Vibration White Finger” (occupational disease as a parable). Musically he worked with the sound engineer David Wrench and Lebanese musicians he had met at a festival: the drummer “Reesa” advised using drum machines so that the guitars would have more room, the bassist Mohammed played; “All The Rage” contains a rap section he wrote himself. Robert Fisher (Willard Grant Conspiracy) recites a poem by Gary Snyder and sings “The Law of Tide”; “In Memory of My Mother” is a poem by Patrick Kavanagh, for his mother, who died in October 2004. For the tour with Cosgrave he is considering a Greek viola player and a Norwegian percussionist. Leven's conclusion: he is less afraid today and writes more powerfully, now that both parents are dead.
zitate_kontext: Leven on his development as a songwriter.

2005-11-16-ostlendingen-leven-uten-brak.kurz: Østlendingen reviews *Elegy for Johnny Cash* briefly: a mix of poet and musician who almost always delivers solid work; only partly a tribute album, often dark, sometimes light, with some spoken-word singing. “Leven means it.”
inhalt: The short review in the paper’s new-records column calls Leven a mix of poet and musician who delivers “solid stuff almost always”. The title *Elegy for Johnny Cash* suggests a tribute album to the late Cash, but it is only partly that: Leven sings a bit in Cash style on a couple of tracks, but the songs are his own, as are the musical surroundings, “often lingeringly dark, but actually a little light and pretty in between”.

He uses his distinctive voice partly for deep spoken-word singing, partly in the usual way. In a couple of places he mixes in a little “hip hop light”, somewhat amusing, but no load-bearing element. The lyrics, the poems, are always worth hearing. The conclusion: “Leven mener alvor” – Leven means it.

2005-12-03-kindamuzik-elegy-for-johnny-c.kurz: Maurice Dielemans (KindaMuzik) gives a mixed verdict on *Elegy for Johnny Cash*: the title misleads, the experiments with electronics are admirable, but most tracks lack impact – Leven's voice saves much.
inhalt: In his review of 3 December 2005, Maurice Dielemans picks up from an interview he did with Leven at Crossing Border a good year earlier, when the Scot spoke of an album he wanted to record in the Lebanese capital Beirut. He has now met Leven again and the ambitious project, to which various musicians contributed, has become reality. It has certainly turned out to be “a special CD”.

The title, however, is “somewhat misleading”: music and lyrics “generally have little to do with the late country outlaw”. The only exception is the partly successful title track, in which a galloping cowboy melody and Leven's bone-dry voice pay a modest tribute to Cash's unique personality. Of interest is “The Law of Tide”, written by Leven but sung by Robert Fisher of Willard Grant Conspiracy, plus contributions from Michael Weston King in the carefree “Glad Go Blind” and from the rapper Martin Okasili in a remarkable combination of trip-hop and hip-hop called “All the Rage”.

That Leven opts for “refreshing experiments” earns admiration. “Unfortunately most tracks lack impact”, something that also showed on previous albums, mostly through the length of the pieces and the choice of unusual arrangements. Leven's “penetrating Celtic singing voice”, which balances at uneven heights and is unusual for the genre, fortunately makes up for much. Oddly enough, Dielemans concludes, this CD is not essentially different from other Jackie Leven albums, despite all the new experiments with electronics.

2005-12-12-kindamuzik-jackie-leven-said.kurz: Bart Breman finds the reading and live music of *Jackie Leven Said* (recorded live in 2004 with Ian Rankin) refreshing, but the studio tracks on the second disc “dull, smooth and overproduced”, dangerously close to a “Sky Radio” sound.
inhalt: Bart Breman reviews the double album *Jackie Leven Said* (Cooking Vinyl/Bertus) for the Dutch site KindaMuzik. Usually little makes a live CD exceptional, but Leven fortunately tries to experiment and give the release something special. Most of the double disc has little to do with music; it is mainly spoken. Alongside Leven, the 2004 live recording features the Scottish author Ian Rankin, whose books are found in the “Suspense” section of the bookshop.

On the first CD Rankin reads the story “Jackie Leven Said”, which is about a Scottish family gathering for a funeral. Rankin has a pleasant voice, and his bone-dry humour lightens the rather gloomy story. Between the chapters Leven makes music, sometimes instrumental interludes, sometimes whole songs. The second CD consists of a few new songs by Leven, supplemented by the cover “I Say A Little Prayer” and previously released work.

The two men from East Scotland complement each other well, and the Crossing Border-style approach (where the two performed together) is refreshing. Leven’s music sounds very pleasant live, with a folky approach, just acoustic guitar, keyboards and his slightly raspy voice. It is different with the studio recordings on the second CD: neither the three new songs nor the older work stick; Leven comes fearfully close to a dated Sky Radio sound. At best it is nice, but “dull, smooth and overproduced” are better descriptions.
zitate_kontext: Bart Breman on how Leven and Rankin work together
Breman on the studio tracks of the second CD

2005-chicago-review-press-heylin-from-th.kurz: In the 2005 edition of Clinton Heylin's history of early American punk, Leven is mentioned in connection with David Thomas of Pere Ubu as Britain's “most consistently original singer-songwriter”.
inhalt: In the 2005 edition (first published 1993) of his history of early American punk, *From the Velvets to the Voidoids*, Clinton Heylin mentions Jackie Leven in connection with David Thomas of Pere Ubu, with whom Leven collaborated. The passage apparently describes him as Britain's “most consistently original singer-songwriter”; the beginning of the sentence is cut off in the available extract, so the attribution of the superlative is not wholly certain. Heylin was among Leven's friends.
zitate_kontext: Phrase in Heylin, apparently referring to Leven

2005-folkworld-sir-vincent-lone-songs-fo.kurz: A very short FolkWorld note: Sir Vincent Lone, alias of the “Scottish folkie” Jackie Leven, serves up “electronic pop but minimalist” with a few lovely melodies and provocative titles.
inhalt: The German-language CD review in FolkWorld no. 31 consists of only a few sentences. It covers Sir Vincent Lone's *Songs for Lonely Americans* (Normal Records, RTS 46, 2004, running time 37:26). The “Scottish folkie” Jackie Leven slips into the role of Sir Vincent Lone “to record songs of a different kind for once”.

The reviewer describes the music as served up “electronic pop but minimalist”, with a few lovely melodies and “such sparkling titles” as “War Crimes of Ariel Sharon” and “Balamory Death Chant”. The closing line says that Jackie Leven has “always been a life and soul of the party” (in German, ironically, a “Stimmungskanone”). In Germany the record is distributed by Normal Records and available from Glitterhouse. The tone is friendly and brief.

2005-jackieleven-com-biografie-chronolog.titel: [Biography] Jackie Leven – with “Jackie's Chronological Listening Line from the 1950s to 2005”
2005-jackieleven-com-biografie-chronolog.kurz: The authorised biography on Leven’s website tells his life in the third person – from Roma roots in Fife through Doll by Doll, the assault and the heroin years to Cooking Vinyl – and ends with his “Chronological Listening Line”.
inhalt: The authorised website biography is written in the third person. Leven is born in 1950 “into a Romany (Roma) family”; his father is “Irish Cockney”, his mother comes from Northumberland. He grows up an outsider in Fife, skips school in the glens and hills, and learns about Lightnin’ Hopkins from his blues-loving mother. His first performances are in local bands and at the Elbow Room folk club in Kirkcaldy, where Archie Fisher and Hamish Imlach encourage him; later he is guitarist for Doris Henderson. A gang feud forces him to leave Fife.

Years of wandering follow: four months in the nooks of the South Bank Centre, Kerry, Berlin and Madrid, where *Control* is made in 1971. He squats houses and meets the mentally ill (with a quotation from Roethke). From 1978 to 1982 he leads Doll by Doll with Joe Shaw, David MacIntosh and Robin Spreafico. After a Charisma session he is attacked in 1983; heroin follows, then withdrawal in 1985 and the CORE Trust, which he ran as manager and chairman and to which he is now attached as patron. The biography tells the anecdote of meeting Princess Diana, for whom he sang “The Bonnie Earl Of Moray”.

It continues via Oban and his return with Cooking Vinyl up to *Elegy For Johnny Cash*. At the end stands “Jackie’s Chronological Listening Line from the 1950s to 2005”, a list of formative music from Fifer folk songs to Amy Winehouse and Johnny Cash. The dates for *Control* (1971) and the Doll by Doll years (1978–1982) are the biography’s own.

2005-moors-magazine-elegy-for-johnny-cas.autor: Holly Moors (according to page metadata; editorial account, individual author not stated)
2005-moors-magazine-elegy-for-johnny-cas.kurz: Moors Magazine praises *Elegy for Johnny Cash* in its winter 2005 round-up as Leven in top form: not a Cash album and not world music, but “simply an old-fashioned good Jackie Leven album” that grabs you at once. Four stars.
inhalt: The short review in the “korte recensies” (short reviews) round-up for winter 2005 is headed “Leven in topvorm” (Leven in top form). It recalls that Leven fronted Doll by Doll about 25 years ago, but found his groove only some ten years ago after a black period in his life, and since then has put out a small masterpiece almost every year.

*Elegy for Johnny Cash* wrong-foots the listener several times: it has not turned out Cash-like, even though the title song was written out of admiration for the bare Rubin recordings Cash made at the end of his life, and guest Robert Fisher (of Willard Grant Conspiracy) sings one song entirely in Cash style. And although the album was recorded in Beirut with musicians from Greece, Lebanon, the USA, Scotland, Ireland, Wales and England, it has not become world music, but simply an old-fashioned good Jackie Leven album. That means passionate vocals, special arrangements and gripping songs. A record that grabs you by the scruff of the neck at once and lets go only a good hour later. The rating is four stars, and the last word is “Wereldklasse” (world class).
zitate_kontext: Verdict on how the album should be classed

2006-03-16-mescalina-elegy-for-johnny-ca.kurz: Christian Verzeletti calls Elegy for Johnny Cash not a tribute or covers album but a set of new Leven songs containing a homage to Cash; despite over-busy arrangements it is, he says, "un signor disco".
inhalt: Christian Verzeletti reviewed the album for Mescalina.it on 16 March 2006, a year after its release, "in unsuspicious times", before the Cash film had stirred up the embers of veneration. They arrive only now, he writes, to reaffirm that Leven's records deserve more attention. First he makes clear that *Elegy for Johnny Cash* is not a tribute album, still less a covers album, but a Jackie Leven album of unreleased songs that contain a homage to the great American songwriter.

Cash is evoked in the title track, where Leven's singing immortalises him in the passage from life to death, and in "The Law of the Tide" with the voice of Robert Fisher of Willard Grant Conspiracy; the same spirit runs through "Blue Soul Dark Road" with acoustic guitar and piano. The elegy has a pop matrix but does not sound rhetorical; it fits a "Johnny Cash style", and Leven shows once more that he is a true voice worthy of respect.

As with much of his recent work (Verzeletti cites *Jackie Leven Said* with Ian Rankin and the large-scale *Shining Brother Shining Sister*), the album follows a broader plan: a group of musicians from different backgrounds open up the songs and increase their already notable pop stature, with percussion, synthesisers, accordion and viola coming from Greece and Lebanon, where the album was recorded. At times Leven stuffs the tracks with choruses and keyboards, letting sounds from the 1980s resurface, but the result is still elegant, worthwhile pop. Highlights: "Museum of Childhood", a noble memory of the Sugar Ray Leonard-Roberto Duran fight; "All the Rage", with a rap insert; "Vibration White Finger", pointing a finger at progress; "King of the Barley", reviving the existential discomforts of Kirkcaldy and all of Britain; and the two moving spoken pieces "In Memory of My Mother" and "Why Log Truck Drivers Rise Earlier Than the Students of Zen" ("great title!").

Criticism: something might have worked better with essential arrangements that better showcased the depth of the songs and Leven's singing, but it remains a "signor disco", a fine record. Though few notice, Leven has once more raised his voice for the benefit of humanity. "Johnny Cash would approve."
zitate_kontext: Verzeletti on what the album is

2006-06-20-gaesteliste-solingen-steinenh.kurz: Ullrich Maurer sees Leven and Michael Cosgrave at the Steinenhaus in Solingen on the night of England v Sweden at the World Cup: vocally convincing, but quieter than usual, with stories that seldom reach a punchline.
inhalt: Ullrich Maurer reports on the concert at the Steinenhaus (the “Cornish Pub”) in Solingen, held on the evening of the World Cup match between England and Sweden. Leven greeted the audience with “congratulations on your football match” and pointed to a Swedish flag stuck in his amplifier: they were supporting Sweden. According to Maurer, the Scot would have backed any team playing England. Michael Cosgrave, who played despite being unwell, had his wife text him the state of the match.

A misunderstanding with the promoter Fritz Kappner delayed the start. Leven, whom even good friends describe respectfully as “rather stout”, no longer tries to hide his bulk and simply uses it as a sound box; his voice still stands strong in the room. Compared with other shows, the evening was fairly quiet. Cosgrave, far from his best, kept to unspectacular accompaniment (with some new gimmicks such as Leven's sampled voice) and gave the troubadour room to unfold.

The programme covered his whole career, opening with the current album *Elegy For Johnny Cash*, whose title song was a highlight. Leven promoted the recent Doll by Doll live CD *Revenge Of Memory*, a bootleg of his 1983 album that Virgin shelved, and the CD *Songs For Lonely Americans*, recorded under the name “Saint Vincent Lone” (as Maurer spells it). From it he played “Moscow Train” and told how, on a train journey in Russia, Bob Dylan told him he disliked the Moscow metro because he felt watched there by women with their eyes closed (Leven's account).

Leven's new stories, about one-eyed window cleaners, Swedish toddlers fighting with teddy bears, Germanwings sick bags and airports haunted by the ghosts of dead ticket inspectors, are still amusing, but lead to a punchline less often than before. Musically he and harmony singer Cosgrave nonetheless convinced, also with the familiar songs from “Single Father” and “Cold Mother Of Lonely Fields” to “Classic Northern Diversions”. The verdict: light summer entertainment and an alternative to the World Cup, but both have been seen more brilliant and inspired. England drew 2-2.
zitate_kontext: Maurer on Leven's stories between songs

2006-06-30-reykjavik-grapevine-dancing-p.kurz: In the Reykjavík Grapevine cover interview, Ian Rankin tells how Leven found himself mentioned in a Rebus novel, got in touch and began performing with him, ending in a double CD shelved next to R.E.M.
inhalt: Sveinn Birkir Björnsson interviews Ian Rankin during his visit to Iceland in June 2006. The long conversation covers Rankin's Channel 4 documentary series on evil (he was exorcised in Rome), its influence on his novel *A Question of Blood*, Edinburgh as a setting, and his more political books such as *Fleshmarket Close* and the G8 novel.

The Leven passage comes from a question about Rankin's musical past. He was singer of a new wave punk band, the Dancing Pigs, for about six months; they recorded five tracks and were “pretty bad”. In his novel *Black & Blue* he turned them into a huge band playing a Greenpeace concert. The dream was only realised recently, he says: the Scottish singer-songwriter Jackie Leven read one of his books, saw himself mentioned – Rebus was listening to Jackie Leven – contacted Rankin's publisher and so got in touch. They began giving concerts together, Rankin reading a long short story and Leven performing songs relevant to the theme. It was so successful that they recorded a double CD. Since then Rankin finds himself in the racks at Virgin or HMV beside R.E.M., “such a buzz”: after all those years of being a frustrated rock star, he got a glimpse of what it might be like.
zitate_kontext: Ian Rankin on how the collaboration with Leven began.
Rankin on seeing the double CD *Jackie Leven Said* in record shops.

2006-07-16-bbc-radio-4-desert-island-dis.kurz: In Sue Lawley's Desert Island Discs of 16 July 2006, the crime writer Ian Rankin picks "Linseed Oil" by Jackie Leven (from Jackie Leven Said) as the last of his eight records.
inhalt: The BBC programme page describes the Ian Rankin edition of *Desert Island Discs* (Radio 4, first broadcast Sunday 16 July 2006 at 11:15; repeated Friday 21 July at 9:00; 45 minutes). Sue Lawley's castaway is the award-winning crime writer and creator of the Scottish detective John Rebus, who had featured in 17 novels to date. Born in Fife into a working-class family in a coal-mining town, Rankin, the blurb says, spent most of his childhood trying to "look like he fitted in"; in his bedroom he lived out a fantasy life, writing poems and stories and creating strip cartoons. He admits many parallels with Rebus: they lived at the same Edinburgh address, both are fond of a drink and now even share the same taste in music, though unlike Rebus, Rankin has never smoked. That is about to change, the text adds, since Rebus has reached retirement age and Rankin's next novel will be the last in the series.

The track list ends with Jackie Leven and "Linseed Oil" from *Jackie Leven Said* (Cooking Vinyl), the joint audiobook-and-concert album by Leven and Rankin. Before it come Dave & Ansel Collins ("Double Barrel"), Mogwai ("Rage: Man"), John Martyn ("Solid Air", his favourite track), Joy Division ("Atmosphere"), Van Morrison ("Snow in San Anselmo"), the Rolling Stones ("You Can't Always Get What You Want") and Belle and Sebastian ("The Boy with the Arab Strap"). His book is Anthony Powell's *A Dance to the Music of Time* and his luxury a traditional American pinball machine. The page says nothing about what Rankin says of Leven in the programme; the recording itself was not heard.

2006-08-the-list-fisher-king-leven.kurz: The Festival-issue preview in The List announces the Fringe evening of Robert Fisher, Michael Weston King and Jackie Leven, trading each other’s songs amid “dark perverse humour”.
inhalt: This short preview by Rachel Devine in The List (Edinburgh/Glasgow) announces an “intimate in-the-round show” by three songwriters. Musical collaborations, it says, are often more for the benefit of the artists than their audiences, but fans of narrative songwriting of the folk-country variety will appreciate the coming together of Fisher, King and Leven.

The three are described as a “triumvirate of pioneers in their respective fields” and old friends and playmates. Robert Fisher is the “rotund leading light” of The Willard Grant Conspiracy, the Americana collective that gravitates to the Californian desert on his say-so, recording epic, gothic tales of whisky and woe. Michael Weston King is best known as lead singer and songwriter of the British alt.country band The Good Sons, often regarded as the first of their breed; lately he has been pursuing a more musically expansive solo career, and his new album *A New Kind of Loneliness* was produced by Leven, here described as “Fife folk maverick and former punk”.

The three will trade each other’s songs in a show that, according to Weston King, will be full of “dark perverse humour, song and stories, maybe some poetry”. Details: Underbelly, 12 August, 9pm, £14.
zitate_kontext: The List on Leven’s role on Michael Weston King’s album
The List on the evening’s programme

2006-09-08-gaesteliste-sir-vincent-lone-.kurz: A short review: Sir Vincent Lone is a kind of “Jackie Light”, less opulent than Leven's Highland folk but built on concrete, partly political stories, the best being “Moscow Train” with its Dylan anecdote.
inhalt: Gaesteliste.de introduces Sir Vincent Lone as an alter ego of the Scottish songwriter Jackie Leven. As Leven tells it at his concerts, he realised one day that he had written more songs than he could release, not least because nowadays you cannot put out as many records as you like but must submit to the “saturation laws” of the market. So he hit on the idea of releasing the surplus under another name. He then torpedoes this, the reviewer notes, by appearing on the cover, unlike on his Jackie Leven albums: “Well, Jackie is a little eccentric.”

Musically, what Leven does with his “partner in crime” Michael Cosgrave is a sort of “Jackie Light”. In harmonic progressions and guitar playing the songs recall his Highland folk of recent years but are less opulent. The lyrics differ: they are not about poetry and dream interpretation but about stories sparked by concrete moments, some of them political. The best story lies behind the opener “Moscow Train”. On a train journey, Leven (pardon, Sir Vincent) says he met Bob Dylan, and they agreed there was nothing lovelier than trains. Only one train did Dylan dislike, the “Moscow Train”, which turns out to be the Moscow metro, because a woman with her eyes closed had been watching him there. The album is released on Cooking Vinyl/Indigo.
zitate_kontext: The reviewer on the lyrics of Sir Vincent Lone
The reviewer on the album's sound

2006-09-08-the-independent-album-sir-vin.kurz: Andy Gill finds Sir Vincent Lone’s (Jackie Leven’s) *Songs for Lonely Americans* most convincing in the familiar Caledonian folk-rock manner; the hip-hop and techno-pop experiments work less well.
inhalt: In The Independent of 8 September 2006, Andy Gill reviews *Songs for Lonely Americans* (Cooking Vinyl) by Sir Vincent Lone. The name is a pseudonym of Jackie Leven, intended as a means by which “this most prolific of songwriters” might release more than his usual complement of poetic insights and laments. It is particularly apt on a collection of reflections on solitude, romantic yearning, the death of illusions and the faltering grasp of dreams.

Mostly Leven delivers these in his usual Caledonian folk-rock manner, with organ or melodica underscoring his guitar. The exceptions are ‘Moscow Train’, on which he experiments with hip-hop techniques, and ‘Straight Outta Caledonia’, whose eighties techno-pop recalls Scots bands from Skids to Simple Minds. Neither is as effective as the troubadour style in which he articulates sentiments such as the haunted recollection of love in ‘The Lights Below’, from which Gill quotes lines. For download he recommends ‘The Lights Below’, ‘Revenge of Memory’, ‘In Search of Stone’ and ‘Balamory Death Chant’.
zitate_kontext: Gill on Leven’s hip-hop and techno-pop experiments
Lines from ‘The Lights Below’ quoted by Gill

2006-09-11-musicomh-sir-vincent-lone-son.kurz: A three-star review of Sir Vincent Lone’s *Songs for Lonely Americans*: the alias lets Leven experiment with 1960s American folk; beautiful fragments but little shape – “a restless ragbag of fascinating scraps”.
inhalt: Fiona Jerome reviews for musicOMH (11 September 2006) the first album by Sir Vincent Lone, alter ego of the “former Doll By Doll frontman, and longtime singer-songwriter” Jackie Leven, and awards three stars out of five. Doll By Doll fans will tell you the band were chronically overlooked in the melee that was punk – intelligent commentators whose voice was drowned out by the louts. This album, if it can be said to have a coherent thread, explores Leven’s relationship with the American folk music of the sixties.

Taking on another persona allows many performers to escape their reputations and expectations. In Leven’s case, according to him, it came from the simple fact that he was writing a lot of material and found waiting to release it as Jackie Leven albums frustrating “because I am a writer of genius”. He is a writer of wryness too, as in “Straight Outta Caledonia”, a kitsch, cornily produced tribute to “My land of songs… songs of sorrow, songs of night”. The new persona lets him try on different musical styles and simplify tunes and settings so the words come to the fore; several pieces are rambling, Dylanesque poems, moments of sensation.

Examples: the opener “Moscow Train”, apparently inspired by a conversation with Bob Dylan about the Moscow underground, lies uneasily over a simple electronic beat; fragments of synthesised voice add to the cold, mechanical feel. “The Lights Below” offers just voice and guitar, Leven’s faintly Scottish, faintly American twang purring then rising sharply, little pinpricks reminding you this is not an album of nice, soft songs. “The War Crimes of Ariel Sharon” shows the politician taking phone calls on the toilet and picking his nose, transported to a childhood moment, described in beatific language, at which he becomes capable of terrible things. The most effective use of traditional overtones is “In Search Of Stone”, about people who have disappeared, presumed dead.

Each song requires dedicated listening; the delivery is not showy, the phrasing careful but rarely inspired, most tunes direct and repetitive. The freedom to do anything is, in its way, the album’s undoing: it has little shape and tails off towards the end. Everything is at least interesting, sometimes sweet, sometimes unsettling, but it jumps from one mood to another relentlessly – “a restless ragbag of fascinating scraps”.
zitate_kontext: Fiona Jerome on Doll by Doll
Leven on the reason for the alias, quoted by Jerome

2006-09-musikexpress-sir-vincent-lone-so.kurz: Peter Felkel retells in Musikexpress Leven’s account of how the pseudonym Sir Vincent Lone came about and judges that the debut sounds “exactly like Jackie himself”: “Moscow Train” is a hit, the Sharon protest song grates, and little is added to the Leven cosmos.
inhalt: Peter Felkel opens his review with Leven’s story, which seems to him far too good not to tell. Two years ago, Leven says, he realised he was writing many more songs than he could ever record and release, especially nowadays when one brings out a studio album only every 18 months. Being a brilliant writer, he found that annoying, so he went to Martin Goldschmidt, the boss of his label, to ask whether he could make more records. Goldschmidt said no. Leven pointed to the Beatles, who released four albums in a year without anyone saying it was too much. Goldschmidt replied: “Jackie, it’s not 1967 any more, and you’re not the Beatles.” At that moment, Felkel writes, Sir Vincent Lone was born, Leven’s alter ego.

The debut *Songs for Lonely Americans* sounds, “surprise!”, exactly like Jackie himself: again that fairly unique mix of pop and poetry, folk and soul familiar from *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West*, *Fairytales for Hard Men* and the other “lovely” Leven albums. The opener “Moscow Train” is a typical heart-storming song, folk underlaid with a kind of hip-hop beat and synth hiss. The protest song “The War Crimes of Ariel Sharon”, by contrast, grates by the second listen, “Straight Outta Caledonia” could easily have come from “a dud like Chris de Burgh”, the spooky “Balamory Death Chant” sounds like a Gregorian chant, and the remaining songs shimmer in quiet acoustic-guitar splendour and enchant with fine melodies.
Verdict: Sir Vincent Lone cannot add all that much memorable to “Master Leven’s” sound cosmos. Release date: 8 September 2006. (Other sources tell the origin of the pseudonym differently.)
zitate_kontext: Martin Goldschmidt, as relayed by Leven
Leven on his surplus of songs

2006-10-10-drammens-tidende-mer-politisk.kurz: Johnny Andreassen reviews Sir Vincent Lone's *Songs for Lonely Americans*: the familiar vocal splendour with a more political tongue, essential for fans but more everyday and less special than much of Leven's work.
inhalt: Drammens Tidende gives a short review of Sir Vincent Lone's *Songs for Lonely Americans* (Cooking Vinyl, in Norway via Bonnier Amigo), the pseudonym under which Jackie Leven releases this material. Johnny Andreassen hears the Scot's well-known vocal splendour, but with a tongue “moistened by a little more politics” than his usual descriptions. The singer-songwriter sings about “The War Crimes Of Ariel Sharon” and “(I've Never Known) Peace On Earth”.

The album is “essential listening” if you are lucky enough to have become a Jackie Leven fan, though it is also more everyday and not as special as much of his other work. Andreassen picks out “Revenge Of Memory” and “Balamory Death Chant” as moments to note. He closes by addressing the “many Drammen people” who have discovered Leven: for them this is a record that completes the picture of the great Scottish artist. The verdict is kind but not euphoric.
zitate_kontext: Johnny Andreassen on *Songs for Lonely Americans*

2006-12-12-plattentests-forum-jackie-lev.kurz: A Plattentests.de forum thread (2006 to 2014): fans praise *The Mystery of Love* and Leven's live shows, find later albums weaker, and after his death post tributes.
inhalt: The thread “Jackie Leven” on the Plattentests.de forum starts on 12 December 2006 with a user calling Leven a “timeless Scottish songwriter”, *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* a masterpiece and “live the man is a bomb”. Another agrees and remembers an “unforgettable evening” at Cologne's Gloria, where Leven played with Richard Thompson and Midnight Choir. A user describes the man sitting on stage “powerfully stocky with a double chin and Bermuda shirts”, a “completely natural presence beyond vanity”, and a gifted entertainer too; you can feel that he has seen a lot of life. *Elegy for Johnny Cash*, by contrast, had not convinced.

In February 2007 a user spots Leven shopping in central Cologne, which prompts speculation about a promo trip. The Plattentests reviewer Oliver Ding finds the then-new album weak: the only really good song is a cover, though Leven has at least turned “I've Been Everywhere” into a “smart German impression”. Another user misses songs of the quality of “Working Alone”, “Gylen” or “The Garden”. In 2009 a user digs out *Defending Ancient Springs* again and finds it a lovely album.

On 15 November 2011 Oliver Ding reports the death, quoting a news site's teaser: “Booze, madness and longing: in the tradition of Johnny Cash the Scottish songwriter sang of self-destruction.” Tributes follow: for one user *The Mystery of Love* and *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West* were milestones that led him to folk music; “Working Alone” and “Gylen Gylen” are “such incredibly sad songs”, and “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” has the “fantastic soul chorus”. In March 2012 a user writes that it is “as if you had lost a very good friend”; being able to see his concerts was a privilege.
zitate_kontext: Forum user “Schäbiger Wurzelsepp” on Leven's stage presence (2006)
Forum user “Don Berger” after Leven's death (2012)

2006-black-and-white-kielty-big-noise.kurz: In Martin Kielty’s oral history of Scottish pop, two contributors mention Jackie Leven: once as someone who helped clear another band’s gear off stage, once for a “brilliant” version of “I’d Rather Go Blind”.
inhalt: *Big Noise: The Sound of Scotland* (Black & White Publishing, Edinburgh, 2006) by Martin Kielty is an oral history of Scottish pop music. Two contributors’ recollections mention Leven: in one, “Doll By Doll’s Jackie Leven” helped get another band’s equipment off the stage; in the other, an evening is remembered at which Leven sang a “brilliant” version of “I’d Rather Go Blind” alongside Clare Grogan. Who is remembering in each case and on what occasion is not known.

2006-cookin-cookin-scottish-musicians-re.titel: Cookin' (cookbook with recipes by musicians and authors)
2006-cookin-cookin-scottish-musicians-re.kurz: In the Edinburgh cookbook *Cookin’*, with contributions from musicians and writers, Leven offers the recipe “Leven’s Paxiot Evening Lamb”, a Greek lamb dish named after the island of Paxos.
inhalt: This Edinburgh cookbook (2006) collects recipes from musicians and writers, among them Boo Hewerdine, Brian Kellock and Colin MacIntyre. Jackie Leven contributes a recipe of his own, “Leven’s Paxiot Evening Lamb”, a Greek lamb dish named after the island of Paxos, where a memorial bench to him now stands.

In another contribution, apparently by Ian Rankin, the author recounts that Leven got in touch after finding himself mentioned in one of his novels. Whether the book served a charitable purpose is not established.
