2006-orion-rankin-the-naming-of-the-dead.kurz: In *The Naming of the Dead*, John Rebus thinks of a few lines from a Leven song about a small boat and a huge sea.
inhalt: In Rankin's Rebus novel (Orion, 2006), Rebus recalls a few lines from a Jackie Leven song about a small boat on a huge sea; the lines are quoted in the book as song lyrics and are not reproduced here. Which song is meant is unclear. The imagery recalls the old Breton fishermen's prayer. The Dutch edition, *Gedenk de doden* (2007), has the same passage.

2006-trafford-barrow-how-not-to-make-it-.kurz: In a self-published musician's memoir the author recalls bands he came across, among them “Doll by Doll, a band fronted by Jackie Leven”.
inhalt: The self-published memoir *How NOT to Make It in the Pop World (Diary of an Almost Has-Been)* (Trafford Publishing, 2006) mentions, in a band or rehearsal-room context, musicians including a band with hits in the early 1970s and “Doll by Doll, a band fronted by Jackie Leven”. The author describes his own rehearsals as chaotic. The text offers little beyond this mention by name.

2007-02-04-bbc-radio-2-johnnie-walker-sh.titel: [Jackie Leven on the Johnnie Walker Show, BBC Radio 2, 04.02.2007]
2007-02-04-bbc-radio-2-johnnie-walker-sh.kurz: Jackie Leven was a guest on Johnnie Walker’s Sunday show on BBC Radio 2 on 4 February 2007, two weeks before the release of *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!*. Only the existence of the recording is documented, not its content.
inhalt: On 4 February 2007 Jackie Leven appeared on Johnnie Walker’s Sunday programme on BBC Radio 2, two weeks before his album *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!* came out on 19 February 2007. A fan site offered the programme as a “listen again” podcast at the time; the MP3 file, about 19.7 megabytes, survives in the Internet Archive in captures from 2007 and 2021.

What was said or played on the show is not documented. The recording documents that Leven was a guest on one of Britain’s biggest stations shortly before the release. The fan site spells the presenter’s name “Johnny Walker”.

2007-02-12-rockol-jackie-leven-oh-what-a.kurz: A short album presentation on Rockol (Italy) for *Oh What A Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!*: eleven folk-rock tracks with Johnny Dowd and Leon Hunt as guests, plus the track list; hardly any verdict.
inhalt: The Italian music site Rockol lists *Oh What A Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!* in its album-review section (12 February 2007). According to the available rendering of the page, it is a brief introduction with a track list: the album contains eleven tracks between folk and rock, with the Texan Johnny Dowd and Leon Hunt named as guests. The visible text contains no actual rating or extended review.
Direct access to the page was blocked (HTTP 403), so it could not be read in the original here; the block was not circumvented.

2007-02-16-gaesteliste-oh-what-a-blow-th.kurz: Ullrich Maurer calls Oh What A Blow That Phantom Dealt Me not revolutionary but a typical, classic Leven album, with Johnny Dowd, a tribute to Kevin Coyne and the funny "I've Been Everywhere".
inhalt: Writing for Gaesteliste.de (16 February 2007), Ullrich Maurer says one should not expect anything revolutionary from the old master Jackie Leven, in recent years one of the most consistent of his kind, yet he manages on every record to bring out new facets of himself.

This time he worked with Johnny Dowd, who is, on a certain level, a kindred spirit, and wrote a tribute to the late Kevin Coyne, whom he always revered as a fellow artist. He also surprises with a good pinch of blues in his guitar playing and serves up the little-known poet Kenneth Patchen, continuing his tireless campaign to bring poetry into music. "I've Been Everywhere", a hair-raising string of the venues Leven usually plays on tour, is one of his funniest songs yet; normally he keeps his musical escapades clearly apart from his clowning.
The album, which also deals with the Scots' favourite pastime, drinking, turns out in the end to be another fairly typical, classic Leven work. Released on Cooking Vinyl/Indigo.

2007-02-16-the-independent-album-jackie-.kurz: Andy Gill, in The Independent, calls Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me! an album of tortured regret spiked with gallows humour, recommending "Vox Humana", "Kings of Infinite Space" and "One Man One Guitar".
inhalt: Andy Gill reviews the album in The Independent of 16 February 2007 (Cooking Vinyl). Like Nico, he says, Leven draws on literary sources for his album titles; the title, derived from Don Quixote, captures the "tortured regret and spiritual deprivation" that lurk behind his work. Unlike Nico, though, a sense of gallows humour at times spikes his melancholy. As evidence Gill quotes "Vox Humana": "I was thinking whisky as I ordered gin / It was a wise decision, and I'd do it again", followed by the darker line "But there's a lonely Scotsman crawling under my skin."

The sense of wretched solitude in songs like "Another Man's Rain" and "One Man One Guitar" is realised in a variety of settings, from the mellow Caledonian soul of "Kings of Infinite Space" to the bluesy folk-rock of "Childish Blues" and "Silver in Her Crucifix", a tribute to the late singer-songwriter Judee Sill. The equally downbeat Johnny Dowd turns up in a couple of tracks to intensify the desolation, but the weirdest piece is the version of the Rolf Harris novelty "I've Been Everywhere", adapted to a journey across Germany. Download picks: "Vox Humana", "Kings of Infinite Space", "One Man One Guitar". The text gives no readable star rating.
zitate_kontext: Leven in "Vox Humana", quoted by Gill

2007-02-19-musicomh-oh-what-a-blow-that-.kurz: Barnaby Smith (musicOMH, 3 out of 5 stars) hears a gruff, boozy, self-deprecating album about ageing in *Oh What A Blow That Phantom Dealt Me*, compared to Bob Dylan's *Modern Times*; Johnny Dowd's guest spots add a gothic touch.
inhalt: Barnaby Smith opens his review (19 February 2007, Cooking Vinyl) with a confession: for years he thought Jackie Leven was a woman, until he saw him in concert – a “large, unkempt, slightly brutish” figure. On the biography he writes that Leven began in the sixties as John St Field, then formed Doll by Doll (wrongly called a punk band that lasted four years), was attacked unprovoked in the street in 1984 and nearly strangled, was unable to speak for two years and became addicted to heroin; he regrouped in 1994 and has since released over a score of albums.

The new album is “gruff, boozy with a hint of utter tragedy”, yet self-deprecating and charmingly confused. Its determination and cheekiness invite comparison with Bob Dylan's *Modern Times*; both know their vocals are pretty shot and use that to bemoan and crystallise the tragedy of getting old, the theme of many songs. The slow road to death seems to be taken lightly, but it is only after a few listens that one is fully impressed by the album's gravitas. “Kings of Infinite Space” addresses the build-up of tumultuous memories in dotage, a song John Martyn might have recorded early in his career, with horns, smooth(ish) vocals and a startlingly simple and sweet melody. Much is typical of an English folk artist – ambiguous, introspective odes to a remote sweetheart (“The Silver in Her Crucifix”) and gloomy lines like those in “Childish Blues”: “Lonely on my own with the news, blues and reviews.”

The special ingredient is Johnny Dowd, the Texan whom Smith calls “a proper genius”. Leven enlists him for backing vocals on a couple of tracks and a spoken narrative on “The Skaters”; Dowd adds a gothic mood that is cinematic and uniquely American. “Vox Humana” and “One Man One Guitar” are, Smith says, masterpieces, telling tales of drifters and travellers with a common perspective on loneliness in a desolate landscape, from two men from “the dustbowls of Fife and Ithaca”.
zitate_kontext: Smith on Johnny Dowd's guest appearances.

2007-02-26-kindamuzik-oh-what-a-blow-tha.kurz: Peer Bataille takes up the ghost motif of *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!*: stylistically unclassifiable, with Johnny Dowd and Michael Cosgrave, mixed in effect – “sometimes you start, sometimes it doesn't do much for you”.
inhalt: Peer Bataille reviews *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!* (Cooking Vinyl/Bertus) on KindaMuzik (26 February 2007), taking up the phantom motif of the title. The inlay warns: “These songs may contain phantoms”. The booklet attributes the title to Don Quixote, which may be a red herring; it credits the line “What kind of fuckery is this?” to Amy Winehouse. The characters in Leven's songs seem to wonder where they have landed this time, and the listener, too, is regularly gripped by an uneasy feeling at the creaking doors, rasping bells and cawing crows.

In the “beautifully dark” opener “Vox Humana” a “lonely Scotsman” (Leven's alter ego?) sits drinking at the bar; “Another Man's Rain” takes its protagonist fifty fathoms deep through the ocean to Norway, and “I've Been Everywhere”, known from Johnny Cash, becomes a tour of Germany with Johnny Dowd as engine driver and tour guide. Dowd also adds his characteristic second voice to “One Man One Guitar” and reads Kenneth Patchen's sinister poem “The Skaters”. Besides him, English banjo player Leon Hunt and above all multi-instrumentalist Michael Cosgrave leave their mark, Cosgrave creating vague sounds that make you wonder where they come from.

Musically the album cannot be pigeonholed: Leven's ghosts feel equally at home in a singer-songwriter song (“Another Man's Rain”), a Bacharach-and-David-like ballad (“Kings of Infinite Space”), an acoustic blues (“Childish Blues”), a folk song (“The Silver in Her Crucifix”, an ode to Judee Sill) and a drum machine (“Here Come The Urban Ravens”, a tribute to Kevin Coyne). The conclusion is undecided: Leven's ghosts unsettle you again and again; sometimes you are startled, sometimes it doesn't do that much for you.
zitate_kontext: Bataille on the album's stylistic range.

2007-02-musikexpress-oh-what-a-blow-that.kurz: Peter Felkel hails Oh What A Blow That Phantom Dealt Me! in Musikexpress as the work of a drinker and bard, sinner and saint, with highlights such as "Kings of Infinite Space" and the Kevin Coyne requiem.
inhalt: Peter Felkel reviews the album in Musikexpress (February 2007). He opens with a character sketch: Jackie Leven is a "drinker and bard, sinner and saint, fool and sage", someone who abhors well-trodden paths and prefers to cut cross-country through his life and art. That he has given us, over the past decade and a half (and some years earlier with Doll by Doll), a stream of enchanting songs drawing on folk, soul, gospel, blues and pop, which breathe "the spirit of a smoky harbour pub as well as the vastness of the sky over the Highlands", is to be stated once more, he writes, and it is just as true of this album. Leven sings "as if at least his life depended on it" and tells stories of rain, guitars and pubs, friendship, childhood and being on the road.

"I've Been Everywhere" is a tongue-in-cheek rockabilly in which Jackie and his partner in crime Johnny Dowd toss city names back and forth like balls - Berlin, Dresden, Düsseldorf, even Schweinfurt and two dozen more. It is fun, but the highlights lie elsewhere: "Kings of Infinite Space", a song of a kind Van Morrison has not written for some years; the heart-wrenchingly beautiful "The Silver in Her Crucifix", a homage to the long-dead folk singer Judee Sill; and "Here Come the Urban Ravens", a moving requiem for the late, great Kevin Coyne, in which Dowd recites a poem by Kenneth Patchen ("The Skaters"), a banjo plinks and a blues harp sighs through the soundscapes gently woven by the multi-instrumentalist Michael Cosgrove (printed "Cosgrove" in the issue). At the end, in "Mellow My Madness", the singer seems to dissolve into thin air, just like the beings the cover warns about: "These songs may contain phantoms". Closing line: "Rave on, Jackie, rave on, you holy fool."
zitate_kontext: Felkel on a highlight of the album

2007-03-02-nojesguiden-jackie-leven.kurz: Patrik Forshage introduces Leven in Nöjesguiden as an overlooked Scottish songwriter, praising his quiet voice, his detail-sharp lyrics and his guests (Johnny Dowd), and concludes that this time there is no excuse for ignoring him.
inhalt: The short review of 2 March 2007 opens with a reproach to readers: if you do not know Jackie Leven, you have only yourself to blame. He made his first record as a Fife folk singer thirty years before James Yorkston and King Creosote and led the “excellent punk band” Doll by Doll in the late Seventies, whose catalogue is to be reissued the following month. He should have been in everyone's mind, had an unprovoked street attack in 1983 not left him mute for two years and then led him into heroin addiction.

Rehabilitated for a good ten years now, he has worked his way, with an endless stream of fine singer-songwriter albums, to something like the status of Scottish national hero. He still has a “lonely Scotsman crawling under my skin”, but his quiet singing voice takes him much closer to a master like Warren Zevon than to his local colleagues. The same reference applies to the “over-clever” sharpness of detail in his lyrics, for instance when he discovers he is standing in a working-class gay bar in Hamburg, drinking ice-cold beer, while men talk quietly to each other (“how did I get here?”).

As usual he bows humbly to his idols, this time Judee Sill and Kevin Coyne, and keeps seeking out exciting collaborators. Johnny Dowd contributes a rasp to the murder story “Skaters”, the dark and charming demo blues “One Man One Guitar” and a “hysterically funny German geography lesson” in Rolf Harris's “I've Been Everywhere” (the song was in fact written by Geoff Mack; Harris made it famous). The album title is not given in the text; from the date and the guests it is probably *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!*. The closing line: this time there is no excuse for passing Jackie Leven by, though there never was before either.
zitate_kontext: Forshage on Leven's path after heroin

2007-03-02-rolling-stone-de-oh-what-a-bl.kurz: Rolling Stone (German edition) on *Oh What A Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!*: a too cosy sequel, “preaching to the converted”; Johnny Dowd, the Judee Sill tribute and “I've Been Everywhere” add variety – the “iron man” has gathered a little rust.
inhalt: The review in the German edition of Rolling Stone, 2 March 2007, opens with a picture: the “gnarled Scot” sits in the bar, knocks one back and watches others do the same, then spins his “flaming yarns”, which he retells on ever new records. For Leven a bar is a gathering place for the stranded and outcast, for ghosts and the driven – just as Leven himself shook off his “merciless demons” only late.

The verdict on the “roughly 23rd album” is mixed: it partly suffers from being an “all too cosy sequel” to the last three or four LPs. The opener “Vox Humana” sounds compositionally like Leven's “building-block principle” and, along with the familiar folk instrumentation, gathers the obligatory keywords (whisky, bar, barman's wife, lonely Scotsman). Fans will be pleased, but it will hardly win new listeners – “Preaching to the converted”. Some variety comes from Johnny Dowd, whom Leven “acquired” over a shared bottle of absinthe: skilful growling into the “successful blues” “One Man One Guitar” and a seven-minute recitation of Kenneth Patchen's poem “The Skaters”. Perhaps Dowd should also have produced a song or two.

Where Leven paid tribute to Johnny Cash on the last LP, this time there is a “tender homage” to Judee Sill (“The Silver in Her Crucifix”, “absolutely successful”) and a song for the late Kevin Coyne (“Here Come the Urban Ravens”, “well meant”). He cultivates his life as a “notorious drifter” who plays a gig in every little pub in the opener “I've Been Everywhere”: the list of German towns he has played is rounded off by the enthusiastic repetition of “Baden-Baden” in the chorus – “What fun!” The conclusion: the “likeable iron man” has gathered a little rust through too frequent recitation of his own works; he should prefer the peace and purity of the Scottish woods to the fusty air of dives again, where at nightfall the myths will soon be felt that supply the material for the next stories.
zitate_kontext: The reviewer on Leven's world of bars.

2007-03-10-bbc-radio-4-loose-ends.kurz: The BBC programme page for “Loose Ends” of 10 March 2007 names no guests; the episode is no longer available, but a fan site circulated a clip featuring Leven.
inhalt: The BBC Radio 4 programme “Loose Ends”, presented by Ned Sherrin, was broadcast on Saturday 10 March 2007 at 18:15 on FM and ran for 45 minutes. The programme page describes it only generally as an eclectic mix of conversation, comedy and music with Sherrin and guests; it lists no guests, and the episode is currently unavailable. That Leven appeared in this edition is documented by a fan site that offered a short MP3 clip (about 3.9 MB). The clip was not listened to, so it is unknown whether Leven played a song or talked.
zitate_kontext: The programme description on the BBC page

2007-03-10-firdaposten-phantom-punch.kurz: A positive review (in Nynorsk) of *Oh What A Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!*: more blues-based yet “unmistakably Leven”, with lyrics about European tours and tributes to Judee Sill and Kevin Coyne. Plus a note that the Doll by Doll CDs arrive on 26 March.
inhalt: Firdaposten (Florø) reviews the album *Oh What A Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!* on 10 March 2007 under the heading “Phantom punch”, as the successor to the “fine” *Elegy For Johnny Cash* of 2005. This time it was made in somewhat safer surroundings than its predecessor, which was recorded in Beirut of all places – showing that Leven simply does what suits him.

Musically Leven is more blues-based than the reviewer has heard him, mixed with the usual touches of pop, jazz and soul and topped by his voice: “This is unmistakably Leven.” The lyrics are as usual of a quality far above average, dealing with things he experienced on tours around Europe, including a train journey from Oslo to Bergen – not the first time Bergen figures in his lyrics: “I think he likes it there.” He also does not shy away from singing about artists more obscure than himself; this time he pays tribute to Judee Sill and Kevin Coyne. Overall the record stays at the standard one has come to expect.

The reviewer also tells how Leven’s girlfriend, some years ago, wanted to introduce him to the hostess of a rather smart gathering where he was to perform as the Scottish edition of Van Morrison; the answer was, “Who is Van Morrison?” And he recalls talking to Leven after a concert in Førde three years earlier. Asked when the four Doll by Doll albums of the seventies and eighties would come out on CD, Leven joked that the label was probably waiting for him to die so that interest would rise. “But now all four are coming out on 26 March. About time.”
zitate_kontext: The reviewer on the album’s sound
The hostess’s reply when Leven’s girlfriend introduced him as the Scottish Van Morrison

2007-03-the-list-5-reasons-to-go-see-jac.kurz: Doug Johnstone introduces Leven in The List with five tongue-in-cheek reasons to see his King Tut's gig in Glasgow on 24 March 2007: underground legend, charity worker, Diana anecdote, Ian Rankin fan and “Fife's answer to Bob Dylan”.
inhalt: The preview in the Glasgow and Edinburgh listings magazine is built as a list of five “reasons” and promotes the show at King Tut's on Saturday 24 March (2007) for the new album *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!* (Cooking Vinyl). First, the 56-year-old singer-songwriter from Fife is an “underground legend” who has spent a lifetime on the periphery of various scenes and genres but has influenced generations; his 1971 debut *Control* is considered a psychedelic folk classic, and his more than two dozen albums since have ranged from punk and blues to hip hop and Americana.

Second, he does a lot of good work for charity: in the Eighties he lost his voice for two years after being strangled in a random attack, slumped into heroin addiction, and eventually cured himself through acupuncture and psychic healing; out of this came the CORE Trust, which helps drug addicts by holistic methods. Third, he once had a set-to with Princess Di, whom he met through the CORE Trust: she said she understood he used to be a singer, he curtly replied that he was a singer, and so she made him sing something on the spot. Records do not state whether they then went on to a karaoke bar together, jokes Johnstone.

Fourth, Ian Rankin is a big fan, so much so that two years earlier Leven released *Jackie Leven Said*, an album of collaborations with the crime writer and fellow Fifer. Fifth, he is “Fife's answer to Bob Dylan”, and the piece asks why we never appreciate what is on our doorstep while a “mumbling tousle-haired oaf” from across the pond gets all the plaudits. The Diana story is Leven's own telling, merely passed on by Johnstone.
zitate_kontext: Johnstone relaying Leven's meeting with Princess Diana
Johnstone's fifth reason: “Fife's answer to Bob Dylan”

2007-04-05-musicomh-jackie-leven-troubad.kurz: Fiona Jerome (4 out of 5) finds Leven at London’s Troubadour a thoroughly wonderful evening despite a miserable journey: a deep, modulated voice, stories and guests such as Michael Cosgrave and Deborah Greenwood.
inhalt: Fiona Jerome describes in the online magazine musicOMH a Leven concert at the Troubadour in London on 5 April 2007 (rated 4 out of 5). Everything went wrong: the wrong bus, undercooked food, a murky, cigarette-fugged venue, an unseemly wait after the brief support act. But the moment Leven sang his first line she forgot all of it. He is now a craggy mountain of a man, a strange combination of twitchiness and confidence, mopping his face between numbers and swigging from a bottle, his voice sometimes falling away during the anecdotes. But when he opens his mouth, deep and beautifully modulated vocals come out, and one senses that he feels completely at home.

He warps his voice for “Elegy For Johnny Cash”, in which he imagines the thoughts of the dying country singer, following it with “Museum of Childhood”. Many songs have stories attached: “Here Come The Urban Ravens” was written as a tribute to Kevin Coyne, and “Moscow Train” was inspired by a chance remark of Bob Dylan’s during a shared European train journey. The less folky, more guitar-driven numbers translate surprisingly well to the small venue thanks to Michael Cosgrave on keyboards and Kevin O’Foster accompanying Leven’s acoustic with his electric guitar; they seem livelier, the lyrics crisp, the imagery incandescent.

The gig is not formal – he sings from a four-inch-high stage, waitresses cross in front of him every ten minutes and half the room cannot see. In between songs Leven regaled the audience with impressions, scurrilous stories about Gordon Brown and tales of pedantic train passengers; he would be in demand on the after-dinner speaking circuit, though he might have to tone down some remarks, such as describing Amy Winehouse’s latest album as “the finest Jewish record made in 30 years”. He asks solicitously whether he is playing what the audience wants to hear but refuses to attempt some older material without preparation. From the new album *Oh What A Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!* he played among others the haunting and complex “Vox Humana” and the soulful “Another Man’s Rain”, plus Jackson C. Frank’s “The Blues Run The Game”, which he heard sung at the Troubadour by its author, and, with Deborah Greenwood, the blues classic “Did Somebody Make A Fool Out Of You?”. There were so many highlights that it is impossible to pick favourites; most of the audience would have sat there all night listening to observations, gossip, tall tales and those sublime vocals.

Jerome on the audience and the songs

2007-04-12-the-telegraph-british-rocks-l.kurz: Neil McCormick uses the reissue of all four Doll by Doll albums on Rhino as an occasion to declare “Gypsy Blood” (1979) the lost masterpiece of British rock: sweeping, tipping from the tender to the terrifying, with Leven's voice gliding between baritone and falsetto; he comp…
inhalt: Neil McCormick uses the reissue of all four Doll by Doll albums on Rhino as an occasion to declare “Gypsy Blood” (1979) the lost masterpiece of British rock: sweeping, tipping from the tender to the terrifying, with Leven's voice gliding between baritone and falsetto; he compares the effect with “Dark Side of the Moon”, “Forever Changes” and “The Bends”. The album came out on the small label Automatic to good reviews and dismal sales; the band harmed itself with its belligerent attitude, made many enemies and changed label after the flop. The master tapes were said to be lost, and some reissues were mastered from vinyl. Leven speaks (self-report) about the band as an alliance of traumatised people (Jung quotation on “matching psychic disturbance”), about the aspiration to be the definitive band of its time, and about the self-chosen images that had closed doors. There follow the attack after the band's end (18 months without a voice), heroin, the cure through acupuncture and “psychic healing”, the founding of the Core Trust in 1985 and anecdotes about Princess Diana, who had urged him to sing. Finally: Jo Shaw now builds hi-tech studios (for Mark Knopfler and Paul Allen, among others), David McIntosh is a potter and furniture maker. Verdict: hymnic.

2007-04-22-rocktimes-oh-what-a-blow-that.kurz: Norbert Neugebauer praises *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!* as another strong but more relaxed album by a “quirky Scot”: less fate-laden than its predecessors, with guests such as Johnny Dowd, a good record whose phantoms may yet grow.
inhalt: Norbert Neugebauer calls Jackie Leven, in RockTimes (22 April 2007), “someone special in the singer-songwriter scene, far from the usual strummer guild”. Active since the late 1960s, including as frontman of Doll By Doll, whose four albums are announced for reissue, the multi-instrumentalist has released around a dozen solo albums since 1994; the good half in the reviewer's collection are without exception first-class. The “quirky Scot” of widely branching Celtic descent has been through a lot and you can hear it: his songs are full of sarcasm and irony yet also paintings of astonishing colour, each a small modern epic with poetic imagery about personal demons.

The new album, he says, is by far not as melodramatic and fate-laden as its predecessors; it sounds loose and relaxed, especially in the middle. Neugebauer describes the “phantoms”: one waits in the bar, another rides the tour bus rolling through a dreary dive until it strands in a faceless hotel (“Standing in Another Man's Rain”). On “I've Been Everywhere” Leven lists to a blasé contemporary all the places in Germany he has played. Two dedications go to Judee Sill, who died in 1979 (spelt “Judee Still” in the text), and to Kevin Coyne, who died in 2004; Johnny Dowd (spelt “Johnny Dodd”), whom Leven met over a bottle of absinthe in a bar in Kufstein, gets the sinister narrator's voice in “The Skaters”. The close, “Mellow My Madness” with D.J. Unfit For Work, is rather untypical and somewhat poppy.

The album skilfully varies folk, rockabilly, chanson and blues, always with soulful melodic arcs and creative arrangements; the guest musicians add many facets without overloading the recordings. Leven recorded some vocals in a Ukrainian church and produced with David Wrench. The conclusion: perhaps not his emotionally densest work – the “dark man” seems to be mellowing with age – but undoubtedly a good one whose phantoms may even grow. They hold no fear, however, in pleasant listening.

2007-04-25-die-welt-unglaublich-schoener.kurz: Stefan Krulle describes in Die Welt an “incredibly beautiful, crazy evening” with Leven and Michael Cosgrave at Hamburg’s Knust: a song evening among friends, cabaret and almost frightening songcraft.
inhalt: Stefan Krulle opens in Die Welt of 25 April 2007 with Leven’s first words at the Knust in Hamburg: he would have understood, says Leven, if people in this weather preferred to sit in a café over a cappuccino contemplating “poor old Boris Yeltsin”. Then his partner Michael Cosgrave is in place, Leven mentions the new album *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!* and begins with a song from *Elegy for Johnny Cash* that would have moved the great American to tears.

What follows, Krulle writes, is a rare atmosphere of a “song evening among friends”, absurdly cabaret-like verbal acrobatics and humanities that never turn mawkish: “Monty Python and Bob Dylan in Sezuan, so to speak.” Leven does not peddle his intellectuality; he peddles having remained, despite it, a man for whom fame gladly passes by as long as he does not lose sight of what really matters. In the 56-year-old’s songs the subject is the offbeat; he sings about the meeting of boxers Sugar Ray Leonard and Roberto Durán and explains the song as a “story about how we all at some point just want to go home”. To his warm voice he plays shimmering melodies and mild bass lines at once and proves a songwriter of almost frightening craftsmanship; Cosgrave mixes a cocktail of keyboard sounds and the occasional dull beatbox.

In twelve years Leven has recorded 20 albums, and stories and anecdotes drop at his feet every ten minutes: the gay limousine driver in California’s Napa Valley whom he asks for an ‘ordinary bar’ and, studying his derailed face, clarifies as “a bar you would never go to”; a Hamburg gay bar he stumbled into; women in Moscow metro trains who observe you sharply with their eyes closed; a gig in London before the association of crazy musicians with headliner DJ Unfit For Work, who could not come because he did not feel well. “After so much virtuoso madness without loud bellowing we really only wanted to hug Jackie Leven happily. And that is what we did.” One sentence of Leven’s opening speech is cut off in the online version.
