2007-04-bluesnews-jackie-leven-apner-blu.kurz: Two-page conversation in the Norwegian blues magazine on the occasion of *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!*, conducted while Leven was on a “flying visit” in Oslo to play a sold-out concert at John Dee (March 2007).
inhalt: Two-page conversation in the Norwegian blues magazine on the occasion of *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!*, conducted while Leven was on a “flying visit” in Oslo to play a sold-out concert at John Dee (March 2007). The introduction sums up the legend: Doll by Doll in 1979 as the hottest live band in London's clubs, four acclaimed albums, then the knife attack with his throat slit open, heroin against the pain, the founding of the Core Trust, in which Leven is said to have cured himself, as one of the first patients, with acupuncture and healing treatment. The royal family became patron, and Princess Diana persuaded him on a visit to sing again. In Norway Leven has a very loyal audience; the author calls his music “hvit keltisk soul”.

Leven says (self-report) that his mother constantly listened to black American blues; while other children listened to Elvis, he grew up with Lightnin' Hopkins, favourite piece “Blues in the Bottle”. With the new album he deliberately opened this box and wanted an “unveiled” blues mood; he had always written from a blues heart. “Childish Blues” was meant to sound like Tom Waits and now sounds like Leon Redbone. A lot of modern blues is lazy and meaningless; one has to work the blues into the contexts of today's world. Andreassen praises the guitar playing and the role of Johnny Dowd, who gives the album “Tom Waits darkness”; Leven hints that English critics demanded more collaboration with Dowd. At the same time the Doll by Doll albums appear on CD for the first time. Verdict: very favourable, the author compares the album with Chris Rea's blues box set of the previous year.
zitate_kontext: Leven on his mother's blues records.

2007-04-tmx-kris-needs-night-of-the-psyc.titel: Doll By Doll: Night Of The Psychotic Woodsmen (2007 retrospective)
2007-04-tmx-kris-needs-night-of-the-psyc.medium: tMx (no. 29), republished on the blog Exile on Moan Street (2021)
2007-04-tmx-kris-needs-night-of-the-psyc.kurz: Retrospective by Kris Needs, who as editor of *ZigZag* had championed Doll by Doll in the late seventies.
inhalt: Retrospective by Kris Needs, who as editor of *ZigZag* had championed Doll by Doll in the late seventies. The text is marked as a 2007 piece ("tMx 29 – 04/07") and was republished on the blog *Exile on Moan Street* on 25 May 2021. Needs recalls that the debut *Remember* got miserable reviews on the whole and did not sell. So a music journalist of the time, not only Leven himself, confirms that the debut was mostly received badly by the critics. The retrospective should not be confused with Needs's *ZigZag* article of the same title from March 1979.

2007-05-09-mescalina-oh-what-a-blow-that.kurz: Christian Verzeletti finds *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!* a decent but not outstanding album: dignified songwriting, but without truly strong songs, from an artist who releases too many records.
inhalt: The Italian review opens with an observation on Leven’s way of working: he lives for music “in every sense”, so he releases at least one album a year and does so because he needs to – unlike many others, not merely out of economic necessity. Still, the fact remains that he releases too many records; the quality is above average, but a leaner discography would do him good. The first half of 2007 saw the Doll by Doll reissues and this new studio album.

Leven never lacks ideas, and every release has a reason to exist, even when less successful. So here: eleven songs that are not among his best, but stand on their own with sense and dignity. He reviews a series of forgotten or little-known spirits – certain ‘particular’ characters met on tour, the American songwriter Judee Sill, the rocker Kevin Coyne, the writer Kenneth Patchen – whose presence creates a strong humanitarian echo. As ever he populates the album with many voices: Johnny Dowd (vocals), David Wrench (production, drum engineering), Michael Cosgrave (keyboards) and Leon Hunt (banjo); the booklet carries quotations from Amy Winehouse and Moby Grape to Don Quixote and Judas Iscariot.

The folk at the base of his writing is extended with pop, blues and more modern keyboard touches (plus trumpet, harmonica, pipes and clarinet). Alongside dense ballads there are exercises in 1950s style such as ‘I’ve Been Everywhere’ and riskier ones like ‘The Long Hard Field’, but truly strong pieces are missing. The programme’s intensity fades in the spoken ‘The Skaters’ and in the closing cameo of ‘Mellow My Madness’, inspired by an association campaigning for the mentally ill (with the DJ Unfit For Work). The verdict: sober, rich in human and musical values, but not among his outstanding works – a decent exercise in updating for lovers of good old songwriting.

2007-06-14-kevin-coyne-home-page-whisper.titel: Whispers From The Offing – A Tribute to Kevin Coyne (Comments and Reviews)
2007-06-14-kevin-coyne-home-page-whisper.autor: Pascal Regis (compilation); press and fan voices
2007-06-14-kevin-coyne-home-page-whisper.kurz: Collected comments and reviews of the 2007 Kevin Coyne tribute album *Whispers From The Offing*; Leven contributes “Here Come The Urban Ravens”, the only track that is not a Coyne cover, which several reviewers single out for praise.
inhalt: Pascal Regis’s page collects comments and reviews of the charity CD *Whispers From The Offing – A Tribute to Kevin Coyne* (Life and Living Records, March 2007). Proceeds go to projects run by Life and Living, an organisation working with psychiatric service users at London’s Maudsley Hospital; Coyne had worked as a psychiatric nurse before his music career and died of lung fibrosis in December 2004. Twenty-two performers appear on the album, among them Nikki Sudden, Chris Connelly, Kevin Hewick, Nigel Burch, Heinz Rudolf Kunze and the site owner himself.

Leven’s connection is a song of his own. A review from the Nuremberg city magazine *Plärrer* (five stars, CD of the month, issue 5/2007), reproduced here in English translation, says that the well-known Scottish songwriter Leven dedicated a song to Coyne on his new CD, and that this song is also on the tribute album. A transcribed article from the *Derby Evening Telegraph* (Sarah Whelan, 14 June 2007) names the new song as “Here Come the Urban Ravens” and says it was inspired by Leven’s friendship with Coyne.

Several fan reviews single the track out. One reviewer, who gives the CD five stars out of five, stresses that it is not a Coyne cover but was inspired by him, and that it sounds great; another praises it as a tribute rather than a cover with “great lyrics”; a German listener adds that Leven did a great job as a songwriter. The page also documents other reactions to the album, such as a more reserved three-out-of-six-star rating in *Record Collector* (May 2007) and enthusiasm from participating musicians. About Leven’s song itself it offers nothing beyond these brief verdicts.
zitate_kontext: Translated review from the Nuremberg magazine *Plärrer* of the Coyne tribute CD
Another fan review of the CD

2007-06-uncut-the-stars-that-fame-forgot.kurz: In June 2007 Uncut devoted a retrospective with an interview by Nick Hasted to Doll by Doll in its “The Stars that Fame Forgot” column, to mark the CD reissue; the standfirst calls the band “too dangerous for punk”.
inhalt: The article by Nick Hasted (later the author of The Independent’s obituary of Leven) appeared in the June 2007 issue of Uncut in its column on forgotten stars and accompanied the CD reissue of Doll by Doll. The standfirst calls the band “too dangerous for punk!” and speaks of the “mad, bad story” of Leven’s “Celtic Soul rebels”. The full text of about 750 words is behind a paywall; it is not clear whether Leven himself or other band members were interviewed.
zitate_kontext: Standfirst of the Uncut article on Doll by Doll.

2007-07-23-halden-arbeiderblad-den-store.kurz: Fact profile from a series that festival organiser Tom Skjeklesæther wrote for Halden Arbeiderblad about the artists of Down on the Farm 2007 (Gribsrød gård, Enningdalen near Halden).
inhalt: Fact profile from a series that festival organiser Tom Skjeklesæther wrote for Halden Arbeiderblad about the artists of Down on the Farm 2007 (Gribsrød gård, Enningdalen near Halden). Header with fact box (Fife, born 1950), listening recommendations (*The Mystery of Love*, *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!*, and by Doll by Doll *Gypsy Blood* and *Doll by Doll*, both on CD for the first time in 2007) and jackieleven.com.

The familiar biography is retold: Leven as a troubadour of “classic Celtic soul” alongside Van Morrison; ten years' pause after the dissolution of Doll by Doll (given here as 1984), because at the start of the recordings for his solo debut in London he was said to have been attacked and almost strangled and unable to speak for almost two years; heroin addiction; in 1988 a single with the new band CBI with two Doll by Doll members and Glen Matlock. At the end of the 1980s he is said to have freed himself from heroin with a method he developed himself, which became the basis of the CORE organisation; Leven sits on its board today and received England's highest civil award for CORE. Indirectly Princess Diana brought him back to music: during a CORE visit he struck up an old Scottish song when she asked him.

Important for Norway: Doll by Doll had a strong Norwegian fan base and in 1982 opened the rock club Ratz in Oslo with a sold-out concert, one of the band's last. Since 1994 twelve official solo albums plus fan-club records; collaborations with Robert Bly, Ian Rankin, David Thomas and Johnny Dowd, the last at Down on the Farm in 1998. Leven is said to be known for improvised collaborations on stage and, together with Robyn Hitchcock and John Paul Jones, is to host the new Campfire Stage.

2007-08-01-vaganavisa-jan-age-johansen-h.titel: [Preview: Jan Åge Johansen brings Jackie Leven to Kabelvåg for the sixth time]
2007-08-01-vaganavisa-jan-age-johansen-h.kurz: Våganavisa profiles the promoter Jan Åge Johansen, who is bringing "his favourite artist" Jackie Leven to Præstengbrygga in Kabelvåg for the sixth time on 26 September 2007.
inhalt: The full-page preview (Våganavisa, 1 August 2007) opens by saying that now and then you should treat yourself to something good, so Jan Åge Johansen is fetching his favourite artist to Kabelvåg. "It just went bang," Johansen says of his first Leven experience; on 26 September the Scottish legend gives his sixth concert at Præstengbrygga. Leven, he says, is one of very few artists who can spellbind an audience with just voice, words and a guitar. A former teacher at the local film school told his students after a Leven concert: "To those of you who were at the concert yesterday: I have nothing more to teach you about communication."

A Leven quotation (source not given): "I don't believe I should keep standing up and saying 'I am Jackie Leven and I am addicted to heroin' when I haven't been for 20 years. I believe in the good company in drinking. But I also spend a lot of time sitting quietly at home not drinking." It is less about drinking alone, he says, than about being alone in public places.

Under the sub-heading "Kritiker-favoritt" the piece says Leven is loved by music critics but overlooked by the broad public; record sales are not impressive, but he has a strong name in the business. The NRK journalist Arne Berg introduced him in a 2005 programme: after four records as frontman of Doll by Doll, things went downhill; with heroin as an aid he tried to medicate his own anxiety, until he had to have it out with himself, and succeeded. On the other side awaited a very strong series of records, self-examining and honest but with a skewed, humorous view of the world and himself. Throughout, Leven asks the basic question: what does it mean to be human, and not least, what does it mean to be a man?

Under "Skriver om mannen" a Dagsavisen interview from the same year is quoted: Leven says he is concerned with men who find life becoming indistinct, old experiences drifting ever further apart so that the personality changes while they try to hold on to who they are. People in his songs often have trouble keeping their sanity; he writes about men who think their inner life is a mystery and relate instead to external mysteries. His songs are full of good drink, and he is known for making his own whisky. Johansen will travel to Scotland on 10 October: "I'm a hardcore fan ... I'm going to see Jackie Leven on home ground. It'll be big!" A box gives a short biography (born 18 June 1950) and a discography with some garbled titles.
zitate_kontext: Jan Åge Johansen on his first Leven experience

2007-08-29-record-collector-remember-gyp.kurz: Kris Needs reviews in Record Collector the 2007 Rhino CD editions of all four Doll by Doll albums. The freely visible opening describes the band as a product of the West London squat scene, with psychedelic soul ballads and frighteningly intense live shows.
inhalt: The joint review (issue 336) covers the CD reissues of *Remember*, *Gypsy Blood*, *Doll by Doll* and *Grand Passion* on Rhino. The author is Kris Needs, who had followed the band in ZigZag magazine in 1978–1981.

The freely accessible opening describes Doll by Doll as an offshoot of the West London squat scene, cutting across the punk explosion. The band mixed epic psychedelic soul ballads with cranked-up guitar cacophonies that reached frightening intensity live. After three albums Leven took a more down-to-earth path.
The rest of the text, including the rating, is visible only to registered users and was not accessible.

2007-09-17-puls-jackie-leven-pa-omfatten.kurz: Espen R. Hovelsen announces in the music magazine Puls Leven’s most extensive Norwegian tour so far: 14 concerts from 19 September to 7 October 2007. He recalls that Leven last hosted the Campfire stage at Down on the Farm.
inhalt: The notice of 17 September 2007 introduces Leven as the former Doll by Doll front man who has by now visited Norway more often than most of the other musicians tagged “Norgesvenn” (“friend of Norway”). He is now ready for 14 concerts “in our long-stretched country”.

On his last visit Leven ran the Down on the Farm festival’s new Campfire stage, guiding the audience through a set of his own and others’ performances, including playing together with John Paul Jones, Robyn Hitchcock and William Hut among others. This week he returns for his “by far most extensive Norway tour ever” and perhaps one of the most extensive that a foreign artist has undertaken here for a while.

The dates: 19 Sept Bergen (Madam Felle), 20 Sept Førde (Pikant), 21 Sept Bremanger (Bremanger Kino), 23 Sept Tromsø (Kaos), 26 Sept Kabelvåg (Præstengbrygga), 27 Sept Bodø (Public), 28 Sept Fosen (Stokkøya), 29 Sept Røros (Vertshuset), 30 Sept Trondheim (Credo), 3 Oct Oslo (Kampen Bistro), 4 Oct Drammen (Buddy), 5 Oct Stavanger (Cementen), 6 Oct Skien (Lundetangen Pub), 7 Oct Oslo (Café Mono). This is the announced state of affairs; the notice does not show whether every concert took place.

2007-09-24-drammens-tidende-jackie-pa-bu.kurz: Drammens Tidende announces Leven's "exclusive" concert at Buddy in Drammen on 4 October 2007, by the paper's count his fourth visit to the city, on a tour of 45 concerts.
inhalt: Under the headline "Jackie på Buddy", Drammens Tidende (24 September 2007) reports that the "legendary Scottish singer" Jackie Leven looks forward to seeing Drammen and his many good friends again. By the paper's count it is the fourth time the former Doll by Doll frontman has visited the city; on Thursday 4 October he gives an "exclusive concert" at Buddy. Leven has a large, loyal audience in Drammen and enjoys being there. He is on a larger tour with 45 concerts in total before Christmas in England, Belgium, Germany, Scotland, Sweden and Norway.

The piece calls him one of the most respected artists in Britain; Dagbladet has dubbed him "Scotland's answer to Van Morrison", while he himself admits deep roots in Johnny Cash and Van Morrison. He is a big man with a big voice and enormous stage presence. The article quotes DT reviewer Øyvind R. Gundersen after Leven's concert at the Working Class Hero festival two years earlier: Leven is a poet, a storyteller and a master of the guitar, with enormous variety in his material, from tough songs full of blue notes in which his voice shows itself, through playful jazz numbers and more exotic touches, to classic singer-songwriter art. The author is Bjørn Zarbell-Engh; a photo is captioned "Blå toner" ("Blue notes").

2007-09-bluesnews-oh-what-a-blow-that-ph.kurz: Bluesnews hails *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me* as one of Leven's best albums: more openly bluesy than ever, with Johnny Dowd, homages to Judee Sill and Kevin Coyne, and songs from his Norwegian travels.
inhalt: The review (Bluesnews no. 51, autumn 2007, no author's name apparent) opens by noting that a wind of renewed attention blows around the “old Doll by Doll bandleader” and “master of Scottish Celtic singer-songwriter poetry and white Celtic soul”. The old Doll by Doll albums, which stand “in a context outside everything else”, are being released on CD for the first time. There was plenty of blues feeling in his “restless, gypsy-born soul” even then, but never has the blues nerve been laid so openly bare as on some tracks of the new solo album. It is named after a “historic remark” by Don Quixote when he had to concede defeat in the fight against the windmills, cultivates America's dark roots soul, staged through several guest appearances by Johnny Dowd, and contains much of Leven's classic Celtic melancholy. In England the critics have gone “surprisingly wild”; together with the coming interest in the Doll by Doll records, the “Norway-friend” Leven, who has written five or six songs from his travels in Norway, faces good times.

Singled out is “Another Man's Rain”, based on his experience of the “most beautiful train journey in the world” from Drammen to Bergen, perhaps the loveliest and finest of the Norway songs if anyone were to gather them on one album. There, and on the strolling blues classic “Childish Blues”, one hears why so many admire Leven's guitar playing: “Brilliant!” He wants mix and production to bring out the detail and naturalness of the playing; “Kelly Joe Phelps and Chris Smither sit on the sidelines and applaud”. The reviewer is “once again impressed beyond most of what is released in music today”: Leven writes from feelings and thoughts very few are able to convey, and uses bluegrass musicians, blues-influenced older British rock musicians and America's perhaps most special roots artist, Johnny Dowd, to get the distinctive mix for which Norwegians love him.

With homages to the singer-songwriter Judee Sill, “the prostituted and heroin-addicted bank robber who never got to shine”, and the recently deceased British blues eccentric Kevin Coyne, the album ranks among Leven's very best, alongside *The Mystery of Love …* and *Shining Brother Shining Sister* (“Sister Shining Brother” in the magazine). Praised are “Vox Humana”, “One Man One Guitar”, “Another Man's Rain”, the 1950s r&b- and swing-flavoured, highly entertaining “I've Been Everywhere” and the blues feeling of “Childish Blues”. The closing line: Leven never stops impressing “as the most important artist of the British Isles”, and the album should be prescribed “on the blue prescription nationwide”.

2007-10-03-vaganavisa-en-annen-manns-reg.kurz: Double-page report with interview, conducted on the day of the concert (Wednesday, 26.09.2007) in Svolvær; published a week later.
inhalt: Double-page report with interview, conducted on the day of the concert (Wednesday, 26.09.2007) in Svolvær; published a week later. Photos show Leven with organiser Jan Åge Johansen (“to gode venner”). Opening: Leven sits in the car, rain on the windscreen; the author recaps the attack of 1983, the loss of his voice and record contract and the way out of heroin via holistic therapy.

Leven says (self-reports): on first entering the Præstengbrygga he had thought the room, with a staircase in the middle of the hall, hopeless – and had been wrong. He told his Norwegian agent he wanted to see not just Oslo and Bergen but the whole country. The relationship between audience and artist is like being in love. Once, on a Saturday night in northern Norway, he played to a noisy audience, so bad that Johansen went home; otherwise the Brygga is a place where people listen, and the friendship with Johansen matters. He writes constantly in a notebook; as occasions for songs he names a woman in a bar who asked him to sell a car and died the same evening, a homeless man by the railway tracks in Trondheim and a man on the Hurtigruten who wanted to go home in the Trollfjord. Norway's nature is frightening to him, Lofoten a brutal version of the Scottish north-west coast; he used to hike alone in the Hebrides, now here. He lives on the English south coast with a view of the Isle of Wight. In Europe he plays with a band, in Scandinavia alone – a band in northern Norway would be too expensive, and he likes the solitude. He has an “almost erotic relationship with rain” and wrote “Another Man's Rain” about it. The evening's concert is being recorded and is due to appear on CD next year; in 2008 a new album is coming and he will return to Kabelvåg.

2007-11-14-gaesteliste-koeln-kulturbunke.kurz: Ullrich Maurer reviews the Cologne concert at the Kulturbunker Mülheim for Gaesteliste.de: Leven as a classic storyteller with Michael Cosgrave, Michael Weston King as support, and plenty of personal material – solid and well attended, but nothing new.
inhalt: Ullrich Maurer opens his report on the concert at Cologne’s Kulturbunker Mülheim on 14 November 2007 with one of Leven’s anecdotes. While recording in Glasgow, the Willard Grant Conspiracy want to eat a nice Angus steak and go to a steakhouse with Leven. The unfriendly waiter notes down “guest wants a gay steak” and, when Leven opts for salad, “gay hippie steak”; the pale Robert Fisher of the band marvels: “My God, it really is a different country here!” Stories like this, Maurer writes, are what set one Leven tour apart from another.

As his friend and that evening’s support Michael Weston King rightly puts it, Leven is a classic storyteller who makes communication with the audience central to what he does. That includes his odd culinary tastes (vodka with red wine that night) and an easy way with colleagues, above all sidekick, keyboardist and lately flautist Michael Cosgrave. Leven partly kept his promise to watch guitarist Markus Segschneider’s set, which offered intricate, jazzy guitar pieces with near-atonal singing, now in English, better in German. For Leven fans used to more down-to-earth fare it was difficult and tiring, and when Segschneider tried to pass one piece off as a country number, nobody could follow. Michael Weston King, in contrast, Maurer calls as down-to-earth as an artist can be; Leven once said King writes remarkably simple songs despite his complicated life. He sang of marital problems, his recently deceased father-in-law and old flames resurfacing (“She’s Still My Weakness”), packing everything into the usual 30 minutes.

Leven and Cosgrave then stayed on stage. Leven, Maurer notes, refuses not only encores but rock-business rituals generally. A mix of moving murder ballads, old and new songs followed, mainly from the latest album (Maurer miscalls it “Oh What a Blow That Phantom Told Me”; the title is *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!*) and from Sir Vincent Lone. Musically there were no great revelations, in Maurer’s view; Leven and Cosgrave are blindly attuned to each other, and only “Moscow Train” used a drum loop. What interested fans was the personal note: stories about his trouble with women, the mugging and the long recovery, and the “royal lunch” with Lady Di, for whom Leven says he had to sing “Main Travelled Roads” to prove he was a singer. There were also explanations of some of his coded lyrics and of the stories behind “Kings of Infinite Space” – though with Leven one can never be sure when his imagination runs away with him.
Maurer’s verdict: a very solid, very good show, well attended by Cologne standards and for an obscure venue, offering nothing fundamentally new but the usual good entertainment.
zitate_kontext: Ullrich Maurer on Leven’s between-song stories
Maurer on the programme and Leven’s Lady Di story

2007-buda-historia-rocka-popu-i-hip-hopu.kurz: In Andrzej Buda's Polish compilation of critics' best-of lists, *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* appears in a list of the best albums, next to Blur's *Parklife*.
inhalt: Andrzej Buda's *Historia rocka, popu i hip-hopu – według krytyków, 1974–2006* (Wydawnictwo Niezależne, Głogów) compiles critics' best-of lists. Leven's *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* appears in a list of the best albums, apparently from 1994/95, next to Blur's *Parklife*. Which magazine compiled the list is not clear from the passage; the book was published after 2006.

2007-kevin-coyne-home-page-news-coyne-of.kurz: A fan news page on Kevin Coyne mentions Leven several times: as Sir Vincent Lone with the tribute song “Coyne of the Realm”, as a contributor to the tribute CD *Whispers from the Offing*, and through a reprinted column about Coyne and a Nuremberg show.
inhalt: Pascal Regis's chronological news page on Kevin Coyne mentions Jackie Leven in several places. In late 2007 it notes that Leven – “an old friend of Kevin”, who contributed to the *Whispers from the Offing* tribute CD – has recorded a new tribute song to Coyne under the name Sir Vincent Lone, “Coyne of the Realm”, included on his 2007 CD *When The Bridegroom Comes: Songs For Women*.

The longest entry dates from May 2006: the page reproduces an extract from “The Deep Pool”, Leven's monthly column on his own website. Leven quotes a darkly comic passage about an institution from Coyne's book *That Old Suburban Angst* and says he re-reads the book every night before bed. It makes him laugh out loud, though not in the usual way: the more you immerse yourself in Coyne's world, the more the images pile up inside you and give a fleeting comic protection from “this terrible world”. He is especially fond of Coyne's interest in sausages. He points readers to the publisher Tony Donaghey and kevincoynebooks.com and suggests buying the book for Christmas to disturb one's loved ones.

Leven writes that he has been thinking about Coyne ever since touring Germany and Austria with Michael Cosgrave the previous month. In Nuremberg, Coyne's adopted home, the venue was very full, possibly too full, but when Leven name-checked Coyne from the stage there was a warm, affectionate round of applause – “a lovely moment”. After the show he met Coyne's widow Helmi and talked with her about Coyne, his respect for him and his own song about him, “Here Come The Urban Ravens”. Helmi, he says, made him think of the resilience of people who stand by outsider and borderline folk geniuses; he then places himself, Coyne and the musician David Thomas in an absurd list of real and fictional figures.

Further down, the page lists two tribute projects. *Whispers from the Offing* appeared in March 2007 as a charity CD for the project “Life and Living”; besides Leven it features, among others, The Mekons, Nicky Sudden, Clive Product, Jowe Head and Alternative TV. It received five stars and was named CD of the month in the Nuremberg magazine Plärrer.
zitate_kontext: Leven in his “The Deep Pool” column (May 2006) on the Nuremberg concert.
Leven on Kevin Coyne's book *That Old Suburban Angst*.
The news page's note on the song on *When The Bridegroom Comes*.

2007-moors-magazine-oh-what-a-blow-that-.autor: Holly Moors (according to page metadata; editorial account, individual author not stated)
2007-moors-magazine-oh-what-a-blow-that-.kurz: Moors Magazine awards *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!* four and a half stars out of five: Leven has been making one little masterpiece after another for years without the wider public noticing.
inhalt: In the Dutch online magazine’s roundup of ‘short reviews’, under the heading ‘Lyrical singer-songwriter’, there is a brief and enthusiastic notice. Jackie Leven has for years been making “one little masterpiece after another” without visibly impressing a large audience – which is “a bit strange”, since he writes beautiful lyrical songs about misery and sorrow, sings them in a warm, deep, soulful voice that is “heart-rendingly beautiful”, and also provides magnificent arrangements combining folk with jazz, blues, rock and soul.

Anyone who discovers Leven, the reviewer says, awaits each next album with longing and is never disappointed: each time there is a new, inspired album of an hour, and one feels the creative stream is flowing as fiercely as ever. The latest too is highly poetic, and again he has invited friends who feel the melancholy mood perfectly: Johnny Dowd is the perfect second voice, even when he merely reads a poem. “Romanticism lives in Leven” – a pun on his name – and the listener is once more carried away and moved. Rating: four and a half stars.

2007-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.titel: [Collected finds, Nasjonalbiblioteket 2007: short news items, announcements, listings]

2007-orion-rankin-exit-music.kurz: In Ian Rankin's Rebus novel *Exit Music* the detective puts on Jackie Leven twice: after Rory Gallagher, and in a conversation about his record collection alongside John Martyn.
inhalt: Jackie Leven appears twice in *Exit Music* (Orion, 2007), then planned as the last Rebus novel by Ian Rankin. First, after Rory Gallagher, Rebus puts on Leven, followed by Page and Plant. In a dialogue about Rebus's record collection, John Martyn and Leven are named, and Rebus talks about his “exit music”.
The book was published in translations, including Dutch (“Laatste ronde”, 2008), Italian (“Partitura finale”, 2011) and French (2010).

2008-01-03-rolling-stone-de-jackie-balfo.kurz: Jörn Schlüter reviews two side projects in Rolling Stone: the cosy folk record by Sir Vincent Lone and the audiobook *Chip Pan Fire* by Jackie Balfour – in the end Leven remains “the storyteller”.
inhalt: Jörn Schlüter begins with Leven’s productivity: because he writes too much music, he took on the pseudonym Sir Vincent Lone last year. One understands the label’s objection – for some years the songs of the veteran Scot have been blurring, and some could have been spared. On the second Sir Vincent Lone record, *When The Bridegroom Comes (Songs For Women)*, recorded in between in the company of old acquaintances such as Michael Cosgrave and David Wrench, things are more reflective than on *Songs For Lonely Americans*. Leven sings a handful of his own songs to mostly quiet folk instrumentation.

There are also covers by Jackson C. Frank, Judee Sill, Donovan Leitch and the contemporaries David Childers and Dan Britton, who sings his own contribution – “a whole song given away!”. That is something one does at most at a concert, but this very generosity shows perhaps Leven’s self-image as a recording artist. All in all, a cosy record for the congregation.

The second album, which Leven smuggles past the release rhythms, comes under a new second alter ego: an audiobook in which Leven appears as Jackie Balfour, a junior reporter on the Scottish local paper the “Glenrodent Gazette”. The colleagues are petty-bourgeois intriguers, nothing much happens, and the whole thing sounds like an autobiography, perhaps that of a later-famous journalist. The semi-literary sketch of Scottish small-town life is probably aimless but develops a certain charm because it is so unabashedly everyday. To tie this new series to the main work, three of the stories that make a Leven concert so funny are appended to the reading: Leven talks himself into trouble on a regional train, is abused as a sex tourist, and makes an Edinburgh audience laugh with local colour. Schlüter’s conclusion: “Forget the many names.” With a little distance the parts become a whole again – Jackie Leven, the storyteller.
zitate_kontext: Jörn Schlüter on Leven’s Sir Vincent Lone album.

2008-01-netrhythms-jackie-balfour-chip-p.kurz: David Kidman reviews *Chip Pan Fire*, a spoken-word disc of monologues by Leven's fictional twin Jackie Balfour plus three older stories: engaging, but probably for a small audience.
inhalt: David Kidman describes *Chip Pan Fire* (Cooking Vinyl, reviewed January 2008) as one of a pair of new releases from Jackie Leven and as a disc of monologues rather than songs, split into two sections. In the first, Leven's “twin” Jackie Balfour – a fictional alter ego – recounts his doomed first job on leaving school: cub reporter on the notorious Fife local paper the Glenrodent Gazette in the mid-1960s. The episodes run from gently observed vignettes to more overtly amusing tales of provincial life and newspaper life, delivered in an initially low-key, diffident manner but with evident affection, and introduce the characters of the new town of Glenrodent and its newspaper offices. They are punctuated by brief, attractive piano interludes by Michael Cosgrave, inspired largely by Scottish dance forms.

The second section brings three stories of Leven's own concoction: the infamous “Sting's Dead”, recorded live before an anything-but-humourless German audience; “Stupid Local Boasts”, culled from the double album of the two-hander show at the 2004 Edinburgh Festival that united Leven with author Ian Rankin (playing the straight man); and “Sex Tourist”, recorded at a club in Sydney in 2001. All three had been released before – the first and third only on hard-to-find Haunted Valley discs – but Kidman finds they complement the Balfour episodes well.

His reservation: he is not sure there is a particularly wide audience for this aspect of Leven's art, beyond the “occasional entertaining listen” status that inevitably attaches to spoken-word recordings, however good.
zitate_kontext: Kidman's closing reservation about the record.

2008-05-pennyblackmusic-jackie-leven-gre.kurz: Ben Howarth sees Leven in London’s tiny Green Note café: an intimate, charismatic show for fewer than thirty people in which the stories between songs are the greatest pleasure.
inhalt: Ben Howarth opens with a rant about London – the rudeness on the tube, the prices, the miserable people – before saying that there are odd times when he is glad he came. Tonight was one. Leven, approaching sixty, sits there with “acoustic hair” and sleeves rolled up and does not look like a rock star, but “by any measure” has lived: heroin addiction, mental health problems, homelessness, a violent and potentially life-threatening assault and four albums with the punk band Doll By Doll.

Howarth reckons Doll By Doll were one of those unlucky bands John Peel did not like, though he lays most of the blame for their failure to reach a mass audience on their label boss, “the man who later funded New Labour and now goes by the name Lord Levy”. Leven has since made a string of albums for Cooking Vinyl, and his live performances have secured a small but devoted following. His work as founder and patron of a mental health charity, Howarth adds, saw him hobnobbing with Princess Diana in the 1990s.

The evening at the Green Note in Camden – a café serving strictly vegetarian food, at most ten metres from the stage – is intimate even by Leven’s standards. He watches the support act, then opens with ‘Another Man’s Rain’ from his latest album, which Howarth thinks might become his favourite of the songs. Leven has consistently stressed that he wants to be seen as a good storyteller, and detailed lyrics are at the heart of even his most melodic songs; yet his music has the passion of Van Morrison, whose lyrics were never more than vague. Fans of one are likely to be fans of the other, says Paul Du Noyer, the former Mojo editor and one of Leven’s best-known fans; Howarth agrees.

The most enjoyable aspect for him is the stories between the songs, among them an account of Leven’s doomed attempts to use his existing ticket after missing a train home from London, insisting he had been hounded off by rowdy Portsmouth supporters. The conclusion: passers-by outside the café can hardly realise that inside “one of Britain’s most gifted songwriters” is giving an outstanding performance to fewer than thirty people. “But I got to see it, so I win.”

2008-07-23-whiskyfun-music-and-whisky-in.kurz: The conversation combines the announcement of “Lovers at the Gun Club” with Leven's musical preferences and his ideas about drinking whisky.
inhalt: The conversation combines the announcement of “Lovers at the Gun Club” with Leven's musical preferences and his ideas about drinking whisky. Leven lists his musical partners to date and singles out Johnny Dowd. For the new album he gives 18 August 2008 as the release date. Afterwards he wants to travel through Europe for several months; the overseas tours mentioned for the following year are intentions at the time of the interview.

As his favourite singer he names Chet Baker, as a particularly admired songwriter Judee Sill; for cleaning he listens to Roland Kirk. His later appreciation of Patsy Cline serves him as an example of how age and circumstances change listening. For him, music and whisky can equally trigger a brief moment of inner harmony.

Leven says his father wrote a whisky book and took him to distilleries as a teenager. Linkwood and Mortlach are particularly important to him, but he now often prefers simple blends in ordinary bars. His answers are directed against status consumption and over-refined connoisseur language. He links places, drinks and music into small scenes; the provocative judgements and comic stories belong to the tone of the interview and are not factual quality assessments.

2008-07-the-list-jackie-leven-doug-johns.kurz: Doug Johnstone profiles Leven in The List ahead of his Edinburgh Festival gig: cheerful, without bitterness about his lack of success at home, and in love with spontaneity.
inhalt: Doug Johnstone's piece in the festival issue of The List (Edinburgh/Glasgow) announces Leven's gig at Cabaret Voltaire in Edinburgh on 8 August 2008 (£8). The hook is neglect: while we heap plaudits on “underground legends from across the pond”, Scotland's own talented outsider remains unheralded. Leven laughs: “I can't get arrested in this country”, but his last single and album both charted in Germany and he does well right across northern Europe. Johnstone credits him with discussing the lack of homegrown success without bitterness; the 58-year-old Fifer would spend the next six months touring the world, taking in China, Australia and Canada, “almost always to larger audiences than in Britain”.

The writer places the work: in a career spanning 35 years Leven has produced an extensive and varied catalogue “somewhere between the wilful artistry of Tom Waits and the curmudgeonly literate folk of Bob Dylan”, all imbued with a quintessentially Scottish self-deprecation. After everything from psych-rock to punk he has recently settled on a consummate bluesy folk, with songwriting and guitar playing on the latest album, *Lovers at the Gun Club*, stronger than ever. In the past he did not have to seek out problems – the biography includes losing his voice for two years after a near-death strangulation, and a subsequent heroin addiction – but in 2008 he is found in cheery mood.

Leven himself says: “I've reached an age where you say, ‘Wait a fucking minute, am I going to trudge around the world being in a sulk?’ You've got to have fun and believe in your own songs, it's as simple as that.” With over two dozen albums he is certainly prolific, but nothing in the studio or on stage is ever carefully planned: he likes “the permanent sense of not quite knowing what's going to happen”. He remains enthusiastic about the new music he sees at festivals and gigs: “There's more effort being made now than for a while. After punk, people were all about attitude, but attitude is not very nutritious and in the end people want to be fed by their music. I know I do.”
zitate_kontext: Leven on his position in Scotland and in Europe.
Leven on his cheerful outlook in 2008.

2008-08-18-musicomh-lovers-at-the-gun-cl.kurz: Jenni Cole calls Leven on musicOMH “the closest the UK is ever likely to get to Johnny Cash”: *Lovers at the Gun Club* holds no surprises, but the dark, rough folk is something he does “very, very well”; four stars out of five.
inhalt: The review of 18 August 2008 (four stars out of five) opens with a recommendation: Jackie Leven is the closest the UK is ever likely to get to Johnny Cash, and if you have not yet fallen prey to his charms, it is about time. He is the sound of dark folk clubs, “the final measure of whiskey in the bottom of the bottle as the door closes on the last vestige of hope”. His career has left a trail of under-appreciated, under-rated gems, from the “Celt punks” Doll by Doll through a vicious street attack that nearly left him unable to speak, to heroin addiction, to a solo career that has been “ludicrously prolific” even without the many fan-club-only releases.

*Lovers at the Gun Club*, his 14th official solo studio release, has no surprises, but with a following as loyal as his none is needed. He has found his formula – dark, gravelly, dirty folk – and does it very well. Recorded in Snowdonia rather than his native Scotland, it would be a fabulous album to listen to in the wilderness of any country. Vocals on the title track are sung by his “absinthe-drinking pal” Johnny O'Dowd (that is, Johnny Dowd), who also helps out on “Dent in the Fender” and “The Wheel of Fate”; Leven describes the opening song as “a psychosexual voodoo redneck tale”, a description that would carry well over the whole album.

What follows is a “truly beautiful collection” of songs; “Dent in the Fender …” sparkles brighter than normal, “My Old Home” should be all you need if you have any soul at all, and the delicate fragility of “Woman in a Car” defies anyone not to fall in love with it. Long since freed from the need to please anyone but himself and his followers, Leven can indulge personal projects such as “To Whom It May Concern”, a setting of words by the late beat poet Kenneth Patchen, and hand the final track to David Childers as a sampler of Childers's own album. The themes seem overtly American at times, despite references to Somerfield carrier bags and Sunderland fans; that enhances the album, which can be measured against the hardest, roughest-edged folk blues and heartfelt alt-folk.

2008-08-22-gaesteliste-nicht-ganz-richti.kurz: Interview on “Lovers at the Gun Club” (2008). Maurer reports that Leven chose the pseudonym Sir Vincent Lone after being annoyed that Will Oldham, and not he, had come up with “Bonnie Prince”; the new album was recorded without the record company's knowledge, which Leven plays down.
inhalt: Interview on “Lovers at the Gun Club” (2008). Maurer reports that Leven chose the pseudonym Sir Vincent Lone after being annoyed that Will Oldham, and not he, had come up with “Bonnie Prince”; the new album was recorded without the record company's knowledge, which Leven plays down. Difference between Leven and Lone: Jackie is more dogged because he has to live from it, Sir Vince has more fun (self-report). Johnny Dowd sings the title song; the two met when both happened to be performing in Kufstein. The title story: a drive through the Shenandoah Valley with the “transsexual killer” Shannon Doyle, children giving the Hitler salute, followed by shooting practice at the shooting club (self-report, evidently invented or exaggerated). Leven wants songs to sound “not quite right”, as with David Lynch or Tarantino; he considers “Innocent Railway” one of his best songs. He chooses poetry out of love, not to convert people. Closing anecdote: “Olivier's Blues” came about with Sir Laurence Olivier, whose son Rich Olivier is a close friend (Leven is godfather to his son); Olivier called him a “jolly green giant” (self-report). Outlook: autumn tour with Cosgrave.

2008-08-24-the-sunday-times-lovers-at-th.kurz: Stewart Lee presents Leven in the Sunday Times as a classic cult artist – a big man in thick socks, an obscure seventies band, a drug problem – and gives *Lovers at the Gun Club* four stars.
inhalt: The comedian and critic Stewart Lee reviews Jackie Leven's album *Lovers at the Gun Club* in the Sunday Times of 24 August 2008. In the freely readable teaser he introduces Leven as a classic cult artist: a big man in thick socks, with an obscure seventies band, a drug problem and stylistically varied solo albums. The remainder, behind the paywall, has not been seen; according to other information Lee gave four stars and judged that the quality of the songs carries the album past the feared sound of “suffocating good taste”.

2008-08-26-ostlendingen-jackie-leven-lov.kurz: Geir Hovensjø recommends *Lovers at the Gun Club* in Østlendingen as a “disquieting”, style-mixing record full of borrowed quotations and with a double bottom in its lyrics.
inhalt: On the music page of Østlendingen (Elverum) of 26 August 2008, Geir Hovensjø recommends the new album *Lovers at the Gun Club*. The review is headed ‘Foruroligende’ (‘Disquieting’). Hovensjø introduces Leven (58) as a poet and musician who started in the sixties as John St. Field, was later singer with Doll by Doll, had a period as a “lost junkie” and has since delivered “one great album after another”.

The new one is “very interesting”: Leven knows no boundaries, mixes styles and borrows other people’s music. In the title track you hear the guitar solo from Them’s ‘Gloria’ (Van Morrison); in ‘Olivier Blues’ Willie Dixon’s blues classic ‘My Babe’ is woven in; and in ‘The Dent in the Fender and the Wheel of Fate’ a verse from ‘Heart in My Soul’ by the American artist and lawyer David Childers appears – Childers’s original recording is also the album’s final track.

Some of it is rocky, some jazzy, some folky, some poetry reading. The lyrics usually have a “disquieting double bottom” which Leven’s dark, vibrating voice brings out in a very special way. The closing advice: “Treat yourself to a concentrated hour.” That Leven began in the sixties is the reviewer’s simplification; his first record as John St. Field appeared only in 1971.

2008-08-29-bergensavisen-jackie-leven-ti.kurz: Bergensavisen's preview of Leven's concert on 9 November 2008 at Madam Felle on Bryggen: lovely songs, absurd stories, plus a quote from the Independent's review of *Lovers at the Gun Club*.
inhalt: The short announcement “Jackie Leven tilbake” (“Jackie Leven back”) appeared in Bergensavisen on 29 August 2008. On Sunday 9 November Leven would be back in Bergen: the Scot, currently touring *Lovers at the Gun Club*, would play Madam Felle on Bryggen, where he had “given some magical concerts before”. The stage was set, it said, for “another solemn occasion with beautiful songs and absurd stories”.

As proof of the new album's quality the item cites the “prestigious” Independent, which gave it four stars out of five and described it with the sentence “Leven's majestic voice is one of the most noble instruments in popular music”. Three biographical markers are given: he released his first album in 1971, led the “semi-legendary” Doll by Doll from 1978 to 1982 and began a new solo career at the start of the nineties – he “has lived a long and hard life as a musician”. The piece is an event preview with no verdict of its own.
zitate_kontext: The paper on Leven's earlier concerts at Madam Felle.
Quote from the Independent's review of *Lovers at the Gun Club*.

2008-08-musikexpress-lovers-at-the-gun-c.kurz: In Musikexpress, Peter Felkel calls Leven a great sympathiser and gifted storyteller; *Lovers at the gun club* contains astonishing and head-shaking moments, but no new “Marble City Bar”. “Still lovely.”
inhalt: Peter Felkel reviews *Lovers at the gun club* (released 15 August 2008) in Musikexpress. Leven, he writes, is a “great sympathiser, gifted storyteller and restless worker in the service of blues, folk, gentle rock, soul and, lately, jazz”, who from the windswept west coast of Scotland (other accounts say he was living in Hampshire at the time) supplies his small but devoted fan community every year with a new batch of music that makes one “rave, marvel and occasionally shake one's head”.

As an example of the latter he cites the experimental piece “The Dentist, the Fender and the Wheel of Fate” (spelt “The Dentin …” in the text), over seven minutes long: the intro recalls Miles Davis's *The Man with the Horn*, then it finds its way via funk to folk, quotes Frank Zappa and calls up distorted voices, sounding “like the Tower of Babel turned into music”. Felkel's verdict: “Love it or skip it.” There is also plenty of stupendous material: the title track, which Johnny Dowd delivers with the greatest possible stoicism, a thoroughly touching “Heart Full Of Soul” by David Childers, which Leven sings himself, and again some of those typical Leven tunes between pub poetry, pathos and subversive pop appeal. The conclusion: there is no new “Marble City Bar” among them, a pity, “still lovely”.

2008-08-netrhythms-lovers-at-the-gun-clu.kurz: Mike Davies praises *Lovers At The Gun Club* as a rich, eclectic album in which Leven shares the stage with guests such as Johnny Dowd and David Childers: “idiosyncratic, intoxicating, fascinating and generous”.
inhalt: Mike Davies (NetRhythms; the review itself is dated February 2009) opens with Leven's own claim that this is one of his best albums and does not quibble with it. It is a little disorienting, he says, that the first voice you hear on the “psychosexual voodoo redneck” title track is not Leven but Johnny Dowd's “liquid sleaze” vocals; the song is a wry observation on the connectivity of firearms, sex and machismo, inspired by a car trip with, and stories told by, the Irish Canadian professional killer Shannon Doyle. Dowd also speaks the verses of “The Dent In The Fender And The Wheel Of Fate”, a sax-soaked slow funk groove about revisiting his dad's old yellow Lada, while Leven sings the chorus.

Several songs look back at the past and lost connections: young crushes and runaway lovers in “The Innocent Railway”, the sense you can never truly go back in “My Old Home” (think Van Morrison doing Springsteen's “My Hometown”), the tender “Woman In A Car”, also inspired by his dad's car and his parents, the aching “I've Passed Away From Human Love” and the gospel blues doo-wop of “Head Full Of War”, which examines destructive inner rage.

Davies calls it a “rich and eclectic album”. “Olivier Blues” is a straight rewrite of the blues chestnut “My Babe”, which Leven claims grew from a fireside lyrical to and fro with Sir Larry; “To Whom It May Concern” is a spoken, Irish-mist setting of a poem by Kenneth Patchen; “Fareham Confidential” is a snapshot of a city of lost souls that borrows the melody of “Top of the World” and is surely the only song to namecheck Somerfield. As a matching bookend, the closing “Heart in My Soul” hands over to the American singer-songwriter David Childers and is actually lifted from his own *Hard Time Country* album. Davies does not know how the royalties work, but concludes that they do not come much more idiosyncratic, intoxicating, fascinating and generous than Leven.
zitate_kontext: Closing sentence of Mike Davies's review
Davies on the title song (as Leven tells it)

2008-08-vanguard-online-jackie-leven-int.kurz: A short question-and-answer interview around *Lovers at the Gun Club*: Leven on guest tracks, collaborations, poems, Robert Bly, melancholy and drink, and his wish to be rediscovered for *Gypsy Blood*.
inhalt: Ross McGibbon puts questions to Jackie Leven in August 2008 for Vanguard Online, on the occasion of the new album (*Lovers at the Gun Club*). Leven describes assembling a “family” of songs without fully understanding the blood ties between them, always including a fairly old song and a fairly new one: “Fareham Confidential” was written in ten minutes in a bar in Fareham, while the title song took ten years. He defends the guest tracks on his records – on the new album a “magnificent” one by the underexposed American David Childers – as a way of spreading community among musicians. Collaborations, especially the spoken-word contributions of Johnny Dowd and David Thomas on *Shining Brother, Shining Sister*, give him access to ideas others do better; you cannot make albums worrying about what “Dave in Sheffield” might think.

For the poems on his albums he draws on a near-library of poetry at home and follows an instinct he does not understand: a Kenneth Patchen poem was already on the previous album *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!* and the new one has another. He remains in constant touch with Robert Bly and regrets missing him in September, when he is touring in Europe. He would love to release a second *Argyll Cycle* volume, perhaps a third, but does not know when – he is already working on an album for 2010 that will not be an Argyll one.

Asked which dead musician he would dig up, he picks Lightnin' Hopkins and a band called “Leven and Hopkins (deceased)”. On whether there is a Celtic melancholy particular to men, he says melancholy has the same tone everywhere: partly a neurosis from knowing you will never fathom the levers that run your life. Asked what he wants to be remembered for, he hopes to be rediscovered for Doll by Doll's *Gypsy Blood*. On drink he is more expansive: modern culture has abandoned the formal initiation of the young into adulthood, so teenagers try to initiate themselves in high-street bars every Saturday night; much of his writing comes from watching the fallout. He quotes his friend Jo Shaw of Doll by Doll – “you got to time your highs” – and finishes with the line “for my gift is a poison …” from “Hell Games”, whose first line producer John Sinclair would not let him keep.
zitate_kontext: Leven on whether there is a Celtic melancholy particular to men.
Leven on what he would like to be remembered for.
Leven on drink and its place in his world view.

2008-09-01-westzeit-lovers-at-the-gun-cl.kurz: Klaus Hübner reviews *Lovers At The Gun Club* in Westzeit: never was Leven so valuable, his interpretations so cheeky and rough – a light-footed assurance in the vein of Tom Waits and Lambchop.
inhalt: Klaus Hübner considers Leven’s new album his most valuable: never were his interpretations so “snotty, skewed, rough”. Leven has outed himself as a “lover from the shooting club” – no holds barred, but with a keen eye for everyday scenes. In the title track, sung by Johnny Dowd, he quotes Van Morrison’s “Gloria”; Leven knows exactly where he can afford quotations and where his own strength counts.

Surprisingly, he achieves a light-footed assurance like Tom Waits, the Go-Betweens or Lambchop (the text writes “Karl” instead of Kurt Wagner) – one would call his music “carefree” were the word not so superficially charged, with all the hooks and eyes of contemporary blues, country and underground music.

2008-09-03-the-independent-jackie-leven-.kurz: Andy Gill calls Leven in The Independent “perhaps our greatest musical poet of loss” and describes a Borderline concert full of anecdotes, poetry and sensitive band backing.
inhalt: Andy Gill begins by asking what lures people out in drizzle and murk in the age of YouTube clips and webcast concerts, particularly if you are a troubadour “blessed – or cursed” with an appreciation of the value of melancholy. Jackie Leven is one such: perhaps “our greatest musical poet of loss”, his songs keenly anatomising the slight but significant shifts of mood, memory and emotion from which we construct our personal histories. Not the most attractive prospect after a long day’s labour, yet Leven pulls a decent crowd of lived-in faces, world-wearied enough to appreciate the ebb and flow of life’s fortunes – or as he puts it in “My Old Home”: “Kingdom come, kingdom go – how that works, I just don’t know.”

To lure and keep an audience the touring troubadour must develop a rapport akin to a stand-up comic. Fortunately Leven has a colourful past to draw upon and the ironic delivery to put across his fund of offhand gags and observations: tales of scary acquaintances (such as the Irish transsexual hitman who inspired the title track of his latest album *Lovers at the Gun Club*) and the recollected wisdom of hecklers – his favourite put-down came from a Glaswegian who answered one of several songs about his late father with “Typical Fifer, showboating about how he knew his dad!”

The song he may have been referring to has Leven returning to the family home but finding no release from the estrangement that clouded their shared history; “Got a head full of headstones, as I stepped down from the train” is about as perfect an evocation as has been coined of the sinking feeling of familial duty. So not just a typical Fifer, but a rarer, more sensitive breed. Elsewhere “Kings of Infinite Space” is introduced via scenes from an old Columbo episode featuring Johnny Cash; the unrequited first love in the backstreets of Fife in “The Innocent Railway” comes with chapter and verse; and “Her Arms Are Full of Broken Things” incorporates verses from A. E. Housman and Charlotte Mew. The band – purring keyboard pads, wistful harmonica and backing vocals – provides “the perfect sepia-tint settings” for his narratives.
zitate_kontext: A Glaswegian’s heckle at a song about Leven’s father, as related by Leven.
Song line about returning to the family home, singled out by Gill.

2008-09-04-rolling-stone-forum-jackie-le.titel: [Thread: Jackie Leven] (Topic 5, tour dates 2008–2011, tour cancellation 2011)
2008-09-04-rolling-stone-forum-jackie-le.kurz: A forum thread collects Leven's tour dates in Germany, Austria and Switzerland from September 2008 to September 2011 and ends on 8 September 2011 with the news that the autumn tour was cancelled because of his illness.
inhalt: The thread in the German Rolling Stone's concert forum has 15 posts. It begins on 4 September 2008 with a fan looking forward to that year's tour with Michael Cosgrave (“I never tire of laughing at his anecdotes”) and listing the German dates from 11 September (Verden, Kornbrennerei Flander) via Völklingen, Ansbach, Karlsruhe, Essen, Berlin, Hannover, Kiel, Hamburg and Bonn to 25 September in Eppstein in the Taunus. Asked whether the tour continues in October, another member supplies the rest of the schedule: Leiden, Amsterdam (Paradiso) and Ottersum at the end of September, then the UK from 11 to 23 October (from Exeter via London, Sheffield, Newcastle, Manchester, Perth and Glasgow to Southampton) and Norway from 29 October to 13 November (Oslo, Trondheim, Kabelvåg, Tromsø, Bodø, Skien, Hardanger, Haugesund, Stavanger, Bergen, Drammen).

In January 2009 a list for February follows (Herbrechtingen on the 6th to Bremen on the 20th, with Zurich, Halle, Stuttgart, Dresden and Munich); in December 2009 and February 2010 the May 2010 dates grow from Kiel (6 May) to Marburg (20 May), taking in Verden, Einbeck, Hannover, Frankfurt, Saarbrücken, Berlin, Singwitz, Munich and Vienna, and in April Solingen on 11 May is added. For September 2010 Amsterdam, Hamburg (Knust), Münster, Bremen, Essen, Stuttgart and Dresden are set; in May 2011 the tour of 16 to 27 September 2011 (Marburg to Hamburg, with Eppstein, Zurich, Munich, Vienna, Ansbach, Münster, Essen, Saarbrücken, Hannover and Kiel) is announced. The posts in between are short remarks from fans pleased about a date or sorry that nothing is near them.

The ending matters most. On 8 September 2011 a member reports that the 2011 tour is cancelled because of an illness of Leven's; he had to go into inpatient medical treatment, nothing more is known, and the tour is to be rescheduled for spring 2012 if possible. On 24 September another member points, as consolation, to the new “official bootleg” *One Long Cold Morning*, available from Leven's website. The thread consists solely of announcements and fan comments; it does not prove that the earlier concerts took place, and the source of the cancellation notice is not given.
zitate_kontext: A fan on Leven's concerts, 4 September 2008

2008-09-10-jaerbladet-lite-leven-med-lev.kurz: A youth-page review (“Scoopet”) of *Lovers at the Gun Club*, half of it a biography: Leven is “almost what we can call a living legend”, lacking only more listeners. The authors have seen him live three times and interviewed him.
inhalt: On the youth page “Scoopet” of the Jæren newspapers (Jærbladet, 10 September 2008; run the next day in Sandnesposten as “Lite leven med Leven”), the authors open by saying the Scot is “almost what we can call a living legend”; the only thing missing is that a few more listeners discover the guy. They then retell Leven’s life, evidently following his own account and with some twisted details and OCR damage: born in 1950, only a few nerdy friends, no school genius but good at English and writing. His mother played “American black blues music” while his friends’ parents hummed along to Elvis Presley. With a local band he played his own blues songs and was envied for gigs alongside Archie Fisher and Hamish Imlach. A local clique then started a “personal vendetta” against him, so bad that he had to leave Fife and Scotland.

In London he lived hand to mouth for months, since street musicians were hardly accepted in the late sixties; after that he lived in Ireland, Berlin and Madrid. His debut album came out in 1971 under the name John St. Field, later came Doll by Doll (1978–1982). In 1983, while recording a solo album, he was attacked on his way home from the studio and almost strangled, unable to speak or sing for months, and lost his record deal, his friends and his composure. He fell into mental imbalance and heroin addiction and lived “his own hell in isolation” for nearly a year. From 1985 he turned to Chinese five-element acupuncture and “psychic healing” and co-founded the CORE Trust, which is still active in London; the authors call him its “manager” and say he sits on the board. Princess Diana blessed the project and showed great interest.

In recent years Leven has visited Norway several times, built a solid name and comes across as a serious balladeer with a twinkle in his eye. The authors have seen him live three times and conducted a “fascinating interview”; between songs he chats willingly with the audience, and there is always room for tall tales. The new album is, as expected, that of a singer-songwriter “with a little more soul, honesty and weight than many others”: “You have to live a hard life to get such a mood onto a record.” Some songs are “a bit too dull”; the authors like the title track and “To Whom It May Concern” best. Fans of Bruce Springsteen, Johnny Cash and credible troubadours will find their favourites here; Leven mostly addresses a more adult audience but might also appeal to younger people.

The authors on the songs of the album

2008-09-bluesnews-jackie-leven-lovers-at.kurz: Bluesnews calls *Lovers At The Gun Club* a good but not especially magical return to the Celtic troubadour: without the Americana tones of earlier records, with Johnny Dowd as guest and “My Old Home” as the loveliest moment.
inhalt: This review in Bluesnews (no. 56, September 2008), the magazine of the Norsk Bluesunion, calls Leven the “Scottish friend of Norway” – “with a positive sign” – a welcome guest at many clubs in Norway. He returns in November with his guitar, his often untidy and holey shirts, and a voice that “must put even God up above in a good mood”. The new album will not be remembered as one of his finest, the review says, but it is more than good enough and indispensable for his many followers.

Gone are the Americana and country beats one could hear on *Elegy For Johnny Cash* and the blues nerve that surfaced on a couple of strong tracks on *Oh What A Blow That Phantom Dealt Me*. What you hear is a more back-to-basics troubadour and Celtic songwriter: slowly winding ballads like “The Innocent Railway”, the troubadour’s “lightly ingenious” observations of comic everyday situations in the shambling ballad style of “Fareham Confidential”, and light, rolling folk/boogie moments like “Head Full Of War”. “Bra hele veien” – good all the way – but perhaps not particularly exciting or as magical as much of what Jackie has done before.

Johnny Dowd, the “Americana brimstone preacher”, turns up once more with his strong-charactered voice; the title track, which he colours most, is perhaps the only song likely to be carried forward onto later Leven compilations. Dowd also appears on the ambitious, jazz-tinged “The Dent In The Fender And The Wheel Of Fate”, a long, charismatic journey through Americana land unlike anything Leven has done before. Leven sings like Aaron Neville in places. Personally the critic is happiest with the emotional and beautiful moments such as “My Old Home”, since nobody sings what he calls white soul with that floating Celtic sound as beautifully as Leven. The album ends with the charming acoustic “Olivier Blues”. The review closes: “Lovers At The Gun Club. Er du en av dem?” (“Are you one of them?”).
