The critic on the overall level

2008-10-29-nordlys-jackie-leven-tromso-c.titel: [Interview: Jackie Leven before the Circa concert and the Madrugada support slot in Tromsø]
2008-10-29-nordlys-jackie-leven-tromso-c.kurz: Double-page preview with quotes from a conversation. Leven is coming to Tromsø at the weekend: first a solo concert at Circa on Saturday afternoon (5 pm), then as support act for Madrugada at their farewell concerts at the Kulturhuset on Sunday and Monday.
inhalt: Double-page preview with quotes from a conversation. Leven is coming to Tromsø at the weekend: first a solo concert at Circa on Saturday afternoon (5 pm), then as support act for Madrugada at their farewell concerts at the Kulturhuset on Sunday and Monday. The unusual afternoon start is explained by Leven's second passion, Liverpool FC: he has to watch the Tottenham–Liverpool match at half past six, he says, laughing.

The article summarises the biography (Doll by Doll, dissolved 1982; solo career; nocturnal attack after a studio session, almost strangled, loss of speech, of friends and of his partner, psychological problems, heroin, isolation; after a year the founding of a foundation for addiction rehabilitation) and calls him an honest, hard-working and unusually well-reviewed musician whom the Tromsø audience has often seen (a caption mentions one of Leven's “many Blårock concerts” and a dog named Basil who stays at home).

Leven says (self-report) that he has liked Tromsø since seeing a report in an English newspaper many years ago and telling his manager that was where he wanted to go. He always stays at the Grand Hotell, where he has written very many songs: wake up, breakfast, walk through the streets, write in the room. Impressions from the street and from pubs are “stored” and come out when he writes in peace. He knows Norwegian music well, used to support Midnight Choir, rates Bertine Zetlitz (a joint appearance in Stavanger, afterwards the same flight to Oslo) and thinks Norwegian music is currently “hip” in Britain. He calls the invitation from Madrugada a great honour; he remembers the day he got their first record.

2008-11-08-varden-en-lun-kveld-pa-puben.autor: unknown (not reliably attributable in the OCR)
2008-11-08-varden-en-lun-kveld-pa-puben.kurz: Varden reports briefly that Jackie Leven played and talked at the Lundetangen pub in Skien: a cosy evening with a good atmosphere for all who had come to hear him again.
inhalt: The short notice covers the concert at Lundetangen pub in Skien on Thursday evening (6 November 2008). Leven had given a Saturday-café concert there the year before, which led the landlord Steffen Steffensen to bring him back for a full concert as soon as he had the chance.

Leven played in Doll by Doll but has been a solo artist for many years and has developed a storytelling style of his own, “suitably matched” to his guitar playing. It was a cosy evening with a good atmosphere for those who had come for another hearing of Leven. The photo caption has Leven “back in Skien” (photo: Per-Åge Eriksen).
zitate_kontext: The writer on Leven’s storytelling style

2008-11-12-drammens-tidende-jackie-leven.titel: [Interview/Preview: Jackie Leven back in Drammen – “Comeback overtalt av Lady Diana”]
2008-11-12-drammens-tidende-jackie-leven.kurz: Culture page (p. 12 of the issue) with interview before the second “Lyttekonsert” at Buddy on Thursday, 13.11.2008, 8 pm.
inhalt: Culture page (p. 12 of the issue) with interview before the second “Lyttekonsert” at Buddy on Thursday, 13.11.2008, 8 pm. Andreassen recalls the sold-out concert there the previous year, calls Leven “Scotland's answer to Van Morrison”, refers to Doll by Doll and to the attack in a London side street with a serious neck injury; a subheading claims that Lady Diana persuaded him to make a comeback. The reports from the ongoing Norway tour showed a Leven in rare form, with a new album and new songs; his voice is comparable to Roy Orbison and Aaron Neville, his stock of stories full of irony equally remarkable.

Leven explains (self-report) that it will not be a blueprint of last year's concert: it is about true stories from his life, about accepting and understanding oneself; one cannot die with feelings of guilt. He touches on the US election (a black president is surely not a bad thing). A longer anecdote is set in the 1970s (in the OCR “…castle”, presumably Newcastle): after a falling-out with his business partner, a man named Keith was shot in broad daylight – a “Shannon” had been hired for it – and that same evening a woman in the hotel bar confided her knowledge to him; a strange friendship grew out of it. In Drammen he always feels “magic”; the town reminds him of the working men's clubs of his youth, where people smoked and drank beer – perhaps remnants of the working class; and he likes the women there.

2008-11-14-drammens-tidende-en-bamseklem.kurz: Drammens Tidende praises the last concert of Leven’s 2008 Norway tour at Buddy, Drammen, as a “teddy-bear hug”: warm voice, good guitar playing, coarse jokes and mastery of words. Only echo effects irritated.
inhalt: The critic reviews the concert on Thursday, 13 November 2008, at Buddy in Drammen, the last on the tour (125 in the audience; the rating is based on the 45 minutes before the interval). The burly figure walks on, and the first five minutes go on praise for Drammen and an anecdote from Haugesund, where Leven slept instead of playing because his support slot for Madrugada fell through when Sivert Høyem had a sore throat. Then the 58-year-old Scot, “formerly of the band Doll by Doll”, finally gets going with his teddy-bear, fatherly voice and fine guitar playing.

“Another Man’s Rain” from *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!* opens the show “brilliantly”, followed by “My Old Home”. There is a song about Johnny Cash and what his thoughts at the end of his life might have been, which the critic finds “highly ordinary” with a train rhythm, and a musical high point about a single father opening with the lines “Let’s stand and drink in a damn good pub …”. A calmer song from the newest album brings Mark Knopfler faintly to mind. Before the interval Leven sings a “delightful ballad” by David Childers, “Heart in My Soul”. The loudest laugh of the night comes with a coarse joke about the Scot who appeared in a porn film.

The only objection: why echo effects at such a concert, which irritated in at least two songs; they did not spoil the pleasure of Leven’s mastery of guitar and words, “a teddy-bear hug and good stories from a big, kindly grandfather”. The photo caption speaks of Leven’s more or less ironic arrogance, with which he conveyed how fantastic his new album is and what a genius the Scot is. The critic hopes the “friend of Drammen” returns soon and tickets sell out again.
zitate_kontext: Critic on the echo effects and Leven’s mastery
Critic on the start of the concert

2008-jackieleven-co-uk-gaestebuch-2008.kurz: The first roughly 45 entries (16.07.–20.12.2008) welcome the new official website and the album *Oh What A Blow That Phantom Dealt Me* or
inhalt: The first roughly 45 entries (16.07.–20.12.2008) welcome the new official website and the album *Oh What A Blow That Phantom Dealt Me* or Sir Vincent Lone's *Lovers at the Gun Club*. The dominant theme is the direct sale of the live album *Live From A Cornish Pub In Germany*: German fans ask how they are to pay without a British cheque, Britons are still waiting for their CD in September. Alongside this, concert greetings from Vienna (Chelsea, 15.09.), Hamburg, Berlin (Quasimodo), Bonn, Eppstein, Leiden, Dublin, Oslo, Bury, Hebden Bridge, London (Borderline, Putney) and Retford; a fan offers home-made Leven badges, a schoolboy from Johnstone thanks Leven for a school visit in December 2008. A Bonn fan raves about the stage story of “Black Bob”, another asks what in the tales is fact and what is fiction. A user who reveals himself as part of the organiser's circle reports the move of the concert on 07.12.2008 from Coffee Bliss (Lenzie) to Bar Bliss (Kirkintilloch) and then its cancellation. A fan from Liverpool thanks Leven, saying his music accompanied him through the end of an addiction.

2008-moors-magazine-lovers-at-the-gun-cl.kurz: Moors Magazine hails Lovers at the Gun Club as another chapter in Leven's grand narrative: a Celtic soul singer who combines folk with jazz, blues, rock and soul, "een absolute aanrader!" (an absolute must).
inhalt: The Dutch online paper Moors Magazine reviews *Lovers at the Gun Club* (Cooking Vinyl, COOKCD464) under the headline "keltische soulzanger maakt weer een meesterwerkje" ("Celtic soul singer makes another little masterpiece"). Leven is a British, lyrical singer-songwriter who has been turning out masterpieces for years without the general public seeming to notice. He is a Celtic soul singer who sublimely combines folk with jazz, blues, rock and soul in his arrangements.

He does not have a strong feel for melody, so his songs sometimes resemble each other, but in his case that is no objection, because his CDs of recent years can be heard in a single long, gripping session: you get the feeling of receiving another small piece of the "big Leven story" each time. The same goes here: the arrangements are as exciting and surprising as ever, Leven swings in a driven manner and the band is as inspired as the master.

For those who do not know Leven, the CD opens somewhat curiously with Johnny Dowd taking the lead vocal on the title track; Dowd makes another prominent appearance later. Perhaps even more curious is the closer, David Childers's "Heart in My Soul", simply "borrowed" from his CD *Hard Time County*. Yet it all fits exactly: Leven makes clear once more that it is purely about the music, and if the title track works better sung by Dowd, then Dowd sings it. Leven himself is back on old-fashioned form, as if he has been in the flow for years, so that one great masterly musical story is emerging. Although the reviewer should by now know what to expect, each new record knocks him flat again. Verdict: "Magnifiek", "een absolute aanrader!"

2008-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.titel: [Collected finds Nasjonalbiblioteket 2008: short notices, announcements, lists]

2008-timezone-moody-endless-beat-new-sar.kurz: The Salisbury music chronicle *Endless Beat* lists three John St Field gigs (1973/74) – among them with Man and the JSD Band – and later also names Jackie Leven among the artists who played there.
inhalt: In *Endless Beat: Voices of the New Sarum Sound, 1970–1999* Frogg Moody and co-authors document the music scene of Salisbury (Wiltshire), with a gig list. It records three appearances by **John St Field**: on 4 July 1973 at the City Hall together with the JSD Band, on 17 July 1973, also at the City Hall, together with **Man**, and on 8 March 1974 at the College of Technology. Later “Jackie Leven” also appears in a list of artists who played in Salisbury.
The list thus provides early dated live evidence of Leven’s beginnings under the name John St Field and shows him in southern England in 1973/74, not in Spain.

2009-01-r2-rock-n-reel-jackie-leven-outs.kurz: David Burke interviews Jackie Leven for R2 (Rock’n’Reel), January 2009: Leven talks candidly about his difficult early years and his heroin experience and says he could make four albums a year if allowed.
inhalt: The interview ‘Outside In’ by David Burke appeared in the January 2009 issue of the British folk and rock magazine R2 (Rock’n’Reel). It runs to almost 1,950 words and is available in full only from the archive Rock’s Backpages behind a paywall. According to the public teaser, Leven talks candidly about his difficult early years and his heroin experience. He also says he could make four albums a year if they let him – a remark that fits his well-known productivity.
Further details of the conversation are not known.

2009-02-13-gaesteliste-the-haunted-years.kurz: Ullrich Maurer reviews the first two Haunted Years double CDs (*Men in Prison*, *Munich Blues*) and calls Leven’s live albums a “double-edged sword”, because the storyteller’s gestures are missing.
inhalt: Ullrich Maurer reviews, for Gaesteliste.de, the reissue of Leven’s Haunted Valley live albums on Cooking Vinyl/Indigo. Leven would like to release even more CDs than he already does, he writes; one way is to put out live recordings, including those he sold through the Haunted Valley Society. The first two reissues come as a double CD.

Leven recorded *Men in Prison* in 2000 – “in the style of Johnny Cash”, to whom he had already dedicated an elegy – inside the men’s prison in Bergen, Norway, playing solo to the inmates “for safety’s sake”. The mood is accordingly a little frosty, perhaps also because Leven held back somewhat on his jokes. Quite different is the 2002 recording from the Muffathalle in Munich, where, accompanied by Michael Cosgrave and Deborah Greenwood, Leven rises to his best as an entertainer.

The verdict remains mixed: Leven’s live recordings are “a double-edged sword”, because the inimitable gestures of the master are missing on disc – he not only tells stories entertainingly but likes to act them out. The set is therefore probably more for fans who were not members of the Haunted Valley Society.

2009-02-17-ostlendingen-fra-bergen-fengs.kurz: Geir Hovensjø recommends the double CD *The Haunted Year – Winter* in Østlendingen: Leven alone in Bergen prison in 2003 is the stronger half – “Bergen is best!”
inhalt: The short review in Østlendingen (Elverum) presents *The Haunted Year – Winter* (Cooking Vinyl). The Scot Jackie Leven, placed in the text with “eighties Doll by Doll” (the band in fact ran from the late seventies to 1983), went off the rails but got himself back in and has since delivered a long run of fine albums where not least the lyrics impress. He evidently feels at home in Bergen.

On the first disc of the double album we meet him “all alone” with guitar at a concert in Bergen prison in 2003. In between he tells of his “crooked” life, and it comes out almost better than usual how well he sings when the music behind is stripped stark naked. The second disc is live from a café in Munich in 2000 with a couple of fellow musicians; the keyboard player lays on more of what we are used to from the studio albums. Hovensjø’s verdict: “Bergen er best!” – Bergen is best.
zitate_kontext: Hovensjø on the Bergen prison concert of 2003.

2009-02-24-bergensavisen-jackie-leven-me.kurz: A short review in Bergensavisen: Bergen finally has a proper prison record; Leven’s concert in Bergen prison is open and honest, the Munich concert more varied. Download tips: “Universal Blue” and “Call Mother a Lonely Field”.
inhalt: In the record column of Bergensavisen (24 February 2009), Frank Johnsen reviews the double CD *Men In Prison/Munich Blues* with the words: “At last Bergen has a proper prison record.” He seems to measure it against Johnny Cash’s famous prison recordings; the comparison is only fragmentarily legible in the scan.

In Bergen prison Leven naturally talks about his dark years as a heroin addict, but with a more positive undertone than many moralists would like. The Munich concert is more varied, since he has fellow musicians on stage. But the Bergen concert has “something open and honest” about it, not least because Leven describes the inmates as “amazingly good looking”. Johnsen’s download tips are “Universal Blue” and “Call Mother a Lonely Field”. The rating is illegible in the scan.

2009-02-netrhythms-haunted-year-winter.kurz: Mike Davies introduces the first of Leven's seasonal double-CD reissues of his fan-club albums for NetRhythms: Munich Blues (live in Munich) and Men in Prison (recorded in Bergen men's prison).
inhalt: Mike Davies reviews *The Haunted Year – Winter* (Cooking Vinyl) for NetRhythms. Over 25 years, he notes, Leven has released 16 solo albums (one as Sir Vincent Lone), most recently *Lovers at the Gun Club*, and listeners will probably know *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*, *Fairytales for Hard Men* and *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me*. Unless you belong to his Haunted Valley appreciation society, though, you will not know that since 1998 he has also made eight limited-edition, mostly live albums. With the demise of the society's quarterly magazine they are now being sold commercially as four double CDs, one per season.

*Munich Blues*, from spring 2000, comes from a show at Munich's Cafe Muffathalle. Judging by the between-song banter it was a playful evening (he remarks that whenever anyone calls from Germany he is on the toilet). The set includes a rousing "Looking for Love", the moody Celtic blues "Stranger on the Square", a haunting "Single Father" and, as a treat, his muscular cover of "You've Lost That Loving Feeling". He was joined by regular collaborators Michael Cosgrave and Deborah Greenwood.

*Men in Prison*, recorded in March 2003 in Bergen men's prison in Norway, is a one-man show apart from the opening choral title track, taken from *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West*, and a lot more intense. Leven introduces himself by recalling his own troubled past of violence, drugs and prisons, then launches into six minutes of "Extremely Violent Man". He loosens up as the show develops: "Poortoun" with memories of his birthplace in Fife, "Call Mother a Lonely Field" about Irish ex-pats in London, the meditative bluesy ballad "The Garden" ("a drinking song"), a punchy "Classic Northern Diversions" and finally the jazzy blues "The Crazy Song", by which time Davies reckons the audience is contemplating a mass breakout to catch his next show on the tour. The review is friendly and informative rather than evaluative.
zitate_kontext: Davies on the plan for the series
Davies on the end of Men in Prison

2009-03-01-record-collector-haunted-year.kurz: Kris Needs welcomes the start of the Haunted Year series in *Record Collector*: *Men In Prison & Munich Blues* find Leven, “the UK's mightiest troubadour”, on top form.
inhalt: In Record Collector (issue 361, March 2009) Kris Needs reviews the double-header *Winter: Men In Prison & Munich Blues* (Cooking Vinyl, COOKCD 483), the opening of Leven's “Haunted Year” series. By way of background, he explains that between 1994 and 2004 Leven, “the UK's mightiest troubadour”, ran an appreciation society called The Haunted Valley, which released an annual members-only live album. With the operation fallen to the internet, the eight albums were being released in 2009 as four double-headers.

Anyone who has followed Leven's “highly-personalised journey” since Doll By Doll confronted the world over thirty years ago will welcome the scene-setting “heavenly chorale” of “Men In Prison”, from 1995's *Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West*, before lapping up a 2000 gig recorded at Bergen Men's Prison, Norway, where Leven is on top form on tracks such as the “starklybeautiful” ballad “The Garden”. *Munich Blues*, in Needs's account, was recorded in 2002 at the Café Muffathalle in Munich, with the multi-instrumentalist Michael Cosgrave and the singer Debbie Greenwood on “intimate gems” including “Universal Blue” and a “heartfelt” version of “You've Lost That Loving Feeling”. The booklet features Leven's “Deep Pool” blogs, which he thinks worthy of a possible book.

For Needs it is a great start to the “much-deserved consummation” of a “fearlessly uncompromising artist” who deserves to be up there with the greats, yet is still playing pubs and probably wouldn't have it any other way. Note: his dates for the recordings differ from other sources, which place *Men in Prison* in March 2003 and *Munich Blues* in 2000.
zitate_kontext: Kris Needs, closing sentence of the review

2009-03-17-laagendalsposten-knut-buen-og.titel: [Kongsberg Jazz Festival 2009: Knut Buen meets Jackie Leven]
2009-03-17-laagendalsposten-knut-buen-og.kurz: Previewing the Kongsberg Jazz Festival 2009, the paper calls the meeting of folk musician Knut Buen and “tough Scot” Jackie Leven the festival's most original pairing, introducing Leven as a “musician's musician”.
inhalt: Terje Jensen reports in Laagendalsposten on the nearly complete programme of the 2009 Kongsberg Jazz Festival. The festival's “most original constellation” will undoubtedly be the meeting of master fiddler Knut Buen and the Scottish singer Jackie Leven (headline: “Knut Buen meets tough Scot”). Leven, whose varied career the article mentions, is described as a “musician's musician” and compared with Mike Scott, Elvis Costello and Van Morrison; others have called him “the toughest Scottish export since malt whisky”. He is very productive, happily releasing one or two albums a year, and enjoys great respect, above all at home, for both records and strong live shows.

Buen is among his admirers: a few years ago he sent Leven three of his records as a Christmas present; Leven was thrilled with what he heard, and the idea of a musical meeting has been in the air since. The article describes Buen, from Jondalen, as one of Norway's leading folk musicians, who has for decades promoted folk music as fiddler, author, composer, columnist and publisher and often crosses genre lines with jazz, blues and art-music players. “Leven/Buen” runs under the festival's blues umbrella at Christians Kjeller on the festival Thursday. Marketing chief Eric Malling says the blues programme, like the whole festival, is meant to challenge boundaries: blues fans get what they ask for, but also something to chew on, if the aim of becoming the country's most interesting blues stage is to be met. The article expects an exciting séance between two strong personalities.
zitate_kontext: Terje Jensen on the festival programme.
How others have characterised Leven, according to the article.

2009-04-27-musicomh-man-bleeds-in-glasgo.kurz: Nic Oliver gives the double CD *Man Bleeds In Glasgow / Greetings From Milford* four stars out of five: Leven is a fine live act whose songs sound better stripped bare; stage patter, covers and “Main Travelled Roads” are praised.
inhalt: Nic Oliver’s review (musicOMH, 27 April 2009, four out of five stars) covers a double CD of two older live releases previously issued through the Haunted Valley website, which has been serving fans of the Scottish singer-songwriter since the late 1990s. Best by far, he says, is *Man Bleeds In Glasgow*, a 1998 release that pairs Leven with The Celtic Soulmen, aka Michael Cosgrave and the virtuoso multi-instrumentalist Steáfán Hannigan.

Leven is a fine live act, his songs better suited to the stripped-down interpretations he performs on stage. The “rather bland” production style that occasionally mars his studio albums is absent; songs such as “Farm Boy”, “Man Bleeds In Glasgow” and “Night Lilies” benefit from the “bare-faced nakedness” of their live readings and give Leven’s “rich Scottish soul vocals” room to shine. Part of the Leven live experience is the on-stage banter, here with stabs at left-leaning music journalists and CNN and larger-than-life tales from the pub and bedroom, in that order. The programme is largely drawn from the same year’s *Night Lilies*, but also casts back to his early solo releases and closes with the “cast-iron classic” “Call Mother A Lonely Field”.

*Greetings From Milford*, recorded, according to Oliver, at the 1999 Haunted Valley Christmas party, features The Stornoway Girls (Kevin Hewick, Dan Britton and Lee Allotson). It reveals Leven as a fine interpreter of other artists’ songs: a stately reading of “Pale Blue Eyes”, an energetic thrash through “Waiting For My Man”, and the chutzpah to attempt Van Morrison’s “Madam George”, to which he brings something new. Among the originals the most pleasing is the closing take on Doll By Doll’s “Main Travelled Roads”, a reminder of how long Leven has been one of the UK’s leading songwriters, “albeit one who has had to live with a cult following”. The final word goes to the man himself – “Genius or nutter, you decide” – and Leven is neither, just another of the country’s neglected national treasures, happy to carry on at his own pace.
zitate_kontext: Nic Oliver on Leven’s live qualities

2009-04-bluesnews-jackie-leven-live-at-b.kurz: An enthusiastic review of the double CD *Live At Bergen Men’s Prison / Munich Blues*: the prison recording is perhaps the best solo recording by Leven the reviewer has heard; by the end of the seven songs even the toughest inmates had surrendered.
inhalt: The Norwegian Blues Union reviews in its magazine Bluesnews (no. 59, April 2009) the double CD with which Leven makes recordings from his now inactive fan club available through regular channels. Through the fan club Leven released many live and special recordings under various titles; now he wants to make several of them available for sale, and the first two arrive as a double CD at the price of a single one.

The first concert is from Munich in spring 2000 with his partner Deborah (vocals) and his “ever faithful” Michael Cosgrave (keyboards, trumpet). More important, however, is the solo recording from the men’s prison in Bergen in February 2003, which the reviewer had seen go for three to four times the normal CD price on eBay. The setting – some of Norway’s toughest criminals who had probably never listened to Leven’s sensitive Scottish soul and singer-songwriter art – was so special that it put “our dear friend of Norway” on his toes. The sound is very good, and Leven speaks quite openly about his relationship with heroin and his years in Scottish and English prisons (a self-report the review merely relays). With some of his very best songs, from “Extremely Violent Man” to “Poortoun” and “Call Mother A Lonely Field”, this is “perhaps the best solo recording I have heard of Jackie”. Bergen is one of his favourite cities in the world, and by the time he finished his seven songs even the toughest prisoners had surrendered.

The Munich concert, three years earlier, is more an ordinary concert from a longer German tour, but also a very sharp evening. Leven himself was “really out of sorts”, anti-social and unusually uninterested in meeting his audience, but fantastic sound and an attentive crowd got him and his musicians to deliver a “razor-sharp show” – with entirely different songs from Bergen, from “Looking For Love” to the lovely “Stranger On The Square” and the magical “Paris Blues”. He closes with one of his rare covers, “You’ve Lost That Lovin’ Feelin’”, which he makes his own. Combined with his storytelling gift and the humorous, ironic comments along the way, these are two of the best concert recordings Leven has released; getting both on a double CD is “a steal”.
zitate_kontext: Reviewer on the effect on the inmates

2009-05-05-soundi-the-haunted-year-men-i.kurz: Timo Kanerva gives the double CD *The Haunted Year – Men in Prison/Munich Blues* four stars out of five in Soundi: Leven is a kindred spirit of Van Morrison, at one with audience and songs in a prison and a café.
inhalt: Kanerva begins with a comparison: Jackie Leven is one of Van Morrison’s kindred spirits. They share much of the same soul fire drawn from Celtic roots, and both have their roots in folk and blues. But whereas Morrison became a star as a youth, big success has always shunned Leven.

He has been making music for a very long time, first as leader of the band Doll by Doll, then as a solo artist, with more than two dozen albums to his name. The large output has meant rather uneven recordings; of the Leven albums that have come the reviewer’s way, only the ten-year-old *Night Lilies* is a flawless masterpiece. *The Haunted Year* is now the second full hit, a live double with two solo gigs, one in a Norwegian prison and the other in a Munich café.

Although the years have not treated Leven with silk gloves, he is present in both concerts in a unique way: he plays his acoustic guitar both forcefully and with nuance, tells stories from his life and sings tenderly and manfully in his deep, expressive baritone. “Only a great artist can be so completely at peace with both his audience and his songs.” The page records publication in Soundi 4/2004; this probably means 4/2009, since the double CD only appeared in 2009.

2009-05-netrhythms-haunted-year-spring.kurz: Mike Davies reviews the double CD *Spring* for NetRhythms (May 2009): *Man Bleeds in Glasgow* (1998) and *Greetings from Milford* (1999). He stresses Leven’s humour and cover versions: a very good year for Leven fans.
inhalt: Mike Davies’s review (NetRhythms, May 2009) covers the second double instalment of the series in which Leven releases previously fan-club-only live recordings generally. By Davies’s account the two discs date from 1998 and 1999. *Man Bleeds in Glasgow* was taped at a Water Rats gig in London with the Celtic Soulmen, Michael Cosgrave (keyboards) and Stephen Hannigan (uilleann pipes), and draws several songs from 1994’s *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*. *Greetings from Milford* records the fanzine’s annual Christmas bash with the Stornoway Girls in the British Legion Club at Milford, Derbyshire.

On *Man Bleeds* Leven quotes a Guardian review (“Don’t go expecting light entertainment”) after warming up the crowd with the arms-linked swayer “Farm Boy”, thereby underscoring his often overlooked sense of humour. Davies agrees with the paper that Leven’s songs carry dark shadings, dwelling on emotional dysfunction, masculinity and the human condition, and that bouncy singalongs do not characterise his shows. What you get is passionate, intense performance drawn from a love of folk, jazz and blues. Highlights, he says, are “Night Lilies”, Hannigan’s showcase in “Glenarm/Burning the Box of Beautiful Things”, the cheery “Deep Choking Wooded Death Fix”, a wailing, Gaelic-infused “Call Mother a Lonely Field” and the brooding title track. A between-song anecdote about “Erotic Football Results” suggests Leven might have had a second career as a stand-up.

*Greetings from Milford*, by contrast, leavens original material with covers that underline his influences: Dylan’s “She Belongs to Me”, Van Morrison’s “Madame George”, a 1970s chicken-scratch funk take on Bill Withers’s “Who Is He and What Is He to You?” and two Velvet Underground songs, a “gorgeously world weary” “Pale Blue Eyes” and a “suitably ragged rowdy” “Waiting for My Man”. From his own songbook come “Walking in Argyll”, “Listening to Crows Pray” and “Paris Blues”. The real treat, Davies says, is a rare return to Doll by Doll days with a heart-stirring revival of their “monumentally majestic classic” “Main Travelled Roads”.
His verdict: with the summer and autumn releases still to come, it is adding up to “quite a very good year for Leven fans”.
zitate_kontext: Davies on Leven’s live performances on *Man Bleeds in Glasgow*

2009-06-04-record-collector-jackie-leven.kurz: Debbie Neech praises Leven's set at Whitstable Folk Club in Record Collector (no. 366): anecdotes, attacking guitar and a voice ranging from poetry to growls, summed up in one word, "Unique."
inhalt: Debbie Neech reviews Leven's gig at Whitstable Folk Club on 4 June 2009 for *Record Collector* (issue 366, online 25 July 2009). With an endless fund of anecdotes, such as how Ralph McTell "put the fear of God" into him at their first meeting, Leven observes life and translates what he sees into music. His own life has been a roller-coaster, battling addiction, homelessness and a mugging that robbed him of his voice, yet he has emerged with his spirit intact and songs that are moving, haunting and uplifting.

"Standing in Another Man's Rain" got the evening off to a flying start and set the standard, maintained throughout, up to the closing number, "The White Bars of Heaven". In between came a flurry of highlights: an elegy to Johnny Cash, a rumination on ravens, and psychedelic blues segueing into the Beatles via Van Morrison and Donovan. All of it was accompanied by great, attacking guitar, while his voice ranged from poetry to barely distinguishable growls. The verdict is a single word: "Unique."

2009-06-10-diskant-jackie-leven-the-haun.kurz: Morten Wamsler finds Leven strong as a songwriter and singer but less compelling as a live entertainer on the double CD *The Haunted Year – Spring*; his verdict is a mixed picture of the “king of Celtic soul”.
inhalt: The Danish reviewer Morten Wamsler opens with his verdict: Leven is an uncannily gifted songwriter and a strong vocalist, but not quite as great an entertainer, and as a live artist not quite as attractive as his songs – so the result is a mixed whole from the “king of Celtic soul”. He headlines the first part, with irony, “Intense but stagnant”: Leven, he says, is to traditional Celtic music what Cliff Richard is to modern pop – very Celtic and very little modern. He is widely called the King of Celtic Soul, and for all the backward-looking, tradition-faithful character, the quality of this double live album, which shows “two sides of the king”, cannot be denied.

The first disc, *Man Bleeds In Glasgow*, presents Leven with the band The Celtic Soulmen, whose backing is solid, dependable and at times almost anonymous, leaving Leven as the focal point and giving the timeless compositions plenty of room; more traditional folk instruments are used. For a concert recording, Wamsler finds it too static: it was probably atmospheric to be there, but listening to the reissue it is “on the edge of boring”. “Glenarm / Burning The Box Of Beautiful Things”, however, brings it to the brink of a folk masterpiece, and the classic “Night Lilies” also works well.

The second disc, *Greetings From Milford*, is more colourful and lively. It is still traditional, with the nearly sixty-year-old Leven as the seasoned anchorman, but The Stornoway Girls pump life into several numbers. “Listening To Crows Pray” is nothing short of outstanding, while “Who Is He And What Is He To You?” has an almost funky feel that swings nicely. There are fine, captivating highlights, but too few for a double live album. Wamsler gives no score.
zitate_kontext: Morten Wamsler on Leven and Celtic tradition.
Wamsler on Leven’s strengths and limits.

2009-06-il-popolo-del-blues-spring-man-b.kurz: Salvatore Esposito praises the spring instalment of the *Haunted Year* series: *Man Bleeds in Glasgow* (1998) and *Greetings from Milford* (1999) show Leven as a compelling performer, with “Main Travelled Roads” better than the original.
inhalt: Salvatore Esposito reviews *Spring* for Il Popolo del Blues, the spring instalment of *The Haunted Year*, in which Leven presents previously unreleased live recordings season by season. The series opened with the double album *Winter*, bringing together two concerts, one in a Norwegian prison and one in a Munich café. The spring concerts too were sold in advance via the internet.

*Man Bleeds in Glasgow* dates from 1998 at the Water Rats Theatre in London, with Leven and the Celtic Soulmen, Michael Cosgrave and the multi-instrumentalist Steafan Hannigan. Esposito calls it an absolutely surprising concert in which all the qualities of the Scottish songwriter as a performer can be appreciated, as in the excellent versions of “Farm Boy”, “Man Bleeds In Glasgow” and “Night Lilies”, at the time brand new and in his view one of the peaks of Leven's career. The ironic closer “Call Mother A Lonely Field”, following the equally irresistible “Erotic Football Results”, is also unmissable.

*Greetings from Milford* dates from the following year, from the annual Haunted Valley Christmas Party at the British Legion Club in Milford, Derbyshire. Covers stand out: Bob Dylan's “She Belongs To Me”, two very personal rereadings of Lou Reed (“Pale Blue Eyes” and the splendid “Waiting For My Man”) and Van Morrison's “Madame George”. The concert closes with an excellent rendition of Doll By Doll's “Main Travelled Roads”, in a version absolutely superior to the original. The series is a thoroughly successful undertaking, Esposito says, and he hopes it will help make Leven known not only as a songwriter but as a compelling performer. The review is followed by the 23-track list of the double CD.
zitate_kontext: Salvatore Esposito on the close of *Greetings from Milford*.

2009-07-02-drammens-tidende-unikt-musikk.kurz: A preview of the concert by Jackie Leven and Knut Buen at the Kongsberg Jazz Festival: a commissioned work conceived by the comedian Jon Gjerde, bringing the Hardanger fiddle together with a Scottish songwriter.
inhalt: Drammens Tidende of 2 July 2009 reports from Kongsberg on the day of the concert: when the Scot Jackie Leven and the Telemarker Knut Buen meet that evening, it is a milestone in the jazz festival’s history. The director is Jon Gjerde of Drammen. According to the piece it is the first commissioned work in the festival’s 50-year history, and the trade magazine Fidelity calls the concert at Christians Kjeller “the cultural event of the year”; the unusual meeting of the famous Scottish singer-songwriter with one of Norway’s leading folk musicians has caused a stir.

Gjerde, 56, a stand-up comedian, copywriter, actor and artist, has believed in the idea since 2005. It came to him while renting a mountain farm in Tuddal one summer: Knut Buen is “a clone of Espen Askeladd and Myllarguten”, a superb folk musician; in the car he was playing Leven as usual, and the thoughts met. “They are both strong tradition bearers with quite different standpoints, but neither of them is an A4 figure. There is something of a fairy tale about both.” He is looking forward “like a child” to seeing whether the bridge between two cultures holds.

The concert includes several newly written Leven songs given the unmistakable character of the Hardanger fiddle. Buen compares himself with Leven: both are free improvisers who need no script, and there is no school for learning the Hardanger fiddle – it is all about what you manage to find. He expects both wistful interplay and wild improvisation, and knows the moment may be hard to repeat. Leven himself is full of enthusiasm for Gjerde’s ideas and artistic abilities: you do not meet many who work entirely without thinking of their ego.
zitate_kontext: Knut Buen on Leven and the Hardanger fiddle

2009-07-03-dalane-tidende-jackie-leven-d.kurz: Profile in the festival programme of the Visefestivalen in Egersund (section “Dalane Brygghus”). Aalbu strings together the Leven legends, expressly as hearsay (“etter sigende”): the first pupil in Scotland to be expelled from school for drug possession; Doll by Doll shortly before the breakthrough; in 1984 on the…
inhalt: Profile in the festival programme of the Visefestivalen in Egersund (section “Dalane Brygghus”). Aalbu strings together the Leven legends, expressly as hearsay (“etter sigende”): the first pupil in Scotland to be expelled from school for drug possession; Doll by Doll shortly before the breakthrough; attacked in 1984 on the way home from the studio and kicked in the larynx; a doctor is said to have prescribed him anabolic steroids, which led him to heroin and into deep depression; exit with a method he developed himself, including Chinese acupuncture, founding of a detox clinic and of The Core Trust; his girlfriend ran off with the Dalai Lama's bodyguard. In 1994 the comeback with *The Mystery of Love…* (with Mike Scott and Robert Bly), plus his own whisky “Leven’s Lament”, which Salman Rushdie is said to have recommended in the booklet. As highlights of the discography he apparently names *Fairy Tales for Hard Men*, *Creatures of Light and Darkness* and *Shining Brother Shining Sister* (titles garbled in the OCR). Live spartan with acoustic guitar, on record opulent and Celtic-masculine.

2009-07-04-laagendalsposten-folkelig-top.kurz: Lars Bryne watches Knut Buen and Jackie Leven at the Kongsberg Jazz Festival: Hardanger fiddle meets folk singer, and despite audience chatter it was “great art”.
inhalt: Lars Bryne reports in Laagendalsposten on the concert by Knut Buen and Jackie Leven on Thursday evening, 2 July 2009, in the backyard of Christians Kjeller at the Kongsberg Jazz Festival. He calls them “two great musicians from different camps”; they had not shared a stage before.

Mixing the Hardanger fiddle with the folk singer Leven may sound a bit odd, but the meeting went quite well. Folk tunes fit nicely into a jazz-festival setting, whether rooted in Africa or in Jondalen. The audience, at any rate, was carried away, and Buen's philosophical humour spread across a backyard full of expectant listeners; Buen is as much a funny man as a fantastic musician.

The festival management was quick the next day to apologise that the two had not been given the right stage, since the music demanded something of its listeners. A crowd in festival mood easily brings chatter with it, which marked the second half of the concert somewhat. But, the verdict runs, it was great art all the same.

2009-07-06-dalane-tidende-fantastisk-his.kurz: Paal Kvassheim hails Leven in Dalane Tidende as a “fantastic storyteller”: a big man marked by life, whose tall tales at the Brygghus in Egersund had the audience cheering, accompanied by rough songs about ravens and the theft of urban souls.
inhalt: The short review (headline “Fantastisk historieforteller – og publikum jublet”, “Fantastic storyteller – and the audience cheered”) covers Leven's show at the Dalane Brygghus in Egersund, evidently as part of the Egersund song festival (Visefestival), on which the same issue reports at length. Kvassheim opens by calling Leven “a big man in several ways”, a fellow who has experienced a lot in life, “and that has perhaps taken its toll”. The benefit for the audience is that it gets to take part in Leven's life through the stories he tells. It was “actually quite fantastic” to sit in the Brygghus in Egersund and share in such musical joy.

Leven tells tall tales, such as that he was thrown out of Alicia Keys's limousine and that he finally wrote a tribute to the man he had hated for many years, Johnny Cash. He talks about sex, drink and a long life in the music business, and his songs are rough: they are about ravens and the theft of urban souls. The anecdotes are Leven's stage stories and unverified. In the same column block follows a review of the Lenny Smith / Larry Norman tribute in Egersund church.

2009-07-07-varden-buen-og-leven-gi-ut-pl.kurz: Karina Hagen reports in Varden on the premiere of the commissioned work by Knut Buen and Jackie Leven in Kongsberg: the pair plan a joint record and another concert in Tuddal.
inhalt: Varden (Skien) reports on 7 July 2009 on the ‘commissioned work’ at the Kongsberg Jazz Festival with the Hardanger fiddler Knut Buen and the Scot Jackie Leven. There was great interest in this meeting, “bringing together folk music and folk music”, and the premiere on the Thursday of the previous week in the garden in front of the small stage at Christians Kjeller drew old and young. The idea came from the blues and folk enthusiast Jon Gjerde, who brought together Leven – a musician many consider among Scotland’s most interesting – and Buen.

The compère said the two had asked to be introduced as “an old geezer from Scotland together with an old geezer from Telemark”, but that he would rather call them two great musical personalities. Leven then took the microphone and, “in true Buen fashion”, charmed the audience with anecdotes and stories between songs. When Buen stepped onto the podium a little under an hour into the concert, the audience was well warmed up and musically ‘tenderised’. He began as usual with a poem reading in the town where he was born 61 years ago. The programme: springar, gangar, folk tunes and songs, “almost all of it bound together by the red thread of love”.

Buen says he had to develop a Hardanger-fiddle foundation specially for Leven’s songs: “He is a shining poet with points from a life most of us can relate to.” They worked a few days at the hotel in Tuddal on rhythm and tone. He is pleased with the interplay and would gladly repeat it. He and Leven have already talked about making a record “with a good deal of Hardanger fiddle”; Leven would also like to play at Tuddal amphitheatre, for which there was no time this time. The headline promises a record and a further concert; whether they happened the text does not say.
zitate_kontext: From the conversation with Buen about the record

2009-07-24-gaesteliste-the-haunted-year-.kurz: Ullrich Maurer reviews the double CD *The Haunted Year – Barefoot Days*: live recordings full of stories plus a few studio rarities – solid, mainly for fans and collectors.
inhalt: Ullrich Maurer first explains the background: since 1994 Leven has collected his live performances on recordings and sold them through the exclusive club The Haunted Valley. Now that the club no longer exists, he has softened up his label to make these live CDs (with studio oddities and other treats) available to “normal” fans too – the Scot would in any case like to release far more records than he does, and even invented an alter ego in Sir Vince Lone.

The double CD, with recordings from Brighton and Yorkshire, offers a few Jackie standards, some guests (David Thomas among them) and above all the absurd stories that make up much of every show – happily ones the fan does not necessarily know already. For hunters and collectors the studio recordings are the real attraction. Verdict: “solid”, at least for the “Elevens” (Leven devotees).
zitate_kontext: Ullrich Maurer on the content of the double CD.

2009-07-25-record-collector-troubadour-h.kurz: In Record Collector, Kris Needs unmasks the supposedly deceased Sir Vincent Lone as Leven “in fanciful mood” and praises *Troubadour Heart* as an intimate, vocally superb record by an underrated talent.
inhalt: Kris Needs reviews *Troubadour Heart* (Cooking Vinyl, COOKCD 478) in Record Collector, issue 366. The album purports to be one of three albums by a recently deceased eccentric drunk called Sir Vincent Lone, available only in person from a London coffee house; in truth, Needs says, it is the incredibly prolific Jackie Leven in fanciful mood, heading for the open road again and taking in some startling scenery on his never-ending journey.

For fans of Doll by Doll, Needs singles out a new acoustic version of “An Honest Woman”, originally a 12-inch B-side but always a behemoth live highlight, now given a different emotional tilt. The rest of the album, which ends with a guest track from Leven's mate Chris Conway, steers with customary bared-soul intimacy through songs such as “Florin/Tweed”, which seem even more to be casting back to a bygone time, depicted with the kind of lyrical detail that makes Leven a unique figure.

None of it would stand up, he adds, without that incredible voice, in heart-tearing form on “His Arms Are Full Of Broken Things”, while Bert Jansch's “Strolling Down The Highway” is an inspired and very suitable choice of cover for this greatly underrated talent.
zitate_kontext: Needs on the voice and the choice of cover

2009-07-30-the-skinny-sir-vincent-lone-t.kurz: Joe Barton awards four stars to *Troubadour Heart*: Leven “kills off” his pseudonym Sir Vincent Lone and produces a “posthumous” album better than the usual retrospectives – “a fine epitaph”.
inhalt: Joe Barton reviews Sir Vincent Lone's *Troubadour Heart* (Cooking Vinyl, released 27 July) in The Skinny (30 July 2009, four stars). Jackie Leven kills off his musical pseudonym and consequently produces a “posthumous” album that is actually better than the kind of retrospective albums released when songwriters actually kick the bucket.

The stripped-down production suits Lone's backstory of having been a regular at the Troubadour Coffee House in London: “Strolling Down The Highway” displays an authentic café blues performer vibe, all plucked harmonics and fingerpicked twiddles. However, it is on “Rove On Wraith Of Raith” that Leven surpasses the Lone persona and moves into the territory of sheer beautiful lyricism: a delicately delivered vocal threaded over gentle guitar work, allowing the lyrics' imagery to come to the fore. That collaborator Ian Rankin gets namechecked in the song is appropriate, since Leven's lyrics are as captivating as the prose of any thriller author, and the creation of Sir Vincent Lone served as a media-bucking outlet for his magnificent songwriting. A fine epitaph.

2009-07-netrhythms-haunted-year-summer.kurz: Mike Davies reviews the double CD *Summer: Barefoot Days / Deep in the Heart of Nowhere*: two live recordings in which Leven’s between-song stories outrun the songs, with David Thomas as a guest.
inhalt: Mike Davies reviews the third of the seasonal double discs with which Cooking Vinyl reissues Leven’s fan-club albums, originally available only through the Haunted Valley appreciation society. Disc one comes from a show at the Black Horse in Otley, Yorkshire, and opens with the studio-recorded title track, Leven “in familiar contemplative downbeat mood”, pondering mortality with death following a few steps behind. The live ‘Desolation Blues’ is no cheerier, with its dead heart and the funeral of his best friend, partly about his old mate Scots John – not to be confused with Scouse John, another friend whose death he discusses in the sleeve notes – who is the subject of a near seven-minute anecdote.

Davies’s central point is that the between-song ramblings often run longer than the songs themselves, but he finds them fascinating. In ‘How He Met Joni Mitchell, Matt Monroe and the Chip Packet/Dirty Underpants’ Leven goes from treading on Joni’s foot in Soho to declining a request because, without the falsetto, it would sound like Matt Munro on smack, then to greasy chip packets, and finally to washing his pants on tour as an intro to ‘Washing by Hand’. That leaves room for only six songs: ‘Billy Ate My Pocket’ (infidelity and a close equine encounter), Leven’s melancholic setting of Robert Frost’s ‘Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening’ and, after a lengthy preamble about English history, the bleak parting shot ‘Exit Wound’.

Disc two combines two studio recordings – the traditional ‘Nottamun Town’ and ‘Rain of Kathleen’, whose lyric mentions ‘defending ancient springs’, the title of his 2000 album – with a recording from The Greys, Brighton. Again there is plenty of banter: the Daily Telegraph, a gender-conflicted New York plugger, regional styles of complaining, a Bethesda chip shop and a school Viking history lesson. This time there are more songs, including ‘Universal Blues’, ‘Marble City Blues’, ‘Single Father’ and ‘Working Man’s Love Song’. ‘Paris Blues’, already on *Winter* and *Spring*, makes it a hat trick and segues into “a rather fine version” of the David Thomas song ‘Down by the River’, with the Pere Ubu singer guesting on falsetto and improvising about how hard it is to be a Brian Wilson fan. Davies regrets that the duet on ‘You’ve Lost That Loving Feeling’ promised in the press release is missing, but concludes that this is still a summer to savour.

2009-08-03-musicomh-barefoot-days-deep-i.kurz: Nic Oliver gives three out of five stars to the reissue of *Barefoot Days* and *Deep In The Heart Of Nowhere*: a “criminally overlooked songwriter” and a live performer of “flawed beauty”.
inhalt: Nic Oliver reviews for musicOMH the latest twofer in the reissue programme, which is “building up a fair head of steam”: *Deep In The Heart Of Nowhere* (dated by him to 2001, originally released through the Haunted Valley website) and *Barefoot Days* (2004 according to Oliver, previously only an official bootleg). Both albums mix specially recorded studio tracks with highlights from Leven’s entertaining live shows.

*Barefoot Days* opens with the studio-recorded title track, a sweeping ballad about death stalking us as we go about our lives, “affecting and sombre in equal measure” – typical Leven, “a criminally overlooked songwriter”. The live section, recorded at Greys in Brighton, is a typical set: witty tall and not so tall tales from his years on the road interspersed with choice selections from his back catalogue. The best anecdote concerns an accidental meeting with Joni Mitchell during a drunken night out; the musical highlights include a stately reading of “Desolation Blues” and the keenly observed story songs “Stopped By Woods On A Snowy Evening” and “Washing By Hand”.

*Deep In The Heart Of Nowhere* starts with two studio tracks, the heartfelt “Rain Of Kathleen”, with excellent picking, and the traditional “Nottamun Town”. The live part is a more complete set and gives a more accurate picture of a typical Leven show: songs from *Defending Ancient Springs*, including “Single Father” and “Working Man’s Love Song”, and “Paris Blues/Down By The River” with David Thomas as a guest, plus earlier highlights (notably “Marble City Bar”) and unreleased material. The flow is less convincing than on *Barefoot Days* but more representative: bathos and pathos lurch along side by side and nothing sounds planned. That is why Leven is such a live draw: forget choreographed stage acts – he is “a living, breathing representation of the human condition in all its flawed beauty”. “Long may he live.”
zitate_kontext: Oliver on *Deep In The Heart Of Nowhere*.

2009-09-11-gaesteliste-sir-vincent-lone-.kurz: Ullrich Maurer declares Sir Vincent Lone “dead”: the alter ego has served its purpose, though *Troubadour Heart* is still a good Leven interim album with humorous “instant Leven classics”.
inhalt: The short review opens with an obituary: “Sir Vincent Lone is dead.” That is no surprise, since the “bastard” never had a proper chance. By Leven's own account, Lone, his alter ego, existed only so that he could release more records. But Leven is now with a label that goes along with every release-related whim of the “master”, so three or four Leven albums appear each year anyway and Lone has served his purpose. There was hardly a musical reason for Lone: he does nothing really different from Leven and does not even disguise his voice.

Accordingly, *Troubadour Heart*, the third Lone album, is more a typical Leven interim record: two or three thoroughly structured and orchestrated numbers, mostly acoustic material that showcases Leven's skills as an instrumentalist, and live recordings. Even so, Maurer concedes without envy, it is not a bad interim album, as it contains some “instant Leven classics” that fully convince especially on the humorous side; Sir Vincent Lone was perhaps less depressive than Leven sometimes is. The album had been available only at concerts until now and is released generally on Cooking Vinyl/Indigo.
zitate_kontext: Ullrich Maurer, opening of the review
Maurer's parenthetical remark near the end

2009-10-22-harknessian-mixcloud-elegy-fo.kurz: An 18-minute interview with Leven from the interval of his concert at the Fife Acoustic Music Club in Kirkcaldy on 22 October 2009, uploaded to Mixcloud later as an obituary. Only the uploader’s description is available, not the conversation itself.
inhalt: The Mixcloud channel Harknessian has put online an 18:14-minute audio piece titled “Elegy for Jackie Leven”: an interview together with a live performance from the Kirkcaldy Acoustic Music Club in October 2009. According to the uploader, the conversation took place during the interval of Leven’s concert at the Fife Acoustic Music Club at the Polish Club on 22 October 2009, which proved to be a memorable home-coming gig.

According to the description, Leven gives “a candid insight” into his itinerant lifestyle, his troubled past and his relationship with Fife, talks about his introduction to music in his formative years and touches on his Romany heritage, the “colourful” reasoning for choosing his first pseudonym John St Field, Doll by Doll’s antagonistic relationship with punk and his respect for his label Cooking Vinyl. The uploader calls Leven one of Fife’s greatest musical exports, an engaging raconteur, a gentleman and a prolific and consummate musician of the highest order; “Sadly there will be no Encore – RIP Jackie Leven”, he ends, closing with the line: “Bury me in the Village Square; where I can hear the feet of the children and the drums of the old men.” The audio itself has not been evaluated here; tags include Ian Rankin, Cooking Vinyl and Doll by Doll.
zitate_kontext: Line with which the uploader closes his description

2009-11-30-diskoryxeion-jackie-leven-gre.kurz: A Greek music blog reproduces Leven's booklet note for *Greek Notebook*, his sketches from the island of Astypalea, and recommends the “significant artist” to fans of the acid-folk album *Control*.
inhalt: The blog post of 30 November 2009 (by Fontas Troussas) consists mainly of Leven's own booklet note for *Greek Notebook*, signed “Jackie 1999”. Leven writes that one of the loveliest things in his long life was spending every May and September for seven years on the remote Greek island of Astypalea, fourteen months in all, “a significant part of my life”. The island is harsh and mountainous and off the tourist track; on a very clear day one can see Rhodes, a hundred miles away, from the top of the old town. From early morning to the golden evening he sat in his ancient hilltop house, “more a cave really”, singing and playing guitar, with occasional breaks to lie on the beach, visit great bars and restaurants, or smell the night lilies.

Much of it he recorded in “glorious lo-fi” on a Sony Professional Walkman, leaving about forty hours of sketches. The album is a selection from those tapes with “all kinds of weird and wonderful moments, including the odd boring bit – I'm not the genius all the time”. Songwriters are welcome to develop any of the notebook ideas into a song of their own, as long as they get in touch with the Haunted Valley so that any royalties can be shared. Leven thought it pointless to list the tracks, “so happy listening”.

The blogger adds two sentences in Greek: those who remember from the Seventies the rare and beautiful acid album *Control* by the Scot John St. Field, as Leven was then called (first released on the Spanish label Movieplay in 1975), have in *Greek Notebook* (Cooking Vinyl) his Greek connection. He ends: “A significant artist. Discover him.”
zitate_kontext: Leven in his booklet note signed “Jackie 1999”
Leven on how Greek Notebook came about

2009-11-netrhythms-haunted-year-autumn.kurz: Mike Davies reviews the autumn instalment of the *Haunted Year* series: the sketchbook *Greek Notebook* and the studio-and-live mix *Only The Ocean Can Forgive*, with Leven’s stage anecdotes.
inhalt: Mike Davies reviews the last of Leven’s seasonal double-disc reissues of his fan-club albums on Cooking Vinyl. Unlike the previous three, this one features only one live recording.

*Greek Notebook* is a collection of 33 musical sketches, all titled “Island”, the result of seven years of Mays and Septembers spent on the island of Astypalea and recorded on a Sony Professional Walkman. They are idea doodles and fragments of works in progress, from a few seconds to almost seven minutes. Davies finds them an interesting example of the creative process as Leven plays around with chord progressions, but not one for the regular Leven playlist.

The second disc, *Only The Ocean Can Forgive*, mixes studio and live material, the latter being five numbers recorded in Germany. Three come from the 2003 Acoustic Stories tour: “Classic Northern Diversions”, preceded by a lengthy spoken intro about the despairing looks on the faces of men in the streets of Belfast; the broodingly powerful “Extremely Violent Man”; and the self-examining “My Philosophy”, which Leven explains was inspired by a fit of depression and two London policemen who got him out of it. The other two, presumably from the same tour but a different venue, are the wheezing, meditative “Paris Blues” (on all four reissues) and “Sting’s Dead (Story Of The Sad Death Of The Well-Known Singer)”, which Davies says is not a song at all but a ten-minute preamble about trouble on a Glasgow train, where Leven, to escape a fellow passenger’s unwelcome advances, announced that Sting had been killed in a helicopter accident. “You probably had to be there.”

The three studio tracks are “Woman In A Car” (later on *Lovers At The Gun Club*), “Autumn” and “Little Brown Box” – the last two warm and reflective and, to Davies’s knowledge, never on a studio album. The closing track, recorded at the 2002 Christmas party in Derbyshire with Joe Shaw and Kevin Hewick, is a full-blooded, wailing, spooked blues version of “Barefoot Days”, previously heard only on the Summer edition. The tone is factual and benevolent, without an explicit verdict.
zitate_kontext: Mike Davies on the first disc.
Davies on the longest live item on the second disc.

2009-12-06-record-collector-haunted-year.kurz: Kris Needs welcomes the final *Haunted Year* instalment: *Greek Notebook* as a unique glimpse into Leven's workshop, *Only the Ocean Can Forgive* as live highlights, monologues and studio ballads – a strong close.
inhalt: Kris Needs reviews *The Haunted Year: Autumn* (Cooking Vinyl COOKCD 486, 2-CD) in Record Collector issue 371. It is the last of four seasonal releases in which Leven bundled, during 2009, eight albums issued annually since 1994 through his appreciation society, The Haunted Valley. Needs calls Leven “the great and often-underrated troubadour” and describes the set as a coupling of esoteric insight with stone classic.

*Greek Notebook* presents aural sketches Leven captured on a Walkman over six years in the early 1990s while sporadically holed up on a remote Greek island: song ideas, lyrical snatches and melodic doodles amounting to hundreds of hours. With no chance of honing such a mass into finished form, Leven released a clutch to the society as 33 numbered snippets and invited members to take them forward. Needs thinks it may be the most unconventional item in his catalogue and a fascinating peek into his creative process.

*Only The Ocean Can Forgive* mixes stellar 2004 live recordings – among them the smouldering “Extremely Violent Man” and the darkly intense epic “Barefoot Days” – with humorous extended monologues, the brilliantly convoluted “Sting's Dead” being particularly hilarious. Three towering studio outings, “Autumn Song”, “Woman In A Car” and “Little Brown Box”, crystallise the wounded ballad form of which Leven has been master for over thirty years, ending this wonderfully intimate series on a major high.
zitate_kontext: Kris Needs on the three studio tracks and the close of the series.

2009-black-and-white-macdonald-scottish-.kurz: A collection of Scottish football quotations includes a 2007 Leven quote about Doll by Doll and being hated.
inhalt: The collection *Scottish Football Quotations 3* (Black & White Publishing, Edinburgh, 2009) includes a quotation from Jackie Leven dating from 2007 about Doll by Doll and being hated, placed in a football context. No original source is given.

2009-dvdfever-haunted-year-spring.kurz: Elly Roberts reviews *The Haunted Year: Spring* (Cooking Vinyl, May 2009), two fan-club live recordings from 1998 and 1999: the first CD with the Celtic Soulmen is far stronger (8/10) than the second (6/10); overall verdict “Very good collection”.
inhalt: Elly Roberts reviews *The Haunted Year – Spring: Man Bleeds in Glasgow / Greetings from Milford – Live* (Cooking Vinyl, May 2009) for DVDfever.co.uk. The two live CDs get a commercial release for the first time; they come from the fan club Leven had set up around the quarterly magazine *The Haunted Valley*, which also issued limited live albums to members. Roberts rates the first disc 8/10 and the second 6/10.

The first CD, recorded in 1998 at the Water Rats Theatre in London, has Leven with Michael Cosgrave and Steafan Hannigan, the Celtic Soulmen, and is by far the better. Its set list is mostly drawn from *Night Lilies* (1998), arguably one of his best solo albums for Cooking Vinyl, but it goes back further too, to “Call Mother A Lonely Field”. There are rustic ballads such as “Farm Boy”, the love ballad “Looking For Love”, the whopping Celtic sound of “Glenarm” with stirring Uilleann pipework by Hannigan, and the country-blues-tinged “Man Bleeds in Glasgow”. The jewel in the crown is the divine ballad “Poor Toun”, his best vocal by a long stretch, enough to bring tears to the eyes; the haunting “Deep Choking Wooded Death Fix” with stylish acoustic picking comes a close second. The set closes with one of his most popular songs, “Call Mother A Lonely Field”, where his soulful voice is at its thrusting best, and all of it is mixed with sharp wit and playful banter between band and audience.

The second disc was recorded at the 1999 Haunted Valley Christmas party at the British Legion club in Milford, Derbyshire, with Kevin Hewick, Dan Britton and Lee Allatson as The Stornoway Girls. Here are covers of Van Morrison (“Madame George”), Lou Reed (“I’m Waiting For The Man”, “Pale Blue Eyes”) and Bill Withers (“Who Is He And What Is He To You?”) along with originals such as “Walking In Argyll” and “Listening To Crows Pray”. “Pale Blue Eyes” follows Reed’s laid-back template, though Leven’s vocals sharpen things up considerably. “I’m Waiting For The Man” keeps the original’s rough-and-ready swagger, but his vocal attack does not catch Reed’s 60s rock pulse; on “Who Is He…” his voice does not match Withers’s soulful angst, though the wah-wah riffs are superb. The verdict: “Very good collection”.
zitate_kontext: Elly Roberts on the first disc

2009-george-yefchak-njaca-corrections-qu.kurz: Troyanovich introduces Leven to an audience from the American correctional system. The piece appears in the newsletter of the New Jersey chapter of the American Correctional Association, Volume 3, Number 1, Spring/Summer 2009, on printed pages 18–19. It opens with the joint project with Ian…
inhalt: Troyanovich introduces Leven to an audience from the American correctional system. The piece appears in the newsletter of the New Jersey chapter of the American Correctional Association, Volume 3, Number 1, Spring/Summer 2009, on printed pages 18–19. It opens with the joint project with Ian Rankin and stresses that Leven is hardly known outside Europe.

The text combines a brief career outline with the CORE Trust and focuses particular attention on “Men in Prison”. Troyanovich describes the recording as a solo concert in Bergen prison and points to Leven's introductory words there about addiction and his own experiences. He also explains the reissue of the fan-club material in the series “The Haunted Year” and announces “Troubadour Heart”.

A further focus is the poetry worked into Leven's recordings. The author names numerous poets and recommends several albums as a starting point. For the collection the article is above all evidence of reception outside the usual music press: Leven is presented here through prison concerts, addiction support and poetry. It is not a scholarly study or an effectiveness evaluation of CORE; its biographical claims therefore gain no additional evidential weight.

2009-greenwood-forshaw-british-crime-wri.kurz: The entry on Ian Rankin in the reference work says literature and music overlapped when Leven found himself mentioned in the Rebus novel *Resurrection Men*; this led to the short story with music “Jackie Leven Said” (2005).
inhalt: In its entry on Ian Rankin, the reference work *British Crime Writing: An Encyclopedia* (ed. Barry Forshaw, Greenwood, 2009) describes how literature and music met in Rankin's work. The occasion was that Jackie Leven found himself mentioned in the Rebus novel *Resurrection Men*. From this came “Jackie Leven Said” (2005), a short story written and read by Rankin with music by Leven. Rankin has also written song lyrics.

2009-jackieleven-co-uk-gaestebuch-2009.kurz: Around 40 genuine entries. The trouble over *Live From A Cornish Pub In Germany* grows: several buyers report that their cheque was cashed in 2008 but the CD never arrived; in June one writes that it has been over a year, a Scottish fan has been waiting since Glenfarg for a paid-for, signed album and letter …
inhalt: Around 40 genuine entries. The trouble over *Live From A Cornish Pub In Germany* grows: several buyers report that their cheque was cashed in 2008 but the CD never arrived; in June one writes that it has been over a year, a Scottish fan has been waiting since Glenfarg for a paid-for, signed album and letter and comments on this with a Fife proverb. Alongside this, thanks for concerts in Essen and Bremen (February, with a question about the track list of an “official bootleg” from Hull 2009), Karlsruhe, Wallingford (Rugfest, June), Sidmouth (August), Milton Keynes (Stables, November, with four new songs) and Glenfarg; a 15-year-old Norwegian girl says she knows Leven through her father. A fan from Langholm recalls Leven's time in Carlisle, a woman from Wales her first concert in 1983 at London's Embassy Club and promotional badges from the manager of the time, a sound engineer from San Francisco writes that he mixed Doll by Doll live in the 1970s. A Kassel fan misses new columns, an Italian woman asks about the missing *Haunted Year* instalments “Summer” and “Autumn”, and in August people welcome Leven back after a “dark time”.
