2009-rough-guides-rough-guide-to-world-m.kurz: The Scotland chapter of the Rough Guide to World Music mentions Leven as a musician who emerged from the wreckage of the post-punk band Doll by Doll to exorcise his own demons and start a solo career.
inhalt: In the Scotland chapter of the handbook *The Rough Guide to World Music, Vol. 2: Europe and Asia* (2009, edited by Simon Broughton, Mark Ellingham and Jon Lusk), Jackie Leven is mentioned among musicians who found their own longevity coming out of the rock scene. He emerged from the wreckage of the post-punk band Doll by Doll to exorcise his own demons and start a solo career. No more than these two sentences were visible in the search extract; the page number and further context are unknown.

2009-vanguard-online-jackie-leven-interv.kurz: Long conversation, conducted in December 2008 before a concert at the pub The Roscoe in Leeds and published eight months later.
inhalt: Long conversation, conducted in December 2008 before a concert at the pub The Roscoe in Leeds and published eight months later. Leven says he is not getting anywhere in Britain, while in Germany things are going well. He lives from music, with outliers such as a royalty cheque for £10,000 because the Doll by Doll song “Soon New Life” became the radio song for births in South America (self-report). The publisher prevents him from re-recording old Doll by Doll songs. He describes Cooking Vinyl as a former “scavenging label” that has become a real label. Sir Vincent Lone sells better in Britain than Jackie Leven; Vince albums are cheaply produced “diffusion Jackie albums”, whereas Scandinavia and Germany expect high production values. Further topics: his sound engineer David Lynch, weaker songs on records, Lovers At The Gun Club as the end point of a sound, politics (Leven calls himself a socialist, brought up in the “communist” mining districts of Fife, Young Communists), songs about broken men as healing, 100 to 120 concerts a year, Scottish identity, Wetherspoon pubs as gathering places for lonely exiled Scots, poetry, the philosopher Charlie Martin, listening habits (Roland Kirk, Stephen Isserlis, Vaughan Williams) and a planned song “I Love Chet Baker When He Sings”.

2010-01-20-sentireascoltare-only-the-oce.kurz: Giancarlo Turra reviews the double CD *Only The Ocean Can Forgive / Greek Notebook* from Leven's “Haunted Year” series, places Leven between British folk and early Leonard Cohen, and gives it 7/10.
inhalt: On SentireAscoltare, Giancarlo Turra reviews the double CD *Only The Ocean Can Forgive / Greek Notebook* from Leven's “Haunted Year” series, which the page gives as released on 1 December 2009. The first disc combines three studio tracks, including “Autumn Song”, with six live recordings from Cologne and Frankfurt in 2003, among which “Barefoot Days” with Kevin Hewick and Joe Shaw stands out. The second disc collects “Walkman” sketches from the Greek islands.

Turra places Leven between British folk and the early Leonard Cohen and calls his cult status “undeserved”: an artist for whom the “cult” is an undeserved condition. The rating is 7 out of 10. Turra writes that Leven spent several months on Greek islands in the 1990s; his stays on Paxos are otherwise documented only from 2003 onwards.

2010-02-24-telegraph-blogs-the-rock-star.kurz: Blog entry by Telegraph rock critic Neil McCormick after Leven's concert at London's Slaughtered Lamb to launch Gothic Road (February 2010).
inhalt: Blog entry by Telegraph rock critic Neil McCormick after Leven's concert at London's Slaughtered Lamb to launch Gothic Road (February 2010). McCormick calls Leven “Britain's lost rock star” and the most talented singer-songwriter who never became a household name, and lists the stations of his life (expulsion over drugs, Doll by Doll, attack, heroin, CORE Trust with Diana). The core is an anecdote Leven told on stage (McCormick stresses that Leven is not always a reliable narrator): in October 2009 Leven accompanied Ralph McTell to his honouring by the All Party Folk Music Group in the House of Commons; there Prime Minister Gordon Brown, Leven's schoolmate from Kirkcaldy, persistently asked McTell whether “Streets of London” should not be called “Streets of Paris” for economic reasons, and praised the situation of the homeless under New Labour. Leven calls Brown a “political hero”. Note on the duet with McTell (“Cornelius Whalen”) on Gothic Road (release 4 April 2010) and listening recommendations from Gypsy Blood to Troubadour Heart.

2010-02-bluesnews-sir-vincent-lone-troub.kurz: Johnny Andreassen in Bluesnews (no. 63) on Sir Vincent Lone's *Troubadour Heart*: songs from the trunk; the alias sounds more and more like a stripped-down version of Leven's Celtic soul; a fine album for “quality time” alone.
inhalt: The review in Bluesnews no. 63 (February 2010) is by Johnny Andreassen (the attribution is not entirely certain because the OCR mixes the columns). Jackie Leven, it says, releases records from time to time under his own alias, Sir Vincent Lone. The first time, it was a way to give a musical outlet to the “politically and socially engaged” songs he had “at the bottom of the chest”: songs that were not so heavily produced, and that might get “completely different and more daring forms under acid bath and arrangement”, in a spirit he sometimes shares with his old partner David Thomas when they appear as Ubudoll. The name reflects their backgrounds in Doll by Doll and Pere Ubu respectively, but the similarities stop there – Ubudoll has never released a recording. “Fortunately Sir Vincent Lone has.”

*Troubadour Heart* is “a more personal version of Jackie Leven”. The cover shows the entrance door of The Troubadour, the London folk club to which Leven has returned for over thirty years – “the only coffee house in Earls Court from the fifties”. With “Rove on Wraith of Raith” as one of the finest songs, Sir Vincent Lone “begins more and more to resemble a stripped version of Jackie Leven's folk song and Celtic soul”; Scots are not known for American-inspired singer-songwriters or for gospel, but Leven “has never gone with the flock of his countrymen”. Leven is fascinated by eccentric songwriters, from Robert Fisher (Willard Grant Conspiracy) to Johnny Dowd; he has worked with Fisher, Dowd, Thomas and Mike Scott.

The verdict: “A fine record to be alone with for an hour or two. Quality time is what it's called, being alone with yourself.” You don't need to raise the door and widen the gate, for this artist reaches everyone who really listens. But in relation to the alias: “always choose a Jackie Leven album over a Sir Vincent Lone album”, should you stand with one in each hand and suffer the agony of choice, because Leven has a lower threshold for what he allows himself on the Sir Vincent Lone albums – “that has its charm too”.
zitate_kontext: Andreassen on choosing between the two names.

2010-03-bergen-sentrum-jackie-leven-pa-m.kurz: Bergen Sentrum announces Leven’s concert at Madam Felle on Friday 9 April 2010: a storyteller “at the highest level” touring his new album *Gothic Road*.
inhalt: The announcement by Isabella Nordbø on the website of Bergen’s city centre presents Leven as a regular visitor to Norway since the first half of the nineties: a welcome “big Scot” with a growing but still modest following, who can therefore keep playing small clubs with a closeness to his listening fans that few artists are granted. The concert takes place on Friday 9 April at Madam Felle.

Leven is often compared with Van Morrison – not a stupid commercial comparison, only Leven is “so much more”, a storyteller at the highest level whose lyrics and music grip you and do not let go until you have digested them long and well. After the cult band Doll By Doll, drugs and rock ’n’ roll in the seventies, a new Jackie Leven appeared with *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* (1994): drug-free after a long hell of pain following a nasty assault, he gave the term “Celtic soul” new and beautiful content. Since then it has been some twenty albums.

In spring he comes with *Gothic Road* (Cooking Vinyl, distributed by Tuba, release date 5 April). The previous album, *Lovers At The Gun Club* (2008), received glowing reviews in Britain: four out of five in The Independent (“Leven’s majestic voice is one of the most noble instruments in popular music…”) and four out of five in Uncut (“Typically brilliant!”). The evening promises “yet another solemn occasion with lovely songs and absurd stories”.
zitate_kontext: Nordbø on the evening at Madam Felle.

2010-04-02-gaesteliste-gothic-road.kurz: Ullrich Maurer calls *Gothic Road* a very solid “Jackie classic”: humorous, sweeping in melody, with Ralph McTell as a guest, and a return to Leven’s Celtic roots.
inhalt: This short album review on Gaesteliste.de (2 April 2010) first notes that, among all his side, touring and reissue projects, Leven regularly finds time for “normal” new records under his own name. *Gothic Road*, it says, has turned out a very solid classic. Thematically he circles, as humorously as ever, the “way of life”, which with him can quickly become a way of death, of the in-between world or a purely metaphysical dream state. What he is singing about each time, Maurer suggests, only Leven knows – and often not even he.

He gets more concrete in the politically motivated “Cornelius Whalen”, the dreamy “Tilda Swinton” and the funny, self-mocking “Mini Bar”. Musically he draws on abundant resources: he invited an old idol, Ralph McTell, as a guest (shared appearances had long featured in his show patter) and spurred his collaborator Michael Cosgrave to peak performances, even remembering to remind him how beautifully he plays flute.

As Leven once said in an interview, he likes “Euro-trash pop melodies” – sweeping melodic arcs with grand gestures – and there are plenty here. That suits his singing and largely compensates for the “often aimless, bluesy noodling” of his recent releases. Verdict: the old Jackie Leven has returned to his roots, which lie in the melancholy-sentimental Celtic, and is on top form there. The album is released on Cooking Vinyl/Indigo.
zitate_kontext: Maurer on the enigmatic quality of Leven’s lyrics

2010-04-08-word-magazine-blog-jackie-lev.kurz: On the Word Magazine readers' blogs, "Fangie" asks for Leven recommendations; a fan grades the albums by stars, and other readers add listening tips and a stage anecdote.
inhalt: On 8 April 2010 "Fangie", a self-described long-term lurker and first-time poster, wrote on Word Magazine's readers' blogs that after seeing King Creosote he was minded to check out fellow Fifer Jackie Leven. He had been working through the catalogue on Spotify and was ready to download a couple of albums, but saw that Leven had made "hunnerds of the rascals". Aside from the new album, what would the "Massive" recommend?

One reply, headed "The Big Man – a brief guide", became a mini discography. The writer has loved Leven's music since seeing Doll by Doll in a grotty pub in Manchester in 1982. Everyone has their own nomination for the great lost superstar of British music, he says, and "Big Jackie" is his: "Such an immense voice, such varied and powerful songs", and live you are reminded what a terrific guitarist he is. His five-star classics are *Fairy Tales for Hard Men*, *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*, *Shining Brother, Shining Sister*, *Control* and the third Doll by Doll album, *Doll by Doll*. Four stars go to *Forbidden Songs of the Dying West*, the live *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow*, *Gypsy Blood*, *Defending Ancient Springs*, *The Argyll Cycle* and *Grand Passion*; from the Haunted Valley fan-club releases he recommends *The Wanderer*, *Deep in the Heart of Nowhere* and *Greetings from Milford*. The only dud, he says, is perhaps *Elegy for Johnny Cash*; otherwise the back catalogue is "an absolute treasure trove". His claim that *Control* first appeared in 1971 under the name John St. Field, when Leven was 17, and only in Spain because he was on the run from the law, is fan legend; Leven was 21 in 1971.

In the comments one reader names *The Haunted Year – Winter* (*Men in Prison* and *Munich Blues*) and the audiobook of Leven and Ian Rankin live at Edinburgh's Queen's Hall (*Jackie Leven Said*), in which Rankin tells a story, Leven plays musical interludes and then a set backed by a keyboard player. Another recommends *Defending Ancient Springs* and "Single Father"; another praises the spoken intro to "The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ"; a reader loves the new album *Gothic Road* and regrets that Word had not reviewed it. One commenter recalls that before a gig Leven had a huge wad of papers, perhaps notes of things he might talk about, and never referred to them; he retells Leven's story of a jealous boyfriend who threatens to kill him after the television programme (Coronation Street) is over, but whose heart gives out during the ad break, leaving a relieved Leven to carry on watching to see what Norris does next. Another comment simply quotes Leven's line "Eternal is the warrior who finds beauty in his wounds".
zitate_kontext: The author of the "Big Man" guide on Leven
The same author on the back catalogue

2010-04-09-haugesunds-avis-jackie-leven-.titel: [Interview and concert report: Jackie Leven at Dikselen, Haugesund] (picture caption “Opp fra rennesteinen”)
2010-04-09-haugesunds-avis-jackie-leven-.kurz: Conversation and short report on the previous evening's performance (08.04.2010) at the Haugesund venue Dikselen, the opening of the 2010 Norway tour. Leven played material from the just-released *Gothic Road* as well as older songs such as “Big Tears” to a “conscious and marginal” audience.
inhalt: Conversation and short report on the previous evening's performance (08.04.2010) at the Haugesund venue Dikselen, the opening of the 2010 Norway tour. Leven played material from the just-released *Gothic Road* as well as older songs such as “Big Tears” to a “conscious and marginal” audience. The author recalls that The Pogues had played at the same venue in 1984, with Elvis Costello as sound engineer.

Leven says he travels through Norway to see the country; friends in London hardly dared leave the city. People envied him his “interesting life” – a misunderstanding, he says; his life has something “cinematically bad” about it. He describes his audience as people who think for themselves and do not let a lifestyle be sold to them; in England many young people come. The article summarises his biography (Doll by Doll 1978–1982 without mainstream success; friendship and collaboration with Ian Rankin, Glen Matlock and Frank Black) and describes the mugging on his way home from the studio during work on his first solo album: two years without a voice, mental problems, isolation and heroin. Leven partly takes the blame on himself, in his own account – he had been drunk and had walked alone despite the engineers' warning; he grew up because of it. About his label he says that indie companies are no better than others and dropped him without hesitation, so he must have done something right. *Gothic Road* is presented as his 16th solo album; Dagbladet's critic Fredrik Wandrup gave it five pips.
zitate_kontext: Leven on the myth of his life.

2010-04-10-haugesunds-avis-underskuddsga.titel: [News item: KUF rejects deficit guarantee for Jackie Leven concert] (subheading “Hvem får underskuddsgaranti?”)
2010-04-10-haugesunds-avis-underskuddsga.kurz: For Leven's concert at Dikselen, the promoter Inventum asked Haugesund's culture agency KUF for a deficit guarantee, was refused, and the case triggered a debate about the funding guidelines.
inhalt: Haugesunds Avis reports (by Roar Eskild Jacobsen) on an application by the promoter Inventum to the municipal body Kultur og festivalutvikling (KUF). Inventum, which works in restaurants and property and stages cultural events at Byscenen, Flytten and Dikselen, had applied for a deficit guarantee for Thursday's Jackie Leven concert: 50 per cent against accounts of 19,800 kroner. The application was turned down at the KUF board meeting the previous Wednesday. At the same meeting the board asked the city council to add a sentence to the guidelines saying that no deficit guarantees or support are given to commercial operators.

KUF's administrative head, Inger Mæland, says this is not about Inventum: “All commercial operators get a refusal from us.” The scheme supports voluntary organisations and events with cultural content that are open to the public, and actors with theatre projects usually receive a guarantee. Applications are invited twice a year and are “complicated and difficult” to assess. The pot is 110,000 kroner a year; KUF received 18 applications in 2009 and granted several guarantees for April, for instance to a chamber opera project, Gamle Slaktehusets Teater and Haugaland Kunstverk, in amounts of around 10,000 to 20,000 kroner.

Inventum's booking manager Helge Bertelsen calls the Leven concert a “guaranteed loss-making project”. He argues that such a concert falls under what the politicians intended with the guarantee scheme: Leven's artistic quality serves a town like Haugesund by being on the bill. Inventum would never apply for a guarantee for concerts by acts like Vassendgutane or Dum Boys, but the city council must show what KUF is for; the audience does not care who the promoter is. It is the first time Inventum has asked KUF for money, “but it will not be the last”.
zitate_kontext: Bertelsen (Inventum) on the Leven concert and the refusal

2010-04-10-itromso-jackie-leven-pa-basta.kurz: A short preview of Leven’s concert at Bastard Bar in Tromsø on Wednesday; booking manager Egon Holstad praises the voice, guitar playing and storytelling of “our Scottish friend”.
inhalt: iTromsø announces under “Spiller på Bastard” (“Playing at Bastard”) a Jackie Leven concert for Wednesday 14 April 2010 at Bastard Bar. The paper quotes booking manager Egon Holstad: “Our Scottish friend is finally back in town, and what could be better for tending delicate Wednesday nerves than this hero?” Holstad praises a voice that puts legendary crooners to shame, breathtaking guitar playing and a storytelling gift that impresses even the most weather-beaten stand-up comedians. Few, he says, combine humour with crushed self-confidence and heavy suicidal thoughts as convincingly as Leven does on stage.

On his last visit to Tromsø, Leven played support for Madrugada on their farewell tour: alone on a huge stage, armed only with a guitar and a voice whose signature is as massive as Hendrix’s guitar and Miles Davis’s trumpet, he enchanted the audience. In the intimate Bastard Bar it will be something quite different, Holstad promises.
zitate_kontext: Egon Holstad, booking manager, on Leven’s return to Tromsø.
Holstad on Leven’s earlier appearance supporting Madrugada.

2010-04-11-rocktimes-gothic-road.kurz: A track-by-track review of *Gothic Road* in RockTimes: typically eccentric, more relaxed, a stretch even for fans. Norbert Neugebauer gives no rating; the album needs time.
inhalt: Norbert Neugebauer reviews *Gothic Road* (Cooking Vinyl, 52:27 minutes) for RockTimes (11 April 2010). He opens with a complaint: “Hard to keep track of such output.” Leven, alias John St. Field, alias Sir Vincent Lone, alias “Jackie Balfort” (correctly Balfour) and a member of Doll by Doll, really does not skimp on his musical talent. The last album under his own name was *Lovers At The Gun Club* (2008), followed by reissues in the “Haunted Year” series with club live recordings and, as Sir Vincent Lone, *Troubadour Heart* (2009). RockTimes had presented *Oh What A Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!* (2007).

The album opens with the German voice of a satnav (“Fahren Sie 260 Kilometer” – “drive 260 kilometres”) sending him onto the “Gothic Road”, to a tin whistle, an oddly kitschy “yeah yeah” ladies’ chorus and dramatic humming in the background – “not necessarily the usual from Mr Leven”. It continues askew with clattering percussion cascades; “Last Of The Badmen” comes more from the familiar ballad cosmos, “John Paul Getty’s Silver Cadillac” is an unusually relaxed road song with a playful arrangement. In “Cornelius Whalen”, about the last participant of the 1936 Jarrow march of the unemployed, Leven, together with Ralph McTell, once again takes up a socially critical theme, but without the earlier bitterness. Hard to grasp for a non-Brit are the surreal verses of “Song For Bass Guitar And Death” with Deborah Greenwood; similarly restrained is “New Wreath”, the warm voice supported only by plucked guitar and simple piano chords. Then come “the next musical joke in a slightly skew country sound” (“Absolutely Joan Crawford”), the elegiac “My Lost Blonde” and the more relaxed “In A Shivering Blaze”. Another German announcement, this time from the captain who flew him to Hamburg, opens the nonsense song “Hotel Mini Bar”; then follow the loop-underpinned “Shadow Of A Man” and, with piano alone, “Island”.

The verdict: the album is “typically Leven” in its eccentricity, yet because of its unusual ingredients takes getting used to even for fans. Leven sounds more relaxed and quotes colleagues and their songs more often, but still has his earlier melancholy and extravagant arrangements. It is hard to place *Gothic Road* in the “reclusive Scot’s” output or to give a rating; that will probably take long-term effect. It is an album you have to listen your way into and which will certainly not ignite at once.

2010-04-13-bergensavisen-gothic-road.kurz: Short review in *Bergensavisen* of *Gothic Road* (2010): Leven has found his very own voice, hardly strays from the winning formula and has an exceptionally strong lyrical vein; guests include Ralph McTell and a Russian choir.
inhalt: The review, in a column of new releases, opens with a quip about the “Bergensvennen” (“friend of Bergen”), who spits out live albums and odd compilations faster than most. Now and then, however, comes a more official release such as the fresh *Gothic Road*, on which, “in the spirit of earlier albums”, he collaborates with a number of people, most noticeably the “Streets of London” troubadour Ralph McTell.

Leven has found his very own voice and hardly moves outside the winning formula. Few artists have as strong a lyrical vein as the Scot; it ranges from the deeply philosophical, through the warmly reminiscing, to the pensively funny in the ode to lonely life on tour, “Hotel Mini Bar”. He even uses a Russian choir of brothers of men who died in the Kursk disaster. As usual with Leven’s records, there are many layers to leaf through. The critic’s download tips are “My Lost Blonde” and “Island”. The author’s name and rating cannot be made out in the newspaper scan.

2010-04-13-haugesunds-avis-gothic-road.titel: Jackie Leven: «Gothic Road» (review in the column “Et hode foran”)
2010-04-13-haugesunds-avis-gothic-road.kurz: Roar Eskild Jacobsen calls Gothic Road "a blue record with black humour" in Haugesunds Avis: Leven has become an elegant gentleman with several ghosts in the closet and an eternal outsider.
inhalt: In the "Et hode foran" column of Haugesunds Avis (13 April 2010), Roar Eskild Jacobsen reviews Jackie Leven's *Gothic Road* (Cooking Vinyl/Tuba) under the headline "Blå humor" ("Blue humour"). The verdict is "Sterkt" ("Strong"), summed up as "Elegant popgryte". The Scot has become "an elegant gentleman with several ghosts living in the closet"; a crooked life, many musical talents and great self-knowledge have made him a continuous supplier of interesting and varied music. Leven and his contemporaries John Cooper Clarke and Wild Billy Childish are eternal outsiders, artists with a different perspective from what is served up in more polished forums: "They see other things."

*Gothic Road* is "a blue record with black humour". The narrator stirs deeply in his own experiences without digging himself in. The melancholy, the big guitar parts and the simple bluesy-jazzy rhythms suit the small stories told by Leven's bright, prominent voice, with a touch of aggression, emotional. The album is a coherent journey; the highlights are "Song for Bass Guitar and Death", "My Lost Blonde" and "Hotel Mini Bar". Leven's sense of humour shines through, and he references Joy Division's Ian Curtis (in the title track, "Gothic Road"), Joan Crawford ("Absolutely Joan Crawford") and Dolly Parton. The star/dice rating is illegible in the scan.

2010-04-13-laagendalsposten-leven-og-bue.titel: [Preview:] Nå samles Jackie Leven og Knut Buen igjen (subheadings “Ny duo”, “Felesjef”)
2010-04-13-laagendalsposten-leven-og-bue.kurz: Laagendalsposten announces that Jackie Leven and the Hardanger fiddler Knut Buen, who made a successful debut in Kongsberg in 2009, will perform together again, at Bergenfest 2010 and in Ulvik.
inhalt: Under the headline “Nå samles Jackie Leven og Knut Buen igjen” (“Now Jackie Leven and Knut Buen come together again”), the Kongsberg local paper reports that the duo, who first performed together at the Kongsberg Jazz Festival in 2009 to a sold-out concert and an “immediate success”, are reuniting. This time they will play together at Bergenfest 2010, a festival with a “very broad programme” that should not be confused with the Bergen International Festival. A photograph shows the two last year in the back yard of “Christians kjeller” in Kongsberg.

The concert on the Småscenen at the venerable Den Nationale Scene is divided into three parts: Leven alone, Leven and Buen together, and finally Buen alone. Under the subhead “Felesjef” (“fiddle chief”), the paper notes that Buen was last seen on stage at this year's Spellemannspris ceremony, where he showed who is boss of the fiddle in the country, whatever the age. Leven and Buen also play in Ulvik on Saturday 1 May, at the newly started Harding Folk event. Buen is not the only local act at Bergenfest: the Kongsberg duo Susanna and the Magical Orchestra, Susanna Wallumrød and Morten Qvenild, also play on 1 May in the western capital.

2010-04-15-karmsund-skotsk-morkemann.kurz: Portrait with quotations from conversation after Leven's concert at Dikselen, Haugesund, the previous week (08.04.2010).
inhalt: Portrait with quotations from conversation after Leven's concert at Dikselen, Haugesund, the previous week (08.04.2010). Sørhus introduces him as “Scotland's answer to Van Morrison”, who turns sixty in 2010. Leven says (in his own account) that Bergen was the first city in which he performed as a professional musician: at 16, in 1966, he toured with the American gospel/blues singer Doris Henderson, and Bergen was the first stop; he recalls arriving through the fjord and the stench of a fish-processing plant, but says he fell in love with Norway at once – the people had the same “madness” as the Scots. One of his favourite poets was Olav H. Hauge, so it was exciting to be close to his home region.

On the origin of “Rainy Day Bergen Women” he says he was woken in Bergen by coughing in the next room, looked out on the rainy street full of hurrying women and wrote the song in half an hour; his father had just died, and it was his first song about his death. In Haugesund some had taken him for an “old punk” and expected punk songs. He loves the studio because he is “incredibly good” in it, but the record company only allows an album every 18 months – hence the pseudonym Sir Vincent Lone.

2010-04-20-romerikes-blad-leven-leverer-.kurz: Rune Westengen praises *Gothic Road* in Romerikes Blad: the veteran keeps delivering fine songs, rooted in folk and song tradition, with impressive lyrics and guests such as Ralph McTell.
inhalt: Rune Westengen reviews *Gothic Road* (Cooking Vinyl, 12 tracks, 52:25) in Romerikes Blad under the headline “Leven leverer igjen” (“Leven delivers again”). The veteran continues to deliver fine songs. “Scotland's best-known gypsy” has released high-quality records ever since he fronted Doll By Doll at the end of the 1970s. He has lived intensely and in part outside society, but since he was nearly killed in a street fight in the mid-eighties he has fought his way back and can now look back on a long line of fine solo albums.

Ralph McTell, Michael Cosgrave, Kevin Foster and David Wrench appear on the album. Leven remains rooted in folk and song tradition and delivers impressive lyrics. Song titles such as “John Paul Getty's Silver Cadillac”, “Absolutely Joan Crawford” and “Song for Bass Guitar and Death” promise much, and deliver. The verdict: an album that bears witness to life experience and love of life, and one “we can live with for a long time”.

2010-04-20-varden-gothic-road.kurz: Helge Ottesen finds good moments on *Gothic Road* in Varden, where storytelling and music become one, but is mixed overall; he names four good songs and Ralph McTell as a guest.
inhalt: The review in Varden (Skien) is headed “Historiefortelleren” (“The storyteller”). The “folk-rocker” Jackie Leven has his good moments, where storytelling and music merge into a higher unity, but is not equally exciting throughout. The critic, Helge Ottesen, notes that this time Ralph McTell (“remember ‘Streets of London’?”) sings on a song and David Wrench helped with the production and in return got an extra track of his own.

Much is catchy, both arrangement and melodies. Leven borrows here and there and makes it his own – for instance the line “The world is a matador and I’m full of bull. I ache in the places I used to ache” (the last part being Leonard Cohen’s) and “Black Is the Colour”, where the song says “heart” instead of “hair”. As good songs Ottesen names “John Paul Getty’s Silver Cadillac”, “Song for Bass Guitar and Death”, “Absolutely Joan Crawford (With a Bit of Tilda Swinton on the Side)” and “In a Shivering Blaze”.
zitate_kontext: The critic on Leven’s use of borrowed material.

2010-04-21-dalane-tidende-jackie-leven-t.titel: [Preview: Jackie Leven back in Egersund – concert at Grand Kjelleren for Verdens bokdag]
2010-04-21-dalane-tidende-jackie-leven-t.kurz: Large preview of the concert on Friday, 23.04.2010, at Grand Kjelleren in Egersund, organised by the Egersund Visefestival in cooperation with World Book Day (Leven performs after a Bokkafé).
inhalt: Large preview of the concert on Friday, 23.04.2010, at Grand Kjelleren in Egersund, organised by the Egersund Visefestival in cooperation with World Book Day (Leven performs after a Bokkafé). Festival director Henning Feyling says Leven felt so comfortable at the festival in summer 2009 – he gave two concerts at Dalane Brygghus, with people standing all the way down the stairs – that he was determined to come back; after the Trondheim concert on Tuesday he will travel down and spend two free days in Egersund. It is the first time the festival has put on a concert outside its July dates, as a test of the mood; the summer programme (including Hanne Boel, Steve Wynn) was to be handed out at the concert. Feyling points to Dagbladet's review, which proclaimed Leven “Scotland's dark master singer” and gave *Gothic Road* five pips.

Aalbu, who by his own account has been to nine or ten Leven concerts (including Stavanger, Bryne), adds a personally coloured portrait: Leven tells so many tall stories that fact and fiction blur; this is followed by the familiar biographical stations (Romani descent, expelled from school for drugs, Doll by Doll, the 1984 mugging with a kick to the larynx, steroids, heroin, depression, self-treatment including Chinese acupuncture, a rehab clinic and the Core Trust, comeback in 1994 with Mike Scott and Robert Bly), the whisky “Leven's Lament” with a Salman Rushdie recommendation in the booklet, and Leven's quirky song titles. Leven is at least as interesting between the songs as when singing, comparable to Van Morrison, Scott Walker and John Martyn. A side column is devoted to his old shorts, always the same ones.
zitate_kontext: on the blurriness of his biography (start of sentence).

2010-04-21-nordlys-stodig-fra-leven.kurz: Danny J. Pellicer finds *Gothic Road* rock-solid, the work of one of the most formidable lyricists alive, but regrets that it too rarely truly sparks; still a good buy, with a voice of old whisky and a life lived.
inhalt: Nordlys (Tromsø) reviews Jackie Leven's *Gothic Road* (Cooking Vinyl) under the title “Stødig fra Leven” (“Steady from Leven”). Danny J. Pellicer calls the album “bunnsolid”, rock-solid, once again. “Joy” may not be the right word, since much of the material is dark as black-painted coal, but it is well worth the money to enter the Scottish veteran's singer-songwriter universe.

Above all because he must be among the most formidable lyricists around: “literary as hell”, with pop-culture references that rain down but are never show-off, always there to say something. He masters existential darkness (“Gothic Road”, “Last of the Badmen”) as well as everyday, slanting observations on touring life (“Hotel Mini Bar”), and humour: “Absolutely Joan Crawford (With A Bit of Tilda Swinton on the Side)”, in which he fantasises about a gloriously promiscuous life with various famous women, is “priceless”.

The objection is that it is too long between the times Leven really sparks. But the craft and a production that is true to genre yet varied and finely tuned make *Gothic Road* a good buy, and one can only doff one's cap to the voice that oozes old whisky, adversity and a life lived. The conclusion: the business needs honourable men who deliver the goods, and Leven is one of them. The rating cannot be read in the newspaper scan.
zitate_kontext: Danny J. Pellicer on Leven's lyrics

2010-04-22-chicago-reader-a-cult-artists.kurz: One of the few North American articles about Leven, published for the US release of Gothic Road (Vol.
inhalt: One of the few North American articles about Leven, published for the US release of Gothic Road (Vol. 39 No. 31 of the Chicago Reader). The critic Cliff Doerksen, who comes from Winnipeg, recounts how Doll by Doll found a small following in his home town in 1979 and defends the first three albums (Remember, Gypsy Blood, Doll by Doll) as the greatest lost rock albums; Grand Passion falls short. From the liner notes of the 2007 Rhino reissues he quotes that John Peel and Paul Morley loathed the band. Discovering the UbuDoll project with David Thomas (2000) led him to Leven's solo work; he considers Leven possibly the most underrated living songwriter. Gothic Road is the 13th solo studio album since 1994; mentioned are Chip Pan Fire, collaborations with Johnny Dowd, Ron Sexsmith and Ian Rankin, and a quotation from David Thomas from the DVD The Meeting of Remarkable Men (2004). Leven talks about touring (formerly 200 days a year, now fewer), about the genre label, and about the fact that lack of attention sometimes makes him angry but that he made his choice.

2010-04-22-karmsund-gothic-road.kurz: Camilla Sørhus describes the “friend of Norway” Leven in *Karmsund Avis* as one of Britain’s hardest-working artists and a gifted storyteller; *Gothic Road* offers Ralph McTell, a Russian choir and a classic Leven tale.
inhalt: Camilla Sørhus reviews *Gothic Road* in the column “Musikk – vurdert av Camilla Sørhus”. The “friend of Norway” Jackie Leven has become a veritable cornucopia in recent years: with a new release every eighteen months and the waiting time spiced with collaborations and bootlegs, he is one of the hardest-working artists in Britain. The Scot is best known as an excellent storyteller, with lyrics that balance on the very edge of poetry, delivered in a deep voice and with sharp humour.

This time he brings a Russian choir of brothers of men who died in the tragic Kursk accident, as well as the man behind “Streets of London”, Ralph McTell. On *Gothic Road* he documents the loneliness of touring life in “Hotel Mini Bar”, while “John Paul Getty’s Silver Cadillac” offers a classic but still gripping Leven narrative, even after countless listens. The rest of the text and the rating cannot be read in the newspaper scan.

2010-04-27-ostlendingen-musikk-til-poesi.kurz: Østlendingen praises *Gothic Road* in a short review headed “Music for poetry”: Leven's lyrics are pure poetry, his vibrating voice gives them a sting, he sets melodies in surprising frames, and Ralph McTell appears on “Cornelius Whalen”.
inhalt: The short review (headline “Musikk til poesi”, Østlendingen, 27 April 2010, page 25, in a box of record reviews next to Roky Erickson, Elin Ruth Sigvardsson and Besnard Lakes) introduces “the Scottish Jackie Leven (60), once a member of Doll by Doll”. He delivers at least one album every year, after having been “down in the darkness” for a period in the Eighties. (Leven turned sixty in June 2010; he was 59 when the review appeared.)

His lyrics can be regarded as pure poetry, and his characteristic voice and vibrating way of singing give the words extra sting and life. At the same time he has a gift for setting melodies in exciting and unexpected frames; he “twists and turns the conventions” and conveys dark moods in his own highly personal way. *Gothic Road* (Cooking Vinyl/Tuba) has some captivating high points that must be played again and again. Finally “Ralph McTell himself”, the man behind “Streets of London” (known in Norway as Finn Kalvik's “En tur rundt i byen”), turns up on “Cornelius Whalen”. A rating is not legible in the OCR, and the attribution of the author's name in the multi-column box is uncertain.

2010-04-29-drammens-tidende-skotsk-pa-bu.kurz: Preview of Leven's appearance at the “lyttekonserter” at Buddy Scene in Drammen, conducted by Johnny Andreassen (who had already done the Fremtiden interview in 1995).
inhalt: Preview of Leven's appearance at the “lyttekonserter” at Buddy Scene in Drammen, conducted by Johnny Andreassen (who had already done the Fremtiden interview in 1995). Leven raves (in his own account) that Drammen is “the holiday I always look forward to”, while many concerts around the world are thankless: the “wonderful Margrethe” (promoter Margrethe Berg), walks over the bridge from the hotel, a town with growing self-confidence and Buddy's unique soul. Berg had to close the door at his concerts every time and send latecomers home.

Leven tells how the album title *Gothic Road* came about: after a wild evening he woke up on all fours on his stone kitchen floor, on which he had written “Something Gothic” with a felt-tip pen; his wife was away, the word would not scrub off, and in the process he heard himself say the phrase that became the title. He also declares his support for Gordon Brown, who he says saved England from economic ruin; they went to school together, and he was present at the rugby game in which Brown lost the sight in one eye. A song about the Jarrow protest march is mentioned (“1938” in the paper). In Norway, *Gothic Road* received fives and sixes on the dice.

2010-04-29-hordaland-gothic-road.kurz: The Nynorsk newspaper Hordaland introduces Leven ahead of the concert with Knut Buen in Ulvik as a ‘Scottish storyteller’ and praises *Gothic Road*: spare, creaking music, with guitar, lyrics and a deep voice as weapons.
inhalt: The newspaper Hordaland (Voss) writes in Nynorsk on 29 April 2010 about *Gothic Road* (Cooking Vinyl/TUBA), ahead of the concert Leven gives on Saturday with Knut Buen in Ulvik. As storytellers both are ‘hardwood’, the paper says, even if their expression is quite different, and together they are to honour Sigbjørn Bernhoft Osa, another great storyteller in words and music. The headline calls Leven a “Scottish storyteller of history”.

Leven’s lyrics are “not exactly suited to putting you in a radiant mood”, but then they are about the shadow side of life. The reviewer describes his background: with an Irish cockney father and a mother from Northumbria he grew up as a classic outsider in Scottish Fife; school – minus English and essay writing – was a drudge, and that still marks his lyrics and music. The humour is “coal-black and intense”.

Leven fights his war with guitar, lyrics and a deep Scottish voice as weapons – “and they are weapons that serve”. The music is rhythmically creaking and rattling, sparingly portioned out. Admittedly tracks such as ‘Absolutely Joan Crawford (With a Bit of Tilda Swinton on the Side)’ and ‘In a Shivering Blaze’ brighten the picture musically, where blues and country swing gain a certain upper hand. The page is interleaved with an excerpt from Lars Osa’s memoir ‘Med pensel og boge’; the passage about the man gnawing a meat bone in the gutter belongs to that, not to the review. The biographical details are the newspaper’s own.

2010-04-netrhythms-gothic-road.kurz: Mike Davies reviews *Gothic Road* warmly and with a wink: an album full of pop-culture references, with Ralph McTell duetting on “Cornelius Whalen” and a closing track by co-producer David Wrench; whether the two-roads metaphysics holds up he leaves open.
inhalt: Davies starts with the concept: according to Leven's own blurb, we all walk two roads, the Royal Road and the Road of Poverty and Death, which form the Gothic Road where they meet. What they stand for stays vague; the reviewer reads it as a search for the balance of yin and yang, the pessimistic and the optimistic, “and it may all just be poetic smoke and mirrors”. One should know by now, he says, not to expect anything shallow from Leven's pen.

The album, he writes, comes loaded with pop-culture references. The slow-march title track, guesses Davies, is about the need for clear emotional communication and quotes both Ian Curtis and Dylan; “In a Shivering Blaze”, bouncy Cat Stevens pop, carries a chorus line from the Temptations and Marvin Gaye song “Too Busy Thinking ’bout My Baby”; “Last of the Badmen” marries spaghetti Western to Eastern European chant, borrows the melody of Dolly Parton's “Jolene” and includes the misquoted line “please don't kill me just because you can”. The spare, bluesy “Song for Bass Guitar and Death” meditates on mortality and even tips its hat to Mud's “Tiger Feet”; among the covers is a brooding, jazzed-over version of “Shadow of a Man” by the punk poet Patrick Fitzgerald. “John Paul Getty's Silver Cadillac”, Celtic-flavoured country blues, again deals with the enormity of masculine need and emptiness and may contain a musical trace of Michael Martin Murphey's “Geronimo's Cadillac”.

Because so many songs are about being dumped by or separated from a lover, Leven's libido “gets quite a working here”: in “Absolutely Joan Crawford (With a Bit of Tilda Swinton on the Side)” he fantasises about both women (Swinton snores, apparently) and about Patsy Cline, but says he will give them up if his departed lover comes home; in “Hotel Mini Bar”, a playful song about life on the road, he dreams of being propositioned by Cher and turns her down in favour of the fridge contents. It is not all sex, death and celebrity names, though. “Cornelius Whalen”, with Ralph McTell on second vocals (the blurb's “fabled English renegade”), is a tribute to the then last living member of the 1936 Jarrow marchers and an inspiration on how to live a life. As on *Lovers at the Gun Club*, Leven gives the final track to another artist: the Welsh singer and co-producer David Wrench, whose meditative, Levenesque piano ballad “Island” may surprise anyone used to his usual diet of camp synth pop.

Davies closes by noting that Leven was apparently a Kirkcaldy High School contemporary of the equally Fife-born Gordon Brown, and adds that when it comes to enriching our lives he knows which of the two gets his vote. (The school claim comes from the press material.)

Davies on the two-roads concept and the album's allusions

2010-06-13-david-belbin-jackie-leven.kurz: “Song of the Week” piece by the writer David Belbin for Leven's 60th birthday. He recounts how he saw Doll by Doll around 1979 at the Ad Lib Club in Nottingham after buying the debut *Remember*: the DJ had played the ballad *Janice* five times before the performance, so the band out of spite did not play it; the concert was harder than any punk band (“Joy Division? Pah.”). Twenty years later he experienced Leven solo in the upstairs room of The Gladstone pub in Nottingham – with his falsetto lost, but a brilliant, earthy and self-mocking storyteller; afterwards Leven confirmed to him that the 1979 concert had been one of Doll by Doll's few good ones.
inhalt: “Song of the Week” piece by the writer David Belbin for Leven's 60th birthday. He recounts how he saw Doll by Doll around 1979 at the Ad Lib Club in Nottingham after buying the debut *Remember*: the DJ had played the ballad *Janice* five times before the performance, so the band out of spite did not play it; the concert was harder than any punk band (“Joy Division? Pah.”). Twenty years later he experienced Leven solo in the upstairs room of The Gladstone pub in Nottingham – with his falsetto lost, but a brilliant, earthy and self-mocking storyteller; afterwards Leven confirmed to him that the 1979 concert had been one of Doll by Doll's few good ones.

Since then he has been a big fan, attends every tour (including Summer Sundae, Derby in June 2010 with stories about Diz Disley, The Flowerpot) and praises the way the albums keep getting better. He repeats Leven's stories about the mugging, heroin, CORE and Princess Diana and remarks that Leven seems to have known an astonishing range of people, from Laurence Olivier to Ralph McTell (a guest on *Gothic Road*). In Derby, Leven spontaneously sang *Strip Show* in the style of Matt Monro. As a listening example he links *Poortoun* in the version from *Men in Prison* (one of the four live double albums of 2009).

2010-06-28-diskoryxeion-jackie-leven-ive.kurz: Greek critic Phontas Troussas introduces Leven: the Astypalea years and *Greek Notebook*, the discovery that John St. Field of *Control* was Leven, the double CD *The Haunted Year / Spring* and the most “American” album, *Lovers At The Gun Club*.
inhalt: This 28 June 2010 post on the Greek record blog Diskoryxeion (Vinylmine) is a personal, very warm tour through Leven’s work. Troussas starts with the album *Greek Notebook* (Haunted Valley Clan, 1999) and calls Leven a resident of the island of Astypalea “for seven years (1991–1997)”. He translates the booklet note, in which Leven writes that one of the best things that ever happened to him was spending May and September on the remote island for seven years – 14 months in all – in a rough, mountainous place untouched by tourism. He recorded around 40 hours of material on a professional Sony Walkman to freeze the “wonderful and strange moments”. The 33 tracks (52:29) strike Troussas partly as sketches, partly as finished, quite “naked” songs with nature sounds, recalling the great folk moments of the past.

The second section deals with *Control*. Troussas had known for years of an album by a Briton called John St. Field as one of the best acid-folk LPs, which in his account was made around 1973 and released only in Spain, on Movieplay, two years later. When a Korean label, Merry-Go-Round/Beatball, reissued it in 2002 as 500 vinyl copies with liner notes by the man himself, he learned for the first time that St. Field was Jackie Leven. Leven writes there that he made the album in 1971 after an intense period of his life when he took LSD under varying circumstances; he chose the pseudonym because he had trouble with “law and order” and wanted to change identity for a while, though he would not advise anyone to change identity by taking acid. What struck him on relistening was how similar the writing of that 20-year-old is to that of the man today. Troussas doubts the date 1971 (“really?”) and raves about the eleven-minute “The Problem”. Doll by Doll he sums up briefly as a mix of acid-folk recipes and punk references.

Most of the post, however, covers newer releases. The double CD *The Haunted Year / Spring* (2009) collects two rare fan-club albums: *Man Bleeds In Glasgow* (1999), recorded live in London in September 1998 with the Celtic Soulmen (Michael Cosgrave, Steafan Hannigan), and *Greetings From Milford* (2002) with the Stornoway Girls (Kevin Hewick, Dan Britton, Lee Allatson), mostly covers – of Dylan, Lou Reed, Van Morrison, Bill Withers. He singles out the ten-minute “Glenarm / Burning the box of beautiful things”. Troussas wrongly places the Milford club in Leicester; Milford is in Derbyshire.

The studio album *Lovers At The Gun Club* (2008), recorded in Wales, includes a setting of Kenneth Patchen and closes with a song by David Childers. With more than fifteen musicians it is one of the most “American” albums of Leven’s career, with echoes of Van Morrison, Lou Reed, Tom Waits and Blind Gary Davis. Troussas closes on an image: Leven too is an “American” who left the Highlands and the shells of the Aegean behind to speed his old banger down the roads of a wilder West. He had not yet heard *Gothic Road* (2010). Reader comments below add further admirers of *Control*.

Leven in his *Control* liner notes, in Greek translation, on the pseudonym

2010-09-22-kindamuzik-jackie-leven-parad.kurz: Peter Bartlema is torn between “aversion, admiration and compassion”: Leven played Amsterdam’s Paradiso in a room far from sold out, as the opening act: plenty of anecdotes, swearing frustration, glowing songs, a phenomenal voice – and no encore.
inhalt: This KindaMuzik concert review (by Peter Bartlema, published 22 September 2010) is subtitled “Gemengde gevoelens” (“Mixed feelings”) and covers the show of 19 September 2010 in the upstairs hall of the Paradiso. Bartlema names three feelings a Leven performance can evoke in a listener “not too devoted” to him: aversion (weerzin), admiration and compassion. Compassion because such a “musical mastodon”, especially in “hip” Amsterdam, is far from selling out and tickets went at half price on the day. Admiration because the “Roma-born” Scottish bard (the reviewer’s words), despite a life of setbacks and addictions, has always carried on and, at the same label for a long time, has been extraordinarily productive. Aversion because on stage Leven airs his frustrations with frequent use of “fuck” and its conjugations, which mostly produces “vicarious shame”.

Most of those present seemed to regard his set mainly as a warm-up for the evening’s second act, the American roots outfit Chatham County Line, and Leven himself seemed aware of it: the show was over after an hour, and a large part went on true-or-not anecdotes and explanations of the songs, such as how aggressive Ralph McTell, guest on *Gothic Road*, supposedly is, or the incomprehensible accent of his American friend David Childers, a lawyer and roots rocker from North Carolina.

The songs, some from *Gothic Road*, nevertheless got a glowing delivery, thanks to an accompanist on keys and melodica but above all to Leven’s inventive guitar playing and the “phenomenal” sound of the robust Scot’s voice, which in timbre and vibrato recalls illustrious predecessors such as Tim Hardin and Aaron Neville. Before his last song Leven announces that he does not do encores – that is for artists with a mental disorder such as Robbie Williams. “Waarvan akte” (“Duly noted”), Bartlema concludes.
zitate_kontext: Bartlema on the end of Leven’s set

2010-12-01-bbc-radio-scotland-stark-talk.kurz: Roughly 26-minute conversational portrait from the BBC Radio Scotland series “Stark Talk” (BBC programme page: https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b00w68bh).
inhalt: Roughly 26-minute conversational portrait from the BBC Radio Scotland series “Stark Talk” (BBC programme page: https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b00w68bh). According to the BBC, broadcast on Wednesday, 1 December 2010 (15:30), repeated on 5 December 2010 and – “Another chance to hear … Jackie Leven, who died recently” – on 20 November 2011; no longer available from the BBC. The YouTube description dates the recording to November 2010 (presumably the month of recording; uploaded on 4.11.2014). Stark introduces Leven with Rankin's quip about the “Bob Dylan of Scotland”, Neil McCormick's praise for “Gypsy Blood” and the new album “Gothic Road”, and then works through his life chronologically: why fame failed to materialise (Leven says he avoids psychotherapy out of the superstitious fear of otherwise losing what is good in his writing), childhood in Leslie and Glenrothes as an outsider family, his mother's blues records, skipping school to be out in nature, the school librarian who slipped him Russian and American poetry, the gift of his first guitar and his own tuning. Next come fleeing a Glenrothes gang, years in Spain and Berlin, the Dorset squats, the London squat Bristol Gardens, Doll by Doll as “genuinely violent music”, LSD (Leven names Grof/Halifax's “The Human Encounter with Death” as his favourite book), tours with Hawkwind and Devo, both of whom threw the band off. Leven recounts the mugging after a studio session (almost strangled, around a year without a voice), depression, heroin as a painkiller, getting off it with five-element acupuncture, the founding of the CORE Trust and meeting Princess Diana, who at a charity lunch asked him to sing – for him the beginning of the comeback. The close: meeting Deborah Greenwood through a fan letter about “The Mystery of Love…”, the story about the girlfriend and the Dalai Lama's bodyguard, and the question of stadium fame, which he calmly dismisses. Overall verdict: a warm, humorous portrait; Leven as a self-mocking storyteller whose statements are throughout his own accounts.

his reply to Diana when she said he had once been a singer.

2010-12-03-the-guardian-albums-of-2010-h.kurz: In the roundup of the Guardian critics' lists for 2010, Mike Atkinson places Leven's *Gothic Road* sixth in his top ten albums.
inhalt: On 3 December 2010 the Guardian published the individual year-end lists of its music critics. In his album list Mike Atkinson has “Jackie Leven – Gothic Road” at number 6, between Glasser's *Ring* (5) and *We Love* by We Love (7). Number 1 is These New Puritans' *Hidden*, ahead of Rumer, I Am Kloot, the joint album by Ali Farka Touré and Toumani Diabaté, and then John Grant, Hot Chip and the Carolina Chocolate Drops. The list carries no comment on Leven; it is evidence of the attention a late Leven album could still attract in the British press.
zitate_kontext: Entry in Mike Atkinson's top ten albums in the Guardian, 2010.

2010-cooking-vinyl-gothic-road-albumtext.titel: Jackie Leven [Artist page with album text “Gothic Road”]
2010-cooking-vinyl-gothic-road-albumtext.kurz: Cooking Vinyl’s promotional text for *Gothic Road* (2010) opens with an invented dialogue about the album title, then describes guests, themes and sounds. The October 2011 tour dates are listed below it.
inhalt: The Cooking Vinyl artist page carries a long, playfully staged promotional text for *Gothic Road*, Jackie Leven’s first studio album since *Lovers at the Gun Club* (2008). It opens as a little stage scene: at a large meeting at Cooking Vinyl a new label manager asks what the title means. Leven answers that everyone walks two roads, the Royal Road and the Road of Poverty and Death, and where the two meet one is on the “Gothic Road”. Asked whether this is all true, label chief Martin Goldschmidt, without looking up from his doodling, says: “It is now …”

According to the text, the album opens with the choral sound of “Ghost Voices of the Kursk”, sung by three young men from Murmansk whose brothers died in the Russian submarine disaster. This is followed by the voice of a German sat-nav guiding Leven’s tour bus out of Hamburg the year before. After that come twelve strong tales from someone who has walked the road for nearly sixty years, many of them at once mystical and locked into the daily grind of emotional survival.

The guests are named: Ralph McTell supplies the second lead vocal and Gibson acoustic guitars on “Cornelius Whalen”, a song about the man who, when Leven wrote it, was the last surviving Jarrow marcher. Elsewhere Leven fantasises about the actress Tilda Swinton, hides in his hotel minibar from the tyranny of endless touring, sings “Shadow of a Man” by the original punk poet Patrik Fitzgerald, and welcomes a guest recording by co-producer David Wrench (described as a great Welsh singer) on “Island”. In the title song Henry Priestman’s massed plucked cellos stand for the royal-road pomp, John Roberts’s skeletal spoons for the poverty-stricken end of the street; in “Last of the Badmen” celestial choir voices carry a Parton-esque refrain, “please don’t kill me just because you can”.

The text ends by claiming that the music is proof that Leven is not merely going from strength to strength but is close to passing out of sight on a road that others fear to tread. Below it is the listing for an October 2011 tour (Manchester, Hebden Bridge, York, Wavendon, Bristol, Derby, Birmingham, later Glasgow). The listing was still online when Leven died in November 2011; several of the dates had already been cancelled.

The label manager asks, Martin Goldschmidt replies
The label text on the album’s songs

2010-jackieleven-co-uk-gaestebuch-2010.kurz: Of roughly 190 guestbook entries for 2010 only about 25 are genuine; spam takes over from September. Fans praise *Gothic Road*, thank Leven for concerts and ask about the undelivered *Cornish Pub* CD.
inhalt: The guestbook on jackieleven.co.uk holds around 190 entries for 2010, of which only about 25 turn out to be real. From early September 2010 spam entries overwhelm the page; in November a fan explicitly asks for the junk to be deleted, and in December dozens of identical “Very impressed!” posts appear.

The genuine entries are short fan letters. Several praise the new album *Gothic Road*: a visitor in Ayr who attended a concert at Bar Libertine in March calls it excellent, a fan from Cologne loves it and looks forward to the Dortmund show, and a fan from Münster is longing to hear the CD and reports outstanding reviews in local music magazines. Others say thank you for concerts: in April in Egersund (Norway), on 16 May in Munich, where Leven played with Michael Cosgrave, in June in Berlin (with thanks for the conversation after the show), as well as Trowbridge (a festival, where Michael Weston King joined in in the tent), Wallingford (Rugfest), Stuttgart and, on 22 November, Strathpeffer. On 18 June fans congratulate him on his 60th birthday. One listener enjoyed hearing “Stripshow” at Derby and suggests a collaboration with Gwyn Ashton, with whom he could revamp early Doll by Doll material.

Two entries offer memories and leads. One visitor recalls early-1980s London shows (the Embassy Club, the Hope & Anchor, Dingwalls) under the name “The Dead Sea Scouts” and asks about the manager of the time; the name is an unverified fan recollection. Another refers to a conversation between Leven and Edi Stark on BBC Radio Scotland in the autumn of 2010.

A recurring theme is irritation: several fans ask whether anyone has ever received the promised *Cornish Pub* CD, ordered nearly two years earlier, and a fan from Kassel complains that columns and replies to questions have dried up. One fan asks Leven to re-record *Grand Passion* with Deborah Greenwood and to play more electric guitar.
zitate_kontext: Visitor from Ayr, entry of 30 March 2010
Visitor from Bletchley, entry of 12 June 2010
Visitor from Berlin, entry of 9 June 2010

2010-metro-cabell-ian-rankin-and-inspect.kurz: Craig Cabell’s Rankin monograph mentions Leven several times: Rankin toured with him, the joint album *Jackie Leven Said* (2005) touches on Rankin’s formative years, and in a Rebus novel a character buys a Leven CD.
inhalt: Craig Cabell’s monograph *Ian Rankin and Inspector Rebus* (Metro Publishing, 2010) contains several passages on Jackie Leven. Rankin does not write songs, but he toured with Leven and read a short story on the tour. *Jackie Leven Said* (Cooking Vinyl, 2005) is not autobiographical in the strict sense but touches on Rankin’s formative years; a footnote wrongly calls the CD “Jackie Leven Says”.

The book also mentions the funeral of Rankin’s mother in connection with the story, and the reference to Siobhan’s CD purchase – Leven, Lou Reed, Mayall – in *Fleshmarket Close*. One footnote is dated 26 July 2009.

2010-time-out-london-jackie-leven-listin.kurz: Time Out London recommends Leven as a “consistently intense and haunting performer” and mentions *Gothic Road* with Ralph McTell as a guest.
inhalt: The entry in Time Out's “Folk, country and blues” listings, marked as recommended, calls Leven an “excellent” Cooking Vinyl-signed, Fife-based folk-soul and roots man who is “a consistently intense and haunting performer”. The text also points to April's *Gothic Road*, which featured a guest spot by Ralph McTell. Venue and date of the announced concert no longer appear on the page. The page shows the date 11 October 2012, probably a migration date; given the reference to the April album, the text belongs to 2010.

2010-virgin-du-noyer-in-the-city.kurz: In Paul Du Noyer's book *In the City: A Celebration of London Music* (2010) a “great song” by Leven appears in a list of London songs; Du Noyer calls him the “barrel-chested bard of Fife”.
inhalt: Paul Du Noyer, music journalist, friend of Leven and later the author of his obituary, treats the city's musical history in *In the City: A Celebration of London Music* (Virgin Books, London 2010). In a list of London songs he names a “great song” by Jackie Leven and describes him as the “barrel-chested bard of Fife”. The song title cannot be seen in the available excerpt; it is probably a song about Soho, such as “Empty in Soho Square”.

2010-wegottickets-jackie-leven-gothic-ro.kurz: A ticket page for a London concert at Union Chapel: Jackie Leven and his band with guest Ralph McTell, with a short biography, notes on *Gothic Road* and a quotation from the Daily Telegraph.
inhalt: The ticket page (promoter: the Electroacoustic Club) advertises an evening at London's Union Chapel: Jackie Leven and his band play from his latest Cooking Vinyl album, *Gothic Road*, joined by the folk legend Ralph McTell. Leven is introduced as a “cult Scottish poet, singer-songwriter and former Doll By Doll singer”, whose fans include Robert Plant and Ian Rankin.

The short biography follows the familiar pattern: born in 1950 into a Romany family, an outsider in the clannish world of Fife; Doll By Doll made five critically acclaimed albums before splitting. In 1983, after a late-night recording session for a solo album, Leven was the subject of an unprovoked street attack in which he was nearly strangled. Unable to speak or sing, he lost his record deal, friends and way, entering a period of psychic disorder, taking heroin and living in isolation for nearly a year. Since re-joining the world in 1985 he has released a string of excellent albums.

*Gothic Road* opens with the choral sound of “Ghost Voices Of The Kursk”, sung by three young Russian men from Murmansk whose brothers all died in the submarine tragedy, “and so the stage is set” for twelve strong tales from one who has walked the road for nearly sixty years. Neil McCormick of the Daily Telegraph is quoted: “a great musical maverick”, “Britain's lost rock star”, “probably the most talented singer-songwriter never to have become a household name, producing neglected masterpieces since 1971”. Ralph McTell is billed as one of the great storytellers with a virtuoso guitar style modelled on Robert Johnson and Blind Willie McTell, celebrating 30 years on the road: debut *Eight Frames a Second* in 1968, an Ivor Novello Award for “Streets of London” in 1974 and a Lifetime Achievement Award at the BBC Radio 2 Folk Awards in 2002.
zitate_kontext: Neil McCormick (Daily Telegraph), quoted in the event text

2011-04-musikzirkus-magazin-jackie-leven.kurz: Stephan Schelle praises the DVD “Live At Rockpalast” of the 2004 Bonn performance as a dense, intimate concert with Michael Cosgrave and Kevin Foster that kept him glued to the television.
inhalt: Stephan Schelle reviews in April 2011 the recording issued by mig (released 25 April 2011). Rockpalast first brought Leven to Bonn in 2004 to record a concert at the Harmonie on 26 March as part of its Crossroads series, which shows, he says, that the makers have a knack for new, unknown acts worth introducing. Leven sings and plays acoustic guitar, supported by Michael Cosgrave on keyboards (and at times second voice) and Kevin Foster on bass. The listing gives 13 pieces and 72 minutes, while the text speaks of “a total of eight songs”.

The three gave an “extremely intimate” concert, helped by the small, well-filled venue. Schelle had not heard Leven’s music before and was curious; Leven played highlights of *Shining Brother Shining Sister* and his “first hit” “Call Mother A Lonely Field”. Leven himself says of the evening (according to the release notes): it was his first visit to Bonn, with his two favourite musicians, it was a good concert, he sang well, and although he has no personal memory of the performance he can see he was happy to be there and the audience was happy too.

Between songs he tells anecdotes, most amusingly the story in which, just left by his girlfriend, he sits depressed at home and a pigeon looking through the window takes him for dead; it fetches its mate and the two move into the room to build a nest. Leven’s “pleasant voice” carries the sensitive songs that get under the skin, and Cosgrave provides a lovely foundation of atmospheric sounds and instrument voices. It is impossible to single out one song, so dense is the concert; Schelle meant only to glance at the DVD and stayed riveted in front of the television.
zitate_kontext: Stephan Schelle on the concert recording.
Schelle on the evening in Bonn.

2011-05-14-music-week-profile-cooking-vi.kurz: A Music Week profile of Cooking Vinyl (14 May 2011) cites Leven as its example of a high release rate: 23 albums since 1994, five in 2009. Label boss Martin Goldschmidt tries to discourage him, but Leven always finds a reason.
inhalt: The label profile in Music Week (14 May 2011, p. 18) looks at Cooking Vinyl: a mix of label, distribution and a newly built-up music publishing arm under Paul Kinder. On release frequency it says no one knows off the top of their head how many albums the Pixies’ Charles Thompson has released through the label as Frank Black and Black Francis – 17 seems about right. Since 1994, “former Doll By Doll man Jackie Leven has notched up 23 – five of them in 2009”. A caption states that the label cannot even remember how many albums it has released by label stalwarts such as Leven and Frank Black.

Label boss Martin Goldschmidt admits some people think he should say no more often, but it is hard: “With Jackie, I’ll try to discourage him but he always comes up with a brilliant reason for making another one.” The profile stresses that Cooking Vinyl puts out a lot of records, 85 per cent of them turn a profit thanks to deals with minimal or no advances, and that the A&R criterion is as simple as “Do we like it?”. The figure of 23 evidently includes Haunted Valley and pseudonym releases. The profile appeared half a year before Leven’s death.
zitate_kontext: Music Week on Leven’s release rate
Label boss Martin Goldschmidt on Leven

2011-05-25-rocktimes-live-at-rockpalast.kurz: Mike Kempf, who did not know Leven before, finds the DVD *Live At Rockpalast* (recorded 26 March 2004 in Bonn) well played and emotive but without a real “cracker”; he recommends sampling it first.
inhalt: Mike Kempf reviews the DVD *Jackie Leven With Michael Cosgrave – Live At Rockpalast* (MIG, 2011, 72 minutes, 4:3, Dolby Digital 2.0) for RockTimes. The concert was recorded as early as 26 March 2004 at the Harmonie in Bonn and released in April 2011 in the Rockpalast Crossroads series. Kempf, to whom Leven was “hitherto unknown”, describes him as responsible for the lyrical delivery, accompanied by acoustic guitar, bassist Kevin Foster and keyboardist Michael Cosgrave. The trio impresses with songs delivered with feeling.

After the opener “A Little Voice In Space” it was clear to him that he should expect no rock spectacle but an intimate concert whose quality he rates as good, without discovering a real cracker; the song structures are staged with great feeling and, as befits the name of the venue, radiate harmony. Besides Leven’s “first hit” “Call Mother A Lonely Field” there are songs from *Shining Brother Shining Sister*; the Scot’s funny stories raise laughter in the audience. His fellow musicians provide a lovely, melancholic foundation for his expressive voice. However, one must be open to a “note costume moving mainly in murky water”; he sees a risk that the DVD will not go down well with all fans, not least since the sound is only 2.0 Dolby Digital.

His conclusion: the musical quality is undisputedly good, the running time of just under an hour and three-quarters not exactly generous (the disc details give 72 minutes), the lyrics, which almost amount to a biography of the main protagonist, are delivered with sophistication, and the instrumentalists, with no drummer, provide thoroughly solid craftsmanship. The trio seems well rehearsed and delivers a flawless evening; sampling it is advisable. Personally the DVD does not quite knock him off his stool. The line-up list at the end swaps Foster and Cosgrave (keyboards and bass).

2011-06-12-musikreviews-de-live-at-the-r.kurz: An enthusiastic review of the live DVD of the 2004 Rockpalast show in Bonn with Michael Cosgrave and Kevin Foster; Jochen König praises the melancholy, humour and storytelling. The comments add memories from readers and editors and criticism of an obituary.
inhalt: In his review on Musikreviews.de, published on 12 June 2011, Jochen König welcomes the first regular live DVD by the man who introduces himself as “the wonderful Jackie Leven and his music”. (Before it there was only *The Meeting of Remarkable Men*, deliberately billed as “Jackie Leven & Friends”.) The DVD shows a Rockpalast appearance at the Harmonie in Bonn in 2004 with Michael Cosgrave on keyboards and Kevin Foster on bass; three long songs from the then-current album *Shining Brother Shining Sister* are at its centre. The trio is enough for a performance that is “as wistful as it is dynamic”, garnished with Leven’s small, witty, subtly barbed stories. König concedes that at other concerts the burly man from Fife talked far more, but praises his eye for land, people and moods and his sense of timing for punchlines.

Musically he describes Leven’s “typical, fervent variant of Celtic folk rock”: charismatic, rousing, sad, tenderly melancholic, with discreet sarcasm and a readiness to be bawdy. As an example he quotes the line about the jukebox playing a terrible song – “ROBBIE WILLIAMS”. He wishes for more music and more stories from “Jackie Balfour” and regrets there is no word from Sir Vincent Lone, whom Leven buried in 2009: after a “Chablis-fuelled” argument about the influence of Wittgenstein’s central ideas on the late work of Kajagoogoo he allegedly became furious and later died in his flat – one of Leven’s stage tales, passed on by the reviewer as a joke. The high point is the energetic version of “Call Mother A Lonely Field”, including the explanation of the title.

In his verdict König calls the show an excellent introduction to the world of a unique musician, though cinematically “solid regional-TV fare” – but what could one do, or experiment with, when Leven sits on a chair with his guitar, flanked by Cosgrave and Foster, doing what he does incomparably well: being Jackie Leven. The only drawback is the running time of barely 75 minutes, a result of the “small” Rockpalast format. The reviewer’s own user score is 13 out of 15; the editorial rating is embedded as a graphic.

The comments are a small document of their time. Editor Thoralf Koß reports having seen Leven live and being “completely finished” afterwards; after nearly an hour’s conversation he knew that the world should look for exactly such musicians, but only the “otherworldly outsiders” would find them. König describes two concerts, one amid a crowd that chatted throughout, the second alone with Cosgrave, where Leven was an “inimitable” storyteller. On 15 November 2011, the day after Leven’s death, a reader who had seen him for 18 years mourns the stories between the songs. On 17 November König lambasts the FAZ obituary, which called Doll by Doll a “wannabe punk band”, as “a bad joke” born of “ignorance” and “incompetence”.
