2011-08-13-theartsdesk-edinburgh-fringe-.kurz: Graeme Thomson sees Leven at the Edinburgh Fringe three months before his death: physically reduced, but able with voice and guitar alone to captivate a small room – “a winning mix overall of the sacred and profane”.
inhalt: The section on Leven in the round-up review (13 August 2011, comedy section, alongside reviews of Jen Brister and Greg McLaren) carries the caption that the Scottish troubadour's talents are “as expansive as ever”. “Physically reduced he may have been”, but with just voice and guitar he could hold a small room captivated. In recent years Leven has released a bewildering range of music under a variety of pseudonyms, often mixing his tales of Serbian prostitutes, Earls Court cab drivers and damaged Dundonian bar-stool philosophers with ironically cheap and synthetic musical textures; on stage he was a far warmer proposition.

His live act is as much about the yarns as the songs: he offered rambling reflections on the “harrowing” *Toy Story 3* and on losing a girlfriend to the Dalai Lama's bodyguard, as well as “wickedly scatological” tales about a Bay City Rollers badge and a Glasgow photo session. Among the deadpan and very funny banter he “succeeded again and again in cutting right to the heart of the matter”. He played fluid acoustic guitar, and his “big, warm, hungry voice” stretched some of his best songs into powerful shapes, particularly the sad and soulful “Exit Wound”.

It was rarely cheery stuff, but it connected: “Poortoun” (spelt “Poortown” in the piece) told of blighted lives over a haunting melody, and “Beware Soul Brother” – the highlight of his forthcoming album *Wayside Shrines and the Code of the Travelling Man* – was both an elegy for a departed sibling and for the past itself. The verdict: “a winning mix overall of the sacred and profane”. The paragraph names neither venue nor date of the performance. The Leven part is by Graeme Thomson, the other parts by Veronica Lee.

2011-08-28-pennyblackmusic-jackie-leven-.kurz: Probably one of Leven's last interviews, by telephone shortly before the release of Wayside Shrines and the Code of the Travelling Man, the joint record with the keyboard player Michael Cosgrave.
inhalt: Probably one of Leven's last interviews, by telephone shortly before the release of Wayside Shrines and the Code of the Travelling Man, the joint record with the keyboard player Michael Cosgrave. Ben Howarth introduces Leven as a “cult artist's cult artist” (quoting Stewart Lee) and recounts how his father discovered Leven at the Canterbury Fayre festival before Willard Grant Conspiracy. Leven explains that the songs arose in German hotel rooms while waiting for soundchecks and were developed with Cosgrave at soundchecks; he normally records at the Welsh studio Bryn Derwen, this time at Cosgrave's studio on Dartmoor, where he deliberately gave Cosgrave free rein. He talks about Germany as his favourite country to tour, about the backgrounds of songs (“Townes at the Borderline” after an encounter with Townes Van Zandt, “Swine Fever Blues” after a bout of swine flu), about songs that are supposed to take shape only in the studio, about a fixed repertoire of stage stories and how true they are, about the “Official Bootlegs” – prompted by Cooking Vinyl so that he himself would earn from them – and about the “death” of Sir Vincent Lone. Guest tracks by other artists (here John Mayfield) are his principle. At the end: a meeting with Randy Newman after a concert in Bergen and the plan to carry on for at least another ten years.

2011-09-09-gaesteliste-wayside-shrines.kurz: Ullrich Maurer on the last studio album, *Wayside Shrines and the Codes of the Travelling Man*: Cosgrave given free rein, synths and beats, sounds like the live shows, “typical Leven fodder”.
inhalt: On 9 September 2011, about two months before Leven's death, Ullrich Maurer reviews *Wayside Shrines And The Codes Of The Travelling Man* by Jackie Leven and Michael Cosgrave (Cooking Vinyl/Indigo). He recalls that Leven once confessed to liking “Euro-trash pop” – what he hears on the radio or in lifts on his travels – so the “twittering synthesisers and plopping electronic beats” should come as no surprise, especially as Leven gave his long-time partner “virtually free rein” this time, as the name of the CD already shows. Cosgrave brought not just keyboards but accordion, tin whistle and percussion to illustrate Leven's songs, and co-wrote as well; Leven limited himself to acoustic guitars and vocals.

In principle it sounds like the countless concerts the two usually play – which, in a studio production, is “a bit of a problem”, because bass and drums naturally get short shrift. Otherwise it is “typical Leven fodder”: songs written in (and about) German hotel rooms, such as “Swine Fever Blues” (properly “Swine Flu Fever Blues”), once again a poem set to music, and a closing humorous reference to the late great Townes Van Zandt, “including flying shoes”.
The verdict is friendly and sober: Leven carries on his way “unswervingly”, with or without Cosgrave – this time with. The review misprints the album title as “Codes” rather than “Code”.

2011-09-27-ostlendingen-morkets-skjonnhe.kurz: The short review “Mørkets skjønnhet” in Østlendingen portrays *Wayside Shrines and the Code of the Travelling Man* as the work of a storyteller who walks the dark paths of existence, honours his dead brother and Townes Van Zandt, and ends in Vienna.
inhalt: This record review (27 September 2011) on the music page of Østlendingen covers the album by Jackie Leven and Michael Cosgrave and shares its page with reviews of Jonas Alaska, Melissa Horn and others. It opens with a question: “Can anyone give a shopping trolley abandoned in the tide textual meaning? Yes, Jackie Leven.” The 61-year-old Scot had a past in Doll By Doll in the seventies before going solo; a subheading, “Rå gatevold” (“Raw street violence”), points to the attack that, according to the text, made him inactive for some years before he started up again “unstoppably”. He now has an estimated 25 albums behind him.

His narrating, distinctive voice is one main element, his lyrical texts the other. He often moves along the dark paths of existence and does not shy from topics others would avoid: hallucinations during swine fever, say, or his own wish for a grave in Frankfurt. He honours his dead brother as well as the music legend Townes Van Zandt, and ends in noisy traffic backstage in Vienna. The headline “Mørkets skjønnhet” (“The beauty of darkness”) and the tone point to a clearly positive verdict; author and rating symbol are illegible.
zitate_kontext: The critic on Leven’s voice and lyrics

2011-09-netrhythms-wayside-shrines-and-t.kurz: Mike Davies praises Leven’s last studio album, made with Michael Cosgrave alone, as slimmer but fully on a par with *Lovers at the Gun Club* and *Fairytales for Hardmen*, and goes through it track by track.
inhalt: NetRhythms writer Mike Davies reviews the album in September 2011 as Leven’s 24th solo studio album (three of them as Sir Vincent Lone). Leven chose to work solely with his long-time collaborator Michael Cosgrave, feeling that his best recent work had come from their interplay. Davies agrees: a “musically slimmer album perhaps”, but up there with *Lovers At The Gun Club* and *Fairytales For Hardmen*. The songs were mostly written in German hotel rooms and recorded in Cosgrave’s home studio in Dartmoor.

He comments on the songs one by one. “Swine Fever Blues” opens in a familiar Celtic folk-blues mood, with lines about being in Captain Beefheart’s band and about a woman walking the Scottish hills in a long black veil – images that raced through Leven’s mind during his delirium. The “Spooky Berlin Hotel Song” is as advertised: a gothic, foreboding chorus of “Knees Up Mother Brown”, ancient bullet holes, the ghost of a child with broken bones. “Deep Purple Cloak”, written in a Hamburg hotel foyer, is one of Leven’s broken-heart numbers, “a sort of slow core Walker Brothers tune”. Of “To Live And Die In Levenland” Davies admits he is not sure what it is about; it was inspired by Frankfurt’s Gothic cemetery, where one grave carries a Blake quotation, and he likes its striking imagery and the lovely melody.

All the songs have an autobiographical element, he says, but “Townes At The Borderline” is among the most specific: in an acoustic style recalling its subject, Leven tells how he accompanied Townes Van Zandt to hear the bells of St Giles, sketching a poignant portrait of the late legend at the gig. More personal still is “Beware Soul Brother”: Leven wrote the chorus years ago in an austere religious hotel in Münster, but the arpeggio-led verses only came this year, after the death of his younger brother – a loss Davies also hears in the downbeat homecoming “The Kirkcaldy Book Of The Dead”.

Of the remaining tracks, the brief “Dagenham Dream” is as lovely as it is reflective. “A Kiss On The Cheek” is not by Leven and Cosgrave at all but a poem written and played by the film composer John Mayfield and spoken by the “mystical humanist” Gola Wolf Richards, all of whom generously share in the album’s royalties. The closer, “Backstage, Chelsea Club, Vienna”, consists only of Cosgrave reading out the band names written on the club’s dressing-room walls over a soundcheck instrumental and Viennese street sounds – bizarre, but more entrancing than it sounds in print. No star rating; the verdict is plainly positive.

2011-11-08-word-magazine-blog-jackie-lev.kurz: The user “Bogart” (later also active in the Afterword) opens a thread on 08.11.2011: Leven is “very poorly in hospital”, and people are asked to collect stories and thoughts about him; he will hear about them and it may help him.
inhalt: The user “Bogart” (later also active in the Afterword) opens a thread on 08.11.2011: Leven is “very poorly in hospital”, and people are asked to collect stories and thoughts about him; he will hear about them and it may help him. He sketches the path from St Judas and John St. Field via Doll by Doll to solo artist and recalls that the Independent once called him Britain's “great lost popstar”. Over the following days around 17 users write: several discovered Leven through “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” on an Uncut cover CD; a reader from Nova Scotia says Leven cancelled an appointment there and calls him “Van Morrison with his inspiration intact”; a man from Birmingham, whose concert two weeks earlier had been cancelled and moved to early January, tells his “Wrapped Up In Blue” anecdote (the same as in the Afterword 2021/2024). “duco01” came to Leven through his songs for Kevin Coyne; asked whether he had ever sung with Coyne, Leven replied that he had preferred to sit in the audience, and he gave a young guitarist from the writer's family a guest-list place and advice.

On 13.11.2011, the day before the death, the user “Turner” copies a notice from Leven's website into the thread: Leven was gravely ill with cancer and had “only a few days to live”; the same biographical paragraph follows (“In a career stretching over forty years …”, with the error “solo resurgence through the 1980s”) that after the death stood on the obituary home page. From 15.11. words of farewell follow; at the end Bogart quotes a line from “Working Alone / A Blessing”.

2011-11-14-jackieleven-co-uk-gaestebuch-.kurz: They begin on the evening of 14.11.2011 (Brussels, Kassel) and peak on 15 and 16.11.; they are written from Scotland and England, Germany (Bochum, Lauterbach, Münster, Düsseldorf, Essen, Frankfurt, Hannover, Kiel, Krefeld, Bremen, Dresden), Norway (Egersund, Oslo, Trondheim, Drammen), Sweden, the Czech Republic, the Netherlands, Belgium, Northern Ireland, Australia, New Zealand and the USA, some in German. The tone is grief and gratitude for songs, voice, guitar playing and above all the stories; many drink to him (“white bar in Heaven”, “best bar in the sky”). Many only heard of it days or weeks later, and some did not know he had been ill.
inhalt: They begin on the evening of 14.11.2011 (Brussels, Kassel) and peak on 15 and 16.11.; they are written from Scotland and England, Germany (Bochum, Lauterbach, Münster, Düsseldorf, Essen, Frankfurt, Hannover, Kiel, Krefeld, Bremen, Dresden), Norway (Egersund, Oslo, Trondheim, Drammen), Sweden, the Czech Republic, the Netherlands, Belgium, Northern Ireland, Australia, New Zealand and the USA, some in German. The tone is grief and gratitude for songs, voice, guitar playing and above all the stories; many drink to him (“white bar in Heaven”, “best bar in the sky”). Many only heard of it days or weeks later, and some did not know he had been ill.

Alongside these are memories from people in his circle. Several write about the Doll by Doll period: visits to the band's squat in Maida Vale or “Clifton Villas” in 1979, where the band, with friends and crew, took in young fans; a man from Edinburgh remembers how Doll by Doll, as support for Hawkwind, raided their catering before Hawkwind walked past in capes and silver helmets; others mention concerts at the Blue Note in Derby (around 1980) and at Brollies, Richmond (around 1976?). The brother of a Doll by Doll musician announces that the latter will be at the funeral. Dan Britton, a member of the backing band The Stornoway Girls, thanks Leven for the collaboration and for including a song of his on *When The Bridegroom Comes*. A musician from Wakefield was proud to have stood on stage with Leven; a harmonica player recalls duo performances in Bournemouth and his contribution to “Uptown”; a reviewer says that Deborah Greenwood had already sent him *Control* for review in 1974. An old companion recalls a Norway tour in 1997 and the WOMAD performance on the day of Princess Diana's death, as well as the CORE years. Further traces: a concert in “your Kingdom of Fife” in March 2011 before 53 people, Robyn Hitchcock dedicated a song to Leven at a concert in Shoreditch, BBC Radio 4 featured him on 20.11. in *Last Word*, a Dutchman watches the 2004 Rockpalast recording, an Australian recalls performances in Sydney, at WOMADelaide, in the Barossa Valley and at WOMAD New Zealand.

2011-11-15-adresseavisen-jackie-leven-er.kurz: The Trondheim newspaper Adresseavisen reports on 15 November 2011 the death of the ‘friend of Trondheim’ Jackie Leven; only the standfirst is freely readable.
inhalt: Adresseavisen (Trondheim) reports at 13.38 on 15 November 2011, under the headline ‘Jackie Leven er død’, the death of the Scottish troubadour, whom it calls a ‘friend of Trondheim’: he died on Monday. The author is the music journalist Vegard Enlid.
Only the standfirst is visible; the article itself lies behind the paper’s paywall and was not read. The label ‘friend of Trondheim’ alone suggests that Leven was remembered there as a regular guest.

2011-11-15-bbc-news-tributes-to-scottish.kurz: BBC News reports Leven’s death at 61 from cancer and gathers reactions from Ian Rankin, Tom Morton, Eddi Reader and Cooking Vinyl, plus a statement from Leven’s own website.
inhalt: On 15 November 2011 the BBC reports that the Scottish singer-songwriter Jackie Leven has died “after a battle with cancer” aged 61. He was a founding member of the punk band Doll by Doll (a label Leven himself rejected) and had a lengthy solo career; among his many releases was a joint album with the crime writer Ian Rankin, who like Leven hailed from Fife. A reformed drug addict, Leven “and his wife” set up a charity for the treatment of heroin addiction – other sources identify this as the CORE Trust, which he co-founded in 1985.

Rankin tweeted: “RIP Jackie Leven. Gentle man, poetic songwriter, skilled guitarist, storyteller. It was an honour to call you friend.” BBC Radio Scotland presenter Tom Morton wished he still had some of Leven’s whisky ‘Leven’s Lament’ to drink to his memory. Eddi Reader asked in disbelief: “Has Jackie gone?? What hard news today!” Cooking Vinyl called him a long-time friend and label artist who had lost his battle with cancer.

The item quotes at length a statement from Leven’s official website from the days before his death: in a career stretching over 40 years he had carved an impressive reputation as a uniquely gifted singer-songwriter, from his emergence as leader of the “underrated” Doll by Doll through addiction problems that he overcame with remarkable strength of will, to a solo resurgence “through the 1980s” (probably meaning the 1990s) to the present. He was the composer of over 400 songs, including arguably his greatest, ‘Call Mother’, from the album *The Mystery of Love*, which Q magazine had ranked among the ‘100 Best Albums of All Time’. If sales did not always reflect the overwhelmingly positive critical reception, he remained a perceptive writer and performer, imbued with restless creativity, with ruminative lyrics laced with humour and melodic grace. As a performer he could enthral audiences with picaresque tales from first-hand experience; those who worked with him knew his mordant wit and very idiosyncratic world view.
zitate_kontext: From the tribute on Leven’s official website

2011-11-15-bergensavisen-jackie-leven-er.kurz: Bergensavisen's short death notice of 15 November 2011: Bergen's “friend” Leven died aged 61 after a long battle with cancer; it recalls his many visits to Bergen and a concert for prison inmates.
inhalt: On 15 November 2011 (19.32, updated the next morning) Ingrid Linde Bakken reports Jackie Leven's death on ba.no. Under the line “Bergensvenn og musiker døde i går” (Friend of Bergen and musician died yesterday) it says that this “friend of Bergen” had suffered from cancer for a long time and died of the illness on Monday evening. He was born on 18 June 1950 and died aged 61.

The Scot had been to Bergen many times, among other things for the Bergenfest festival; the archive photo shows him “ready for Bergenfest in 2005”. In 2003 he played for the inmates of Bergen Landsfengsel (prison), where he expressed great love for the city. He is quoted: “Bergen has a very special place in my heart. I love the city, its surroundings and the women there. The whole atmosphere reminds me of the one I experience in my own Scotland.” Beyond that the item offers no appreciation of his work; it is a local obituary that shows Leven chiefly as a returning guest of the city.
zitate_kontext: Leven on Bergen, in 2003 at the prison concert.

2011-11-15-boards-ie-jackie-leven-r-i-p.kurz: On the Irish forum boards.ie a user opens a memorial thread after Leven’s death, praising him as an underrated singer, guitarist and songwriter and recommending his catalogue, Doll by Doll included.
inhalt: The opening post of the thread “Jackie Leven R.I.P.” on the Irish forum boards.ie, posted on 15 November 2011, the day after Leven’s death, is by the user “wezzopalooza”. The author pays tribute to Leven as an underrated singer, guitarist and songwriter and urges readers to explore his catalogue, explicitly including the Doll by Doll albums. According to the available information, the publicly accessible page showed only this opening post and no replies. The text is a short forum-style obituary and contains no new biographical information.

2011-11-15-caught-by-the-river-caught-by.kurz: Mick Houghton, who in 1978 was responsible for Doll by Doll in the press department of Warner Bros and in 1994 again worked as Leven's press man, remembers on the day after the death.
inhalt: Mick Houghton, who in 1978 was responsible for Doll by Doll in the press department of Warner Bros and in 1994 again worked as Leven's press man, remembers on the day after the death. The first meeting in spring 1978 with Leven and Jo Shaw, both visibly on LSD, the concert at the tiny Rock Garden before a handful of onlookers and interviews with the music press (Hugh Fielder of Sounds; Shaw walked out of an interview in a fish-and-chip shop in Burton upon Trent without a word) paint a picture of a band that intimidated its audience rather than merely threatening it, as punk did. Houghton describes the concept: making the suffering of the soul public, benefit concerts for R. D. Laing's Philadelphia Association instead of Rock Against Racism, flyers and Artaud pictures, plus the aborted NME cover story with Nick Kent. After the debut Remember his involvement ended; in 1994 he worked again with the now gentler Leven on two albums. At the end comes the Dylan story (alleged train journey Berlin–Saint Petersburg in 1988, song after “One Too Many Mornings”), which Houghton never believed. Overall tone: affectionately ironic, Leven as a lovable rogue.

2011-11-15-classic-rock-jackie-leven-die.kurz: Classic Rock's short news item of 15 November 2011 reports Leven's death at 61 after a long illness with cancer and recalls Doll by Doll and his solo career since 1994.
inhalt: Classic Rock reported Leven's death on 15 November 2011 (12:19 pm) in its news section under the headline "Jackie Leven Dies". The item is only a few sentences long: the Scottish singer Jackie Leven has died aged 61, having been suffering from cancer "for some while".

As to his career, it says he first made his name with the cult band Doll by Doll during the punk/new wave era and subsequently established his reputation as a soulful, dramatic storyteller with a considerable number of solo albums released since 1994. It closes by pointing readers to Leven's website. The byline is "mdome"; a reader comment attached adds no further information.
zitate_kontext: Classic Rock on the solo career

2011-11-15-cooking-vinyl-jackie-leven-ju.kurz: The label's official obituary, published the day after the death. It begins with the same sentence as the obituary home page of jackieleven.co.uk (death on Monday, 14 November, “at 8 o'clock in the evening”, cancer) and the same Leven quotation about “spiritual” and “soulful” storytellers.
inhalt: The label's official obituary, published the day after the death. It begins with the same sentence as the obituary home page of jackieleven.co.uk (death on Monday, 14 November, “at 8 o'clock in the evening”, cancer) and the same Leven quotation about “spiritual” and “soulful” storytellers. A detailed account of his life follows: birth in Kirkcaldy, outsider childhood in Glenrothes (father “Irish Cockney”, mother from Newcastle, Romany background), essay prize and expulsion from school for drugs, marriage at 16, rocket factory, driven out by a gang at 17, wandering years (farm work, Berlin, Kerry, Madrid with *Control*), Doll by Doll (four albums, the last with David Gilmour, split in 1983), solo contract with Charisma/Virgin, the mugging in Market Street in Islington (strangled and injured in the throat), loss of the falsetto, several years of heroin, getting clean with five-element acupuncture and “psychic healing”, CORE Trust; from 1994 *Songs From The Argyll Cycle* and *The Mystery Of Love…*, then 24 further albums, *Jackie Leven Said* with Ian Rankin, Ubudoll with David Thomas, Leven's Lament (bottled by Islay Mist), annual walks, five albums in 2009 (Haunted Valley double and Sir Vincent Lone), *Gothic Road* and *Wayside Shrines* with Michael Cosgrave, which Martin Goldschmidt considers the best since *The Mystery Of Love*. Close: Leven's description of *Wayside Shrines* as a “homeopathic record”.

2011-11-15-faz-nachruf-auf-jackie-leven-.kurz: In a short, rather detached obituary in the FAZ, Edo Reents calls Leven one of the most luckless songwriters, undone by a false name, the wrong moment and an assault.
inhalt: Edo Reents of the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung's arts pages opens his short obituary by saying that Jackie Leven will go down in history as one of the singers and songwriters most dogged by bad luck. He started early, but under a false name (John St. Field), so that his folk – in Reents's view not as varied and intense as that of his Scottish compatriot Gerry Rafferty – could not be permanently attributed to him; his debut *Control* sold little and was quickly forgotten.

The founding of the “wannabe punk band” Doll By Doll came, in Reents's account, at the wrong time, since after 1975 one had to offer “disco, wave or really hard stuff” to stay in business. When Leven was about to make a second solo attempt in 1983 he was assaulted and was practically out of action for two years. Even the heroin he fled into could not prevent the “bear of a man with a tender soul” from still becoming a performer who, in his late phase, took his cue from Johnny Cash's “destructive musician's strategy”. His records, released regularly from 1994, did not reach a mass audience but were valued by lovers of “unobtrusive, moderate country and folk”. The first was called *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*; Leven and his followers can now get to the bottom of this truth separately, in the hereafter and in the here.

On Monday Leven, who came from the barren country of Fife, a “descendant of a Roma family” (Reents's words; the ancestry rests on Leven's own account) and a welcome guest in Germany until the end, died aged 61. The tone is detached; the standfirst calls him a folk singer, Cash epigone and wannabe punk who never found the large audience. Doll by Doll are otherwise usually classed as a new wave band; the label “wannabe punk band” is Reents's own sharpening.
zitate_kontext: Opening sentence of Edo Reents's FAZ obituary.

2011-11-15-leonardcohenforum-jackie-leve.kurz: On the Leonard Cohen fans' forum, members report Leven's illness and death and share memories: the whisky he poured at the Celtic Connections festival club, a concert in Bournemouth and the correct pronunciation of his name at the funeral.
inhalt: The forum thread “Jackie Leven RIP” in the “Other music” section has six posts between 15 November 2011 and 25 September 2012. The thread starter, Diane, first reports Leven's serious illness, copying the announcement from his website, and then his death, with the opening of the Guardian obituary.

One member recalls how Leven generously poured samples of his whisky for the whole audience at the Celtic Connections festival club in Glasgow. Diane says she once handed him her water bottle at a concert in Bournemouth, and praises the way he combined poetry with down-to-earth comedy. Another member reports on the funeral in Hampshire, where the celebrant mispronounced the name: “Leven” should rhyme with “grievin'”, after the river and the town in Fife. In 2012 Diane points to Paul Du Noyer's obituary.

2011-11-15-musikkbloggen-jackie-leven-19.kurz: Rune Letrud announces Leven’s death on the blog Musikkbloggen, calling him a “tragically overlooked songwriter” who had a devoted audience in Norway.
inhalt: The short obituary on the Norwegian music blog by Rune Letrud appears on 15 November 2011. The Scottish “gentleman and songwriter par excellence” had been seriously ill with cancer, and it was “with sorrow” that one must report he had left the day before “in favour of the Great Gig in the Sky”, where he now joins an increasingly star-studded band in the hereafter. Leven was a “tragically overlooked songwriter” who had played in Norway several times and has a “devoted audience” there.

Letrud himself became aware of Leven through Ian Rankin’s Rebus novels, in which Inspector Rebus repeatedly highlights Leven as “some of the best that Scotland has produced”. The two also made a joint record, *Jackie Leven Said*. The career began with the record *Control* under the name John St. Field – dated 1975 in the text – and then as songwriter of the “punk-influenced” Doll by Doll; later he released nearly forty records as a solo artist, commercial albums as well as live records issued exclusively for a very devoted fan club. Leven died on 14 November at 8 pm.
The blog pays tribute with a small video, an added pointer to the obituary at The Arts Desk, and an embedded interview including the song ‘Empty in Soho Square’.
zitate_kontext: Letrud on how he found Leven

2011-11-15-nickchurchill-org-uk-remember.kurz: The Dorset journalist Nick Churchill published a short obituary on the day of the death (blog post of 15.11.2011, updated 2016) and documented beneath it three interviews he had done with Leven for the Bournemouth Echo.
inhalt: The Dorset journalist Nick Churchill published a short obituary on the day of the death (blog post of 15.11.2011, updated 2016) and documented beneath it three interviews he had done with Leven for the Bournemouth Echo. In the obituary he recalls a performance before about 30 people in the skittle alley of his village pub in Dorset (Bere Regis), near the farm where Leven once lived.

- **May 2006** (before a concert at Club Hobo, Bournemouth, 20 May, with Joe Shaw): Leven on former places of residence (Westbourne, Parkstone, Corfe Mullen), a “lifetime lack of achievement award”, the Q Awards, a major German prize with a string-quartet arrangement of “St Judas”, a planned album of songs by Judee Sill and Lightnin' Hopkins, and the Doll by Doll reissues, which hinged on Warner having lost the legal papers.
- **October 2008** (Lovers At The Gun Club, concert at the Opera House): Leven would like to produce Amy Winehouse; explanations of “Fareham Confidential” (drum loop from “Ruby Don't Take Your Love to Town”), of his relationship with Cooking Vinyl and of his Dorset years (farmhouse near Blandford after Control).
- **March 2010** (Gothic Road): Leven on a feared schoolmate, on Gordon Brown, whom he supports, the concept of the “two roads” behind the album title, Ralph McTell and the Jarrow March, the dedication to the musician Tim Mycroft from Blandford.

2011-11-15-rolling-stone-de-jackie-leven.kurz: Rolling Stone’s German edition reports Leven’s death on 15 November 2011 in a few sentences, quotes his remark on spiritual and soulful storytellers and mentions his dark last album. Age and place are partly wrong.
inhalt: The short text reports that the Scottish songwriter Jackie Leven, who had cancer, “died on Monday at eight in the evening in Southhampton” and was 62 years old. Both details are imprecise: Leven died on Monday 14 November 2011, aged 61; “Southhampton” is misspelt (evidently Southampton, a place not mentioned anywhere else), as is “Kilkcaldy” for his birthplace Kirkcaldy.

As one of his better-known quotations the editors give a remark Leven made about himself more than once: there are spiritual storytellers and soulful storytellers, and he hopes to belong to the latter. “Spiritual” means striving upwards, heaven, God and all that; his stories, by contrast, reach into the earth, have juice and are nourishing.

Finally the piece points to his last album, *Wayside Shrines and the Code of the Travelling Man*, released only in September 2011 and recorded with his keyboardist Michael Cosgrave, and describes it as a collection of dark songs about illness, hallucinations and death. The photo is credited to Cooking Vinyl.
zitate_kontext: Leven (quoted in German translation), as cited by Rolling Stone
Rolling Stone on the final album

2011-11-15-spiegel-online-songwriter-jac.kurz: A short Spiegel obituary: Leven sang of heroin addiction, alcoholism, madness and depression, was a “colossus of a man” with a “filigree voice”, and toured Germany regularly with loyal fans.
inhalt: The Spiegel Online obituary of 15 November 2011 names as Leven’s great themes heroin addiction and alcoholism, madness and depression, eternal restlessness and pathological longing, worked out in folk, blues and country gospel. At a concert one saw a “colossus of a man – with an extremely filigree voice”. Born in Fife in 1950, Leven released more than two dozen solo albums, including a live album from a Norwegian prison – he probably took the idea from Johnny Cash, whom he honoured in 2005 with *Elegy for Johnny Cash*.

His last album, *Wayside Shrines and the Code of the Travelling Man*, had come out only in September, songs about illness, hallucinations and death, partly recorded in German hotel rooms. In Germany he had loyal fans and toured regularly. The “son of an Irishman and a Roma” began his career in the late seventies in the “punk band” Doll By Doll (a simplification); it released four albums and broke up over friction with the label. Leven died on Monday aged 61 of cancer.
zitate_kontext: Spiegel Online on Leven’s German audience.

2011-11-15-the-guardian-jackie-leven-obi.kurz: The most important British newspaper obituary, written by the Guardian folk and world music critic Robin Denselow, who had known Leven since the late 1970s and had interviewed him himself in 1988.
inhalt: The most important British newspaper obituary, written by the Guardian folk and world music critic Robin Denselow, who had known Leven since the late 1970s and had interviewed him himself in 1988. Denselow calls Leven a brilliant outsider with a loyal cult following but without the success he deserved. He sketches the background in Kirkcaldy (Roma descent, in Leven's own account), the early marriage at 16, the wandering years as a labourer and the stage name John St Field. Doll by Doll guitarist Joe Shaw is given extensive space: getting to know each other in a folk club in Bridport (Dorset), a shared squat in Dorset, a meeting in Hamburg, a rehearsal room in the Maida Vale squat. Denselow quotes his own characterisation of Leven at the time as a mixture of Van Morrison and psychopath, and mentions Gypsy Blood and the U2 support slot at the London venue. Next come the 1984 mugging in north London (ribs broken, larynx almost destroyed), the heroin addiction (Leven told Denselow of £150 a day), the cure through acupuncture and reflexology, and the founding of the CORE Trust with Carol Wolf, supported by Pete Townshend and Westminster City Council. At a meeting in 1988, Leven preferred to talk about CORE rather than Concrete Bulletproof Invisible (with Shaw and Glen Matlock). Cooking Vinyl boss Martin Goldschmidt says it took him two years to sign Leven, and that he released 26 albums; he calls the whisky brand “Leven's Lament” and the Dylan song story on the train to Moscow “scams”. Mentioned are Mystery of Love with Robert Bly and Mike Scott, Sir Vincent Lone, Deborah Greenwood, David Thomas and Jackie Leven Said with Ian Rankin. Overall tone: warm, respectful, with the expectation that the music will find a larger audience.
zitate_kontext: Denselow's own description from the Doll by Doll period.

2011-11-15-the-spill-readers-recommend-r.kurz: The opening post pays tribute to Leven as a songwriter who encouraged other musicians to write themselves.
inhalt: The opening post pays tribute to Leven as a songwriter who encouraged other musicians to write themselves. More productive than the short announcement of his death is the comment thread: it shows several ways in which listeners discovered Leven. tincanman2010 expressly names the music references in Ian Rankin's Rebus novels. Others came to him through Doll by Doll or through the music selection of the Readers Recommend community.

notsosourpus reports on his contact via the songwriter Dan Britton and on talks about possible performances in Budapest. These did not come about; no tour date can therefore be inferred from them. An anonymously posted comment recalls Britton's participation in a Haunted Valley Christmas concert and makes the connection to “Greetings from Milford” and other live releases.

The thread also contains a reference to a planned Leven tribute on Johny Brown's “Mining for Gold” on Resonance FM the following Friday. That is a concrete lead for radio archives, but not yet proof of a broadcast. The page shows 22 comments or replies in all. As a source it documents the networking of the fan community; their memories and attributions of records are in each case statements by the users concerned.

2011-11-15-theartsdesk-jackie-leven-1950.kurz: Tribute by Graeme Thomson on the morning after Leven's death. He calls Leven one of the country's most distinctive songwriters with a stubbornly low commercial profile and describes the cast of his songs (Serbian prostitutes, Earls Court taxi drivers, convicts, pub philosophers from Dundee), with whom Leven identified; as his best songs he names “Poortoun” and “Universal Blue”. Leven was an ex-junkie, brawler and enthusiastic drinker, the late records often uneven, the concerts with their digressions (Laurence Olivier, a photo session in a Glasgow alley) always worth seeing. Thomson last saw him in August 2011 in Edinburgh, physically weakened.
inhalt: Tribute by Graeme Thomson on the morning after Leven's death. He calls Leven one of the country's most distinctive songwriters with a stubbornly low commercial profile and describes the cast of his songs (Serbian prostitutes, Earls Court taxi drivers, convicts, pub philosophers from Dundee), with whom Leven identified; as his best songs he names “Poortoun” and “Universal Blue”. Leven was an ex-junkie, brawler and enthusiastic drinker, the late records often uneven, the concerts with their digressions (Laurence Olivier, a photo session in a Glasgow alley) always worth seeing. Thomson last saw him in August 2011 in Edinburgh, physically weakened.

The original version (preserved in the LiveJournal reproduction) was followed by an edited version of an older Herald profile by Thomson, in which the 56-year-old Leven tells at length: being an outsider because of his Roma family in the Fife of the 1950s, nights spent fleeing gangs, LSD years and episodic mental illness during the Doll by Doll period, the 1984 mugging after a bottle of Canadian Club on the way to Maida Vale, two years without a voice and with heroin, healing through acupuncture and “psychic healing”, CORE Trust (Lady Diana, Westminster City Council award), monthly acupuncture to this day, a visit to Oslo and the forthcoming Doll by Doll CD reissues, including musings on a reunion. The current page contains only the obituary part.
zitate_kontext: Leven on his Doll by Doll years (Herald profile).

2011-11-15-theartsdesk-kommentare-jackie.kurz: Beneath Graeme Thomson's obituary (15.11.2011) there were around 30 reader comments up to March 2012; they are no longer visible on the live page today, but are complete in the Wayback capture of 2021.
inhalt: Beneath Graeme Thomson's obituary (15.11.2011) there were around 30 reader comments up to March 2012; they are no longer visible on the live page today, but are complete in the Wayback capture of 2021. A Viennese fan (“Rodja”) learned the news through Michael Cosgrave's Facebook page; Leven's Vienna concert in September had been cancelled. Several commenters name the Southsea Folk and Roots Festival as a regular meeting place, others concerts in Otley, New Brighton, at the Green Man Festival, in Hebden Bridge, Glasgow, Stornoway (1990s) and at the Chimney Boy in Faversham.

Two entries come from Leven's professional circle: the documentary maker Mark Kidel says that Leven had seen his Channel 4 film *Kind of Blue* about melancholy and depression in the 1990s and invited him to show and discuss it at a centre for addicts in Marylebone; Kidel describes Leven's charisma and empathy with those affected. A musician who played on Leven's albums thanks him for introducing him to Yeats's line about the “rag and bone shop of the heart” (February 2012). A Belgian fan describes how in 2008, seriously ill, he set off at short notice for Leven's concert in Eeklo in order to shake his hand.

2011-11-15-word-magazine-blog-jackie-lev.autor: MarkHagen; Amigoman; stevedickychap; Burt Kocain (thread starter)
2011-11-15-word-magazine-blog-jackie-lev.kurz: After Leven’s death on 14 November 2011, four threads about him appeared on the reader blogs of Word magazine within days: grief, pointers to songs and concerts, surprise at how little known he was, and a failed joke that sparked a debate about decency.
inhalt: After the news of Leven’s death, readers of Word magazine’s online blog opened four threads within two days. In “Jackie Leven RIP” (started by MarkHagen on 15 November) the opening post says he died the previous night, only hours after his battle with cancer had been made public. The comments honour a man who was always out of step, always the bridesmaid, but made seriously good music and poignant lyrics. Links include Doll by Doll’s “Main Travelled Roads”, a concert recording about a year old and a note on Tom Morton’s tribute on his afternoon BBC Radio Scotland show. One reader had tickets for a Wakefield gig in December; another had planned to see him in late October, the gig cancelled and apparently rescheduled for January. One reader came to Leven only through the double CD *Exit Wound* with Ian Rankin and calls him “an upgrade on Van Morrison, better person, better songs”. Others love *Defending Ancient Springs* or call his version of “I Say a Little Prayer” the best they have ever heard.

The second thread, “RIP Jackie Leven” (Amigoman, 15 November), has praise for the singer and guitarist (“a true maverick”) but also the barbed question of who he was and why anyone should be upset. One reader replies that he knew him as a Roy Harper-style folk singer and was surprised to find he had also played in the new-wave band Doll by Doll; he saw him live once and found him a thoroughly nice bloke. Another honours the courage to write “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” and names *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*. “Lament for Leven” (stevedickychap, 16 November) consists solely of a song lyric ending “RIP Jackie”.

The fourth thread, “Jackie Leven Update” (Burt Kocain, 17 November), opens with the joke “Still dead, apparently” and triggers a debate about taste: several users call it crass, the author defends it as a comment on the many parallel threads. One reader points out that Leven himself had a mordant sense of humour, recalling his infamous joke story about Sting being dead, and quotes Leven’s last tweet (“Aliive alive alive o”).

Reader comment, headed by *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*
A reader who discovered Leven through *Exit Wound*
Reader in the debate over the joke thread

2011-11-16-bbc-blogs-stuart-bailie-jacki.kurz: The BBC journalist Stuart Bailie recalls in a short obituary Leven’s Borderline gig in a kilt serving his own whisky, Doll By Doll, the life-changing advice “get on the bus” to Mike Scott, and the CORE Trust.
inhalt: Stuart Bailie, music journalist and BBC Radio Ulster presenter, pays tribute to Leven on 16 November 2011 in his BBC blog. He remembers seeing Leven at The Borderline in London, wearing a kilt and serving up his own whisky: poetry and intense music, all fastened by the great physical presence of the man who was reared in Fife but had Irish and Romany roots.

Doll By Doll, he says, were a cult act in the years after punk, spiky and individual but also prone to mystical asides in the Van Morrison tradition. His old NME colleague Stuart Maconie was a big fan, and Leven was celebrated in the sleevenotes to The Waterboys’ *Fisherman’s Blues*: Mike Scott had been complaining about the stresses of life as a commercial rock star in 1986 and said he would rather be on a bus in Ayr, savouring the fresh air of home. Leven’s response was life-changing: “Well, get on the bus then.”

Bailie mentions the violent attack in the Eighties that nearly cost Leven his voice through strangulation, and his heroin addiction. He spent a memorable afternoon in west London in 1992 hearing Leven’s stories about the dark side, illuminated by information about his rehabilitation charity, The CORE Trust. Leven was friends with Robert Bly of Iron John fame; his solo records of recent years were full of Celtic expanse, name-checking Van and Louis MacNeice, performing with Ian Rankin and also releasing music as Sir Vincent Lone. You didn’t need to know him well, Bailie ends, to be impressed by the vigour of the man.

Leven’s response to Mike Scott when Scott complained about rock-star life in 1986 (according to Bailie)

2011-11-16-dagsavisen-jackie-leven-er-do.kurz: Dagsavisen reports Leven’s death in brief and honours him as a “great friend of Norway” who toured the country, recorded in Bergen prison and came to his joint album through Ian Rankin’s Rebus.
inhalt: The print edition of Dagsavisen for 16 November 2011 carries a short item on its culture page: the Scottish singer and songwriter Jackie Leven died on Monday aged 61. He broke through in 1979 as frontman of the group Doll By Doll, then vanished for many years with personal problems, but returned in 1994 and has since released 24 albums, “mostly of a high standard”.

Most of the item concerns Leven’s relationship with Norway: “Leven was a great friend of Norway.” He played the length and breadth of the country, often sang about places he visited, translated Rolf Jacobsen into English and recorded an album in Bergen prison. On a flight to Tromsø, the paper says, he discovered that he was one of the favourite singers of Ian Rankin’s fictional detective John Rebus; Rankin and Leven afterwards made the album *Jackie Leven Said* together.

The details are the paper’s own. That Leven ‘translated’ Jacobsen is probably a simplification: on *Fairy Tales for Hardmen* he recites Robert Bly’s English translation of Jacobsen’s poem ‘Sunflower’. The item sits among brief notes on other subjects on the culture page.
zitate_kontext: Dagsavisen on Leven’s ties to Norway

2011-11-16-david-belbin-jackie-leven-rip.kurz: The Nottingham writer David Belbin (young-adult and crime novels) writes a personal obituary two days after Leven's death.
inhalt: The Nottingham writer David Belbin (young-adult and crime novels) writes a personal obituary two days after Leven's death. He says he met Leven several times over the years and could hardly reconcile the affable, very funny man with the fearsome singer he saw in 1979 with Doll by Doll at the Garage in Nottingham – Leven told him twenty years later that it had been one of their few good gigs. Belbin mentions the John St Field album from the early 1970s, the assault, the heroin addiction and Leven's return as a prolific songwriter and storyteller, who he says made him laugh more than any current stand-up comedian.

He had a ticket for a concert in Derby in October 2011 that had been postponed – now he knew the reason. Leven, he says, never played encores (at most granting a single request), but after concerts he would hug and kiss fans and sign autographs. He points to the obituaries in the Guardian and the Herald and to Kevin Hewick's piece at Louder Than War, and posts the song *To Live and Die in Levenland* as an MP3. In the comments one reader recalls a concert at Jim's Café in Colne; in 2021 Belbin adds a reply pointing to the new tribute album.
zitate_kontext: Belbin on Leven as a storyteller.

2011-11-16-fan-lexikon-jackie-leven-ist-.kurz: A short news item of 16 November 2011: Jackie Leven died on Monday 14 November aged 61 of cancer; his latest albums were *Gothic Road* and *Wayside Shrines…*, 24 albums in all, many under pseudonyms.
inhalt: The portal Fan-Lexikon reported on 16 November 2011 (dateline London): “Jackie Leven is dead.” The Scottish singer and songwriter died on Monday 14 November at the age of 61. Leven had suffered from cancer for a long time and had now lost the fight against the disease.

His most recent albums were *Gothic Road* (2010) and *Wayside Shrines And The Code Of The Travelling Man* (2011). In total he released 24 albums, many of them under pseudonyms; he had called himself John St. Field or Sir Vincent Lone, for instance.

2011-11-16-gaffa-jackie-leven-er-dod.kurz: Espen Strunk reports Jackie Leven’s death at 61 for GAFFA, recalling the five-star review of his last album *Wayside Shrines and the Code of the Travelling Man* and the concert planned at Kinross.
inhalt: The Danish music magazine GAFFA reports on 16 November 2011, under the headline “Jackie Leven er død” (“Jackie Leven is dead”), that the 61-year-old songwriter has lost his battle with cancer. Author Espen Strunk recalls that only a few months earlier GAFFA’s reviewer had given five stars to the latest album by the “somewhat overlooked, but highly productive and critically acclaimed” Scottish guitarist, singer and songwriter. The premise was simple: apart from two exceptions, all the songs were written in various German hotel rooms and then recorded at home in Dartmoor – “Resultatet er fremragende” (“the result is outstanding”).

On the following Friday Leven was due to play the Green Hotel in Kinross. Shortly before his death his website carried a statement that the great Scottish songwriter was seriously ill with cancer and probably had only a few days left. Strunk speaks of an at times turbulent life marked, besides music, by heroin and alcohol abuse, both of which Leven had put behind him by the time he died. The career began in the late Sixties under a pseudonym and continued in the group Doll By Doll; after a violent assault and the ensuing slide, Leven returned as a solo artist in 1985. In recent years he worked closely with the multi-instrumentalist Michael Cosgrave, including on *Wayside Shrines and the Code of the Travelling Man* from autumn 2011, which thus became his last album. With a few lines from it, the obituary lets Leven have the last word. The article gives his early stage name wrongly as “St. John Fields” (correctly John St. Field), and its 1985 return as a soloist conflates recovery with the later fresh start.
zitate_kontext: From GAFFA’s review of *Wayside Shrines and the Code of the Travelling Man*, quoted in the obituary
Statement on Leven’s website shortly before his death, given here in Danish translation

2011-11-16-gonzo-circus-bij-de-dood-van-.kurz: The Dutch music journalist Peter Bruyn explicitly writes not an obituary but a personal recollection.
inhalt: The Dutch music journalist Peter Bruyn explicitly writes not an obituary but a personal recollection. He says he began listening to Leven seriously around the turn of the millennium, after a Doll by Doll LP had sat gathering dust on his shelf for years. He was first moved by the idiosyncratic melodies and the voice (compared with Scott Walker, David Thomas and Robert Fisher of Willard Grant Conspiracy), then by the themes: ordinary people groaning under the weight of life, losing work, wife and ideals, and taking stock in front of a bottle of whisky. Bruyn briefly recounts the biography (the near-strangling in the eighties, damaged vocal cords, heroin, founding a holistic detox clinic, the voice returning in the nineties).

In 2005 Bruyn visited Leven in Münster for an interview, a week before a gig at the Patronaat in Haarlem; he describes him as driven by deep compassion and at the same time very funny, with introductions that lasted longer than the songs. Another Patronaat concert had been planned for the end of September 2011, but the tour was suddenly cancelled because Leven was ill.

The main part is an anecdote: in January 2006 Leven played at a private party that Bruyn held in Haarlem for his own 50th and his partner's 40th birthday, and kept around eighty guests quiet for an hour. Afterwards he only wanted to take his guitar back to the hotel briefly, but got stuck at the bar of the Proeflokaal De Blauwe Druif with an old man, then lay down for a moment at the hotel, fell asleep and woke only shortly before his flight from Schiphol; the next evening he phoned and apologised profusely. The text ends with the sentence that Leven will now never wake up again. Tenor: warm, humorous, sad.

2011-11-16-herald-scotland-jackie-leven-.kurz: Standalone, unsigned Herald obituary (headline “Musician; Born: June 18, 1950; Died: November 14, 2011”), separate from the news report of the same day.
inhalt: Standalone, unsigned Herald obituary (headline “Musician; Born: June 18, 1950; Died: November 14, 2011”), separate from the news report of the same day. It calls Leven one of Scotland's most underrated songwriters and a soulful singer and guitarist. Background according to the text: father Irish-Cockney, mother from north-east England, Roma roots that made him an outsider in the Fife of the 1950s and 60s; Leven tells (as a quotation) of the night in the allotment when he hid from a gang. He was already on the road married at 17, having previously been thrown out of Kirkcaldy High School for drugs, where he was in the same year as Gordon Brown. Then come Berlin, Madrid and Control as John St Field (on a Spanish label), the founding of Doll by Doll in London in 1975, being thrown off tours with Devo and Hawkwind, a solo contract with Virgin in 1984, the mugging on the way home from the studio, two years without a voice, heroin and the cure through acupuncture, CORE Trust with Princess Diana as patron. After that a fresh start with his family, Cooking Vinyl, the 1994 comeback, over 20 albums in 17 years, collaborations with David Thomas, Johnny Dowd and Ian Rankin (Usher Hall 2005). Leven was a crowd-puller in Europe, especially in Germany, and remained a cult figure in Britain. Stage anecdotes (losing his girlfriend to the Dalai Lama's bodyguard, Bay City Rollers badge). The text ends with the 2011 Edinburgh Fringe show, at which Leven was emaciated, and the closing line of “Main Travelled Roads”. Several formulations coincide with Graeme Thomson's Herald profile (c. 2006, reused in the theartsdesk obituary); Thomson as author is plausible but not proven.

2011-11-16-herald-scotland-scots-folk-si.kurz: A news report in The Herald: Leven died on Monday night after a long battle with cancer. Ian Rankin and Eddi Reader pay tribute; the report briefly recounts his career, the 1983 attack, heroin addiction and his co-founding of the CORE Trust.
inhalt: The report by Victoria Weldon opens by saying that the Scottish folk singer and songwriter Jackie Leven has died after a long battle with cancer. The 61-year-old, whose album *Mystery of Love* was listed by Q magazine among the 100 best albums of all time, died on Monday night. Friends, colleagues and fans paid tribute the next day; one music critic described him as “the most talented singer-songwriter never to have become a household name”.

The crime writer Ian Rankin, who recorded the album *Jackie Leven Said* with Leven in 2005, wrote online: “RIP Jackie Leven. Gentle man, poetic songwriter, skilled guitarist, storyteller. It was an honour to call you friend.” The singer Eddi Reader added: “What hard news today. RIP Jackie Leven, here’s to him.”

Brief biography: Leven came from Kirkcaldy, Fife, and began his career in the late 1960s under the pseudonym John St Field. In 1983 he lost his voice for two years after being attacked in the street and became addicted to heroin during that time; he overcame the addiction years later. According to the paper he wrote more than 400 songs and enjoyed success with Doll by Doll and as a solo artist; his albums included *Songs For Lonely Americans* and *Elegy For Johnny Cash*. He also co-formed the addiction support centre CORE Trust, which uses holistic therapies.
zitate_kontext: An unnamed music critic on Leven

2011-11-16-louder-than-war-jackie-leven-.kurz: The Leicester musician Kevin Hewick, a fan from the first hour, pays tribute to Leven as the true “Celtic soulman”: he recalls the 1979–80 Doll By Doll shows, the Warwick Avenue squat, the fanzine *The Haunted Valley* and Leven’s late triumph as a solo artist.
inhalt: Kevin Hewick, a singer-songwriter from Leicester, writes a personal appreciation for Louder Than War. There is no air of distant nostalgia about Leven’s legacy, he says, from his teenage duo Saint Judas in 1969 through Doll By Doll to the solo work of the Nineties and after: a timeless edge, vivid insights into the human condition, funny and scary and beautiful all at once. Blessed with a rich, unique soulful voice and a dazzling percussive guitar technique, Leven delivered, between some downright filthy stories and the inevitable triple vodkas, ballads “full of power rather than power ballads”; Hewick feels utter bafflement at how comparative micro-talents like Sheeran, Blunt and James Morrison got away with it. Van Morrison, he adds, showboated for years next to Leven, the real Celtic soulman.

On Doll By Doll: in the post-punk, post-Sid Vicious climate of early 1979 they released *Remember*, the classic album that many forget or never heard, still a sonic slap in the face – the house band from hell killing their guitars at the end of the world, headswirling psychedelic blues rock meeting psychotic poetry down a very dark alley. It reached a displaced, disenchanted audience, soon a hardcore bunch of lads and girls from Derby and Leicester who followed the band almost anywhere and saw in them the match of the mythical bands their generation was too young for: the Velvets, the Doors, the Stooges. Only Adrian Borland and The Sound, and Joy Division, came close at the time.

Hewick tells anecdotes. The chisel-like gouges in Leven’s Burns guitar, Leven told him, he made on acid, believing them to be beautiful carvings. When Jo Shaw smashed his vintage Stratocaster he was not a millionaire rocker doing auto-destructive theatre but followed where the strobe-lit, epileptic-fit-inducing feedback climax of “The Palace Of Love” took him. Jackie, Shaw, drummer Dave McIntosh and bassists Robin Spreafico and the late Tony Waite kept this intensity up into the Eighties, until Leven tried a softer version of Doll By Doll with a short-lived new line-up. Hewick himself saw more than fifty shows; he remembers the night in Barbarella’s, Birmingham, when only eleven of the faithful turned up and the band got flung off a Hawkwind tour support slot, “having U2 as their support act”. Most of all he treasures their insane generosity: loads of fans kipped on the floor of their Warwick Avenue squat, and the band were their acid agony aunts and true friends.

Leven’s comeback in the Nineties was one of the finest ever, if less noticed than it deserved: a prolific solo career of studio and live albums. Mick Nolan, another Doll By Doll mega-fan, turned Leven’s pre-internet information service and “trashzine” *The Haunted Valley* into a cottage industry; at the annual Christmas party at the social club in Nolan’s native Milford, Derbyshire, Hewick and fellow Leicester players Dan Britton and Lee Allatson had their moment as The Stornoway Girls with Leven, and in 2002 Hewick played a one-off trio with Leven and Jo Shaw. Leven matured like a fine wine – or rather a kickass malt whisky – happy with his devoted partner Deborah, his dogs, his music and a good bar. When Hewick last saw him, at the Musician in Leicester in June, Leven was clearly not well but still made everyone laugh, “cruder and ruder than ever”.
zitate_kontext: Kevin Hewick on Leven’s voice and songs
Hewick on the last time he saw Leven, June 2011

2011-11-16-medicine-show-jackie-leven-co.kurz: Rob Ellen's Highland radio show “Medicine Show” paid tribute to his friend after Leven's death; its core is a concert recording from Strathpeffer made about a year earlier.
inhalt: On Mixcloud, Rob Ellen's “Medicine Show” appears as a tribute edition for Jackie Leven. In the description Ellen writes that he and the “late great” Leven travelled the Highlands many times; he still finds it hard to believe he will never see him again, but can now at least listen to his music without feeling too much pain and appreciate “just what a gigantic talent he was”. He sees his face and hears his songs in every place he visits around “this country of ours”, so it is overdue to play this show.

The show was first broadcast on 16 November 2011, in Ellen's words “the day after his death” (Leven died on 14 November), and features a concert recorded in Strathpeffer “almost exactly a year before and in much happier times”. It was broadcast from the Scottish Highlands on North Highland Radio, 2 Lochs Radio Gairloch and Lochbroom FM Ullapool, as well as on Celtic Music and Sunny Govan Radio in Glasgow, Sheppey FM in Kent and across the UK country music fraternity. The page gives no track list, and the content of the recording is not described.
zitate_kontext: Rob Ellen in the show's description

2011-11-16-rock-town-hall-jackie-leven-d.kurz: The owner of the US rock discussion site Rock Town Hall writes on Leven's death that he knows only the album Control by John St. Field; four commenters recall John Peel, Gypsy Blood and Ian Rankin.
inhalt: "Mr. Moderator", who runs the rock discussion blog Rock Town Hall, posted "Jackie Leven Dead at 61" on 16 November 2011. He had never heard of Leven until a fellow user, KingEd, turned him on a few years earlier to *Control*, an obscure 1975 album Leven released as John St. Field. The two listened all the way through, "leaning forward and grinning at all the right licks", and the next day he downloaded it from eMusic. He never downloaded another song by Leven: that one album was surprise enough, straddling very English hippy-dippy folk and pub rock - nice to find an oddball album and simply enjoy its oddball pleasures.

A couple of years earlier he had tried to contact Leven for a chat for the site but never heard back, and wonders who he was, a man who never bought more than one record by an unknown artist, to drag him into "our scene". Only from the obituary did he learn that Leven did a duet on "You've Lost That Loving Feeling" with "my man David Thomas", and that they shared the same birthday. He is glad to have happened upon Leven and that one album's worth of songs.

Four comments follow. One British reader remembers hearing Doll by Doll on John Peel; Leven was due to play a venue near him about a month earlier but the gig was postponed and filed under "to look forward to", and he is shocked that yet another artist who apparently shunned success in the name of art has gone. A second reader knows Leven's work up to the early 1980s and calls Doll by Doll's *Gypsy Blood* his masterpiece and "truly one of the great lost albums of that era"; the complication was that the band was marketed as new wave, which they were not; unlike *Control*, it has hooks and melodies, his singing is incredible throughout and the lyrics mature and evocative. He links a YouTube track. A third commenter notes that Ian Rankin mentions Leven several times in his Rebus novels.
zitate_kontext: The site owner "Mr. Moderator" on Control

2011-11-16-telegraph-blogs-jackie-leven-.kurz: Neil McCormick, the Telegraph's chief rock critic, calls Leven "Britain's great lost rock star": as talented as a man can be, and in a well-ordered universe a legend.
inhalt: Neil McCormick, then the Telegraph's chief rock critic, published this obituary on his blog on 16 November 2011. He opens by calling Leven Britain's great lost rock star, now lost for ever. Leven was not a household name, "which is the loss of every household who never heard of him". When successful musicians tell McCormick that the cream always rises to the top, he answers with two words, "Jackie Leven", which usually shuts them up. Leven was "as talented as a man can be": a passionate, eloquent, brilliant songwriter with incredible musical ability and a fluid, rich and extraordinary voice, also hugely charismatic, a deep thinker, an inspired and hilarious raconteur, a brave vagabond soul and, in his own estimation, which McCormick cannot dispute, "a ****ing genius".

McCormick first saw Doll by Doll in a club in Dublin in the late 1970s: "Imagine the Beach Boys if they were a Celtic heavy rock band with a metaphysical bent." Live they were positively scary, the tenderness of the songs counterbalanced by the toughness of Leven's persona. He and his musician friends worshipped the band, and *Gypsy Blood* is a masterpiece that still sounds powerfully resonant decades later. For a while awestruck critics seemed certain Doll by Doll would be the next big thing, but Leven was a complicated character, more interested in creating works of terrible beauty than in following sound business principles. The critic Robin Denselow once described him as "Van Morrison crossed with a psychopath", which McCormick finds a little harsh but which captures something of his compelling intensity.

On the life story: an official obituary will appear in the Daily Telegraph, but Leven's wayward life deserves a book, which he often claimed to be writing ("I hope he left those pages somewhere"). Born in 1950 and raised in Kirkcaldy, he went to school with the future Prime Minister Gordon Brown, of whom he told many an amusing tale, and was the first schoolboy in Scotland to be busted for drugs. His life as an itinerant musician almost ended in the early 1980s, when a random mugging damaged his larynx and left him unable to talk or sing for nearly two years. In pain and despair he became a heroin addict but cured himself through an effort of will, using acupuncture and meditation, and went on to found the addiction charity CORE, which was so successful that Princess Diana became its patron. He always credited Diana with persuading him to return to music in the early 1990s.

Leven made "over thirty albums" and played thousands of gigs to a small but devoted audience; he was "the patron saint of lost causes" and admitted to McCormick that he never felt like a success. McCormick says he championed Leven in the Telegraph many times. For newcomers he recommends *Gypsy Blood* and *Doll by Doll* and the solo albums *Fairy Tales for Hard Men*, *Defending Ancient Springs* and *Creatures of Light and Darkness*. He ends with the first verse of "Main Travelled Roads", Leven's "most perfect and elegiac song". He gives the date of death as "Tuesday, 14 November", which is wrong: 14 November 2011 was a Monday.

2011-11-16-the-daily-telegraph-jackie-le.kurz: Classic Telegraph obituary. Leven was said to be one of the most colourful and distinctive talents in rock and folk, without the success he deserved; a Telegraph critic (Neil McCormick) is said to have called Doll by Doll “the greatest band you've never heard of”.
inhalt: Classic Telegraph obituary. Leven was said to be one of the most colourful and distinctive talents in rock and folk, without the success he deserved; a Telegraph critic (Neil McCormick) is said to have called Doll by Doll “the greatest band you've never heard of”. Biography: born into a Roma family in Kirkcaldy, father London-Irish, mother from Northumbria; truant, walks in the hills near Kirkcaldy, his mother's love of the blues, folk clubs, hitchhiking through Europe, busking in London, Control in 1971 as John St Field. With themes such as mental illness and homelessness, Doll by Doll set themselves apart from punk and split up after four albums. In 1983 an assault by a group of strangers on the way home from a recording session in north London; Leven says he thought he was going to die. Then separation, withdrawal, heroin, after two years recovery through Chinese treatment and “psychic healing”, co-founding of the Core Trust in Marylebone. Move to Oban, where the material for Mystery of Love (1994) came into being. Overview of the work: Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West (1995, male voice choir, Eddi Reader, Andy White), Fairy Tales For Hard Men (1997), Night Lilies (1998), Defending Ancient Springs (2000, Kathleen Raine, duet with David Thomas), Elegy For Johnny Cash (2005), Lovers At The Gun Club (2008) and the last album with “German Hotel Rooms” in its subtitle.

2011-11-16-the-granville-chambers-jackie.kurz: A short personal obituary on a private blog from Bournemouth. The author, who interviewed Leven several times, describes him as always friendly and talkative in conversation, as generous in listening as in telling stories.
inhalt: A short personal obituary on a private blog from Bournemouth. The author, who interviewed Leven several times, describes him as always friendly and talkative in conversation, as generous in listening as in telling stories. He remembers a tiny concert that Leven let himself be talked into: in the skittle alley of his village pub in Dorset, not far from the farmland where Leven is said to have lived once, in front of 30 people at most. Leven played the full emotional range there and told stories – from life on the road to the claim that Bob Dylan had spat in his Guinness, and about a Great Dane from the neighbouring pub that stole his pie. The post closes with a farewell and links five of his own pieces in the Bournemouth Echo: interviews in 2006 (“Leven it up”, about Dorset and Doll by Doll), 2008 (about Amy Winehouse and *Lovers at the Gun Club*) and 2010 (about Gordon Brown and *Gothic Road*), as well as 2009 reviews of Sir Vincent Lone (*Troubadour Heart*) and of the *Haunted Year – Summer* double CD.

2011-11-16-the-scotsman-obituary-maveric.kurz: Personal obituary by the Scotsman music journalist Colin Somerville, who first met Leven in 1994 in a telephone interview about Mystery of Love and was friends with him.
inhalt: Personal obituary by the Scotsman music journalist Colin Somerville, who first met Leven in 1994 in a telephone interview about Mystery of Love and was friends with him. He describes childhood in the new town of Glenrothes with an Irish-Cockney father and a “Geordie” mother (north-east England), Leven's aversion to his old home (he looked grimly across the Forth from the Old Chain Pier in Newhaven), expulsion from school for drug possession, marriage at 16 and being driven out by youth gangs. There follow years of wandering, Berlin, Spain, Control as John St Field and Doll by Doll, who were said to be neither punk nor New Wave. Somerville moves the assault to Islington: Leven was throttled from behind at a cash machine and permanently lost his falsetto range. Then heroin, healing with a Chinese method, CORE with the Princess of Wales as a supporter. Somerville stresses Leven's closeness to Robert Bly and the Men's Movement, the collaborations with Mike Scott, David Thomas, Robert Fisher and Ian Rankin, and the unusual loyalty between Leven and Cooking Vinyl boss Martin Goldschmidt. Anecdotes: two fans from Teesside, in front of whom Leven did not want to play at a late-scheduled Fringe show and who sat in the front row the following year; the beer glass with a mystery cocktail on stage; the poet Paul Reekie before a Leven festival show. Tenor: affectionate, Leven as an unsung Scottish hero.

2011-11-17-efe-eme-fallece-el-cantante-y.kurz: The Spanish music site Efe Eme reports in a short item on Jackie Leven's death on 14 November 2011, aged 61, from cancer, and summarises Doll by Doll, the attack and the heroin addiction.
inhalt: The short death notice in the “Obituarios” section calls Leven a Scottish singer and composer who died on 14 November, aged 61, of cancer. In 1977 he formed the punk band Doll by Doll, with whom he released four albums between 1979 and 1982. He then began a solo career in which he played and recorded both under his own name and under the pseudonym John St. Field.

While he was recording his first solo record – the item dates this to 1984 – he was assaulted in the street and an attempt was made to strangle him. As a consequence he lost the power of speech for two years, during which he became addicted to heroin. The item places the pseudonym John St. Field after Doll by Doll (it was in fact before) and gives 1984 as the year of the attack (elsewhere 1983); no songs or albums are discussed.

2011-11-17-tagesspiegel-zum-tod-des-musi.kurz: The Berlin music journalist H. P. Daniels pays tribute to Leven in the Tagesspiegel as a songwriter who never stopped writing even in the darkest phases of his life and grew “ever more imposing” and “ever better” with the years.
inhalt: The obituary (as of 17 November 2011, 9.12 pm) by H. P. Daniels, a Berlin music journalist, is freely readable only in its standfirst and first paragraph; the rest is behind the paywall (Tagesspiegel Plus). It says that Leven never stopped writing songs, not even in the darkest phases of his life, and that over the years he became, physically as well as artistically, “ever more imposing” and “ever better”.

Beyond the first paragraph there is only a secondary source: according to a review on musikreviews.de (2024), the piece stresses art, literature and poems and the mixture of anger, pain, grief, consolation, lust and humour in Leven's songs. The full text was not seen; the obituary also has a Berlin connection (Leven's Berlin concerts).
zitate_kontext: H. P. Daniels on Leven's late years

2011-11-17-terrorverlag-saenger-songwrit.kurz: On Leven’s death Terrorverlag prints the German version of Cooking Vinyl’s promotional biography: from an outsider childhood in Glenrothes through Doll by Doll, the attack, heroin and the CORE Trust to 24 albums since 1994 and the last album with Michael Cosgrave.
inhalt: On 17 November 2011 the online magazine Terrorverlag publishes the complete German version of the promotional biography sent out on Leven’s death; the source named is the agency “Community Presse-Promotion”, the German press agency for Cooking Vinyl. The text tells the life story in the tone of label copy: an outsider childhood in Glenrothes, a school essay prize and expulsion over drugs, marriage at 16, factory work, flight from a gang, more than ten years of wandering life on farms, in Berlin by the Wall, in County Kerry and in Madrid, where *Control* was made as John St. Field. Then come Doll by Doll in London (with David Gilmour as a guest on the last album) and a solo deal with Charisma/Virgin.

Then the strangulation attack in Market Street, Islington, on the way home from the studio, heroin, and withdrawal by five-element acupuncture, followed by the co-founding of the CORE Trust. The rebirth in 1994, it says, came with *The Argyll Cycle* (a Scotland-only release) and *The Mystery of Love* (with Mike Scott and Robert Bly); 24 albums have appeared since, including *Jackie Leven Said* with Ian Rankin, Ubudoll with David Thomas, the whisky “Leven’s Lament” from Islay Mist, the annual walks starting from a randomly chosen railway station, five albums in 2009 alone, the Haunted Valley series and the Sir Vincent Lone albums. The close concerns the last album with Michael Cosgrave, written mostly in German and Austrian hotel rooms according to the text; label boss Martin Goldschmidt considers it the best since *The Mystery of Love*, and Leven calls it “the world’s first homeopathic record”.

Parents: an “Irish Cockney” father and a “Geordie” mother, with links to the world of the Roma. The childhood details ultimately come from Leven himself and are not independently verified. The text spells “Kilkcaldy” and is a translation of the English Cooking Vinyl biography.
zitate_kontext: Leven on *Wayside Shrines and the Code of the Travelling Man*

2011-11-17-the-independent-musician-whos.kurz: Obituary by the music journalist Nick Hasted, who had interviewed Leven in 2007 and quotes from that interview.
inhalt: Obituary by the music journalist Nick Hasted, who had interviewed Leven in 2007 and quotes from that interview. He describes Leven's songs as the inner lives of “disappointed hard men” (Rankin's formula), often set in the rough landscapes of his childhood, and as partial self-portraits of a life marked by addiction and exile. Biography: Kirkcaldy, father from London-Irish stock, mother from Northumberland, both Roma according to the text; his mother's blues records, folk clubs at 16, a brief first marriage, prize-winning pupil in the same year as Gordon Brown and allegedly the first Scottish schoolboy expelled for drugs, driven out by a gang. He met the Doll by Doll members in squatted farmhouses in Dorset; in 1975 the band came together in a squat in Bristol Gardens (west London); Leven describes the street full of damaged but funny Scots. The second album, he said, gave him a place in the world. In 1983 he was throttled and cut on the neck, voiceless for over a year, dropped by the label, spending weeks in silence at Marylebone station. 1985 recovery, CORE Trust, meeting with Diana, retreat to the Scottish west coast among fishermen, 1994 fresh start with 24 albums at Cooking Vinyl, Bly's influence, concerts with tall tales (Sting's alleged death on the commuter train to Kirkcaldy), The Haunted Year in 2009 as the best overview of his work.

2011-11-18-bbc-radio-4-last-word-jackie-.kurz: BBC Radio 4's obituary programme “Last Word” of 18 November 2011 leads with Jackie Leven; Ian Rankin pays tribute in an eight-and-a-half-minute segment.
inhalt: The programme page for “Last Word” (BBC Radio 4, presented by Matthew Bannister) lists the edition broadcast on Friday 18 November 2011 at 4pm, repeated on Sunday 20 November at 8.30pm. The half-hour programme carries obituaries of the singer-songwriter Jackie Leven, the cosmetics executive Evelyn Lauder, the actress Dulcie Gray, the Guardian chairman Richard Scott and the florist Jane Packer.

The programme text describes Leven as a Scottish singer and songwriter, front man of the band Doll By Doll, who became addicted to heroin after a mugging that damaged his windpipe. Ian Rankin pays tribute. In the chapter list the Leven segment comes first and runs for 8 minutes 30 seconds, followed by Lauder, Gray, Scott and Packer, for whom Sarah, Duchess of York pays tribute. The page shows the edition as available; what Rankin actually says is not reproduced there.
zitate_kontext: The BBC's programme text for the Leven segment

2011-11-18-jackieleven-co-uk-nachruf-sta.kurz: The official website announces Leven’s death on Monday 14 November at eight in the evening after cancer, with his quote on “soulful story tellers” and a short career summary.
inhalt: The homepage of Leven’s official website announces, unsigned, that the great Scottish singer and songwriter died on Monday 14 November at eight in the evening; he had suffered from cancer. Below is a quote from Leven himself: there are spiritual and soulful storytellers, and he hopes to be a soulful one – spiritual is ascending, sky and God, whereas his storytelling goes down into the earth, is wetter and has more moisture. Further information is directed to jackie-leven.com.

The biographical paragraph salutes a career of more than forty years as a uniquely gifted singer-songwriter: from leader of the underrated Doll by Doll in the seventies, through well-documented addiction problems he overcame with remarkable strength of will, to a “solo resurgence through the 1980s” (a loose dating; his solo career came later). He composed over four hundred songs, including arguably his greatest, “Call Mother” (that is, “Call Mother A Lonely Field”) from *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*, an album the page says Q ranked among the “100 Best Albums of All Time”.

If sales did not always match the overwhelmingly positive critical reception, he remained a perceptive writer and performer, imbued with restless creativity and always seeking new settings for ruminative lyrics laced with humour and melodic grace. As a performer he could enthral audiences with picaresque tales from first-hand experience. Those who worked with him will know his mordant wit and idiosyncratic world view. His latest release, *Wayside Shrines and The Code of the Travelling Man*, made with multi-instrumentalist Michael Cosgrave (Cooking Vinyl, mid-September), was further proof of his enduring talent.

The page also still carries the order offer for the “official bootleg” *One Long Cold Morning* (five new studio recordings plus live performances and stories, with a link to the title track) and Leven’s remark on the Cosgrave album: everybody needs a code to live and die by; his life is built around hotel rooms and the rigours of touring, and the songs are “the code of the travelling man”.
