zitate_kontext: Jackie Leven, quoted on the page.
Leven on *Wayside Shrines and The Code of the Travelling Man*.

2011-11-18-music-week-jackie-leven-dies-.kurz: Music Week reports Leven’s death on 18 November 2011: born 18 June 1950 in Kirkcaldy, successful with Doll By Doll (four albums, the last featuring David Gilmour), a fresh start in 1994 with two albums.
inhalt: The British trade magazine *Music Week* reports the musician’s death on 18 November 2011 (4.15 pm) under the headline “Jackie Leven dies following battle with cancer”. The freely readable opening says that Leven was born on 18 June 1950 in Kirkcaldy and had success with Doll By Doll; the band released four albums, the last featuring David Gilmour, and split in 1983. Leven made his fresh start in 1994 with two albums: *Songs from the Argyll Cycle Volume 1* (according to the sleeve released only in Scotland) and *The Mystery of Love*. The rest of the article is reserved for subscribers.

2011-11-18-musiczine-jackie-leven-nous-a.kurz: The Belgian magazine Musiczine reports Leven’s death on 14 November 2011 from cancer and sketches his career, the assault and his last album in a few lines.
inhalt: Bernard Dagnies’s short obituary reports that Jackie Leven died on Monday 14 November 2011 from the effects of cancer, shortly after celebrating his 61st birthday. He had made more than twenty albums under his own name and began his career under the pseudonym John St Field before living through the explosion of punk and new wave in London with Doll by Doll. Later he worked, among others, with David Gilmour (Pink Floyd) and David Thomas (Pere Ubu).

The text says the Scottish-born musician was attacked in 1984 as he left the recording studio; because of the injury to his throat his voice turned into a falsetto. At that time, probably as a result of the attack, he became addicted to drugs and, paradoxically, began to favour folk-rock in his repertoire. The article names *Wayside Shrines and the Code of the Travelling Man*, recorded with Michael Cosgrave and released on 19 September 2011, as his last album.

The piece is a news-style brief obituary. Two claims should be read with caution: the collaboration with David Gilmour is hardly documented elsewhere, and the claim that the attack turned Leven’s voice into a falsetto contradicts accounts that he was unable to sing at all for a long time afterwards.

2011-11-18-the-times-jackie-leven-obitua.titel: Jackie Leven (obituary; subheading: Scottish singer and songwriter who drew on his wanderings to produce a rich stream of poetic and mysterious anthems)
2011-11-18-the-times-jackie-leven-obitua.kurz: Unsigned Times obituary. It presents Leven as an outsider with a 40-year career, masterly but neglected albums and labels such as “Britain's greatest lost rock star”.
inhalt: Unsigned Times obituary. It presents Leven as an outsider with a 40-year career, masterly but neglected albums and labels such as “Britain's greatest lost rock star”. Biography according to the Times: father an Irish Cockney of Roma descent, mother from Northumbria; Kirkcaldy High School with Gordon Brown, whom Leven briefly outshone when he won the Scottish Round Table's national school essay competition – with an essay about his dream of setting out as a wandering musician. Expelled from school over drugs, from 1967 a decade of wandering through Britain, Ireland and western Europe, Control as John St Field recorded in Madrid “in the mid-1970s”. 1977 founding of Doll by Doll in a London squat; Gypsy Blood is said to have impressed David Gilmour, who then played on Grand Passion (1982). 1983 solo contract with Charisma/Virgin, assault after a night session at a studio in Islington, loss of falsetto, heroin, CORE Trust with Diana as patron. Diana is said to have persuaded him to return to music by urging him to sing backstage at an official engagement; 1994 Cooking Vinyl, over 20 albums, Sir Vincent Lone, Jackie Leven Said with Rankin, who chose Leven on Desert Island Discs. The whisky “Leven's Lament” was named after him by Islay Mist.

2011-11-23-mzpjsinclair-jackie-leven-sto.kurz: A concert video uploaded nine days after Leven's death: after “Single Father” he tells how his drug-help charity was taken over over the years by “politically correct” staff, with a canteen anecdote as the punchline.
inhalt: The YouTube channel MzPJSinclair uploaded a video titled “Jackie Leven Story” on 23 November 2011, nine days after Leven's death. The description says only that after the song “Single Father” during his live performance he carries on to say this. Venue and date of the concert are not given.

It is a stage story of a little over three minutes in which Leven – by his own account – tells of his drug-help charity, which he says he helped to run for ten years and which, over the years, was taken over by “politically correct” staff. He points it up with a canteen anecdote about a book called “Hitler's Henchmen”, through which he reduces his colleagues' non-judgemental stance to absurdity. It is a typical example of his coarse, self-mocking stage humour, which stood alongside the songs at Leven's concerts.

2011-11-27-the-guardian-letter-jackie-le.kurz: In a letter to *The Guardian*, Roy Warne recalls an anecdote Leven told at a concert about a Blackpool landlady and a minuscule portion of honey.
inhalt: Roy Warne’s letter supplements Robin Denselow’s *Guardian* obituary of Leven of 16 November 2011, which had mentioned his story-telling prowess. He recalls an anecdote Leven told between songs at a concert a few years earlier: he was staying in digs in Blackpool and was being ribbed by his landlady about his Scottish origins. Scots, she said, were mean and had no sense of humour. He asked for some honey with his breakfast toast and received a minuscule portion on a saucer. His reply: “Thank you. I see you keep a bee …”
zitate_kontext: Leven’s punchline in his Blackpool anecdote, as recalled by Roy Warne

2011-11-cooking-vinyl-kommentare-zum-nac.titel: [Comments on the Cooking Vinyl obituary “Jackie Leven June 18th 1950 – 14th November 2011”]
2011-11-cooking-vinyl-kommentare-zum-nac.kurz: 16 reader comments from 15.11. to 01.12.2011 beneath the label's obituary, in English and one in German.
inhalt: 16 reader comments from 15.11. to 01.12.2011 beneath the label's obituary, in English and one in German. Fans from Great Britain, Austria, Germany and Norway mourn and remember: a Viennese learned of the death through Michael Cosgrave's Facebook entry and mentions a cancelled Vienna concert in September 2011; a man from Birmingham describes how, after a Doll by Doll concert in London, Leven gave a friend the lyric sheet he had just sung from; Mike Plumbley (author of the 1997 Winchester concert review) recalls a CORE benefit concert to which he came because of Townes Van Zandt and where Leven played “Men In Prison”, whereupon hard men wept; the Hanover radio presenter Uli Kniep thanks him for many encounters since *The Mystery Of Love*; Jan Myrvold (Norway) promises to pass the legacy on to younger generations; others recall Doll by Doll in north London and in York in 1979, a cancelled Dingwalls concert, a raffle at the 12 Bar Club, Leven's tattered “lucky shirt” and cancelled concerts in 2011 (York, Vienna). A German comment (Leo Lambrecht) mentions performances at the “Lab” in Stuttgart.

2011-11-folkworld-muensterland-festival-.kurz: FolkWorld's report on the Folk Night of the Münsterland Festival with the band Cara mentions Jackie Leven only in its introduction: he cancelled through illness, and so did his support act Paul Armfield.
inhalt: The report "Cara's kleine Nachtmusik" appeared in FolkWorld no. 46 (November 2011) and covers the Folk Night at the Steverhalle in Senden on 15 October 2011. The Münsterland Festival took place for the sixth time in September and October 2011; under the motto "Zusammenrücken" ("moving closer together") there were about 40 events at some 30 venues. After Scandinavia, the Black Sea region, the Adriatic, the western Mediterranean and the Maghreb, this year's focus was England, Ireland and Scotland, with the Scottish band Breabach and the fiddler Rua MacMillan among others.

About Leven the report says only: "The English singer-songwriter Jackie Leven, however, cancelled because of illness, and with him the support act Paul Armfield with his Tennyson settings." (Leven was a Scot from Fife, not an Englishman.) The rest of the piece is about the Folk Night itself: Jackie Oates, Seth Lakeman and above all the band Cara of Gudrun Walther, Jürgen Treyz and Rolf Wagels with new members such as the Orkney fiddler Jeana Leslie and the piper Ryan Murphy. The sentence is contemporary confirmation that Leven's German dates in autumn 2011 were called off because of his illness, a few weeks before his death.

2011-11-jackie-leven-com-jackie-leven-19.kurz: On a plain memorial page in November 2011, a woman named Deborah asks that flower money instead go towards a small memorial at the spot in the village where Leven sat, wrote and watched the water.
inhalt: The page consists of a single message under the heading “Jackie Leven, 1950 – 2011”. Above it stands a motto: “Eternal is the warrior who finds beauty in his wounds”. Below, a woman signing herself only as Deborah writes that many people have asked where to send flowers for Jackie, but that they would very much like to have a small memorial to him, possibly where he used to sit in the village with the dogs, look at the water and write.

She asks people to consider directing their flower money to this end: for both his family and his many friends it would be “truly lovely” to have a permanent, physical reminder of this unique man. Donations can be made with a PayPal button, or alternatively to the Musicians Benevolent Fund. There is no book of condolence, no tributes and no further pages.
zitate_kontext: Deborah, appeal on the memorial page

2011-11-musikreviews-de-jackie-leven-nac.kurz: Short obituary by Jochen König on Musikreviews.de, 16 November 2011: Leven died on 14 November aged 61 of cancer; König praises his “true Celtic soul”, his live storytelling and asks whether the big breakthrough was denied or spared him.
inhalt: On 16 November 2011 Jochen König reports on Musikreviews.de that Jackie Leven died on 14 November aged 61 of cancer. He calls him an exceptional artist who, with his band Doll by Doll in the early eighties, “almost” enjoyed great success. A knife attack that robbed him of his voice for nearly two years, and the heroin addiction that followed, knocked him off course but did not stop him from recording “a multitude of great albums” after his recovery: “true Celtic soul, sometimes sparse, sometimes opulent, but always moving”. (Other accounts describe a strangling attack rather than a knife.)

The obituary stresses the esteem of the crime writer Ian Rankin, shared by his detective John Rebus, which gave Leven “a perfect template” for his inimitable live shows. König's picture is that of the concert performer: an overweight man in baggy clothes who needed only a chair, his guitar and occasionally a colleague – latterly mostly Michael Cosgrave, with whom he made his last album – to conjure up moving, funny, simply magical moments, even when he told more than he played and sang.

Despite a large and devoted circle of friends and fans, König writes, the big breakthrough he deserved more than anyone eluded him (the original says “vergönnt”, presumably meaning “versagt”) – “or was he spared it?” With Leven's death, music has lost a great, but also one of those people who make life worth living. The piece ends with a quoted line about a guest being called back into the pub (“Hey Jackie – we were looking for you … So why don't you come back in?”) and “Farewell und Danke!”. It is short and personal, but it captures how Leven was seen in Germany: a revered insider's tip whose evenings are remembered.
zitate_kontext: König on Leven's albums after his recovery.
König on the missing breakthrough (original wording, “vergönnt”).

2011-11-pennyblackmusic-jackie-leven-195.kurz: A tribute on Pennyblackmusic by the brothers Ben and Charles Howarth: how an overrunning festival set made their father a Leven fan, and Charles's account of his first Leven gig in a Bath pub.
inhalt: Ben Howarth, a writer for Pennyblackmusic, and his brother Charles pay tribute to Jackie Leven, who died of cancer in November 2011. Ben begins by noting that the closest musical relationships often begin by chance: his father only came across Leven because his set overran at a festival. Heading the opposite way from the crowd gathering for Robert Plant, and never a Zeppelin fan, the father was following Ben's recommendation to see Willard Grant Conspiracy in a tent. As he walked in, Leven, alone with an acoustic guitar, was ending his set, his “rich booming voice and fantastical stage banter” a revelation. Backstage, Leven and Robert Fisher, the WGC frontman, were bonding; Leven had ended with an impassioned plea for the audience to stay in the tent rather than watch Plant. Not many did, but the pair soon started appearing on each other's albums.

The father ploughed through Leven's back catalogue and chased up rarities, and Ben's conversion followed. His suggested introduction is “Classic Northern Diversions”, a freewheeling epic that sums up Leven's musical and lyrical fascinations. He heard of the death in a press release; he was one of the last journalists to speak to Leven and points readers to that interview in the archive, saying that had he known it would be his last chance he would have insisted on it lasting far longer. His brother Charles had become something of a “Jackie Leven missionary”, dragging friends along to shows.

Charles describes the first time he saw Leven, a Sunday lunchtime in a pub in Bath, half full of young families and old men at the bar. A large, dishevelled man stooped onto a stage perhaps a foot high, greying hair damp from the rain, hands fidgeting with sheets of scrawled paper; he reminded Charles of the oilskinned fishermen of the North Cornwall coast. When he began to play, “It was as if some Divine kenosis had emptied the weight of his wanderer's soul”: song after song was a story etched from a hard life, told by a man who has seen suffering and begun to come through the other side, and although Charles had never heard them, each felt like a favourite from years past.

He singles out “Museum of Childhood”, the image of a man walking through the memory of his own childhood as though each event were an exhibit in a museum, intertwined with the boxing rematch between Sugar Ray Leonard and Roberto Duran, which Duran ended with “No más”. Leven's best songs, he writes, were earthed in the spiritually profane; he was a storyteller and his songs poems to the lonely. Perhaps the greatest compliment is that he understood what it meant to be human and could express it so that everyone could understand. Travelling home from Bath, Charles was sure that “these songs spoke to the hearts of all men”.
zitate_kontext: Charles Howarth on Leven's gig in Bath
Ben Howarth recommending a starting point

2011-11-sammeldatei-musikerreaktionen-no.medium: Twitter, blogs, musicians' websites – preserved in BBC News, Herald Scotland and other sources

2011-12-01-cooking-vinyl-wayside-shrines.autor: Cooking Vinyl (unsigned, “admin”; with quotations from Leven)
2011-12-01-cooking-vinyl-wayside-shrines.kurz: Cooking Vinyl’s release text for Leven’s last studio album: recorded with Michael Cosgrave in Dartmoor, songs written in German hotel rooms, a title about ‘pagan shrines’ and “the world’s first homeopathic record”.
inhalt: Cooking Vinyl’s text introduces *Wayside Shrines and the Code of the Travelling Man*, by Jackie Leven and Michael Cosgrave. It was recorded “by the light of the spring moon”, out in the wilderness of Dartmoor, in Cosgrave’s home studio. Leven says he had felt on his last few albums that the best work on them was the creative interplay between himself and Cosgrave, “a world class multi-instrumentalist and best friend”, so the two decided to make the whole album between them – engineering, producing and mixing – and, in his opinion, the result is a very focused body of work.

On the title: touring Germany, the pair noticed that most German hotels have displays of flowers and art in reception and other public rooms of a kind seen nowhere else in the world. Staff, when asked, always say they do not know what the displays are for; they were there before they started work. Leven’s reading is that these are pagan shrines, where pagan Germany can be seen “in a small but very powerful way”. The songs are not about shrines, but nearly all were written in German hotel rooms on tour over the previous two years.

The album is also billed as “the world’s first homeopathic record”. Leven explains that they took a sound representing grief – something the West is not good at – and diluted it in the songs so far that it can no longer be heard, though its ‘memory’ remains; the more you listen, the better you will feel about the real sadness in your life.

The text singles out the hallucinations of ‘Swine Flu Fever Blues’ and the ode to his brother, who had died earlier that year, ‘Beware Soul Brother’, as showing the “master craftsman” at his most confident. The post is dated 1 December 2011, after Leven’s death; the wording comes from the press text issued for the autumn release.
zitate_kontext: Leven on the flower and art displays in German hotels
Leven on “the world’s first homeopathic record”

2011-12-02-mzpjsinclair-jackie-leven-lit.kurz: A three-minute YouTube clip, "Jackie Leven, little bird": Leven tells on stage the story of the bird flying through the Vikings' hall, then a "Scottish version" with a coarse punchline.
inhalt: The video "Jackie Leven, little bird" was uploaded on 2 December 2011, a little over two weeks after Leven's death, by the channel "MzPJSinclair" and runs about three minutes. The description reads: "Jackie Leven tells a story that he heard of a Little Bird. Well, two, actually."

The clip presents a stage story told after a tour through Scandinavia and Germany. Leven recalls the parable of the bird flying through the hall of the feasting Vikings (life as a brief flight), which he heard at school aged eleven, and then tells a "Scottish version" with a coarse punchline. Place and date of the recording are unknown. Title, description and length of the video are the secure facts.

2011-12-06-bhcr-real-music-club-18.kurz: Episode of the Brighton community station BHCR, 6 December 2011, shortly after Leven's death: Tim Rundall played two tracks from *Wayside Shrines and the Code of the Travelling Man*.
inhalt: “Real Music Club 18” is an episode of “The Real Music Club” on Brighton and Hove Community Radio (BHCR), presented by Tim Rundall and uploaded to archive.org on 6 December 2011. The description contains only the playlist, with no accompanying text. From Leven's last album, *Wayside Shrines and the Code of the Travelling Man* (with Michael Cosgrave), two tracks are played: number 5, “To Live and Die in Levenland”, and number 8, “Backstage Chelsea Club”. Around them sit Thee Headcoats, Monsoon Bassoon, Knifeworld, Bonnie Prince Billy, Fairport Convention (“Meet on the Ledge”) and Frank Zappa and the Mothers of Invention (live, 1974).
The episode appeared three weeks after Leven's death on 14 November 2011; whether the programme mentions it cannot be seen from the description, and the audio itself was not listened to.

2011-12-09-gaesteliste-michael-weston-ki.kurz: Ullrich Maurer reports on a Cologne house concert by Michael Weston King that was largely devoted to Leven, who had died a few weeks earlier: memories of their collaboration and a reworked Ronnie Lane song whose lines were read at Leven’s funeral.
inhalt: Under the heading “Erinnerungen an Jackie” (“Memories of Jackie”), Ullrich Maurer reports for Gaesteliste.de on the house concert with which Michael Weston King and his long-time sidekick Alan Cook ended their German tour in Cologne on 9 December 2011. There were a few Christmas songs, such as Robbie Robertson’s “Christmas Must Be Tonight”, but in Maurer’s impression the evening was less about the season than about remembering “his friend, the Scottish songwriter Jackie Leven, who died a few weeks ago”.

King recalls their joint projects: Leven produced his 2003 album *A Decent Man*, recommended the poet Langston Hughes for his protest-song album *I Didn’t Raise My Boy To Be A Soldier*, and appeared with him repeatedly, most recently in August 2011 at the last concerts Leven gave, as King told the audience. King plays no Leven song but weaves in tributes, the loveliest being Ronnie Lane’s “She’s Leaving”, which he rewrote as “He’s Leaving”. The lines “Oh may the road rise up to great him and the wind be at his back. The sunshine warm upon his lovely face. The rain fall soft upon the fields until we meet again” from that piece were read as a eulogy at Leven’s funeral. Maurer calls Leven “the gentle giant”.

Otherwise the report describes a good-humoured tour through King’s repertoire – Townes Van Zandt’s “Rake” as an opener, protest songs by Phil Ochs and originals – plus material from the new album *My Darling Clementine*, a collaboration with his wife Lou Dalgleish in the style of Dan Penn and Spooner Oldham. Alan Cook plays mandolin and pedal steel, which for long stretches sounds like an organ. Between songs King tells anecdotes about Jackie and the tour; the encore is “I’ve Just Seen A Face”.
zitate_kontext: Ullrich Maurer on the character of the evening
Lines from King’s “He’s Leaving”, read at Leven’s funeral

2011-12-17-music-week-gedenkanzeige-jack.kurz: Memorial advertisement in Music Week (16 December 2011, p. 51): “Our dear friend Jackie Leven has passed away” – his family asks for donations towards a memorial where he used to sit with the dogs and write music.
inhalt: The trade magazine Music Week carried an advertisement on page 51 of its 16 December 2011 issue marking Jackie Leven's death. It is headed with a line from “Main Travelled Roads”: “Eternal warrior who finds beauty in his wounds”. Beneath it: “Our dear friend Jackie Leven has passed away. Jackie's family has asked for donations to erect a memorial to the great man.” Donations can be made via PayPal at jackie-leven.com or to the Musicians Benevolent Fund.

The ad then quotes a line saying it would be “truly lovely for his family and many friends to have a permanent, physical reminder of this unique man where he used to sit in the village with the dogs, look at the water and write his music”, followed by “JACKIE LEVEN, June 18th 1950 ~ 14th November 2011”. No sponsor is named. The advertisement shows that the appeal was also placed in the British music-industry press.
zitate_kontext: Text of the advertisement on the planned memorial.
Headline of the advertisement, a line from “Main Travelled Roads”.

2011-jackieleven-co-uk-gaestebuch-2011-v.kurz: Around 35 genuine entries that reflect Leven's last year from a fan's perspective. In the first half of the year, declarations of devotion dominate (a fan from Leeds saw him in 1994 at the Duchess of York pub and remembers “Gylen Gylen”), along with questions about Australian tours and memories from old acquaintances: a Yorkshireman, now in Saigon, says he stayed overnight in the Doll by Doll flat in Maida Vale and arranged gigs for the band. In summer *One Long Cold Morning* is sent out by post; delivery to Germany takes a long time, and the old resentment about the never-delivered *Cornish Pub* CD flares up again. One guest announces a free concert on 12.08.2011 at Jolly's Bar, Kilmarnock; a Canadian is looking forward to the Halifax Urban Folk Festival (HUFF), a Swede to the Scandinavian tour in October.
inhalt: Around 35 genuine entries that reflect Leven's last year from a fan's perspective. In the first half of the year, declarations of devotion dominate (a fan from Leeds saw him in 1994 at the Duchess of York pub and remembers “Gylen Gylen”), along with questions about Australian tours and memories from old acquaintances: a Yorkshireman, now in Saigon, says he stayed overnight in the Doll by Doll flat in Maida Vale and arranged gigs for the band. In summer *One Long Cold Morning* is sent out by post; delivery to Germany takes a long time, and the old resentment about the never-delivered *Cornish Pub* CD flares up again. One guest announces a free concert on 12.08.2011 at Jolly's Bar, Kilmarnock; a Canadian is looking forward to the Halifax Urban Folk Festival (HUFF), a Swede to the Scandinavian tour in October.

From 10.09.2011 the tone changes: fans from Munich, Hamburg, Lauterbach, Bremen, the Netherlands and Münster write that Leven is in hospital and the entire 2011 German tour has been cancelled; a woman from Münster who had planned to go to the Hot Jazz Club on 22.09. had his CD played there instead. One fan wishes him to “get oot the hospital”, Norwegians still hope in October for the concert at Buddy in Drammen, a man from Burnley regrets the cancelled concert at the Trades Club (October), a Londoner asks for news on 04.10. On 14.11.2011, the day of his death, the first words of farewell appear.

2011-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.titel: [Collected finds from Nasjonalbiblioteket 2011: short news items, announcements, listings]
2011-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.kurz: In 2011 the Norwegian press mentions Leven in 26 issues, mostly obituaries after his death on 14 November and the announcement of an October tour that never happened; by these findings no concerts took place in Norway.
inhalt: In the digitised Norwegian newspapers and magazines of the National Library, "Jackie Leven" appears in 26 issues in 2011, only 9 of them freely readable. By these findings no concerts took place in Norway in 2011; the autumn programme of the Buddy club in Drammen, however, still listed a date on 5 October 2011 (Drammens Tidende, 12 August), matching the Scandinavian tour in October that was no longer realised and whose performance is not documented. *Wayside Shrines and the Code of the Travelling Man* (with Michael Cosgrave) appears in new-release lists in September (Bergensavisen on 9 September, Tidens Krav on 16 September among them); a short review in Østlendingen (27 September) covers the album.

After Leven's death on 14 November came obituaries, all of which, apart from the short Dagsavisen item of 16 November, are not freely readable: Bergensavisen (16 November, 5 mentions), Nordlys (16 November with 7 mentions, also 17 November and 7 December), Adresseavisen (16, 21 and 22 November), Lofotposten (22 November, 5 mentions), Dagbladet (26 November, opinion page, 4 mentions) and Stavanger Aftenblad (30 December). The print editions of Adresseavisen and Bergensavisen probably match or expand the web obituaries of 15 November. Other freely readable finds: a Dagsavisen year-end review on 27 December listing Leven among the dead of 2011, a year's balance by Lasse Skjoldal in Karmsund (15 December) with *Wayside Shrines* as his last album and a short obituary paragraph, and a survey on the Egersund Visefestival (Dalane Tidende, 29 June) in which Leven is named among the best concert experiences.

2011-simon-and-schuster-viner-cream-teas.kurz: In his book on the British holiday, the journalist Brian Viner retells a story Leven told him: Leven’s agent had booked him a gig in 2002. Leven is also thanked in the acknowledgements.
inhalt: The journalist Brian Viner (*The Independent*) tells in *Cream Teas, Traffic Jams and Sunburn: The Great British Holiday* (Simon & Schuster, London, 2011) an anecdote Jackie Leven confided to him: Leven’s agent had booked him a gig in 2002. How the story continues is not available. Leven is also named in the book’s acknowledgements.

2012-02-21-jackieleven-co-uk-robberies-o.titel: [Notice] Robberies of the Rain – profits go to Jackie Leven Memorial Fund
2012-02-21-jackieleven-co-uk-robberies-o.kurz: The official website's home page after Leven's death: news of his death, an obituary text and a sale notice for 100 rare CDs of *Robberies of the Rain* in aid of a “Jackie Leven Memorial Fund”.
inhalt: The archived copy of the official website, dated 21 February 2012, shows a home page given over to Leven's death: the “great Scottish singer and song writer” died on Monday 14 November at 8 o'clock in the evening, after suffering from cancer. Below it is a quotation from him: there are spiritual story tellers and soulful story tellers, he hopes to be a soulful one, his story telling going down into the earth, wetter, with more moisture.

The obituary text that follows praises a career of more than forty years, from leading the “underrated” Doll by Doll in the seventies, through addiction problems he overcame with remarkable strength of will, to a solo resurgence. It credits him with over four hundred songs and singles out “Call Mother” from *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death*, which Q magazine is said to have ranked among its “100 Best Albums of All Time”. If sales did not always match the critical reception, he remained a perceptive writer and performer, imbued with restless creativity and able to enthral audiences with picaresque tales from first-hand experience. His last release, *Wayside Shrines and The Code of the Travelling Man*, made with Michael Cosgrave, is called further proof of his energy; Leven himself says everybody needs a code to live and die by, and that these songs are “the code of the travelling man”.

At the bottom come the sales notices. *One Long Cold Morning* is offered as Leven's new “official bootleg” with five new studio recordings plus live performances and stories (UK £12.50 up to £14.50 for Australia and New Zealand). In addition, 100 very rare CD-only copies of *Robberies of the Rain* are available, “found a box in attic”, with profits going to the “Jackie Leven Memorial Fund”, first come first served (UK £14.50 up to £16.50). The page does not say who runs the fund.
zitate_kontext: Leven, as the motto on the home page
Leven on his last album, *Wayside Shrines and The Code of the Travelling Man*

2012-02-uncut-jackie-leven-1950-2011-too.kurz: Graeme Thomson’s tribute in Uncut’s February 2012 issue, headed by the quotation “I’m too connected to the pain of other people”, sees Leven as a songwriter who captured the raw extremes of human behaviour with poetic soulfulness. Full text paywalled.
inhalt: Graeme Thomson’s tribute appeared in the February 2012 issue of Uncut and runs to 2,738 words. Rock’s Backpages classes it as a “Retrospective and Interview”. The freely visible teaser describes Leven as a songwriter who documented in life and music the raw extremes of human behaviour with poetic soulfulness; Uncut honours a “wild and brilliant talent”.

The title quotation, “I’m too connected to the pain of other people. It really breaks me up.”, probably comes from an interview Thomson did with Leven for the Herald around 2006, which other obituaries have also drawn on. The full text was available only behind a paywall and was not read.
zitate_kontext: Leven, title quotation of the tribute

2012-03-03-rolling-stone-de-leserbrief-n.kurz: A reader accuses Rolling Stone of not devoting “even a line” to Jackie Leven’s death and pays tribute to him as songwriter, guitarist and “sensational storyteller”.
inhalt: On the letters page of the German edition of Rolling Stone (here the version of 3 March 2012), under the heading ‘Nachruf’ (‘Obituary’), there is a short letter from Frank Germer. He complains that the singer-songwriter Jackie Leven died on 14 November 2011 and the magazine did not find it worth “even a line”: “That is bitter!”

Leven, he writes, was not only an outstanding songwriter and performer but an outstanding guitarist and “above all a sensational storyteller”. The writer hopes that a worthy obituary may yet follow – Leven would have deserved it. The letter was “a matter of the heart” for him; he signs off “Cheers, Jackie”.

The letter is a rare testimony to how Leven’s death was perceived in the German music press: the reader speaks for a loyal German following who felt the missing obituary in the magazine as an omission.

2012-03-31-david-belbin-jackie-leven-ran.kurz: Nottingham novelist David Belbin posts a recording from Essen, made a year before Leven's death, of an introduction about Randy Newman and Joni Mitchell, and laments that he can no longer see Leven live.
inhalt: The novelist David Belbin writes in his blog series “Song of the Week” that, sorting through unlistened-to live recordings in his collection, he found a Jackie Leven show recorded in Essen a year before Leven died. Leven's shows, he says, were as renowned for his storytelling as for his singing: often laugh-out-loud funny, always in a thought-provoking manner.

A description listed one song introduction as being about Randy Newman, of whom Belbin is a huge fan, but it turns out also to be about Joni Mitchell, of whom he is an even bigger fan, and features one of his all-time favourite Joni Mitchell songs. So he posts the story as audio, with Leven's “Walking in Argyll”, Mitchell's “Shades of Scarlet Conquering” (from *The Hissing of Summer Lawns*) and Newman's “The Girls in My Life (Part 1)”.

The post turns personal at the end: four weeks earlier his diary had the rescheduled Leven show at the Flowerpot in Derby, where he had seen Leven twice, and it is a bummer that he won't see him play, and talk, again. Still, there is the music and the stories. His wife Sue had just come back with a bottle of one of Leven's favourite tipples, Co-op Les Jamelles Viognier, so that evening he would raise another glass in memory of the big man.
zitate_kontext: Belbin on the cancelled Derby show.

2012-03-folkworld-news-and-gossip-47.kurz: FolkWorld’s obituary section (issue 47, March 2012) reports Leven’s death on 14 November after cancer, summarises his career and quotes a reader calling him “the gypsy Van Morrison”.
inhalt: The item appears in “News & Gossip”, where FolkWorld in spring 2012 collects short obituaries of musicians from the scene, here alongside entries on an Irish concertina player, a flamenco guitarist and an Irish sculptor. The editorial note on Leven (1950–2011) says the Scottish singer-songwriter died on Monday, 14 November, having suffered from cancer. He began his career as a folk musician in the late 1960s, first found success with the new-wave band Doll by Doll and later released more than twenty albums as a solo artist, under his own name or the pseudonym Sir Vincent Lone. *Songs for Lonely Americans* and Leven’s website are linked.

Above it stands a contribution from the reader David “Dai” Woosnam, who in one collective note mentions Cesária Évora and then Leven. Of Leven he writes that “the gypsy Van Morrison” has “just died of cancer at 61”. He was never really a fan, but can see that Leven had an intense quality that brought him a cult following. Woosnam’s preceding sentence about Ann Wroe’s “magnificent obituary” in The Economist belongs to the Évora obituary, not to Leven.

2012-03-the-word-the-jackie-leven-obitua.kurz: The most literary obituary, written by the music journalist Paul Du Noyer, who met Leven in 1979 and was his friend for 32 years.
inhalt: The most literary obituary, written by the music journalist Paul Du Noyer, who met Leven in 1979 and was his friend for 32 years. Published in The Word (March 2012) together with the cover CD “Heroes Can Be Any Size”, compiled by Du Noyer; the website version contains the track list at the end. Du Noyer asks who Leven actually was, and interprets the persona “Jackie Leven” as a deliberately built house into which Alan Moffatt had moved. He describes the background (English parents with Roma and Irish roots, according to Leven), reading from John Clare to the Russian poets, singing exercises with “Rescue Me”, the squats in north London in the mid-1970s, his own experiences in 1979 (frightening pubs, drugs, conspiracy theories), Doll by Doll and the name after e. e. cummings. Leven is said to have burst into tears when Du Noyer asked him about the closing line of “Main Travelled Roads”. There follow the assault, heroin, CORE (with the expansion of the acronym) and Diana's alleged interest in Leven (his own account), Cooking Vinyl from 1994, the Men's Movement phase after the Robert Bly tape from the Dalai Lama's bodyguard, “Levenland”, bars as places of devotion, Ian Rankin. Deborah Greenwood speaks at length about Leven's restlessness, the “electric fur”, life in the village in Hampshire and some fans' expectation of seeing him suffer. Conclusion: diagnosis in September 2011, death on 14 November, funeral in a country church with “Working Alone / A Blessing”, and Leven's probably last online message about a “Belfast Of The Mind”.

2012-10-06-my-vintage-rock-doll-by-doll-.kurz: A blogger recalls seeing Doll by Doll around 1979 in Middlesbrough and as Hawkwind’s support in Newcastle, calls them in hindsight a unique, underrated band, and two readers add Reading and Gateshead.
inhalt: The short post on the concert-memory blog “Vintagerock’s Weblog” (6 October 2012, not quite a year after Leven’s death) opens by calling Doll by Doll an intriguing band. Led by the “late and sadly missed” Jackie Leven, they surfaced around the time of punk, but their music was much deeper than the punk label suggests. A mate had been raving about their first album, so the writer went to see them at Middlesbrough Rock Garden, he thinks around 1979. He also seems to recall seeing them as a support act at Newcastle City Hall, the same year, on a Hawkwind tour.

Looking back, he says, it is clear they were a pretty significant and very under-rated band. Leven came from a folk-roots background and blended this with psychedelia, some great guitar and a smattering of punk. The first album, *Remember*, is “pretty special” and unlike anything else at the time. He did not think Doll by Doll anything particularly special when he saw them, but he owned that album, played it often, and now realises how unique the band were. The post ends with Leven’s statement about “soulful” rather than “spiritual” storytellers, with no source given.

In the comments a reader (Peter) recalls seeing the band at that Hawkwind gig, at Reading that year and a while later at Gateshead Stadium; the blogger replies that he too was at Reading and at the Rock on the Tyne gig, and had forgotten seeing Doll by Doll on those occasions. All dates rest on the writers’ memories.
zitate_kontext: The blogger on Leven’s musical roots.
Leven, quoted by the blogger at the end.

2012-10-11-orion-ian-rankin-standing-in-.kurz: In a video of under two minutes, published by his publisher, Ian Rankin explains how a misheard chorus from Leven’s “Another Man’s Rain” gave his novel *Standing in Another Man’s Grave* its title.
inhalt: The publisher Orion put a short video on YouTube (title: “Standing in Another Man’s Grave: Ian Rankin on how Jackie Leven inspired the book title”; description: Rankin talks about how some misheard song lyrics inspired the title). Rankin explains that the title is a “mondegreen”: for years he heard the chorus of Leven’s song “Another Man’s Rain” as “Standing in Another Man’s Grave”, and only noticed his mistake when he looked at the lyric sheet. According to the video, his character Rebus mishears it in the same way at the start of the novel.

The book is dedicated to Leven, and each section opens with a line from one of his songs. Rankin calls Leven a great guitarist and storyteller who is “not well enough known”. The video appeared not quite a year after Leven’s death, as a tribute to his friend.
zitate_kontext: Description of the video on YouTube (Orion Publishing Group).

2012-11-21-the-quietus-crime-plays-write.autor: Luke Turner; conversation with Ian Rankin
2012-11-21-the-quietus-crime-plays-write.kurz: Ian Rankin chooses “Creatures of Light and Darkness” for the “Baker’s Dozen” series. His reasoning leads directly to his writing: Leven's male characters, who are poor at expressing their feelings, seemed to him fitting music for Rebus.
inhalt: Ian Rankin chooses “Creatures of Light and Darkness” for the “Baker’s Dozen” series. His reasoning leads directly to his writing: Leven's male characters, who are poor at expressing their feelings, seemed to him fitting music for Rebus. Rankin recalls that Leven in turn read the novels and got in touch via the publisher after his name was mentioned. From this developed their personal meeting and the joint recording for Cooking Vinyl.

A second focus is “Standing in Another Man’s Grave”, the new Rebus book dedicated to Leven. Rankin explains the title as his own mishearing of a Leven song title. He also describes how he built the misunderstanding into the novel: after a funeral, Rebus listens to Leven in the car and likewise mishears the words. Rankin also says that different Leven songs open the sections of the book.

Finally he connects the album title with the moral ambivalence of human action, which also interests his crime novels. The source thus documents Rankin's own interpretation of the connection between Leven's music and Rebus, a year after Leven's death.

2012-2020-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-lev.titel: [Collected finds Nasjonalbiblioteket 2012–2020: short notices, announcements, lists]

2012-chicago-review-press-simmonds-encyc.kurz: Jeremy Simmonds's encyclopedia of dead rock stars lists Leven under 2011 as a “journeyman folk/rock musician and songwriter” from Kirkcaldy, Fife, with Doll By Doll, Sir Vincent Lone and death from cancer.
inhalt: In the expanded 2012 edition of *The Encyclopedia of Dead Rock Stars*, Jackie Leven appears under the year of his death, 2011. The entry begins “Jackie Leven (Kirkcaldy, Fife, Scotland, 18 June 1950)” and describes him as singer and guitarist of Doll By Doll, who released four albums in four years, and as a “journeyman folk/rock musician and songwriter”. He was born into a Romany family and began as John St Field with a “long-forgotten” debut, later also releasing as Sir Vincent Lone. He died after a “two-year battle” with cancer; the two-year figure is inaccurate, as the diagnosis came only in the autumn of 2011.

2012-frances-lincoln-westwood-the-great-.kurz: The young-adult novel *The Great and Dangerous* by the former music journalist Chris Westwood is dedicated to the memory of Jackie Leven (1950–2011).
inhalt: Chris Westwood, a former music journalist (among other things he wrote about Doll by Doll for Record Mirror in 1979), dedicated his young-adult novel *The Great and Dangerous* (Frances Lincoln Children's Books, London, 2012) to the memory of Jackie Leven 1950–2011. No further references to Leven were visible in the excerpts checked.

2012-jackieleven-co-uk-gaestebuch-2012-2.kurz: The guestbook on Leven’s website gathers belated condolences, concert memories and a call for a memorial gig in 2012; from 2013 genuine entries dry up and spam takes over.
inhalt: The guestbook on jackieleven.co.uk stayed online after Leven’s death in November 2011. The early entries of 2012 are mostly belated condolences from people who learned of the death only weeks or months later – one at the end of December, another in April 2012 while searching for a new album. From spring 2012 the page is increasingly swamped by spam; only about 25 genuine entries remain, and by 2015 there is little but single characters and advertising.

Many entries are small Leven stories. A promoter from Palma de Mallorca recalls shows in 2002 and 2003 and sends warm regards to Leven’s wife, Deborah. A fan from Brighton, who saw Leven more than twenty times, caught the penultimate gig there in August 2011 and barely recognised him: the voice was of the same pure quality, but not “the aggressive bolshy Jackie” of the stage; he had no idea Leven had cancer. He suggests a London remembrance night with Michael Weston King, Tom Robinson, Andy White and possibly Martyn Joseph playing Leven’s songs. An Australian remembers a show in Katoomba where Leven stopped singing mid-song when his four-year-old daughter dropped a drink in his lap, asking whether he would like him to wait while everything was sorted out. A woman from Saxony who attended nine concerts in Dresden and Singwitz asks where his grave is; a Londoner asks the administrators to repost Leven’s old monthly diary entries from the former Haunted Valley site.

Other entries mark his birthday (18 June) and the first anniversary of his death (14–17 November 2012). In June 2012 a fan writes who found Leven through Ian Rankin’s Rebus novels; in August a German fan sends greetings to everyone who has posted; in 2013 a new listener from Atlanta introduces himself. The guestbook is less a source of fact than a portrait of a mood: it shows how far Leven’s audience reached – Britain, Germany, Spain, Australia, the USA – and how personally many had experienced his concerts.
zitate_kontext: A Brighton fan on the penultimate gig
Australian fan on a show in Katoomba

2012-orion-rankin-standing-in-another-ma.kurz: Ian Rankin's first Rebus novel after Leven's death, Standing in Another Man's Grave (2012), is dedicated "RIP Jackie Leven"; its title derives from Leven's "Another Man's Rain", which Rebus at first mishears.
inhalt: *Standing in Another Man's Grave* (Orion, London, 2012) is the first Rebus novel after Leven's death. It carries the dedication "RIP Jackie Leven" and a copyright notice for Leven song lines (CV Publishing). The title comes from a Leven song that Rebus at first misunderstands: he hears "standing in another man's rain". Rankin himself has confirmed that the scene is autobiographical and that the title goes back to Leven's "Another Man's Rain" (on the album *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!*, also a single in 2006); the song also appears as "Standing in Another Man's Rain" on *The Wanderer* in a version by Andy White.

In the novel Rebus thinks that Leven is now dead too, a year or two younger than himself. The Leven CD plays several times in the car. The book appeared in translation, including *Mädchengrab* (German, Manhattan), *Debout dans la tombe d'un autre* (French, 2014) and *Cold case* (Dutch, 2013), plus a US edition in 2013, each with the dedication and the passages. Rankin also explains the choice of title in an Orion video and in a Guardian piece of 20 July 2021.
zitate_kontext: What Rebus at first believes he hears in the novel

2012-seren-carson-call-mother-a-lonely-f.kurz: Liam Carson’s memoir about his family and the Irish language takes its title from Leven’s song “Call Mother a Lonely Field” and is dedicated to Jackie Leven (1950–2011).
inhalt: *Call Mother a Lonely Field* is a memoir by the Irish author Liam Carson of Belfast about his family and the Irish language (Hag’s Head Press / Seren, 2012). The title is borrowed from Leven’s song, and the book is dedicated “in loving memory of Jackie Leven 1950–2011”. Carson thanks Leven for permission to use the title and lines, reports that Doll By Doll were played in his parents’ house in the early Eighties, and relates what Leven told him about how the song came about. It is regarded as the most extensive literary echo of a Leven song outside Ian Rankin’s work.

2013-03-15-djay-buddha-jackie-leven-back.kurz: A short YouTube video, "Jackie Leven Backstage Vienna", uploaded in 2013 by the channel Djay Buddha; the description speaks of a "strange eclectic collection of words names and phrases" by Leven.
inhalt: The video "Jackie Leven Backstage Vienna" was uploaded on 15 March 2013 by the YouTube channel "Djay Buddha" and runs 3 minutes 54 seconds. The description reads: "Couldn't find this strange eclectic collection of words names and phrases by Jackie", and the uploader adds that he does not own or claim rights to the video, which is shared purely for the listening pleasure of Jackie Leven fans.

Title and description do not reveal what kind of announcements or recording this is, and there is no recording date. The title points to backstage material in Vienna, where Leven performed several times. The video itself was not evaluated.

2013-03-folkworld-my-top-50-psychedelic-.kurz: In his list of the 50 best psychedelic folk albums (1966–1982), David Hintz ranks John St. Field’s *Control* at number 46 and considers it Leven’s brightest work.
inhalt: For FolkWorld’s fiftieth issue, the writer David Hintz offers in March 2013 a personal top 50 of psychedelic folk albums from the “classic psyche-folk era” of 1966 to 1982. He uses the term liberally: any folk album with elements of folk rock or progressive folk and a full or partly psychedelic sound and spirit qualifies. He sees the list as a snapshot in time; tomorrow it will change. He recommends Jeanette Leech’s *Seasons They Change* and Rob Young’s *Electric Eden* for further reading.

At number 46 stands John St. Field’s *Control* – the pseudonym is Jackie Leven. The short comment runs: Ian Rankin’s favourite musician was Jackie Leven, who had an interesting band, Doll by Doll. But it is this first effort that shines brightest, released under a mysterious pseudonym “due to various nefarious stories”. What the ‘nefarious stories’ refer to, the author does not say.

The placement, next to Tim Buckley’s *Goodbye and Hello* at 45, marks *Control* as a collector’s record of the psychedelic folk scene. The entry is brief but shows that Leven’s early album is regarded among genre connoisseurs as a discovery.

2013-07-15-plain-and-fancy-john-st-field.kurz: A collectors' blog post on *Control* (1971) by John St. Field, with a long biography of the young Jackie Leven: an outsider in Fife, folk clubs, years of wandering across Europe.
inhalt: In July 2013 the blog Plain and Fancy presented John St. Field's *Control* as “beautiful acid psych folk rock”. The post gives the track list, the musicians and a longish biography of Leven's youth. The credits are John Haines (drums), Joe Kuccer (flute, baritone sax), Jackie Leven (guitars, keyboards, bass, vocals), Phil Ryan (organ, Moog), Alex Atterson (piano) and Jesse Ballard and Juliet Lawson (vocals). All songs are by Leven, from “Soft Lowland Tongue” and the ten-minute “The Problem” to the short “Sleeping In Bracken”.

The biography starts in 1950: Leven was born into a Romany family and, as a child and teenager, was clearly marked out as an outsider in the clannish, insular world of Fife. Neither parent came from the area; his father was an Irish Cockney and his mother came from a large Geordie family in Northumberland. He was hopelessly wayward at school but outstanding at English and essay writing, and the truanting days spent alone in glens, hills and by rivers still form the imagery of his songs. His mother, unusually for the time and place, loved American black blues, so he came home from school to Lightnin' Hopkins while his friends' homes resounded to Elvis's “Wooden Heart”.

Soon he was playing in local bands, part of the first real electric scene in that part of the world, and singing his own blues songs in folk clubs such as the Elbow Room in Kirkcaldy, where Archie Fisher and Hamish Imlach encouraged him and where he played a few shows as guitarist for Doris Henderson. That activity also brought him to the attention of local gangs; one started a baseless vendetta against him and he had to leave Fife and Scotland. Years of rootless wandering followed, sleeping rough and living hand to mouth, including four months in corners of London's South Bank Centre, busking in the late sixties when street musicians were far less accepted than now.

He also lived in County Kerry, Berlin and Madrid, where *Control* was released in 1971 under his stage name of the time, John St Field, and is now regarded as a psychedelic underground classic. In squats around the UK he met people with serious mental illness, and he often quotes Theodore Roethke's line “for what is madness but nobility of soul at odds with circumstance?”. Seven comments follow, several written after Leven's death, among them “one of the nicest/greatest guys in music” and “a great storyteller as well as a singer and guitarist”. The biography is plainly Leven's own embroidered narrative and is not independently confirmed.
zitate_kontext: The blog's biography on Leven's mother and his childhood
The biography on Leven's time in squats

2013-07-17-plain-or-pan-six-of-the-best-.kurz: In the blog series “Six Of The Best”, Ian Rankin picks “Exit Wound” as one of six favourite tracks: Leven was a fan of his books, which led to friendship, a joint album and a tour.
inhalt: Craig McAllister’s post on the Scottish music blog Plain Or Pan is number 15 in the series “Six Of The Best”, in which musicians, authors and other figures pick six favourite tracks – “a mini, groovier version of Desert Island Discs”. The blogger first introduces Ian Rankin as the creator of the Rebus novels and a well-known music fan whose book titles often quote songs and albums (*Let It Bleed*, *The Hanging Garden*, *Exit Music*, *Dead Souls*), and tells a longer anecdote about how he himself came to Rebus through his father-in-law.

Rankin explains that when Desert Island Discs asked him for his top eight songs he began with a shortlist of forty; here he chooses six that may not be all-time favourites but mean something to him and should be listened to more often. They are Hawkwind’s “Silver Machine”, the Rolling Stones’ “You Can’t Always Get What You Want”, “Theme from Shaft”, The Cure’s “The Hanging Garden”, King Creosote’s “Ankle Shackles” and Jackie Leven’s “Exit Wound”.

On Leven, Rankin says Jackie was a fan of his books, which he did not know; he himself was a fan of Leven’s music, and so was Inspector Rebus. Eventually they became friends, made an album and toured together – “and then Jackie was gone, dead too soon”. He saw him do this song many times; it is “moving, powerful, classic Jackie”. As a bonus the blogger adds a live recording of “Exit Wound” by Leven and Rankin from their 2005 tour.
zitate_kontext: Ian Rankin on “Exit Wound” and his friendship with Leven

2013-08-cambridge-105-smelly-flowerpot-j.kurz: A tribute programme of just under two hours forty from Davey Hammond's radio show “The Smelly Flowerpot” (Cambridge 105, August 2013), with Leven's songs and messages from friends and colleagues, including members of Doll By Doll.
inhalt: In August 2013 Davey Hammond's show “The Smelly Flowerpot” on Cambridge 105 devoted an edition to “the late, great and much missed Jackie Leven”. Under the title “When The Stars Began To Fall – A Jackie Leven Tribute”, Hammond played some of Leven's greatest songs (he writes it was hard whittling the list down) and added exclusive messages and interviews with friends and artists who worked with him, including members of Doll By Doll.

In September 2013 Hammond put the show on Mixcloud in its entirety with extra material, including songs not previously aired; it runs to a little over two and a half hours. He asks listeners to help keep Leven's music and memory alive by sharing, and jokes that the show was produced with his trusty laptop, “some dodgy editing software and several bottles of red wine”. It is dedicated to the memory of his mother and stepfather, who died a few weeks either side of Leven in 2011. The page's tags are “Eternal Warrior” and “Celtic Soul Brother”. The description does not say who exactly speaks in the programme.
zitate_kontext: From the programme description on Mixcloud.

2013-09-26-orion-saints-of-the-shadow-bi.kurz: In a short publisher’s video, Ian Rankin explains that the title of his novel *Saints of the Shadow Bible* comes from a line by his friend Jackie Leven, and that both men’s work is about men who cannot show their emotions.
inhalt: In September 2013 the publisher Orion put online a 98-second video for Ian Rankin’s Rebus novel *Saints of the Shadow Bible*. The description says it is the second time Rankin has used a lyric from his “good friend Jackie Leven” as the title of a book. Leven’s songs and Rankin’s books deal with similar themes: “Men who can’t show their emotions, men who make mistakes, men who screw up.”

In the video itself, Rankin says, according to the available account: Leven died while Rankin was planning the novel *Standing in Another Man’s Grave*. Their friendship rests on mutual admiration. *Saints of the Shadow Bible* was one of four or five possible Leven quotations for a title, and stands for ghosts, alcohol and the love of Rankin’s detective John Rebus for Leven’s music; some Leven lines appear as an epigraph to the book.
The video shows how closely Rankin’s Rebus series was bound up with Leven’s work – a connection that had already produced their joint album *Jackie Leven Said*.
zitate_kontext: Description of the video on YouTube
Description of the video on YouTube

2013-12-29-the-new-vinyl-villain-big-tea.kurz: A guest post by Phil of The Corn Poppy on The New Vinyl Villain celebrates the only single by Concrete Bulletproof Invisible, in effect Doll by Doll with Glen Matlock, as a neglected cult classic.
inhalt: The "Cult Classics" post was submitted by Phil from the blog The Corn Poppy and published by the blog's owner, JC, on 29 December 2013. Phil wonders whether anyone else ever heard this record and says that in a parallel universe *Big Tears* by Concrete Bulletproof Invisible would have been a smash. CBI were really Doll by Doll with Glen Matlock on bass. A long quotation from Wikipedia follows: a London band formed by Leven in 1975, largely ignored by the press of the day, with Jo Shaw, Robin Spreafico, David Macintosh and later Tony Waite, the albums *Remember*, *Gypsy Blood*, *Doll by Doll* and *Grand Passion* (with David Gilmour), the split in 1983 and the 1988 single.

In his own words, Phil says that in 1983 Jackie ("from the Kingdom of Fife") was mugged and half strangled, lost his voice for a time and gave up singing altogether; nothing followed until the mid-1990s, when he began a string of albums that won him a genuine cult following. "Big Tears" was a Matlock song; the B-side, "Braid on My Shoulder", was written by Leven. Phil calls them a cracking pair, with all the punch of Matlock's best powerpunk swagger and "Jackie's still powerful voice". A UK 12-inch added "Good Thing", a US 12-inch "Love Kills". It was the group's only record, though the name was later used as the title of a John Foxx instrumental credited to Foxx/Leven.

His closing paragraph: Leven had a chequered career, often on the verge of greater success and never quite grasping it, sometimes seemingly through deliberate sabotage. Around 2000 he settled in the Hampshire village of Botley, opposite the pub, often popping out for a pint (usually with a vodka in it) or to tour Germany or Norway. His friendship with Ian Rankin led to Rankin naming his last two novels after Leven lyrics. He died in November 2011, six weeks after releasing one of his best albums, *Wayside Shrines*. One day, Phil predicts, a song of his will be used in a car advert and suddenly everyone will love him.

JC adds that Leven was very much a cult artist with many fans in the blogger's part of the world and points to an April 2010 piece on the now defunct Helpless Dancer blog. In the comments a reader who bought the single on release recalls the B-side as the lasting impression: the tale of a soldier serving in Belfast during the Troubles who finally escapes when he travels to Galway Bay. Several details come from Wikipedia and are partly inaccurate (e.g. the 1975 founding date, the 1983 mugging).
zitate_kontext: Phil on "Big Tears" and "Braid on My Shoulder"

2013-heinemann-fletcher-boy-about-town.kurz: In his memoir *Boy About Town*, the music journalist Tony Fletcher tells how, as a teenager, he met “Jackie Levan”, singer of Doll By Doll, a band with a reputation among the music press.
inhalt: In *Boy About Town* (William Heinemann, London, 2013) the music journalist Tony Fletcher, founder of the fanzine *Jamming!*, looks back on his youth. In one passage he describes meeting “Jackie Levan”, singer of Doll By Doll, a band that had made a name for itself with the music press. The name is misspelt in the book; how the encounter continues cannot be seen in the available extract.

2013-orion-rankin-saints-of-the-shadow-b.kurz: Ian Rankin's novel *Saints of the Shadow Bible* carries lines from Leven's “One Man, One Guitar” as its epigraph; by Rankin's account the title too goes back to a Leven line.
inhalt: Ian Rankin's Rebus novel *Saints of the Shadow Bible* (Orion, 2013) opens with lines from Jackie Leven's “One Man, One Guitar” as an epigraph, reprinted by permission of CV Publishing. The prologue follows immediately. The French edition (“On ne réveille pas un chien endormi”, 2015) carries the same epigraph.
According to Rankin himself (The Guardian, 20 July 2021), the book's title also comes from a Leven line about the “saints of the shadow bible”; he never asked Leven what it meant.

2013-polygon-galloway-songs-in-the-key-o.kurz: Jackie Leven is mentioned in Vic Galloway’s book *Songs in the Key of Fife* on the Fife scene around the Fence Collective only in a list of Fife musicians whose story the book explicitly does not tell.
inhalt: The book (Polygon, Edinburgh, 2013) is by the BBC Scotland presenter Vic Galloway and deals with the intertwining of the Beta Band, King Creosote, KT Tunstall, James Yorkston and the Fence Collective. In the visible excerpt Jackie Leven appears only in a list of Fife musicians, alongside Nazareth, the Skids and Big Country, whose story the book explicitly does not tell.
No section on Leven of his own is evident. The hit mainly serves as a pointer that Leven is counted among the well-known names of music from Fife.

2014-01-25-distorsioni-outsider-di-gran-.kurz: Two-part portrait in the Italian web magazine Distorsioni, a good two years after Leven's death.
inhalt: Two-part portrait in the Italian web magazine Distorsioni, a good two years after Leven's death. Part 1 (Jackie Leven) tells the career: “Control” in 1973 as John St. Field on the Spanish label Movieplay, founding of Doll by Doll in 1975, four LPs 1977–1983, at the end of 1983 a street assault with an attempt at strangling and over two years without the ability to speak or sing, heroin addiction, the band Concrete Bulletproof Invisible with Glen Matlock (single “Big Tears”, good review in Melody Maker), a collaboration with John Foxx, in the early nineties overcoming the addiction with the help of his wife Carol through acupuncture and holistic therapy, then the return in 1994 with “Songs from the Argyll Cycle” and the Cooking Vinyl album “The Mystery of Love…”. Highlighted are, among others, “Fairytales for Hard Men”, “Creatures of Light and Darkness”, the Haunted Year series and “Wayside Shrines…”, collaborations with Michael Cosgrave and Ian Rankin, the pseudonym Sir Vincent Lone and support slots for Willie Nile and Lloyd Cole. Sfondrini compares Leven's vocal range with Demetrio Stratos (Area).

Part 2 (Doll by Doll) describes the band as neither commercial nor compatible with punk, discusses “Remember”, “Gypsy Blood”, “Doll by Doll” (MCA, released late) and “Grand Passion” (Magnet, with Helen Turner, Mel Collins and David Gilmour; Turner is judged disparagingly) and mentions the live CD “Revenge Of Memory” (Sheffield Limits Club 1977, released 2006). Tenor: appeal for rediscovery, Leven as an “outsider” of great class.
zitate_kontext: Closing appeal of the Leven part.

2014-06-26-mylondon-former-addicts-celeb.kurz: The local paper reports on the Core Trust's annual garden party in Marylebone on 19 June 2014, with about 50 former and current clients marking 29 years; founded in 1985 by Leven and his partner Carol Wolf, part of the Westminster Drug Project since 2007.
inhalt: Alix Culbertson reports on 26 June 2014 for the London local paper on the summer gathering of The Core Trust, the addiction charity in Marylebone set up by the Scottish singer. On Thursday 19 June, the charity welcomed former users of the service to its annual party at its headquarters in the Lisson Cottages: about 50 former and current service users, staff and volunteers enjoyed food, live music and a tombola and celebrated 29 years of the charity's work.

A former client, a mother of two (the piece gives only her first name), tells how the trust helped her. She had struggled with addiction problems from a young age and became a heroin user; she began treatment at Core in 2010 and has now been clean of drugs and alcohol for three years. Life had been about surviving, and her decisions were dictated by addiction; by coming to Core something in her was awoken again, and the people there really wanted the best for her and her children.

On history, the piece says the Trust was founded in 1985 by the late songwriter and musician Jackie Leven and his partner Carol Wolf after he became addicted to heroin – at first as a way of dealing with their own addiction by creating “a place where change happens”. Since 2007 it has been part of the London-wide charity Westminster Drug Project (WDP) and offers abstinence-based rehabilitation programmes, specialising in direct support to the families and children of those attending. Service manager Lynn Turner calls the party a fantastic chance to see former and current users and celebrate their recovery, a family get-together where people from the wider community can see what Core is about. Leven's own account of the founding is not the subject here.
zitate_kontext: A former client (first name in the piece, withheld here)
Lynn Turner, service manager of the Core Trust

2014-07-bbc-music-artist-page-jackie-lev.kurz: The archived BBC Music artist page shows a short Wikipedia-derived biography, the latest tracks played on BBC Radio Scotland in 2014, and the BBC programmes that have played Leven, including Late Junction, Bob Harris Sunday and Desert Island Discs.
inhalt: The BBC Music artist page (archived July 2014) lists Jackie Leven with dates 18 June 1950 to 14 November 2011. The short biography comes from Wikipedia: a Scottish songwriter and folk musician who began as a folk musician in the late 1960s, first found success with the new wave band Doll by Doll and later released more than twenty albums under his own name or the pseudonym Sir Vincent Lone. The links come from MusicBrainz (official website, Facebook, MySpace, Discogs, Last.fm, Wikipedia); Doll By Doll is listed as a band he was a member of.

The most useful part is the section on BBC airplay. The latest tracks played, all on Iain Anderson's BBC Radio Scotland programme, are “Poortoun” (7 July 2014), “One Man Guitar” (2 July 2014), “Nottamun Town” (11 March 2014) and “Soft Lowland Tongue” and “Elegy For Johnny Cash” (both 10 March 2014). Besides Iain Anderson, the programmes named as having played Leven are Late Junction (Radio 3), Bob Harris Sunday (Radio 2), Tiompan (Radio nan Gàidheal), The Late Show with Stuart Bailie (Radio Ulster), Desert Island Discs (Radio 4) and Alex Lester (Radio 2). Similar artists are given as Doll By Doll, Sir Vincent Lone, Kevin Coyne and Chip Taylor. The page itself notes that the play-count information is incomplete at present.
zitate_kontext: Opening of the short biography on the BBC page (from Wikipedia).

2014-bloomsbury-thorne-dictionary-of-con.kurz: Tony Thorne’s slang dictionary illustrates the entry “heat” (police, pressure of pursuit) with a line from “Endgame”, a 1979 Doll by Doll song.
inhalt: In the *Dictionary of Contemporary Slang* (Bloomsbury) Tony Thorne gives, under “heat” in the sense of police or pressure of pursuit, a line from “Endgame”, a 1979 Doll by Doll song, as his illustrative quotation. It is a curious lexicographical record of Leven’s lyrics; the lyric itself is not reproduced here.

2014-suhrkamp-the-beat-goes-on-2015.kurz: The German calendar book *The Beat Goes On 2015* lists Leven under a commemoration date with all his pseudonyms and calls him an “industrious” Scottish musician.
inhalt: In the pop calendar *The Beat Goes On 2015* (Suhrkamp, Berlin, 2014) an entry under one date – probably his birthday or death day – reads “2011 Jackie Leven (*18.6.1950) aka John St. Field aka Sir Vincent Lone aka Jackie Balfour”, characterising him as a “busy-as-a-bee” Scottish musician; the continuation is not visible. It is notable that a German mass-market book lists all of Leven's pseudonyms in full.

2015-06-16-the-guardian-cult-heroes-jack.kurz: Tribute for his (almost) 65th birthday in the Guardian series on cult musicians. Graeme Thomson recalls Leven's concert at the Cabaret Voltaire in Edinburgh on 11 August 2011, which turned out to be a farewell; three months later Leven died of pancreatic cancer.
inhalt: Tribute for his (almost) 65th birthday in the Guardian series on cult musicians. Graeme Thomson recalls Leven's concert at the Cabaret Voltaire in Edinburgh on 11 August 2011, which turned out to be a farewell; three months later Leven died of pancreatic cancer. Relatively well known in Germany and Norway, under the radar in Britain, but with high-calibre admirers: David Thomas, Johnny Dowd, Ron Sexsmith, Ian Rankin (two Rebus titles taken from Leven songs) and Mike Scott, who gave Thomson a statement of his own. Thomson characterises the songs as poetry of unfulfilled lives with moments of transcendence and recommends “Poor Toun” and “Universal Blue” (live version from The Haunted Year: Winter), as well as the Sir Vincent Lone version of Judee Sill's “When the Bridegroom Comes”. Biography: father London-Irish, mother from north-east England, school in Kirkcaldy like Gordon Brown, Roma heritage; left home at 16, by the early 1970s had left two marriages behind him. Doll by Doll (with Joe Shaw and Dave MacIntosh) in the squat in Maida Vale, contract with Automatic (Warner), thrown off a Hawkwind tour, drug excesses. After the split in 1983 a contract with Virgin, assault on the way home from a session, never regained his falsetto, heroin, recovery, CORE Trust. Return to music in 1992, around 30 releases in two decades. Thomson's stage memories and Rankin's perception of “pent-up energy”.

2015-06-16-the-guardian-kommentare-cult-.titel: [Reader comments on: Cult heroes: Jackie Leven found musical beauty in his wounds]
2015-06-16-the-guardian-kommentare-cult-.kurz: Twenty comments (16–18.06.2015) under Graeme Thomson's “Cult heroes” piece. To one reader's charge that a dead man is being mythologised, fans reply that Leven did most of that himself.
inhalt: Twenty comments (16–18.06.2015) under Graeme Thomson's “Cult heroes” piece. To one reader's charge that a dead man is being mythologised, fans reply that Leven did most of that himself. “Kevin1957”, who followed the band as a fan and was allowed to stay overnight in Maida Vale, reports that co-founder Robin Spreafico died of cancer in early 2015 and his successor Tony Waite a few years earlier; Doll by Doll, he says, did get front covers of Disc and Record Mirror at the time. Another reader remembers that Leven played regularly at the Brighton Folk Club in the early 1970s.

The most detailed is “simonhop”, a songwriter who supported him several times at the 12 Bar Club in the mid-1990s and booked Leven for a series in Bromley. Leven stayed overnight with him and, over vodka and orange juice, explained his storytelling technique: the audience does not want ordinary heroes; the storyteller must have experienced extraordinary things, and the truth must not get in the way. Leven later asked about printing one of simonhop's lyrics on an album cover, which never happened. Another reader was at the 12 Bar concert that was released as *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow*, saw Leven at the release concert for *The Mystery of Love* at the Borderline with an electric guitar, and in the 1990s exchanged letters with him about poetry (recommendation: Sharon Olds, *The Father*; conversation about Kenneth Patchen). TatankaYotanka announces the tribute evenings by Michael Weston King and Michael Cosgrave in Winchester and Birmingham.

2015-06-18-the-afterword-jackie-leven-wo.kurz: Forum thread marking Leven’s 65th birthday on 18 June 2015: fans raise a glass, name favourite songs and recall gigs, a cancelled last concert in Birmingham and Graeme Thomson’s Guardian tribute.
inhalt: On The Afterword’s forum, the user “Baron Harkonnen” opens a thread on 18 June 2015 for what would have been Leven’s 65th birthday. Leven would have bollocked him or anyone else for being sentimental, he writes, but let us raise a wee dram to Jackie and his legacy; as a listening sample he posts *Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West*. Twelve replies follow. Kaisfatdad drinks to “the big man’s memory”, Wheldrake calls him a brilliant, sadly missed songwriter and links a favourite. duco01 is glad of how many fans of the “Big Man from the Kingdom of Fife” there are on the board and posts “Desolation Blues” live in Glasgow, 18 years earlier. Feedback_File has followed Leven since the Doll By Doll days, names a track that still makes him misty-eyed, and praises Leven’s version of “I Say A Little Prayer” as almost definitive (“but don’t tell Aretha”); Baron Harkonnen agrees that he really was a one-off.

SteveT, who misses him terribly, had a ticket for Leven’s last gig in Birmingham, cancelled about a week before he died, with no idea that he was ill; he looks forward to an evening of Leven songs by Michael Weston King and Michael Cosgrave the following month. retropath2 says it was a privilege to see him in Birmingham, never more than a handful of people, who would nevertheless be “converted, effortlessly”; he later learned Leven lived only miles from his parents on the Hampshire coast, and went for a drink in the village pubs in the hope that he might be there. He never was.

duco01 also links Graeme Thomson’s piece on Leven in *The Guardian* of 16 June 2015 (“Cult heroes”); retropath2 calls it a lovely piece and Baron Harkonnen a fine tribute to a fine man. Gary recalls posting one of his favourite lines from Leven’s lyrics on the board when Leven died, and cannot believe it was over three years ago.
zitate_kontext: retropath2 on Leven’s concerts in Birmingham

2015-07-13-three-chords-and-the-truth-uk.kurz: The blog Three Chords and the Truth UK reports on the tribute evening at the Kitchen Garden Café: Michael Weston King and Michael Cosgrave play an hour of Jackie Leven songs and an hour of Townes Van Zandt.
inhalt: The blog post of 13 July 2015 opens with thoughts on the immortality of song when “the great architects” are taken too soon. Jackie Leven and Townes Van Zandt at least lived in the era of multi-dimensional recording; Van Zandt’s presence has thrived since his death in 1997, and Leven too left “a massive vault of legacy-laden songs” that will keep the spark going for many years. The personal link between them is Michael Weston King, one of the UK’s most sincere and scholarly practitioners of roots music, who has teamed up with the multi-instrumentalist Michael Cosgrave, a long-time associate of Leven.

At the show on Sunday 12 July 2015 at the Kitchen Garden Café in Kings Heath, Birmingham, the first hour was devoted to Leven. Weston King’s vocals worked “in divine cohesion” with Cosgrave’s guitar, piano and accordion, and Cosgrave chipped in with occasional comment. Leven had played the venue many times before his death in 2011, and the well-attended show was clearly frequented by many of his fans. The songs ranged from the popular ‘Main Travelled Roads’ to slightly hidden album tracks such as ‘Ireland for Losers’. In his usual slightly dry delivery Weston King paid many humble personal respects to his late friend, including a stark reference to his style as ‘Celtic soul’. The first half closed with the song Leven wrote for a Townes tribute album, ‘Townes at the Borderline’ – ironically a project in which the invited practice was to cover one of his songs, but the true songwriting maverick had other ideas.

The second hour was Van Zandt, with whom Weston King worked and played in the early 1990s: ‘Tecumseh Valley’, ‘White Freight Liner Blues’, ‘A Song For’ and ‘Lover’s Lullaby’ from *No Deeper Blue* (1994), King’s own ‘Riding the Range’, covered by Townes, and the morbidly sad ‘Maria’. The writer admits being far more familiar with Van Zandt and therefore felt the shorter liaison with Townes was the evening’s greater legacy; yet two hours after the pair left the stage his awareness of Leven had been “lifted tenfold”. He apologises for the piece being a little Townes-heavy and closes with full respect for Leven’s body of work: with this marker down, you never know where your own musical adventure heads next.
zitate_kontext: On the Leven half of the evening
The writer on the evening’s effect

2016-06-18-born-to-listen-jackie-leven-w.kurz: On what would have been Leven's 66th birthday, the blogger Hallgeir recalls a concert shortly before his death, a CD signed “To my big viking friend”, and shares five YouTube performances.
inhalt: The post on the music blog Born To Listen marks the day on which Jackie Leven would have turned 66. The author, signing himself “Hallgeir”, calls Leven “brilliant and truly under-appreciated”; he says he never tires of the music, that the lyrics stand as poetry of the highest order and that Leven's life ended much too soon. He was lucky enough to see him in concert about a year before he died, and calls him a master story-teller both in his songs and between them.

He tells how Leven asked his name after the show. When he said “Hallgeir”, Leven answered “What?”, tried to say it, laughed and asked what it meant. Hallgeir explained that it is an old viking name meaning literally “stone spear”, and Leven signed his CD “To my big viking friend, Hallgeir!” He was, the author says, a sweet, funny and very talented man.

The rest consists of YouTube finds “to celebrate a fine songwriter”: “Empty in Soho Square” with an interview (2004), an Ancient Misty Morning medley from the Tramway, Glasgow (1995), “Kings Of Infinite Space” (23 July 2010), “Poortoun” (25 July 1999) and “Single Father” (20 September 2000). In between sits a Wikipedia-style biographical paragraph (18 June 1950 to 14 November 2011; folk musician, then success with Doll by Doll, later more than twenty albums under his own name or as Sir Vincent Lone; he often complained that his record company would not let him release as many albums as he wanted). The post concludes that he never achieved the success he deserved: “We miss him.”
zitate_kontext: Hallgeir at the start of his post
Leven's dedication in the signed CD

2016-08-01-fast-n-bulbous-between-the-cr.kurz: The blogger A. S. Van Dorston celebrates Doll by Doll as a band that fell through the cracks between new wave and post-punk: *Gypsy Blood* is an “unsung classic”, followed by a short account of Leven's later path.
inhalt: “Between The Cracks Part 3” belongs to a blog series on bands that slipped between the cracks of new wave, power pop, punk and post-punk in 1978–82. Van Dorston, who opens with “Trends are bullshit”, also covers The Flys, Holly and the Italians and The Distractions.

Doll By Doll, he writes, definitely had trouble fitting in. Leven had already released a solo album, *Control*, in 1971 as John St. Field, progressive folk and R&B influenced and, he says, available only in Spain. Like Graham Parker, he had more in common with Van Morrison, Bruce Springsteen and the former pub rockers Nick Lowe and Elvis Costello than with the current crop of new wave bands.
