The debut *Remember* (1979), with Antonin Artaud on the cover, has long, meandering songs of poetic lyricism and raw guitar, a structural bridge from Free to Gang Of Four and a spiritual link between Dr. Feelgood and Joy Division; since forming in 1977 the band had toured with Hawkwind and Devo. The dualling guitars are out of tune and the production is sloppy, but it is a memorable debut that crescendoes with the raging “Palace of Love”.

*Gypsy Blood* (1979) then fulfils that promise “and then some”. “Teenage Lightning” (2:28) joins sleek pop harmonies and girl-group backing vocals to a raw rock edge, on “Stripshow” Leven switches between baritone and falsetto with ease, “Human Face” blossoms into a power pop anthem, “Binary Fiction” (properly “Binary Friction”) is guitar funk of the kind Robert Fripp would soon bring to King Crimson, “Forbidden Worlds” recalls Television and “Highland Rain” balances folk and post-punk fury. Two very short acoustic numbers, with poetry by Anna Akhmatova, close the album. It is easy to see why some did not know what to make of it, he says, but one close listen leaves no doubt that it is an unsung classic.

The third, self-titled album (Magnet, 1981), delayed by label contract issues, is sleeker and tighter, a progression but a slight downgrade in passion. He praises “Figure It Out” (Springsteen romanticism), the motorik “Caritas” and the neo-skanking “Soon New Life”, but finds the ballad “Main Travelled Roads” disappointing. *Grand Passion* (1982) was basically a solo album, and a fifth album was recorded but never released. A brief account of Leven's “wilderness years” follows: drug addiction, setting up the addiction charity CORE Trust, encouragement from its supporter Princess Diana, the band Concrete Bulletproof with Jo Shaw, David McIntosh and Glen Matlock, eight more years in Scotland involved in Robert Bly's men's movement, and a first solo release in 1994. He counts nearly twenty solo albums, three of them as Sir Vincent Lone, collaborations with David Thomas and Ian Rankin, and Leven's death in 2011.

2016-black-dog-margotin-rolling-stones-a.kurz: In *The Rolling Stones: All the Songs* Leven is quoted on a Stones track as someone for whom it is his favourite Stones song, with a football-chant rhythm; the source is a Mojo interview of September 2007.
inhalt: In the book by Philippe Margotin and Jean-Michel Guesdon (Black Dog & Leventhal, New York 2016; French original *Les Rolling Stones, la totale*), Jackie Leven is quoted on a Stones track: for him it is his favourite Stones song, and it has a football-chant rhythm. According to endnote 47 the source is a Mojo interview with Leven from September 2007. Which song is meant does not emerge from the available extract.

2016-dedalus-meehan-geomantic.kurz: In the notes to her poetry collection *Geomantic* (2016), Paula Meehan records that several poems were presented with music by Jackie Leven at the 2007 Imram festival.
inhalt: In the notes to *Geomantic* (Dedalus Press, Dublin, 2016), the Irish poet Paula Meehan records that some of the poems – “The Fever”, “The Lists” and “The Singer” are named – were presented with music by Jackie Leven at the 2007 Imram festival. The note documents a collaboration between the poet and Leven at that festival.

2016-wickham-festival-jackie-leven-tribu.kurz: The Wickham Festival's artist page for a “Jackie Leven Tribute” consists of a death notice (died on Monday 14 November at 8 pm, of cancer), a Leven quotation on “soulful” rather than “spiritual” storytelling, and a biographical text.
inhalt: The Hampshire festival's page carries the note “appeared in 2016” and describes no programme but pays tribute to Leven. It begins with the news that the great Scottish singer and songwriter died on Monday 14 November at eight o'clock in the evening, having suffered from cancer. It continues with a statement of his own on storytelling: there are spiritual and soulful storytellers; he hopes to be a soulful one – “Spiritual is ascending. Sky, God and all that. I hope my story telling is going down into the earth, is wetter, has more moisture.”

The biographical text follows the official website: a career of more than forty years as a “uniquely gifted singer-songwriter”, from leading the “underrated” Doll by Doll in the Seventies through “well documented” addiction problems, which he overcame with remarkable strength of will, to a solo resurgence. He is the composer of over four hundred songs, including arguably his greatest, “Call Mother”, from the album *The Mystery of Love …*, which Q magazine allegedly ranked among its “100 Best Albums of All Time” (an unsubstantiated promotional claim). If sales did not always reflect the overwhelmingly positive reception, he remained a perceptive writer and performer, imbued with restless creativity, with ruminative lyrics laced with humour and melodic grace. As a performer he could enthral the audience with picaresque tales from first-hand experience. Last comes *Wayside Shrines and the Code of the Travelling Man*, made with the multi-instrumentalist Michael Cosgrave, as further proof of his talent. The page does not say who played at the tribute.
zitate_kontext: Leven on his storytelling, quoted on the festival page
The biographical text on Leven on stage

2017-02-13-bergensmagasinet-nese-for-det.kurz: In a profile of Bergen concert promoter Frank Nes, he recalls being Leven's Scandinavian agent from 1994, calls him “every record label's nightmare”, and describes the funeral where “Main Travelled Roads” was played.
inhalt: Magne Fonn Hafskor profiles Frank Nes, head of Bergen Live, who has been involved since 1993 with what is now the Bergenfest, for Bergensmagasinet. The piece covers Nes's habit of booking artists before they are famous (John Grant, Hawksley Workman, Royal Blood), the firm's figures and the headline acts of summer 2017. Within it, Jackie Leven gets a section of his own: an artist who played several concerts in Bergen before he died in 2011, aged 61.

Nes says he was Leven's agent in Scandinavia from 1994 and spent much time with him. Leven was “every record label's nightmare” because he released album after album on a conveyor belt, and the song catalogue of this “big man in every way” holds a great deal of gold. The journalist remembers Leven best from the Doll by Doll era and says he has read that some of their records were made in an LSD haze; Nes will only say that Leven told a good deal about it. The solo records are more “Celtic soul”, he says, singling out *Fairytales for Hardmen* (1997), *Shining Brother, Shining Sister* (2003) and *Gothic Road* (2010), and above all the comeback album *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* (1994): so much beauty on it, and track three, “Call Mother A Lonely Field”, is simply lovely.

The journalist recounts the background to that album as the article gives it: after Doll by Doll went their separate ways in 1983 Leven began work on his first solo record, was then knocked down in the street and almost strangled, could not speak for two years, was in great pain and eventually became addicted to heroin. Nes started working with him in 1994, when the first solo record could finally be released, and followed him until his death from cancer.

The funeral was “powerful”, Nes says: in the church they played the Doll by Doll song “Main Travelled Roads” over the loudspeakers. He fetches the programme from the ceremony, which prints the almost self-prophetic words from Doll by Doll's debut album: “Eternal is the Warrior / who finds beauty in his wounds”. The writer sees in Leven the romantic Scot, probably raised on Robert Burns, William Blake – and Van Morrison.
zitate_kontext: Frank Nes on Leven as an artist.
Words from Doll by Doll's debut, printed in the funeral programme.

2017-06-28-scotch-whisky-magazine-ian-ra.kurz: In the Scotch Whisky Magazine interview, Ian Rankin matches each whisky with a piece of music; with the Laphroaig comes Leven’s *Exit Wound*. Rankin recalls how Leven made contact, their collaboration, and how Leven dealt with his cancer diagnosis.
inhalt: The conversation with Ian Rankin takes place in the rooms of the Scotch Malt Whisky Society in Edinburgh, with Rankin choosing a piece of music for each dram. It ranges over Rebus, Edinburgh, the Scottish gothic tradition (Hogg, Stevenson, Muriel Spark), Rankin’s writing process, ageing and loss. Jackie Leven features in one short passage.

The interviewer summarises that after Leven’s songs began appearing on the late-night Rebus playlist, Leven contacted Rankin. A working relationship followed, including stage shows and the CD *Jackie Leven Said* (dated 2004 in the text; it was released in 2005), and ended with Leven’s sudden death from cancer in 2011. Rankin recalls that they were meant to do an event together; Leven’s manager phoned to say he could not make it, and three days later he was dead. Leven had dealt with the diagnosis by getting a bottle of whisky and going for a walk. “He was a lovely man.” (The timing is vague; a concert was cancelled only after Leven’s death.)

They then listen to *Exit Wound* with a pair of Laphroaigs. The whisky might be too intense for some, Rankin says, but when Rebus isn’t listening to John Martyn he will be drinking Laphroaig and listening to Jackie Leven. Leven’s album *Fairy Tales for Hard Men* he sums up as “that’s Rebus”. The rest of the interview covers John Martyn’s *Solid Air* with Highland Park, Iain Banks and Glenfiddich, Rankin’s year off writing and Rebus’s ageing.
zitate_kontext: Ian Rankin on Laphroaig and Leven

2017-07-cambridge-105-choice-threads-jac.kurz: Mixcloud entry for a near-hour-long episode of Cambridge 105’s “Choice Threads” in which Chris Duerden and Dave Hammond discuss Leven’s long career, playing tracks by Doll By Doll and Jackie Leven.
inhalt: Radio presenter Chris Duerden’s Mixcloud page lists an episode of the Cambridge 105 Radio show “Choice Threads”, titled “Choice Threads – Jackie Leven ft Dave Hammond” (July 2017, running time 57:57). According to the description, Duerden is joined in the studio by Dave Hammond to discuss the long and fruitful career of the Scottish singer-songwriter Jackie Leven. The tracklist says only that tracks by Doll By Doll and Jackie Leven are played. The content of the programme itself is not accessible from the page, and the description names no topics or specific conversations.

2017-08-16-no-more-big-wheels-doll-by-do.kurz: The long retrospective combines an in-depth appreciation of the Doll by Doll albums with the author's recollections and older passages of conversation.
inhalt: The long retrospective combines an in-depth appreciation of the Doll by Doll albums with the author's recollections and older passages of conversation. At its centre at first is “Gypsy Blood”, which the author calls his irreplaceable favourite album. He describes its shift from accessible songs to menacing, many-layered soundscapes and explains its commercial ineffectiveness partly by the band's difficult public image.

Next comes the third album, of the same name as the band: the text emphasises the attempt at the time to write more comprehensible songs without giving up emotional intensity. In the reproduced answers Leven explains his changed idea of entertainment and the relationship between personal experience, psychedelia and song construction. The author describes his own encounters with Leven as friendly and funny, alongside his intimidating stage presence.

The account extends beyond the end of the group to the later solo career. It ends with the note that Jo Shaw and Dave McIntosh played with friends in a pub in Cricklewood in 2012 in memory of Leven. This adds to the existing trail to the tribute evening, but gives neither an exact date nor the name of the pub here. Older interview quotations and retrospectives from 2007 are interwoven with the narrator's present of 2017.

2018-01-17-norman-lamont-jackie-leven-be.kurz: The Scottish singer-songwriter Norman Lamont (self-description: “came of age in the early 70s”) tells how he discovered Leven twice without hearing him first: in 1981, after a press review, he bought Doll by Doll's single “Main Travelled Roads”, and in 1994 likewise the EP *Songs from the Argyll Cycle*, which…
inhalt: The Scottish singer-songwriter Norman Lamont (self-description: “came of age in the early 70s”) tells how he discovered Leven twice without hearing him first: in 1981, after a press review, he bought Doll by Doll's single “Main Travelled Roads”, and in 1994 likewise the EP *Songs from the Argyll Cycle*, which remains among his favourite recordings to this day. In the 1990s he wrote a song inspired by “Main Travelled Roads”, sent Leven a cassette and received a handwritten letter back immediately (as an image in the post, with a note from Leven about a new album “out on Sept 18th”). The song “Touched Again” was later recorded by Lamont's band The Invisible Helpers and can be heard in the post.

The main part is an outline of the work from a fan's perspective: Doll by Doll (with a longer quotation from Neil McCormick), assault and addiction, founding of the CORE Trust with Carol Wolf (now WDP), support from Princess Diana – Leven credited her with getting him singing again. Lamont stresses that he had heard the Diana story in several versions, which grew with the telling; an embedded audio recording gives the best version (backstage at a charity event, with Wayne Sleep). Then follow Robert Bly and the men's movement, Leven's own open guitar tuning, for which there is no tablature, the relationship with Ian Rankin, the pseudonyms and Leven's notebook text on the “code of the travelling man”, which Deborah Greenwood gave to Paul Du Noyer after his death.
zitate_kontext: Lamont on Leven's way of telling stories.

2019-01-20-the-afterword-jackie-leven.kurz: Gary links a short YouTube video in which Leven speaks (first announced as a documentary, then corrected: “just him talking”).
inhalt: Gary links a short YouTube video in which Leven speaks (first announced as a documentary, then corrected: “just him talking”). From this develops a thread of memories with a good 25 posts (Jan.–June 2019). “Artery” owns all the CDs, claims to have seen Leven almost a hundred times and wishes for vinyl or box-set editions from Cooking Vinyl. SteveT describes Leven's stage image – barefoot, in shorts, seemingly indifferent – and relays a statement by Michael Weston King: Leven was a perfectionist, sober before concerts, and expected the same of fellow musicians. retropath2 half disagrees: he says Leven often asked the audience on stage for a large vodka with lime in a pint glass. A debate follows about the pronunciation “Leeven” rather than “Levven” and a running gag with Leven's stage line “Sting is dead”.

retropath2 says Leven drew him into the old blog of The Word magazine, where he met a community of Leven devotees – forerunner of the Afterword community. Kaisfatdad saw Leven in Stockholm, most recently at the club Debaser. Baron Harkonnen says he discovered the band through an NME review of the album *Doll by Doll* in a pub in Wigan, found Leven again through Mike Scott's thanks on *Fisherman's Blues* and bought *The Mystery of Love* in Rhyl in 1994. Nick L says his future wife named Leven as her favourite musician when they met. Feedback_File and Gary name “Main Travelled Roads” as their favourite song; a link leads to the (according to YouTube comments, only) Doll by Doll film footage.

2019-04-10-norman-lamont-drinking-with-j.kurz: Norman Lamont publishes, with permission, the recollections of a reader, “Tom in Glasgow”.
inhalt: Norman Lamont publishes, with permission, the recollections of a reader, “Tom in Glasgow”. Tom knew Doll by Doll only vaguely and discovered Leven in the mid-1990s through the library CD *The Mystery of Love*; “Call Mother A Lonely Field” blew him away. After that he saw him regularly in Glasgow and Edinburgh. In 2000 he got tickets for a recording at the Glasgow club The Ferry, filmed by STV – as he remembers it, for an episode of the programme *Artery* about Leven; on watching it again on YouTube, however, the concert excerpts did not come from the Ferry, possibly because of technical problems.

Through a companion he met the painter Allan there, whose pictures Leven used for Haunted Valley live albums; Allan later introduced him to Leven, and the three of them occasionally sat in the bar after concerts or watched the main act together when Leven was playing as support (named: Caravan at the Ferry). Away from the stage Leven was somewhat milder, but a masterly storyteller, of whom one never knew whether a story was true. Tom says Leven mocked a musician who had asked him about his guitar before a concert as nosy, right there on stage. In 2009 he saw him with his future wife at the Tolbooth in Stirling. The high point was a concert at the Woodend Bowling and Tennis Club in Glasgow in November 2010: Leven talked as much as he played, overran heavily, and a coarse story about a night-time photo shoot behind the central station brought the house down. He missed the summer 2011 gig at King Tut's; tickets for another Woodend concert in autumn 2011 expired because Leven died a few weeks before. He says he knew Leven was ill, but not how seriously.

2019-12-07-cca-glasgow-leventime-a-celeb.kurz: The CCA Glasgow's listing for “Leventime”, a night of music on 7 December 2019: Leven's songs played by friends and admirers, with profits going to the refugee charity Refuweegee.
inhalt: Glasgow's Centre for Contemporary Arts announces “Leventime: A Celebration of Jackie Leven” for Saturday 7 December 2019, part of its “Sounds in the Suburbs” programme. The text describes Leven as a Scottish songwriter and folk musician, born in Fife in 1950 and died in 2011, a “larger than life character” whose live performances, with their “extravagantly embroidered tales and tall tales”, were “something to cherish”.

The short biography has him starting as a folk musician in the late 1960s, finding his first success with the new wave band Doll by Doll, and later releasing more than twenty albums under his own name or the pseudonym Sir Vincent Lone. The evening offers songs by artists who played with him or were influenced by him: Andy White, Jinky Gilmour, the Doghouse Roses and Dumb Instrument are on the bill, performing some of their own songs and some of Leven's. The second half is a set led by Deborah Greenwood, “Jackie's partner in life and music”, who is assembling a band that includes Jinder of Fisherman's Friends. All profits go to the Glasgow charity Refuweegee. Doors 7pm, £15 plus a £1 booking fee, theatre, 18+.
zitate_kontext: The CCA's programme text on Leven's concerts

2020-03-09-fife-today-why-johnny-cash-wo.kurz: Allan Crow reports in Fife Today on the first Cash Back In Fife festival in Aberdour, where Ian Rankin brought to life the story of Jackie Leven, "an all-too forgotten Fifer".
inhalt: Allan Crow writes in Fife Today (9 March 2020) about the first Cash Back In Fife festival at the Woodside Hotel, Aberdour. Organiser Dean Owens, an Edinburgh singer-songwriter, wrapped it up saying "Maybe my daft wee idea wasn't so daft after all." His notion of celebrating the Man in Black's Fife links and musical legacy produced, in the writer's view, arguably one of the most enjoyable events of 2020; the hotel buzzed with music and chat all weekend. Performers included Owens, Rab Noakes and Fay Fife, alongside acts rooted in Americana.

The Leven connection came on Saturday afternoon, when Ian Rankin took the stage "with a handful of CD covers, all from the late, great Jackie Leven, the celebrated singer-songwriter Fife seems to have forgotten". Leven started out as a folk singer before forming the new wave band Doll by Doll, and he, too, discovered the joy of Cash's music later in life, bringing the set full circle. Next year marks the tenth anniversary of Leven's death at just 61; Rankin, who collaborated and performed with him, brought his turbulent but richly creative story to life, which Crow hopes inspired more people to seek out the music.

Elsewhere: Friday opened with Martha Healy and Al Shields, then Owens and the Celtabilly Allstars (Kevin McGuire, Craig Ross, Amy Geddes) played songs from his Cash-inspired album *Cashback*, the festival's namesake, ending with "Walk the Line" and an encore of "Hurt". On Saturday night a songwriters' circle with Owens, Noakes and Hannah Rose Platt (Noakes recalled seeing Cash in concert in the late 1960s); cover of the weekend was The Marriage (Dave Burn and Kirsten Adamson) turning "Ring of Fire" into a ballad. On Sunday came Kirkcaldy's David Latto and, to finish, the Countess of Fife led by Fay Fife of the Rezillos. Verdict: the festival has tapped into something special, and the writer hopes it returns in 2021.
zitate_kontext: Allan Crow on Ian Rankin's appearance
Crow on Leven and Johnny Cash

2020-03-13-americana-uk-cash-back-in-fif.kurz: Paul Kerr reports on the first Cash Back In Fife weekend in Aberdour, where Ian Rankin remembered his friend Jackie Leven with Dean Owens on guitar.
inhalt: Paul Kerr reviews for Americana UK the first Cash Back In Fife weekend (6–8 March 2020) at the Woodside Hotel in Aberdour. It is the brainchild of Leith singer-songwriter Dean Owens, who had earlier released an album of Cash songs; the occasion was Johnny Cash’s delight at discovering ancestors from the ancient kingdom of Fife. Not a “tribute” event but a weekend acknowledging Cash’s influence on artists, with a nod to those with a Fife connection – among them Rab Noakes, Fay Fife, Kirstin Adamson and David Latto. Kerr is enthusiastic overall.

Crime writer Ian Rankin, another Fifer, spoke of his late friend, the Fife-born Jackie Leven, whom Kerr calls a tremendous (and tremendously underrated) artist. Rankin toured and recorded with Leven; they became friends after Rankin showed his hard-bitten Edinburgh cop Rebus relaxing by listening to Leven. Ostensibly the talk was about the album *Elegy for Johnny Cash*, but by Kerr’s account most of it was Rankin reminiscing and reading favourite lyrics, accompanied by Owens extemporising wonderfully on acoustic guitar.

Kerr calls Leven a maverick with a convoluted career and a complicated personality, yet someone one cannot help admiring for writing lines such as the title “Absolutely Joan Crawford (With A Bit Of Tilda Swinton On The Side)”. Rankin also retold the classic Leven yarn of announcing Sting’s death on a Kirkcaldy train – a stage anecdote. Like Cash, Leven sang of “embittered men”, and Rankin with Owens briefly brought him back to life that afternoon.
zitate_kontext: Paul Kerr on Leven, during Rankin’s reading.
Kerr’s closing remark on the Leven session.

2020-06-18-the-afterword-remembering-jac.kurz: Opening post by the forum user “Moonidus” for Leven's 70th birthday (18.06.2020): he says he organised a bench in London's Soho Square in his memory, near the bench for Kirsty MacColl – both wrote songs about the square.
inhalt: Opening post by the forum user “Moonidus” for Leven's 70th birthday (18.06.2020): he says he organised a bench in London's Soho Square in his memory, near the bench for Kirsty MacColl – both wrote songs about the square. He calls on people to listen to a song, drink a “wee dram” and visit the square after lockdown.

Eleven replies, all from 18 to 20.06.2020. The regular users (Artery, SteveT, Baron Harkonnen, Vulpes Vulpes, Lando Cakes, retropath2) express admiration, call Leven one of the best British songwriters and storytellers and miss unreleased material at Cooking Vinyl. retropath2 reports Facebook mentions, including at the Wickham Festival – Wickham in Hampshire was Leven's home in his late years; Deborah Greenwood is pleased when his memory is kept alive. Sitheref2409 tongue-in-cheek criticises a lyric line. The most important is the post by “Bogart” (20.06.): on Thursday evening (18.06.2020) there was a virtual concert, organised by Deborah Greenwood and Jinder, with cover versions by musicians from Leven's circle – named are Deborah, Jinder, the former Doll by Doll members Jo Shaw and Kevin Foster, Tom Burgess – as well as Ian Rankin, who read Leven's lyrics. Available in the Facebook group “Burning The Box Of Beautiful Things” and on YouTube. Toasts to Leven were drunk with “toffee vodka”.

2020-06-19-jindersongs-jackie-leven-at-7.autor: Jinder (JinderSongs) with Deborah Greenwood and others
2020-06-19-jindersongs-jackie-leven-at-7.kurz: A video of a good 85 minutes, compiled for Leven's 70th birthday from contributions the participants recorded at home (Covid period).
inhalt: A video of a good 85 minutes, compiled for Leven's 70th birthday from contributions the participants recorded at home (Covid period). The opening is spoken by a woman in Leven's music room in a house built around 1700 in Botley, Hampshire, with Leven's Morgan guitar – from context Deborah Greenwood; she sings “Universal Blue” and tells how the song came about in the kitchen of friendly hosts after a long walk up the Cheviot. Ian Rankin reads song lyrics (“My Spanish Dad”, later “The Innocent Railway” from “Lovers at the Gun Club” and a piece from “Forbidden Songs of the Dying West”). Iona of the Doghouse Roses remembers seeing Leven as a guest of Willard Grant Conspiracy and plays “Elegy for Johnny Cash”. Henry Priestman (The Yachts) reads from his diary of 12 April 1979 about a Doll by Doll concert at Eric's in Liverpool, tells of keyboard recordings in Bryn Derwen with producer David Wrench and of Leven crediting him on later albums for instruments he never played, and plays “Paris Blues”. Further contributions: “Revenge of Memory” in Leven's tuning, a reading of “The Dent in the Fender and the Wheel of Fate”, “Main Travelled Roads”, a poem, Rachel Taylor-Beales with a song of her own about Leven, a duo with Kevin Foster from Cricklewood with a song Leven wrote at 16, a contribution on “Silver Blaze” and, at the end, a song by the host with Jinder as backing voice. Tenor: loving, private memorial event of the inner circle.
zitate_kontext: Priestman relays the producer's explanation for Leven's imaginary credits.

2020-07-03-klof-mag-watch-rachel-taylor-.kurz: KLOF Mag features Rachel Taylor-Beales’ single “Jackie’s Coming Around”, a tribute released on what would have been Leven’s 70th birthday, together with her memories of him.
inhalt: KLOF Mag makes “Jackie’s Coming Around” its Song of the Day. The single by the Welsh songwriter Rachel Taylor-Beales came out in June 2020, on what would have been Jackie Leven’s 70th birthday. In the video her husband Bill Taylor-Beales conjures up an ink-and-dip-pen drawing of the late singer. The article quotes the song’s opening (“Blackbird on this tavern roof …”, and “And Jackie said ‘keep following the muse’”) and summarises Leven’s life: a Fife-born singer-songwriter who started out in the seventies with Doll by Doll after having to flee his hometown because of local gang violence; after the band imploded and a serious mugging damaged his larynx and nearly cost him his voice, he became addicted to heroin, but eventually got clean and went back on the road as a solo artist.

The song merges elements of Taylor-Beales’s own songwriting journey with a musical biography of Leven and weaves in multiple references to tracks from his 2007 album *Oh What A Blow That Phantom Dealt Me*. It was recorded and produced at the couple’s Hushland Studio, with Rachel on guitar, banjo, harmonica, soprano saxophone and Rhodes, and Bill on slide and electric guitar, bass and percussion.

In her statement, Taylor-Beales recalls meeting Leven in 2008 when she opened for him at Cardiff Barfly; she was blown away by his songs and storytelling – the dry humour and the characters he evoked, wrapped up in a voice that could soar ethereally one moment and punch you in the guts with gravitas the next. After the gig they chatted about Kevin Coyne; Leven pointed her towards Karen Dalton and Judee Sill, and he was right. She left saying it was a crime that Jackie was not better known.

On 14 November 2011 she was working with the composer Gill Stevens when a blackbird crashed into the glass conservatory roof and died; at that moment she read on social media that Leven had gone – hence the blackbird in the song. In today’s uncertain times she is moved by how Leven seemed to revel in defiance, rebuilding his life against all odds and following the muse; she herself had to rebuild after a serious accident in 2012. The single is available on Bandcamp.
zitate_kontext: Rachel Taylor-Beales on seeing Leven in Cardiff in 2008.

2020-09-04-popklikk-en-musikalsk-helt.kurz: Long conversation from 2007 in the bar of the former Hotel Viking in Oslo, (re)published on Popklikk.
inhalt: Long conversation from 2007 in the bar of the former Hotel Viking in Oslo, (re)published on Popklikk. Occasion: the spring album *Oh What a Blow That Phantom Dealt Me!* (title after Cervantes), Doll by Doll reissues and many concerts in Norway. Leven says he deliberately works with blues ideas in order to become more direct, and keeps around 150 small red notebooks; what goes on an album is decided by intuition. Melancholy is a necessary part of life (he takes up the Greek term “pothos”), music a kind of therapy; Munch's “Scream” runs through as a comparison.

On songs: “Another Man's Rain” goes back to a train journey to Bergen on which he was overwhelmed by memories of youth at a glacier; the same day he saw a defeat of the Norwegian football team in Bergen and heard Bertine Zetlitz in Førde. “The Kings of Infinite Space” was inspired by Bacharach and 70s crime series (Rockford, Columbo), the title by Shakespeare, his hairdresser contributed lines. He praises Judee Sill's *Heartfood*, wrote a song for a Kevin Coyne tribute and says he discovered Böcklin's “Isle of the Dead” (cover of *The Mystery of Love*) in New York; because the painting had belonged to Hitler, the album sold unexpectedly well in Germany – a typical Leven punchline. On the voice he names Fontella Bass's “Rescue Me”; he does not see Doll by Doll as punk but alongside Dexys and The Pop Group; *Gypsy Blood* is the best album, and an album lost by Warner should be released with further material. Norwegian matters: a refused whisky in a pub in Kabelvåg, amazement at Norwegian drinking customs, favourite authors Rolf Jacobsen, Olav Hauge and Hamsun's *Sult*.
zitate_kontext: Leven on his way of working.

2021-03-09-wikipedia-ja-doll-by-doll.kurz: The Japanese Wikipedia article (9 March 2021) presents Doll by Doll as a London rock band founded by Jackie Leven in 1977, listing line-ups, albums and the 1988 Concrete Bulletproof Invisible single; it translates the English article of the time.
inhalt: The Japanese Wikipedia describes Doll by Doll as a London-based rock band formed by Jackie Leven (rendered in katakana) in 1977, which came to prominence in the New Wave period but was largely ignored by the music press of the time: their emotional, psychedelic-tinged music was judged out of step with other bands. Genres: rock, art rock, new wave; labels: Automatic and Magnet; active 1977 to 1983.

The original line-up was Leven (vocals, guitar), Jo Shaw (vocals, guitar), Robin Spreafico (vocals, bass) and David Macintosh (vocals, percussion). It recorded only one studio album, *Remember*, before Tony Waite (given as 1958-2003) replaced Spreafico; this line-up made *Gypsy Blood* (produced by John Sinclair) and the eponymous third album, *Doll by Doll*. By the final album, *Grand Passion*, only Leven remained from the original band, joined by Helen Turner (vocals, keyboards) and Tom Norden (vocals, guitar, bass) and guests including Pink Floyd's David Gilmour; Mark Fletcher (bass) and Chris Clarke (drums) played live.

The band fell apart in 1983. In 1988 Leven, Shaw and Macintosh, together with ex-Sex Pistol Glen Matlock, released the single "Big Tears" as Concrete Bulletproof Invisible, and Leven went on to become a prolific solo artist with more folk-oriented material. In 2005 a live recording by the original line-up appeared, *Revenge of Memory*: all but one song of *Remember*, recorded in 1977 at the Limit Club in Sheffield. All four studio albums came out on CD for the first time in March 2007 (WEA/Rhino). The discography lists *Remember* (1979, Automatic), *Gypsy Blood* (1979), *Doll by Doll* (1980, Magnet), *Grand Passion* (1982, Magnet) and *Revenge of Memory* (2005, Haunted Valley). The article inherits errors of its English source (founding year, Waite's dates, dating the live album to 1977). There is no Japanese article on Leven himself.

2021-05-jackieleven-co-uk-biography-grae.kurz: Essay by the Scottish music journalist Graeme Thomson, dated “Edinburgh, May 2021”, as the official biography of the revived website.
inhalt: Essay by the Scottish music journalist Graeme Thomson, dated “Edinburgh, May 2021”, as the official biography of the revived website. Thomson begins with his first meeting: Leven came back from Norway, shaken by the homeless people and addicts at Oslo bus station, and said he was “too connected to the pain of other people”. He characterises Leven's music as a journey between consolation and despair, and his themes (angry, damaged men, loneliness, violence, but also tenderness, humour, political anger). Life: born Alan Moffat on 18.06.1950, father a London Irishman, mother from north-east England, Kirkcaldy High School like Gordon Brown, feeling of being branded because of Romany background, left home at 16, *Control* in 1971 (he chose the pseudonym, by his own account, to evade the authorities), from 1975 in London, Doll by Doll with Joe Shaw and Dave MacIntosh in the squat in Maida Vale, thrown off a Hawkwind tour, Leven's later admission that he had been episodically “genuinely mentally ill” at the time; split in 1983, Virgin contract, assault in 1984 (colleagues looked for him and rescued him), two years with barely a voice, lost his falsetto, several years of heroin, CORE Trust; from 1994 over 30 albums including fan-club CDs and Sir Vincent Lone. Thomson describes the stage presence (Johnny Dowd: “Jackie was real”) and his own last concert experience at the Cabaret Voltaire in Edinburgh on 11.08.2011; Leven died three months and three days later of pancreatic cancer. Ending with Ian Rankin and the line from “Main Travelled Roads”.

2021-06-18-jackieleven-co-uk-new-website.kurz: In June 2021 the placeholder page jackieleven.co.uk announced further projects from Cooking Vinyl after the compilation Straight Outta Caledonia, including a tribute album of new music.
inhalt: In June 2021 the site www.jackieleven.co.uk carried the heading "New website coming soon...". The text says that following the announcement of *Straight Outta Caledonia*, the compilation collated by Night School Records on its archival label School Daze, Cooking Vinyl Records is teasing more upcoming projects that aim to introduce Leven's music to new generations. A tribute record with new, unheard music will be available to pre-order soon. Visitors are invited to sign up to the new "Jackie Leven Official mailing list" for more information; the page offers a sign-up form asking for email address, first name and last name.

2021-07-20-the-guardian-ian-rankin-jacki.kurz: On the occasion of the compilation *Straight Outta Caledonia*, Ian Rankin (as told to Robin Denselow) recounts his relationship with Leven.
inhalt: On the occasion of the compilation *Straight Outta Caledonia*, Ian Rankin (as told to Robin Denselow) recounts his relationship with Leven. He says he was a late discoverer: Doll by Doll passed him by, and only a review about a songwriter “from Fife” made him curious. While working on a Rebus novel he listened to *Shining Brother Shining Sister* and had Rebus listen to Leven in the next book. Leven read the mention on a plane over Scandinavia and got in touch via the publisher; Rankin then attended a midnight concert at the Edinburgh Fringe in a converted church and at first took the shuffling Leven for the roadie – until he heard the voice.

Rankin sums up Leven's life as a series of reinventions (folk troubadour, Doll by Doll, assault in Camden, heroin, founding an addiction-aid charity, solo career) and describes his themes: fragile masculinity, the ballad tradition, estrangement on tour, provocation (*The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ*). Leven was a “magpie” who played with African, Arab and jazz musicians, and a great Johnny Cash fan.

On the stage show: Leven proposed a joint reading with songs for Celtic Connections; Rankin proposed writing a story specially on Leven themes, to which Leven would respond with new songs – this is how *Jackie Leven Said* came about, performed and recorded several times; Leven wrote *The Haunting of John Rebus* specially for it. The rider anecdote: the first tour stop was the Southbank in London, and Leven ordered “one uncooked haggis for every venue” for Rankin. After Leven's death Rankin named *Standing in Another Man's Grave* after a misheard Leven title and *Saints of the Shadow Bible* after a Leven line. Further collaboration would certainly have come. Rankin laments the ignorance of the British media; in Norway Leven is revered.

2021-07-20-the-guardian-kommentare-ian-r.titel: [Reader comments on: I don't know why Jackie Leven isn't better known – he should be revered]
2021-07-20-the-guardian-kommentare-ian-r.kurz: Beneath Ian Rankin's piece (as told to Robin Denselow) are 151 reader comments from 20/21.07.2021 – the most extensive publicly readable thread of memories about Leven.
inhalt: Beneath Ian Rankin's piece (as told to Robin Denselow) are 151 reader comments from 20/21.07.2021 – the most extensive publicly readable thread of memories about Leven. It falls into three layers. First, Doll by Doll memories: one reader (“Kevin1957”) claims to have seen the band 58 times and says fans from the Midlands were allowed to stay overnight in the band's squat in Maida Vale; several readers describe the Hawkwind tour around 1979 at the Hammersmith Odeon, where Hawkwind fans shouted down the support band, threw objects and some stormed the stage until the curtain fell; according to others the band was later thrown off the tour (allegedly because of Hawkwind's beer, according to Kevin1957 after sabotage of sound and lights). Further traces: concerts at the Red Cow (Hammersmith), Taboo Club Scarborough (in front of about 20 listeners), Albany Empire Deptford, Dingwalls 1982, The Venue, a cancellation at Futurama 1981 in Stafford and a fight with a heckler in Chesterfield.

Second, memories of the solo artist: appearances at the 12 Bar Club (Leven threw chattering guests out himself; an evening of audience requests only), at The Bell in Bath (Leven is said to have called it “family”), at the Queen's Hall Edinburgh with David Thomas and Linda Thompson, in Sidmouth, Otley, Trowbridge 2010, Exeter, Tavistock, Hebden Bridge, Manchester shortly before his death and several times in Bergen. A former CORE Trust funding officer remembers weekly morning sessions in Leven's kitchen in Ladbroke Grove; a female musician thanks Leven for getting her into a major festival in Bergen. “mikeollier” relays Leven's claim that Princess Diana brought him back to singing – he insisted it was the plain truth. Third, debates about fame, Rebus and the free CDs from Uncut (2000/2001) and The Word.

2021-07-21-at-the-barrier-straight-outta.kurz: John Barlass welcomes the first “Greatest Hits” collection *Straight Outta Caledonia* (23 July 2021) as an overdue tribute to an overlooked talent and walks through its ten tracks from “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” to “Single Father”.
inhalt: In his review for At The Barrier, John Barlass presents the compilation *Straight Outta Caledonia* (released 23 July 2021 on CD and vinyl, including a limited clear-vinyl edition), the songwriter’s first-ever greatest-hits collection. Leven, he says, is one of those talents loved by those in the know and unjustly ignored by most people; the ten tracks are the perfect chance to catch up. He agrees with Ian Rankin, who calls Leven one of the most astonishing lyricists Scotland has produced and, in his later years, a true troubadour.

He praises Leven’s voice as one of the richest, most sonorous and most versatile around, and places the songs between traditional folk, eighties pop and white soul; fans of Warren Zevon, early Fairport Convention or Hall and Oates should enjoy it. On the biography, he writes that Leven began in the late 1960s making psychedelic, progressive music as John St. Field (according to the author; John St. Field in fact belongs to the early Seventies), formed Doll By Doll in 1977 with Jo Shaw, Robin Spreafico and David Mackintosh and recorded four albums with them. In 1984 a horrific assault left him unable to speak for two years, and he developed a heroin addiction in that period. His fortunes turned in 1988 with the single “Big Tears”, made with former Doll By Doll members and Glen Matlock; with his wife’s help he overcame the addiction and relaunched himself as a solo artist. By his death from cancer in 2011 he had released more than 25 solo albums and EPs, never achieving the mainstream success Barlass thinks was his due.

He then goes through the selection. The opener “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” retells its protagonist’s life not as that of a pure, sinless messiah but of a sexually frustrated, solitary human being, set to hard-edged percussion and synthesised orchestral effects. The eighties theme continues in the title track, a bright and poppy ode to his homeland, and in “Snow in Central Park”, which merges a traditional folk theme with Tomita-like synth flushes. Those who prefer their folk less adulterated get “Heartsick Land”, with mandolin, harp and acoustic guitar, recalling Fairport’s “Reynardine”, as well as “Dagenham Dream” and, best of all, the fingerpicked “Poortoun”, whose lyrics confront poverty, homelessness, street crime and drug abuse.

“Irresistible Romance” sounds like Hall and Oates with jangly guitars, until Leven name-checks favourite European cities (Vienna, Stockholm, Amsterdam, Oslo), brings the tour home to Dundee and the band bursts into “Scotland the Brave”. For lovers of ballads he recommends the Zevon-like “Live or Die”, the closing “Single Father” and the timeless “Some Ancient Misty Morning”. All of it is delivered in that tremendous voice, which Barlass describes with a long quotation from a profile: a multi-octave instrument that, though damaged in the savage assault, he used with flair, a baritone touched by his gentle Kirkcaldy accent. He could not put it better, he says.
zitate_kontext: Ian Rankin on Leven, quoted by John Barlass

2021-07-21-the-afterword-jackie-levens-g.kurz: The occasion is Ian Rankin's Guardian piece of 20 July 2021 on the compilation *Straight Outta Caledonia*.
inhalt: The occasion is Ian Rankin's Guardian piece of 20 July 2021 on the compilation *Straight Outta Caledonia*. The thread (about 35 posts, 21–27 July 2021) first clears up the confusion between the compilation (Leven recordings only, ten tracks, track list posted) and the tribute album *The Wanderer*, announced at the same time; SteveT reports that Michael Weston King had spoken on Facebook of three Leven releases. Several users praise the free CD given away by The Word magazine after Leven's death as their way in.

The question of Leven's best-selling record leads to reminiscences: Kaisfatdad tells (as a retelling of Leven's stage anecdote) of an uninterested US marketing woman in New York and of concerts in Sweden before tiny audiences; retropath2 heard “I Say A Little Prayer” in 1994 on Janice Long's show on Radio Glastonbury. Jaygee links Neil McCormick's Telegraph blog about Leven and Ralph McTell meeting Gordon Brown at 10 Downing Street. Baron Harkonnen describes his path from “Main Travelled Roads” on the radio, via Mike Scott's thanks on *Fisherman's Blues*, to chancing upon *The Mystery of Love* in Rhyl in 1994; SteveT reads Scott's thanks as encouragement in a crisis.

The most personal contribution is Artery's: a fan since about 1995, he says he saw Leven over a hundred times in 15 years and knew him well, though he found him somewhat reserved in conversation; Leven played two sets at his 50th birthday party in 2005 (rider: one bottle of Smirnoff Black Label, untouched), and he was at the funeral – a deeply spiritual experience. SteveT tells the Midlands Arts Centre anecdote: during the interval he requested “Wrapped Up In Blue”, and Leven announced the song crudely as an audience request; Artery and retropath2 were at the same concert (audience about twelve). Artery also remembers a woman in the audience demanding her money back over his language while Leven was supporting the Oyster Band.
zitate_kontext: Artery on the concerts he attended.

2021-07-23-god-is-in-the-tv-straight-out.kurz: Ed Jupp recommends the compilation *Straight Outta Caledonia* on God Is In The TV as an ideal introduction to a “cult artist”, praising Leven's balanced voice and tracks such as “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ”, “Irresistible Romance”, “Snow in Central Park” and “Poortoun”.
inhalt: The review of 23 July 2021 begins by pondering the term “cult artist”: is it a cliché applied so that those too cool for school can ringfence what they see as theirs, or music too difficult for a wider audience, or a label for things that should be more successful? Leven certainly has his admirers, including the writer Ian Rankin, who collaborated with him and made his troubled cop Rebus a fan, and musicians as different as Glen Matlock and James Yorkston. The compilation is an introduction to Leven, who died of cancer in 2011, with over thirty albums across a career of more than forty years: a whetter of the appetite for those who can nod and say “told ya”, even if they go on to criticise the tracklisting.

Jupp starts with the voice – “soulful without being too gruff or too slick”, rich without being overpowering, showing its Scottish roots without overdoing it – and with material worthy of it. The record opens with “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ”, an eighties-tinged track produced by Pere Ubu's David Thomas: Jesus is shown not as a pure and sinless messiah but as a sexually frustrated, solitary man condemned to an existential loneliness no one else will experience. “Irresistible Romance” is “like a celtic Hall & Oates”, with a nod to “Scotland the Brave”, and cleverly fades out before it gets twee; “Snow in Central Park” impresses with its cinematic brilliance without feeling overbaked. “Poortoun”, the only track wholly in a folk idiom, evokes a small Scottish town where a mother grieves for the narrator's brother who died from heroin, while the singer loses himself in drink – a measured reflection rather than a “woe is me” piece.

With ten tracks and forty-five minutes, the record recalls the days of putting together one side of a tape for your Walkman. Kudos goes to Michael Kasparis of Night School, who was so moved by the songs that he released the record to introduce new people to Leven's songbook. It is an ideal easing-in to a back catalogue that may seem as labyrinthine as The Fall's but, like a Leven song, brings the listener in without smothering them, and it should open this revered but under-appreciated artist to a wider audience. No mark is given.
zitate_kontext: Jupp on one of the tracks

2021-07-23-the-wee-review-straight-outta.kurz: Alistair Maxwell calls the compilation *Straight Outta Caledonia* (Night School Records, 2021) an intelligent introduction to “Scotland’s greatest hidden gem”: slim but cleverly chosen, showing Leven’s gift for singing about dark subjects without being dour.
inhalt: In The Wee Review, Alistair Maxwell takes on the compilation *Straight Outta Caledonia*, out in July 2021. He begins with Leven’s unusual gift: few artists could sing about heroin addiction, single fatherhood and “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” without being dour, but Leven does it with humanity, empathy and a genuine smile. Maxwell sketches the career: Leven started as a troubadour, founded the “Celtic inspired post-punk band” Doll by Doll and even made an album with Ian Rankin, who thought his lyrics so good that he borrowed some for the title of a Rebus novel, *Saints of the Shadow Bible*, without ever finding out what they meant. At one point, Maxwell says, Leven’s output was so great that he persuaded his label to let him use a pseudonym.

The selection is slim: ten songs, under fifty minutes. Fans will lament omissions (no “Call Mother a Lonely Field”), but no album shy of ten hours could offer more than a taste. Its job is to paint the broad shapes and invite listeners to seek out the minute brushstrokes themselves. Leven paints Scotland’s highs with the title song and its lows with “Heartsick Land”, and in between a myriad of stories and feelings thanks to his authorial style and ear for dialogue. His songs have roots in his native soil but flower abroad. “Poortoun” sits alongside Billy Joel’s “Allentown” and Springsteen’s “Youngstown”, an aching portrayal of a declining industry and its people; Leven is rarely compared to international singer-songwriters, but at his best he deserves a place among them.

Maxwell notes that Leven died in 2011, a few days before his next gig, and that his partner Deborah Greenwood afterwards found notebooks full of lyrics (a claim given without a source). His verdict: for the uninitiated an intelligent cross-section of work from Scotland’s greatest hidden gem; with luck the compilation will help the sensitive giant move from hidden gem to national treasure.
zitate_kontext: Maxwell on the compilation’s purpose and limits

2021-07-24-the-courier-jackie-leven-the-.kurz: Feature by the Scottish music journalist David Pollock on the compilation Straight Outta Caledonia.
inhalt: Feature by the Scottish music journalist David Pollock on the compilation Straight Outta Caledonia. Deborah Greenwood, Leven's partner for the last 15 years, describes how much his origins mattered to him: he always had himself announced as “Jackie Leven from the Kingdom of Fife” and opened concerts with a joke about the wind in Fife. Michael Kasparis (Night School Records, Apostille) says Molly Nilsson played him Leven on a car journey to Manchester; “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” was a revelation to him, the compilation is a personal selection from around 35 albums, and the title is a nod to NWA. A short biography follows (Control 1971, Doll by Doll, Gilmour recordings discovered later, Concrete Bulletproof Invisible with Glen Matlock). Greenwood relates that a school librarian led the boy, who was often banished to the library, to the Russian poets; his imagery (sky, reservoirs, hills) and characters such as “Jim o' Windygates” came from Fife. Kasparis compares Leven's devotion with soul (Otis Redding) and his kinship with Big Country, the Waterboys and Bert Jansch.

2021-07-27-cooking-vinyl-tribute-album-g.kurz: Cooking Vinyl announces the tribute album *The Wanderer* (22 newly recorded tracks, 17 September 2021) and the first “Greatest Hits” collection *Straight Outta Caledonia*, with press verdicts from MOJO, Uncut and Ian Rankin.
inhalt: Cooking Vinyl’s blog of 27 July 2021 combines two pieces of news. On 23 July *The Wanderer: A Tribute to Jackie Leven* was announced, a tribute record of 22 specially recorded new tracks reimagining Leven’s songs, featuring among others Eliza Carthy, Ralph McTell, Boo Hewerdine, Tom Robinson and Ian Rankin. It is due digitally and on CD on 17 September; the first single, “Sick Harbour Lament” by Ralph McTell and Graham Preskett, is already available.

The Friday before, *Straight Outta Caledonia*, the first commercially available Jackie Leven “Greatest Hits”, had been released. The compilation was collated by Night School Records and is out on CD and black vinyl on its archival label School Daze and digitally on Cooking Vinyl. Three press quotes are given: *MOJO* (four stars) calls the “thoughtful comp”, with a sleevenote nod from friend and fan Ian Rankin, a timely Leven awareness campaign showcasing his fearless lyrical acuity on “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” and the self-explanatory, bleakly beautiful “Single Father”. *Uncut* (9/10) praises a long-needed, career-spanning set by “one of Scotland’s finest songwriters”. And Ian Rankin tells *The Guardian* he does not know why Leven isn’t better known, he should be revered; he hopes the compilation makes a difference, a lovely introduction that just scratches the surface, after which people might explore the discography, where you could spend your whole life getting to know this guy.
The post closes by pointing to the mailing list and the official Facebook and Twitter pages, promising there is still more to come.
zitate_kontext: Ian Rankin in The Guardian, quoted in the blog

2021-08-03-jockrock-jackie-leven-straigh.kurz: The Scottish site jockrock announces the compilation *Straight Outta Caledonia* (Night School/School Daze, 23 July 2021) as Leven's first commercially available “Greatest Hits”, quoting Ian Rankin on one of the most astonishing lyricists Scotland has produced.
inhalt: The news item of 3 August 2021 (by the “News Team”) says that the “Scots musical legend” Jackie Leven has his career celebrated in the compilation *Straight Outta Caledonia*, described as his first commercially available “Greatest Hits” collection. It comes from Night School Records, run by Michael Kasparis, who records as Apostille and is part of the team at Monorail in Glasgow, via the archive offshoot School Daze, as stream, download, CD and limited vinyl edition. The album, subtitled *The Songs of Jackie Leven*, has ten tracks; it was released on 23 July 2021.

Highlighted is “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ”, produced by Pere Ubu's David Thomas and incorporating samples of unemployed workers in Glasgow after the closing of the Clyde shipyards. Leven's dedicated international fans, the text says, include the Sex Pistol Glen Matlock and the musicians James Yorkston and Molly Nilsson. Among his non-musical acolytes it names the novelist Ian Rankin, who said he is “one of the most astonishing lyricists Scotland has ever produced” and in his latter years a true troubadour, a balladeer of “sad, unsettling and uplifting songs, songs that blossom and bear fruit as you listen to them”.

The Kirkcaldy musician began making psychedelic, progressive music in the late Sixties and recorded more than thirty albums, including four with Doll by Doll and several under aliases such as John St Field and Sir Vincent Lone “to avoid record contract restrictions” (a claim of the item). He also played house shows, often spoken-word events, in Europe after or instead of official concerts. His multi-octave voice was damaged in a serious assault “in Fife” (the attack took place in London); he died in 2011 aged 61. The track list follows: “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ”, “Straight Outta Caledonia”, “Heartsick Land”, “Irresistible Romance”, “Live or Die”, “Some Ancient Misty Morning”, “Snow in Central Park”, “Poortoun”, “Dagenham Dream” and “Single Father”.
zitate_kontext: Ian Rankin on Leven, quoted in the item

2021-08-04-backseat-mafia-album-review-j.kurz: An enthusiastic review of the best-of *Straight Outta Caledonia…The Songs of Jackie Leven* on Night School: ten songs as an ideal introduction to a unique, under-appreciated artist whose strengths are narrative range and the vulnerability of his characters.
inhalt: Gannon reviews on Backseat Mafia (4 August 2021) the first commercially available “greatest hits” selection of Jackie Leven, compiled by Night School Records on its archival label School Daze. He recalls vividly hearing “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” for the first time in 2001: totally unprepared and “utterly mesmerised by the sheer audacity” of Leven’s artistic reach and the epic sweep of his lyrics and music. Some artists never achieve across a whole album the musical brilliance Leven achieved in that one song. It comes from *Creatures of Light and Darkness* (2001) and now opens the selection.

The reviewer describes the selection as “a brilliant primer” for a genuinely unique but massively under-appreciated artist. Genius often fails to get the attention it deserves in an artist’s lifetime; that was the case with Leven, who remained largely obscure even in his homeland despite his massive output of amazingly observed stories nested in epic, sad, unsettling and soaring tunes. Leven died in 2011, leaving behind over 30 albums under different guises or with his New Wave band Doll by Doll. He quotes Ian Rankin as authority: “one of the most astonishing lyricists Scotland has ever produced”.

On Leven’s style: his voice can traverse octaves and sometimes adds a staccato, percussive effect; he is often put into the folk-rock or Celtic-rock boxes, but his songs do not meet neat categorisation well. If there were a category called “epic tuneful visceral alienation” it might work. All his work is riven with vulnerability, openness and a reality of life; his characters have led lives full of joy, despair and loss and “really get you in the gut”. Singled out: “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ”, which recasts the protagonist as a sexually frustrated man rather than the pure messiah; “Straight Outta Caledonia”, like a poppier version of Dougie MacLean’s “Caledonia”, full of yearning and love for his homeland; and the almost hymnal, elegiac “Heartsick Land” with a distant choir, gentle mandolins and Leven’s super-smooth vocals.

In the closing paragraph Leven’s skill is said to be taking everyday stories of the brutality and joy of life and dreaming up characters who tell them; he turns every listener into an “imagineer”. The selection is a wonderful introduction for anyone who does not know him. Despite his ferocious creativity, Leven never got the attention his genius deserved; artists such as James Yorkston and Molly Nilsson now acknowledge his influence.
zitate_kontext: Gannon on the difficulty of categorising him

2021-08-13-fife-today-new-compilation-al.kurz: Allan Crow introduces the compilation *Straight Outta Caledonia* in Fife Today, the first “greatest hits” showcase for the Fife-born songwriter, with a short biography and a nod to *Jackie Leven Said* with Ian Rankin.
inhalt: Allan Crow reports in Fife Today (published 12 and updated 13 August 2021) on a new album celebrating the music of the Fife-born Jackie Leven, released just months before the 10th anniversary of his death. *Straight Outta Caledonia* is the first “greatest hits” showcase for a prolific songwriter who never achieved the recognition many believe he deserved. Leven died of cancer, aged just 61, in November 2011 and left behind an “astonishing” catalogue. The selection, collated by Night School Records, features just ten tracks from the hundreds he recorded and is hailed as the perfect introduction to Leven the wordsmith, troubadour, storyteller and songwriter, with his Fife roots woven deep into his lyrics.

The article sketches his career: the folk circuit of the 1960s, rising to prominence in the 1970s with Doll By Doll (four albums), a mugging in London in 1984 that badly crushed his larynx and left him unable to speak, then heroin, recovery and the founding of the Core Trust to help addicts with alternative medicine. His comeback, *The Mystery of Love Is Greater than the Mystery of Death*, was, the paper says, ranked by Q Magazine among the “best 100 albums of all time” (a claim it does not support).

With fellow Fifer Ian Rankin, Leven made the album and stage show *Jackie Leven Said*; Rankin used several song titles for his Rebus books, and Leven responded with “The Haunting of John Rebus”. Rankin spoke about his favourite Leven tracks last March at the Cash Back In Fife event in Aberdour. Leven's final album, *Wayside Shrines and the Code of the Travelling Man*, came out in September 2011, two months before his death; he was due to play the Green Hotel in Kinross, near home, on the Friday after. A Bandcamp link closes the piece.
zitate_kontext: Crow on the selection by Night School Records

2021-09-09-the-scotsman-album-reviews-th.kurz: Fiona Shepherd gives the tribute album *The Wanderer* four stars: a heartfelt, largely stripped-down homage casting new light on Leven's “undersung” catalogue, with Deborah Greenwood's “Universal Blue” the standout.
inhalt: Fiona Shepherd leads a round-up of album reviews in The Scotsman (9 September 2021) with *The Wanderer – A Tribute to Jackie Leven* (Cooking Vinyl), awarding four stars. Marking ten years since his passing, it is a heartfelt tribute to the cult Fife songwriter, curated and compiled by Michael Weston King, who called on Leven's contemporaries and next-generation folk artists to interpret songs from his “extensive, undersung catalogue”.

The contributions were recorded during the pandemic in largely stripped-down format. James Yorkston offers a bare-bones rendition of “Empty in Soho Square”, Kathryn Williams the delicate seduction of “The Crazy Song”, Boo Hewerdine the gentle yearning of “A Little Voice in Space”. Ralph McTell adds pavement café accordion to his soulful storytelling, while Eliza Carthy showers “The Garden” with lashings of tremolo. King himself applies Celtic soul to “The Final Reel” and his partner Lou Dalgleish lends a classy intimacy to “One Long Cold Morning”. The grittier corners of the catalogue are represented by The Membranes' pared-back but pugnacious cover of “More Than Human” by Leven's band Doll By Doll, and Tom Robinson, who brings some ragged glory and a serving of sardonic relish to “Classic Northern Divisions” (properly “Diversions”).

Leven's talent for the musical snapshot is showcased in “Edinburgh Winter Blues”, gracefully recited by Ian Rankin with soft accompaniment from Dean Owens, while Rab Noakes brings empathetic authority to the grim portrait of a post-industrial wasteland in “Poortoun”. All the voices are sensitive to the weight of the words, but none more so than Leven's partner Deborah Greenwood on a rich and soulful “Universal Blue”.

2021-09-10-uncut-straight-outta-caledoni.kurz: Jon Dale gives the compilation Straight Outta Caledonia 9/10 in Uncut and traces Leven's path: Night School boss Michael Kasparis came to him through Molly Nilsson, and Leven's voice is "liquid mercury trapped in jagged basalt".
inhalt: Jon Dale reviews *Straight Outta Caledonia... The Songs of Jackie Leven* for Uncut (online 10 September 2021), the compilation Glasgow's Night School released on its archival imprint School Daze; the standfirst calls it a "solo career-spanning set, long needed, by one of Scotland's finest songwriters". Rating: 9 out of 10. Revelations come from unexpected corners: for Michael Kasparis, who runs Night School, the keys to the kingdom were gifted to him by label artist Molly Nilsson. "I instantly knew I was listening to a miracle," Nilsson writes in the liner notes of her first encounter with Leven's music; the opening track, "The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ", is "the best song ever written". Hearing it for the first time was so profound for Kasparis that he almost crashed his car.

That is a familiar story, Dale says, and it makes sense: Leven always engendered strong responses, and his backstory is grimly compelling. He first found attention in the punk-adjacent Doll by Doll, survived a mid-'80s mugging that damaged his larynx but turned to heroin addiction, and after kicking his habit formed the Core Trust, an organisation that treated addicts. A short stint with ex-Sex Pistol Glen Matlock in Concrete Bulletproof Invisible followed, but the shackles really came off in 1994, when his solo career started properly with a string of quixotic, magical albums. After more than twenty albums, his seemingly endless fount of song ended when he succumbed to cancer in 2011. (Dale dates the mugging to the mid-1980s; elsewhere it is placed in the early 1980s.)

Yet it feels reductive, Dale writes, to use Leven's autobiography to explain the statuesque, deeply human songs he wrote. *Straight Outta Caledonia* introduces the multiple sides: the questing troubadour reeling out visions as infinite horizons in "The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ"; the intimate folk singer in near-direct lineage from figures such as Dick Gaughan in "Poortoun"; the deeply felt (inter)personal admissions of "Single Father" and "Heartsick Land"; the soul swagger of "Irresistible Romance". Kasparis: "Leven's songs always sound so full to me, fit to burst. Full of comedy, sadness, several lives lived in one, full of love... He never leaves anything out when he's writing or delivering the song."

Some might have trouble with the '90s tinges in the production; in lesser hands it would date the material and strand it in its era. In Leven's case, however, it gives the songs a spectrality, a peculiar, flickering radiance, that this burly, imposing character, "a voice like liquid mercury trapped in jagged basalt", can harness such intimacies from this base material. It is also a world-warping voice, as the litany of cities in "Irresistible Romance" tells us, yet Leven always returns, ever loving, to his Kingdom of Fife.
zitate_kontext: Dale on reading Leven through his biography
Michael Kasparis (Night School) on Leven's songs

2021-09-15-the-telegraph-strong-on-the-o.kurz: The major retrospective for the tenth anniversary of Leven's death, published in the week of the tribute album The Wanderer.
inhalt: The major retrospective for the tenth anniversary of Leven's death, published in the week of the tribute album The Wanderer. Graeme Thomson notes that Leven's death in 2011 went almost unnoticed but that his reputation has been rising since (the compilation Straight Outta Caledonia, a tribute album with Rankin, Kathryn Williams, Tom Robinson, James Yorkston, Eliza Carthy, Ralph McTell). Michael Weston King explains his initiative for the album. Kathryn Williams, who supported Leven in Aberdeen in 2000, stresses his love of experimentation. Biography: Alan Moffatt, father London-Irish, mother from north-east England, Kirkcaldy High School in Gordon Brown's time, left home married at 16, Control 1971, Doll by Doll at Automatic/Warner, thrown off a Hawkwind tour. Tom Robinson describes Leven at the Reading Festival in 1979, staring down the booing crowd and draining a can of beer. Mick Houghton tells how Nick Kent disappeared into a squat in Maida Vale for an NME cover story. After the split, a contract with Virgin, the 1984 attack after a night session, heroin, withdrawal in 1985, the Core Trust with Carol Wolf in Victorian cottages in Marylebone, now part of the Westminster Drug Project and recipient of half the proceeds of The Wanderer. Diana, as patron, urged Leven to sing at a charity lunch; he sang “The Bonnie Earl of Moray”. Over 30 albums from 1994. Rankin reads the songs as a dissection of Scottish machismo; anecdotes about raw haggis as Rankin's rider and kalimotxo as Leven's drink. Verdict: a decade on, Leven's music seems more urgent than ever.
zitate_kontext: Ian Rankin on Leven's male characters.

2021-09-17-bandcamp-the-wanderer-tribute.kurz: The Bandcamp page for *The Wanderer – A Tribute to Jackie Leven* (17 September 2021) lists 22 specially recorded reinterpretations of Leven’s songs by friends and admirers. Proceeds go to the Westminster Drug Project.
inhalt: *The Wanderer – A Tribute to Jackie Leven* was released on 17 September 2021 on the artist’s Bandcamp account. The page describes it as a 2CD digipak with a 16-page booklet. It holds 22 specially recorded new tracks “reimagining the brilliance of Jackie Leven”, played by “big names and big fans”, among them Eliza Carthy, Ralph McTell, Boo Hewerdine, Tom Robinson and Ian Rankin. Each artist has also contributed sleevenotes to the extensive booklet, describing their experiences of knowing and working with Leven and why they wanted to contribute. Proceeds benefit the Westminster Drug Project, a charity that continues the work of Leven’s own charity, the CORE Trust.

The track list: Andy White (with Stefan Hannigan), “Standing in Another Man’s Rain”; Ralph McTell and Graham Preskett, “Sick Harbour Lament”; Dog House Roses, “Elegy for Johnny Cash”; Eliza Carthy, “The Garden”; Jeb Loy Nichols, “The Working Man’s Love Song”; Johnny Dowd, “Farm Boy”; Boo Hewerdine, “A Little Voice in Space”; Tom Robinson, “Classic Northern Diversions”; Michael Weston King, “The Final Reel”; Rab Noakes, “Poortoun”; Henry Priestman, “Paris Blues”; Kathryn Williams, “The Crazy Song”; Arksong, “Honeymoon Hill”; Jinder, “Main Travelled Roads”; James Yorkston, “Empty in Soho Square”; Levi Henriksen and Babylon Badlands, “Just Like Jack”; Lou Dalgleish, “One Long Cold Morning”; Mike Cosgrave, “The View from Shit Creek”; Ian Rankin with Dean Owens, “Edinburgh Winter Blues”; Liam Carson with Knut Buen, “I Weep”; Deborah Greenwood, “Universal Blue”; The Membranes, “More Than Human”. The tracks can be streamed individually, the CD is offered for sale (£14), and individual tracks have their own pages.
zitate_kontext: Description of the album on the Bandcamp page

2021-09-20-cover-me-review-the-wanderer-.kurz: Detailed track-by-track review of the tribute album by a self-declared fan who saw Leven live several times.
inhalt: Detailed track-by-track review of the tribute album by a self-declared fan who saw Leven live several times. By way of introduction the author sketches Leven's biography (Doll by Doll, the attack, heroin, CORE Trust; half the proceeds to the Westminster Drug Project) and his output, which Martin Goldschmidt at Cooking Vinyl is said to have supported against commercial good sense; he assigns the alter ego Sir Vincent Lone to the Glitterhouse label and *Chip Pan Fire* to the pseudonym Jackie Balfour. He describes Leven's solo performances (guitar technique, microphoned foot-stomping, stories between the songs).

On the project: Michael Weston King, whose album *A Decent Man* (2003) Leven produced and whose live band he is said to have led, always praised Leven and played Leven tribute nights of his own. The two CDs are titled “Gentle Man” and “Hard Man”. The author praises Disc 1 almost throughout (Eliza Carthy's Brecht/Weill-like *The Garden*, Jeb Loy Nichols, James Yorkston, Lou Dalgleish, Ian Rankin's spoken *Edinburgh Winter Blues* with Dean Owens, which sounds eerily like Leven, Deborah Greenwood's *Universal Blue*). Disc 2 is said to be more uneven; highlights are Dog House Roses (*Elegy for Johnny Cash*), Johnny Dowd's *Farm Boy* and Michael Cosgrave's own composition *The View from Shit Creek*; he is less convinced by Tom Robinson, Rab Noakes, Levi Henriksen's *Just Like Jackie Leven* and Liam Carson's spoken *I Weep*. Verdict: largely very good, a little too long; the booklet contains reminiscences from almost everyone involved.

2021-09-30-the-afterword-seeing-double.kurz: In a forum thread about giveaway duplicate CDs, fans sum up what is happening around Leven in autumn 2021: the tribute album, a new website and YouTube channel, a reissue of his solo debut and two memorial shows.
inhalt: On the forum The Afterword, the user retropath2 offers duplicate Bandcamp albums for free on 30 September 2021, among them “the excellent Jackie Leven tribute” (that is, the album *The Wanderer*). This develops into a small exchange about what is currently going on around Leven.

The user Kaisfatdad quotes a post from the Facebook page: there is a brand new website, jackieleven.co.uk, and a new official YouTube channel with interviews, live performances and upcoming releases. Another poster (Bogart) writes that a lot is happening “and not before time”: Leven's debut solo album under his own name, *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* (ignoring *Control*, credited to John St Field), is being reissued on vinyl and CD, the CD including the EP *The Right To Remain Silent*. Two Jackie-related shows are also planned, in London on 11 November and in Glasgow on 9 December, with no venues or line-ups yet; Deborah Greenwood, Leven's widow, will perform.

He adds that a few bootleg videos are floating around, most not yet on YouTube, and that “Finest Hour” by Alan Moffatt, as Leven would later be known, from a 1971 folk compilation, is also doing the rounds. He mentions the original Facebook group “Burning The Box Of Beautiful Things” as a refuge for many members of the old Yahoo group, the “Levenites”. Another post sums up the mood: playing the tribute album reminds him that there has never been anyone quite like Jackie, and “I truly miss the Big Man.” The rest of the thread is the forum members swapping CDs.
zitate_kontext: Forum post on the news around Leven
Another fan in the same thread

2021-10-01-dag-og-tid-arkivet-jackie-lev.kurz: In the series “Arkivet” in Dag og Tid, the Bergen author Vågnes counts Leven’s solo shows in small clubs among the finest musical experiences of his life and presents him as a songwriter, guitarist and storyteller faithfully revered in Norway.
inhalt: This personal piece by the Bergen media scholar and author Vågnes appears in the music series “Arkivet” of the weekly Dag og Tid (1 October 2021). He counts Leven’s solo concerts with acoustic guitar in small clubs among the finest musical experiences of his life. He presents Leven (1950–2011) as a songwriter, outstanding guitarist and gifted storyteller who is widely unknown but faithfully revered in Norway, and quotes Ian Rankin’s piece in The Guardian from summer 2021.
Only the teaser of the text is freely accessible; the rest of the article is behind a paywall. The language is probably Nynorsk.
zitate_kontext: Ian Rankin (Guardian, summer 2021), quoted by Vågnes with reference to Norway

2021-10-06-the-afterword-atm-jackie-leve.kurz: “ATM” stands in the forum for a request for recommendations (“Ask The Members”): fitterstoke, who has just been given the tribute album, asks where a newcomer should start.
inhalt: “ATM” stands in the forum for a request for recommendations (“Ask The Members”): fitterstoke, who has just been given the tribute album, asks where a newcomer should start. Around 25 replies (6/7 October 2021) add up to a kind of collective fan discography. Mentioned are *Oh What A Blow That Phantom Dealt Me* (a way in via Ian Rankin), *Defending Ancient Springs* (for “Single Father” and the cover of “You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin'”), *Lovers at the Gun Club*, *Shining Brother Shining Sister*, *Fairytales for Hard Men*, *Night Lilies*, *Creatures of Light and Darkness*, *Forbidden Songs*, *Gothic Road* (with Ralph McTell), the four double CDs of the *Haunted Year* series as an entry to the Haunted Valley fan-club releases, and *Wayside Shrines* with Michael Cosgrave. retropath2 recommends the LP-length version of *Songs From the Argyll Cycle* and warns that Robert Bly's narrating voice on *The Mystery of Love* may put people off.

Bogart relays Leven's own story, expressly given with a caveat, that there was meant to be a video for “You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin'” in which Leven and David Thomas dance in women's clothes on the beach at Brighton; he points to *Chip Pan Fire* (as Jackie Balfour) with the stage speech “Sting Is Dead” and to the whisky “Leven's Lament – The Lonely Spirit of the Glen”. retropath2 explains that the first CD edition of *The Mystery of Love* was a double jewel case with an empty second tray, which he only filled with the “Mystery Supplement EP” (promo). Vulpes Vulpes came to Leven by buying Doll by Doll's *Grand Passion* from a bargain bin.
