2021-10-09-dagsavisen-jackie-leven-var-e.kurz: Geir Rakvaag in Dagsavisen (Nye Takter, 9 October 2021) on the tenth anniversary of Leven's death: gladness at hearing the songs of “one of the world's best cult heroes” again, prompted by *The Wanderer* and the compilation *Straight Outta Caledonia*.
inhalt: The music column “Nye Takter” in Dagsavisen appeared on the tenth anniversary of Leven's death and covers the tribute album *The Wanderer* and the first compilation, *Straight Outta Caledonia*. Only the standfirst and a photo caption are visible; the main text is for subscribers. The writer, Geir Rakvaag, says in the standfirst: “Det er godt å høre sangene til en av verdens beste kulthelter igjen” – it is good to hear the songs of one of the world's best cult heroes again. The photo shows Leven in 1998 on one of his many visits to Norway, where he won many friends with melancholy songs. The rating is unknown.

2021-10-09-dagsavisen-jackie-leven-var-e.titel: [Print version] Jackie Leven var en av verdens beste kulthelter
2021-10-09-dagsavisen-jackie-leven-var-e.kurz: Fully legible print version of the Plus article. Double-page spread with photos (Leven in Norway in 1998, Doll by Doll in 1981, the whisky “Leven's Lament” – with the note that it has been claimed these were his own labels on other people's bottles –, Levi Henriksen).
inhalt: Fully legible print version of the Plus article. Double-page spread with photos (Leven in Norway in 1998, Doll by Doll in 1981, the whisky “Leven's Lament” – with the note that it has been claimed these were his own labels on other people's bottles –, Levi Henriksen).

Rakvaag reviews the tribute album *The Wanderer – A Tribute to Jackie Leven* and the compilation *Straight Outta Caledonia* (both Cooking Vinyl) and recalls Leven's Norwegian connection: *Fairy Tales for Hardmen* reached number 40 on the VG chart in 1997, which a British magazine noted as a near-improbable event; the album ends with Rolf Jacobsen's “Sunflower” in Robert Bly's translation. Leven had already played in Norway in 1966 as guitarist for the blues singer Doris Henderson (his own statement to Dagsavisen: his first trip abroad as a professional musician), and later liked playing in small places on the periphery. Mentioned are “Rainy Day Bergen Women”, the live album *Men in Prison* from Bergen's county prison, and the discovery, on a flight from Bergen to Tromsø, that he appears in a Rankin novel as John Rebus's favourite artist; Leven said at the time that he and Rankin wrote about men who experience their inner lives as a mystery. The compilation shows him from the crooner side, at times like a Roy Orbison of our time.

The second focus is Levi Henriksen, who discovered Leven late through an Uncut interview with a CD, listened to nothing else for a month and sensed a kinship in background and view of humanity. His contribution to the tribute, “Just Like Jackie Leven”, is a translated version of his Babylon Badlands song “Jackie Leven sier det snart skal snø”, the first song he wrote for the band, about the healing power of music. Other tribute contributors: Ralph McTell, Kathryn Williams, James Yorkston, Tom Robinson.

2021-10-09-el-pais-jackie-leven-belleza-.kurz: Major Babelia article for the tenth anniversary of Leven's death, prompted by the compilation “Straight Outta Caledonia” and the tribute album “The Wanderer”.
inhalt: Major Babelia article for the tenth anniversary of Leven's death, prompted by the compilation “Straight Outta Caledonia” and the tribute album “The Wanderer”. It opens with Ian Rankin's farewell tweet of 2011; Leven, it says, was ignored by the public (apart from Scandinavian and German fans), not by the critics. Fernández Escobar describes the stylistic breadth (rock, British folk, Celtic soul, Americana, sixties pop) and opens with “The Sexual Loneliness Of Jesus Christ”, which contains the voices of laid-off shipyard workers.

Biographically the text largely follows Leven's own account of himself: he felt pushed to the margins by his mixed background (Irish and Roma blood) and led a nomadic life between Cornwall, Glasgow, Dublin, Berlin and Madrid; in Franco's Spain his debut “Control” appeared in 1973 on Movieplay (Madrid) as John St. Field, the pseudonym being due to a police matter. Doll by Doll came from the London squatting scene, four studio albums, “Gypsy Blood” as the high point; thrown off tours with Devo and Hawkwind, John Peel turned away; the last album effectively a Leven solo project with David Gilmour. Then a Virgin contract for a solo album, then the attack, loss of voice, heroin. After withdrawal, the founding of the CORE Trust; Leven says the visit of Princess Diana brought him back to music; the band attempt Concrete Bulletproof Invisible with Glen Matlock. On “The Wanderer”: contributions from Rankin (spoken word), Johnny Dowd, Michael Cosgrave, Ralph McTell, Eliza Carthy, James Yorkston and others; David Thomas and Ron Sexsmith are absent. Three song boxes: “Main Travelled Roads”, “The Sexual Loneliness Of Jesus Christ”, “Single Father”. Tone: a passionate rehabilitation.
zitate_kontext: Mishima quotation from “Main Travelled Roads”, giving the title.
Leven quotation about his life path (Spanish translation).

2021-10-19-blabber-n-smoke-the-wanderer-.kurz: Paul Kerr reviews the double tribute *The Wanderer*, curated by Michael Weston King for the tenth anniversary of Leven’s death: a labour of love with 22 tracks that mainly shows what a fine songwriter Leven was, but lacks Leven himself.
inhalt: The blog Blabber’n’Smoke calls *The Wanderer – A Tribute to Jackie Leven* “something of a labour of love”. For the tenth anniversary of his friend’s passing, Michael Weston King has compiled 22 songs: all Leven covers bar his own tribute *The Final Reel* and contributions by Levi Henriksen & Babylon Badlands and Liam Carson with Knut Buen. As with most tribute albums the takes vary in success, and what the album is really missing, Kerr says, is Leven himself, “such a unique and powerful character”. Ironically it is Weston King who gets closest to him, on *The Final Reel*, which captures some of Leven’s Celtic vagabond ways. The Scottish crime writer Ian Rankin, accompanied by Dean Owens, sounds most like Leven on the spoken-word *Edinburgh Winter Blues*, one of Kerr’s favourite moments.

The two discs are subtitled “Gentle Man” and “Hard Man”, reflecting the dual personality most people attribute to Leven, though apart from a couple of rowdier numbers on disc two there is little to tell them apart. Singled out on the first are Deborah Greenwood, Leven’s partner, with a touching *Universal Blue*, Boo Hewerdine’s plaintive *A Little Voice In Space*, Kathryn Williams’s ethereal, dreamlike *The Crazy Song*, Arksong (Marc Pilley) with *Honeymoon Hill*, James Yorkston with *Empty Square In Soho* (as the blog has it; the song is *Empty In Soho Square*) and Lou Dalgleish’s “majestic” solo-piano *One Long Cold Morning*.

The “Hard Man” disc opens with Andy White’s rocked-up *Standing In Another Man’s Rain*, wrestling with fuzzed guitar and bagpipe-like squirls, “like The Go-Betweens on amphetamine”. Tom Robinson tries something similar on *Classic Northern Diversions* with less success; Johnny Dowd’s unhinged, robotic Farfisa-fuelled romp through *Farm Boy* is the furthest from Leven and perhaps the one he would have liked best. The Membranes hark back to Doll by Doll days on *More Than Human*, Henry Priestman offers *Paris Blues* as a beatified busker, Eliza Carthy gives *The Garden* a Brechtian turn, Jeb Loy Nichols makes *The Working Man’s Love Song* laid-back and Caribbean, Rab Noakes turns *Poortoun* into a docudrama with acres of acoustic guitar, and the Scottish Dogtown Roses play *Elegy For Johnny Cash* banjo-driven, Appalachian and gothic.

In conclusion, Weston King has honoured Leven’s memory well; the album works as an enjoyable listen in its own right and, Kerr hopes, may send people to Leven’s own albums, with the best-of *Straight Outta Caledonia* and the reissue of *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death* due in November as occasions. Proceeds go to the Westminster Drug Project, which continues the work of Leven’s own charity, the CORE Trust.

Kerr on the album’s two-disc structure

2021-10-jackieleven-co-uk-news-twitter-f.kurz: The news page of the new official website mirrors tweets from autumn 2021 on the tribute record *The Wanderer*, the reissue of *The Mystery of Love* for the tenth anniversary of his death, and a new YouTube channel.
inhalt: In October 2021 the news page of the relaunched official site jackieleven.co.uk is nothing but the Twitter feed of @LevenJackie, with retweets added. It documents the revival of Leven’s work around the tenth anniversary of his death.

At its centre is *The Wanderer – A Tribute to Jackie Leven*, released on 17 September 2021 digitally and on CD (with a 16-page booklet) on Cooking Vinyl: 22 specially recorded tracks “performed by many big names and fans”, including Eliza Carthy, Ralph McTell, Boo Hewerdine, Tom Robinson, Michael Weston King, Rab Noakes and Ian Rankin (@Beathhigh). Participants’ thanks and promotion are retweeted: Michael Weston King thanks Ralph McLean for featuring the album on his BBC Radio Ulster show, and Graeme Thomson points to his Telegraph article on the life and death of the genius Jackie Leven, with contributions from several of the performers.

Other items: on 22 September the record shop Monorail Music announces that Cooking Vinyl is repressing Leven’s “mercurial debut” *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death* for the tenth anniversary of his passing, on marble 2LP and 2CD; on 15 October an edit of ‘Call Mother a Lonely Field’ is released, with pre-orders for the collector’s edition. On 29 September a new official YouTube channel with interviews and live performances is announced alongside the new website. The feed contains no texts of its own, only links and promotion, but it is a period document of the commemorative year.

Its description calls it a remembrance ten years after the death of Jackie Leven on 14 November 2011 and a tribute to the course of the Scottish musician, from the 70s to the 00s. The tracks played and the wording of the presentation cannot be gleaned from the description; the recording was not listened to.

2021-fatea-straight-outta-caledonia.kurz: Mike Davies presents *Straight Outta Caledonia* for FATEA as a long-overdue introduction to Leven’s work, goes through the ten tracks, and concludes that it is about time the world realised Leven was a giant.
inhalt: Mike Davies reviews the best-of *Straight Outta Caledonia: The Songs of Jackie Leven* (School Daze, ten tracks) for FATEA Magazine. When Leven died of cancer in 2011 he left behind 26 commercially available albums (including three as Sir Vincent Lone and his 1973 debut as John St. Field) along with four as leader of Doll By Doll, of which “Main Travelled Roads” remains Davies’s personal favourite. Born in Kirkcaldy, Fife, as Alan Moffatt, he never enjoyed chart success but commanded immense critical respect and a steadfast loyal following.

Davies finds it surprising that a retrospective took ten years to appear, and that it comes from a small independent offshoot rather than Cooking Vinyl, the label he had been signed to since his 1994 solo debut, after he lost his voice for two years following an attempted strangulation in 1984, which led to a heroin addiction. The title cheekily echoes N.W.A’s *Straight Outta Compton*. Given the vast amount of material, a single disc cannot do full justice to his Celtic folk-blues songwriting, the often metaphysical, empathetic lyrics veined with tragedy and comedy (“fairytales for hard men”, as he described them), or the warm malt-whisky intimacy of his baritone, but as an introduction it does a sterling job.

Davies goes through the selection. The opener, “The Sexual Loneliness Of Jesus Christ” (from the David Thomas-produced *Creatures of Light & Darkness*, 2001), retells over six minutes, beginning with church organ and spoken-word samples of unemployed Glasgow shipyard workers, the biblical story as that of a sexually frustrated, solitary man. The tumblingly melodic title song follows, from the Sir Vincent Lone album *Songs For Lonely Americans* (2006), then “Heartsick Land” and the cinematic “Snow In Central Park” from *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death* (1994), which features Mike Scott and Anthony Thistlethwaite of The Waterboys. “Irresistible Romance” from *Shining Brother Shining Sister* (2003) underlines why Leven was often regarded as Scotland’s answer to Van Morrison; “Live Or Die” hints at the Righteous Brothers, whose “You’ve Lost That Loving Feeling” he covered on *Defending Ancient Springs*. “Some Ancient Misty Morning” has a Velvets feel, “Poortoun” is an acoustic reflection on childhood memories of Fife, “Single Father” an uptempo meditation on loss and loneliness, and the 113-second “Dagenham Dream” from his final album, with Michael Cosgrave, closes the set. Davies mixes up some albums and dates (for instance he dates *Night Lilies* to 1996 and gives the last album as *Wayside Shrines and the Dreams of the Travelling Man*).

Countless other songs could be argued for – “Call Mother A Lonely Field”, “Men in Prison”, “John Paul Getty’s Silver Cadillac” – but until the definitive box set comes along, this will do very nicely. A posthumous compilation had already appeared in 2012 as a magazine cover-mount, *Heroes Can Be Any Size*. It is about time the wider world realised that Leven was a giant.

Davies on the value of the collection

2021-michael-weston-king-the-wanderer-st.kurz: The sales page for the tribute album *The Wanderer* (2021): 22 new recordings by Eliza Carthy, Ralph McTell, Boo Hewerdine, Tom Robinson, Ian Rankin and others, with proceeds going to the Westminster Drug Project.
inhalt: Musician Michael Weston King's website offers *The Wanderer: A Tribute To Jackie Leven*, a double album marking the tenth anniversary of Leven's death in November 2021. The introduction calls Leven one of the world's “most prolific and accomplished singer songwriters”, whose recordings ran from folk to Celtic soul, driving rock to lyrical ballads, and says the legend of this uniquely talented artist grows every year as more people discover his catalogue.

The album features 22 specially recorded tracks reimagining Leven's work, by “big names and big fans” including Eliza Carthy, Ralph McTell, Boo Hewerdine, Tom Robinson and Ian Rankin. Each artist has also contributed sleeve notes to an extensive booklet describing their experiences of knowing and working with Jackie and why they wanted to take part; each will promote the release through their own channels. Proceeds go to the Westminster Drug Project (WDP), a charity that continues the work of Leven's own charity, the CORE Trust.

Disc 1 lists, among others, “Sick Harbour Lament” (Ralph McTell & Graham Preskett), “The Garden” (Eliza Carthy with David DeLarre), “A Little Voice In Space” (Boo Hewerdine), “The Final Reel” (Michael Weston King), “Edinburgh Winter Blues” (Ian Rankin with Dean Owens) and “Universal Blue” (Deborah Greenwood). Disc 2 has “Standing In Another Man's Rain” (Andy White feat. Stefan Hannigan), “Farm Boy” (Johnny Dowd), “Classic Northern Diversions” (Tom Robinson), “Just Like Jackie Leven” (Levi Henriksen & Babylon Badlands), “I Weep” (Liam Carson with Knut Buen) and “More Than Human” (The Membranes).

2021-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.titel: [Collected finds Nasjonalbiblioteket 2021: short notices, announcements, lists]
2021-nasjonalbiblioteket-jackie-leven-sa.kurz: In October 2021 Norwegian newspapers mention Jackie Leven repeatedly: the tribute album *The Wanderer*, the compilation *Straight Outta Caledonia*, Geir Rakvaag’s double-page piece in Dagsavisen and an NRK radio programme for the tenth anniversary of his death.
inhalt: Twenty-four issues of Norwegian newspapers name Jackie Leven in 2021, almost all in October, around the tenth anniversary of his death, the tribute album *The Wanderer* and the compilation *Straight Outta Caledonia* (Cooking Vinyl). The highlight is Geir Rakvaag’s double-page piece in Dagsavisen of 9 October 2021, which also ran in Demokraten, Moss Dagblad and Rogalands Avis.

The other October hits are mostly radio listings: on Saturday 23 October 2021 NRK P2 broadcast a tribute to Jackie Leven – a ‘Jackie Leven-hyllest’ – in its magazine ‘Musikklivet’ (14.03, repeated at 00.05 and on 30 October at 07.03), alongside items on ‘Stjernekamp’ and the Rostrum competition. The programme pages appear in Aftenposten, VG, Bergens Tidende, Adresseavisen, Stavanger Aftenblad, Fædrelandsvennen, Harstad Tidende and Innherred. Dag og Tid ran an archive column on Leven on 1 October (five mentions).

There were no concerts in 2021. The radio item itself is not available here. The finds show that Leven’s name in Norway a decade after his death was still enough to move newspapers and broadcasters to pay tribute.

2022-01-29-glasgow-life-leventime-tribut.kurz: Glasgow Life announced “Leventime: A Tribute to Jackie Leven” for 29 January 2022 at Òran Mór, led by Deborah Greenwood and Ian Rankin; it was cancelled because of Omicron.
inhalt: The event page describes the tribute evening “Leventime” on Saturday 29 January 2022 at 7.30 pm at Òran Mór in Glasgow (over-14s only, £19.80 including booking fee). Ten years after his death, Leven’s partner Deborah Greenwood and friend and colleague Ian Rankin were to lead friends and admirers through a selection from his extensive song catalogue. Named are Boo Hewerdine, Rab Noakes, Jinder, Michael Weston King, Malcolm Lindsay, Doghouse Roses and Dumb Instrument.

Leven is described as “the cult artist’s cult artist” and “Scotland’s answer to Bob Dylan”, whose work is now starting to gain wider recognition with three albums released in the last year alone. The promised ingredients were laughter, a few tears, some tall tales and great, great music. A notice at the top of the page announces the cancellation: the show was called off because of the ongoing impacts of the Omicron variant, with the box office to be in touch with ticket buyers.

2022-02-11-jackie-leven-official-rankin-.kurz: The official channel publishes a video of just over two minutes in which Ian Rankin reads Leven’s lyrics to “Classic Northern Diversions”, recorded in 2020 for Leven’s 70th birthday; the description points to Tom Robinson’s version on the tribute album.
inhalt: The video on the YouTube channel “Jackie Leven Official” (running time 2:13, published 11 February 2022) shows a reading by the writer Ian Rankin: he reads the lyrics of “Classic Northern Diversions” from Leven’s album *Shining Brother Shining Sister* (2003). According to the description, Rankin recorded the reading in 2020 to celebrate what would have been Leven’s 70th birthday.

The description quotes Rankin: “Jackie was an amazing lyricist and not every great lyricist work works when you take the music away, but Jackie’s words work as poetry.” It also notes that Tom Robinson’s version of “Classic Northern Diversions” features on *The Wanderer – A Tribute to Jackie Leven*, with a link to the album, and points to the official social media pages and website. The content of the video itself is not reproduced here.

2022-03-25-americana-uk-interview-michae.kurz: Weston King explains how “The Struggle”, his first solo album in ten years, came about.
inhalt: Weston King explains how “The Struggle”, his first solo album in ten years, came about. For Leven research the conversation about “Theory of Truthmakers” is the most productive. King says their mutual friend Alan Black had kept an unpublished handwritten lyric by Leven. Leven had written it during a train journey they made together and left it with Black. When King approached the artist about the cover of the tribute record “The Wanderer”, he learned of this text.

King wanted to set it to music and release it on the memorial record but did not finish in time. So he recorded the piece for “The Struggle”. By his account the handwriting is reproduced in the booklet. The string-like sounds were contributed by Michael Cosgrave; King had expressly asked him for a sound reminiscent of Leven's records. For the brightening in the chorus King also had Scott Walker in mind.

The rest of the interview deals with King's orientation towards songwriters of the late sixties and early seventies and the recordings with Clovis Phillips in Wales. The story of the Leven lyric is King's recollection; the manuscript itself was not examined here.

2022-04-12-americana-uk-michael-weston-k.kurz: Tim Martin gives Michael Weston King’s album *The Struggle* 8/10; “Theory Of Truthmakers”, built on an unused Jackie Leven lyric, strikes him as a conscious evocation of Leven’s spirit.
inhalt: This Americana UK review is not about Leven but about *The Struggle* (Cherry Red, 2022) by Michael Weston King, otherwise one half of the duo My Darling Clementine. Reviewer Tim Martin sees a pronounced singer-songwriter album that showcases sides of King we do not see in his day job. He names John Prine among the touchpoints for the songwriting; “Sugar” was written with Peter Case.

The Leven connection: “Theory Of Truthmakers” uses unused lyrics from King’s “late collaborator Jackie Leven”. The song, Martin says, stands slightly apart in feel from the rest of the record – “almost as if King was consciously evoking the spirit of Jackie Leven”. Lou Dalgleish, King’s My Darling Clementine partner, shares the chorus and lifts the song’s rather despondent atmosphere.

Overall Martin praises the range: a folk song of the English North East with whistle and mandolin, a forties-style number, 1970s touches, the opener “Weight of the World” that returns at the close as a “Ghostwriter remix”, plus guests such as Steve Nieve, Jeb Loy Nichols and King’s daughter. King’s “rich velvety voice” links it all. He is one of those artists who fly just under the notice of the wider album-buying public who would love him. Rating: 8/10.

Martin on the origin of the lyric

2022-05-09-gubberock-michael-weston-king.kurz: The blog Gubberock gives Michael Weston King's *The Struggle* 8.5 out of 10 and points to two Leven links: “The Final Reel” recalls Leven, and “Theory Of Truthmaker” sets Leven's handwritten lines to music.
inhalt: The Norwegian blogger behind Gubberock reviews *The Struggle*, Michael Weston King's first solo album in ten years, which he says has been there for him over recent weeks “when I have not been ready for other music”. It was recorded in rural Wales with the multi-instrumentalist Clovis Phillips; guests include Steve Nieve, Jeb Loy Nichols, the trombonist Barnaby Dickinson, Lou Dalgleish and daughter Mabel on flute. He hears a singer-songwriter and folk album in the vein of Mickey Newbury, Jesse Winchester and John Prine, with great lyrics, songs and production; highlights are “The Hardest Thing” and “Just Another Dying Day”, about depression.

The Leven connections: “The Final Reel” has flutes and points towards Ireland, while its lyrics make the writer think of the late Scottish artist Jackie Leven. Leven is also the man behind the lyrics of “Theory Of Truthmaker”: Weston King has set a melody to handwritten lyrics by Leven which he recently received from a mutual friend, and the song can also be heard on the album released the year before on which many artists make their versions of Leven's songs. Overall verdict: a brilliant collection, food for the soul in a volatile world, 8.5/10.
zitate_kontext: The blogger on the Leven contribution to the album

2022-05-18-say-it-with-garage-flowers-mi.autor: Say It With Garage Flowers (blog; interviewer not named)
2022-05-18-say-it-with-garage-flowers-mi.kurz: Telephone interview with Michael Weston King about his first solo album in ten years, *The Struggle* (2022, recorded in Newtown, Wales, mixed with Colin Elliot in Sheffield).
inhalt: Telephone interview with Michael Weston King about his first solo album in ten years, *The Struggle* (2022, recorded in Newtown, Wales, mixed with Colin Elliot in Sheffield). Two songs concern Jackie Leven directly.

*The Final Reel* was written about Leven, in the style of a “Celtic soul singer” who was strongly influenced by Van Morrison. Weston King tells how it came about: in the week before Leven's death he was on his way to a concert in Perth, drove past Loch Leven, stopped, walked along the shore and phoned Leven, who by then was in hospital and was not to leave it. They chatted and laughed; it was their last conversation. The song draws on that scene and their years together as wandering singers – they played “hundreds” of concerts together. (The song had previously also appeared on the tribute album *The Wanderer*, 2021.)

*Theory of Truthmakers* is based on unpublished Leven lines: Leven wrote them on a journey they made together and gave them to the Glasgow painter Allan Black, whose picture he had also used for an album. Black kept them as a souvenir and sent them to Weston King, who set them to music. The song was originally meant for the tribute album he curated but was not finished in time. Musically, for the chorus he aimed at something “big” like *Heroes* or a Scott Walker song.

2022-05-27-x-twitter-ian-rankin-bench-so.kurz: On 27 May 2022 Ian Rankin shares a photograph of a memorial bench for Jackie Leven in London’s Soho Square and calls it “Poignant”.
inhalt: The crime writer Ian Rankin, a friend of Leven’s and partner on their joint album *Jackie Leven Said*, posts a photograph on X (formerly Twitter) on 27 May 2022. He writes: “Just been sent this by James McAon. Bench in Soho Square dedicated to Jackie Leven. Poignant.” The bench in Soho Square, a small park in London’s West End, is dedicated to Leven; the photograph was sent to Rankin by an acquaintance whose name is spelled ‘McAon’ in the tweet (probably a typo).

The tweet is brief but revealing: it shows that more than ten years after his death Leven’s memory had been tied to a visible place in London. The wording makes clear that Rankin was sent the photo rather than visiting the bench himself. Leven’s song ‘Empty in Soho Square’ carries the name of the place in its title.

2022-06-02-the-afterword-jackie-levens-7.kurz: Moonidus invites people to an informal gathering at Leven's bench in Soho Square (south side of the gardens) for his 72nd birthday (Saturday, 18 June 2022), at midday, possibly followed by the Nellie Dean pub in Dean Street.
inhalt: Moonidus invites people to an informal gathering at Leven's bench in Soho Square (south side of the gardens) for his 72nd birthday (Saturday, 18 June 2022), at midday, possibly followed by the Nellie Dean pub in Dean Street. The replies (2–6 June 2022) are mostly apologies because of distance, combined with toasts and reminiscences. Gatz relates that in the Facebook group “London Urbanist Oddities” a cousin of Leven's responded to a photo of the bench; he had not known about it. Razor Boy and others only came to Leven through the free CD from The Word magazine. SteveT again mentions his ticket for a Birmingham concert that was cancelled shortly before Leven's death.

The most productive strand concerns the second bench, on Paxos: Bogart was on Corfu in 2022 and wanted to visit the bench and the taverna that Leven is said to have frequented there; Moonidus had read that the bench had been damaged. Bogart then relays a notice (translated from Greek) from the Paxos municipality: the bench designed by Sam Khaleq and paid for by Deborah Greenwood, at the entrance to the Old Customs House in Loggos, suddenly disappeared in early November 2021; a fisherman from Gaios found the backrest on the shore; the residents wanted to restore it at their own expense. Chrisf finally quotes from an Ian Rankin interview in The Times (4 June 2022) in which Rankin calls Leven underrated and points to *Straight Outta Caledonia*.

2022-06-23-paxos-festival-the-songs-of-j.kurz: Announcement of an evening of Leven songs on 23 June 2022 at the Old School House Yard in Loggos, Paxos, performed by Jinder, Michael Weston King and Deborah Greenwood; the text presents Leven as a great lover of the island and a songwriter.
inhalt: The Paxos Festival announces “The Songs of Jackie Leven” for 23 June 2022 at 8 pm in the Old School House Yard, Loggos, Paxos. Performers are to be Jinder, Michael Weston King and Deborah Greenwood, plus special Paxos guests. Leven, who died in 2011, is introduced as “one of Scotland’s finest songwriters” (Uncut) and “the Scottish Bob Dylan” (Ian Rankin). He was a great lover of Paxos, wrote many songs and poems there, and played a concert at the Old School House that will never be forgotten by anyone who saw it.

Jinder and Weston King, both highly regarded songwriters with many albums to their names, worked with Leven regularly and have performed his songs many times since he died, most recently on the new tribute album *The Wanderer*, alongside Ralph McTell, Tom Robinson, Eliza Carthy and Ian Rankin. Deborah Greenwood is described as Leven’s partner in life and music and the female voice on most of his twenty or so albums. The three have played the songs at festivals in the UK and will be joined by Paxos musicians who knew and loved him; the evening promises music, laughter and perhaps the odd tear or two.

The background text claims that Leven’s work has gained acclaim and followers since his death. *The Mystery of Love is Greater than the Mystery of Death* is said to have been chosen by *Q* as one of the top 100 albums of all time, he has been the subject of features in the Telegraph, Times, Guardian and Scotsman, among others, and a retrospective in July’s *Mojo* (out in June) is due. Leven was a prolific writer of lyrics, music and poetry, an inventive and dazzling guitarist, with a voice that blended a great single malt with the sweetest honey. The most recent releases named are the best-of *Straight Outta Caledonia* and the tribute album *The Wanderer*.
zitate_kontext: Announcement text on Leven’s ties to Paxos

2022-06-29-americana-uk-video-michael-we.kurz: Americana UK presents the video for Michael Weston King’s ‘The Final Reel’, a tribute to his “much missed dear old pal” Jackie Leven, illustrated with photographs of Leven over the years.
inhalt: The Americana UK piece of 29 June 2022 introduces Michael Weston King’s album *The Struggle*, his first solo release in ten years. It praises the songcraft and the inspiration drawn from the soulful country sounds of the 1960s and 1970s; his voice is described as rich and sonorous, pulling listeners into the stories with lovely melodies and warm harmonies. After ten years and five albums with his wife, Lou Dalgleish, as My Darling Clementine, King looked to storytellers and songwriters such as John Prine.

From the album the piece singles out ‘The Final Reel’, a song that “delivers real emotional impact”. King says it is a musical homage to his much missed dear old pal Jackie Leven. The depth of their connection, the writer says, is clear from the heart-breaking video, which presents a series of photographs of Leven over the years.

The piece ends with listings: King plays the new album at the Kitchen Garden Café in Birmingham that evening, 29 June, followed in July by shows with Lou Dalgleish and Steve Nieve in Liverpool (9 July) and Edinburgh (10 July), playing songs from *Country Darkness*. For readers of Leven the item shows how alive his memory remained in King’s circle eleven years after his death.
zitate_kontext: Michael Weston King on ‘The Final Reel’

2022-08-01-noejesguiden-manadens-baesta-.kurz: A short paragraph in Nöjesguiden’s monthly round-up on the vinyl reissue of *The Mystery Of Love*: Forshage calls Leven Scotland’s sharpest singer-songwriter and compares him with Warren Zevon; missing him was largely his own fault.
inhalt: In his column “Månadens bästa musik, enligt en föredetting” (July 2022), Forshage devotes a paragraph to the vinyl reissue of *The Mystery Of Love (Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death)* (Cooking Vinyl/Playground). The chances that you missed “Scotland’s sharpest singer-songwriter” while he was alive are high, he writes, and frankly that is largely his own fault.

After some success with his old punk band Doll by Doll he sank into the heroin mire, and when he came back – “with a vengeance” – he went on tripping himself up. The pent-up need meant the records came out too fast for anyone to keep up (Forshage mentions five double albums in 2009 alone) and often hid behind pseudonyms such as Sir Vincent Lone. As a result too few noticed that he had grown into a master of sharp, clever literary rock songs, “comparable only with Warren Zevon”. A good ten years after Leven’s death his solo debut is now re-released on vinyl, so there is another chance to discover him: “Take that chance.” There is no numerical rating.

2022-10-mojo-jackie-leven-the-truth-is.kurz: Aizlewood's retrospective accompanies the reissue of “The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death”.
inhalt: Aizlewood's retrospective accompanies the reissue of “The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death”. The freely readable opening presents Leven as a well-read songwriter and impressive stage presence whose stories shaped his songs as much as his voice and guitar playing. Aizlewood visits Deborah Greenwood and describes the literary surroundings of Leven's work; Rilke is expressly named.

Greenwood comments on several of Leven's self-presentations. The well-known train encounter with Bob Dylan and the false news of Sting's death appear in the context of his invented stories. The legends on records and in side projects are also put into perspective: “Leven’s Lament” was ordinary Bell’s whisky with his own label. “Elegy for Johnny Cash” was recorded in Wales, contrary to the information on the sleeve; according to Greenwood, the involvement of Lebanese musicians explains the Beirut reference. Henry Priestman did in fact play on “Defending Ancient Springs”, but other corresponding album credits are inaccurate.

The opening section thus already offers concrete starting points for checking Leven's stories. These are statements by Greenwood in conversation with Aizlewood, not production records independently verified here. The later questioning of further companions in the full article remains unread.

2023-01-16-americana-uk-celtic-connectio.kurz: Americana UK's preview of the 30th Celtic Connections in Glasgow lists “Leventime: A tribute to Jackie Leven”, with Michael Weston King, Boo Hewerdine, Doghouse Roses, Dumb Instrument and Ian Rankin, among the most anticipated events.
inhalt: Paul Kerr reports on 16 January 2023 on the start of the 30th Celtic Connections festival in Glasgow, opening on Thursday 19 January for three weeks. It is the first full-scale edition since pandemic restrictions ended: in 2021 the festival moved online, and the year before further restrictions had stopped several shows. This time some 1200 musicians are to play more than 300 events at over 25 venues, from traditional folk through roots, Americana, jazz and soul to world music. Festival producer Donald Shaw calls the edition a testament to the strength of the Scottish music industry after an extremely tough period.

In the section on Americana acts (Lucinda Williams, Bonny Light Horsemen, Aoife O'Donovan, Nickel Creek and others, plus Dean Owens and the Transatlantic Sessions) the piece says that “highly anticipated” is *Leventime: A tribute to Jackie Leven*, featuring Michael Weston King, Boo Hewerdine, Doghouse Roses and Dumb Instrument, and the crime writer Ian Rankin. The text is an announcement and says nothing about the evening itself; it ends by recalling the recently deceased Rab Noakes.
zitate_kontext: Paul Kerr in the festival preview

2023-01-17-the-sunday-post-he-just-soake.kurz: Jamieson traces Leven's life from a conversation with Deborah Greenwood and links her retrospective with the announcement of the memorial evening “Leventime”.
inhalt: Jamieson traces Leven's life from a conversation with Deborah Greenwood and links her retrospective with the announcement of the memorial evening “Leventime”. The starting point is Greenwood's view that recognition of Leven could still grow after his death. She estimates his output at more than 300 songs and reports on the plan to compile song lyrics into a volume of poems. The article documents a plan in January 2023, not a publication that had already appeared.

Greenwood recalls her first personal meeting with Leven at London's 12 Bar Club in the mid-1990s. Before that she had sent him a fan letter. She describes a well-read, nature-loving person of very varied temperaments; the text sets admiration and difficult sides side by side. The details are her recollections, not an independently established chronology.

A separate section contains Stuart Maconie's appreciation of Leven's voice and his portrayal of male vulnerability. The announced tribute evening is to take place on 4 February 2023 at Òran Mór, with Ian Rankin, Boo Hewerdine, Jinder, Malcolm Lindsay and Greenwood, among others. The report also explains that the event was postponed from the previous year, when it was cancelled because of the pandemic.

2023-03-13-cd-junkie-215-doll-by-doll.kurz: In the video “CD Junkie #215”, Stephen Schnee surveys Doll by Doll's four studio albums (1979–1982): *Gypsy Blood* as the emotional centrepiece, the third album as the most melodic, *Grand Passion* as the weakest.
inhalt: In the first part of a two-part video series on Jackie Leven's albums, the American journalist and collector Stephen Schnee (“The CD Junkie”) covers the four Doll by Doll studio albums released between 1979 and 1982. The video runs just under 14 minutes and was published on 13 March 2023; its tags name Jo Shaw, David McIntosh and Tony Waite, *Remember*, *Gypsy Blood* and *Grand Passion*.

Schnee tells how he came across *Remember* and *Gypsy Blood* as a record buyer in Los Angeles in 1979/80. He describes the band as uncategorisable between new wave and rock, and calls *Gypsy Blood* the emotional centrepiece and the best album to start with. The self-titled third album is the most melodic (released in the USA on MCA) and *Grand Passion* the weakest, dated in its production. A medley closes the video. The tone is an enthusiastic recommendation. Schnee is unsure about the first bass player (“Robin Spreafico”) and speculates that Helen Turner might be the later Style Council musician.

2023-03-14-cd-junkie-216-jackie-leven-so.kurz: Stephen Schnee gives a 19-minute overview of Leven’s solo albums in his YouTube series “CD Junkie”, from *Control* to *Wayside Shrines* (2011): a fan’s tribute praising the warmth of the late work and Leven’s generosity.
inhalt: Episode #216 of “CD Junkie” on Stephen Schnee’s channel is the second part of a two-part portrait. According to its description Schnee dives into Leven’s solo career; the first part (episode #215) focused on his band Doll by Doll.

The video runs through the studio albums in about 19 minutes: from *Control* (which Schnee dates to 1971; it was recorded in 1971 but released only in 1975, in Spain), issued under the name John St. Field, via the 1983/84 singles and Concrete Bulletproof Invisible (1988) to the Cooking Vinyl years and *Wayside Shrines* (2011), including the pseudonym albums as Sir Vincent Lone and Jackie Balfour. It ends with a medley.

Schnee praises above all the warmth, tenderness and variety of Leven’s late work and his generosity in giving label-mates space on his albums. He guesses that Cooking Vinyl released the pseudonym albums because of a one-album-a-year contract, which is speculation. The tone is that of a fan who wants to bring Leven closer to a new audience.

2023-04-07-pere-ubu-bandcamp-lore-jackie.kurz: The official Pere Ubu Bandcamp page releases on 7 April 2023 a recording of a duo concert by Jackie Leven and David Thomas at the Hôtel du Nord in Paris on 17 May 1999.
inhalt: On 7 April 2023 Bandcamp carries the album *Lore (Jackie Leven and David Thomas)*, a 12-track release under the UbuDoll label. The accompanying text reads: Jackie Leven and David Thomas in concert on 17 May 1999 at the Hôtel du Nord, Paris. “Magic happened.” Thomas has kept several of the original recordings of their shows, but this was the one he chose to put out in refined form.

The track list names ten pieces: “Perfumed Road”, “Cry For Me”, “Green River Under A Morbid Sky”, “Working Alone / A Blessing / Deer Blinks”, “I’m Working Now”, “Man In Darkness”, “C’est Lui C’est Lui”, “Down By Weird River”, “Gershwin For A Dying Man” and “Bus Into Millennia”, plus the extras “Approximately Wig Alley” and “Brunswick Parking Lot”. Personnel: David Thomas on vocals, melodeon and percussion; Jackie Leven on vocals, guitar and percussion.

According to the credits all songs were written by David Thomas (Hearpen Music) except “Working Alone / A Blessing” and “I’m Working Now”, which are by Leven (Warner/Chappell). A supporter comments that, as a huge fan of both, he finds it “absolutely essential” and thanks Thomas. The page itself offers nothing on the quality of the performance beyond its description and credits.
zitate_kontext: Release note on the album page.

2023-11-14-the-afterword-levenland-debor.kurz: A forum post announces “Levenland”, an evening of Leven's songs and stories with Deborah Greenwood and Jinder at the Betsey Trotwood in London on 18 November 2023, twelve years after his death.
inhalt: On the forum The Afterword the user Bogart posts on 14 November 2023 – twelve years to the day since Leven's death – about the evening “Levenland”. Deborah Greenwood, Leven's wife, and Jinder, a good friend and fellow performer, will play at the Betsey Trotwood pub in London on Saturday 18 November, celebrating “his songs, stories and all things Levenland”. Bogart invites readers to join the “Church of Leven”, listen and raise a glass of Toffee Vodka.

The pub's event page gives the start as 7 pm, finish 11 pm, with tickets at £12 plus booking fee. Three readers comment: two regret that they cannot come because of distance or cost or another engagement, and a third says he would be there if he lived in London.
zitate_kontext: The forum user Bogart inviting readers to “Levenland”.

2023-11-18-betsey-trotwood-levenland.kurz: Event listing from the London pub The Betsey Trotwood: “Levenland” on 18 November 2023, an evening in which Deborah Greenwood and Jinder celebrate the life and music of Jackie Leven.
inhalt: The page of the London pub The Betsey Trotwood announces “Levenland” for Saturday 18 November 2023, 7pm to 11pm. The text is a single sentence: Deborah Greenwood and Jinder celebrate the life and music of Jackie Leven. Tickets are £12 plus booking fee in advance, sold through WeGotTickets. The page names no other performers and gives no programme.

2023-11-22-wikipedia-no-jackie-leven.kurz: The Norwegian Wikipedia article (November 2023 version) is a stub: one introductory sentence with life dates and a discography running from Doll by Doll through the Cooking Vinyl albums to the fan-club releases.
inhalt: The version of 22 November 2023 is marked as a stub. It calls Jackie Leven – born 18 June 1950 in Kirkcaldy, Fife, died 14 November 2011 – a Scottish singer, composer and folk musician, citing an obituary from Classic Rock Magazine. The infobox lists composer, singer, songwriter, guitarist and folk musician, Kirkcaldy High School as his school, and Cooking Vinyl as his label.

The rest is a discography. Under “John St Field” stands *Control* (“Cooking Vinyl, 1971”, mixing up recording year and reissue). For Doll by Doll it lists *Remember* (1979) and *Gypsy Blood* (1979) on Automatic, *Doll By Doll* (1980) and *Grand Passion* (1982) on Magnet, and the live album *Revenge of Memory* (Sheffield Limits Club, 1980; Haunted Valley, 2005).

As a solo artist the list runs from *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery of Death* (1994) to *Gothic Road* (2010), covering all the Cooking Vinyl albums, among them *Forbidden Songs of The Dying West*, *Fairytales For Hardmen*, *Night Lilies*, *Creatures of Light And Darkness* (here “2000”), *Shining Brother, Shining Sister*, *Jackie Leven Said* (with Ian Rankin), *Elegy for Johnny Cash*, *Lovers at the Gun Club*, the four *Haunted Year* albums, the Sir Vincent Lone albums and *Chip Pan Fire* as Jackie Balfour. Separate headings list the fan-club albums from *Saint Judas* (1998) to *Men in Prison* (2003) and the DVD *The Meeting of Remarkable Men* (2005). Links lead to the official website and the MySpace profile. There is nothing on his life, music or any Norwegian connection.
zitate_kontext: Introductory sentence of the Norwegian Wikipedia article

2023-12-01-obladada-revisio-john-st-fiel.kurz: An enthusiastic review of Guerssen's reissue of *Control* (John St. Field) on the blog Obladada: an uneven album that is twisted and brilliantly produced at its best, somewhere between pop and prog.
inhalt: The blog Obladada gives the reissue of *Control* by the Catalan label Guerssen (vinyl only, 7 December 2023) a long review in its “Revisio” series. It opens by reflecting on albums as “a document of a space and place in time”: they are almost always uneven yet can still be great “as long as the good bits are really good”. *Control*, it says, fits this idea of “imperfect perfection” superbly. When it hits its stride it is “one of the most unusual, amazingly produced, twisted, and bizarre treats” to come their way in a long time – a sub-genre of pop and prog with lysergic, spiralling lyrics delivered in a gentle, elaborate, radio-friendly voice.

The reviewer retells the backstory: recorded in 1971 in the midst of an intensive exploration of LSD, with the artist in trouble with the police and therefore credited as John St. Field; the record was shelved for a few years and briefly released in Spain (the review says 1975); later Leven changed the running order and reissued it under his own name in the late nineties; Guerssen now reissues it 52 years on in its original order. Highlights are “Soft Lowland Tongue”, a skewed journey through Scottish Borders history and the border reivers, with odd hooks, close harmonies and a friendly, almost pop surface that sits at odds with its lyrics – to the writers, living a few miles from the places named, “a strange but very welcome strain of local psychedelia”; the near eleven-minute “The Problem”, with avant-garde droning, rumbling explosions, a menacing rock throb and a sudden elongated flute groove; “Dune Voices”, with backward vocals, droning smears and howling gales, “as bewildering as it is stunning”; and “Raerona”, a “multiheaded monster” of squelchy electronics, peeling guitars and acerbic lyrics. “Ruins”, “I'm Always a Prinlaws Boy”, “Mansion Tension”, “Dog Star” and the closer “Sleeping in Bracken” fall away or sound like attempts at something more commercial.

The verdict: had it appeared in 1971 it would probably have made “tiny but noticeable waves” among the most adventurous listeners, alongside Meddle, Hunky Dory or Maggot Brain. After *Control*, the review says, Leven endured years of isolation in lighthouses, living on water and dog biscuits (an anecdote without a source), before reappearing with Doll by Doll in the late seventies and later as a prolific folk artist; it wrongly gives 2001 as the year he died aged 61 (it was 2011). Nothing later comes near “that wild half an album of perfection”. *Control* is “a spectacular square peg in an ongoing sea of round holes”, an actually unearthed classic in a sea of copyists. A reader's comment adds that he first met the album through tape-trading of rare psych records in the late eighties; nobody knew who John St. Field was, and when it turned out to be Leven it was a shock, but in retrospect it all made sense.
zitate_kontext: The reviewer on the album's nature.

2023-12-13-wikipedia-de-doll-by-doll.autor: Wikipedia authors' community (basis imported from the English version by Semming)
2023-12-13-wikipedia-de-doll-by-doll.kurz: The German Wikipedia article (version of December 2023) presents Doll by Doll as a London rock band founded by Jackie Leven in 1975, lists line-ups, albums and successor projects, and reproduces a US fanzine review of *Gypsy Blood*. Several dates are questionable.
inhalt: The article describes Doll by Doll as a rock band from London founded by Jackie Leven in 1975 and active until 1983. It says they became known in the new-wave era but were largely ignored by the media, because their emotional, psychedelically tinged music was regarded as out of date.

The original line-up was Leven (vocals, guitar), Jo Shaw (vocals, guitar), Robin Spreafico (vocals, bass) and David Macintosh (vocals, drums). They recorded the album *Remember* before Spreafico was replaced by Tony Waite. With that line-up they released *Gypsy Blood* (produced by John Sinclair) and the self-titled third album, *Doll by Doll*. The Daily Telegraph, the article says, called the group a “lost masterpiece” because it was quickly forgotten. By the last LP, *Grand Passion*, only Leven remained of the original line-up, joined by Helen Turner and Tom Norden and guest musicians including David Gilmour of Pink Floyd; Mark Fletcher and Chris Clarke played live with the band. Doll by Doll fell apart in 1983. In 1988 Leven, Shaw and Macintosh released the single “Big Tears” with ex-Sex Pistol Glen Matlock under the name Concrete Bulletproof Invisible; Leven went on to a solo career with more folk-oriented albums.

The text also mentions the 2005 live album *Revenge of Memory*, said to contain all but one of the songs on *Remember* and to have been recorded in 1977 at the Sheffield Limit Club, and the CD reissue of the four studio albums by WEA/Rhino in March 2007. A section headed “Style” reproduces a review of *Gypsy Blood* from the American fanzine *Touch and Go*: the band belonged to no camp but enjoyed cult-like devotion from a small following, sounded “mainstream-ish”, yet wrote intelligent, deep lyrics. The discography lists *Remember* and *Gypsy Blood* (1979), *Doll by Doll* (1980), *Grand Passion* (1982) and *Revenge of Memory* (2005).

Errors and inaccuracies: the Telegraph’s “lost masterpiece” comes from a 2007 article by Neil McCormick about a single album, not the band. A 1977 recording date for *Revenge of Memory* is hardly tenable given the band’s founding and release dates; the third album probably appeared only in 1981; and the dates given for Tony Waite (1958–2003) differ from other accounts (1953–2002). The fanzine book title is given as “’79–’93”, which seems wrong.
zitate_kontext: The article’s assessment of the band’s position
The article’s paraphrase of the *Touch and Go* review of *Gypsy Blood*

2023-12-guerssen-records-john-st-field-c.kurz: Label text for the *Control* reissue (Guerssen, December 2023): the complete track list in original running order and a new insert with unseen photos and the recollections of musicians involved.
inhalt: The shop of the Spanish label Guerssen offers the black LP of John St. Field's *Control* as a “psychedelic, progressive folk-rock masterpiece” from 1971, recorded in London by John St. Field aka Jackie Leven “(of Doll by Doll fame)” but only released in Spain at the time. The text says that before becoming a cult singer/songwriter in the 90s, Leven debuted in the early 70s with *Control*, issued under the pseudonym because of “problems with the forces of law and order”.

The album was recorded in London with the help of musicians from Man and other friends (Phil Ryan, Juliet Lawson, Jesse Ballard, Joe Kucera), the songs written after Leven's years of wandering and taking copious amounts of LSD. Unlike earlier reissues, this one presents the complete tracklist in original running order and a new insert with previously unseen photos and memorabilia, plus recollections from some of the musicians involved. A press quotation calls it one of those special LPs that “stands off in its own space”. Side 1 runs “Soft Lowland Tongue”, “Ruins”, “The Problem”, “Dune Voices”; side 2 “Raerona”, “I'm Always A Prinlaws Boy”, “Mansion Tension”, “Dog Star”, “Sleeping In Bracken”. The purchase does not include a digital download.
zitate_kontext: Press quotation (source not named) in the label text

2024-02-24-alastair-mckay-substack-punks.kurz: The journalist Alastair McKay publishes in 2024 an interview he conducted with Leven in March 1994, re-transcribed as a continuous first-person account without questions; in the opening Leven says he was born in Kirkcaldy but feels more like a Glenrothes person.
inhalt: Alastair McKay, a Scottish journalist, posts in his Substack newsletter a conversation he had with Jackie Leven in March 1994. The text has been re-transcribed and presented as Leven’s first-person account without questions; the title quotes a punchline about Doll By Doll: punks hated them because they weren’t punk, everybody else because they thought they were. In the freely visible opening Leven says he was born in Kirkcaldy but feels more like a Glenrothes person. The rest of the text can only be read after a free registration.
zitate_kontext: Headline of the piece, Leven’s punchline about Doll By Doll

2024-04-18-rocktimes-jackie-leven-live-i.kurz: RockTimes announces a 4-CD box for 26 April 2024 with two Leven concerts recorded by Radio Bremen (1999 and 2004) and briefly outlines his career.
inhalt: Markus Kerren (initials “mk”) reports on 18 April 2024 at RockTimes, in the section “Angekündigt”, the box *Live Or Die – Live In Bremen* (MIG Music) with two concerts that Radio Bremen is said to have recorded “in its usual strong quality”. It comes out as a 4-CD set on 26 April 2024. The years vary within the text: headline “1994 & 2004”, body text “1999 and 2004”, box title “1995 & 2004”; 1999 is the correct one.

A brief career sketch follows. The singer-songwriter, born in Scotland in 1950, began in the late sixties as John St. Field; the text dates his first album, *Control*, to 1973 (it is normally given as 1971). Later in the seventies he was strongly influenced by punk and founded Doll By Doll, who went down well on stage but sold hardly any records; their psychedelic-tinged new wave interested “hardly anyone” by the end, and the band split in 1983. Personal and health blows kept setting back his solo career until *The Mystery of Love Is Greater than the Mystery of Death* appeared in 1994. Leven died in 2011 aged 61.
zitate_kontext: Kerren on the contents of the box

2024-04-26-mig-music-kuenstlertexte-jack.kurz: MIG Music's label texts for *Live Or Die – Live In Bremen 1999 & 2004* (4 CDs) and *Live At Rockpalast 2004*: a short biography, concert details and track lists that include the spoken introductions.
inhalt: The Hanover label MIG Music describes two archive releases on two product pages. *Live Or Die – Live In Bremen 1999 & 2004* came out on 26 April 2024 as a 4-CD set (running times 45:53, 49:25, 58:14, 49:17). The accompanying text sketches Leven as a “singer-songwriter, folk musician and storyteller”, born in Kirkcaldy in 1950, the son of an Irishman and a Roma; he began in the late sixties under the pseudonym John St. Field and recorded his first album *Control* in 1973. “Inspired by punk”, he founded Doll by Doll in London in 1978; their emotional, psychedelic-tinged new wave went down very well live, but their four albums did not reach the expected sales. After the band disbanded in 1983 he concentrated on a solo career, which took off only eleven years later, after “a number of personal and health-related strokes of fate”, with *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*. As Sir Vincent Lone he released three albums of songs too unusual for his folk image. He died in 2011 aged 61 “after a long, serious illness”. (The dates for the band's founding and end and for *Control* differ from other sources, which have Doll by Doll ending in 1982 and place *Control* later.)

The two concerts were recorded by the broadcaster: solo at Club Moments in Bremen on 27 May 1999, and on 29 March 2004 in the Radio Bremen Sendesaal with Michael Cosgrave on keyboards, “his long-time friend and companion”. The track lists give the spoken introductions as separate titles (“ad lib”), for instance about football, the Irish singer Andy White, city life, his son Simon, St Kitts & Nevis, a butterfly, or “Glen Matlock is drinking…”; the songs include “Stranger on the Square”, “Call Mother a Lonely Field”, “Poortoun” (as “Universal Blue – Poortoun”), “Single Father”, “Men in Prison”, “Gylen-Gylen”, “My Philosophy”, “Alvis Green”, “Empty in Soho Square”, “A Little Voice in Space”, “Classic Northern Diversions”, “Exit Wound”, “Tied-Up House” and “Live or Die”.

*Live At Rockpalast 2004* (CD+DVD, 27 September 2024; the DVD had already appeared on 25 April 2011) is described as recorded in March 2004 at Club Harmonie in Bonn, with highlights from *Shining Brother Shining Sister* and “the first Jackie Leven hit”, “Call Mother a Lonely Field”. The promotional text calls Leven “perhaps Scotland's greatest singer/songwriter”, a master of mature melody blurring the lines between pure folk and sophisticated pop, with melancholic, biographical songs and an ironic humour shown in great stories on stage. The track list includes the spoken pieces, among them “The Butterfly Story”, “Jackie's Bad Depression (A Funny Story)”, “Jackie Talks About Kiel And His Mother”, “Jackie Has A Moment Of Silence” and “Jackie Talks About Norwegian Prisoners”. It notes his death on 14 November 2011.

2024-05-07-musikreviews-de-live-or-die-l.kurz: Editor-in-chief Thoralf Koß hails the box *Live Or Die – Live in Bremen, 1999 & 2004* as the legacy of one of the most likeable musicians ever, compares Leven to Scott Walker and adds a personal memory from Dresden.
inhalt: Thoralf Koß, editor-in-chief of Musikreviews.de, reviews the four-CD box *Live Or Die – Live in Bremen, 1999 & 2004* (MIG Music, 26 April 2024, about 200 minutes), which contains two complete Bremen concerts: a solo show from 1999 and a 2004 show at Radio Bremen’s Sendesaal with the pianist and friend Michael Cosgrave. He praises the excellent sound, the attentive audiences and the lovingly produced twelve-page booklet.

The text opens with three quotations: a friend’s comment under the obituary at theartsdesk.com, ending with the last line of “Main Travelled Roads”, a passage from the Tagesspiegel obituary of 17 November 2011 about Leven’s devotion to art, literature and stories, and comments from the site’s guestbook. There Koß himself had written that he saw Leven live once, was “completely wrecked” afterwards, and after nearly an hour’s talk knew: these are the musicians the world should look for, but only the “otherworldly outsiders” find them. His colleague König recalls two concerts, the first amid a chattering crowd, the second alone with Cosgrave, where Leven was more the storyteller, a one-off who for the moment blots out the entire music business. A reader writes after Leven’s death that he will miss the stories between the songs he experienced over 18 years. König also attacks the *FAZ*, which called Doll By Doll a “would-be punk band”, while *Spiegel Online* ran a respectful obituary.

In his own words Koß rates Leven among the most likeable, honest and entertaining musicians of all time, one who in lyrics and music could easily have outdone Bob Dylan; add “cynical” and he stands next to Frank Zappa. On stage the former Doll By Doll singer always appeared in a “tramp outfit” with unruly hair, and still swept the audience up into the highest singer-songwriter regions. He played long sets but on principle gave no encores, since only “idiots like Robbie Williams” did; that is exactly what one hears at the end of the box, when he bids the audience goodbye before the title song “Live Or Die”. Between songs he tells stories from his eventful life, with black Scottish humour.

Koß praises Leven’s guitar playing, passionate yet always tender, and his voice, which at times sinks into the baritone depths of Elvis Presley’s “In The Ghetto” and then soars into heavenly heights. The only point of reference he can think of is Scott Walker; both are incomprehensible, yet we keep trying to catch them out. His verdict is the highest praise: a wonderful memento of one of Scotland’s most moving singer-songwriters, who combines black humour with the pensive sadness of Scott Walker.

In a postscript Koß recalls meeting Leven about fifteen years earlier at the Beatpol in Dresden and talking at length. Leven signed a copy of *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow* for him “Kossi % With Love. Jackie x”, after they first had to look for a pen because Koß’s own would not write on the booklet. He gives the title as *The Peace Comes Dropping Slow*, which is a slip for *For Peace Comes Dropping Slow*.

2024-05-21-betreutesproggen-de-jackie-le.kurz: Juergen Meurer presents the four-CD box *Live Or Die (Live in Bremen)* on BetreutesProggen.de: two radio recordings from Bremen (1999 solo, 2004 with Michael Cosgrave), carried by Leven's lovely voice and his anecdotes; 10 out of 15 points, with a second reviewer's initials giving 12.
inhalt: The review (21 May 2024) begins by saying the listener gets “so much material thrown at them” that the musician, who died in November 2011, deserves a fuller introduction. The author first explains the many names: they are stage names, not fellow musicians. The Scottish songwriter “Alan Moffatt” (as the text has it) began as John St. Field, whose first work *Control* was recorded in 1971; other pseudonyms were Jackie Balfour and Sir Vincent Lone. In 1977 he founded the new wave band, at which, incidentally, a certain David Gilmour once guested – “perhaps that alone is reason enough” for this singer-songwriter album to appear on a prog site – and which dissolved in 1983.

His solo career, Meurer writes, began under a very bad star: during the recording of his debut he was attacked at night and nearly strangled, and for almost two years he could neither speak nor sing, which led him into drug addiction. Fortunately he got out again, and in 1994 – “eleven years later than originally planned” – came his first success with *The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death*. As a notable album he mentions the one with the Fife-born crime writer Ian Rankin. The box (MiG Music, 26 April 2024) consists of two concert recordings of two CDs each: Club Moments on 27 May 1999 and the Sendesaal on 29 March 2004. The first two CDs are solo performances “in the truest sense”: a man with a guitar, a very beautiful voice and a talent for being extremely entertaining.

That is part of it: the Scot tells many anecdotes, so all four CDs are loosened up with funny stories. This sometimes seems slightly irritating, because witty announcements are followed now and then by very sad-sounding songs. Individual songs such as “Men in Prison” remind the reviewer a little of later Amazing Blondel titles or of Tír na nÓg, whom MiG has also recalled. The two concerts have only one overlap (“Single Father”); at the 2004 gig he is discreetly accompanied on keyboards by Michael Cosgrave. (According to the track list “Call Mother a Lonely Field” also appears in both.) Verdict: “For the fan, but also as an introduction, a very nice compilation.” Rating 10/15 points, the second reviewer's initials (KR) giving 12.

2024-06-20-eats-drinks-and-leaves-doll-b.kurz: Tim Cooper introduces Doll by Doll’s “Butcher Boy” with an admiring, anecdote-rich portrait of Jackie Leven: cult band, assault, heroin, recovery and storytelling.
inhalt: Journalist Tim Cooper’s blog post of 20 June 2024 is about the song “Butcher Boy” and doubles as a portrait of Leven. Doll By Doll, he writes, were something of a cult band in the punk/New Wave era, thanks mainly to the larger-than-life personality of their Scottish front man: a singer, songwriter, storyteller, traveller and raconteur, a formidable fingerstyle guitarist and an even more formidable drinker who even published the names of his favourite pubs on his album sleeves. His voice, which rose from a mellifluous baritone to a tremulous falsetto, could frighten a crowd, make grown men weep and lull an infant to sleep.

Despite an eclectic sound that sometimes veered into prog, there was a punk-like element to their incendiary live performances, especially the fiery onstage attitude of Leven and guitarist Jo Shaw, who would often physically threaten audience members. Leven peppered performances with engaging stories from his epic life – the road, miners, shop workers, farmers, history, folklore, lost and displaced people, the shelter and harshness of the natural world, terminal loneliness and the insights of barroom philosophers.

Cooper retells the Leven myth: part Romany gypsy, expelled from school, married and a father at 16, then years busking and sleeping rough in Scotland, Ireland, Berlin and Madrid – where he recorded an acid-folk album as John St Field – and London, squatting in the South Bank Centre. Doll By Doll were doomed to cult status: a record contract failed to curb his hedonistic inclinations; pickled in alcohol, wasted on psychedelic drugs and haunted by violence at gigs, they were kicked off tours with Devo and Hawkwind (“quite an achievement!”) and finally split. Leven then recorded an album with guests including David Gilmour but deleted it as soon as it was released; while mixing his first solo album he was jumped in an alley after leaving the studio, had his throat slashed and was savagely beaten by a gang. The damage to his larynx left him unable to sing, he fell into despair and heroin addiction, and beat it through will power, acupuncture and reflexology, going on to found the CORE Trust charity (patron: Princess Diana and, after her death, Prince Charles). Still bad fortune followed: he lost his girlfriend to the Dalai Lama’s bodyguard, who left him a tape of Robert Bly’s men’s-movement manifesto *Iron John*, which so impressed Leven that he became a spokesman for the movement.

Cooper closes with collaborations (Glen Matlock, Mike Scott, David Thomas, Peter Hammill, Ron Sexsmith, and Ian Rankin, whose Rebus listens to Leven) and highlights such as *Elegy For Johnny Cash* and the song “The Sexual Loneliness Of Jesus Christ”. He wrongly dates *Forbidden Songs Of The Dying West* to 1992 (it appeared in 1995) and calls “Butcher Boy” the opening song of the 1979 debut “Romance” (the album is *Remember*). Leven died in 2011 aged 61.

2024-07-07-rocktimes-live-or-die-live-in.kurz: Markus Kerren praises the four-CD box *Live Or Die*, with Bremen concerts from 1999 and 2004, as “a very successful affair”: fingerpicking, a soft dark voice, and stories you can follow even with little English.
inhalt: In the online magazine RockTimes (7 July 2024), Markus Kerren reviews the four-CD box *Live Or Die (Live In Bremen 1999 & 2004)* on MIG Music. He first introduces Leven: starting out in the late sixties as a twenty-something under the name John St. Field, *Control* recorded in 1971 but, in his account, released only two years later and only in Spain; a founder member of Doll By Doll in 1978 (the band actually formed in 1977), who made four studio albums and a live album into the early eighties. Fate then dealt him a bad hand: in 1984 (1983 is the usual date), in the middle of recording a solo album, he was attacked in the street and nearly strangled to death; for about two years he could not speak, became depressed and fell prey to heroin. Only at the start of the nineties did he get back on his feet, and in 1994 he released *The Mystery Of Love Is Greater Than The Mystery Of Death*.

The first two CDs come from the Club Moments in Bremen (1999), CDs 3 and 4 from Radio Bremen's broadcasting hall (2004). Kerren describes Leven as a man with an acoustic guitar, his voice, good songs and many funny stories, for whom going to a concert was “definitely worth it back then”. The tracks are varied, melodic and well played, and despite the melancholy one listens gladly. The tour-life stories can be followed even with little English, a technique also used by masters such as Townes Van Zandt. Leven switches deftly between fingerpicking and strummed guitar and delivers his stories in a softer, darker voice; interaction with the audience repeatedly offers him “penalties” for spontaneous asides.

At the second concert five years later his long-time friend Michael Cosgrave accompanies him on keyboards and vocals, which adds extra colour. One has to like such sparsely instrumented performances, but then nearly three and a half hours of entertainment give plenty in return: “All in all, a very successful affair.” The track list includes “Stranger On The Square”, “Call Mother A Lonely Field”, “Single Father”, “Men In Prison”, “Classic Northern Diversions” and the title song “Live Or Die”.

2024-07-28-the-afterword-live-or-die-in-.kurz: A forum post recommends the four-CD set *Live or Die* (radio recordings from Bremen, solo in 1999 and with Michael Cosgrave in 2004) as the best bargain of the year, followed by other fans’ memories of gigs and of Leven’s stage persona.
inhalt: On the forum The Afterword a member (Jaygee) recommends the 35-song, four-CD set *Live or Die* as “the best £20 you’ll spend this year”. Last Thursday he had seen Bruce Springsteen at Wembley and thought of an equally deserving songwriter most of the crowd had probably never heard of: “the late, great Jackie Leven”. Leven’s adeptness at balancing often caustic lyrics and frequently gorgeous melodies, he writes, exceeded his acclaim and commercial success; criminally under-rated in the UK, he earned and enjoyed cult-hero status in Germany and Norway through his relentless gigging. The author only discovered Leven around *Oh What A Blow That Phantom Dealt Me* (dated 2006 in the post) and never saw him live.

The recordings were made for a local radio station: the first two CDs present a “wonderfully intimate” solo show from 1999, discs three and four his songs embellished five years later by long-time accompanist Michael Cosgrave. In between come the famous, often “hilariously outlandish” shaggy-dog stories. He picks two highlights: the bittersweet *Jim O’Windygates*, about Leven’s time in a Haig whisky factory (“We didn’t get hangovers, we got haigovers”), as an introduction to the softer, melodic side, and the ferocious *Classic Northern Diversions* for the more acerbic one.

The replies bear out the picture. One user says Leven did go on a bit between songs; others call him a superb raconteur. One recalls the Midlands Arts Centre, where Leven granted a request for *Wrapped Up In Blue* in the second set with a coarse remark, and a ticket for the Kitchen Garden Cafe about a week before Leven’s death. Another relays what Michael Weston King told him: Leven always seemed relaxed, even slightly ramshackle, but as soon as he got on stage he was the most professional person King had ever worked with. A Stockholm fan last saw him in the back room of the club Debaser and is glad he never sold out football stadiums. The tribute album *The Wanderer* and Weston King’s *The Final Reel* are also mentioned.

2024-09-12-dmme-live-or-die-live-in-brem.kurz: A five-star review by Epstein on DMME.net of the double set *Live Or Die: Live In Bremen, 1999 & 2004*: Leven as a matchless storyteller and singer who never played the same show twice.
inhalt: Epstein reviews the 2024 MiG release *Live Or Die: Live In Bremen, 1999 & 2004* for DMME.net (Let It Rock) and gives it five stars. The standfirst sums up the tone: the “Caledonian troubadour” brings his “spellbinding tales to the banks of the Weser where captive listeners drink the water of Fife wisdom”. Leven's death in 2011 at 61 robbed the world not simply of one of the greatest singer-songwriters but of one of the most immaculate storytellers – and provocateurs, as “The Sexual Loneliness of Jesus Christ” suggested in style. His run of albums that began in 1994, after Doll by Doll, Concrete Bulletproof Invisible and “a battle with smack”, remains unprecedented: more than twenty records in under twenty years, some as Sir Vincent Lone, plus collaborations.

That meant a plethora of songs to pick from, so Leven never repeated himself on stage, and these four discs are the best illustration of how different his concerts could be. The earlier show (Club Moments, May 1999) captures him solo, the later one (Sendesaal Radio Bremen, March 2004) with Michael Cosgrave at the piano. What counts, Epstein says, is the attitude audiences can still enjoy. It is best sampled on two cuts that appear in both sets, “Call Mother a Lonely Field” and “Single Father”, which tackle family issues “in a magnificent fashion”, even for Bremen listeners to whom the nuances of English could seem a bit alien. Then there are the melodies – the folk-informed refrain of “Gylen Gylen” and the acoustic guitar flourishes leading into “Stranger on the Square”.

Without the hard-hitting, highly poetic lyrics and the anecdotes that preceded almost every song, however, much of Leven's charm would feel diminished; those introductions are lost on digital platforms and available only in the physical format. His deep voice booms and stretches resonant notes in “Looking for Love” and croons in “Exit Wound” as though measuring the room's dynamics; he weaves dramatic motifs and a quote from “Yesterday” into “Jim O'Windygates”, while a light whistle and robust strum lift the gloom off “Marble City Bar”. Church organ turns “My Philosophy” into a hymn, piano ripples make “Alvis Green” an emotionally charged tragedy, and “A Little Voice in Space” soars beyond the traditional pale where the “faux jolly” “Classic Northern Diversions”, spiced with a mention of Gerhard Schröder, resides. With the title track, Leven's greatness and his absence become “unbearably tangible”.

2024-10-12-bbc-radio-4-inheritance-track.kurz: The seven-minute Radio 4 “Inheritance Tracks” episode has Ian Rankin choose Jackie Leven’s “Another Man’s Rain” as the song he wants to pass on. The programme page gives only the framework; what Rankin says about Leven is not reproduced there.
inhalt: “Inheritance Tracks” is a BBC Radio 4 feature (Saturday Live) in which guests choose a piece of music inherited from their parents and one to pass on to their children. The episode with Sir Ian Rankin aired on 12 October 2024, lasts seven minutes and is available to stream and as a podcast. It was produced by Ben Mitchell and Noa Dowling.

The programme text introduces the guest as the “king of Tartan Noir”: the best-selling crime writer grew up surrounded by food (his father ran a grocery in Fife, his mother worked in a school canteen), reviewed wine as a young writer, and changed his style, and his life, with the hard-drinking, stubborn Edinburgh detective Inspector John Rebus. Since *Knots and Crosses* in 1987 there have been 25 Rebus novels, as well as TV dramas and stage plays, mainly dealing with Scotland’s dark and dangerous underworld.

The chosen pieces: as inherited track “Seven Drunken Nights” by The Dubliners, and as the song to pass on “Another Man’s Rain” by Jackie Leven. It is known from other remarks by Rankin that a misheard line from this song gave his novel *Standing in Another Man’s Grave* its title. What he says about Leven in the programme itself cannot be gathered from the programme page.
